title: Paris Perdikaris: When And Why PINNs Fail To Train
speaker: Paris Perdikaris
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. One popular way is to let a learning program (a program with millions of dials it tunes by trial and error until its answers look right) also receive the laws of physics as it learns. This talk is about why that approach, called a PINN, so often refuses to learn well: the trial-and-error tuning gets stuck because some of the physics rules 'shout' much louder than others, so the program never lands on an answer that respects all of them.
core_problem: PINNs turn a physics prediction problem into a learning task: fit data, respect the boundary conditions (the fixed facts at the edges), respect the initial conditions (what things looked like at the start), and satisfy the physics rule all at once. That sounds sensible, but the computer's trial-and-error process may not push each of these demands equally. The direction and strength that tell the learning program which way to adjust its dials (what we call a gradient signal) can be weak or even point different ways for different constraints. High-frequency wiggling, multiple scales, and boundaries especially suffer because the signals pointing toward satisfying each constraint can be weak or work against each other.
first_principles_model: A PINN uses a learning program to represent the answer to a physics rule. A special mathematical trick called automatic differentiation lets the computer compute what the rule demands at any spot, turn that demand into a score for how wrong the answer is, and then nudge the dials in the direction that makes the score go down. The real problem being solved is not just the physics rule itself; it is a constrained guessing game: many simultaneous goals must be met by adjusting the dials. If that guessing process is stubborn (needing tiny nudges) or biased (strongly preferring some wiggles over others), the physics rule can be simple while learning still fails.
key_claims: Physics can be added through the learning program's structure (certain shapes of dials work better) or through the score (certain penalties favor physics). PINNs mostly use penalties in the score.
PINNs are unusual in that they penalize the program's output and how fast it changes, not just the dial settings themselves.
Even simple physics rules can fail if the trial-and-error tuning cannot satisfy the boundary conditions or the rapid wiggles.
The trial-and-error process for PINNs can require tiny adjustment steps, making training impractically slow if done the usual way.
Different demands in the score can produce vastly different adjustment signals, so one requirement gets met while another is nearly ignored.
A mathematical tool called neural tangent kernel analysis explains spectral bias: the learning program picks up smooth, slow wiggles before sharp, fast wiggles.

important_terms.meaning: A learning program trained to guess an answer to a physics rule while also being punished when the physics rule is violated at the edges or start.

A single score made by adding up several different scores: how wrong the guess is on the data, how badly the boundary conditions are violated, how badly the starting conditions are violated, and how badly the physics rule is violated.
A tuning problem where the continuous trial-and-error process has some parts that change very fast and others that change very slowly, forcing stable methods to take tiny steps.
A failure where different demands in the score produce very different adjustment signals, so some physics demands are effectively ignored while others make the program change.
The tendency of learning programs trained by trial-and-error adjustment to pick up smooth, gentle changes in their input before sharp, rapid changes.

stanford_connections: This is the starting point because it shows the difference between the idea of a PINN and whether it can actually learn in practice.
It connects to later talks about alternative math forms, automatic rebalancing of demands, learning operators instead of single answers, and learning program designs that respect physical laws.
It teaches a habit: never ask only whether the physics rule is correct; always ask whether the trial-and-error process can actually use it to improve the program.
practical_caution: Do not trust a low score for physics rule violations as proof that the learned answer is correct in the real world. The choice of how to weight different demands, where to check the physics rule, the structure of the learning program, the tuning method chosen, and the types of wiggles that exist in the true answer can all determine whether this method actually solves what you care about.
selected_evidence: Failure can happen at any time even for the simplest problems.
This gradient flow problem becomes very stiff.
Stiffness leads to imbalance gradients during back propagation.
The network cannot really change the parameters in order to fit the boundary condition.
Neural networks are known to suffer from spectral bias.
takeaway: PINNs are optimization systems that must balance many goals at once, not automatic solvers. They succeed only when the trial-and-error process can send each physics demand into the right parts of the learning program.
worked_example:
A fully connected neural network with four hidden layers trained on the 2D Helmholtz equation achieves about 20% relative error in the L2 norm. The network struggles particularly at domain boundaries—gradient signals for fitting boundary conditions collapse to near-zero during backpropagation, preventing the solver from satisfying boundary constraints. For a simple 1D Burgers equation with viscosity 0.01/π, training takes only seconds on a GPU and produces accurate predictions across the domain interior.

When applying the adaptive weighting strategy to a wave equation with three loss terms (initial condition, time derivative, residual), the method balances the neural tangent kernel (NTK) spectrum across loss components. Without balancing, eigenvalues of the boundary term have magnitude 10^3 while residual eigenvalues reach 10^5, causing the network to learn residual satisfaction 100x faster than boundary fitting.
deeper_mechanics:
PINNs formulate a composite loss function combining data fit, PDE residual, and boundary/initial conditions. During gradient descent, this becomes a stiff ODE system in the neural network parameters. The Neural Tangent Kernel—the Jacobian of network outputs with respect to parameters—governs training dynamics and remains nearly constant during optimization. Spectral analysis shows fully connected networks exhibit spectral bias: eigenvectors corresponding to large NTK eigenvalues preferentially capture low-frequency modes, while high-frequency components are learned extremely slowly (eigenvalue decay is steep).

The discrepancy in NTK spectral properties across loss terms creates imbalance: the kuu block (boundary) and krr block (residual) have mismatched eigenvalue magnitudes. Adaptive learning rates λb and λr scale each loss term to equalize spectral convergence rates, making the gradient flow well-conditioned. This is analogous to choosing adaptive step sizes for stiff numerical ODEs—explicit integration requires very small learning rates (10^-6 or smaller) unless the problem is preconditioned.
failure_boundary:
Spectral bias makes PINNs fail on problems with high-frequency solutions or multi-scale features. A solution exhibiting strong anisotropy (more frequencies in one direction) or steep gradients requires the network to simultaneously approximate both smooth and oscillatory components—a task for which low-frequency-biased eigenvectors are poorly suited. Forward problems are particularly vulnerable: with data only at boundaries and initial conditions, the domain interior is extrapolation, and unbalanced loss terms cause the network to over-fit residuals while ignoring boundary constraints.

Inverse problems perform better because interior observations regularize the solution—data distributed throughout the domain reduces the spectral imbalance problem. Out-of-distribution parameters (very different from training conditions) expose the fundamental limitation: the learned kernel depends on initialization and network width, and there is no guarantee it captures the target PDE's structure. Convergence stalls when the NTK's rank deficit forces additional regularization.

title: Donsub Rim: Distilling Nonlinear Shock Waves
speaker: Donsub Rim
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples. One common trick is to use a learning program (a huge network of dials that tunes itself by trial and error until it predicts correctly) to build a small, fast version of a big simulator. This talk focuses on why that fails for one specific type of problem: when something moves or a shock wave travels across the space — linear tricks don't work because motion makes the snapshots messy and high-dimensional, but the actual motion itself is simple. This lecture shows how to find the right low-dimensional description by tracking how things move through space instead of memorizing field values.
core_problem: Imagine a camera recording a wave or pulse moving across a domain. Each photo looks different from the last, so if you collect many photos and try to fit them into a low-dimensional space (like finding 5 or 10 shared patterns to explain all photos), you need many patterns — the ranking is high. But the underlying motion is simple: the same shape just slid left or right. The problem is that standard tricks assume all solutions cluster around smooth, simple directions. When things move or translate, the snapshots are nearly perpendicular to each other in the math space, so the counting of independent directions explodes even though the physical motion is straightforward.
first_principles_model: For moving waves and shocks, the real low-dimensional object is not the field values in a photo but the map that describes where information flows. Instead of saying 'the temperature here is 25 degrees in photo 1, 24 in photo 2,' think of it as 'the hot spot is moving forward by one grid cell per time step.' The transport map (how fast and in what direction the wave travels) or the deformation map (how the whole shape stretches and shifts) may be simple and low-dimensional, while the snapshots are complicated. Nonlinear model reduction tries to directly capture that moving geometry — the flow paths and transformations — rather than trying to squash moving snapshots into a fixed basis.
key_claims: When things move or interfaces evolve, traditional small models struggle because motion spreads the snapshots across many independent directions, even though the motion itself is simple.

A mathematical measure called Kolmogorov n-width shows why a linear basis can need many modes even for basic moving discontinuities: it quantifies how well the solution set fits into an n-dimensional linear subspace.
The set of all solution snapshots can be high-dimensional and complicated, while the map describing how things transport or deform can be low-dimensional.
Small nonlinear models can be built by combining a basis for shape with a learned or constructed map for motion.
Shock formation adds extra difficulty because the map that tracks motion can develop breaks or lose smoothness at the shock.
Neural networks can be understood as a way to compress a large solution representation into a smaller nonlinear model.

important_terms.meaning: A physics rule (PDE) where motion, waves carried by flow, shocks, or sharp interfaces control what happens.
A measurement of how well a set of solutions can fit into an n-dimensional linear space — high n-width means you need many independent directions.
A description of how points and features move through space under the motion or flow.
A small model that uses nonlinear coordinates or transformation maps to capture solutions more efficiently than a linear basis alone.
A compact neural network designed to approximate a family of solutions more cheaply than a large generic network, by learning the essential structure of that solution family.

stanford_connections: This connects directly to the concept of small models that capture solution structure, and introduces the first major way that linear small models fail.
It prepares later talks on curved solution sets, registration-based reduction (aligning solutions so they line up), and simulation in learned spaces.

It also explains why data-driven simulation cannot ignore how things are arranged: the same physical motion can look expensive and high-dimensional in one choice of coordinates but cheap and simple in another.
practical_caution: If your small learned model fails when predicting how a shock or wave moves, don't automatically blame lack of data or say the network needs to be bigger. The real issue might be the coordinate system. The low-dimensional structure may live in how things transport through space, not in linear combinations of snapshots. Choosing the right description of the solution — finding the right coordinates — often matters more than collecting more examples.
selected_evidence: Transport dominated problems are hard to handle with traditional reduced models.
Low-dimensional reduced spaces cannot exist.
The solution manifold itself is not low rank.
There is still a low dimensional structure available.
When there's shock formation.
takeaway: The lecture's core message is: separate what the physics does (the actual low-dimensional behavior) from the rank of the snapshots (how many independent directions you need to write them down). A moving wave can be simple when described in terms of its transport and deformation, even if collecting raw photos makes it look high-dimensional and tangled.
worked_example: Transport equation with smooth speed c(x,t)=constant±sinusoids, hat-shaped or piecewise analytic initial profile with discontinuity at s-th derivative → n-width lower bound n^(-s/2). With 10 POD basis functions composed with 4 transport modes, reduced deep network evaluates only at interpolation points (no underlying grid scaling): runtime per timestep constant even when basis grid refined 2^6→2^10 points. Burgers equation shock case: 4-layer RDN with ε error requires ~log(1/ε) parameters.
deeper_mechanics: Kolmogorov n-width bounds best linear basis approximation of solution manifold {u(·,t) : t∈[0,T]}; for transport-dominated PDEs decays slowly (~n^(-1/2) for jump). Key insight: shift representation from global basis C_R to adaptive composition C_R∘T_t^(-1), where T_t is low-rank diffeomorphism tracking characteristics x_c(t). Weight matrices have structure W_l=U_l Γ_l V_l^T (frozen U,V, small Γ_l); enables efficient backprop through specialized layer. Depth separation: shallow 1-layer RDN fails (Kolmogorov width too small), deep 2-3 layer RDN succeeds by factoring transport maps.
failure_boundary: Method breaks at shock formation (Burgers): characteristics become singular, plateau in T_t emerges, n-width of transport map degrades from fast decay. Practitioner sees: error grows exponentially over time, reduced model drifts from full solution, velocity/position magnitude discrepancy. Requires nested transport maps (4-layer RDN) to capture shock as traveling feature. Beyond 1D: extension via Radon transform discretization (ADRT) unproven at scale; continuous Radon transform loss of invertibility at large grid resolution.

title: Jan Hesthaven: Non-Intrusive ROMs Using Physics-Informed Neural Networks
speaker: Jan Hesthaven
one_sentence: This whole series is about making computers predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. This talk focuses on a concrete bottleneck: when you must speed up repeated simulations but can only watch what a simulator produces, not see how it works inside (because it's old, proprietary, or too complex). One way forward is to train a neural network (a program with millions of little dials you adjust by trial and error) to predict the answer instantly. This talk shows how adding physics rules to that trial-and-error process can make the predictions more reliable when the simulator itself is hidden from view.
core_problem: Simulators that run slow step-by-step through a physical problem can be sped up by learning a compressed shortcut: instead of running the full simulation, predict the answer using a smaller set of numbers. If you have access to the simulator's internal equations, you can work out the shortcut math by hand. But in real engineering, simulators are often locked away — written by other companies, classified, or so tangled with decades of code that nobody dares to touch them. In those cases, you only see the inputs going in and the answers coming out, with no way to touch the gears inside. When problems are nonlinear (meaning the answer does not scale linearly with the input), even the best hand-derived shortcuts still force you to run expensive calculations at full scale, choking the speedup.
first_principles_model: The goal is to build a fast shortcut: a map that takes in the problem's parameters (like wind speed or material stiffness) and directly outputs the answer as a small set of numbers representing the solution. If you can see the simulator's equations, math tells you exactly how those numbers should change with parameters. If you cannot see inside, you run the full simulator many times with different parameters and watch what outputs you get. Then you train a neural network (millions of adjustable dials) to imitate those input-output pairs. As it learns, if you also tell it the physics rules, you can nudge it to find answers that obey the laws while still matching the data.
key_claims: A reduced shortcut can represent solutions to repeated parameterized physics problems using just a small set of basis shapes, giving you speed without redoing the full simulation each time.
Nonlinear physics creates a stubborn problem: even after you shrink the math down to those few numbers, calculating the physics terms still forces you back to the full scale of the problem.
When you can only observe the simulator's inputs and outputs, not its internal structure, you must build your shortcut by watching examples, not by working out the math by hand.
A neural network can learn the direct mapping from parameters to the small set of numbers that represent the solution in the simplified basis.
If the basis captures the essential patterns in solutions, the learned mapping should be smooth enough that a small neural network can pick it up reliably.
Physics rules built into the neural network's training can steer it toward physically sensible shortcuts rather than letting it chase any pattern that fits the data.

important_terms.meaning: A speed-up technique that requires you to look at the simulator's equations or rewrite parts of it.
A speed-up built entirely from watching the simulator's inputs and outputs, without changing or examining how it works inside.
A small set of numbers that, when multiplied by key patterns in the solution, reconstruct an approximate answer without storing the full, huge array of values.
The cost or barrier that appears when the physics rules themselves depend on the solution in complicated ways, forcing you back to the full scale even in a sped-up version.
When a neural network learns the specific examples it saw during training so well that it fails on new examples, like memorizing test answers instead of understanding the concept.

stanford_connections: This talk describes the core workflow that threads through the whole series: collect examples from the full simulator offline, identify the essential patterns, then use a fast predictor online.

It places neural networks in a concrete engineering role: solving the specific problem of hidden solvers and nonlinear bottlenecks, not as a replacement for numerical simulation but as a tool to sidestep particular obstacles.

It connects to design workflows because the speedup only pays off when you must run many different parameterized versions of the same physics problem in sequence, such as exploring design options or optimizing a component.
practical_caution: This shortcut only works if two things are true: first, the full solution must have a simple underlying shape that you can capture with just a few essential numbers, and second, the learned map from parameters to those numbers must work reliably on new parameter values it has never seen before. Machines are notorious for one mistake: making the neural network too large or complex without feeding it enough examples. When you do that, the network memorizes the specific training examples rather than learning the true pattern, so it fails on fresh parameters you did not show it during training.
selected_evidence: Creating the reduced model becomes intrusive.
All you have is a piece of code that can provide you input output.
The key problem becomes how to go from choosing a parameter.
Let's use a neural net for this exercise.
When you don't have enough data... you're overfitting.
takeaway: The central lesson is practical: neural networks become your tool when classical mathematical shortcuts hit a wall, especially when the solver is only available as a closed program you cannot modify, or when the physics creates expensive side calculations that even shortcuts cannot avoid. Use this method to sidestep those specific obstacles, not to replace numerical simulation itself.
worked_example: A feed-forward neural network maps PDE parameters (boundary conditions, material properties) to reduced basis expansion coefficients. For a 1D viscous Burgers equation with 2 parameters, using 50 randomly chosen data points and 8000 residual points, a small neural network (2 layers, 10-30 neurons, hyperbolic tangent activation) achieves L2 error of 1e-2 to 1e-3 after 5,000 iterations using Adam optimizer followed by L-BFGS. For a 2D Stokes flow with non-uniform domain mapping, training 200-300 solutions for a 2D Navier-Stokes reduced model with 6 basis functions, the neural net predicts velocity and pressure with 1000x speedup compared to full Galerkin projection, though accuracy is limited to roughly 10e-2 percent error.
deeper_mechanics: The non-intrusive ROM uses a neural network Θ to learn the map μ → α(μ) where μ are parameters and α are expansion coefficients in a reduced basis V. Loss function combines data mismatch L_data = ||u_measured - Σ α_i v_i||² and PDE residual L_PDE = ||∂u/∂t - N[u]||² evaluated via automatic differentiation. For time-dependent problems, an LSTM network learns the memory term: the convolution kernel K accounting for discarded high-modes through projection P onto the reduced space, outputting the correction term to the Galerkin ROM that enforces energy balance. The projection error decomposition breaks total error into: (1) finite-element approximation error (PDE discretization), (2) reduced basis projection error ||u - Π_V u||, and (3) neural network approximation error for the parameter map.
failure_boundary: Accuracy plateaus around 1e-2 to 1e-3 error due to high-dimensional non-convex optimization even with adaptive learning rates; spectral accuracy (1e-4 or better) is difficult to achieve. When reduced basis doesn't well-represent solution manifold (bad linear space), neural networks cannot compensate—garbage in, garbage out. For long-time integration without memory correction, reduced ROM solutions drift rapidly and can show completely wrong amplitude/phase; adding LSTM correction gains 4-6 orders of magnitude accuracy. Training data volume and neural network size involve overfitting plateau: too few snapshots or oversized networks cause spurious overfitting visible in validation curves beyond ~25 neurons for small problems.

title: Nils Thuerey: Differentiable Physics Simulations For Deep Learning
speaker: Nils Thuerey
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of only hand-built math. This talk shows how to connect simulators and learning by making the simulator compute gradients — think of them as tiny signals showing which direction to nudge inputs to get closer to a desired physical outcome — so those signals can guide learning, answer puzzles about what caused an observation, and improve how we control things.
core_problem: Simulators are programs that step through physical situations (air flowing, heat spreading, water sloshing) moment by moment to predict what happens next. Most people use simulators just to create training data: run it many times with different inputs and collect results. But this misses something important. Many real problems ask: if I change an input, a parameter, or a control action, how would the physical result change? To answer that question precisely, you need gradients — numerical signals that flow backward through the simulator showing how much each earlier step contributed to the final answer.
first_principles_model: A simulator takes a starting state, parameters, or control actions and predicts what the physics will do next. Most simulators can only run forward: plug in numbers, get answers. A differentiable simulator also computes gradients — which inputs and parameters mattered most to the final result. This opens up new possibilities. You can reverse the question: start from an outcome you want and work backward to find what starting state or control action would produce it (this is called an inverse problem). You can reduce errors built into the numerical method itself by training a learning program to spot and fix them. You can train learning programs inside the physics loop by having gradients flow from the simulator back to the program's dials. The simulator stops being just a tool to generate data and becomes a step in the optimization process itself.
key_claims: Physics models and the numerical methods used to solve them have real value and should be kept when possible, with learning handling measurement noise, gaps in observations, and effects we don't know about.
Running a simulator forward shows what will happen; asking inverse problems means finding what starting conditions or actions would create a desired outcome.
Learning from data made by simulators is helpful but loosely connected to the actual physics.

Telling a learning program the physics rules in its loss function (a score measuring how wrong its answers are) creates a tighter link, but building the simulator itself into the learning process creates the closest connection.
What matters most is the gradient showing how the simulation's final result would change if you tweaked the starting conditions or control action.
Solvers (programs that compute physical predictions) that can compute gradients can be used inside the training loop for learning, control, and fixing errors in approximate numerical methods.

important_terms.meaning: A program that runs physics forward and also computes gradients showing how much each input, state, control signal, or parameter affected the final answer.
A learning system where a program that predicts physics runs as part of training and passes back gradient signals to guide how the learning program tunes its dials.
A method for efficiently calculating what change in an earlier step would have been needed to cause a small change at the end — the reverse direction of a forward simulation.
A puzzle where you start with an outcome (measured or desired) and work backward to find the hidden causes, parameters, or actions that would produce it.
Training a learning program to spot and fix errors that come from using coarse grids, simple mathematical approximations, or fast but imprecise solvers.

stanford_connections: This is the differentiable-simulation foundation for the seminar series and extends earlier talks about adding physics to learning by moving the solver into the learning process itself.
It connects to controlling systems, designing objects better, simulating fluids, and upcoming talks about machine learning applied to science.
It also bridges adjoint methods from classical scientific computing to today's automatic differentiation tools (programs that compute gradients automatically).
practical_caution: Gradients are useful only if they truly reflect what happens in the real physics and if calculating them stays fast. Physics code that mixes many different types of physics, makes predictions far into the future, has sudden jumps (like objects colliding), or uses math that grows unstable can make this approach impractical. The nice theory works best when the simulator is stable and relatively simple.
selected_evidence: Ideally there shouldn't be much of a boundary between learning and simulation.
We have a gradient of this simulation.
This actually lets us combine simulation very neatly with the deep learning process.
The first example... is this solver in the loop project.
Differentiable solvers is a very useful tool.
takeaway: Gradients let you optimize through simulation instead of just using it as a data source. This is why differentiable physics matters for inverse problems (finding what caused an observation), control (making something behave as you want), and machine learning applied to science.
worked_example:
2D cylinder wake flow with obstacle: domain 128x64, 10-32 timesteps, Re ~ 100-200. Solver-in-loop approach reduces mean absolute error from ~0.14 (naive supervised) to ~0.013 (with neural correction). 3D flow requires ~900s CPU reference simulation vs 13-14s hybrid (source + network correction) = 60-70x speedup. Network trains under 100 epochs to stabilize double integrator control task.

Smoke plume fire exit control: 2D domain 128 sq, 16 timesteps, 5000+ continuous control parameters. Solver-in-loop enforces differentiability through entire unroll, enabling gradient-based optimization where RL fails. Achieves sub-optimal but satisfactory control solutions vs reinforcement learning instability.
deeper_mechanics: PDE-aware solver loops integrate automatic differentiation through numerical schemes. Forward pass: solve PDE residual |∂u/∂t - N[u]|² using neural network correction C[u; θ] added to coarse solution. Backward pass: compute adjoint of entire solver stack to backprop sensitivity ∇L/∇θ. Key: replace naive supervised l2 loss (reference data only) with solver-in-loop loss that sees denoised but evolving system states. Adjoint computation uses same discretization (e.g., Runge-Kutta 4) for both forward and backward to preserve accuracy.
failure_boundary: Method struggles with chaotic systems where small state perturbations diverge exponentially; adjoint instability can emerge with long unrolled horizons (100+ steps). Shifting distribution problem occurs when network sees only source simulator during supervised training but must generalize to hybrid dynamics during deployment. For 3D flows at high fidelity, memory footprint for storing full trajectory during backpropagation becomes prohibitive; wall-clock cost of reference solver generation can dominate if problem requires many training episodes.

title: Pawan Goyal: Physics-Informed Learning For Nonlinear Dynamical Systems
speaker: Pawan Goyal
organization: Max Planck Institute for Dynamics of Complex Technical Systems
one_sentence: This whole series is about teaching computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of hand-written math. One powerful way to learn fast models is to build in what we know about the physics structure from the start. This talk focuses on a technique that learns a small reduced model—one that captures the main patterns of how a system changes over time—by studying real data, and it automatically keeps the physics structure that simplified models should have.
core_problem: To design machines, control them, optimize them, or test how they handle surprises, engineers need models that predict how systems evolve over time. But the most detailed models—ones with millions of small pieces that track every tiny part of the system—take hours or days to run. Older simulators or commercial software often hide their internal equations; you only see the output numbers. Classical techniques exist to build small, fast versions of big models, but they need the full detailed equations to work, and many data sources (old codes, vendor software, specialized tools) do not give you access to those.
first_principles_model: Most systems have a key insight: only a handful of patterns actually matter for predicting what happens next. Imagine a spinning turbine: you do not need to track every molecule; you just track a few shapes that move and evolve. The technique here learns those core shapes and their rules directly from measurement data. It works by assuming the small model has the same structure a classical reduction would have built, then solving backward from the data to find what those equations must be.
key_claims: To understand how systems evolve and respond to new operating conditions, you need equations that can be run repeatedly and modified.
Two stubborn problems: turning a messy real system into equations is hard work, and detailed accurate models are so huge they take forever to run.
Instead of deriving equations by hand or running expensive detailed simulations, you can jump straight from measurement data to small, fast equations.
The core idea is to learn those small equations from data while enforcing that they follow the structure physics would predict.
If your data samples enough different behaviors (fast and slow, different starting points, different stresses), the learned equations match what older mathematical methods would have found.
This approach shines when your data come from older software, commercial tools, or one-of-a-kind simulators where you cannot reach inside to see the math.

important_terms.meaning: A technique that figures out the equations of a small simplified model by studying how a real system moves and changes over time in recorded data.
A detailed mathematical description with so many pieces and variables that running it once can take hours or days, making repeated use nearly impossible.
The few most important patterns or shapes that describe how a system behaves; like the lowest notes that define a song even though many more notes could exist.
Old software or a simulator that produces output numbers you can measure, but does not show you the equations or internal rules that created those numbers.
Training a model to fit data while also obeying the known laws and rules of physics, rather than letting it find any pattern that fits.

stanford_connections: This continues earlier talks about building small, fast models from big ones, but now focuses on learning the small model's equations from data alone.
It connects to talks on tools that can take derivatives through a simulation and on solving inverse problems, because a learned small model becomes the fast engine for steering a system.

It reinforces a repeating thread: when you have real data and physical laws, use both together; let data fill in what is missing or too costly to compute by hand, but keep the physics rules where you know them.
practical_caution: This is not just drawing a smooth curve through points. If you guess the wrong structure for the reduced model, or if your data only shows the system in a narrow set of conditions (say, only low-speed flows, not turbulent ones), the small model may look perfect on short simulations but break down when you try longer runs or push the system in new ways.
selected_evidence: We have focused on operator inference approach to learn dynamical systems.
We need dynamical models to analyze transient behavior.
There are two main bottleneck.
Can we go out of these two steps?
Compute reduced order model directly from the data.
takeaway: When you have data from a system but no access to its full equations, you can still build a small, fast model by learning it directly from the data while insisting it follows the structure that physics-aware reduction should have—no guessing, no hand-tuning, but honest about what the data can and cannot teach.
worked_example: For a tabular reactor model learning nonlinear dynamics from data, the method collects 513 snapshots over 30 seconds. A reduced order model of dimension 10 is trained to capture concentration (phi) and temperature (theta) fields. The full finite element model requires accessing discretized operators, whereas operator inference learns the ROM directly without the high-fidelity matrices. Testing on held-out time interval 30-60 seconds shows prediction error under 1 percent—demonstrating generalization without overfitting—while compression preserves the coupling structure across both species.
deeper_mechanics: Operator inference formulates a quadratic form PDE where discretization yields x-dot = Ax + f(x), but instead of solving for A and f directly, it finds reduced operators A-hat and f-hat by minimizing ||M(A-hat, f-hat) - residual||^2 subject to regularization. The method exploits that if data snapshots X and time derivatives X-dot are available, the reduced model A-hat = V^T A V and f-hat projected onto reduced basis V satisfy a least-squares problem with a Tikhonov regularizer. This avoids ill-conditioning by balancing fit against parameter norm. Gray-box variants add known physics like diffusion structure to the objective, keeping only unknown reaction terms unstructured.
failure_boundary: Operator inference degrades when the underlying PDE has unknown nonlinearities or when data is sparse in poorly sampled regions. The method assumes access to uniform time-step snapshots; missing or irregularly sampled data requires preprocessing. For advection-dominated problems (high Reynolds number flows), the quadratic form assumption breaks down and the ROM cannot capture sharp gradients or transport phenomena without special treatment. Parameter extrapolation fails outside the training regime since the inferred operators have no embedded physical constraints—only data-driven relationships.

title: Youngsoo Choi: Efficient Nonlinear Manifold Reduced Order Model
speaker: Youngsoo Choi
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. One fast approach is a reduced-order model: a program that learns to turn a huge simulation (millions of numbers) into a tiny stand-in (a few numbers) and back again. This talk is about why these stand-ins fail on flows where material gets pushed around fast, and how to fix both the shape problem (use a curved map instead of a straight one) and the speed problem (only evaluate the residual—the mismatch between the model and reality—at sampled spots instead of everywhere).
core_problem: Linear-subspace reduced-order models are fast when the solutions cluster near a flat low-dimensional space. But flows where material gets pushed around (advection-dominated), shocks, and moving structures usually do not cluster that way. A curved manifold (a nonlinear space) can show these solution families more faithfully, but a simple curved-manifold model can run slower than the full simulation because the decoder (the neural network that rebuilds the big state from the tiny one) and the residual (the mismatch between the model and the actual behavior) still need full-dimensional work—that is, they touch every number.
first_principles_model: A full simulation tracks a very large state (all the numbers). A reduced-order model swaps that for a small latent coordinate (a handful of numbers that stand in for the full state). In a linear version, you rebuild the big state by multiplying a basis (a fixed set of directions) by small coefficients (one number per direction). In a curved-manifold version, you rebuild it using a learned nonlinear map, often built as an autoencoder—two neural networks working together, one that compresses the full state into a handful of numbers (the encoder) and one that expands those numbers back into a full state (the decoder). The remaining slowdown is that evaluating the residual still requires visiting every entry, so hyper-reduction picks only the entries you actually need to approximate the residual accurately.
key_claims: Surrogate models (quick stand-ins for expensive simulations) matter for multi-query tasks like design optimization because full simulations can take too long.
More invasive surrogate models (ones that dig into the physics equations) can be more accurate but usually demand more access to the equations and are harder to speed up.
Curved-manifold reduced-order models use nonlinear maps, like autoencoder decoders, instead of linear basis times coefficients.
Without hyper-reduction, curved-manifold reduced-order models stay impractical because nonlinear terms still scale with the full simulation size.
Gappy POD (a sampling method where you pick a few key spots instead of using the whole field) can shrink how many decoder outputs you have to compute.
On a flow with both pushing (advection) and smoothing (viscosity) like Burgers equation, the curved-manifold reduced-order model matches the full simulation better than a flat-subspace one.

important_terms.meaning: A reduced-order model (a tiny stand-in for a huge simulation) that rebuilds full states from a few numbers using a curved map instead of a straight line (a linear basis multiplied by coefficients).
The part of a neural network (a program with millions of little dials) that takes a handful of numbers and expands them back into a full state by learning the pattern from examples.
A speed-up trick that cuts the cost of calculating mismatch (residual) by only computing at a sampled subset of spots instead of everywhere.
A method that rebuilds a full field by taking samples at chosen spots and combining them using a reduced basis instead of storing every number.
A flow where material gets pushed around and travels fast, which tends to destroy the flat low-rank structure (the idea that everything stays close to a flat space) that linear methods assume.

stanford_connections: This continues the shock-wave lecture: if pushing (advection) breaks the flat low-rank structure, switch to curved coordinates.
It ties to later latent-space and autoencoder reduced-order model talks by making the decoder cost visible and real.
It also reinforces a recurring DDPS theme: getting the shape right (representation) is only half the job; the actual running speed also matters.
practical_caution: A curved latent code can look accurate on paper but still run slower than the original solver if you don't also cut the cost of residual evaluation. Real reduced-order model design must measure both how close the approximation is to the truth and how fast it actually runs.
selected_evidence: One full simulation takes 7.4 days.
More intrusiveness means more accuracy.
NM ROM uses a non-linear manifold representation using non-linear map G.
These non-linear terms still scale with the full order model size.
NM ROM achieves less than 1% maximum relative error.
takeaway: The lecture's core lesson is that curved manifolds solve a shape problem (how to represent the solutions faithfully), while hyper-reduction solves a speed problem (how to make it run fast enough). A useful reduced-order model needs both.
worked_example: A smooth particle hydrodynamics (SPH) simulation for shape charge penetration originally requires 7.4 days per simulation. The nonlinear manifold ROM reduces this substantially by combining three components: (1) autoencoder-based nonlinear map G for solution representation, (2) hyper-reduction to handle nonlinear terms, and (3) gappy POD with neural network sparsification. Testing on an advection-dominated 2D viscous Burgers' equation shows the NM ROM achieves less than 1% maximum relative error compared to the full order model, while the black-box surrogate approach reaches around 38% error.
deeper_mechanics: NM ROM substitutes the nonlinear manifold representation u ≈ G(α) into the governing equations, producing an overdetermined system that is closed by minimizing the residual norm ||r|| = ||∂u/∂t - N[u]||^2, where N[u] represents nonlinear operators. The critical issue: nonlinear terms still scale with full-order size N. Hyper-reduction addresses this via gappy POD, selecting a subset of nonlinear outputs (shown as orange discs in the decoder) to avoid full-size evaluation. A mask is applied to create a sparser network, reducing the hidden nodes needed to compute selected outputs.
failure_boundary: The method currently falls short on instability problems like Rayleigh-Taylor instability. Even with hyper-reduction, the approach traditionally suffered from NM ROM being slower than the full order model, making it impractical for multi-query design optimization—the main motivation for surrogate building.

title: Jesse Chan: Entropy Stable Schemes For Nonlinear Conservation Laws
speaker: Jesse Chan
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from data instead of pure hand-written math. One challenge: when you use fancy, high-accuracy math on systems with sharp features (shock waves, wild turbulence, details too small to capture), the method can break and give nonsense. This talk is about building methods that stay correct near those breaking points by baking the physics rules—especially one rule about energy increasing over time—directly into how you solve the equations.
core_problem: High-order numerical methods (fancy math that should be very accurate) work great when solutions are smooth, but fail on problems with shock waves, turbulent eddies, or gradients so steep you can't capture them on your grid. To keep the solution from exploding, engineers add damping filters, limiting rules, or fake extra friction. These patches work, but they force a painful choice: turn them up and you stay safe but lose accuracy; turn them down and you regain accuracy but risk instability.
first_principles_model: A nonlinear conservation law says that certain quantities (like mass or momentum) move through a system via flow across boundaries—they don't appear or vanish for no reason. For most real physics (air flow, shallow water, heat and fluid mixing), there's a secondary rule: an energy-like quantity—call it entropy—should always increase or stay the same, never decrease. An entropy-stable method is designed so that the numerical solution (the grid-based approximation the computer calculates) automatically obeys this energy rule. That means stability is a built-in guarantee, not a last-minute fix you add when things go wrong.
key_claims: Systems from Burgers flow to shallow-water waves to full air flow (Navier-Stokes) and even magnetic fluids (MHD) all fit a common mold: nonlinear conservation laws with an energy rule underneath.

High-order discontinuous Galerkin methods (a way to break the solution into separate pieces on each grid cell and connect them via fluxes) combine geometric flexibility with high accuracy, making them attractive.
When gradients are unresolved (too sharp for your grid), shock waves and turbulence make simple high-order methods produce garbage.
Traditional stability patches—adding fake friction, filtering, or slope limiters—reduce accuracy and require tedious parameter tuning.

Entropy-stable schemes use a change of variables (entropy variables), carefully designed flux rules between grid cells (numerical fluxes), and discrete energy inequalities to make stability automatic.
The idea extends beyond simple collocation-style methods toward more structured approaches (modal discontinuous Galerkin) and reduced-order models that capture only the dominant modes.

important_terms.meaning: A rule saying that certain quantities (like mass or momentum) move through space via flow; they are never created or destroyed.
A mathematical rule stating that an energy-like quantity (representing disorder; in thermodynamics called entropy) must increase or stay the same, never decrease in physical solutions.
A rescaled set of variables obtained by measuring how the entropy changes when you shift the conserved quantities; they change the perspective on the equations in a useful way.

A way to solve equations on a grid by treating each grid cell as its own region, writing the solution separately in each cell using basis functions, and connecting cells with carefully designed flux values at the boundaries.
Fake extra friction added to the numerical method to smooth out wiggles and keep solutions from exploding, but at the cost of washing out fine details and accuracy.

stanford_connections: This talk brings a numerical-analysis lens to the machine-learning focus of the series: reliable predictions depend not just on data and learning, but on the underlying structure of the discretization scheme.

It matters for fluid surrogates and reduced-order models because learned or simplified versions of a system inherit stability issues unless they respect the conservation and energy structure of the original equations.

It's essential context for anyone building learned simulators: before training a learning program to mimic a system, make sure you understand which conservation and stability properties the numerical scheme must preserve, otherwise the learned model will be brittle.
practical_caution: When you train a learning program to mimic a fluid system, don't judge it only by short-term error. If it doesn't respect the true structure of the equations (conservation) or the energy behavior, then over many timesteps under-resolved shocks and turbulence will grow in nonsensical ways or violate the conservation laws you assumed were true.
selected_evidence: They generally blow up whenever they encounter under-resolved solutions.
Shocks and turbulence... are highly under-resolved solutions most of the time.
I wanted to avoid the common metrics used for higher schemes... artificial viscosity filtering... slope limiting.
They can tend to reduce the amount of the accuracy.
A class of nonlinear conservation laws which all admit an entropy inequality.
takeaway: Reliability must be built in from the start by respecting the physics of the equations, not bolted on as a patch when a method starts to fail.
worked_example: 8th-order method on Burgers equation with 25-175 POD basis modes; Euler equations and compressible Navier-Stokes with Reynolds 10000, Mach 1.5 flow over cylinder; 2D smooth Kelvin-Helmholtz instability with 400,000 grid points, viscosity 1/1000, 75 modes achieving 1% relative error; Gaussian pulse in 2D with 25 modes yielding under-1% error; Riemann problem shock resolution with 50 modes; Jacobian autodiff computation speedup from 400 ms to 3 ms (133× faster) on 50x50 matrix for Burgers equation.
deeper_mechanics: Entropy stable schemes built on entropy conservative fluxes satisfying discrete entropy condition: difference in entropy variables times flux equals difference in entropy potentials. Hadamard product structure: skew-symmetric differentiation matrix Q (zero row-sum, conservative) combined with flux matrix F via Q ⊙ F (element-wise product). Summation-by-parts operators with boundary matrices enforce entropy stability. Modal discontinuous Galerkin formulation: L2-project entropy variables before flux evaluation to handle non-polynomial entropy variables. Proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) reduction with Galerkin projection and two-step hyper-reduction (compress via test basis, then project onto empirical cubature sample points) preserves entropy conservation. Jacobian formula as explicit Hadamard product: ∂F/∂u ⊙ (∂f/∂v + small diagonal) avoids dense autodiff.
failure_boundary: High-order DG methods oscillate and blow up at shocks without stabilization (unrealistic Burgers simulations crash during discontinuity formation). Gibbs phenomenon persists near shocks even in entropy stable schemes, risking negative thermodynamic variables (density, pressure) that invalidate equations of state and break stability theory. Under-resolved Riemann problems show poor shock capturing in reduced-order models (relative errors >10%, oscillations present). Reduced-order models become more expensive than full-order for explicit time stepping despite size reduction: sampled matrix becomes dense (loss of sparsity in Q), requiring many more flux evaluations. Entropy variable enrichment incurs cost in singular value decay (50+ modes needed vs 25 for accuracy). Modal DG schemes require hybridization technique to avoid all-to-all coupling when interior quadrature nodes (not boundary nodes) are used.

title: Irina Tezaur: Schwarz Alternating Method For Concurrent Multiscale Coupling In Solid Mechanics
speaker: Irina Tezaur
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. Sometimes an object has tiny details in one spot (like a crack growing through metal, or stress bunching at a weld) that control what happens to the whole thing, but simulating every tiny detail everywhere is too slow. This talk is about a trick to solve this: split the object into pieces, let each piece use its own solver and detail level, and pass information back and forth at the boundaries until all pieces agree on what happens at their edges.
core_problem: When a physical object has small-scale events happening in one region while most of the object stays simple, you need both a detailed picture in the critical zone and a simpler, faster picture everywhere else. But here is the hard part: if you try to glue a fine-grain simulation to a coarse one at the boundary, information traveling across that line can cause errors, the two solvers might not speak the same language, or the combined prediction can blow up and become wrong.
first_principles_model: A domain decomposition approach (the words just mean: split the problem into pieces) cuts the region into chunks. Then the Schwarz alternating method solves each chunk's equation while swapping boundary information with its neighbors repeatedly. Imagine sitting at the boundary between a coarse zone and a fine zone: the boundary of one zone is the information the other zone gets, and you iterate—pass data, solve, get new boundary data, pass it back—until both sides agree on what they see at their shared line.
key_claims: When a local small-scale event controls what happens to the whole object, you need to solve that detail in real time, not after the fact.
You should be able to use different solvers (the programs that do the math) and different speeds of time-stepping in different zones.
The boundary handoff should not introduce errors that do not exist in the real physics.
The Schwarz alternating method divides the big domain into smaller pieces and iteratively passes information until the global answer is consistent.
This method has a proven convergence recipe for problems with big deformations and strongly nonlinear physics.
Small overlapping regions where the zones mix can be enough, but cases with just touching zones or contact require extra care.

important_terms.meaning: Solving different levels of detail (coarse and fine) in different parts of the object at the same time, with each part informing the others.
A repeating process where each region solves its own local equations and swaps boundary information with neighbors until they all converge.
A band where two zones share space; used to pass solution values back and forth and speed up the repeating process toward a steady answer.
A situation where the material bends or stretches so much that the shape itself changes the math—not just small jiggles.
A fake, unphysical behavior that pops up at the seam where two zones meet because they do not connect correctly.

stanford_connections: This lecture expands DDPS beyond just learning replacements for old solvers—sometimes the best answer is to keep the physics-based solver but split the job across zones.
It ties to hybrid twins: real machines often have small patches where you need exact answers stitched into a bigger, rougher model.
It reinforces a lesson that keeps showing up: the boundary or interface between pieces is not just geometry—it is part of your model and can make or break the answer.
practical_caution: Even if each model is correct on its own, the handoff at the interface—how boundary values pass from one zone to the next—is part of your overall model. A sloppy handoff makes the global answer untrustworthy, even if every piece was solved correctly.
selected_evidence: A small-scale event will eventually determine the performance of the entire system.
Allow us to use different solvers and time integrators in different regions.
We don't want the coupling to introduce any non-physical artifacts.
The earliest known domain decomposition method.
You decompose that domain into simpler subdomains.
takeaway: Multiscale modeling is really an interface problem: your global prediction is only as good as how well information moves between the coarse and fine pieces.
worked_example:
A cuboid problem couples two cube-shaped domains with different mesh refinements and overlap regions. Schwarz iterations converge with linear rate until solutions match in the overlap to a specified tolerance, requiring typically 2-4 iterations for the voltage joint problem even with tiny overlap around bolts. Displacement errors reach machine precision (10^-13) in stress when coupling is tuned correctly, with error about 0.1% in the notch cylinder problem due to geometric discretization, not coupling artifacts.

The tension specimen couples 200,000-node high-fidelity model (fine tetrahedral mesh in gauge, coarse hex mesh in ends) with inelastic J2 plasticity. Schwarz converges in 3 iterations per time step. Production-scale fastener/bolt problems show speed comparable to single-domain solutions even though method is iterative, sometimes actually faster (line 1618-1620) due to reduced individual subdomain complexity, though analysis varies by mesh resolution.
deeper_mechanics:
The overlapping Schwarz method solves each subdomain's PDE independently: solve in Ω1 using boundary conditions on outer boundary and arbitrary BC on internal boundary γ1; then solve in Ω2 using prescribed BC on outer boundary and Dirichlet BC on γ2 interpolated from Ω1's solution. This iterates (boundary solution from Ω1 → BC for Ω2, reverse) until solutions match in overlap to convergence tolerance. For quasi-statics, an outer loop increments load while an inner Schwarz loop enforces compatibility (line 506-525). For dynamics, a controller time stepper synchronizes domains at global time steps; each subdomain advances with its own time discretization, requiring space-time interpolation of displacement, velocity, and acceleration at boundaries (line 1167-1173).

Theory guarantees convergence if single-domain problem is well-posed and overlap region non-empty (line 614-617). Proof constructs sequence of solutions with curly feet till parameter n, applies Schwarz iteration, shows convergence to unique minimizer of energy functional Φ (line 622-631). Stability for Newmark integration requires sufficiently small time step Δt to make second variation of action functional positive definite (line 1209-1229). Convergence rate is linear and improves with larger overlap fraction (line 800-805).
failure_boundary:
When overlap region becomes very small (voltage joint case), requirements on stability and well-posedness may dominate, though practically this has not been limiting (line 1988-2010). Material model inconsistencies in overlap cause convergence issues: plastic deformation spilling into overlap where only elastic model expected produces artifacts (line 938-942). When different material models coexist in overlap, users must carefully position decomposition so overlap stays in elastic region; theoretical convergence then assumes same material model throughout (line 944-954).

Boundary transmission conditions for contact (non-overlapping) differ fundamentally from solid-coupling case and require Robin or alternating Dirichlet-Neumann conditions (line 1731-1732). Coupling structural elements (shells) to continuum requires separate algorithm development; current work addresses this as ongoing research (line 1710-1713).

title: Steven Brunton: Interpretable And Generalizable Machine Learning For Fluid Mechanics
speaker: Steven Brunton
one_sentence: This whole series asks: can computers learn to predict how physical things behave by studying examples, instead of just relying on hand-written math? This talk focuses on one specific goal: when teaching a computer to predict how fluids move and change, prefer models that you can actually read and understand. A model that is easy to read usually works on new situations the computer has never seen before, while a hidden locked-box model often fails when conditions shift—new speeds, different shapes, changed temperature.
core_problem: Measuring fluids produces enormous amounts of numbers, and running exact simulations takes forever. But just teaching a computer to match numbers it has already seen is not good enough. A model can repeat past observations while completely breaking down when the conditions change—when you use a new control, change the shape, or vary a parameter—if it has only memorized patterns instead of truly learning how fluids actually work. The real structure hiding inside fluid motion is often surprisingly simple: just a handful of important directions and perhaps only a few key forces matter, but most models never find that simplicity.
first_principles_model: Real fluid systems carry tons of measurement data but almost always boil down to just a few essential directions; the hidden rules that govern them also usually rest on only a few key pieces instead of using every possible term. Interpretable machine learning hunts for those few crucial directions, determines which forces truly matter, finds hidden terms that are missing from our approximate rules, or spots where our simple models need small fixes. The alternative is building a secret system that just converts inputs to outputs without you ever knowing why it works.
key_claims: Applying machine learning to engineering is essentially optimization: find the dials and numbers that make your predictions as close to the real measurements as possible.
For a model to work on new situations, it must capture the true hidden simplicity, not just memorize old training examples.
Simple is better: build models with as few terms as required, but no fewer.
One specific method called SINDy (Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics) watches how a system changes and automatically picks out which forces and interactions are actually doing the work.

The way you choose to describe and measure a fluid—your coordinate system—can either hide the simple structure or expose it; picking the right way of measuring turns a huge complicated problem into something small and clear.
Machine learning can also focus on finding mismatch: what is the difference between our approximate rules and what actually happens in reality.

important_terms.meaning: The principle that a good explanation should be as simple as possible to describe what you see, without unnecessary details.

A method that takes measurements of a system and automatically discovers which forces and interactions matter. You give it a long list of candidate pieces (linear terms, multiplication terms, etc.), and it systematically removes the ones that contribute almost nothing, leaving only the few that actually drive the behavior.
A type of fitting that pushes most candidate contributions toward zero, keeping only the few that truly matter for prediction.
Finding new ways to measure and describe a system so that complicated high-dimensional motion becomes simple and clear.
Learning the gap between an approximate rule (like a simplified physical equation) and what you actually observe in the real world; the correction term that fills the hole in your theory.

stanford_connections: This is the core thread linking reduced-order models (stripped-down simpler versions that keep the essential behavior), operator inference (learning how operations transform the system), and scientific machine learning: the shared idea is to learn true structure rather than just memorizing outputs.
It directly connects to talks about surrogates and closure because closure terms are often exactly discrepancy models for physics happening below the scale you can measure.

It also sets a clear test for interpretability: can you actually inspect and understand what you learned—as explicit equations, as a list of important directions, as a balance of forces, or as correction terms?
practical_caution: A computer model that predicts the next snapshot of a fluid flow may look impressive on graphs but still be scientifically hollow if it never reveals which variables are actually driving the flow, how different forces combine and interact, or what physics pieces we left out. To truly test if a model works in new regimes, you must try situations it has never encountered—not just check whether it predicts numbers in between the training examples.
selected_evidence: It would not generalize beyond fall.
Things should be as simple as possible and no simpler.
Mathematically today in my opinion is sparsity.
Sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics or SINDy.
If we pull out the right coordinate system you can get a very very simple model.
takeaway: The deep lesson from this talk is that when a model is easy to read and inspect, that is not extra decoration—it is often the exact thing that makes it work on new situations. In fluids especially, once you can see the structure and write it down clearly, the model begins to transfer to problems it has never trained on.
worked_example: SINDy discovered the Lorenz 63 model from noisy measurement data. Using only 2-3 trajectories collected in a couple of hours on a laptop, the algorithm recovered the three core equations (x dot, y dot, z dot) with correct coefficients without ever seeing the equations. For the cylinder wake system, researchers measured lift and drag and used sparse identification to discover a spring-mass-damper model—achieving both the highest accuracy (nearly perfect quantitative match) and simplest description ever written for this canonical problem.
deeper_mechanics: SINDy builds a library of candidate terms (polynomials, derivatives, products) organized as a matrix Theta. Given time-derivative data X_dot, it solves a sparse regression: find the minimum number of columns of Theta such that Theta @ c = X_dot. The loss enforces skew-symmetric structure for energy conservation; when combined with cubic and higher-order closure terms, it captures how truncated low-energy modes couple back to retained modes. The constrained sparse selection uses iterative least squares with hard zeros: minimize ||X_dot - Theta @ c||^2 subject to ||c||_0 being small.
failure_boundary: SINDy struggles with discontinuities and shock waves—piecewise constant data requires many more terms or fails entirely. For turbulent flows without coherent structure, it cannot extract the small number of dominant terms needed; full isotropic box turbulence is beyond reach. Systems with weak coupling or slow timescale separation lead to ambiguous term selection and require careful hyperparameter tuning. Measurement noise introduces false terms that must be pruned, and extrapolation beyond the training regime (new parameter ranges) is unreliable because the discovered equations encode only the dynamics observed.

title: Alfio Quarteroni: The Mathematical Heart
speaker: Alfio Quarteroni
one_sentence: This whole series is about teaching computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of only using hand-written rules. This talk focuses on the heart: an organ where electricity triggers muscle contraction, which squeezes and deforms tissue, which pushes blood around, with valves opening and closing, all while blood vessels feed the muscle itself. The challenge is that these five processes (electricity, mechanics, blood flow, valves, vessel perfusion) all happen at different speeds and scales, and they all affect each other—so a real heart model is not one simple rule, but five interconnected simulators (programs that step a physical situation forward in tiny increments) that must stay in sync.
core_problem: The heart is not one physics rule or one simulator. An electrical wave spreads through heart muscle and tells it to contract. That contraction deforms tissue, bending and stretching it. The bent tissue moves blood sitting in the heart chambers. Valves snap open and shut to guide that blood flow. At the same time, tiny blood vessels feed oxygen and nutrients back into the contracting muscle. Each of these five processes runs at a different speed (some fast, some slow), uses a different spatial scale (some tiny vessels, some whole chambers), and needs its own equations and numerical tricks to solve. Putting them together in one model means that electricity, mechanics, flow, valves, and perfusion all touch each other—change one, and all the others shift.
first_principles_model: To build a heart simulator on a computer, start with the organ's actual shape from a CT scan or MRI. Chop that shape into millions of tiny boxes (a mesh—like graph paper wrapped around the heart). Then add five separate physics modules: (1) An electrical rule that spreads an activation wave through muscle, powered by ions flowing in and out of cells. (2) A mechanics rule that says muscle fibers contract when activated, pulling the tissue; the tissue also has stiffness and resists being bent (elasticity). (3) A fluid-dynamics rule that governs how blood flows inside the heart chambers, following the same principles that govern water rushing through pipes. (4) A valve rule that opens and closes at the right times to keep blood moving the right way. (5) A perfusion rule that tracks blood supply through large coronary arteries splitting into millions of capillaries feeding the muscle. Link all five together so that electrical activation triggers contraction, contraction deforms the chambers, deformation guides blood flow, flow pulls on the walls, and vessel pressure feeds back into the muscle.
key_claims: Hand-written math rules can describe how electricity spreads through heart muscle, how muscle contracts and deforms tissue, how blood moves inside the heart and vessels, how valves open and close, and how blood feeds the muscle.
The heart is a coupled multiphysics problem (several distinct physical processes affecting each other) with multiscale behavior (processes happen at vastly different speeds and sizes).

The exact shape of a patient's heart can be traced from medical scans (CT or MRI), or approximated using statistical average shapes built from many healthy hearts, or hand-designed as a simplified CAD model.
Electricity and contraction may need different spatial grids (mesh divisions) than blood flow, because the detail needed is different in muscle tissue versus flowing liquid.

A complete heart model needs six components: electrical activation, active muscle contraction (the muscle's own pulling force), passive tissue stiffness (resistance to bending), blood flow in chambers and vessels, valve mechanics, and blood supply through coronary arteries.

Solving the full model on a computer is expensive, so scientists build simpler surrogate simulators (reduced-order models) for clinical studies and when uncertainty matters—these trade some accuracy for speed.

important_terms.meaning: The study of how electrical signals spread through heart tissue, triggering muscle cells to contract. Think of it like a wave of activation rippling across the heart, powered by charged atoms (ions) moving in and out of cells.

The actual pulling and pushing force that a muscle fiber generates in response to electrical activation. When a nerve signal arrives, the muscle fiber burns chemical energy and contracts—this is the active part.

The stiffness and resistance of tissue when it is stretched or compressed by external forces (like blood pressure pushing against the heart wall). Every material resists being bent; this rule describes that resistance.
The two-way coupling between a flowing liquid (blood) and the solid walls and valves it touches. The blood pushes on the tissue; the tissue moves and shapes the blood flow.

The delivery of blood to tissue through vessels of many different sizes—wide coronary arteries branch into progressively smaller vessels down to capillaries the width of a single cell. Modeling this requires describing large vessels with one method and tiny vessels with another.

stanford_connections: The heart is the clearest example in this series of a real multiphysics simulator (many interacting physics pieces) where machine learning methods must respect all the coupled modules, not ignore them.

It ties to reduced-order models (ROM) because doctors need fast surrogates—simplified stand-in simulators that run in seconds instead of hours—to do patient studies and answer 'what if' questions about variations in a treatment.

It ties to differentiable simulation (the ability to run a simulator backward to ask 'what patient parameters would have caused these measurements?') and inverse problems because clinical diagnosis often means estimating patient-specific numbers from measured data, not just forward-predicting outcomes.
practical_caution: Each of these five physics pieces can be solved correctly on its own—the math is sound, the computer code runs—but the model will give wrong answers if the handoff between them is wrong. Electrical activation and mechanical contraction must stay locked to each other with the right timing. The fluid pressure in the heart chambers must balance the pulling and pushing of the deformed tissue. Coronary vessel pressure must feed blood into tissue that is squeezing and releasing. The biggest difficulty is not solving one piece; it is making sure the time steps, boundary edges (fixed values at the borders), and feedback loops between all five pieces stay consistent. Miss this coupling, and a patient's prediction based on the model will be dangerously wrong.
selected_evidence: Electrical, mechanical and fluid-dynamical processes occurring in the heart.
A classical multi-physics problem featuring multi-scale solutions in space and time.
They include the electrophysiology, the active mechanics... the passive mechanics... the fluid dynamics.
We need however a second grid... for simulating the fluid dynamical processes.
You have to account for variability and uncertainty.
takeaway: This talk shows what a real first-principles scientific simulator looks like when it is built for a living system: not a single learned guessing program, but multiple interconnected physics solvers that must be tuned together. Any approach—whether hand-built math or machine learning or a hybrid—eventually must respect this coupled reality.
worked_example:
The team reconstructed the geometry of an actual human heart using CT/MRI scans and created a computational mesh with 60 million tetrahedral elements in the myocardium alone. This extremely fine discretization was necessary to accurately simulate electrical propagation. When solving the electrophysiology model, they used time steps of 0.01 milliseconds to capture the fast ionic dynamics. The complete heart model involves 4 different state variables and 16 parameters describing ion channel behavior.

For clinical arrhythmia detection, they simulated a heart with ventricular arrhythmia—an irregular electrical pattern—and the numerical model identified late activation zones and conduction block lines that corresponded to biomarkers surgeons needed to find. The prediction required solving 10 to the power 7 degrees of freedom, which took approximately 6 hours on a modest cluster with standard cores. After identifying these biomarkers, doctors could then perform ablation (burning specific points) to restore normal rhythm.
deeper_mechanics:
The electrical propagation in cardiac tissue is governed by the monodomain equation: a reaction-diffusion PDE where the transmembrane potential u(x,t) evolves under an elliptic component (divergence of conductivity tensor times gradient of u) coupled to a reaction term describing ionic activity. The conductivity tensor is anisotropic—it depends on the local fiber orientation—which means heart muscle conducts electricity much faster along fibers than perpendicular to them.

The mechanical deformation follows Lagrangian elastodynamics: the second time derivative of displacement equals the divergence of the Piola-Kirchhoff stress tensor (which is the derivative of a strain energy function). The constitutive models used were hyperelastic (Guccione and Orthotropic energy functions), capturing both passive and active mechanics. The active force is generated when calcium binds to contractile proteins, and this calcium concentration comes from solving the ionic model. The problem is fully coupled: electrical activation drives mechanical contraction, deformation changes geometry (moving the domain), and the altered geometry feeds back into the electrical propagation.
failure_boundary: The integrated heart model becomes computationally intractable for clinical use without severe simplifications. Even solving the full coupled system for a single heartbeat (about 1 second) takes on the order of 100 hours. Forward simulations are possible but clinical decision-making needs real-time or near-real-time answers. The model also requires extensive patient-specific data (fiber orientation, material properties, initial conditions) that are often unavailable or noisy from imaging. When fiber orientations are estimated from atlas or rule-based methods rather than measured, the electrical predictions become less accurate. Additionally, the model's high dimensional nonlinearity makes sensitivity analysis and uncertainty propagation extremely expensive—addressing any of these requires solving the model many times over.

title: Byungsoo Kim: Data-Driven Methods For Fluid Simulations In Computer Graphics
speaker: Byungsoo Kim
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of just hand-written math. One version of this is building a simulator that guesses the next moment of a fluid like water or smoke. This talk is about a shortcut: instead of doing all the math for every tiny piece of the fluid, you train a learning program (a huge bank of dials the computer tunes by trial and error until its answers look right) on examples of fluids, and let it predict or speed up pieces of the simulation. The goal is not scientific accuracy; it is convincing motion that artists can control and that runs fast enough for a movie or game.
core_problem: Movie and game studios need to simulate fluids like water, smoke, and splashes that both look convincing and run fast enough to finish on time. The old way—solving the physics step by step for every tiny piece—works but is slow. The main question is not 'does every number match the physics equations exactly' but 'does the motion look right, can the artist steer it, and will it finish before the deadline?'
