first_principles_model: A physics simulator takes the laws of motion and pressure (rules for how something changes from moment to moment) and steps the fluid forward in tiny increments. A data-driven shortcut: train a program on many examples of fluids in motion, and let it learn to predict the next moment directly, or learn to speed up parts of the step-by-step math. You can teach a program to work in compressed space—a smaller, squeezed version of the full fluid field that is cheaper to evolve. You can add surface turbulence or splashes that would be too detailed to simulate by hand. You can tune how forces affect the fluid (art direction) by taking gradients through the simulator—poking the numbers in directions that push the result toward what you want—instead of re-running the whole calculation.
key_claims: Physics-based animation has been around for decades, but studios still need fast and controllable ways to simulate fluids on set.
In graphics, losing some accuracy is acceptable if you gain speed, artist control, and visual appeal.
A learning program can speed up the particle solvers (tracking many tiny bits of fluid) and the pressure step (the expensive calculation that keeps fluid incompressible).
You can train a program to work on compressed representations of the fluid field—smaller versions that are cheaper to advance in time—then decode them back to full resolution.
A learning program can add detail—turbulent swirls, water splashes, sharp motion—that would take forever to simulate by hand.
By computing gradients through a simulator, you can tune starting states or force settings to reach a target motion without re-running the full calculation repeatedly.

important_terms.meaning: A simulator that artists can steer by adjusting forces, starting conditions, or parameters, and the result stays physically plausible enough to look real.
Applying artistic choices to how a fluid flows or looks—like changing the turbulence style, thickness, or color—without re-running the core physics.
Training a learning program on pairs of low-resolution and high-resolution fluid simulations so it learns to add sharp detail when given a coarse version.
A simulator that compresses the full fluid field into a smaller squeezed form (like compressing a video), evolves the squeezed form (much cheaper), then expands it back to full size for display.

Taking gradients (directions of change) backward through a simulator so you can tweak starting conditions or forces in ways that push the final motion toward a target without running the whole calculation over.

stanford_connections: This talk reveals that data-driven simulation has different goals depending on the field: graphics optimizes for control and convincing appearance in ways that engineering prediction does not.
It shows a concrete example of differentiable physics—using gradients through a simulator to enable artists to steer the result toward what they want.
It also demonstrates compressed-space approximation and super-resolution as real practical ways to make simulation fast enough for production while keeping visual quality.
practical_caution: A shortcut that works for movies may not work for engineering or safety predictions. A motion that looks visually convincing in a graphics demo may fail badly when you need precise numbers—like predicting how a real flood will behave, or designing a dam. The opposite caution is also true: demanding engineering accuracy for a movie animation wastes time and money.
selected_evidence: For visual effect artists it is necessary to have a physically plausible but computational efficient and also art-directable simulation tool.
It's allowed to sacrifice accuracy to some extent for performance and controllability.
Deep learning methods can provide faster realistic and more controllable simulations.
Latent space fluid solvers with auto encoders and LSTM architectures.
Differentiability... optimize its motion controller or initial parameter settings to achieve a target state.
takeaway: The deep lesson is that your choice of what to measure drives the entire design. A graphics simulator measures 'does this look convincing and do artists have control?' and optimizes for speed and creativity. An engineering simulator measures 'is this prediction accurate?' and optimizes for truth. They are solving different problems, even though they both simulate fluids.
worked_example:
A CNN generative model for parametrized Eulerian fluid simulations achieves 700x speedup on GPU compared to CPU solvers. The network trains on 3750 unique velocity frames across 5 inflow velocities and 3 buoyancy values, then performs interpolation at unseen velocity values (e.g., intermediate buoyancy not in training). With compression ratios exceeding 1000x compared to standard floating-point methods, a coarse smoke simulation on a low-resolution mesh can be upsampled and refined to higher resolutions while maintaining consistency in plume shape and dynamics.

For liquid simulations, the model interpolates across discontinuous boundaries (liquid-air interfaces). Testing across 10-14 sample positions shows that reconstructing splash features improves as resolution increases, even for positions not in training. The follow-up frequency reconstruction work adds high-frequency details by fitting in spectral domain, recovering lost waviness that the initial model reproduced too smoothly.
deeper_mechanics:
The core architecture uses skip connections and leaky ReLU activations to map forced parameters (source position, inflow velocity, buoyancy, time) through a generative CNN to velocity fields. To enforce incompressibility, the loss includes a curl constraint: taking curl of the network output forces it to learn a stream function whose derivatives implicitly reconstruct divergence-free velocities. A Jacobian loss term L_jacobian = ||∂u_pred/∂params - ∂u_truth/∂params||^2 is added to match spatial gradients, critical for stream function fields since derivatives determine the final velocity.

For complex parameterizations where direct mapping becomes intractable, an autoencoder reduces the parameter space to a latent code. A latent-space integrator—a fully connected network—maps sequential latent codes forward in time, enabling temporal prediction by iteratively advancing through latent states. Temporal velocity fields are reconstructed by interpolating latent codes between time steps, creating smooth animations at unseen velocities through learned non-linear interpolation.
failure_boundary:
The model produces overly smooth reconstructions in high-frequency regions; spectral features (fine wrinkles, small-scale turbulence) are lost in the initial baseline approach. This is addressed post-hoc with Fourier-space loss, but the fundamental issue is spectral bias: the network learns low-frequency structure first.

Interpolation quality degrades sharply when test parameters fall far outside the training parameter range. Boundary conditions introduce discontinuities (e.g., liquid-air interfaces) that violate the smooth manifold assumption. For autoencoder-based parameterization with latent-space time integration, complex source motions not seen during training degrade fidelity; the latent integrator's per-timestep prediction compounds errors over long rollouts.

title: Karthik Duraisamy: Towards Robust, Accurate And Tractable Reduced-Order Models
speaker: Karthik Duraisamy
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. One popular shortcut is to replace a huge, slow simulation with a tiny one—think of fitting the whole behavior into fewer dials. This talk shows why that shortcut has three sticky rules: the tiny model must stay accurate when things change, it must match the real physics with low error, and it must still run fast enough for engineers to use.
core_problem: Reduced-order models are tempting: replace a giant system that takes hours to run with a shrunken version that finishes in seconds. But real flows like combustion or detonation pack many hard things at once—equations that change at wildly different speeds, waves bouncing around, heat releasing from chemical burning, solid shapes warping or tearing, and leftover errors (the gaps between the true rules and the approximate model) that jump around violently. A model tuned perfectly for one set of conditions may start acting wild, break the rules that should always hold (mass stays the same, energy does not vanish), or stay just as slow when the conditions or parameters shift.
first_principles_model: A reduced-order model moves the governing equations onto a smaller geometric space—imagine projecting a high-resolution picture onto a lower-resolution grid, but for the physics. For tricky nonlinear systems, having fewer dimensions does not automatically make the leftover error cheap to compute, stable when you step the model forward in time, or conservative (keeping mass and energy intact). Robust models therefore need: variables built to respect the physical laws, a method for fitting residuals (the gap between the true rule and the model) that keeps the model stable as it evolves, a way to shift the model when parameters change, and a trick to evaluate the expensive nonlinear pieces at only a handful of locations instead of everywhere.
key_claims: A reduced-order model solves the same governing equations on a smaller geometric space rather than discarding the equations entirely.
Difficult flows with many types of physics create problems for reduced models through equations at different timescales, layers of structure at different sizes, wave transport, and shape changes.

Standard Galerkin reduced models (one common way to build reduced models by projecting the equations onto a smaller space) can look stable in theory but become unstable when flows are hard or parameters drift far from the training data.

Least-squares Petrov-Galerkin methods improve stability by measuring how badly the approximate equations fail at selected points, rather than just checking that residuals are perpendicular to the reduced space.
Evaluating the expensive nonlinear pieces takes cost; you must do this work at only a small number of sample points instead of everywhere, or the speed gain vanishes.
Running time matters most when the full simulation is so expensive that even collecting training examples becomes the bottleneck.

important_terms.meaning: A shrunken version of a full simulation that solves the same physics rules but on fewer dials, so it runs in seconds instead of hours.

A method for building a reduced model by measuring how badly the approximate equations fail at certain spots, then adjusting the model to lower this failure score rather than enforcing a standard geometric alignment.
A change of variables or a method built so that laws that should always hold—like total mass stays the same or energy does not disappear—continue to hold in the reduced model.
A trick to speed up reduced models by computing expensive nonlinear pieces at only a few hand-picked spots instead of at every grid point.
A reduced model built for one part of a larger system, which can then be connected to other reduced or full-size pieces.

stanford_connections: This talk ties together earlier reduced-model talks into a practical checklist: speed and small size are not enough without stability.
It connects to digital twins—copies of real systems running on computers—by showing that a digital twin that works reliably in the field needs stable reduced pieces, not just fast guesses.
It links to entropy-stable schemes and models you can train with gradients by showing that reduced models must match the structure and conservation laws of the full system.
practical_caution: A model can fail even if you found a good reduced basis if the leftover error does not match the physical laws, the nonlinear terms are not evaluated at just a few spots, or the operating conditions change the flow in ways your training data never showed (say, whether swirling vortices appear). Always test stability, runtime cost, and how well the model handles parameter shifts together, not one at a time.
selected_evidence: The first part is on robustness and accuracy.
The third part of the talk is on tractability.
How to handle things like chaotic flows and big parameter changes.
For many problems stability is a major issue.
Hyper reduction... ensuring that the residual is only evaluated at a few points.
takeaway: The core lesson is that fewer dimensions does not make the problem simpler. Real models must preserve physical laws, adapt when physics changes, and cut the cost of evaluating the expensive nonlinear pieces.
worked_example:
A rocket combustor with 15 million degrees of freedom gets reduced from ~100 million spatial points to 4-60 basis coefficients. The least-squares Petrov-Galerkin ROM with hyper-reduction shows 3-4 orders of magnitude speedup: without oversampling the speedup is ~10x, but with careful QR-pivoting-based sample selection and oversampling, the speed is maintained while keeping reconstruction error low (during training intervals). Temperature predictions in true future-state mode show error jumps visible at timestep 20 and 60 modes, but projecting small perturbations at inlet conditions still demonstrates stability.

On a 1D combustor simplified test: the ROM stays stable across chamber lengths, trained on truncated domain with many forcing frequencies (sinusoids). The full system assembly then handles geometry changes by switching the acoustic region to full-order while keeping the reaction zone as component ROM.
deeper_mechanics: The method uses three-level symmetrized reduction. First, variable transformation (q→s, primitive/conservative forms) via dual-time stepping ensures conservation while allowing flexible variable choices. Second, least-squares Petrov-Galerkin projection: if φ(q) = V·c + q_ref is the ROM ansatz, then minimize residual r(c) = L[V·c + q_ref] over Galerkin test space W, producing Jacobian-symmetrized system (W^T·L_φ·V)·c_dot = -W^T·r. This inherits stability from discrete consistency without requiring symmetric governing equations. Third, hyper-reduction samples the residual at m << n points: introduce basis for residual representation, use QR pivoting to find critical sample points, then carefully oversampling (2-3x the basis count) maintains fidelity while keeping online cost O(n·m·k) for n FOM DOF, m sample points, k ROM modes.
failure_boundary: In chaotic flows (shear layers), the spectrum of POD basis does not decay: with 0.167 ms training data, spectral magnitude stays large; more data doesn't fix it. Static manifolds (linear or nonlinear) cannot handle flow topology changes when inlet conditions change. Hyper-reduction fails if samples miss localized reaction zones: QR pivoting alone can miss sharp gradients in multi-scale problems, requiring manual tuning of oversampling ratios. Forward prediction error jumps sharply beyond training window—even with many modes, long-term drift accelerates when manifold cannot follow system state.

title: Mario Ohlberger: Model Reduction With Adaptive Enrichment For Large Scale PDE-Constrained Optimization
speaker: Mario Ohlberger
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of hand-written rules alone. One way to do that is to build a faster stand-in (a simplified version that runs quickly) for the slow mathematical rules that describe real physics. This talk is about adaptive enrichment: instead of building one giant simplified model upfront (which costs a lot), you start with a small cheap one and grow it as you need it during optimization, so you only pay for accuracy where the algorithm actually looks.
core_problem: When you want a computer to optimize a design (say, the shape of a wing) while obeying physics, you must solve the physics rules (written as equations describing how air flows or heat spreads) many times, each time with different design choices. To make this fast, you can build a simplified stand-in model that runs in seconds instead of hours. But building that simplified model itself costs a lot of expensive full solves upfront (the 'offline' stage), and if you do build it, the simplified model might be wrong in the parts of design-space the optimizer actually visits. For hard problems like battery degradation, uncertainty handling, or multiscale systems, even the initial setup is too expensive to afford.
first_principles_model: A PDE-constrained optimization problem (a math puzzle where you change design or control variables while a physics equation keeps being solved) must solve that physics equation over and over. A simplified stand-in model can speed this up, but the optimizer needs to know when to trust it. Adaptive enrichment works like this: start with a small simplified model. During optimization, watch how wrong it is (using error estimates that you can compute quickly after each solve). When the simplified model's error is small, use it; when error grows large, pay for a full expensive solve and add that solution to your simplified model to make it better for next time. Often you wrap this in a trust-region step: a safety zone where you only use the simplified model if you know its error is controlled.
key_claims: Adaptive enrichment steps beyond the old split where you do all the expensive work upfront and then queries are cheap.
The focus is on large-scale optimization problems governed by physics equations, plus related problems like uncertainty quantification (testing how sensitive answers are to small changes in inputs).
Building a rich simplified model ahead of time can require solving the full physics so many times that it is too expensive to afford.
To know when a simplified model is accurate, you need a quickly-computable error estimate that tells you how far off the simplified solution is.
Trust-region methods (a way to limit optimizer steps to regions where you trust the approximate model) can control whether the simplified model is reliable enough.

For certain types of physics (like shocks that form suddenly, or equations where the width of the essential information decays slowly), a linear simplified model might not work well and needs nonlinear extensions.

important_terms.meaning: A math puzzle where you want to pick the best design or control variables (like wing shape or material thickness), but the variables must satisfy a physical rule written as an equation (a PDE: a rule that says how something changes across space and time, like how heat spreads or air flows).
Growing your simplified model during the optimization by adding new physics solves when the current simplified model is not accurate enough in the region where the optimizer is looking.

A low-dimensional simplified model built by collecting solutions from expensive physics solves and finding the common patterns (like a compressed picture that captures the essential idea without storing every detail).
A quickly-computable score that tells you how wrong your simplified model's solution is after you have already computed it, so you know when to trust it and when to do a full expensive solve instead.

A safety zone in the design space where you believe the simplified model is accurate enough to guide the optimization algorithm's next step, so you only use the simplified model in that zone and do expensive full solves elsewhere.

stanford_connections: This extends the earlier talks about simplified models (reduced-order models) from just prediction to optimization loops, where you must solve the physics equation repeatedly and guarantee the simplified model is reliable.
It connects to inverse problems and control design because optimization means deciding which solves can use the cheap simplified model and which need the expensive full physics.

It also hints at the later talks on nonlinear simplified models: when the physics has sharp changes (shocks) or certain mathematical properties (slow Kolmogorov-width decay), a linear simplified model cannot keep up and needs nonlinear tricks.
practical_caution: Do not build a giant simplified model upfront without asking: do I actually need it? If the optimization algorithm only visits a small corner of the design space, adaptive enrichment saves money by spending expensive full solves only where the algorithm actually goes, not everywhere.
selected_evidence: A new paradigm that goes beyond the classical offline online splitting.
Large scale PDE constraint optimization.
The classical approach has limitations because in the offline stage we usually need to solve very large scale problems.
Reduced basis trust region approach.
You will never beat the Kolmogorov... with a linear method.
takeaway: Reduced-order models (simplified stand-ins for expensive physics solves) in optimization must be managed on the fly: use the cheap model when it is accurate enough, enrich it (make it better by adding more data) when needed, and let error estimates control when to switch.
worked_example:
For lithium-ion battery degradation modeling with a 1.7 million degree-of-freedom finite volume discretization, the full high-dimensional charging sweep took 6.5 hours of computation. Applying reduced basis methods with adaptive enrichment and empirical operator interpolation brought this down to 1.5 seconds maximum simulation time, yielding a relative L2 error of 10^-3 in both ion concentration and electrostatic potential. This represents approximately 280-290× speedup while maintaining fidelity across complex pore-scale electrode geometries.

The offline phase requires solving several parameter-dependent snapshots to construct the reduced basis via POD-Greedy algorithm. For a 2D parameter domain in heat transfer optimization (trust region method with 710 optimization steps), local subdomain enrichment required solving only 709 local sub-problems across the domain without ever solving the full global high-dimensional model—averaging about 11 local problems per subdomain per optimization step.
deeper_mechanics:
The method combines three ingredients: (1) reduced basis projection—expressing high-dimensional solutions u_h in a low N-dimensional space spanned by basis functions φ_i, so u(μ) ≈ Σ c_i(μ)φ_i; (2) offline-online decomposition exploiting affine parameter dependence to precompute reduced operators A_h^red = V^T A(μ) V where V contains basis functions; and (3) empirical operator interpolation (DEIM) for non-linearities, replacing expensive nonlinear operators with interpolated surrogates A_μ^DEIM = ΣV_r a_r(μ) with discrete basis V_r.

The trust region approach for optimization minimizes a corrected reduced functional that accounts for non-conformity between primal and dual reduced spaces. The key correction is to the Lagrangian: J_corr = J_red + (ψ_red, r_primal)_L2, where r_primal is the residual of the primal state equation tested against the dual solution from a different space. Error estimates for the functional and gradient exhibit quadratic convergence in primal-dual residuals, guaranteeing certified model quality within adaptively growing trust regions.
failure_boundary:
Classical offline-online reduced basis methods fail in large-scale optimization because the offline phase requires solving many high-dimensional problems to populate the basis, which becomes prohibitive for expensive simulations (e.g., 6.5 hours per solve). The greedy POD algorithm assumes fast decay of Kolmogorov width—failure occurs with hyperbolic problems exhibiting shocks or slow polynomial decay, where even N=100 basis functions cannot capture the solution manifold's richness.

Adaptive enrichment can stagnate if the trust region radius shrinks too aggressively or if the error estimator overestimates, causing the optimization solver to stop early without reaching sufficient accuracy. For multiscale or strongly nonlinear problems where the kernel structure is unknown, DEIM hyper-reduction introduces an additional approximation layer that can accumulate error if the number of interpolation points is chosen too small, leading to observable loss of accuracy in gradient information.

title: Tommaso Taddei: Registration-Based Model Reduction Of Parameterized Advection-Dominated PDEs
speaker: Tommaso Taddei
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples. When material flows and carries features (like heat, moisture, or a shock wave) from place to place, simply learning the solution directly becomes expensive. This talk shows a trick: first nudge the coordinate system so the moving features line up at the same spot, then learn a fast model in this new coordinate system where features stay still.
core_problem: Some physical problems involve material flowing and carrying features from one place to another—think of a heat pulse traveling down a rod, or a shock wave moving through air. As you change the problem's settings (like initial temperature or flow speed), these moving features slide to new positions. When you try to build a fast model (using a small number of basis vectors—the building blocks the computer uses to glue together its approximation), a fixed set of basis vectors cannot describe where the feature will be at each setting. This means you need enormous numbers of basis vectors, which defeats the speed gain you want, or you lose the sharp features altogether.
first_principles_model: Registration solves this by finding a coordinate transformation that shifts and stretches the space so that moving features appear in the same location no matter what settings you chose. Imagine drawing a grid on paper and scribbling where a shock wave is; registration warps the grid to slide the shock back to the same spot on each drawing. Once this coordinate shift is done, the solution snapshots (the states at different settings, now in the transformed space) become much easier to compress. A reduced model can then do three things together: apply the registration transformation, express solutions as linear combinations of a small set of basis vectors, and use hyper-reduction (computing the answer at only a few important points instead of everywhere) to save time.
key_claims: When material flows and carries features, moving features at different settings cannot fit neatly into a single fixed low-dimensional space, so standard basis-vector reduction becomes slow or inaccurate.
Registration works by finding a coordinate transformation that nudges features to the same location across all the different settings, making the solution set much more compressible.
The method is general enough to work across different transport equations, focusing on geometric alignment before applying dimension reduction.
Registration can be stacked with basis-vector reduction and multifidelity approaches, which mix fast rough models with slower accurate models to gain both speed and correctness.
The method includes hyper-reduction steps where you pick the most important points to compute and skip the rest, speeding up the approximation even more.
The transcript is corrupted enough that the abstract is the most reliable source for what the talk claims.

important_terms.meaning: A procedure that finds coordinate transformations (like a grid warp) to slide and stretch the solution features so they sit in the same position across all different settings.
A shared, fixed coordinate system where moving features have been aligned and now sit still, making them easy to describe with a small set of basis vectors.
A rule that predicts how fast something changes from moment to moment, in a situation where flowing and carrying of material (like a pulse or a wave) is the main action happening.
How well you can take many solution snapshots and describe them all using a small fixed list of building-block solutions, added together in different amounts.
A method that combines a slow, accurate simulator with a fast rough approximation, letting you learn from both to gain speed without throwing away correctness.

stanford_connections: This is the geometric counterpart to talks on nonlinear manifold reduction: instead of learning a new shape in space (a manifold) to describe solutions, you warp the coordinate grid first to make solutions fit a simpler shape.
It directly addresses the problem of moving shocks and transport: these appear to need many dimensions because the feature location varies, but registration collapses this by alignment.

It shows a recurring pattern in scientific machine learning: sometimes the single best improvement comes from a preprocessing step that respects what the physics actually does, before you try any learning.
practical_caution: The speech-to-text transcript for this talk contains many errors and missed words. The deep dive below is a first-pass reading that leans heavily on the talk's abstract, treating the transcript as rough until a corrected version or written notes are available.
selected_evidence: Parameterized advection-dominated problems.
Parameter-dependent discontinuities that cannot be adequately represented through linear approximation spaces.
Registration procedure to align local features in a fixed reference domain.
Improve the linear compressibility of the solution manifold.
Registration based projection based multi fidelity model.
takeaway: Transport problems where material flows and carries features are only reducible to a fast small model after the features are aligned in a shared location first. Registration reduces the motion itself before reducing the number of dimensions your model needs.
worked_example:
Illustrative (the transcript is a heavily garbled auto-transcription, so no clean spoken numbers survive; the structure below follows the method the talk describes). Take a parametric shallow-water / advection problem where a shock sits at position s(mu) that slides across the domain as the parameter mu (an inflow angle or free-stream setting) changes. If you build a plain reduced basis from snapshots at, say, 7 parameter values, the shock sits at 7 different places, so a linear combination of those snapshots smears into a staircase rather than a sharp front, and you need dozens of modes to resolve one moving discontinuity.

The registration idea instead learns a mapping Phi(x; mu) that warps each snapshot's domain so the shock always lands at the same reference location before you compress. Concretely: pick a reference configuration, solve a small optimization per snapshot that finds the warp aligning that snapshot's front to the reference, then do POD on the aligned (registered) snapshots. Now one or two modes carry the front shape, and mu only has to drive the cheap warp plus a few coefficients.

The talk pairs this with a multi-fidelity training trick: generate many cheap low-fidelity snapshots to learn the registration map (which is the expensive offline part), then use a small number of high-fidelity snapshots only where accuracy matters. The claim shown is that with on the order of a handful of high-fidelity runs (the speaker mentions building the map from roughly seven simulations) you recover the parametric front behavior that a linear ROM misses entirely.
deeper_mechanics:
The registered approximation is u(x; mu) approx sum_i a_i(mu) * phi_i( Phi(x; mu) ), where phi_i are POD modes computed in a reference frame and Phi is a parametric diffeomorphism of the domain. Phi is found by minimizing a proximity objective ||registered_snapshot - template||^2 plus a regularization that penalizes distortion of the map, subject to a hard constraint that the Jacobian determinant of Phi stays positive (det(grad Phi) > 0) so the warp never folds the mesh. That bijectivity constraint is what keeps the transformed problem well posed.

Because a linear trial space cannot represent a translating discontinuity with few modes (the Kolmogorov n-width decays slowly for advection-dominated PDEs), registration moves the nonlinearity into the geometry: the solution manifold becomes low-dimensional after you factor out the transport. The reduced model is then a Petrov-Galerkin or least-squares projection of the governing operator N[u; mu] onto span{phi_i} composed with Phi, and the front is handled by a shock-aware discretization (an ENO-type stencil giving second-order accuracy so gradients stay bounded / total-variation-bounded) rather than by adding modes.

The map itself is parameterized (spectral-element / polynomial building blocks over a partition of the reference domain), and a regression / interpolation learns Phi as a function of mu offline. Space-time registration is used when a single spatial warp cannot align multiple interacting shocks: you register in the coupled space-time domain so an incoming wave and its interactions line up, at the cost of a larger offline computation.
failure_boundary:
Registration stays trustworthy while one continuous warp can align the features. It degrades when shocks collide or multiply (multiple discontinuities appearing, merging, or changing topology as mu varies) because no single diffeomorphism can simultaneously straighten fronts that cross each other; the speaker flags multi-shock interaction and changing wave topology as the open hard case. It also breaks if the Jacobian-positivity constraint is pushed to the edge: near-folding maps make the optimization non-convex and can converge to distorted or non-unique solutions, and the box constraints that keep the warp sane can bind and stall the alignment.

Practically, the offline registration optimization is the fragile part: it needs a good initial guess (the talk warms it up from a nearby parameter and marches), and for parameters far from the training set the learned map extrapolates poorly, so the front lands slightly wrong and the reduced solution shows spurious oscillations or an offset shock. Boundary regions are also weaker, since enforcing the warp near non-periodic boundaries can inject small false gradients.

title: Francisco Chinesta: Empowering Hybrid Twins From Physics-Informed Artificial Intelligence
speaker: Francisco Chinesta
organization: ENSAM Institute of Technology / ESI Group
one_sentence: This series is about teaching computers to predict how things behave in the physical world by learning from examples instead of using only hand-built math. One approach is to start with the math that engineers already know (the physics model), then add a learning program that figures out what the physics model misses — the real-world messy bits that the simple math cannot capture — so the computer gets closer to what actually happens.
core_problem: Physics models are approximations. They describe the big rules — how heat flows, how stress builds in material, how a machine wears — but real systems behave differently because of things the model did not account for: uneven loading over time, hidden material changes, or effects too detailed to write down. Engineers need digital twins that combine the known physics with a separate piece that learns the gap between what the math predicts and what the actual machine does. A pure physics model leaves the gap uncorrected. A pure data-learning program can be unreliable and may not respect the physical rules that the system must follow.
first_principles_model: The core idea is a simple picture: what actually happens equals the known physics plus the unseen gap. A hybrid twin keeps two parts working together. Part one is the original physics model — the trusted equations engineers built over years. Part two is a learning program trained on measurements to predict just the difference: prediction from physics minus what we actually measured. When you add these two parts together, the twin matches reality better. Now the twin can do two jobs: diagnosis (figuring out what is wrong or different right now by comparing physics + learned gap to the real measurement) and prognosis (predicting what will happen next by running both models forward).
key_claims: Industry is shifting from selling a product once to guaranteeing how it performs during actual real-world use.
A physics model always misses something, so treating the mismatch between prediction and measurement as a real phenomenon to model directly makes sense.
The best digital twins combine trusted physics equations with a learned model that predicts the gap.
When a learning program predicts the gap, it should still obey physical laws, including the rules about energy and mass that govern the system.
Once the twin matches reality, it can help you figure out what is wrong now (diagnosis) and what will happen next (prognosis).
Model reduction, curve fitting, and data learning are related techniques for building accurate approximations when you combine physics and data this way.

important_terms.meaning: A digital copy of a real machine or system that combines two prediction engines running side by side: a model built from known physics equations, and a separate program trained on data that learns to correct or fill in what the physics misses.
The difference between what the physics equations predict and what happens in the real system, measured by comparing predictions to actual sensor data.
Using measurements from right now to figure out what the current state of the system is, or to spot something unusual or broken.
Using the twin to predict what the system will do in the future, or to estimate when it might fail.
A rule that any learned model must follow: it cannot violate the basic laws about energy, heat, and mass that must hold true in any real system.

stanford_connections: This is the clearest direction in DDPS for hybrid physics-and-learning systems: learn only the missing piece instead of trying to learn everything from raw data alone.
It connects to fast reduced-order models because these lean physics models often become the core backbone of a real-time twin that needs to run quickly.
It also connects to uncertainty and control because diagnosis and prognosis require the twin to stay correct as the real system changes and new measurements arrive.
practical_caution: A digital twin is not just a screen showing numbers or a single learning program trained on old data. If the twin does not split physics from learned corrections, you cannot tell when the model is guessing far beyond the range of examples it saw. That breaks trust. You need to know when the learned part is being asked to predict something it has never seen before.
selected_evidence: Reality... is equal to the things that you know... plus the things that you ignore.
The physics-based model... can be enriched with a data-driven model of the gap between predictions and measurements.
When you put both together... you obtain the physical reality.
Digital twin of the deviation.
Data serves in order to make diagnosis... and... prognosis.
takeaway: The central idea is this: hybrid twins are gap models wrapped around physics. Keep the physics you know. Learn what you do not. Train the twin on real measurements so it can correct itself and match the real system.
worked_example:
A composite material crash simulation with 5+ million finite elements and 20 parameters (thickness, material properties, design geometry) normally requires days or weeks per run. Using proper generalized decomposition (PGD) with sparse sampling, the method generates a parametric solution with approximately 20 simulation runs—one per parameter. A Hyundai car crash example demonstrates real-time parameter exploration: sliders control structural thicknesses and show impact on peak stress and energy absorption instantly. A resin infusion (RTM) process exhibits filling time that scales inversely with permeability; inverse analysis identifies the actual permeability from observations in seconds by interrogating the parametric solution, matching experimental flow front position to within measurement uncertainty.

For a tensile test with stochastic material parameters (k, ε₀, n following distributions), the method computes not just one traction curve but a 95% confidence corridor—the range within which results fall with 95% probability. The fracture point probability corridor is obtained by adding variance to parameter distributions while keeping the base parametric model fixed.
deeper_mechanics:
The hybrid paradigm decomposes reality as: Real system = Physics-based model + Deviation (ignorance). Model order reduction via PGD treats parameters as extra coordinates; a solution u(x,t,μ₁,...,μₘ) is approximated by separable form: Σᵢ Xᵢ(x)·Tᵢ(t)·Pᵢ₁(μ₁)·...·Pᵢₘ(μₘ). This tensor decomposition avoids the curse of dimensionality by solving low-dimensional univariate problems. Sparse regularization (elastic net or Lasso) selects which basis functions contribute, avoiding overfitting in low-data regimes where sampling ≈ number of parameters.

When model predictions diverge from measurements, the deviation is learned as a separate data-driven model (neural network, polynomial regression, or kernel method) preserving physics: new models are trained to satisfy conservation laws (energy), entropy production, and symmetries via Hamiltonian + dissipation structure. The final prediction combines high-fidelity fast physics with corrective deviation model: prediction = parametric PDE solution + learned_gap_model.
failure_boundary: The method assumes the high-fidelity model captures the dominant physics correctly and deviations are small perturbations. If the model is fundamentally wrong (missing coupling, incorrect PDE form), no regression can fix it—deviation learning only works for unmodeled-but-small effects. Sparse sampling (≈ p samples for p parameters) relies on the assumption that a rich basis exists and sparsity will select the right terms; if the true solution has dense dependence on all parameters, underfitting occurs. Parametric solutions are only accurate within the sample range; extrapolation beyond observed parameter values is unreliable. For highly nonlinear or bifurcating systems (where small parameter changes cause large qualitative shifts), interpolation on manifolds can fail if the dimension of the manifold is underestimated or if transitions are sharp rather than smooth.

title: Priya Donti: Incorporating Power System Physics Into Deep Learning Via Implicit Layers
speaker: Priya Donti
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from data instead of only hand-written math. One approach is to add physics rules directly into a learning program's structure. This talk shows how to build a learning program with special layers that solve real-world power-grid decision problems step-by-step as the program runs, so the program's predictions automatically obey what a real power system must do.
core_problem: Learning programs can predict numbers with high accuracy, but those numbers often break rules that power grids must follow. A real electricity grid has hard requirements: supply must equal demand, power lines can only carry so much current, equipment must stay stable, and physical limits cannot be crossed. A prediction is only useful if it solves the actual optimization problem that grid operators run to make decisions.
first_principles_model: Usually a layer in a learning program is a direct calculation: multiply inputs by numbers, add them up, apply a squashing function. But a layer can also be defined differently: as the answer to a hidden problem—an optimization task (pick the best choice given constraints), a rule for how things change over time (how voltage adjusts when power flows), a balance point (a state where forces stop shifting), or a control rule (what action should the system take). If that hidden problem can be solved in a differentiable way (meaning we can compute how to nudge the program's dials based on the solution), the entire program learns end-to-end while preserving the real domain structure.
key_claims: Special network layers can encode complex operations like optimization problems, rules for how things change, and other structured tasks.
Power-grid physics and hard requirements can be built into learning programs rather than checked only after predictions are made.

The main power-grid optimization problem (choosing generation and power flow with all limits enforced) can be embedded inside a network by working through a sequence of optimization steps or by differentiating through its optimality conditions.
Programs trained to optimize actual system outcomes perform better on what operators care about, not just raw prediction error.
Special layers give the program prior knowledge by reflecting how the domain actually works.
They also enforce rules that cannot be broken and support stable control in real physical systems.

important_terms.meaning: A part of a learning program that is defined by solving an equation, optimization problem, or system of rules rather than by doing a direct calculation.
An optimization problem that decides how much power each generator produces and how it moves through lines while respecting all physical limits and network rules.
Mathematical rules that describe when a constrained optimization has found its best solution, and how to compute the impact of small changes to that solution.
Training a prediction program by measuring how good the choices that result from the predictions are, not just the distance between the prediction and the actual number.
A requirement that must be true exactly, enforced by the rules themselves, not just encouraged by adding extra penalty points to the score.

stanford_connections: This talk extends physics-informed learning beyond penalty scores that measure how badly rules are broken to optimization layers and requirements that must be met during actual operation.
It connects to inverse problems and control because the program learns by measuring success in the decision or control problem it serves, not by prediction accuracy alone.
It also complements differentiable simulation: both treat a structured physical computation as a step inside the learning process.
practical_caution: Low prediction error alone is not enough for grids. The learned program must be tested by checking whether it produces decisions that are feasible (physically possible), stable (safe to operate without damage or failure), and useful under the actual rules and constraints of the power system.
selected_evidence: Incorporate physics and hard constraints from the electric power system into deep learning methods using... implicit layers.
Layers that encode... optimization problems.
Incorporate ACOPF into a neural network.
Differentiate through it... KKT conditions.
Implicit layers can be a really powerful tool for physical applications like energy systems.
takeaway: The core lesson is that a learning program for real infrastructure should include the operational decision—what the system is required to do—baked into its structure, not just predict numbers that come before the actual problem.
worked_example: AC optimal power flow on 14-bus system, 200 hourly demand snapshots. Naive RMSE-optimized forecaster (2 unit error) yields 40% higher generator scheduling cost than decision-driven model. Decision-driven pipeline: predict demand y_hat → solve ACOPF via sequential quadratic programming (relaxed linearization, ~3-5 iterations) → extract z*(schedule) → compute actual cost against true y → backprop through KKT conditions. Result: cost reduction ~40% despite lower RMSE.
deeper_mechanics: AC optimal power flow: min c^T p subject to linearized power balance (nonconvex in full form). Sequential QP solves relaxed convex QP at each iteration with optimality KKT: ∇L(z*,λ*)=0, Aw=b, μ_i s_i=0. Implicit differentiation through fixed point (z*,λ*): d(z*,λ*)/dθ obtained by solving [∇^2 L | A^T] [dz* dλ*]^T = [b_θ]. Embedded as neural layer: forward pass runs SQP, backward solves linear system with KKT Jacobian. Non-convex problem relaxed via linearization around current iterate.
failure_boundary: Discrete decisions (unit commitment: on/off generators) not differentiable; requires combinatorial relaxation or heuristics. Ramping constraints (max ramp-rate ΔP_max per hour) couple time steps; errors at hour 1 propagate → by hour 8-10, constraints become infeasible, cost blows up (observed threshold effect). Scalability beyond ~5000 buses: KKT system Jacobian becomes dense, backward pass inversion grows O(n³). Non-convex relaxation loses global optimality guarantees; local optima differ from true minimum.

title: Traian Iliescu: Large Eddy Simulation Reduced Order Models
speaker: Traian Iliescu
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. This talk focuses on a specific challenge: when you build a simplified model (a reduced-order model) that captures only the largest motion patterns in turbulent flow, the small-scale motion you threw away still affects what happens—so you need to add a model of those missing effects to get correct predictions.
core_problem: Turbulent flows—think of water or air swirling at many different scales—have large patterns mixed with tiny wiggling patterns, and they all influence each other. A simplified model that represents only the large patterns cannot capture what the small patterns do. The small-scale motion that was skipped over still feeds back and changes how the large scales move, making predictions unstable or wrong. A basic shrinking-down of the equations does not automatically account for this missing influence.
first_principles_model: Large eddy simulation starts with a mathematical filter that divides motion into two groups: large-scale patterns you will track, and small-scale patterns you will skip. You then add an extra term that estimates how the skipped small patterns affect the tracked large ones. To apply this same idea to a simplified model (a reduced-order model), you use filters to decide which motion patterns the model represents, evolve only those patterns forward in time, and add models for how the untracked patterns influence the full motion.
key_claims: Simplified modeling for turbulence remains an open problem with no single method everyone agrees on.
One common approach expresses the solution as a sum of basis patterns (computed from data) and projects the governing rules onto those patterns.
When you mathematically filter nonlinear rules, the small scales you filtered out create an extra term that must be guessed or modeled.
Models for the missing effects can add a dissipation-like term to the equations or alter the equations themselves.
Practical tricks like pressure stabilization may not have clean theoretical backing but are needed to make real simulations work.
Scaling rules for models of missing effects often depend on the specific problem rather than working across all flow speeds and geometries.

important_terms.meaning: A method that directly solves for large flow patterns and adds a model to account for how the small-scale motion it does not track affects the large-scale patterns.
A mathematical dividing line in a simplified model that specifies which sizes and speeds of flow motion the model can represent.
The difficulty of figuring out how the small-scale motion you cannot represent in your model affects the large-scale motion you can represent.
A model that adds a damping or friction-like term to represent how small-scale turbulent swirling motion stirs and smooths out the large-scale flow.

A method that combines the mathematics of handling multiple scales of motion with patterns learned from actual or simulated flow data to estimate the effects of small scales the model does not represent.

stanford_connections: This connects to entropy-stable fluid schemes, interpretable machine learning for fluids, and simplified models of flow around the shared challenge of accounting for motion scales you cannot directly resolve.

It is a central warning for neural surrogates (learning programs trained to mimic fluid behavior): the small scales you do not track still have real effects on the large scales, even if the model ignores them.
It also explains why testing a neural flow surrogate over long prediction spans matters—the effects of the missing small scales pile up over time.
practical_caution: Do not assume one set of tuned numbers or a simple scaling rule will work when the flow speed, the shape you are simulating, or the flow conditions change. Simplified models of turbulent flow must be adjusted and tested separately for each type of flow you care about. The numbers that work for one situation often do not transfer to another.
selected_evidence: Reduced modeling is not... for turbulence... a settled field.
When you filter nonlinear equations you're gonna get the closure term.
The non-linear term... you have to model.
Functional means physical eddy viscosity type of thing and structural... mathematical.
Our models should not be expected to be valid over a range of Reynolds numbers.
takeaway: Turbulence simplified models are inherently filtered models. When you ignore the small scales, the simplified version is not just smaller; it is actually missing real physics that affects what happens. You cannot just shrink and hope—you have to actively model what the removed scales would do.
worked_example: Large eddy simulation of a red sea overflow (geophysical flow) requires resolving 10 km length, 1 km height/width domain; naive calculation shows 10^18 degrees of freedom needed for all scales. Using 6 reduced basis modes (POD), a coarse mesh element method discretizes the filtered Navier-Stokes, and a Magorinsky eddy-viscosity closure adds turbulent stress. Compared to fine-mesh spectral element solution (polynomial degree 16-17 per element), the LES-ROM simulation achieves 10-100x speedup while capturing mixing with factors of 2-3 higher than fine mesh. For 3D flow past a cylinder at Re=1000, using 6 modes with dynamic Smagorinsky model shows energy spectrum matching reference solution, with error of ~0.1 relative L2 across entire prediction horizon.
deeper_mechanics: LES filters Navier-Stokes equations with operator ∂u/∂t + ∇·(u⊗u) = -∇p + ν∇²u + ∇·τ_SGS where τ_SGS = -2νₜ(S - 1/3 S δ_ij) is the subgrid stress modeled via eddy viscosity νₜ. ROM projects onto POD modes V via Galerkin: ȧ = M a + B(a⊗a) + closure term. The data-driven approach uses two-scale decomposition: y₁ (large modes, ~4 modes) and y₂ (small modes, discarded), then learns correction ã_tilde and b̃_tilde via least-squares on true closure ≡ A_true a + B_true (a⊗a) - (M a + B a⊗a). Physical constraints enforce: matrix A is dissipative (diffusion), nonlinear term B is conservative (Skew-symmetric for incompressible flow).
failure_boundary: Under-resolved channel flow (Re_τ=395, Re_bulk~5600) with 10 modes fails: Galerkin ROM alone shows 40% error in mean velocity profile and completely wrong Reynolds stress tensor components. Pure data-driven closure (least-squares fit only) performs poorly; only hybrid approach (eddy-viscosity component + data-driven correction with physical constraints) recovers statistics. At very high Reynolds numbers without enough basis modes, spectral bias occurs: ROM eigenvalue decay plateaus rather than decays, indicating inadequate basis. Closure models are problem-dependent; no universal model works across vastly different Reynolds numbers (cylinder flow vs turbulent channel).

title: George Karniadakis: Approximating Functions, Functionals, And Operators Using Deep Neural Networks
speaker: George Karniadakis
one_sentence: This whole series is about teaching computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. This talk jumps to a harder problem: a learning program (a huge bank of dials the computer tunes by trial and error) can learn single guesses, but real physics often needs to learn an entire solution map—a rule that takes a function (like an initial temperature across a bar) and spits out another function (like the temperature everywhere later). This talk shows how to teach neural networks to do that using DeepONet, which uses two smaller learning programs working together—one that digests the input function, one that knows the output location—to build the full solution map.
core_problem: Many real physics problems do not have one fixed rule that takes a handful of numbers and gives an answer. Instead, there are huge families of related problems where the input itself is a function—an initial shape, a forcing pattern, a property changing from place to place, or a record of measurements from sensors. Simulation means learning a solution operator, a rule that takes one function as input and produces another as output. A learning program needs to handle this: the same governing equations with different starting states, different boundaries, different geometries. Standard neural networks were built to turn numbers into numbers. Here we need to turn functions into functions.
first_principles_model: Start with three kinds of maps. A function takes one point and gives one value—the temperature at a spot, the cost of a stock. A functional takes a whole function and gives one number back—the total energy stored in the system, the cost summed across time. An operator takes a whole function and gives another whole function—the PDE solver that takes initial temperature and gives future temperature everywhere. DeepONet builds an operator by using two learning programs working together. The branch network takes the input function (often represented as measurements at a few specific points) and squeezes it down to a short list of numbers that capture its essence. The trunk network takes the location where you want an answer and also produces a short list of numbers. Multiply the two lists together, add them up, and you get the predicted value at that location. Repeat for every location and you have the full output function. When data are scarce or noisy, add the physics rules themselves as loss terms—penalize the learning program if its answers break the governing equations.
key_claims: Real scientific learning often relies on physics rules or priors when data are limited or noisy, not just raw examples.
PINNs work especially well for inverse problems because measurements help steer the trial-and-error tuning toward the right answer.
Operator learning is broader than a single guess; it learns the entire mapping from input function spaces to output function spaces.
DeepONet learns operators by combining a branch network (which ingests the input function through measurements) and a trunk network (which encodes the output location) to predict values everywhere.
How you represent the input function—which points you measure, which basis functions you choose—shapes whether the learned rule will work on new data.
Neural operators can power digital twin models, where a learned fast rule replaces or speeds up slow simulation for large systems.

important_terms.meaning: A rule that takes a whole function as input and produces a single number as output—for example, a rule that sums up temperature across an entire bar, or totals energy over all time.

A rule that takes one function as input and produces a different function as output—the most common example is a PDE solver, which takes initial conditions and produces the solution at all future times and places.

A learning program designed to learn operators by splitting the job: one smaller program (branch) digests the input function (often as measurements at specific points), another (trunk) knows the output location, and together they predict the value there.
The choice of a few measurement points to stand in for an entire function—how the learning program is told what the input function looks like during training and when making predictions.
Adding the governing equations themselves into the loss signal—penalizing the learning program if its answers violate the physics rules—so it learns to respect them even when data are scarce.

stanford_connections: This talk is the main anchor for operator learning in the early seminar sequence and extends the PINN talks from solving a single PDE to learning the entire solution operator that solves a whole family of PDEs.
It connects to graph simulation and ROM-net because all three ask how to represent physical states compactly and build fast maps between them.
It links to hybrid twins because a learned operator can serve as the fast learned component inside a larger twin that mixes learning and classical simulation.
practical_caution: Operator learning still depends on which input functions the learning program saw during training and how those functions were represented. A DeepONet trained only on small initial temperatures may fail badly on large ones. A network trained with measurements at ten sensor points may not transfer to a different sensor layout. A learned rule for one geometry may not work on a shifted geometry. Always test on input functions that look different from training.
selected_evidence: Approximating functions functionals and operators using deep neural networks.
Unlike other approaches that rely on big data, here we learn from small data.
A branch associated with this... and then there's a trunk.
We map from an infinite dimensional space to an infinite... space.
How you represent the input space is important.
takeaway: The lesson is that real science and engineering often need to learn maps between spaces of functions, not just guess single numbers. Building neural operators—programs that take functions to functions—is how we extend learning to the full complexity of physics.
worked_example: DeepONet learns integral operators from data: 10,000 functions sampled from Gauss random field, 100 sensors per function input representation. MSE converges to 10^-5 (excellent accuracy) with exponential convergence on interior; drops to 1/√n algebraic convergence after network width saturation. Bubble dynamics (Rayleigh equation): maps pressure difference Δp to radius r(t) evolution, handles oscillation and viscous decay across three regimes (continuum, stochastic, optimistic) seamlessly. Hypersonic flow chemistry (Mach 8-10): beats CFD solver 100,000x using only 100 trajectories for training; predicts species evolution and velocity avoiding stiff chemistry solver.
deeper_mechanics: Operator approximation via branch-trunk network: branch net φ(u) encodes infinite-dimensional input u evaluated at m sensor locations; trunk net ψ(y) maps output query location y; output G[u](y) = Σ_k φ_k(u)·ψ_k(y) (inner product in latent space). Extends single-layer universal operator theorem (Chen-Chen) to deep networks composed with nonlinearity g: G ≈ σ(ψ)·σ(φ) alternating. Key: many sensors per function (typically 100+) are needed; input space representation (GRF, orthogonal polynomials) critically affects convergence speed (2 orders magnitude difference with fractional polynomial basis).
failure_boundary: Curse of dimensionality: beyond ~20 input parameters, data requirements explode unless problem has low effective dimension (sensitivity-based dimensionality reduction needed). Non-compact input spaces (e.g., Gaussian random fields) require careful sampling strategy; uniform random sampling breaks down without active learning. Model fails catastrophically on discontinuous operators (multi-scale bubble nucleation regime switch); requires separate training on each physics regime or hybrid multi-fidelity approach. Cannot extrapolate beyond training distribution: shown on Mach 13 case only succeeds via fine-tuning with 5 new data points, not from Mach 8-10 training alone.

title: Alvaro Sanchez-Gonzalez And Tobias Pfaff: Learning Physical Simulation With Graph Networks
speaker: Alvaro Sanchez-Gonzalez and Tobias Pfaff
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples. One way is to represent a physical system as a network of points and connections—particles or mesh corners linked by their neighbors—and train a program to pass information along those links to predict what happens next, then run that prediction many steps ahead.
core_problem: Learning programs that predict what physics does can be fast, but they often fail when you try them on systems larger or shaped differently than what they saw during training. Physical simulations come in many forms: loose particles, triangular meshes, brick-shaped meshes, cloth that bends. An architecture that can handle all of these, including systems the program has never seen before, is rare and hard to build.
first_principles_model: You can describe a physical system as a network: each point (particle or mesh corner) is a node, lines between neighbors are edges, and numbers attached to each node and edge hold the actual physics (position, velocity, force). A message-passing program reads those edges and nodes, updates each edge based on what its two endpoints say to each other, and updates each node based on messages from all its connected edges. After enough rounds of this talking-to-neighbors, you decode the numbers back into the next step of the simulation. Run this prediction step over and over to see how the system evolves.
key_claims: A single architecture can learn to simulate particles, triangular meshes, solid meshes, and deformable cloth—just by changing which nodes and edges the network uses.
You train it to predict one step ahead, then roll that prediction forward many times to see the full trajectory.
Passing messages between connected nodes mirrors how physics itself works: each piece only directly affects its immediate neighbors.
The calculation gives the same answer no matter how you order or relabel the nodes and edges—the only thing that matters is who is connected to whom.
Because it learns relative positions and local interactions, it can extrapolate to bigger domains and different object placements than it saw during training.
A network-based representation generalizes better than treating space as a fixed grid (like photographs) when the system has an irregular or changing shape.

important_terms.meaning: A program that operates on points (called nodes), the connections between them (called edges), and optionally properties of the whole network. It updates these pieces by having each point talk to its neighbors.

A way of computing where each connection between two points learns something from both endpoints, and each point learns something from all its connections. Information flows back and forth across the network.

A three-step pipeline: first, turn a physical state (positions, speeds, forces) into a network. Second, run many rounds of neighbor-to-neighbor message passing to update that network. Third, turn the updated network back into the next physical state.
Taking a one-step prediction program and running it many times in a row to see how a system evolves over many steps—like a long simulation starting from an example the program has never seen.
The property that the prediction stays the same if you relabel or reorder the points and connections. What matters is who is connected to whom, not arbitrary names or numbering.

stanford_connections: This talk introduces a way to represent physics using network structure as an alternative to grids or mathematical bases—the network directly tracks which parts of the system touch each other.
It connects to work on operator learning because both learn reusable maps between physical states, but graph networks focus on the local connection structure that the physics already has built in.
It also connects to concerns about long-term stability raised in talks on fluids and turbulence: errors from one-step predictions pile up over many steps, so the program must handle that compounding.
practical_caution: When you test a graph simulator, look at how well it stays stable when you run many prediction steps in a row—not just whether its first prediction is close. Also test it on systems with different shapes and sizes than it trained on. Passing messages between neighbors helps the program generalize, but it does not by itself ensure that the physics rules are respected (like that energy doesn't vanish) or that the simulation stays stable as you run it forward in time.
selected_evidence: We learn a next step prediction model.
The model is an encode process decode graph network.
They are learned using the same model with the same architecture.
Graph networks were based on something called message passing.
This property allows the model... to be used on systems that are much larger.
takeaway: Physical systems are built on local interactions: particles push only their nearby neighbors, heat spreads only to touching surfaces, forces act between connected mesh corners. Graph networks exploit this by learning to calculate these local, pairwise interactions using the same network structure that the physics already uses.
worked_example: A cylindrical wake flow around a cylinder with 513 snapshots spanning 0–2 seconds is learned via graph neural networks. The full finite element model requires 1100 large linear solves on a 160k-unknown grid; the reduced model needs only 180 solves to build a 360-dimensional basis, yielding 4x cost reduction. Pressure field reconstruction shows less than 1 percent error in the domain interior, with graceful degradation outside training bounds. For a 2D water particle system trained on 128×128 pixels, generalizing to a much larger scene with continuous inflow generates vortex dynamics never seen during training—demonstrating mesh-independent, scene-agnostic learning.
deeper_mechanics: Graph neural networks encode a physical system as nodes (particles/mesh vertices), edges (interactions), and global features (parameters). Message passing updates each edge by concatenating source/target node features and applying a shared MLP to compute forces/interactions. Node aggregation sums incoming messages (superposition principle) and updates each node using another MLP. Encoder maps raw state to graph, processor runs message-passing layers, decoder extracts accelerations or field updates. Inductive bias from encoding relative distances in edges grants translational equivariance; local neighborhoods reduce receptive field complexity; permutation-equivariance lets the same weights apply to any subset of particles.
failure_boundary: Graph networks struggle with long-range dependencies or global coherence—information needs multiple message-passing steps to propagate. Scaling to very large particle counts (millions) becomes memory-prohibitive. Turbulent regimes with Reynolds numbers >1000 remain untested; high-frequency instabilities violate the smooth-dynamics assumption. Models trained on single Reynolds/material parameter may fail catastrophically outside that regime. Boundary conditions and contact dynamics (particle overlaps) require careful initialization with training noise; without noise injection, models accumulate error into physically impossible states (interpenetration, divergence) that weren't observed during training.

title: Romit Maulik: Neural Architecture Search For Surrogate Modeling
speaker: Romit Maulik
one_sentence: This whole series chases one goal: getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of hand-written math. One way to do that is with surrogate models—simplified programs that act like the real simulator but run much faster. The problem is that designing the architecture (the overall shape and size of a learning program with millions of dials the computer tunes by trial and error until its answers look right) takes forever and often locks you into the default choices humans happen to try first. This talk shows how to automate that design by trying thousands of different shapes and sizes, and how to use many different designs together to measure how much uncertainty there is in the prediction.
core_problem: Building a fast surrogate model (a learning program trained to mimic what a simulator does) usually means someone has to sit down and decide the overall shape and size of the neural network by hand: how many layers, how wide each layer should be, whether to include shortcuts that skip ahead, which parts should squeeze information down, how much randomness to add during training. All these choices (called the architecture, hyperparameters, bottlenecks, and symmetry assumptions) get decided once at the start, often based on whatever worked on a different problem or what the person nearest to the computer happened to build last time. That manual decision-making can eat up months of the project. And it hides better designs that nobody would naturally guess, especially for weather forecasts or autoencoders (learning programs that squish data down to find its simplest patterns, then rebuild it from those patterns).
first_principles_model: A neural network can be drawn as a flowchart with no loops: each box is one operation (multiply, add, randomly drop some dials, jump ahead to a later box), and arrows point forward. The space of all possible networks is everything you could draw this way—varying how many boxes, how wide they are, where the jumps go, what operations each box does, how randomly things turn on and off during training, and all the numbers that control how the trial-and-error tuning happens. An optimizer like aging evolution picks candidate flowcharts, trains each one on real examples, scores how well each one predicts on held-out data it never saw, then mutates the good ones (small random changes), removes the bad ones, and repeats. After many rounds, better networks bubble up. When you keep many different trained networks from this search—not just the final winner—you can see how much the prediction wiggles when you change the network's shape. That wiggle tells you how uncertain you should be about the answer.
key_claims: DeepHyper automates the search over thousands of possible neural-network shapes, sizes, and training settings across many kinds of networks.
Searching over architectures can find surrogate models that work well without needing the physical laws built into the network structure itself.
The space of all possible networks can be drawn as a flowchart showing every operation and connection the search is allowed to build.
Aging evolution keeps the best candidate networks, mutates them slightly, removes the worst ones, and repeats until networks stop getting better.
Architecture search can question default choices—like the idea that if a network squishes data down, it must rebuild in exactly the reverse way.
Using many different trained networks together lets you see how much the prediction changes when you pick a different network shape—that change is your uncertainty.

important_terms.meaning: Automatic trial of thousands of different network shapes and sizes by a computer, instead of one person deciding the shape by hand at the start.
Every possible network shape, operation, and training-control number that the search is allowed to build and try.

An algorithm that picks candidate networks at random, trains each one, scores how well it predicts, keeps the good ones, mutates them slightly, removes the weak ones, and repeats; it mimics how populations evolve over time.

A collection of many different trained networks, each with its own shape, run together on the same data; seeing how much the prediction moves when you switch between them shows you how much the network shape matters.

A learning program that squishes data down in its first half (the encoder) and rebuilds it in its second half (the decoder), where the decoder does not have to be the mirror image of the encoder—it can be a completely different shape.

stanford_connections: This builds on earlier work showing that the shape of a reduced-order model (a simplified program that mimics the real simulator but runs faster) is something the scientific workflow should search over and optimize, not just assume at the start.
It ties to uncertainty and robustness: by running many different network shapes and seeing how much the prediction changes between them, you learn how much your uncertainty should be.
It also connects to hyper-reduction (using only a few of the most important directions in the data) because finding smaller, efficient networks means predictions run faster in real applications.
practical_caution: Neural architecture search does not replace the need to check whether predictions make physical sense. If the search only rewards how well the model fits test data it was shown, it can find networks that look accurate on the tests but predict crazy things when deployed in the real world, or grow so huge they are impractical to run, or produce answers that violate the laws of physics.
selected_evidence: Automate the construction of neural networks and the optimization of its hyper parameters.
Represent the neural network as a directed acyclic graph.
The aging evolution algorithm actually interprets... neural networks as a genetic algorithm.
Uncertainty quantification and deep learning is a big issue.
By losing the restriction of symmetry our auto encoders were actually able to get far better performance.
takeaway: The real lesson is that the shape and size of a learning program is a design choice—just like picking a solver, boundary conditions, or a method to compute things faster. Neural architecture search searches over that choice instead of hoping a human default design is good enough.
worked_example: POD-LSTM surrogate for sea surface temperature forecasting on the Optimum Interpolation (OI) dataset (180×360 grid, daily data). Evolved architecture found via aging evolution (genetic algorithm on DAG encoding) shows R² ~0.95 within minutes, converging across multiple random seeds. Compared to US DoD HiCom (800 CPU-hours/day for 1-day forecast on Cray XC40) and Community Earth System Model (30-member ensemble), the POD-LSTM delivers 8-week forecasts with lower RMSE in the eastern Pacific during El Niño. Top-100 architectures post-trained on separate GPU resources until convergence.
deeper_mechanics: Proper Orthogonal Decomposition extracts low-rank basis: snapshot matrix Φ ∈ ℝ^(N×m) (N DOFs, m snapshots) → SVD → truncated POD basis {φ₁,...,φᵣ}. Coefficients a(t) evolved via LSTM: a(n+1) = f_θ(a(n)) learned on training data. DAG-encoded architecture (array of integers) represents operations: variable LSTM nodes, skip connections, connection operations. Aging evolution interprets genome as architecture array, applies mutations to maximize validation accuracy or minimize validation loss, evaluates in parallel (128 nodes × 1 architecture each).
failure_boundary: LSTMs are not systems of ODEs and lack time-integration structure, causing long-term forecast divergence after 8 steps. POD convergence is slow for advection-dominated problems (high Kolmogorov width). Convolutional autoencoders + LSTM better handle sharp advection but lose orthogonality guarantees. Cost-benefit trade-off: ~10% accuracy gain over hand-tuned LSTM may not justify HPC wall-clock investment for marginal improvements.

title: Harbir Antil: Applications Of Fractional Operators From Optimal Control To Machine Learning
speaker: Harbir Antil
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of hand-written math.
