One way this series explores is using nonlocal operators (tools that measure how far apart two things can still influence each other, or how the past echoes into the present) to build better learning programs for images, geological data, systems you can control, and deep neural networks (programs with millions of dials tuned by trial and error).
core_problem: Real physical systems often show nonlocal behavior: one spot influences another far away, the past matters to what happens now, or something spreads in weird ways that don't match the normal rules. Standard calculus uses only the local slope at one point, but that misses the long-distance reach. If you ignore how a material's properties at one place affect its neighbor miles away, or how layers of rock store memory, or how fluids flowing and reacting jump between scales, you get the wrong prediction.
first_principles_model: A fractional operator is a way to measure change that doesn't have to be integer (like the 1st or 2nd derivative you learn in school). Instead of just looking at one spot, it can reach back through time or across distance to see how things influence each other. One example is the fractional Laplacian: instead of diffusion (things spreading out evenly in all directions), it models diffusion that has long-range reach—information or particles scatter farther or linger longer than the simple model predicts. You can also treat the fractional exponent (the number that says how far back or how far the reach goes) as a tunable dial you fit from data, or even as a random variable to capture what you don't know.
key_claims: Fractional calculus handles spreading that deviates from normal (anomalous diffusion) and systems where effects reach into the past or across distance.

In some cases, fractional operators can replace complicated nonlinear ways of smoothing images with simpler linear fractional differential equations (rules about change that use fractional derivatives).
Controlling systems with fractional differential equations raises new mathematical and computational questions that engineers didn't face before.
Unknown fractional exponents can be tuned like dials from data or treated as random variables when you need to capture uncertainty.
Fractional operators can be built into deep neural network layers (the computational parts that learn).
Chemical processes that react and flow show sudden jumps in how fast things happen at different scales, where fractional neural models may catch these shifts.

important_terms.meaning: A mathematical operation with a non-integer exponent (like 0.7 instead of 1 or 2), designed to measure how influence spreads across distance or how the past echoes into the present.
A version of the Laplacian (a tool measuring how things spread and change) that works across distance rather than just at one spot; used to model spreading or influence that reaches far.
Spreading of particles or information that breaks the normal rules; particles wander farther or slower than standard diffusion predicts.
The system remembers and depends on what happened before; the current state carries marks from the past.
A neural network layer built using ideas from fractional operators to capture patterns that depend on distant neighbors or past steps (nonlocal and time-dependent patterns).

stanford_connections: This talk widens the conversation about operator learning by focusing on operators that capture how things influence each other across distance (nonlocal physics).

It connects to optimal control (steering systems toward a goal) and uncertainty quantification (capturing what you don't know) because fractional exponents and long-distance effects can become uncertain parameters that change how you control things.
It also relates to graph networks: both are ways to represent how things in a system influence each other beyond just their immediate neighbors on a grid.
practical_caution: Fractional models fit numbers well, but you have to make choices: how fractional should it be (what exponent), how do you handle the edges (boundary conditions), and how do you actually compute it. These choices change the answer. Use fractional operators only when your physics actually shows this long-distance or memory behavior—not as a generic knob to twist just to fit harder problems.
selected_evidence: Applications of fractional operators from optimal control to machine learning.
Long-range correlations or hereditary material properties.
Modeled by fractional-order differential operators.
You have to solve a more challenging problem with the fractional Laplacian.
I started with several applications of fractional operators in imaging in geophysics... and machine learning.
takeaway: Not everything that happens depends only on what is at one spot right now. Fractional operators give both machine learning and science a way to describe things that reach across distance, remember the past, and spread in anomalous ways.
worked_example: Image denoising with fractional Laplacian (exponent s ≈ 0.4) solved in approximately 0.01 seconds (five to six lines of MATLAB code with FFT/IFFT). Total variation approach took significantly longer. Bayesian inverse problem: 2 parameters inferred; full model solving took 40 minutes, fractional DNN reduced to 2 minutes. Second example: inverse problem requiring 30,000 solves determined initial vorticity of Navier-Stokes system in 2.5 minutes (fractional DNN approach), compared to 18 hours for standard solver.
deeper_mechanics: Fractional Laplacian operator (Δ^{s/2}) with spectral and integral definitions. Euler-Lagrange equations for minimization replacing nonlinear total variation (L1 norm of gradient) with linear fractional PDE. Dirichlet and spectral fractional Laplacian computed via eigendecomposition. Bi-level optimization for learning exponent s and regularization parameter α. Fractional deep neural networks replace standard time derivatives (dX/dt) with fractional time derivatives where history from 0 to current time must be tracked. Non-local operators and their relationship to Fourier transforms. Gradient flow for constrained minimization with Lagrange multipliers.
failure_boundary: Fractional operators lose smoothness compared to classical operators—inherently non-smooth even with smooth boundary conditions and data (no H^1 regularity guaranteed). Non-locality requires dense numerical linear algebra (not sparse systems). Discretization of integral operators computationally challenging in arbitrary domains. At large exponent values (close to 1), behavior approaches classical case but loses fractional benefits. Memory requirements and parameter complexity scale poorly for state-constrained problems. Gradient issues arise with measures on RHS of adjoint equations in state-constraint formulations. Theory incomplete for fractional DNNs on general problems.

title: David Ryckelynck: Model Order Reduction Assisted By Deep Neural Networks
speaker: David Ryckelynck
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from data, instead of (or alongside) slow hand-written math. One popular approach uses simplified models that run fast by working in a smaller number of dimensions—but picking the right simplified model for different input data is hard. This talk is about a method that uses a learning program (a bank of dials tuned by trial and error) to automatically pick the right simplified model for each input, like an image showing where damage is happening.
core_problem: When you simulate something real—how a structure breaks under stress, how air flows around a wing—the answer depends heavily on input data that can look messy and complicated, like an image or a medical scan. You could build one global simplified model that works in a lower number of dimensions, but it might not work well across all the different inputs, or it might be hard to understand why it works. On the other hand, if you use a learning program as a complete replacement for the simulation, you lose speed and the clear structure that comes from the classical mathematical approach (a simplified simulation that solves in fewer dimensions).
first_principles_model: ROM-net combines learning with simplified-model selection. You start by building a dictionary: group your simulation data by how similar it is, and for each group, compute a reduced basis—a small list of directions that capture the main pattern in that group. A learning program (with millions of dials) takes the input data, such as an image showing damage, and decides which group it belongs to, which tells it which simplified model to use or how to blend models together. The result is a piecewise-linear reduced model: made up of separate flat regions (linear pieces) stitched together, where each piece solves much faster than the full simulation. This approach also works with a further speedup trick that cuts not just the dimensions but the number of calculations needed.
key_claims: This method extends simplified-model selection to cases where inputs are high-dimensional and image-like.
Building a collection of local simplified models can be understood as creating a lower-dimensional space made of separate flat pieces joined together.
Grouping data before building simplified models allows each group to have its own tuned simplified basis.
Collections of local simplified models are easier to understand and work with compared to learning programs that compress data to a single code and uncompress it.
Further calculation reduction becomes straightforward when the simplified space is made of separate flat pieces.
The method works with simulation data you already have, while keeping the clear structure that comes from classical mathematical models.

important_terms.meaning: A method that uses a learning program to connect input data to the right simplified model (a simulation that runs much faster by working in fewer dimensions).
A collection of simplified models from which the right one is picked or blended for a given input.
Learning simplified representations using only a small number of local lower-dimensional models or pieces.
A lower-dimensional representation made of several local flat regions (linear subspaces) joined together, rather than one single flat region.
A high-dimensional input, such as a scan or damage map, used to tell the simulation what to predict.

stanford_connections: This talk sits between methods that build simplified models from data alone (without changing the original simulator), automatically finding good learning-program designs, and simplified models that handle curved shapes instead of flat ones: it uses learning programs to route among structured simplified models.
It connects to digital twins because images or sensor readings can pick the right simplified behavior.
It reinforces a recurring theme in this seminar series: learning programs work best when they help classical simplification methods instead of replacing them.
practical_caution: The number of groups and how well they're built matter a lot. Too few groups and you'll miss important variations in the input; too many and you'll need more memory and more time to train the learning program. The learning program that picks which model to use also needs to be tested carefully to make sure it still works right when the input changes in ways it hasn't seen before.
selected_evidence: Model order reduction assisted by deep neural network so-called ROM-net.
Images are input parameter for numerical models.
Sparse dictionary learning can be understood as a piecewise linear latent space.
For each cluster we can use... SVD... to get... a proper reduced basis.
A ROMnet is a feed forward artificial neural network that ends with a reduced order model.
takeaway: Neural networks can pick the right simplified model for each input, while keeping the speed and structure that come from simplified-model selection and further calculation reduction.
worked_example:
ROM-net trained on thermomechanical turbine blade problem: high-fidelity finite element model has 200,000 degrees of freedom; reduced order model achieves 60x speedup with 5% error in predicting plastic strain. Clustering uses 6 clusters, each with 2-mode reduced basis, achieving dissimilarity (Grassmann distance) well-separated from single-global-basis (red curve) approach. CNN classifier achieves 74% accuracy in mapping temperature field images to clusters. Offline training cost amortized across many online parameter queries.

Elastoplastic problem initially requires 100 loading cycles taking 300 days with full FEM. ROM-net acceleration makes parametric uncertainty quantification tractable. Local reduced bases computed per cluster via SVD on simulation subsets, cluster labels learned by CNN from thermal field images, then projection into local ROM space and Galerkin assembly replace expensive residual evaluations.
deeper_mechanics:
ROM-net couples three distinct operations: (1) Offline clustering in Grassmann manifold using ideal reduced basis per simulation and k-medoid algorithm to partition data by angles between subspaces. (2) CNN classifier trained to map input parameter μ (thermal field as image) to cluster label, with loss = supervised classification error. (3) For each cluster k, local reduced basis V_k obtained by SVD; solution projection: minimize ||r(q)|| where q = V_k z_k and r is FEM residual restricted to cluster's basis.

Dimensionality reduction replaces high-dim latent space (true solution manifold) with piecewise-linear approximation (k clusters × local basis). Galerkin projection: V_k^T r(V_k z) = 0 solved at each parameter query. Hyper-reduction via reduced integration domain (energy sampling) or DEIM further reduces residual assembly cost. Grassmann distance d_G(V_i, V_j) = angles between column spaces, computed as SVD of V_i^T V_j; small distance ⇒ good local basis overlap.
failure_boundary:
With insufficient data points in database, oscillations appear in constitutive response due to sparse coverage of latent space (line 687-701). Single global reduced basis (no clustering) shows higher dissimilarity (red curve line 792-810) than clustered approach, increasing approximation error where single basis fits poorly. CNN mislabeling (74% accuracy line 827) can direct wrong cluster; however, near-cluster misclassifications cause small errors since neighboring bases are geometrically close (line 838-844).

Temporally expensive: when k << n (6 modes vs 200k DOFs), complexity scales as k^3 due to dense reduced system (vs sparse FEM), limiting mode count. Memory scales linearly with k clusters × basis size, requiring storage per cluster (line 1156-1165). Method assumes smooth latent manifold with well-defined cluster boundaries; abrupt parameter-dependent transitions in physics may violate piecewise-linear approximation.

title: Matthew Zahr: Model Reduction Of PDEs Via Optimization-Based Feature Tracking
speaker: Matthew Zahr
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples. Some hard problems have sudden jumps—shocks in explosions or flow around objects—that move around as time goes on. This talk is about a trick: instead of trying to compress a fixed grid that watches shocks zoom past, warp the grid so the shocks sit still in a new coordinate system, then compress that simpler view. The method writes this as an optimization problem—find both the physical solution and the grid deformation that work together.
core_problem: When a physical rule (a PDE—a rule that says how something changes from moment to moment or place to place) has shocks or sharp jumps, model reduction is hard. Model reduction means taking all the data from a full simulation and boiling it down to a smaller, faster program that still predicts well. Normally you keep the same grid (the points in space where you measure) and try to compress the results. But when shocks move around, you need a huge number of different 'modes' (different ways to wiggle the solution) to capture them all, and the reduced model either gets fat and slow or smears out the sharp features into blurry wiggles instead.
first_principles_model: Instead of watching shocks zip past a fixed grid, this method warps the grid itself so the shocks line up. Think of it like moving your camera so a fast-moving object stays in the same spot on screen. The method writes down an optimization problem: find values for both the physical solution and for how to deform the grid, such that everything stays consistent with the physics. When you compress this setup, you reduce not just the numbers describing the solution, but also the numbers describing how the grid bends.
key_claims: Shock tracking can be written as an optimization problem—you solve for both the solution and the grid deformation simultaneously.

High-order methods (advanced techniques for numerical solving) keep their nice properties like accuracy and conservation of physical quantities even when you write shock tracking as an optimization constraint.
Warping the domain lines up sudden jumps across different time steps, so fewer modes are needed to capture the motion.
The reduced model optimizes both the compressed solution and the compressed mesh deformation.
The grid warping must preserve the domain edges so interior point movement does not damage the physical boundary.
Feature tracking keeps simple compression tools like SVD (a standard matrix trick for data reduction) useful on hard problems where shocks move.

important_terms.meaning: Warping the grid in space so sharp features like shocks stay in the same spot as time goes on, instead of moving around.
A method where you write an optimization problem to find the shocks by solving the physics and grid together, rather than manually drawing the shock front.
Bending the computational domain (the region in space you are simulating) to line up moving features.
A small set of numbers that control how the grid bends when you are working with a compressed model.
A grid transformation that moves interior points around while keeping the edges of your domain fixed and valid.

stanford_connections: This talk is the optimization-based cousin of registration-based reduced models: both reduce the problem by lining up moving features.
It ties to entropy-stable schemes because handling shocks is not just about learning, but also about how you discretize (break space into steps) and how you move the geometry.
It also connects to nonlinear reduced models on curved subspaces because grid deformation creates a nonlinear representation, yet keeps simple linear tools like SVD still working.
practical_caution: Tracking features is not free. The optimization itself costs computing time, and bending the grid can cause real problems. If you bend the grid badly, you might keep the model small but break the edge boundaries of your domain, lose conserved quantities (like total mass or energy), or make the solver unstable and unreliable.
selected_evidence: Optimization based implicit feature tracking.
Formulated as an optimization problem over the DG solution and mesh coordinates.
We want to deform the domain... to align... the shock.
Minimizing over the ROM state... and the mesh.
Introduce this mapping... to guarantee that the boundaries are preserved.
takeaway: The main idea is that for shocks and sudden jumps, you can first let your coordinate grid flow with the physics before compressing. Moving the grid is itself an optimization problem you solve alongside finding the solution.
worked_example: For the 1D advection equation with a moving step function, implicit feature tracking aligned a coarse mesh (far fewer elements than shock-capturing) to track the discontinuity. Without tracking, naïve linear combinations produced a jagged staircase error. With tracking, the method recovered the solution almost exactly on a handful of elements. For transonic flow over an airfoil (Mach 0.8–0.87), tracking reduced offline cost from prohibitive to tractable; tangential interpolation further reduced computational overhead by factor 1.7. Online evaluation gave 100x+ speedup over full-order CFD.
deeper_mechanics: Implicit feature tracking solves a PDE-constrained optimization: minimize ||X_k+1 - X_rom||^2 + mesh regularization over both the solution coefficients and mesh node positions. The enriched residual formulation includes test functions of degree p+1 to penalize non-physical oscillations on unaligned meshes. Sequential quadratic programming updates both solution and mesh simultaneously via full-space coupling (not reduced-space, which fails on aligned problems). For ROMs, each snapshot maps to a reference domain via smooth deformation; projecting all snapshots onto aligned domains enables linear POD to work better, requiring far fewer modes than naïve POD.
failure_boundary: Implicit tracking requires finding initial mesh guesses; complex geometries with multiple interacting discontinuities demand element collapse operations and reinitalization of oscillating regions, adding robustness overhead. For problems with genuinely distributed features (turbulence, disperse interfaces) rather than sharp moving fronts, the localized nature of the deformation provides diminishing returns. Unsteady systems where features separate or merge dramatically challenge the topological assumptions. For highly nonlinear problems, the optimization may converge to local minima with misaligned features, especially if initial conditions are poor.

title: Tan Bui-Thanh: Model-Constrained Deep Learning For Inference, Control And UQ
speaker: Tan Bui-Thanh
one_sentence: This whole series chases one goal: getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples. One approach is to write down the math rules (the laws of physics) and use them to guide the learning, so the program respects the real science while also learning from data. This talk is about embedding those physics rules directly into a learning program to solve inverse problems—figuring out hidden causes from limited measurements—and to make control decisions when you also need to measure your uncertainty.
core_problem: Many real problems need you to work backward from measurements to figure out what you can't see. Imagine measuring the temperature at a few spots and trying to figure out where a heat source is hidden inside a metal block. The catch: you get only a handful of readings, those readings contain errors, and each one depends on many hidden causes mixed together. The hidden causes (what we're trying to find) can also be enormous—thousands or millions of possibilities. If you want to be sure about your answer, you have to check thousands of scenarios, and each check means running a physics simulator step by step. That's unbelievably slow.
first_principles_model: Start with a forward simulator: a program that takes in parameters (like: where is the heat source?) and runs the physics rules to predict what you'd measure. A physics rule is a recipe that says how something changes moment by moment or place by place—for instance, how fast heat spreads through a metal bar. Working backward (the inverse problem) means: given some measurements, find the hidden parameters that would have produced those measurements. In a Bayesian approach, the answer isn't a single number but a cloud of plausible possibilities—a probability distribution over all the parameters that fit the data reasonably well. The challenge: computing this probability cloud is expensive because you have to run the forward simulator many times. A new idea is to wire the forward simulator directly into a learning program (a network of adjustable dials that learns by trial and error) or into a fast approximation of it, so the learning respects the physics while you avoid running the simulator thousands of times.
key_claims: Combining physics rules (written as equations) with learning from data (finding patterns) gives you the speed of learning plus the certainty that the physics is respected.
Forward problems use the physics rules to predict what you'd measure from known parameters. Inverse problems work the other way: use the measurements to back out the hidden parameters.
When the hidden quantities are numerous and the measurements are limited, there are endless possibilities—too many to check one by one.
Making a Bayesian probability cloud over the hidden parameters (showing which ones are likely) requires running the forward simulator over and over, and this is prohibitively expensive.
A simpler approximation can replace the expensive probability cloud by fitting it to a distribution that's quick to compute—no need to run the full simulator each time.
The key move is placing the physics simulator inside the learning architecture so the learning automatically respects the physics and avoids recomputing it for every trial.

important_terms.meaning: A learning approach where the program's guesses are forced to obey a physics simulator or scientific equation—instead of the program guessing anything, it guesses only answers that satisfy the law.
A simulator that takes in parameters (like: position of a heat source) and runs the physics rules to calculate what you'd measure.
Taking measurements and working backward to find the hidden parameters or causes—for example, finding where the heat source is by measuring temperature at a few spots.
A cloud or spread of plausible parameter values—each one weighted by how well it matches your measurements—showing which parameters are more or less likely.
A technique to replace an expensive probability calculation (running a simulator thousands of times) with a simpler, faster approximation that still captures how uncertain you should be.

stanford_connections: This talk brings together two big ideas: running physics simulators backward through neural networks (so gradients flow from the answer back through the physics) and embedding entire equations inside neural networks as layers.
It connects to digital twins because real digital twins need to infer the current state of a real system and measure how sure you are, not only predict the future.
It also connects to control because making a good control decision (how hard should the robot push?) depends on first inferring what state the system is in and how uncertain that inference is.
practical_caution: A physics-aware learning system is only trustworthy if two things work: the forward simulator must correctly capture the real physics that matters, and the fast approximation must correctly estimate how confident you should be in your final answer. If either one fails, your downstream decisions—where should a robot move? how much material do we need?—could be wrong.
selected_evidence: Model constrained deep learning approaches for inference control and uncertainty quantification.
The forward problem... you just solve for the electromagnetic waves or field.
The inverse problem is more difficult.
The posterior is the solution... probability density.
Put the underlying mathematical model inside the variational encoder.
takeaway: Inference and control need learning systems that obey the physical laws while making uncertainty computation fast enough to actually use in practice.
worked_example:
When solving a 2D heat conduction inverse problem, the team trained on 5,000 pairs of training data (each pair a one-step mapping from current state to next state). They used fully connected feed-forward neural networks and compared three approaches: direct inverse mapping, auto-encoder architecture, and model-constrained learning. For the same problem with full domain observations, they achieved a relative error between 1-2% when using the model-constrained approach compared to solving the full high-fidelity model. The speedup ranged from approximately 10x for reduced order models to 35x for coarse-grained systems capturing 99% of variance.

In a 3D seismic inversion problem with 6-dimensional parameter space, they compared performance against the baseline inverse problem solution. The neural network trained on 20,000 synthetic samples achieved comparable accuracy to traditional parameter estimation but ran 300 times faster for deployment.
deeper_mechanics:
The model-constrained deep learning approach combines a physics-based regularization with data-driven learning. The loss function is structured as: minimize mean square error between network output and observed data PLUS a physics constraint term that enforces the predicted state satisfies the forward model. Mathematically, if G is the forward map (the true PDE solution operator) and N is the neural network inverse map, the loss is: ||N(y) - u_true||^2 + λ||G(N(y)) - y||^2, where y is the observation and λ weights the physics constraint.

For problems with missing observations (partial state variables), they employ memory: storing the past m timesteps as input. The multi-step encoder-decoder architecture processes sequences where the encoder learns compact latent representations of dynamics and the decoder reconstructs high-dimensional states. The key insight is avoiding X as a function of absolute time; instead, learning one-step transition maps x_{n+1} = F(x_n, x_{n-1}, ...) prevents the network from overfitting to training time window boundaries and enables long-horizon prediction.
failure_boundary: Purely data-driven approaches fail on high-dimensional problems because they require enormous amounts of training data. For 3D problems with many features, the dimensional curse manifests immediately—the network cannot distinguish between many equally plausible solutions that match the noisy observations. Performance degrades sharply when test-time conditions diverge from training distribution. The model-constrained approach itself fails if the forward model is itself biased or inaccurate; if G is wrong, enforcing G(N(y))≈y drives the inversion toward an incorrect solution. Additionally, with limited training data (as is typical in practice), the network may overfit and memorize noise rather than learn the underlying inverse relationship. The reduced-order model approach creates an additional modeling gap: if the ROM truncates important dynamics, no amount of neural correction can recover them.

title: Rui Wang: Physics-Guided Deep Learning For Dynamics Forecasting
speaker: Rui Wang
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. One approach is to inject known physics rules directly into a learning program: ideas like how fluids can't compress, how things look the same under rotation, and tricks from engineers' step-by-step calculators. This talk is about why mixing physics and deep learning produces better forecasts when systems evolve in space and time, and which diagnostics you need to trust the model.
core_problem: Predicting how physical systems evolve over time is hard. A system like fluid flow happens at many scales at once—big swirls carry small eddies inside them. A learning program trained only on examples might capture the big patterns but miss smaller ones. It might also break the rules that should always hold, like incompressibility (the idea that fluid can't vanish). Tiny errors early on balloon into huge mistakes later, so a model that looks good for a few steps ahead might fail after many steps.
first_principles_model: A dynamics forecasting model is a program that takes a picture or description of how things look now and predicts how they'll look next. Physics-guided learning teaches it better by baking in physics ideas: using numerical recipes from classical engineering (like how to step a system forward in small increments), enforcing symmetries (if you rotate the input, the output rotates the same way), adding penalties when fluid rules are broken (like when divergence is nonzero when it should be zero), and making sure the program learns both large and small features separately instead of blurring them together.
key_claims: Combining deep learning with known physics rules makes forecasts stay physically realistic for longer.
Neural networks can be redesigned to include numerical methods and symmetries, not just fitted to data.
For fluids that can't compress, enforcing zero divergence (as a penalty during learning) keeps predictions grounded in physics.
Symmetries like rotation and translation help the model generalize to new situations it hasn't seen before.
Training purely on pixel errors can hide the fact that a model gets the big patterns right but botches small scales.
Even with physics guidance, forecasting fails when test conditions drift too far from training—a problem without a complete solution yet.

important_terms.meaning: Predicting how a physical system will look or behave at future moments, given snapshots from now or the past.

Using a program with millions of adjustable dials (tuned by trial and error until its answers look right) while also telling it physical facts—like 'this fluid can't change density' or 'rotating the input must rotate the output the same way'—so it learns answers that respect both data and physics.

When you apply a transformation to the input (like rotating or sliding it), the output is transformed in exactly the corresponding way—a property that keeps the model's answers physically sensible under changes in perspective or position.

A score for how much a predicted fluid field disobeys the rule that incompressible fluids can't have fluid disappearing or appearing at a point; the program tries to push this score down during learning.

When test conditions differ from training conditions—for example, a model trained on slow flow is asked to predict fast flow—accuracy typically drops because the model learned only what it saw, not the underlying rules.

stanford_connections: This talk sits alongside research on building simulators as differentiable programs (you can compute gradients through them) and learning reduced-order models (stripped-down versions that capture the essential physics but run faster) by insisting on long-horizon physical consistency.

It takes the next step beyond PINNs, which fit equations; this approach uses physics to sculpt both how the neural network is built and what losses steer learning, for forward forecasting rather than solving given equations.
It reinforces a recurring theme in this series: a model can interpolate well within its training regime but completely fail when conditions shift—a hard problem still being solved.
practical_caution: Don't judge a forecasting model only by how pixel-by-pixel errors stack up over a few steps. Instead, check the physics by hand: Is the divergence staying small for incompressible flow? Are the frequencies (the wiggles at different scales) staying realistic? Are conserved quantities (things that should never change) actually staying constant? Does it still work when you train on fluid flowing one way and test it flowing sideways or faster?
selected_evidence: Physics guided deep learning for dynamics forecasting.
The divergence is supposed to be zero.
The model may... with the MSE loss... only focus on the large scale component and overlook these small eddies.
We see improved prediction accuracy and physical consistency by incorporating... physics-based modeling.
The theories for forecasting... non-stationary and chaotic dynamics is still missing.
takeaway: Forecasting future states is not just sliding frames forward in time. The model must preserve the rules and symmetries that make future states physically believable. Learning from examples is powerful only when those examples are combined with the structures we already know must be true.
worked_example:
A physics-guided TurblenceNet (TFNet) for Rayleigh-Bénard convection jointly learns velocity components and filters them using trainable spatial and temporal filters inspired by large-eddy simulation. On 2D synthetic data at high Reynolds numbers, the model achieves divergence errors near zero across all prediction horizons (compared to baseline models with diverging divergence), and energy spectrum errors remain closer to ground truth. The model, when applied autoregressively, remains stable 300+ frames into the future, whereas standard deep learning baselines begin to diverge earlier.

For symmetry-incorporated models handling three-dimensional transformations (rotation, uniform motion, scaling), equivalence constraints allow the model to automatically generalize to unseen rotations (e.g., 90-degree rotations) and scaling factors (e.g., 3x scale change) without retraining. On real ocean dynamics, the symmetry-informed model maintains predictive consistency across these transformations, whereas non-equivariant baselines fail to generalize.
deeper_mechanics:
TFNet uses a three-level decomposition via spatial and temporal filters: velocity u is split into large-scale u*, fluctuation u', then u* is further split into temporal average u_bar and fluctuation u_tilde. Each component (u_bar, u_tilde, u') is encoded separately, then a shared decoder learns interactions. The divergence constraint L_div = ||∇·u||^2 penalizes compressibility, enforcing the continuity equation. Energy spectrum loss ensures the model captures multi-scale Kolmogorov structure.

For symmetry, group correlation replaces standard convolution: h(x,y) = ∫ ψ(ρ(g)x - y) φ(y) dy where g ∈ G. Scaling equivalence applies kernels at multiple scales λ in {1/3, 1, 3}; rotation equivalence uses regular representations of cyclic groups (C4) where each rotation maps to a permutation matrix. Uniform motion covariance is achieved by centering: shift input to zero mean, apply convolution, shift output back—this is a learned inductive bias that respects conservation laws.
failure_boundary: At very high Reynolds numbers (Re >> 1), even with multi-scale decomposition, small-scale dynamics become harder to predict accurately. Distribution shift is a fundamental challenge: the model trained on one Rayleigh number or buoyancy value degrades on others unless explicitly trained via meta-learning. Symmetry enforcement comes at computational cost (multiple scale/rotation kernels per layer); scaling breaks down if the assumed transformations don't match the physics (e.g., non-uniform scaling). Long rollouts accumulate error despite the constraints; the model cannot recover from phase drift in chaotic regimes.

title: Yeonjong Shin: A Mathematical Understanding Of Modern Machine Learning
speaker: Yeonjong Shin
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. This talk focuses on the math behind machine learning: when we teach a computer to solve science problems using learned rules and physics, we can break down exactly where mistakes come from—some come from the model's shape, some from not having enough data, some from learning only what was in your examples, and some from the training process getting stuck. This talk is about understanding each type of mistake so we know when these methods work and when they fail.
core_problem: Machine learning often works through trial and error on real problems, but when we use it for science—to solve equations, predict material behavior, or simulate physical systems—we need to know when it actually gets the right answer and when it fails without warning. A popular approach is to build a learning program (a set of dials tuned by trial and error) that is also given the laws of physics while it trains. These methods look promising in experiments, yet without math we cannot tell if they truly solve the equations correctly, whether they will work on new situations, or whether the trial-and-error tuning will actually discover a good solution.
first_principles_model: Every learning method makes mistakes in different ways. Approximation error: the model class (the range of shapes the learning program can take) might not be wide enough to capture reality, no matter how good the training. Estimation error: you only see a finite batch of examples, not infinite samples, so your view of reality is incomplete. Generalization error: the gap between what the model learned on your examples and how it behaves on new, unseen situations. Optimization error: the trial-and-error tuning stops at some answer but not the best possible answer the model class could reach. When we combine learning with physics, we need to track all four errors together and ask how they change as we get more data, train longer, and pick better models.
key_claims: Machine learning's success comes from the model design, the training method, the data available, and the computing power to run it.
Scientific machine learning adds a new constraint: the learned model must also obey the laws of physics.
Physics-informed learning methods show strong results but need mathematical proof about when they work and proof that training will find a good solution.
Generalization error and optimization error are distinct problems and must not be mixed up.
The talk develops mathematical theory for physics-informed learning using techniques from regularization and classical rules for differential equations.
Understanding the math can lead to new and better algorithms for training these learning programs.

important_terms.meaning: The gap between what the best possible model in your chosen set of shapes can express and the actual target you are trying to learn. If your set of shapes is too narrow, approximation error will be large no matter what.
Mistakes that arise because you learn from a limited number of examples, not an infinite amount of data. More data shrinks this error.
The gap between how well your learned model performs on the data you trained it with and how well it performs on new data the program has never seen before.
The difference between the answer your training algorithm actually finds and the best possible answer that exists within your chosen model class. A slow or stuck training process causes this.

A mathematical property that says: if we gather enough data and train long enough under the right conditions, the solution found by a physics-informed learning method will approach the true solution of the physical equations.

stanford_connections: This talk provides the mathematical proof for when physics-informed learning should work in theory, complementing an earlier talk about why these methods fail in practice.
It connects to robustness and uncertainty because dependable scientific machine learning requires us to separate and measure each type of error, not just check overall accuracy on examples.

It helps explain later talks about advanced methods (like learning operators that map between functions) by distinguishing between a model's ability to express solutions and its ability to train successfully.
practical_caution: A mathematical proof about the ideal best solution does not mean a real training algorithm will find it. When using physics-informed learning methods, we need both the math showing the ideal solution exists and practical checks during training to spot when the search is getting stuck or going the wrong direction.
selected_evidence: Lacks theoretical understanding and also it has some potential issues in optimization procedure.
Combining these two errors together we call it generalization error.
The difference between these two is called optimization error.
First convergence theory of the physics informed neural network.
Mathematically it will give you the correct answer if you can get a good optimizer.
takeaway: The first step in reliable scientific machine learning is tracking the error budget. Approximation failure, data failure, generalization failure, and optimization failure are four separate types of trouble, and each needs its own remedy.
worked_example: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) solving a wave equation: using a 2-layer ReLU network with 100 neurons, training with Hölder regularization (α=1, Lipschitz penalty), the method achieved relative L2 error ~10^-3 while training loss drops to ~10^-6. For a 2D function approximation (the Buhnke function with discontinuity and values reaching 0-200), the Active Neuron Least Squares method converged in 100 iterations with 4 orders of magnitude better training loss than gradient descent or Adam—reaching ~10^-6 loss vs 10^-2 for Adam. Generalization error was also smallest among all methods tested. For the absolute value function approximation using a 10-layer ReLU with width 2: standard initialization causes dying ReLU in 9 of 10 runs (probability 0.9), but randomized asymmetric initialization drops dying probability to ~0.4, improving successful training rate from ~20% to ~55%.
deeper_mechanics: PINN minimizes composite loss L_PINN = ||u_NN(x) - y_data||^2 + ||∂u_NN/∂t - N[u_NN]||^2 + ||BC[u_NN]||^2 over interior PDE residual, boundary data, and initial conditions. Hölder regularization bounds expected loss: E[L_PINN(θ)] ≤ L_Hölder(θ) + O(1/√m) by space-filling argument; minimizing the upper bound guarantees consistency as m→∞. Training dynamics split into two phases: (1) plateau phase where activation patterns (which neurons fire on which training points) stay fixed—loss stagnates in orthogonal complement of loss gradient but decays exponentially on signal subspace; (2) phase transition when neuron biases shift, enabling new activation patterns. Dying ReLU occurs when random initialization places neurons outside training data support, making their gradients zero; deep networks (L>>1) die with probability→1, wide networks (n>>1) have probability→0.
failure_boundary: PINNs fail when gradient imbalance: different loss terms (PDE residual vs boundary condition) produce mismatched signal strengths, so one term dominates training early, leaving others unsatisfied. Dying ReLU traps neurons: if neuron bias b is far from training points x_i, then σ(w·x_i + b) is either always 0 or always linear, killing gradient flow. Spectral bias: ReLU networks preferentially fit low-frequency (smooth) components before high-frequency sharp features, so discontinuities like those in the Buhnke function remain approximated poorly. Boundary handling: PINNs don't enforce boundary conditions exactly—only penalize them, so weak maximum principle must be invoked separately to guarantee boundary convergence, adding restrictive assumptions.

title: Marta D'Elia: Data-Driven Learning Of Nonlocal Models
speaker: Marta D'Elia
one_sentence: This series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of hand-written math. This talk focuses on a harder case: materials and systems where distant particles reach out and influence each other, not just neighbors touching. The problem is figuring out the right weight to give each distant effect so that a simplified model (which ignores tiny details) still predicts the big-picture results. This talk shows how to learn those weights from high-resolution data.
core_problem: Most everyday math treats change as local: what happens at one spot depends only on what's right there. But many real materials and complicated systems break this rule—a particle feels the tug of others far away, not just its neighbors. You can write down a new kind of math rule using integrals (adding up weighted contributions) to capture this spread-out influence, but you have to guess what those weights are. This talk is about pulling those weights from real, fine-grained measurements of how the system actually behaves.
first_principles_model: A nonlocal operator works by adding up effects from all the other pieces touching or nearby, each effect weighted by how far away it is. The weighting function (called the kernel) is the recipe—it says which distant partners matter most and by how much. When you train this on pairs of detailed measurements (what you see) and what forces caused the change, you get a simplified model that predicts large-scale results without simulating every tiny detail.
key_claims: Nonlocal models build distance scales directly into addition operators that span regions.
They work well when small-scale activity drives overall results but is too expensive to compute directly.
The real job is finding the weighting function that defines how influence spreads over distance.
Peridynamic operators generalize nonlocal ideas to solid mechanics by including material properties.
Learning programs designed to learn operators can speed up simulations of molecular motion and problem-size reduction.
Nonlocal weighting ideas inspire new designs for neural-network layers that respect how physics works.

important_terms.meaning: A math rule where the state at one point is affected by values spread across a region, not just what's at that one spot.
A rule that assigns weights to how much each distance and direction affects the total influence in a spread-out operator.
A simplified model that correctly predicts large-scale results without tracking every small-scale detail.
A mechanics theory that describes how materials behave by tracking forces traveling over distance, rather than only pointwise stress.
A learning program design inspired by learnable nonlocal weightings, where each layer computes weighted averages across a neighborhood.

stanford_connections: This talk ties together fractional calculus, network graphs with learned connections, and operator learning all through the common idea of spread-out interaction.
It extends the many-scales-working-together theme by replacing the need to simulate fine details with learned operators that copy their effects.
It also touches on understanding what learning programs actually learned because inspecting learned weightings can reveal the underlying physical interaction rules.
practical_caution: A learned weighting only captures real physics if your training examples actually exercise all the important long-range effects and if your chosen weighting shape can truly match the real physical law. Otherwise you have a model that fits your training examples but fails on new situations it hasn't seen.
selected_evidence: Data-driven learning techniques for nonlocal equations.
Complex systems where the small scale dynamics...
The real goal is to find the optimal kernel k.
We collect measurements... high fidelity pairs of solution and forcing function.
Linear peridynamic solid operator.
takeaway: The central idea is learning the interaction law—the rule for how distant parts push and pull on each other—not just curve-fitting to numbers. The weighting function bridges the gap between small-scale behavior and large-scale prediction.
worked_example:
For single-layer graphene material property recovery at 0 K using molecular dynamics data, the optimal kernel learning recovered Young's modulus and Poisson ratio consistent with literature, with a fractional-order non-local model achieving 9% accuracy when tested on geometries completely different from training (different loading, zero forcing inside domain, non-zero forcing outside). The non-local model with tunable fractional singularity and sign-changing coefficients outperformed classical PDE models even on homogeneous samples where simple advection-diffusion fails at coarse scales.

For image classification on CIFAR-10 using non-local kernel networks (the proposed architecture with integral operators), the network remained stable and improved accuracy across 256 layers (where graph kernel networks stagnate), demonstrating resolution independence: training on fine images (32×32) and validating on coarse (16×16) yielded superior cross-resolution performance compared to CNNs that excel only at matched resolution.
deeper_mechanics:
Non-local diffusion operators take the form L_δ[u](x) = ∫_{B(x,δ)} k(x,y)(u(y) - u(x)) dy where δ is the interaction horizon and k(x,y) is a sign-changing kernel to be learned. The optimization minimizes the residual ||L_δ[u] - f||_L2 subject to solvability constraints from unified non-local calculus ensuring well-posedness. Kernels are represented as linear combinations of Bernstein polynomials: k(r) = Σ c_m B_m(r), with coefficients c_m determined by optimization.

For peridynamic solid operators (richer than non-local Laplacian), the model incorporates material properties: linear elastic bonds with Young's modulus E and Poisson ratio ν, plus a tunable fractional term with exponent α controlling singularity strength. Neural ODE view: ResNets ≡ Euler discretization of continuous dynamics dh/dt = σ(W h + b). Non-local kernel networks replace this with dh/dt = ∫_D k_θ(x,y)(h(y) - h(x)) dy + r_θ(x,h(x)), where k and r are shallow networks, achieving continuous resolution independence and stability via unified calculus.
failure_boundary:
Classical PDE models fail catastrophically at coarse-grained scales even for mildly heterogeneous media because the homogenized constitutive law differs fundamentally from the fine-scale physics—advection-diffusion predictions diverge sharply from coarse-grained data. Non-local models with fixed, known kernels (e.g., fractional-α) remain expensive because computing fractional operators requires integration over infinite domains.

Graph kernel networks (prior art) stagnate in accuracy as network depth increases (128+ layers) because the fixed non-local operator lacks a dissipative term (missing h_i difference in their formulation). Non-local kernel networks achieve stability but only if the solvability constraints enforcing well-posedness are correctly embedded; incorrect constraint specification leads to ill-posed inverse problems where the optimizer finds spurious solutions. Additionally, the method assumes high-fidelity reference data (MD simulations or fine-grid solutions); if reference data is corrupted or sparse at certain scales, the learned kernel becomes resolution-dependent and fails under out-of-distribution loading conditions.

title: Dmitriy Anistratov: ROMs For Thermal Radiative Transfer Based On Moment Equations And POD
speaker: Dmitriy Anistratov
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. One key problem in radiation heat transfer is that the full prediction equation is so tangled and expensive to run that people resort to simpler guesses that miss important effects. This talk shows how to build a middle road: keep the physics structure simple, but train it on data from expensive full simulations so it stays accurate while running fast.
core_problem: Radiation heat transfer depends on many things at once: where you are, when it is, which direction light travels, and what energy the light has. Change any of those, and the answer changes. The full equation describing this (called the Boltzmann transport equation, a rule saying how radiation spreads and changes) is nonlinear (the answer does not scale in proportion to the input) and couples tightly to material temperature (hotter things glow brighter and change how radiation travels). Running the full equation directly wastes compute. Faster shortcuts like diffusion (treating radiation like heat spreading through material) or P1 approximation (a rough formula that assumes radiation travels somewhat evenly in all directions) save time but lose some real effects.
first_principles_model: The method starts with the Boltzmann transport equation (a rule saying how radiation spreads and changes across space, direction, energy, and time). Instead of solving it all at once, you squeeze out some details: you integrate (sum up) over all directions, keeping only how much total energy reaches each spot. This creates simpler equations called moment equations. But squeezing throws away information. The moment equations now need extra guesses to stay accurate—especially the Eddington tensor, which captures the pattern of how radiation actually travels in different directions. POD (proper orthogonal decomposition: a method that finds the most important patterns by decomposing data into pieces and keeping the biggest ones) or DMD (dynamic mode decomposition: a method that finds repeating time-patterns in data) compress these guesses using examples from expensive full simulations run once, offline.
key_claims: Thermal radiation heat transfer is a useful testing ground for extreme-energy and radiation-coupled gas dynamics problems.
The main cost comes from solving the high-dimensional transport equation.
Nonlinear projection can derive low-order moment equations for radiation intensity.
The Eddington tensor supplies the closure that moment systems need.
POD and DMD can approximate closure information across different conditions and time.
Removing the expensive transport equation from online calculations can bring cost down to match simple models while keeping predictive quality under control.

important_terms.meaning: How radiation energy (light, heat) moves through material while the material heats up or cools down by absorbing or emitting that energy.
A rule describing how radiation intensity (the amount and direction of light energy) changes across space, direction, energy, and time.
A simpler rule created by summing up the transport equation over some of its variables (like direction), reducing the number of unknowns.
A guess or correction term that captures how radiation actually travels in different directions; needed when you simplify a transport equation into moment form.

Using data-compression methods (proper orthogonal decomposition: extracting the dominant patterns from data; or dynamic mode decomposition: finding repeating patterns in sequences) to approximate the missing terms from training simulations.

stanford_connections: This talk extends reduced-model ideas beyond fluids and structures to a transport-heavy application.
It parallels large-eddy simulation (LES) reduction: both take a high-dimensional physics model and replace removed details with a learned or data-fitted correction term.
It demonstrates hybrid physics-data modeling, where the equations set the low-order structure and data fills in the missing correction term.
practical_caution: A simplified radiation model is only as good as its guesses for the missing pieces. To compress the Eddington tensor (the term that says how radiation travels in different directions) with POD or DMD, you must give the method training data that covers all the real conditions where you will actually use the model. If your training data misses a scenario, the simplified model will stumble there.
selected_evidence: Reduced models for thermal radiative transfer problems based on moment equations and POD DMD of Eddington tensor.
High dimensionality non-linearity different scales in time and space and energy strong coupling.
The main burden here is actually the transport equation.
Data compression techniques for approximative closures... Eddington tensor.
The transport equation is removed from calculations.
takeaway: The core insight is that moment-based reduced models work by keeping the low-order structure of the physics and using data to learn or compress the closure terms that appear when you squeeze out details.
worked_example:
The speaker runs a 2D flat-source (Fleck-Cummings-style) thermal radiative transfer test on a square domain [0,6] x [0,6] cm, with incoming Planckian radiation at 1 keV on the left boundary and the domain initialized cold at 1 eV (10^-3 keV). The full simulation uses 300 time steps of 2 x 10^-2 ns each (0 to 6 ns), a 20 x 20 spatial grid, 17 frequency groups, and an S-quadrature with 36 angles per octant = 144 directions. Multiplying it out (cells x directions x groups x time) gives roughly 10^6 unknowns for the high-order transport solve; the reduced moment system lives in a space thousands of times smaller.

He generates snapshots of the Eddington-tensor grid functions across all groups, all cells, and all time, stacks them into a data matrix, and takes its POD (an SVD). Truncating by an energy criterion: keeping enough modes so the discarded singular-value energy is below 10^-2 needs about rank 15; below 10^-4 needs about rank 40 (out of the full rank 300). So a 300-dimensional time history of the closure collapses to ~15 numbers.

Feeding that low-rank Eddington closure back into the moment equations, the reduced model's temperature error versus the full solve tracks the tolerance: psi = 10^-2 gives about 10^-4 relative error in temperature, 10^-4 gives about 10^-6, 10^-6 gives about 10^-8 -- roughly two orders of magnitude better than the truncation tolerance, and convergence is clean and near-uniform in time. DMD gives similar accuracy at slightly lower rank but starts picking up numerical noise as the rank approaches full.
deeper_mechanics:
The Boltzmann/radiative-transfer equation is integro-differential: L psi + S psi = q, where L is the streaming (hyperbolic) operator and S the scattering/coupling integral. Instead of reducing psi directly, the method takes angular moments (integrate over direction omega with weights 1 and omega) to get equations for energy density E and flux F. Those aren't closed -- the second moment needs the Eddington (quasi-diffusion) tensor D = <omega omega I> / <I>, i.e. the direction-averaged outer product of the travel direction weighted by intensity. D is the exact closure, and the trick is that D is a stable functional (insensitive to variations in the high-order solution), which makes the coupled nonlinear iteration converge fast.

The multilevel hierarchy is: high-order transport -> multigroup low-order quasi-diffusion (closed by the group Eddington tensor) -> effective one-group ('gray') equations (closed by an energy-averaged Eddington tensor and effective gray opacities), coupled at the gray level to the material energy balance. Data compression enters only at the closure: build a snapshot matrix G of Eddington-tensor grid functions, take G = U Sigma V^T, keep the rank-r truncation D approx sum_k u_k sigma_k v_k^T. DMD instead fits a linear evolution operator B (from shifted snapshot matrices X, X', B = X' X^+ via pseudo-inverse) so the closure is reconstructed as an expansion in eigenmodes of B; an equilibrium-subtracted variant fits deviations from the near-steady final state.

Because only the closure is approximated (the moment equations themselves stay exact), the reduced model inherits the physics and the error is controlled by the singular-value spectrum, converging back to the full solve's own iterative tolerance (~10^-15) as psi -> 0.
failure_boundary:
Trust erodes in two ways the speaker names. DMD becomes sensitive as the retained rank climbs toward full: the small singular values it must invert are numerically noisy, so instead of getting more accurate the DMD closure picks up spurious oscillations -- more rank stops helping and starts hurting. Equilibrium-subtracted DMD is better at low rank but even more sensitive at high rank. The spatial error is largest at the radiation front (where the wave is, gradients are steep and the low-rank closure resolves it least well), so the method is least trustworthy exactly at the moving boundary you care about.

The bigger open boundary is parametric extrapolation. All the shown results are reproductive: the ROM replays a case whose snapshots it already saw. For new incoming temperatures or opacities the speaker only has 1D interpolation between pre-sampled parameter points, and DMD did not give reliable interpolation when the time step changed. So outside the sampled parameter mesh, and for stiff regimes where the Eddington closure varies faster than the retained modes capture, the reduced model is not yet dependable.

title: Christopher Earls: Gaining Mechanistic Insight Through Learning Green's Functions
speaker: Christopher Earls
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from data and examples instead of only hand-written equations. This talk shows how you can learn what's called a Green's function — a special response pattern that captures how a system reacts to a poke — and use that pattern to reverse-engineer the hidden rules that govern the system and understand what's actually happening inside.
core_problem: Deep learning programs can predict what a system will do next, but real science needs to understand why it happens. When the equation that controls the system is unknown or too hard to write by hand, you can learn the solution operator — a map that says 'given this input, the output will be that' — sometimes called a Green's function. Once you have that map, you can study it like a fingerprint to read off what physical laws might be hiding in the data.
first_principles_model: For a simple (linear) rule — one where changes add up straightforwardly — a Green's function is the answer you get when you poke the system with a single quick impulse, like a hammer tap. Once you know that single-poke answer, you can reconstruct the response to any other input by carefully adding up (integrating) the Green's function's response scaled by that input, like building the answer from overlapping echoes. Teaching a computer to learn this kernel (the pattern inside the integral) from observed data gives you a compact, human-readable operator that can tell you what hidden equation is probably controlling the system, and which predictions you can test in reality.
key_claims: Patterns in how systems actually respond to inputs contain clues about hidden mechanistic structure.
The goal is not just to predict what happens next, but to learn response patterns and compact integral kernels that can be decoded back into rules.
Green's functions are a classical, time-tested bridge connecting single impulses to the equations that govern complex behavior.
Deep learning can take the old Green's function idea and apply it to new problems and kinds of data.
Operators pulled out by learning can be examined like fingerprints to find features that suggest what mechanisms are at work.
This method is related to other neural operator techniques but distinct in how it prioritizes operator interpretability.

important_terms.meaning: The answer you get when a linear rule is poked once with a single quick impulse; acts as a response pattern you can combine and layer to build the answer to any other input.
A map that says: given a source, forcing, or input, here is the corresponding output or system response.
A function placed inside an integral (a summing operation) that converts input data into output data.
An unknown rule that controls how a system changes, inferred indirectly by studying the data, never given to you upfront.
Understanding the actual gears and levers behind observed behavior — the physical or mathematical mechanism — rather than just predicting what happens.

stanford_connections: This talk brings together operator learning and interpretability: the operator you learn should teach you something real about what physics is hidden underneath.
It connects to nonlocal kernels because both involve learning integral kernels by studying how systems respond to inputs.
It also complements equation discovery methods by learning the solution pattern itself rather than trying to manually pick and name individual PDE terms.
practical_caution: A learned Green's function works best for simple, straightforward systems where changes combine by addition. When the system has wild, chaotic nonlinearities where small changes cause big surprises, you have to test the learned operator carefully or only use it near the specific conditions where you trained it.
selected_evidence: Gaining mechanistic insight through learning Green's functions.
Uncovering the solutions to hidden PDEs.
This kind of reminds me of a Green's function.
If I put a source term here and I have an impulse response.
Learn linear solution operators compact integral functions integral kernels.
takeaway: An operator you can actually read and interpret — one that you learn from data — is often more useful for doing science than a pure prediction box, because it points back toward the actual mechanism driving the system.
worked_example:
For the 1D Poisson equation with Dirichlet boundary conditions, empirical Green's function learning recovers the analytical Green's function with 0.01 relative error (noise-free data). When Gaussian white noise with standard deviation equal to the mean response is added to every measurement, error grows to 0.03 relative error—modest degradation despite significant contamination. The 1D Helmholtz equation (k=15 on unit interval) achieves 0.03 error; the Burgers equation at θ=10 reveals antisymmetry and fine structure in the learned Green's function matching the self-adjoint operator property.

A multi-physics domain (one quarter Helmholtz, three quarters Poisson) shows the learned Green's function shadows both diffusion-like structure (top right) and wave-like structure (bottom left) in different regions. Manifold interpolation at unobserved parameter θ=7 (using library entries at θ=1,5,10) yields interpolated Green's function matching the truly learned one at θ=7 with 0.04 relative error—demonstrating data-free prediction.
deeper_mechanics:
Green's function theory: for linear operator L, the Green's function G(x,x') satisfies L*G = δ(x-x'). Solution u = ∫ G(x,x')f(x')dx' + homogeneous boundary contribution. Spectral decomposition via Fredholm theory: G = Σₖ (conjugate(eigₖ)·eigₖ)/λₖ. Empirical approach replaces orthonormal eigenbases with POD modes extracted from data ensembles. For each parameter θᵢ, collect snapshots under random Gaussian process excitations, compute SVD to get left singular vectors (spatial POD modes), and solve for diagonal coefficient matrices Σₖ minimizing least-squares fit between observed and reconstructed data.

Deep rational neural networks further relax self-adjoint requirement: learn G and homogeneous solution u_h as separate 3-2 rational networks (rational functions replace ReLU/tanh activations) trained on superposition loss: ∫G⊗f + u_h ≈ observed_solution. Rational poles cluster at singularities in the true solution, providing mechanistic insight. Training uses only 100 cause-effect pairs via Gaussian process excitations with tight covariance kernels—over-sampling guarantees rank-k approximation almost surely per randomized linear algebra theory.
failure_boundary: Method requires self-adjointness for spectral decomposition (empirical phase). Advection-dominated or non-self-adjoint operators violate this—though deep learning extension removes this constraint. Passive observation (no control over excitation) reveals only a narrow subspace of the Green's function; Gaussian process excitations must have high-frequency content (small covariance kernel width) to ensure rank-k coverage. With sparse or missing data (e.g., excluding shock region), recovery degrades but rational networks show surprising robustness—poles still cluster at discontinuities via extrapolation through nearby observations. Computational bottleneck: rational network training requires second-order optimization (L-BFGS combined with Adam) for convergence near singularities; first-order gradient descent fails. Systems of PDEs (Stokes flow, coupled ODEs) are tractable but require learning block-matrix Green's functions; coupling strength determines conditioning.

title: Jesse Capecelatro: Turbulent Disperse Two-Phase Flows
speaker: Jesse Capecelatro
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. One problem: when you have a gas or liquid with particles floating through it—like smoke in air or spray from an engine—the particles and the fluid push on each other in complicated ways. This talk asks: how do you write a math rule that captures both what the fluid does AND what the particles do, when they're constantly talking to each other?
core_problem: Dispersed two-phase flows show up everywhere you look: smoke stacks, spray engines, sediment stirred up in the ocean. The puzzle is hard because particles do more than just float along. Each particle stirs up a wake behind it, gets shoved around by the fluid's churning, bumps into other particles, clumps together in spots, and bounces off walls. If you only write down the math for the fluid alone, you miss all of this. Add real particles to the mix, and suddenly the old math stops working because the particles actually change how the fluid churns.
first_principles_model: A gas-particle flow splits into two players: the carrier gas (which does all the churning) and the particles scattered through it (the tiny drops or solid bits). Each particle feels a drag force from the fluid trying to slow it down, but here's the key: each particle also shoves back on the gas through its wake and by stealing momentum. When you try to write down one averaged rule that works everywhere instead of tracking every particle separately, you run into a wall. The averaged equations have terms you cannot compute without knowing the tiny details that got averaged away. This is where learning from data comes in: train a program to guess those missing pieces while keeping all the physics you already know.
key_claims: Particles can change the intensity of turbulent churning by a factor of two or more.
Most models for averaged flows just tack on particle terms to the single-fluid equations without rethinking the whole picture.
Those tacked-on additions break down when particle density swings from very sparse to very dense, where the push-back from particles becomes too big to ignore.

Learning from data is now being used in real applications: training a program to guess missing closure terms, detecting when the model is drifting from reality, and patching models when you don't know all the physics.
The talk shows ways to use learning that go beyond having a program simply guess a single number for each missing term.
Putting randomness into particle-force models helps the math keep the right spread in particle speeds and how far particles get scattered.

important_terms.meaning: A flow where tiny droplets or solid particles are spread throughout and tumbling around inside a liquid or gas.
When the fluid pushes on particles AND the particles push back on the fluid hard enough to change how the fluid moves—neither one ignores the other.
A rule that averages out all the tiny wiggles in a two-phase flow to find the overall average gas motion and overall average particle motion, instead of tracking every speck.
The job of guessing or approximating the pieces that show up in your averaged equations because the tiny details that were averaged away are actually mattering.
A rule for particle forces that includes randomness—tiny random nudges—to match the real jiggling and spreading that you see in actual or simulated flows.

stanford_connections: This talk carries forward a pattern from earlier talks in the series: whenever you average a rule or filter it down, you throw away information, and you have to guess what you threw away. Here you're averaging a two-phase flow; before it was one-fluid turbulence.
It connects to data-driven model repair, where the learned part only patches the missing pieces instead of learning the whole answer from scratch.
It shows a real-world case where forgetting that particles and fluid push on each other leads to huge errors in what your model predicts.
practical_caution: A math model trained only on flowing gas (no particles) or on flows where particles are spread thin will often fail when you switch to dense swarms of particles that really change how the gas behaves. Before you trust any model, always check it against both sparse cases (few particles) and dense cases (lots of particles). Test whether it gets right not just the average gas speed but also how wide the particles spread out and where they actually go—not just which way they're drifting.
selected_evidence: Particles have an order one effect on the background turbulence.
Data-driven modeling has exploded... closure modeling uncertainty quantification model augmentation.
Multiphase turbulence modeling has really... lags the development.
Extensions of single-phase turbulence.
Treating the force stochastically is showing promise to guarantee certain statistics.
takeaway: The real problem in multiphase turbulence is not guessing the particles or guessing the fluid—it's getting the statistics of how particles and fluid trade momentum right. Particles are not just hitchhikers. They actively reshape the turbulent eddies and swirls that the fluid makes.
worked_example: Direct numerical simulation: 1-5% volume fraction gas-solid suspension, particle Reynolds Re_p~10-50, density ratio ~2000. Homogeneous cooling: ~100 particles, granular temperature evolves from T(0)=0.5 to steady-state; stochastic drag model (Langevin force) predicts transient and steady-state velocity variance across Re_p and ε_p. Channel flow Re_τ=10,000, mass loading φ=1-20: at φ=20 clustering forms, fluid TKE spectrum shifts from k^(-5/3) (single-phase) to broadband suppression. Heat-transfer entrance length reduced 40% by particle clustering.
deeper_mechanics: Drag force on single particle: F_d=6πμr v_slip (Stokes). In dense suspension: mean drag correlated by Tennetti-Garg (ε_p, Re) but variance ~equal to mean. Model decomposition: F_i = F_mean(Re,ε_p) + ΔF_i where ΔF_i~Langevin: dΔF/dt = -(ΔF/τ_f)dt + σ_f dW. Timescale τ_f from collision theory (granular temp, radial distribution), σ_f normalized by isolated particle drag. Multiphase RANS derived via phase-averaging Navier-Stokes: unclosed drag production (ρ_p φ u_d·τ_particle) and drag dissipation (ρ_p φ F_d·(u_p-u_f)). Sparse regression identifies algebraic closure: β_i T_i basis with L1 penalty.
failure_boundary: Deterministic drag laws (mean-only) cannot capture velocity variance or dispersion; variance underestimated 2-3x. Stochastic model loses pairwise spatial correlations (radial distribution function, drafting-kissing-tumbling); fails when two-particle interactions dominant. Volume fraction >10% or clustered regimes: sparse regression training data from homogeneous settling may not transfer (transient channel flow showed ~15% error). DNS limited to ~500M particles; reactor-scale ~10^12 particles requires closures at RANS scale. Radiative heat transfer in dense suspensions unmodeled (end-body optics problem).

title: Ionut-Gabriel Farcas: Learning Hierarchies Of Reduced-Dimension And Context-Aware Models For Monte Carlo Sampling
speaker: Ionut-Gabriel Farcas
one_sentence: This whole series asks: can computers learn to predict how physical things behave by studying examples, instead of using only hand-written math rules? This talk takes up a specific question: when you need to know how uncertain a prediction is (like how much a structure might bend), you often have to run expensive simulations many times to get a good answer. What if you ran some cheap, rough approximations first to figure out which expensive runs matter most? This talk shows how mixing cheap approximate models with expensive accurate ones cuts the total cost while still getting a solid uncertainty estimate.
core_problem: Running expensive accurate simulations over and over to measure how uncertain something is costs a lot of computer time and money.
