You can add a cheap rough model (an approximation that runs fast) to cut total cost, but only if three things happen: the rough model's answers stay close to the expensive model's answers, the rough model is actually cheap enough to run many times faster, and the rough model makes sense in the region of inputs you are testing.
first_principles_model: A two-level sampler mixes together answers from expensive simulations and cheap approximations. The cheap approximation might be systematically off by some amount (that is what biased means — consistently wrong in one direction), but if its answer still follows the expensive one closely and costs much less to run, it shrinks down how scattered your final estimate is (spread is also called variance) for the same amount of computer work. Context-aware methods build or swap out which cheap model to use, adapting it on the fly to fit the exact region or single sample you are evaluating right now.
key_claims: In two-level methods, cheap and expensive models work as a team; one does not just replace the other.
The job of a cheap model is to cut the total amount of expensive computation you need.
How good your answer is depends on how closely the models agree and how much each one costs to run.
Simplified models built by extracting patterns from expensive simulations can be accurate but may still take noticeable time to run.
Models fit by regression (straight-line fitting) are cheaper but need many data points before they become reliable.
Building models that change based on what you are currently solving gives you more options than one model that works for everything.

important_terms.meaning: A way to estimate an answer by mixing samples from cheap rough models with samples from expensive accurate ones, so you get a better answer for less total work.
A cheap approximation that runs fast but may have some systematic error; used to spot which expensive computations are worth doing.
A model chosen or rebuilt based on the specific inputs or job at hand, tailored to what you are solving right now instead of one fixed model for all cases.
A single score that adds together how far off your answer is on average (bias) and how much it jumps around (variance).
A number from zero to one that says how tightly the cheap model's output tracks the expensive model's output; higher numbers mean the cheap model is more helpful.

stanford_connections: This talk ties simplified models (smaller versions extracted from full simulations) with uncertainty work to show that simplified models are sources of knowledge, not just faster stand-ins.
It extends targeted sampling: put expensive accurate runs only where the answer changes the most.
It also connects to digital twins, since digital twins need to know how uncertain their predictions are, but often have limited computing power available.
practical_caution: A biased cheap model (one that is systematically off) can still help you, but you must test it: Does how closely it tracks the expensive model times how much money you save actually make your final answer better? Do not assume a fast approximation helps just because it runs quickly.
selected_evidence: Low- and high-fidelity models are used together.
The primary purpose of low-fidelity models is supporting computations with the high-fidelity models.
The mean squared error... depends on the correlation coefficients and the evaluation costs.
Low fidelity models are contextual.
If you need to invest only 10 high-fidelity runs and 1 million... runs then you can do it.
takeaway: The core question is: how do you split your computation budget to get the best uncertainty estimate? A useful cheap model cuts how wrong your estimate is, measured per unit of computing cost, even if by itself it is not accurate enough to replace the expensive simulator.
worked_example: Plasma microturbulence simulation (GENE code, 250,000 DOF, 14 uncertain parameters: device geometry, particle species) with budget B=50k to 1M GPU-seconds. Multi-fidelity sampling uses: high-fidelity model (GENE simulation, w₀=1), sparse-grid adaptive interpolation (S-grid, 14D, reduced-dimension models with 9, then 6 parameters based on Sobol sensitivity). For 1M budget allocation: 200 high-fidelity runs, 50k sparse-grid evaluations on 14D model, 100k on 9D reduced, 200k on 6D reduced. Compared to standard Monte Carlo (only 100-300 high-fidelity samples), multi-fidelity with all three models achieves near-2x reduction in mean-squared error; computational speedup ~8 days → 1 hour for same accuracy level.
deeper_mechanics: Multifidelity estimator θ_MF = θ_HF + Σᵢ ρᵢ(θ_LF,i - c_i θ̂_LF,i) where ρ is control variate weight maximizing variance reduction. Mean squared error: MSE = Var(HF) · [1 - Σᵢ (ρ²_i r²_i / (c_i w_rel,i))], r_i = correlation(HF, LF_i), w_rel,i = cost(LF_i)/cost(HF). Reduced-dimension models built adaptively: full high-fidelity training set projected onto basis chosen by greedy algorithm retaining most energetic modes (POD + sensitivity screening). Context-aware algorithm finds n₁ (HF evaluations for model construction) minimizing bound: MSE_bound ∝ n₁^(-α) + (B-n₁)^(-β) where α, β = accuracy and cost rates. Optimal n₁ independent of total budget B beyond threshold; separates exploration (model building) from exploitation (sampling).
failure_boundary: If low-fidelity model accuracy degrades sharply or becomes worse than high-fidelity over part of parameter space (large negative correlation), variance reduction fails and algorithm inverts, making error worse. Reduced-dimension models constructed via sensitivity screening can miss important interactions if second-order or higher-order parameter couplings not captured by first-order screening; parametric uncertainty not well-separated. Coarse surrogates (e.g., 6-parameter model) trained on limited data may have systematic bias far from training region, reducing correlation r_i and negating speedup. Method assumes low-fidelity models available or constructible; if only one model exists, no multi-fidelity benefit.

title: Peter Benner: Identification Of Nonlinear Dynamical Systems From Noisy Measurements
speaker: Peter Benner
organization: Max Planck Institute for Dynamics of Complex Technical Systems
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. This talk focuses on a tricky case: figuring out the hidden rules of a system by watching it move over time, especially when the measurements you're seeing are blurry or incomplete. The challenge is that if you try to work backward from the data to find what the rules are, small errors in measurement get blown up and lead you astray—so instead, you step the equations forward through time in tiny increments to find rules that could have generated all the data you actually saw.
core_problem: Imagine watching a system move—a pendulum, a heated rod, a chemical reaction—and you want to write down the hidden rules that govern it. You write down what you see at different moments, but your measurements aren't perfect. The big headaches: if you try to compute how fast things are changing by looking at your data (the way you might compute speed from position readings), small measurement errors explode into huge errors in your answer. Also, there are infinitely many possible rules you could write down—how do you pick the right ones? And when there's noise in the data, it's easy to accidentally pick rules that really just describe the noise, not the true physics.
first_principles_model: Any system that moves has a hidden rule: at each moment in time, the rule says how fast the system's state is changing, depending only on what the state is right now. To discover this rule from data, you make a big list of candidate terms (maybe powers, products, sines, anything you think could be useful) and ask: which terms from the list are actually active in the real rule? Instead of taking derivatives directly from noisy data (which gets unreliable), you try stepping the equations forward through tiny time steps (using a procedure like Runge-Kutta, which estimates the state by taking weighted averages of how fast things are changing at a few points within each step) and checking whether the stepped-forward states match what you actually observed. This turns the problem into picking the right terms from your list.
key_claims: Discovering the rules that govern a physical system is essential if you want to predict what it will do, optimize it, or control it.
One practical approach is sparse identification: look at all your candidate terms and use math to pick only the few that are really active.
Measurement errors and sparse, incomplete observations are the biggest practical obstacles when trying to reverse-engineer nonlinear systems.
Stepping the equations forward through time, rather than computing derivatives from the raw data, leads to more stable and reliable discovery.
Automatically choosing which candidate terms to offer is still an unsolved problem.
Different types of systems (like waves spreading through space or material flowing) need different time-stepping methods to get stable results.

important_terms.meaning: The process of figuring out a mathematical rule that describes how a system behaves by comparing the rule's predictions to measurements you've made.
Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics—a method that searches a list of candidate terms and picks only the few that best explain the observed behavior.
A list of candidate building-block functions (like x, x squared, x times y, sine of x) from which the discovery method selects the true terms in the rule.

A procedure that steps a system forward in time by computing the rate of change at several points within each time step and combining them into a weighted average—used to approximate how a system evolves.
Real-world data that is corrupted by sensor error, rounding, or other imperfections; the extra error hides the true signal and can trick identification methods into picking the wrong terms.

stanford_connections: This talk picks up where earlier talks about interpretability ended, diving into the numerical and mathematical details of how to actually find equations from data.
It relates to talks about Koopman operators and Green's functions because all three aim to uncover the hidden structure of a system from what you can measure.
It also connects to control theory, since you almost always need an accurate model of a system before you can design a strategy to steer it or keep it stable.
practical_caution: When you discover equations this way, you might end up with rules that look perfectly reasonable but actually just fit the noise in your data, not the true underlying physics. The list of candidate terms you choose, the method you use to step through time, and how you treat measurement errors are all assumptions—pick them wrong and you'll find an equation that's wrong. There's no automated way to tell if your candidate list is complete enough or if you've accidentally picked noise instead of signal.
selected_evidence: Identification of nonlinear dynamical systems from noisy measurements.
Sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics approach.
We will focus on one issue with this approach and suggest a new variant.
We will add a higher level of noise.
Optimizing the choice of the dictionary automatically... is an important question.
takeaway: Finding the hidden rules of a system by watching its behavior is not just a matching problem—you can't just fit an equation to the numbers. You have to combine it with physics-based reasoning, careful handling of measurement errors, and good choices about which candidate terms to offer the discovery method.
worked_example:
Cubic oscillator (2D ODE, cubic terms only): standard SINDy fails at large timesteps (h=0.1), inserting spurious quadratic and quintic terms; Runge-Kutta CINDY maintains pure cubic form with small coefficient error at same h. FitzHugh-Nagumo spiking model: ground truth cubic right-hand side. Standard SINDy identifies extra unwanted terms at h=0.05; RK4-CINDY recovers correct model. Parametric bifurcation (μ-dependent normal form, bifurcations 1-3): identifies parsimonious model across test parameters outside training range; Gaussian noise 5% amplitude tolerated, higher noise shifts identification failure.

Denoised FitzHugh-Nagumo with 40% noise: raw trajectory appears as scattered cloud; implicit neural network filters noise, Runge-Kutta scheme regularizes, recovers limit cycle attractor structure.
deeper_mechanics:
RK4-CINDY formulation: replace derivative data (noisy, requires differentiation) with discrete constraint x_{i+1} = Rk4[Φ(x_i)·ψ; h]. Minimize ||x_{i+1} - Rk4||^2_2 + λ||ψ||_1 over sparse vector ψ (feature selection). Sequential thresholding: solve LASSO, zero small components, refit without those terms, iterate until convergence. Handles parametric ODEs by augmenting state x := [x, μ] (parameter dynamics dx_μ/dt=0). Rational functions: two separate sparse selectors for numerator and denominator polynomials.

Denoising hybrid: implicit network g_θ(t) fits noisy time series; Runge-Kutta scheme constrains consistency with dynamics φ_θ(x) representing RHS. Loss = ||g_θ(t) - y_noisy||^2 + ||g_θ(t_i+1) - RK4[φ_θ; h]||^2 + weighted gradient penalty.
failure_boundary: SINDy requires known dictionary structure; missing nonlinear terms (e.g., rational functions) not in library causes systematic bias. High noise (>5%) without denoising produces false positives in feature selection, over-fit models. Dictionary explosion: polynomial degree explosion in multivariate systems makes brute-force search intractable; adaptive dictionary discovery open problem. Stiff systems (wide timescale separation) ill-suited to explicit RK4: method suggests switching integrators (e.g., implicit BDF) but implementation details deferred. Long rollout prediction: learned models can diverge from true attractor if trained on finite windows; chaotic systems especially vulnerable.

title: Youngsoo Choi: libROM For Physics-Constrained Data-Driven Physical Simulations
speaker: Youngsoo Choi
one_sentence: This series chases one goal: getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from data instead of only writing down the hand-built rules that engineers have always used. One way to do this is to build a smaller, faster stand-in for a big, slow simulator—a reduced model that keeps some of the original math constraints baked in so it stays close to reality. This talk is about libROM, a working software toolkit that handles all the messy details: finding the hidden patterns in your data, speeding up calculations for tricky nonlinear systems, and tying pieces together so you can actually use reduced models in real simulations.
core_problem: Getting a computer to predict how air rushes over a wing, how heat spreads through metal, or how water sloshes is slow and costly if you start from scratch each time. You could train a learning program (a system with millions of dials the computer tunes by trial and error until its answers look right) on examples and skip the hand-built math—but that often fails because the program has no clue about the physics laws and breaks them. Or you could bake those laws directly into the training as hard rules and make the program respect them—but then you need working code, standard recipes, and ways to check that your result is trustworthy. LibROM steps in to give you that machinery.
first_principles_model: The core idea: you have a full, detailed simulator that works but is too slow for repeated use. You gather a bunch of example runs from that simulator and look for hidden patterns—the handful of directions in the data that capture most of what's happening. You project all your data onto those directions, which shrinks the problem to a handful of numbers instead of millions. You build a small rule (a smaller version of the original) that evolves those few numbers over time. Finally, you unshrink the result back to the full size so a human can read it. For tricky nonlinear systems (where the rule isn't a simple straight line), this speedup breaks unless you're smart about which parts of the rule you actually calculate each step—that's called hyper-reduction, and it samples only the expensive parts that matter most instead of computing everything. LibROM bundles all these ingredients into one toolkit so you don't rebuild it yourself every time.
key_claims: Physicists and engineers have always mixed real data with their written rules—think of tuning a weather model against measurements or calibrating an engine to match tests.
A learning program trained only on examples ignores the physics and often breaks in new situations; a program that also learns from the governing equations stays honest.
LibROM includes several recipes for finding hidden patterns in data—some that process all data at once, some that update as new data come in, and some that are fast but randomized.
When a system has tangled, nonlinear behavior, you must skip most of the expensive calculations each step, keeping only the few that change the answer—libROM does this.
The toolkit ships with ready-to-run examples: heat spreading through a rod, diffusion that eats itself, and fluid sloshing in a box.
For long simulations where material gets pushed far from its start, libROM can split time into windows or build a curved reduced model instead of a flat one.

important_terms.meaning: A working toolkit from Lawrence Livermore National Lab that builds smaller, faster stand-ins for physics simulators by blending data patterns with the governing equations.
A small, fast stand-in for a physics simulator that uses both real examples and the actual governing equations to stay accurate.
A step-by-step recipe that finds hidden patterns in data as new examples arrive, updating the answer each time without redoing all the math from scratch.
Discrete Empirical Interpolation Method—a trick to skip most of the expensive calculations in a small model by computing only the tangled nonlinear parts that actually matter.
A small model made from several even-smaller pieces that each describe one part of the system, wired together to work as a whole.

stanford_connections: Earlier talks in this series showed what's possible in theory—finding hidden patterns, speeding up tangled nonlinear models, and building models from linked pieces. This talk shows how to actually do it with real code you can run.
It connects to talks on finding hidden patterns in data, hyper-reduction for speed, and assembling linked systems by showing them as reusable ingredients in libROM.
It also completes the arc of the whole series: concepts alone don't matter—you need a toolkit you can hand to someone and say, 'Use this to build a smaller, faster, trustworthy simulator.'
practical_caution: A toolkit makes the workflow smoother, but it can't think for you. You still have to decide: which hidden patterns to use, which sampling points to take, what physics to bake in, and how to verify your answer is close to the full simulator. The software just does the bookkeeping—the judgment calls are yours.
selected_evidence: libROM has greedy algorithm capability.
A library for reduced models.
Efficient proper orthonormal decomposition using various singular value decomposition techniques.
In order to achieve the efficiency we have to apply the hyper reduction.
Black box approach... and physics constraints approaches.
takeaway: Building computers that learn to predict physics requires two things: working code and human insight. LibROM is the engineering layer that turns the math ideas into something you can actually repeat, share, and trust.
worked_example: A shaped charge penetration simulation takes 7.4 days per full-order solve. Using POD-based projection onto 20 basis modes reduces a 160,000-dimensional system to 20 ODEs. With hyper-reduction via DEIM sampling only 360 quadrature points instead of all 160k, speedup reaches 14.6–87.8× across Lagrangian hydrodynamics test cases while maintaining <0.1 percent relative error. For a Rayleigh–Taylor instability problem, speedup improves as problem size grows—from 10× on a smaller grid to 100×+ on fine meshes—because compressibility of the solution manifold outpaces dimensional growth.
deeper_mechanics: Projection-based ROM approximates state as u ≈ V c where V contains POD modes and c are time-dependent coefficients. Galerkin projection onto V^T of the residual R(u) = 0 yields reduced system M c-dot + K c + Q(c) = 0, where M = V^T E V, K = V^T A V, and Q is the reduced nonlinear tensor. Hyper-reduction (DEIM) selects r << n sample indices via greedy algorithm, replacing Q(c) with Z Q-bar(Z^T c) where Z samples only the important modes. The sampling matrix enforces that nonlinear residuals vanish at selected DOFs, balancing accuracy against cost. Regularization tuning (SVD truncation, Tikhonov) handles ill-conditioning from near-collinear basis vectors.
failure_boundary: ROM fails when the dominant modes don't span the solution manifold—happens in transport-dominated (high-Re) flows where sharp fronts move unpredictably. Linear projection cannot capture moving localized features; mode alignment requires training data spanning the full parameter space. For parametric problems, basis constructed at one parameter may be inaccurate at distant points; greedy parameter sampling helps but is expensive. Offline cost (computing POD, assembling M/K/Q, DEIM selection) becomes prohibitive for very high-dimensional systems (>10M DOFs). Nonlinear model order reduction via manifold learning or autoencoders adds further computational overhead and loses physical interpretability.

title: Masayuki Yano: Reliable, Efficient, And Automated Model Reduction Of Parametrized Nonlinear PDEs
speaker: Masayuki Yano
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical systems behave by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math rules. One challenge: to learn correctly from examples, you often start with a smaller, simpler model that captures the essence of what matters. This talk is about how to automatically build such simplified models for complex physics problems (where behavior changes in weird ways, not just linearly), control the mistakes that slip in during simplification, and know which new examples to test next to make the model trustworthy.
core_problem: When you want to predict how something physical will behave—say, air flowing over a wing or heat spreading through a metal block—you write down the rules that govern it. These rules (called differential equations, or PDEs) are so complicated that solving them for many different setups takes forever. So engineers build a smaller, faster copy of the full model that captures the essential behavior. But this smaller copy can betray you: if the full model wasn't built carefully enough, or if the simplification threw away the wrong details, the smaller copy gives wrong answers. Building these smaller copies by hand takes months and needs someone who understands both the physics and the tricks—and for tangled, unpredictable flows, you might not even know which tricks will work.
first_principles_model: This talk describes a method that makes computers do the hand work. Instead of trying to predict every detail everywhere, you first pick the one thing you actually care about—maybe lift on a wing, or the maximum temperature reached. The method then: carefully divides the space into small pieces (a finer or coarser mesh) using an automatic rule that judges whether the answer is good enough; finds a smart choice of 'basis shapes' (simple building blocks that get mixed together to form the final answer) by looking at examples across different parameters and cutting out shapes that barely matter; speeds up the expensive calculation of leftover errors (how badly the physics rules are violated) by checking them only on a few pieces instead of all; and uses information from running the physics rules backwards to weight where mistakes hurt most. Finally, a loop greedily picks the next example to test by choosing the setup where the method predicts the biggest potential mistake.
key_claims: When you build a simplified model, you pick up mistakes from three places: the way you chop up space into pieces, the way you pick your simple building blocks, and the way you compute the numbers. You have to watch all three.
Using curved pieces and adjusting their size based on current errors can make the expensive practice phase—where you compute the examples the model learns from—much faster.
Solving the physics rules backwards (a technique called the adjoint or dual problem) tells you where mistakes matter most for the answer you care about.
You can speed up the expensive calculation of leftover errors by computing them only on a handful of pieces instead of the whole space.
A step-by-step loop can automatically build the mesh, the building blocks, and the integration rule all at once.
When you have many knobs to turn or flows with sudden jumps, the challenges are much harder and stay mostly unsolved.

important_terms.meaning: A smaller, faster version of a full physics simulator that you build by keeping the most important pieces and throwing out the rest.
A way of dividing space into pieces and solving the physics rules on each one, where the computer automatically decides how fine to make the pieces based on where the answer is most uncertain.
A method to measure mistakes by running the physics rules backwards and using that backward solution to weight where forward mistakes hurt the answer you care about most.
A trick to speed up calculations by computing expensive sums (like errors) on just a few chosen pieces instead of every piece.
A simple but effective strategy that picks the next example to test by always choosing the one where the method guesses the error will be largest.

stanford_connections: This work continues earlier talks in the series about building simplified models, but switches focus: instead of explaining how an expert tunes a model by trial and error, it shows how to make the tuning itself automatic and trustworthy.

It builds on earlier talks about controlling errors and picking training examples through principled choices—especially the idea of working backwards through the problem to understand where mistakes matter most.
It also touches talks about complex, choppy flows (where air rushes or shocks appear) because those are the problems where automatic tools are most needed and hardest to get right.
practical_caution: The language in this talk says 'certified'—meaning the method gives you a bound on error—but some of these bounds are careful estimates, not ironclad guarantees. When you run the whole automated pipeline on a real problem, especially one with many knobs to turn or sudden jumps (shocks), you still need to run sanity checks by hand and think about whether the answer makes sense.
selected_evidence: Reliable efficient and automated model reduction of parameterized nonlinear PDEs.
Control all three sources of the error... finite mesh... reduced basis... reduced quadrature.
Adaptive high order method enables efficient offline training.
Evaluate it in a very small subset of elements.
Certified here in quotes because we don't have error bounds these are simply estimates.
takeaway: The lesson is this: if you automate the building of simpler models, you have to automate the checking too. You must know exactly what you're squeezing out and what you're keeping, have a way to measure mistakes in the thing you care about, and pick new test cases that fill the biggest gaps. Automation without that thinking is dangerous.
worked_example: Illustrative: A parametric PDE (e.g., nonlinear diffusion with parameter μ) is sampled at training points in parameter space. A POD basis {ϕ₁,...,ϕᵣ} is extracted from full-order snapshots. The reduced solution u_rom(μ) = Σᵢ αᵢ(μ)ϕᵢ is projected via Galerkin: find α such that (∂u_rom/∂t + N[u_rom], ϕⱼ) = 0 for all j ∈ [1..r]. The greedy algorithm adaptively selects parameter samples where certified error bounds exceed a tolerance.
deeper_mechanics: A posteriori error bound ε(μ) provides guaranteed rom accuracy: ||u_fom(μ) - u_rom(μ)|| ≤ ε(μ). Dual-norm (residual-based): ε(μ) ~ ||∂u_rom/∂t + N[u_rom]||*_{H'}/α_LB(μ), where α_LB is the coercivity lower bound. Greedy loop: sample μ with largest ε(μ), add FOM solve, augment POD basis. Nonlinear term evaluation via hyper-reduction (gappy POD or DEIM: Discrete Empirical Interpolation Method) maps N_full(u_rom) → N_red(u_rom) using interpolation indices.
failure_boundary: Coercivity lower bound α_LB is expensive to compute rigorously; many implementations use heuristic estimates. For strongly nonlinear systems (shocks, bifurcations), certified bounds become loose and greedy sampling loses effectiveness. Parameter space exploration scales poorly in high-dimensional μ ∈ ℝ^P.

title: Misha Khodak: Automatic Architecture Design For Emerging Machine Learning Tasks
speaker: Misha Khodak
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of only using hand-written math. Most successful learning programs were carefully designed to work on pictures, using a trick called convolution that forces the network to look at small local patches and share what it learns across space. This talk is about how to automatically redesign these building blocks so they work on completely different problems — graphs, sequences, equations that describe change over time — without an expert having to invent new operations by hand each time.
core_problem: We have neural networks that were brilliantly tuned to see patterns in pictures by using a technique called convolution, which forces the network to notice the same small local features everywhere in the image. But real science deals with sequences (measurements over time), graphs (connected networks of things), differential equations (rules that describe how things change), and other structures that don't look like grids of pixels. For each new structure, experts have to invent new operations by hand — a slow process that only works if someone understands both the science and neural networks. Standard tools for automating network design only change which operations are plugged in, not what those operations themselves can be.
first_principles_model: Think of a neural network architecture as a recipe that says which patterns the network can recognize. Convolutions work by making the network look at small neighborhoods and reuse what it learns across space — that forces the network to find spatially local features. The idea here is to flip this: instead of asking 'how do we wire together fixed building blocks?', ask 'what properties does the problem itself have?' — is it symmetric? Does shifting matter? Is it about neighbors being related? Then design or search for operations that bake those properties in. This turns picking an architecture into finding the right operations that match the problem, rather than inventing them by guesswork.
key_claims: Neural networks designed for pictures are very good at pictures but don't transfer cleanly to sequences, graphs, or physics equations without custom operations.
Different problem structures need different neural operations — what works for images wastes effort on trees or time series.
You can design operations that keep the good properties of convolution but work on many different problem types.
You can automate the search for which operations to use in a network for a new problem.
The best choice of operations depends on both how much data you have and the structure of the problem itself.
Searching over both how to connect operations and what the operations can do is possible but computationally expensive.

important_terms.meaning: Taking successful design patterns from one problem type (like images) and adapting them to work on a different problem type (like time series) by changing the operations the network uses.

A type of neural operation designed to generalize the core idea of convolution — making the network share what it learns and focus on local structure — so it works on many different problem types beyond just pictures.

A built-in rule that reduces the number of tunable knobs in a network by forcing certain structure into it: for instance, making weights identical at different locations, or making the network treat neighbors the same way everywhere.
Automatically trying different ways to connect neural operations together — different wirings of the network — to find which arrangement learns best for a given task.
The choice of which operations to use in a network and how to wire them together; this choice determines what kinds of patterns the network can learn and which patterns it misses.

stanford_connections: Earlier in this series you learned about neural architecture search as changing how operations are wired together; this talk goes deeper by asking whether the operations themselves can be designed or searched automatically.

It connects to the talks on graph networks, Fourier neural operators, and physics-aware solvers because all of them start with a question: what structure does the problem have, and how can we build a network that respects that structure?

This reinforces the central theme: the decisions you make when designing a network act like training wheels or blinders — they decide what patterns the network can catch and what it will miss, which often matters more than how much you train it.
practical_caution: Making architecture search automatic sounds great, but the computer has no way to know what actually matters for your science unless you tell it explicitly. The search algorithm only sees one number you hand it — like 'make predictions match the true answer'. It can't care whether the predictions obey the physics, whether the model trains too slowly, or whether the answer is actually believable in the context of your field. You have to choose what success means: match the data, run fast, stay stable during training, respect physical laws, all of the above?
selected_evidence: Towards automatic architecture design for emerging machine learning tasks.
Manual design of task-specific neural operations.
XD-Operations that mimic the useful degree-of-freedom constraints of convolutions.
If you don't have a lot of data... you can use XD.
Discrete continuous optimization simultaneously... difficulty there.
takeaway: Architecture is the language the network uses to think about a problem. Automatic architecture search finds the right language to match each new problem.
worked_example: Burgers equation on domain [0,1] with neural PDE solvers: tested on 1D (100 to 10,000 cells) and 2D (100 to 400 cells). XD operations consistently maintain L2 relative error across resolution changes, outperforming CNN baseline and matching or exceeding Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) performance. Navier-Stokes across viscosities: XD maintains accuracy better than CNN, slightly outperforms FNO. Training on 32 trajectories for 4,800 time steps with 32-step unrolling. Speedup vs CNN: 2x-5x on protein folding; FNO is ~3 orders of magnitude faster than traditional solvers, XD is ~2.5 orders of magnitude faster. Memory overhead: 2x-5x more expensive than CNN; inference currently slower but trainable overhead is quantifiable.
deeper_mechanics: Expressive Diagonalization (XD) search space based on Kaleidoscope (K) matrices—generalization of FFT structure allowing complex number entries instead of roots of unity. K matrices express: Fourier transforms, graph convolutions, sparse operations, low-rank operations, permutations, wavelet transforms. XD operations parameterized by learnable K_L, K_M matrices initialized as DFTs but varied via gradient descent. Continuous (not discrete) architecture parameters—no binary variables. Single-level simultaneous optimization of model weights and architecture parameters. Linear operations (7 of 8 DARTS operations) amenable to diagonalization; non-linear activations and max pooling excluded. Fourier Neural Operators contained in XD space as special case (identity in frequency domain).
failure_boundary: XD slower to train (5x on PDE, 2x on protein folding) and infer compared to CNN—K-matrix software immature vs decades-optimized FFT libraries. Cannot express nonlinear activations or self-attention (quadratic complexity operations). Does not generalize to well-studied tasks (standard image classification, audio classification where CNNs already work). Discrete NAS approaches (DARTS, AutoDeepLab) fail on PDE tasks even with architecture search—poor baseline consistency. Large memory costs associated with K-matrix implementation. Padding overhead in kernel multiplication. Permutation asymmetry of DFT cannot be exploited with K matrices. No principled method to decide between XD initialization strategies (FNO vs CNN initialization produces different results).

title: Steve Sun: Data-Driven Constitutive Updates From Model-Free Poroelasticity To Level Set Plasticity
speaker: Steve WaiChing Sun
one_sentence: This whole series asks: can computers predict how physical systems behave by learning from examples instead of only using hand-written math? This talk looks at one specific part—the material laws that say how a piece of rock or soil responds when you stretch it or squeeze it or push fluids through it—and shows how to teach those laws directly from experimental data.
core_problem: When you simulate how materials behave—a rock that's being squeezed, soil with water flowing through it, metal that's bending—you need equations that say how much the material deforms when you push on it, how pressure and flow are related, and what happens inside. For many real materials, nobody has written down these equations with confidence, or the experiments to measure them cost too much, or you only have a handful of data points. Using data directly to skip the written-down equation sounds simple, but the answer has to make physical sense and obey the laws of motion.
first_principles_model: The material law (called a constitutive update—a local rule for how one small piece responds) lives inside a bigger simulation that solves how the whole thing moves and deforms. For poroelasticity—which means a solid rock or soil that squeezes and also lets water or oil flow through its pores—you can use data to learn: when the rock is pushed this hard, how much does it squish, and when there's a pressure difference, how fast does the fluid flow? Instead of writing an equation, a data-driven method looks at the actual data points and finds a pattern that makes physical sense. Neural networks (programs with millions of dials the computer tunes by trial and error until their answers look right) or level-set functions (surfaces that slide and change shape to track where a material stops bending elastically and starts deforming permanently) can do this learning when you only have limited measurements.
key_claims: Using data and neural networks to learn how materials behave has been done for decades.
The goal is to make the learned material law readable (so you can see what it's doing) and to work with the limited experimental data you actually collected.
Simulating fluids moving through solids requires two equations: one for how the solid deforms and one for how the fluid flows.
Depending on how much data you have, you can switch between a data-driven learned rule and a hand-written equation inside the same simulation.
Fast computer tricks (like KD-trees, which split space into smaller boxes to speed up searching) can make data-driven updates run quickly enough for real simulations.
Level-set plasticity (using a moving surface to mark where material stops bending elastically) can learn yield behavior from higher-resolution simulations when you don't have direct experiments.

important_terms.meaning: An equation or model that says how a material responds locally: when you push on it (stress and strain), how much does it deform, and for fluids, how pressure and flow relate.
Simulation that uses measured material data directly instead of writing down a specific equation first.
The behavior when a solid material (rock or soil) squeezes and deforms at the same time that a fluid (water or oil) flows through its tiny connected holes.
The set of all physically real material states—either measured in experiments or captured by a learned model.
A method to represent when material stops bending temporarily and starts bending permanently (yielding) by using a moving surface that marks the boundary.

stanford_connections: This lecture adds material-law learning to the broader goal of the series: the learned model is the material response, not the entire physics rule.
It connects to hybrid systems because mixing data and written-down physics works smoothest at the material-response level.

It also connects to model-constrained learning because the full simulation (the big math problem of motion and deformation) decides which learned material responses are actually allowed without breaking.
practical_caution: A material law learned from data can break the full simulation if it says something physically impossible (like negative energy), if the math becomes inconsistent step by step, or if it wastes or creates energy it shouldn't. The learned material law must be tested inside the complete coupled calculation—soil deforming AND water flowing through it together—not just checked against a graph of stress-versus-strain in isolation.
selected_evidence: Data-driven constitutive updates from model-free poroelasticity to level set plasticity.
Relationship between the strain and the effective stress.
Relationship between the pressure gradient and the Darcy velocity.
Identifying the constitutive manifold.
We want something very easy to interpret but... work well with limited data.
takeaway: The insight is that data-driven mechanics often does its job at the material-law level—the local response of one small piece of material. Learn what the material does from measurements, but make sure it fits with the overall physics rules.
worked_example:
Model-free poroelasticity on sandstone with naturally high variance porosity-permeability relationships (variance ~1 order on log scale). Hybrid approach uses model-based J2 plasticity for solid mechanics (tractable stress-strain from triaxial tests) and model-free search for hydraulic response. Heterogeneous domain with porosity fluctuations generates pole pressure buildup; at each quadrature point, k-d tree search identifies nearest material database point in transformed space, replacing smooth prediction with discrete data interpolation. Stress relaxation test on linear problem validates implementation; nonlinear comparison shows model-free response oscillations when data coverage sparse, resolved by adding database points.

Level-set plasticity: neural network trained to identify yield surface evolution with cumulative plastic strain. Hamilton-Jacobi PDE solved once offline; result reusable across many simulations replacing classical return-mapping. Trained on polycrystal elastoplasticity; comparison shows results nearly identical to FFT simulation but without expensive per-quadrature-point FFT evaluation.
deeper_mechanics:
Model-free approach minimizes distance from physical constraint manifold (balance of linear momentum, balance of mass) to material data manifold. Optimization has two steps: (1) Continuous: for fixed data point, find physical field minimizing residual, solved via Lagrangian multiplier; (2) Discrete: identify closest material point in database by k-d tree search using factorized energy norm. Energy norm uses c = inverse of compliance tensor; rewrite as c = L^T L via Cholesky, then transform material space and apply L2 distance to accelerate k-d tree (line 599-612). Hybrid formulation: when constitutive law tractable, use model-based approach; when high variance or complex, switch to model-free for that variable only.

Level-set plasticity formulates yield-surface evolution as Hamilton-Jacobi equation with state = principal stress, parameter = cumulative plastic strain. Neural network solves once to give u-surface implicit representation. Return-mapping uses this learned yield function + learned elastic energy. Enforce physics via material frame indifference test (rotation tensor in deformation gradient unchanged), acoustic tensor eigenvalue check (wave speed > 0 for stability), and symmetry verification. Training uses multi-layer perceptron with relu then hybrid activation (scaled relu layers) to achieve sufficient C² continuity for tangent stiffness derivatives (line 1077-1102).
failure_boundary:
Model-free approach fails when database has gaps: forcing solution outside data cloud produces oscillations (line 687-712, 851-862). Manifold-based distance (not norm-based) required for nonlinear constitutive response; standard L2 norm may prefer wrong points on curved manifold (line 815-828). Different material models in overlap region incompatible; must position decomposition carefully (from dive 036).

Level-set approach: LSTM recurrent networks for yield-surface evolution show oscillations with limited data (line 1276-1289); multilayer perceptron with level-set avoids these. Assumption that yield surface is smooth (scientist function) is strong—some hardening paths may not satisfy this. Interpolation to points outside training stress space unreliable (line 1673-1688 physics-informed NN example: PINNs fail on stiff equations, longer times, parametric changes).

title: Igor Mezic: Koopman Operator Theory For Dynamical Systems, Control And Data Analytics
speaker: Igor Mezic
one_sentence: This whole series aims to get computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples. One major challenge: many real systems change in complicated, nonlinear ways—the next step doesn't follow a simple rule, so prediction and control are hard. This talk introduces Koopman operator theory, a trick that rewrites these complicated systems as if they were simple and linear, but in a specially chosen space of observations. The cost: that space can be infinite-dimensional and tricky to find, but when you find the right one, you turn a hard problem into an easier one.
core_problem: Nonlinear dynamical systems (systems where the way things change from one moment to the next depends on where they are in a complicated, twisted way, not a straight-line way) are very hard to predict, break down into simpler pieces, or steer. Engineers and scientists have a tool: instead of watching how the state itself changes, watch how specific measurements or functions built from the state change. Koopman theory shows that when you pick the right measurements, these functions follow linear rules (straight-line rules)—but the space of all possible measurements is infinite-sized, so the real work is finding which measurements matter and understanding the deep structure of how they connect.
first_principles_model: Start with an observable: just a function—a formula that takes the current state and outputs a number, like 'the distance from center' or 'the temperature at one point'. The Koopman operator takes that observable and shows what it will equal one time-step later, by composing it with the system's actual evolution. Special observables, called eigenfunctions, are ones that evolve in the simplest way: they just get multiplied by a fixed number (an exponential factor) at each time step. If you can find enough of these eigenfunctions, you can rewrite the whole nonlinear system as a linear system—a system where the next state is just a multiplication by a matrix. Methods like DMD (dynamic mode decomposition—a recipe that learns patterns from time-series data) give you a way to guess what those eigenfunctions and factors are, starting only from recorded data.
key_claims: Koopman theory restates nonlinear systems by tracking how measurements of the state evolve, rather than how the state itself evolves.
The Koopman operator is linear (follows straight-line rules) even when the system it describes is wildly nonlinear.

Special measurements called eigenfunctions evolve in the simplest way—they get multiplied by the same number at each time step—so they give you coordinates where everything follows straight-line rules.
Koopman decompositions break things up by how they change over time (the spectrum in the time direction), not necessarily by how they spread through space.
DMD is one recipe for learning the Koopman operator's behavior from recorded data, picking out the most important pieces.

POD (proper orthogonal decomposition, a common method that finds patterns based on how spread-out things are in space) can miss important structure if that structure moves and rotates in a Koopman way that POD does not capture.

important_terms.meaning: A tool (a mathematical map) that shows how any measurement built from the state will evolve forward in time by applying the system's actual flow and then reading the measurement.
Any function or measurement you can compute from the state—like 'the height', 'the speed', 'the distance from the center'—whose time-evolution you want to study.
A special observable that evolves in the simplest possible way: multiply by a fixed number at each time step. Finding these is the goal because they let you write the whole system in linear form.

Dynamic mode decomposition: a recipe that starts with recorded data over time (like a video of a system evolving) and extracts the Koopman operator's most important pieces by spotting repeating patterns.
Organized, repeating behavior (like a whirlpool or a wave) that stays stable over time and can be captured by Koopman modes—the building-block patterns of how the system moves.

stanford_connections: This talk shows how equation-discovery, Green's functions (special solutions that show how systems respond), and reduced-order models (simple copies of big systems) all fit together through the structure of the Koopman operator.
It connects to control (steering a system) because linear representations of nonlinear dynamics make feedback and planning much simpler—you can use old, reliable linear control recipes.
It offers a different way to simplify systems than POD: instead of keeping the directions where energy spreads the most, you keep the directions where Koopman modes move in simple ways.
practical_caution: Koopman methods only work as well as the measurements (observables) you choose. If you pick the wrong ones or miss some, your linear model looks clean but hides important behavior. A finite (limited-size) approximation can seem linear on paper yet still fail to capture the system's true motions if the space of measurements is incomplete.
selected_evidence: Koopman operator theory... for dynamical systems control and data analytics.
A reformulation... in terms of evolutionary observables.
The operator is linear.
Eigenfunctions are special functions... governed by linear equations.
DMD is... ways of approximating the Koopman operator.
takeaway: Nonlinear systems can become linear if you measure the right things. Koopman theory is the systematic search for what to measure and how.
worked_example: For a jet exiting a circular orifice (a noisy flow with cross-flow), the Koopman operator spectral analysis extracted clean eigenvalues represented as colorized structures overlaid on the messy flow field—bright blue and red dots showing coherent vortex dynamics embedded in apparent randomness. For the van der Pol oscillator, the method recovered the periodic limit cycle and its stability properties directly from data without solving ODEs. Power grids with 10 generators were analyzed to find coherent generator pairs (generators 2-3, 6-7-9, 10 formed distinct blocks) that must be stabilized as synchronized units.
deeper_mechanics: The Koopman operator U acts on observables f as U f(x) = f(phi(x)); its eigenfunctions phi satisfy phi(phi^t(x)) = e^(lambda*t) phi(x). Eigenvalues form a lattice: for stable systems, the lattice lives in the left half-plane; for limit cycles, eigenvalues are products of integers times base frequencies. Spectral analysis uses the Hankel matrix constructed from impulse response sequences; singular value decomposition yields eigenvalues and modes. For nonlinear systems with unknown dynamics, spectral factorization of the Hankel matrix bypasses explicit matrix construction, enabling data-driven extraction of the entire spectrum.
failure_boundary: Koopman methods collapse on systems with strong continuous spectrum (turbulence, noise-driven chaos). The separation between discrete eigenvalues and continuous spectrum—critical for clean mode extraction—vanishes when noise dominates or dimensions become very high. Finite-time data provides noisy spectral estimates prone to spurious peaks; spectral truncation requires choosing a cutoff (number of modes, eigenvalue threshold) and no principled method exists for chaotic systems. Bifurcation phenomena with zero-real-part eigenvalues and the interplay with continuous spectrum remain theoretically open and numerically fragile.

title: Miles Cranmer: The Problem With Deep Learning For Physics And How To Fix It
speaker: Miles Cranmer
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. A popular way is to feed a learning program (a huge bank of dials the computer tunes by trial and error) the laws of physics as it trains. This talk asks: when you use this approach to solve a physics problem, do you end up with an answer that works well but stays hidden inside the network — and if so, does that help science or hurt it?
core_problem: A learning program can predict what happens in high-dimensional, complicated situations — like how a fluid flows around an object with many shapes and forces — better and faster than writing out all the math by hand. But if the answer is completely hidden inside millions of tuned dials, science gets stuck. Future researchers don't know what physical rule the program learned, whether that rule is actually true in the real world, or whether the program just found a sneaky shortcut that works for the data it saw but breaks on new situations. This accumulated debt — knowing it works but not why — is what blocks science from moving forward.
first_principles_model: Physics has a language built in: mathematical rules. Instead of hiding the answer inside a neural network, you can build physical structure into how the network itself works. One way: a Lagrangian neural network is a program that learns a single number (like energy) and then applies the known laws of physics to predict how things move from that energy value. Another way: after training a network, you can search for simple math formulas that match what the network learned, using a process called symbolic regression — this turns the network's hidden decision into an equation you can read and test. The goal is to turn the patterns the program found into statements a scientist can inspect and check.
key_claims: A learning program without guidance can delay the hard work of truly understanding the physical problem.
Methods that worked well for explaining images don't work well for physics, because physics has built-in mathematical structure that images don't.
Placing constraints on what a model can learn steers it toward solutions that act like real physics.
Lagrangian neural networks learn a physical quantity (energy-like) by baking in the existing laws of motion.
Networks built as graphs (nodes connected like particles) match natural systems well, because real systems are built on relationships between parts.
You can take what a trained network learned and approximate it with simple math formulas that humans can read.

important_terms.meaning: The gap between knowing a model works and actually understanding why it works — the unpaid cost that blocks science.
A constraint you build into a model beforehand that restricts what answers it's allowed to learn, steering it toward physically sensible patterns.
A computer search that tries to build simple, readable math formulas that fit the data or approximate a trained network.
A network designed to learn a single physical quantity (energy) and then apply motion equations to predict what happens next.
Pulling simple math formulas out of a trained network so you can see and test them instead of leaving them hidden.

stanford_connections: This talk goes against the idea of using learning programs purely as fast replacements for physics simulations — a theme running through the whole series.

It connects to talks on SINDy (a method to extract equations from data), Green's functions (a classical physics tool), and kernel methods, because all of them prioritize learning rules you can inspect and verify.
It ties back to physics-guided forecasting: you can't treat constraints as a nice extra — they're what makes a model useful to actual science.
practical_caution: Even when you build physics into a network, it can still fail if your built-in constraints are too weak or if the data doesn't contain enough information to pin down the quantity you're trying to learn. If you create a method to see what's inside the network, it should produce equations you can actually test, not just diagrams that look nicer than before.
selected_evidence: The problem with deep learning in physics and how to fix it.
We are postponing our need to understand that problem.
Physics has a good symbolic model... math.
An inductive bias is some kind of prior on what possible functions your model can learn.
Symbolic regression... searching for equations.
takeaway: Scientific machine learning has a debt: it must repay the cost of not understanding. Use learning programs to uncover the mechanisms at play — not to hide them behind numbers.
worked_example:
The team trained a graph neural network on three-body particle systems governed by spring laws and one-over-r squared forces. Using symbolic regression with the PySR package, they discovered that the internal message vectors (which should encode forces) were tightly correlated with the true Newtonian forces. Specifically, when they regularized the message dimensions with L1 loss to enforce sparsity to just 2-3 dimensions, the learned internal representations matched analytical force computations with high fidelity.

For dark matter halo distribution, they applied the scattering transformation followed by symbolic regression and recovered the equation: sum of surrounding halo masses divided by a distance-weighted scaling. The discovered formula generalized better to held-out data than the original neural network—when they masked 20% of training data, the symbolic equation maintained accuracy while the graph network's performance degraded substantially.
deeper_mechanics:
The core method uses symbolic regression—specifically genetic algorithms and evolutionary search—to approximate the learned behavior of internal neural network layers. The approach represents equations as binary trees where operators (like sine, cosine, multiplication) are nodes and leaves are variables. For a layer's internal representation, symbolic regression searches the space of possible analytic expressions by iteratively mutating candidate trees, scoring them by how well they fit the layer's output given its input.

The scattering transform is a handcrafted wavelet decomposition followed by nonlinear modulus operations and absolute value: it applies a cascade of wavelet convolutions at multiple scales with modulus nonlinearities, creating what amounts to a convolutional hierarchy that is stable to small deformations. The logarithm of this output produces better numerical properties for downstream regression. For high-dimensional problems, they impose disentangled sparsity—forcing each output feature to depend on as few input features as possible by sparsifying the Jacobian matrix.
failure_boundary: Symbolic regression becomes computationally infeasible in very high dimensions. If a problem has 100+ input features and no prior structure, the combinatorial explosion of possible equations makes search intractable even with sophisticated pruning. The inductive bias of the network architecture matters tremendously: if you use a graph neural network with pooling operations, those pooling choices (summation, max, mean) appear explicitly in discovered equations as assumptions, not discoveries. When symbolic equations are forced to fit noisy training data, they may overfit to spurious patterns in the noise. Additionally, even if a correct equation is discovered, explaining WHY that equation appears—why it's physically meaningful—requires domain insight that symbolic regression cannot provide; a formula like (sum of masses)/(distance^2.5 + constant) may fit data but its physical interpretation remains unclear without human theory.

title: Greg Beroza: Towards Complete Machine-Learning-Based Earthquake Monitoring Workflows
speaker: Greg Beroza
one_sentence: This whole series is about teaching computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. One place this matters is earthquake monitoring: seismic sensors record ground shaking, and a computer needs to turn those wiggly recordings into a list of earthquakes (when each happened, where, how big). This talk shows how machine learning—a program with millions of dials it tunes by trial and error until its answers look right—can handle each step of this job better than older methods. But here's the catch: the whole system only works if training data, realistic variations on that data, model design choices, and final checking of the earthquake list all work together.
core_problem: Earthquake monitoring is not one prediction question, it is many chained together. A seismic network runs continuously, recording every ground wiggle. A real monitoring system has to clean up those signals, spot the moment each seismic wave arrives, group wave arrivals from many sensors so they are recognized as coming from the same earthquake, pinpoint where that earthquake happened, estimate how big it was, and keep accurate records over time. If you swap in a learning program to handle just one of these steps, errors pile up: a mistake in spotting wave arrivals breaks the grouping, which ruins the location, which ruins the final catalog. You cannot ignore this chain.
first_principles_model: A monitoring workflow takes raw seismic recordings and turns them into a structured earthquake catalog. The information shape-shifts at each step: raw signals become wave arrivals (the moment each seismic wave type lands at a sensor), wave arrivals become events (a group of arrivals from one earthquake), events become locations and details about the earthquake. Machine learning shines when it learns these transformations by studying labeled seismic data and artificially created variations on that data that look realistic. But the output that matters is the earthquake catalog, the list geophysicists will actually use. So the right way to score how good a model is should measure the whole workflow, not just how well a single piece works in isolation.
key_claims: Standard earthquake monitoring works as a chain: clean up signals, find wave arrivals, group those arrivals into earthquakes, calculate earthquake locations, and estimate earthquake sizes.
Deep learning (a program with millions of adjustable dials tuned by trial and error) can handle individual steps and often finds many more earthquakes than older methods did.

High-quality training labels, the shapes and sizes of the learning program, and creating realistic variations on training data are not small details; they decide whether the model works on real seismic networks it has never seen.
Replacing one piece of the workflow at a time is simplest to put into real systems because each step can be upgraded alone.
Building one learning program that handles several monitoring tasks together, instead of several separate programs, can work better because different seismic tasks share information.
Better earthquake catalogs reveal small and previously missed earthquakes that show patterns and tell us where earthquake hazards are located.

important_terms.meaning: A complete list of earthquakes that were detected, showing when each happened, where, how big it was, and other measured properties.
Finding the exact moment when each type of seismic wave (the main types are called P and S waves) lands at a sensor in the ground-motion recordings.
Grouping wave arrivals that many sensors recorded so they are recognized as coming from one earthquake instead of separate events.

Creating new training examples by modifying known seismic recordings in realistic ways so a learning program sees what stays the same even when conditions change, instead of memorizing one specific setup.
A learning program design where several related monitoring tasks are learned together in one program instead of as separate independent programs.

stanford_connections: This talk builds on earlier lectures about using physics to guide learning and about surrogate models (programs that imitate expensive calculations): a learned system must fit into the actual workflow scientists use, not stand alone.
It connects to active learning and smart ways to collect data because training labels and realistic data variations are essential for machine learning in science.

It connects to understanding what we do not know and to inverse problems (figuring out what caused something we measured): how good the earthquake catalog is determines what conclusions downstream about earthquakes and hazards can be trusted.
practical_caution: Do not judge a monitoring model only by how well it spots wave arrivals at sensors. A model can score high at detecting waves but still produce a bad earthquake catalog if it fails at grouping arrivals into events, locating them accurately, estimating magnitudes correctly, or working on a seismic network it has never been tested on before.
selected_evidence: Standard earthquake monitoring workflows can be described with... pre-processing, phase detection, event-phase association, location, and characterization.
Machine learning methods, particularly deep neural networks, have been shown capable of replacing these steps.
Generate earthquake catalogs that are far more comprehensive than those developed using standard approaches.
Appropriate architecture, accurate data labels, and data augmentation all play an important role.
The simplest approach... is modular.
takeaway: Machine learning for earthquake monitoring should be judged as a complete measurement system, the way you would judge a thermometer or a scale. The output is not a score or a percentage; it is an earthquake catalog that scientists and hazard forecasters will base decisions on.
worked_example:
PhaseNet, a deep convolutional neural network, picks P-wave and S-wave arrival times on seismic waveforms with accuracy within a few hundredths of a second (±0.03 seconds for P-waves, ±0.05 seconds for S-waves). Compared to expert human picks (ground truth), the distribution is narrow and centered near zero, whereas classical automatic pickers (AR picker) show larger tails and bias. On the Ridgecrest, California aftershock sequence (300 seconds of data), the deep learning catalog finds 10× more events than the standard USGS catalog and 50% more than prior machine-learning catalogs, all from the same instrumental data but with more careful signal processing.

Using the deep catalog for earthquake sequence analysis reveals a spatial-temporal diffusive pattern consistent with fluid pressure diffusion in induced seismicity (Guy Greenbrier fault, Arkansas). Fitting parabolic arc-shaped structures in space-time gives diffusivity estimates of 10–100 m²/s, explaining the temporal evolution of seismicity as fluid propagates through a fault zone.
deeper_mechanics:
PhaseNet uses a CNN encoder-decoder with three input components (3D velocity). The encoder extracts features from raw waveforms; the decoder predicts P-wave and S-wave arrival times by reconstructing truncated Gaussian distributions centered on phase onsets. The loss trains the classifier to assign high probability at the true arrival time and low probability elsewhere. For the Gaussian mixture model (GMM) association step, each phase measurement is treated as a distribution with mean at the picked time and variance reflecting uncertainty. Soft clustering iteratively assigns phases to events by maximizing the likelihood of a fixed number of events, iterating until convergence.

The workflow is embarrassingly parallel: phase picking and association on different time windows run independently. HypoDD performs precise relative locations using waveform cross-correlation and double-differences, providing sub-meter precision for nearby events.
failure_boundary: PhaseNet struggles with heavily clipped waveforms (telemetry saturation) or extremely noisy background (e.g., during volcanic eruptions). In swarms where waveforms overlap significantly, picking individual onsets becomes ambiguous; the model must infer which energy belongs to which event. Manual catalog errors (misidentified phases, mislabeled onset times) in training data propagate as a ceiling on accuracy. Out-of-distribution shifts—e.g., teleseismic waves, unusual velocity structures—can degrade phase picks. The GMM association assumes a Poisson process for event times, which breaks down for foreshock-aftershock clustering. Long-term deployment requires retraining on new station networks and instrument types.

title: Pat Langley: Computational Scientific Discovery
speaker: Pat Langley
organization: Institute for the Study of Learning and Expertise / Stanford Center for Design Research
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of relying only on hand-written math. One approach is to have a learning program (a system with millions of little dials the computer tunes by trial and error until its answers look right) search through many possible scientific laws and equations, guided by what we observe and what scientists already know about how things work. This talk is about how that search works, what makes a discovered law real enough for science to use, and why just finding an equation that fits the data is not enough.
core_problem: Most computer learning chases one goal: make predictions as correct as possible. But science wants something different. Scientists need a law or model they can write down, read, understand, and use in new situations—not just a machine that predicts well. A true scientific discovery has to explore an organized space of possible laws or models, explained in language scientists already trust and use. Finding a curve that matches your measurements is easy; finding something that tells you WHY things happen is hard and much rarer.
first_principles_model: A discovery system needs three parts: observations you are trying to explain, a space of possible laws or models you can search through (not infinite guesses, but a structured set built from known mathematical forms and rules), and decision rules (called heuristics) that guide which candidate to check next. The core requirement is that the final result must be something a scientist can grasp and use: an equation, a description of how something works step-by-step, or a model stated in forms science recognizes. Knowledge about the domain—the specific area you are studying—narrows down the space and makes sure candidate models make sense in that field.
key_claims: Scientific discovery can be reframed as a guided search through candidate laws or models—a systematic exploration aimed at the most promising candidates, not random guessing.
What separates a discovery system from a simple data-matching algorithm is that it produces something close to a scientific theory: a result stated in a form scientists recognize and can work with.

When searching for equations, the goal is mathematical relationships; when searching for models of how things work, you must also capture the qualitative pieces—what causes what and how processes unfold step-by-step.
Qualitative models (descriptions of cause-and-effect or structure) often matter more than exact numbers because they show you how and why something happens, not just that it does.

One powerful variant, called process modeling, learns equations that describe how a system changes over time by studying sequences of measurements and using existing knowledge to infer the governing rules.
Domain knowledge is not something to get around or ignore; it is what makes the search manageable, sensible, and ensures the result will actually be useful to practicing scientists.

important_terms.meaning: A method of exploring a vast set of possibilities by using simple rules or scoring to favor candidates that seem most promising, instead of checking every single option.

A discovered relationship written in compact scientific form—an equation, a process description, or another format scientists accept—rather than a hidden prediction machine that gives answers but no insight.
The process of searching for mathematical equations that match observed data and capture an underlying law or relationship in nature.
A model that explains mechanism and structure—how or why something happens—even when exact numeric values matter less than understanding the cause-and-effect chain.
Learning equations that describe how systems change over time by examining sequences of measurements and using existing scientific knowledge to infer the governing rules.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects to SINDy (a method for finding sparse equations from data), symbolic regression (automated equation search), Koopman analysis (finding hidden patterns in dynamic systems), and researchers like Miles Cranmer who argue science needs better automated tools for discovery.
It bridges the gap between fitting numbers to data and the way science has always explained nature through laws and mechanisms.
It explains why surrogate models (simplified stand-in models humans can read) matter: a tool that predicts well is not the same thing as a scientific discovery.
practical_caution: A short equation that fits your data does not automatically count as a real discovered law. If you choose the space of possible equations poorly, use weak background knowledge, or set bad search rules, the system will churn out compact equations that look good on paper but have no meaning in actual science. The danger is mistaking a lucky coincidence for a discovery.
selected_evidence: Discovery involves heuristic search through a space of candidate laws or models.
Those are stated in some established scientific formalism.
That distinguishes work in this area from pretty much everything else in machine learning.
The interesting thing here is not the parameters... the qualitative structure of these laws.
Inductive process modeling... multivariate time series... background knowledge.
takeaway: The main lesson: scientific machine learning should search and speak in science's own language. Observations put limits on what's possible, but the mathematical forms you allow and the domain knowledge you feed in are what turn a fitting equation into something a scientist can actually trust and use.
worked_example:
The BACON system reconstructed Kepler's third law (d³/p² = constant) from Borelli's observational data on Jupiter's moons: given distances d and periods p across moons, the system noticed d and p both increase together, examined ratios d/p (decreasing), then products, and found d³/p² constant. For ideal gas law: holding moles n and temperature T constant while varying pressure P, found pV = const(n,T). Varying moles led to const/n = new_const, then varying temperature yielded the law pv ≈ cn·T (ideal gas law). BACON also rediscovered Coulomb's law, Ohm's law, conservation of momentum, and Black's law of specific heat—all quantitative forms with non-obvious algebraic structure—from small datasets with minimal noise.

RF5 (neural network version) and later genetic programming systems similarly reconstructed laws from numerical data, but reached beyond simple equations to differential equation models and mechanistic explanations.
deeper_mechanics: Heuristic search through space of mathematical forms: bacon starts with raw variables, applies mental operators recursively (ratio, product, power combinations) to generate composite variables, evaluates each candidate law L using statistical fit residual ||data - L(vars)||². When fit quality improves below threshold, system promotes that law to a base level and continues searching. Search is guided by regularities in the data: correlations suggest which operations to try next (if x increases as y increases, try y/x or x·y). For ideal gas law: each stage fixes some variables (n,T) and performs univariate searches, enabling dimensional hierarchy (laws for single variables → laws combining variables → dimensional composition). Output is communicable: algebraic form directly translatable to scientific literature, unlike decision trees or neural nets.
failure_boundary: BACON fails when quantitative laws don't exist or are disguised by noise: if physics is truly nonlinear at the observation scale, polynomial/rational forms cannot capture it. No mechanistic explanation: system finds correlations (descriptive laws) but cannot infer causation or unobserved processes without external structural knowledge. Variable selection: if the right variables are not in the dataset, discovery is impossible (e.g., can't find ideal gas law without pressure, volume, moles, or temperature). Combinatorial explosion: with 20+ variables, the search space of composite forms becomes intractable even with heuristics. Fails on qualitative data: sparse, non-numerical phenomena (food webs, geology) require supplementary inductive logic programming or causal inference, beyond pure equation discovery.

title: Ashesh Chattopadhyay: Deep Learning Meets Data Assimilation
speaker: Ashesh Chattopadhyay
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave—air, water, heat, structures—by learning from data rather than only hand-written step-by-step math. Weather and climate are especially hard because they are chaotic: tiny errors become huge mistakes in days. This talk shows how to combine learning (a program with millions of dials tuned by trial-and-error to match patterns) with a crucial first step called data assimilation: using real noisy measurements and old predictions to estimate a good starting point before you forecast forward.
core_problem: Weather and climate span many scales—from tiny eddies to global patterns—and are chaotic: a small change now can lead to a completely different outcome later. You cannot forecast by starting from 'perfect truth' because real measurements are noisy (each one is a guess plus error), sparse (we measure only a few spots), and uneven (some places have many sensors, others have none). Whether you use a traditional step-by-step physics model or teach a program to learn the patterns, both have mistakes.
