Before you can forecast anything, you must solve the hard first problem: turning noisy spotty measurements and an imperfect guess into a good starting state.
first_principles_model: Data assimilation is a way to combine what you already believe (prior knowledge) with new measurements to get a better estimate of the real state right now. Imagine you know roughly what the weather is (a background forecast from yesterday or an hour ago), but also some new thermometer and pressure readings just came in. Data assimilation asks: how do I weight these two sources fairly? It gives more trust to sources that have proven reliable before. Deep learning fits in as follows: a program can learn to predict missing small-scale details (like turbulence or cloud effects that the coarse model skipped), or learn to correct forecast mistakes, or learn to fix noisy measurement errors, or even learn to update many parallel guesses using data (a method called ensemble Kalman filtering, where 'ensemble' means many copies). The key danger: if you let the learning program run free, small starting mistakes can amplify fast in chaotic systems, breaking predictions weeks ahead. So the learned parts must respect the laws of motion.
key_claims: Weather and climate are hard to forecast because they spread across many sizes of motion and because tiny changes now grow into huge mistakes later.
You cannot start a forecast from a perfect state because real sensors give noisy spotty readings, and a model (whether traditional math or learned) is never perfectly right.
Data assimilation merges a rough forecast from the model with new real-world measurements to estimate a usable starting point.
Learning programs can discover how tiny-scale processes (like water droplets and air movement) affect the big-scale weather by studying high-resolution simulations or lots of measurements.
The smartest forecasts pair learned prediction with traditional numerical models rather than throwing away the physics entirely and trusting only the learning program.

Keeping predictions physically consistent and using ensemble methods (running many parallel forecasts and updating them together with data) are the tools that make learned predictions reliable in real operations.

important_terms.meaning: A technique that blends a model's rough prediction with noisy real-world measurements to produce a better estimate of what the system is actually doing right now.
The improved state estimate you get after you merge observations into an older forecast prediction.
The model's prediction before you add corrections based on new observations.
A data assimilation method that runs many parallel predictions simultaneously and updates all of them together using new measurements, so you can track how uncertain your predictions are.

Combining a traditional physics-based model (the slow hand-written step-by-step math) with learned data-driven parts (a program that tuned itself by trial-and-error) to get faster and better predictions.

stanford_connections: This talk builds on physics-guided learning because the structure of how you design a learning program matters enormously when small starting errors can explode as the system evolves forward.
It also touches neural operators and reduced-order models: any learned piece must cooperate with state estimation, not just predict far into the future on its own.
The lecture pairs with discussions of uncertainty because the starting state is uncertain (your measurements are noisy), and that uncertainty is a root cause of forecast errors down the line.
practical_caution: A learning program trained on clean made-up data can seem perfect in a lab test—but collapse when you feed it real noisy spotty measurements or run it forward for many days. If you ignore how errors grow in chaotic systems and build a pure learning predictor without checking each step against physics rules, the program will confidently make garbage predictions.
selected_evidence: Weather and climate system... is a multi-scale chaotic dynamical system.
Observations... could be noisy, it could be sparse.
Data assimilation... ensure that information from both the background forecast and the noisy observations are properly weighed.
Hybrid sample Kalman filters for weather forecasting.
You can learn the effects... of these small scale processes.
takeaway: Prediction always starts with state estimation: you cannot skip the hard work of turning messy data into a good starting point. For chaotic physical systems like weather, learning what the system will do next and learning how to set up the starting state correctly are two sides of the same coin—you must solve both together.
worked_example:
For a two-layer quasi-geostrophic flow (canonical mid-latitude dynamics model with 36,000 states), a regular ensemble Kalman filter using 20 numerical ensemble members produced a divergent filter with normalized RMSE trending upward. Switching to 5,000 ensemble members yielded convergence with error decreasing at each assimilation step. The hybrid deep learning ensemble Kalman filter traded 10 numerical ensembles (cost ~1 solver step each) for 2,000 data-driven ensembles (cost ~1/200 of a numerical solve), achieving approximately 4× reduction in forecast error over 60-day cycles with no increase in total computational cost.

For weather re-analysis at 2,048 dimensions (low-resolution ERA5), an SO(3)-equivariant neural network trained on 12-hourly data achieved 5 days of forecast skill (0.6 ACC threshold), compared to ~4 days for standard UNet. Using hierarchical multi-model data assimilation with virtual observations (treating 12-hourly forecasts as synthetic observations to update hourly predictions), the filter converged for 4,000 ensemble members with correlation coefficient >0.7 even under high observational noise.
deeper_mechanics:
Ensemble Kalman filtering computes Kalman gain K = PH^T(HPH^T + R)^-1 where P is background error covariance, H is observation operator, and R is observation noise. High-dimensional systems suffer from rank deficiency when using few ensemble members—the sample covariance P becomes corrupted by sampling error causing spurious long-range correlations. The hybrid approach: (1) compute P from thousands of cheap data-driven ensemble forecasts; (2) compute background forecast from fewer accurate numerical ensembles; (3) combine via analysis state x^a = x^b + K(y^obs - Hx^b).

Deep learning forecasting uses autoregressive integration: given state u_t, predict u_{t+Δt}. For spatiotemporal weather fields, SO(3)-equivariant transformers maintain rotational variance by embedding spatial transforms in latent space. Training horizon determines prediction skill: 12-hourly models have longer forecast skill (slower error growth) than hourly models due to coarser temporal sampling. Virtual observations exploit this multi-scale difference: intermittently assimilate high-fidelity 12-hourly predictions as synthetic observations y_virt to correct drift in hourly forecast chains.
failure_boundary:
Pure data-driven ensemble Kalman filters fail when the surrogate model loses accuracy beyond its training horizon. A data-driven model trained for 1-day forecasts cannot reliably predict covariance structure at 5+ days, causing filter divergence. Additionally, convolutional architectures fail on weather systems because they lack rotational equivariance—they cannot distinguish between a low-pressure anomaly above a high-pressure zone (potentially triggering extreme events) from the reverse configuration, leading to misclassification of critical dynamic patterns.

Data-driven weather models exhibit unphysical long-term drift and climate instability even when forecast skill is 5+ days; they cannot reproduce observed climate statistics. Transfer learning between climate regimes (e.g., pre- vs. post-climate-change initial conditions) requires retraining because the model shows distributional shift sensitivity—Reynolds number changes or parameter shifts cause complete loss of generalization. Sparse, noisy observations coupled with a high-dimensional system (10^8 states in operational weather) forces impossible ensemble sizes; practical systems use localization and inflation hacks rather than principled solutions.

title: Sergei Tretiak: Machine Learning For Materials And Chemical Dynamics
speaker: Sergei Tretiak
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. One common problem in chemistry and materials science is that running accurate quantum physics simulations is very expensive—you need thousands of them to hunt for new materials, and each one takes hours. This talk shows how a learning program can learn to mimic those expensive simulations, running millions of times faster. But there's a catch: the program can only learn what the examples showed it. If atoms are far apart in a molecule, they can influence each other through electric charge or attraction—but if the program was trained only to look at each atom and its close neighbors, it will miss those long-distance effects and give you wrong answers.
core_problem: Getting precise predictions from quantum physics and molecular simulations costs a lot of computer time. To discover new materials, you need to run thousands of these simulations, each testing different atomic arrangements and conditions. A learning program can learn to connect a structure's shape directly to its properties much faster, but it breaks in two common ways. First, if the training examples didn't show a particular arrangement of atoms, the program has no idea what to predict. Second, atoms can influence each other across distance—through spread-out electric charge, attraction between distant molecules, or changes in electronic states (how electrons occupy energy levels). If the program only looks at each atom and its immediate neighbors, it will miss all those long-distance effects.
first_principles_model: A molecular learning program takes the positions of atoms as input and predicts how much energy the structure has, what forces push on each atom, or what properties it has. The simplest approach—local models—treats each atom's energy as coming mostly from atoms sitting nearby. This is fast and can handle huge molecules, but real chemistry doesn't work that way. Atoms can influence each other across the whole molecule through several channels: electric charge spread throughout (not pointlike), how that charge reshuffles itself, attraction pulling distant molecules toward each other, and shifts in electronic energy levels. To capture these longer-distance effects, researchers add layers that let each atom receive information from all other atoms, step by step. Some models use a cycle where a prediction for one atom feeds back and helps predict another atom, repeating until everything stabilizes. Others add a charge-equilibration step: a calculation that figures out how electric charge actually spreads through the molecule to satisfy the forces it creates.
key_claims: A learning program can be trained to mimic expensive chemistry simulations, producing answers in milliseconds instead of hours.
The program can only predict configurations it has seen before, so where and how you gather training data sets a hard ceiling on accuracy.
Active learning (having the program flag cases where it is least sure, running a real simulation at those cases, and retraining) automatically fills in the worst gaps.

If you design the program to predict each atom's energy only from nearby atoms, it runs fast but will miss electric charge spread across the molecule, how charge redistributes itself, attraction between distant molecules, and changes in electronic energy levels.
You can add mechanisms to capture long-distance effects: layers where atoms exchange information step by step, cycles where predictions feed back and re-adjust, or a charge-equilibration calculation.
Running a learned model in a real simulation requires it to stay stable as atoms move around, not just to match static measurements in the lab.

important_terms.meaning: A program trained on examples to predict how much energy a molecule has and what forces push on each atom, based on where the atoms sit.
A loop: the program makes a prediction, flags the configurations where it is most uncertain, you run a real (expensive) simulation at those cases, then retrain the program with the new data.
A simplification where you assume each atom's energy depends mostly on atoms sitting right next to it, not on atoms far away in the molecule.
A physical effect where atoms or charge far apart in a molecule influence what happens at one location, such as electric attraction or charge that spreads across distance.
A calculation step that figures out how electric charge distributes itself through a molecular system to match the forces and attractions it creates.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects to learning from data: deciding which examples to collect is as important as choosing what the program looks like.
It also relates to multiscale modeling, where the rules for single atoms must combine to give right answers at the material scale.
It reinforces the series theme that when you cannot collect data for every possible case, teaching the program the actual physics rules you do know helps it extrapolate safely.
practical_caution: A program that looks good when tested on held-back data can suddenly fail once you use it to simulate chemistry over time. As the simulation runs, atomic positions shift, and the program encounters arrangements it never saw during training. If the simulation ventures into a regime where distant atoms and overall charge distribution dominate the behavior, the program will stumble because its design only lets it see nearby atoms.
selected_evidence: Machine learning... provides a surrogate model trained on the dataset of some reference data.
Designing high-quality training data sets is crucial to overall model accuracy.
Active learning strategy... new data are automatically collected for atomic configurations that produce large ML uncertainties.
A major drawback of the current machine learning framework... is locality.
Overcome nonlocality... interaction layers, self-consistent cycles, or charge equilibration schemes.
takeaway: Molecular learning is a stand-in tool for expensive quantum and molecular physics. Whether it works depends on two things: where you collected the training examples (which configurations did you actually show the program?) and what kinds of physics interactions the program's design can represent (just nearby atoms, or long-distance effects too?).
worked_example:
Illustrative (the talk states orders of magnitude but not a single benchmarked table of numbers). A machine-learned interatomic potential is trained to reproduce quantum (DFT-level) energies and forces for a molecule or material. Where one DFT single point of a modest system might take hours on a cluster, the trained surrogate returns energy and per-atom forces in milliseconds -- the speaker's claim is roughly a million-fold speedup, which is what lets you run the thousands-to-millions of evaluations a materials search or a molecular-dynamics trajectory needs.

Active learning is the loop that decides which expensive calculations to actually run. You start with a small training set, run molecular dynamics with the current model, and at each configuration estimate the model's uncertainty (for example the disagreement across an ensemble of models). Whenever the uncertainty crosses a threshold, you flag that configuration, run one real DFT calculation there, add it to the training set, and retrain. The gaps that hurt most get filled automatically, so accuracy rises where the trajectory actually goes rather than uniformly.

The failure mode made concrete: a local model that only reads each atom's near neighbors can look excellent on a held-out test set of static structures, then drift once you run dynamics. As atoms move, the trajectory wanders into configurations the training never showed, and any regime dominated by long-range charge or electrostatics -- which a nearest-neighbor model structurally cannot see -- gives wrong forces, so the simulation becomes unstable or unphysical.
deeper_mechanics:
A machine-learned potential approximates the potential energy surface E(R) as a function of atomic positions R, and forces come from its gradient: F_i = -dE/dR_i. The locality approximation writes E = sum_i epsilon_i where each atomic energy epsilon_i depends only on neighbors within a cutoff radius. That is what makes the cost scale linearly with system size and lets you reach huge systems, but it structurally cannot represent effects that reach beyond the cutoff: delocalized (spread-out, non-pointlike) charge, charge redistribution, dispersion attraction between distant fragments, and shifts in electronic occupation.

To restore nonlocality the talk names three mechanisms. Message-passing / interaction layers let each atom's representation receive information from all others in repeated rounds, so influence propagates step by step across the molecule. Self-consistent cycles feed a prediction for one atom back to re-adjust others and iterate until the fields stabilize (a fixed-point iteration). Charge-equilibration schemes solve an explicit electrostatics problem -- distribute charge q_i to minimize an electrostatic-plus-chemical-hardness energy subject to total-charge conservation -- so the model computes how charge actually spreads to satisfy the forces it creates, rather than assuming fixed per-atom charges.

Training minimizes a combined loss on energies and forces, roughly L = sum ( E_pred - E_DFT )^2 + lambda * sum || F_pred - F_DFT ||^2 over the reference set. The force term matters because dynamics is driven by gradients, not by matching energies alone.
failure_boundary:
The hard ceiling is the training distribution: the model can only predict configurations similar to what it was shown, so wherever you sampled data sets the reliability. A model validated on static held-out structures can pass and still fail in a running simulation, because time evolution pushes atoms into unseen arrangements -- the practical caution the speaker stresses. Stability under dynamics, not static test error, is the real test.

The second boundary is physics the architecture cannot represent. If a regime is governed by long-range electrostatics, charge transfer, dispersion, or changes in electronic state, a purely local model will be wrong there no matter how much local data you add; you need interaction layers, self-consistency, or charge equilibration built in. Active learning mitigates coverage gaps but cannot invent a physical channel the model has no terms for.

title: Kaushik Bhattacharya: Multi-Scale Modeling And Neural Operators
speaker: Kaushik Bhattacharya
one_sentence: This whole series is about teaching computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from data instead of writing down all the rules by hand. In engineering, materials have behavior that depends on incredibly tiny details—atoms, defects, the arrangement of crystals—but you can't actually simulate every single atom when you're designing a bridge or an airplane wing. This talk is about a learning program that learns the effective, simplified rules that capture what a zillion tiny details do, and then plugs those learned rules into the big-scale simulation, keeping accuracy without the crushing cost.
core_problem: When you try to predict how a material will behave, the real physics happens at many different scales at once—the level of individual electrons, the level of atoms, the level of tiny defects and crystal structures, and all the way up to the size of a real part. You could try to simulate every single detail, but that takes forever and costs too much. You could just average everything and ignore the details, but then you miss the important stuff that actually controls whether the material breaks or bends. So the real problem is: how do you capture the tiny-scale physics without having to compute it all?
first_principles_model: Multiscale modeling is a strategy that breaks the problem into layers. The big layer (the scale that engineers actually care about) sends information down to the tiny layer and asks, 'Given these conditions, what effective response do I get?' The tiny layer does the hard work and sends back an answer. A neural operator is a learning program that learns exactly that map—from the tiny-scale physics to the coarse, effective answer. Instead of writing down the equations by hand or running the expensive tiny-scale simulation every time, you train a program to learn this map. If you train it carefully on examples that match the cases you'll actually encounter, you can drop it into the big-scale simulation and get accurate answers for a tiny fraction of the cost.
key_claims: Material behavior is controlled by physics happening at many different scales at the same time—tiny details like atoms and defects all the way up to the size you can see with your eyes.
Multiscale modeling splits the job into layers: the big scale controls what questions to ask the tiny scale, and the tiny scale returns what actually happens.
The practical problem is that running the tiny-scale simulation over and over inside the big-scale simulation is too slow and too expensive.
Neural operators learn the map from input to output as functions—like learning a whole physical rule, not just learning numbers in a fixed list.

This is different from ordinary learning programs because you are learning a rule that applies to whole functions (fields that vary in space or time), not just learning a single answer from fixed-size numbers.
If trained correctly, a neural operator can keep the important tiny-scale details while making the big-scale simulation run fast enough to be useful.

important_terms.meaning: A way of predicting what happens by connecting physics descriptions that work at different sizes—from tiny atomic scales up to human-sized or building-sized scales.

A learning program that learns the connection (the map) between one set of functions and another. For example, it learns how a stress field at the tiny scale determines the material's response at the big scale.

A collection of all possible functions (mathematical rules that vary smoothly in space or time) rather than just a list of numbers. When learning programs work with function spaces, they are learning rules that apply everywhere, not just at discrete points.
The large-scale view that engineers use—the level of a whole bridge, airplane wing, or building—where you want the final answer.
The small-scale physics—like atoms, defects in crystals, or microscopic structure—where the detailed behavior happens but is too small and numerous to compute directly.

stanford_connections: This talk is a centerpiece in the series' journey through operator learning and connects directly to earlier talks about specific operator methods like Fourier Neural Operators and DeepONets, but from the viewpoint of what multiscale modeling actually needs.
It roots operator learning in classical physics and materials science instead of treating it as a generic trick that works on any data.

It also touches on uncertainty and trust: when you use a learned approximation of the tiny-scale physics, errors from that learned piece get passed up to the big-scale prediction, so you need to understand what you learned and whether it is honest.
practical_caution: A neural operator only works if it has learned the right map on the right kinds of cases. If you train it on one kind of microstructure or one range of loads and boundary conditions, but then test it on a completely different microstructure or load, it can fail badly. The program might fit the training data perfectly but give nonsense on new situations. You need to be honest about which scenarios the learned map is reliable for, and test it hard on cases it has never seen.
selected_evidence: The behavior of materials involve physics at multiple length and time scales.
Multiscale modeling seeks to understand this complexity with a divide and conquer approach.
The maps we are interested in learning is from one function space to another.
We are trying to learn a non-linear operator.
Capture all the details of the small scale but can be directly implemented at the coarse scale.
takeaway: When operator learning works, it works because the thing the program learned to do matches what the physics actually does: it learned a true map between changing fields (like temperature or stress) at one scale to the response at another scale, and it correctly handles the constraints and boundary conditions. That alignment between the learned computation and the physical reality is what makes the whole thing work.
worked_example:
For an elliptic operator (map from coefficient field a(x) to solution u(x)) on 421×421 grids, FNO training on downsampled 64×64 data achieves ~5% relative error. The learned operator generalizes to test data at 64×64, 100×100, 256×256 resolutions—the same error (~5%) regardless of resolution, showing the architecture captures the true functional operator rather than grid-dependent weights. A crystal plasticity example with 3D FFT calculations and 30,000 training trajectories (strain history to stress history) achieves ~10% total error. DFT electronic structure: learning electronic fields reduces reconstruction error from direct energy prediction by ~10x when evaluating total energy.

For single-processor performance: traditional Johnson-Cook material model costs 50 seconds per Taylor anvil simulation; the learned neural operator material model costs 450 seconds (~9x slower). Offline cost: generating 10^6 trajectories + training (~10^4 GPU steps) amortizes over many runs; one full concurrent multiscale simulation would cost ~10^8 single-CPU units.
deeper_mechanics:
PCANet architecture: projection P (via PCA or autoencoder) maps infinite-dimensional function space to finite-dimensional latent space with dimension d; neural network θ operates in latent space; lifting operator L reconstructs output function. For operator ψ: ψ ≈ L ∘ network ∘ P, enabling resolution independence. The PCA step captures statistical structure of the data distribution and is the key to generalization across grid resolutions.

Recurrent Neural Operators (RNO) replace full-history input with state-update dynamics: σ(t) = f(F(t), dF/dt, ζ(t)); dζ/dt = g(F, dF/dt, ζ), where ζ is learned hidden state. Fourier Neural Operators use integral kernels in Fourier space: (Kv)(x) = F^(-1)[K̂(ω) ⊙ F[v](ω)], learning spectral convolution directly—this is a Fourier-domain integral operator approximating the Green's function for PDE solution operators.
failure_boundary: PCANet requires sufficient training data; higher-dimensional reduced spaces need exponentially more trajectories. Higher PCA dimensions d → error first decreases then increases (overfitting regime) when training data is small. Architecture is non-causal by design; while data teaches causality through examples, extrapolation beyond training deformation range is unreliable. Constraints: (1) must know entire strain/deformation history a priori; (2) separate model needed for each initial microstructure; (3) inertial effects not modeled in micro-scale; (4) Fourier operators expensive at evaluation time (O(n log n) FFT per forward pass). For vastly different physical regimes (linear vs. nonlinear PDE, bifurcations), transfer learning fails. Hidden state discovery works for weakly-nonlinear systems but struggles with strongly chaotic or switching regimes.

title: Lexing Ying: Prony's Method, Analytic Continuation, And Quantum Signal Processing
speaker: Lexing Ying
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of only hand-written rules. One hard version of this is: given only a few snapshots of a measurement over time, recover the hidden ripples and decay rates that created those snapshots, even when noise corrupts the data. Prony's method is an old shortcut that does exactly this by spotting patterns in equally spaced samples, and this talk shows how the same idea also helps in quantum computing and in extending functions beyond the region where we know them.
core_problem: Many science and engineering questions boil down to: given a limited set of measurements, find the hidden frequencies and decay rates underneath. Why is this hard? Noise always creeps in, we can only sample so many times, and small mistakes in the data can explode into huge mistakes in the answer (a property called ill-conditioning). On top of this, physicists sometimes want to extend a function beyond the region where they measured it—another version of the same challenge. Quantum computing adds one more twist: to make quantum algorithms work, you need to factor certain mathematical expressions in a stable way, and that's actually the same problem in disguise.
first_principles_model: Prony's method starts with a simple assumption: what you measured is just a sum of exponentials (signals that grow or decay at steady rates). If that assumption is correct, the frequencies and decay rates are locked into algebra that shows up in your equally spaced samples. The core insight is: instead of trying to guess the frequencies directly, convert the hard problem into spotting patterns, then solve for the frequencies from those patterns. This works because structure (exponentials have a very specific form) is easier to find than trying to fix something without knowing its shape.
key_claims: Prony's method recovers the decay rates and ripple frequencies that are hidden in equally spaced time samples.
This method is old but too often forgotten, even though it solves hard problems simply.
Noisy measurements can be cleaned up and extended to regions you didn't measure using these same structure-spotting ideas.
Quantum computing needs the underlying algebra of Prony's method to reliably factor certain expressions.
The same mathematical thinking connects three different fields: old signal processing, extending functions into the complex plane, and quantum circuits.
Noise and measurement error are the real practical enemy, because the problem is sensitive—small changes to the data change the answer a lot.

important_terms.meaning: A recipe for identifying the decay rates and ripple frequencies in a signal that is a sum of exponentials, by spotting patterns in equally spaced samples.
Extending a function beyond the region where you directly measured it, by using the relationships between the values you did measure. This is easy if data are clean but fragile if noise is present.

A method for steering quantum computers by sending them carefully chosen phase shifts (twists in the quantum state) in sequence, similar to how you might amplify or suppress certain frequencies in a radio signal.
Figuring out what ripple rates or decay rates are present in a measured signal—the inverse of building the signal from known ripples.

A situation where tiny mistakes in measurement lead to huge mistakes in the answer. Like trying to draw a line through two dots that are very close—small shifts in where the dots are move the line a lot.

stanford_connections: This talk builds on the series' theme of recovering hidden information from incomplete measurements—that problem runs through inverse problems and imaging talks.
It connects to other talks about finding special frequencies and rates of change because all of them hunt for the 'skeleton' inside messy data.
It reminds us that not every solution to learning from data comes from neural networks; sometimes the oldest, simplest ideas from algebra and signal theory work best.
practical_caution: Prony's method can give great answers if the real data match the exponential model and the noise is small. But if your actual signal is not a sum of exponentials, or if noise is too big, the method can make errors much larger instead of smaller—it amplifies the noise rather than filtering it out.
selected_evidence: Prony's method is a powerful algorithm for identifying frequencies and amplitudes from equally spaced signals.
How many frequencies do you have in the signal... can you figure out what is... the weights.
Applying Prony's method to do noisy analytic continuation.
Stable factorization of the phase factors for quantum signal processing.
The classical solution... goes back more than 200 years.
takeaway: Good algorithms spot the structure hidden in your data before they start tweaking numbers. Prony's method works because it trades a hard, formless problem (find frequencies from samples) into a structured one (find parameters that fit a known pattern). The same pattern-spotting idea shows up in how physicists extend functions in the complex plane and how quantum computers process information.
worked_example: Prony's method on signal f_k = sum_j r_j e^(i ω_j k), k=0,1,2,... Hankel matrix H constructed from data snapshots: rank of H reveals d (number of modes). Null space yields polynomial m_z with roots = e^(iω_j); Fourier frequencies pop out. Analytic continuation: green function G(z) with poles at z_j with residuals r_j, sampled on imaginary axis with Gaussian noise. Mobius transform maps to unit disk; apply Prony to recover pole locations (0.1% noise: exact recovery; 10^(-2) noise: 1-2 pole location errors). QSP example: approximate e^(iτx) using d~1000-5000 phase angles, error ~10^(-12).
deeper_mechanics: Prony's method: given f_k, form Hankel matrix H=[f_0 f_1...f_d; f_1 f_2...f_{d+1}; ...]. Rank = d reveals mode count; null space gives polynomial m(z)=prod(z-e^{iω_j}) coefficients. For noisy analytic continuation, Mobius transform w(z)=(z-a)(z+b)/(b-a) maps imaginary axis→unit circle, poles→interior circles. Conformal map preserves pole structure in {residual, w_j form}. Compute moments via Fourier coefficients (contour integral by residue theorem). Prony extracts pole locations w_j from moments using Hankel structure. QSP: split function f(x) into even+odd parts, approximate by polynomials p_d(cos t), q_d(cos t); extract phase angles via Prony applied to reciprocal 1/sqrt(1-a²-b²) (coefficients ~ pole moments).
failure_boundary: Root finding in Prony becomes ill-conditioned when noise level ≥ 10^(-4) (Hankel singular values collapse). Poles distant from sampled axis (imaginary axis) unrecoverable—exponential decay of Fourier coefficients hides far poles. QSP: high-degree polynomials (d>5000) require extended precision arithmetic (O(d log d) bits); optimization approach converges only if matrix condition number κ ≤ O(d). Noisy continuation on small Matsubara grid (N~100 points): reconstruction fails for spectral features far from grid (edge effects dominate center recovery at noise 10^(-2)).

title: Ming Zhong: Machine Learning Of Self Organization From Observation
speaker: Ming Zhong
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of hand-written math. In many systems—schools of fish, flocking birds, crystal growth, traffic flow—large patterns emerge from simple local interactions between neighbors, but we don't know exactly what those neighbor-to-neighbor rules are. This talk is about teaching a computer to reverse-engineer those hidden interaction rules just by watching the motion trajectories.
core_problem: Self-organization happens in systems such as flocking, crowds, crystals, superconductivity, and social behavior. The large-scale pattern emerges and is visible, but the microscopic interaction rule among individual agents—what each agent actually does based on its neighbors—is hidden. The challenge is to work backward: look at the observed motion, and figure out what local rules must have generated it. This is harder than just predicting motion forward, because many different rules could produce the same observed pattern.
first_principles_model: A collective system is built from individual agents whose speeds or accelerations depend on distances to neighbors, what state each agent is in, and what type each agent is. These relationships are described by interaction kernels—functions that capture how one agent influences another (like: a fish copies its neighbors' direction more when they are close, less when they are far). Given trajectory data (records of where each agent moved over time) from many different starting setups, the learning problem is to estimate those kernels so that when you run a simulation using them, it reproduces what you actually observed. Theory studies how good the estimated kernels become as you collect trajectories from more and more different starting conditions.
key_claims: Self-organization can be studied by watching how individual agents move and interact.
The goal is to discover clear, interpretable rules about how agents interact, not just predict future motion without knowing why.
Learning the interaction rules can test whether existing theories about collective behavior are correct.
How well you can recover the rules depends on having trajectories from many different starting conditions and on how you discretize—break up the trajectory data into measurable pieces.
The method works for systems where all agents follow the same rules and also for mixed systems like predators and prey that follow different rules.

Even when you only observe steady-state behavior (where nothing seems to be changing), there is information hidden in those observations about the interaction rules, though you need to add extra constraints to solve the inverse problem reliably.

important_terms.meaning: Large-scale patterns and order that form by themselves from many small interactions between neighbors, with no central boss directing the outcome.
A function that encodes the rule for how one agent affects another—for example, how strong the influence is based on distance, or what state the neighbor is in.
Individual agents that all follow the same interaction rules.
Agents of different types—such as predators and prey—where each type follows its own set of interaction rules.
A timestamped record of where each agent is and what state it is in, recorded over time, showing the actual motion that you observe and want to learn from.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects to discovering equations and learning symbolic rules because it extracts governing laws directly from data rather than from human-written theories.
It links to nonlocal kernels and graph-based physics because collective behavior depends on how agents relate to and influence each other over distances.
It complements talks about predicting the future by emphasizing understanding and explaining the rules rather than just forecasting what happens next.
practical_caution: Inferring interaction laws from observed motion is an inverse problem—working backward from results to causes. Matching the observed motion does not guarantee you found the unique or physically correct rule, especially when you only have trajectories from a few starting conditions or when you only see steady-state behavior where nothing appears to change.
selected_evidence: Self-organization... can be found in studying crystal formation, superconductivity, social behaviors.
Can we actually derive from observation data... the interaction rules between all the agents.
Develop a learning framework to derive physically meaningful dynamical systems.
Analyze the convergence... from various different initial conditions.
Handle a system of heterogeneous agents.
takeaway: Collective patterns are compressed recordings of what the interaction rules must be. Scientific machine learning should recover the rules themselves—understanding why the pattern exists—not just repeat the pattern by memorizing it.
worked_example: Flocking model: N=50 agents, each with position x_i and velocity v_i, system evolves via ∂x_i/∂t = v_i, ∂v_i/∂t = Σⱼ≠ᵢ φ(r_ij) with pairwise interaction kernel φ. From snapshots of observed dynamics over T=10 time units (training interval), the algorithm recovers φ using 100 different initial conditions and roughly 1D regression rate convergence. Learned kernel φ̂ achieves ≈0.1 relative error compared to true φ. Prediction at T=20 (beyond training) shows dynamics remain accurate up to T=15, with phase and amplitude well-preserved. For predator-prey (1 predator, 20 prey), 4 different kernels learned (prey-prey, predator-prey, prey-predator, predator-predator); algorithm correctly identifies zero kernel for predator-predator (no self-interaction data).
deeper_mechanics: Pairwise interaction system: ∂x_i/∂t = Σⱼ φ(r_ij) e_ij where r_ij = |x_i - x_j|, e_ij = (x_j - x_i)/r_ij. Error functional L(φ) = ΣₘΣₜ ||∂x_i^m(t)/∂t - Σⱼ φ(r_ij^m(t)) e_ij^m(t)||²_L2 over M initial conditions and time. Convergence rate M^(-1/3) equals 1D regression rate; dimension-independent because only pairs interact. Basis expansion: φ(r) ≈ Σₖ aₖ ψₖ(r) using uniform splines or polynomials on learning interval [r_min, r_max]. Condition number of linear system Σⱼ a_j ∫ ψⱼ(r)ψₖ(r) ρ(r) dr = ... is well-controlled when data richness ρ(r) (pairwise distance distribution) is properly sampled.
failure_boundary: If solutions are non-mixing (particles cluster into separated groups), pairwise distances concentrate in narrow range and ρ(r) becomes singular; convergence collapses. For high-dimensional state vectors d >> 1, learning general kernels φ(x_i, x_j) becomes intractable (curse of dimensionality); only distance-dependent kernels learnable. Long-time prediction (T >> training time) fails when system transitions to novel regimes (e.g., from flocking to milling to polarization); kernel valid only in regimes observed during training. Presence of external noise or model mismatch (system not purely pairwise) causes biased kernel estimates and divergence during prediction.

title: Alice Cicirello: Interpretable, Explainable And Non-Intrusive Uncertainty Propagation
speaker: Alice Cicirello
one_sentence: This seminar series chases getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. One key challenge: when you run a simulation and the inputs (like material stiffness or heat source intensity) might change slightly, how do you find the range of outputs that could happen without running the simulation thousands of times? This talk shows a method that uses machine learning to pick the smartest few simulation runs to find that range, then explains to engineers exactly why those bounds are what they are.
core_problem: Engineering decisions rest on knowing whether a system will stay safe or perform well when real-world conditions wiggle. Realistic physics simulations can run for hours or days each, so trying thousands of runs to map out all possible outcomes is not practical. Finding the upper and lower bounds on performance usually requires either running the model vastly many times, rewriting how the solver works (which changes what you're testing), or simplifying the physics in ways that may hide the truth.
first_principles_model: Uncertainty propagation means watching how small changes in inputs (like tolerances in a design or errors in sensors) turn into changes in outputs as they travel through a simulation. If you can't rewrite the simulation's code or replace it with a simpler one, you still need to pick which runs matter most. Machine learning optimization can hunt through the input space for which combinations give the highest and lowest outputs. Once you find them, you build a fast replacement model (a surrogate) — a simpler mathematical description that mimics the expensive one's behavior. You can then point at that simpler model and explain: 'Here's why the output gets so high' or 'Here's why it gets so low.'
key_claims: Uncertainty quantification answers a vital question: when inputs vary (due to measurement error, manufacturing tolerance, or operating conditions), how far do the outputs spread? This variation ripples through the entire calculation.
For simulations that run slowly (hours or days per run), the bottleneck is not math—it is the sheer cost of testing many input combinations.
Non-intrusive methods don't rewrite the simulator's code or replace the physics with a simpler version; you just run it as-is and learn from the results.
Interpretability means a human can follow the chain of logic: 'We ran the simulation with these inputs, here's what came out, and here's why.'
Explainability means packaging the results in forms engineers actually need: 'When temperature can vary this much, performance is guaranteed to stay between these bounds.'
Machine learning can find the input combinations that make outputs as large or as small as possible, rather than blindly testing every combination.

important_terms.meaning: Tracking how small wobbles or ranges in inputs (like a measurement being off by 5%, or a material property changing with temperature) flow through a calculation to create wobbles or ranges in the answer.
A method that treats the simulator as a sealed tool—you feed it inputs and read off outputs, but you don't rewrite any of its code or swap out any of its physics.
Describing uncertainty as a simple range: 'The output will be between 100 and 150.' This is simpler than saying 'The output has a bell-curve probability distribution' but less detailed.

A strategy for picking which experiments or simulation runs to do next when each run is expensive: instead of testing all possibilities, you build a fast statistical guess-model that predicts which untried runs might give the most useful information, then try those.
A guaranteed limit—like 'this system cannot fail worse than X' or 'this system cannot perform better than Y'—that applies when inputs are allowed to vary within specified ranges.

stanford_connections: This talk addresses the seminar series' core theme by showing how to handle variability: when inputs shift or wobble, how do we still know the system stays within safe bounds?
It connects to talks on smart sampling: both use strategies to decide which experiments or simulation runs are worth the cost when resources are scarce.
It builds on talks about interpretability by showing that explaining uncertainty results—not just computing them—is what engineers actually need to trust and use the answers.
practical_caution: If your search strategy overlooks some regions of the input space, or your replacement model doesn't truly capture all the physics's behavior, you might miss the real highest and lowest values. Only trust your output bounds after confirming that your search strategy actually visited the important parts of the input space and your replacement model can reproduce the physics on a variety of test cases.
selected_evidence: Uncertainty models are used in conjunction with a computational model to compute the effects of uncertainties on a system performance.
Interpretable: a human can understand how a prediction was made.
Explainable: the results are presented in a format that is understandable by humans.
Non-intrusive: no modifications of the computational model are carried out.
Select the minimum number of physics based models to run in order to get performance bounds.
takeaway: Finding the extremes of model outputs with a limited computing budget is hard. The real work is picking your simulation runs wisely to find the bounds that matter, then showing engineers a clear picture of why those bounds are correct.
worked_example:
Single-DOF structural system with 4 uncertain parameters (interval bounds): 330 numerical simulations needed for brute-force grid. Bayesian optimization with Gaussian process reduces to 14-20 simulations to identify upper and lower bounds (response extrema). Percentage error <0.01% when bounds matched; stopping criterion: expected improvement acquisition function below 10^-2.

Multi-zone building control: 20 room temperatures, 4 uncertain parameters (material properties, boundary conditions). Supervised lower and upper bounds separately: 12 simulations (lower), 29 simulations (upper). Combined approach (same GP, both extrema tracked): 14 simulations total. Percentage errors ~1-2%. CPU memory 15 GB vs 100+ GB for full grid.
deeper_mechanics:
Gaussian process regression on finite response evaluations: given observed w = [w(b_1), ..., w(b_k)] at k parameter locations b_i, predict w*(b) at untested b via conditional normal distribution with mean and variance. Covariance kernel K encodes smoothness assumption (squared exponential, RBF); output variance quantifies model uncertainty from sparse sampling. Acquisition function (expected improvement): EI(b*) = E[max(0, w(b*) - w_best)] marginalizes GP posterior to balance exploitation (high expected value) vs exploration (high variance).

Stopping criteria: (1) acquisition function max value below threshold; (2) distance from current extrema to acquisition-suggested next point satisfactory. Interval response bounds computed as mean ± k·variance; over-predicts upper, under-predicts lower guarantees physical consistency.
failure_boundary: Gaussian process scales poorly beyond 20 dimensions (curse of dimensionality); sparse inducing points or dimensional reduction needed. Kernel choice critically affects accuracy; wrong kernel (e.g., smooth when response has sharp corners) leads to systematic bias requiring manual kernel tuning or ensemble. Non-monotonic response (global max not at domain boundary) requires dense sampling near extrema; uniform grid initialization inefficient. Mixed parametric/non-parametric or probabilistic/interval uncertainty descriptions untested—combining PDF and interval bounds requires careful formulation. Noisy evaluations (experimental data) reduce convergence rate; assumes clean simulator calls.

title: Yannis Kevrekidis: No Equations, No Variables, No Parameters, No Space And No Time
speaker: Yannis Kevrekidis
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from data and examples instead of only hand-written math. This talk asks: do you always need to know the step-by-step rules written down as equations, or can you sometimes find useful shorthand descriptions of a complex system directly from observations, without writing any equations at all?
core_problem: The normal way to study a complex system goes like this: watch what happens, choose some numbers to track (called variables: for instance, temperature at three spots), write down rules that say how those numbers change over time, pick the numbers that go into the rules (called parameters: things like how heat spreads through metal), and then work through the math to predict what happens. But for many real systems, this gets stuck. Nobody agrees on which numbers are really important to track, or they're hidden deep inside millions of pieces of data. The tiny, detailed simulation (like tracking every atom's motion) might run perfectly, but nobody can write down a simple closed-form rule (equations) that says how the system behaves at the big-picture level. The right shorthand description might live in such a twisted, high-dimensional space that you can't spot it by guessing.
first_principles_model: Here is the flip: forget about starting with equations. Start with the goal: do you want to predict the future, trace how the system stays stable or jumps to a different mode as something shifts, or control it? Then ask: can I build the actual computational operators I need directly from data, or by running the detailed simulation in short bursts? Several tools can do this without equations. Manifold learning is the idea that real complex systems often live on a simpler, curved surface hidden inside high-dimensional data (like how many different movies can be described by a small set of hidden genres, even though each movie has thousands of pixels). Autoencoders are neural networks - programs with millions of little dials tuned by trial and error until their answers match the data - that squeeze data into a much smaller, compressed representation (like summarizing a long movie plot into a few key story beats), then unsqueeze it back out. Diffusion maps build simple coordinates by watching how fast disturbances spread across the data (the same logic that tells you how far gas has diffused through a room: far means time has passed). Neural ODEs are networks that describe how variables change moment by moment (using a rule: at each step, the next state depends on the current state according to a formula the network has learned). Operator learning teaches a network to map entire functions or states directly to other states (like learning that if the temperature distribution looks like X, it will look like Y a moment later), skipping the need for intermediate equations. Together, these can recover the low-dimensional shorthand and the evolution rules from raw data.
key_claims: Modern neural networks have older roots in the study of how to identify nonlinear systems (real-world systems where a change in one part can cause wildly different effects depending on context).

A computational approach to modeling can hit the same analysis goals - prediction, detecting when behavior jumps to a different mode, control - by working with data or short bursts of detailed simulation instead of assuming you have a closed-form equation at the top level.
The right numbers to track in a system can be discovered by learning from data, rather than guessed by intuition or tradition.
Low-dimensional curved surfaces, where real complex systems live, can be revealed by studying the patterns in high-dimensional observation data.
Diffusion maps (a method that uses spreading patterns in data to extract simple coordinates) show one way to learn coordinates that work as useful high-level summaries.
The phrase 'no equations, variables, parameters, space, or time' means: the representation you need for your task can be learned rather than assumed or guessed ahead of time.

important_terms.meaning: A computational approach where you perform high-level analysis and prediction using data or short runs of detailed simulation, instead of finding and writing down the closed-form equations for the whole system.
A single number or small group of numbers that summarize what the system is doing at the large scale (like temperature averaged across a room, or the main direction a flock is moving).

Methods that discover that a complex system's behavior actually lives on a simpler, curved surface - like how a flat sheet of paper, even when crumpled, is still fundamentally two-dimensional - hidden inside high-dimensional data.
A method that learns simple coordinates from data by measuring how fast patterns spread and change (diffusion), the same logic physicists use to measure how gases or heat move through space.

A computational shortcut that advances the high-level description forward in time: translate the abstract description to the detailed level, run the detailed simulation for a short time, translate back to the abstract level.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects directly to talks on learning effective dynamics (how to predict a system's behavior when you only care about the large-scale motion, not every tiny detail) and data-driven methods for dynamics.

It also relates to work on reduced-order models (simplified versions of complex systems that still capture the important behavior) and learning operators (teaching networks to map entire system states to future states), because both search for lower-dimensional or operator-based descriptions of dynamics.
Broadly, it reframes scientific machine learning: before you hunt for equations or build a simulator, first figure out what numbers or coordinates even make the problem solvable.
practical_caution: Learning the shorthand from data only works if your data actually cover the important curved surfaces and operating conditions. A low-dimensional structure that fits your training data perfectly can fail completely when you encounter new situations, rare jumps the training data missed, or parameters your data never saw.
selected_evidence: No equations no variables no space no time.
Obtaining predictive dynamical equations from data lies at the heart of science and engineering modeling.
Operate directly on observations -data-.
Machine learning on the data to find out what the right macro observables are.
Diffusion Maps... learn low dimensional curved manifolds passing through the data.
takeaway: Equations are one tool to write down dynamics, not the only tool. The real goal is to find the shorthand descriptions and operators that make prediction and analysis possible. Sometimes data or quick simulations can give you those shortcuts without writing a single equation.
worked_example: A micro-scale plankton model with birth, death, random walk, and ocean currents generates stochastic agent trajectories. Without writing the governing equation, coarse-projective integration solves the macroscopic pair-correlation function P(r) by lifting: construct particles matching target P(r), run microscopic simulator for Δt_micro, measure derivative dP/dt at macro scale, then step macro variables by Δt_macro >> Δt_micro using Euler with estimated derivative. Result: macro-scale solution evolves smoothly as observed PDE, 100–1000× speedup compared to direct micro-simulation while maintaining accuracy in statistics and bifurcation structure.
deeper_mechanics: Coarse-projective integration requires (1) lifting: given macro state (moment/correlation function), construct ensemble of micro-realizations consistent with it; (2) micro-burst: short-time forward integration to accumulate micro-statistics; (3) restriction: project evolved micro-ensemble back to macro observable and estimate its time derivative via finite difference. The key insight is that macro dynamics are robust to microscopic details—many micro-realizations drive similar macro evolution. Mathematically, the macro system is a hidden Markov process; estimating dP/dt from noisy micro-data requires ensemble averaging. Optional tagging (e.g., stochastic particles with slow/fast splitting) can improve efficiency.
failure_boundary: Equation-free fails when micro-realizations don't converge to macro observables—incompatibility between lifting and restriction operators causes artificial drift. If the macroscopic observable is poor (e.g., first moment only for a multi-modal distribution), lifting is underdetermined and multiple micro-ensembles map to same macro state, introducing error. Multi-scale separation breaks down: if macro and micro timescales overlap, no clear time-scale hierarchy exists to justify large Δt_macro. For partial-differential equations with spatial coupling, lifting microscopic particles on a coarse grid requires ad-hoc boundary conditions that may not match the true PDE. Method requires strong intuition about which observables matter—wrong choice leads to information loss and prediction failure.

title: Weinan E: Machine Learning And Multi-Scale Modeling
speaker: Weinan E
one_sentence: This whole series asks whether computers can learn to predict how physical things behave instead of (or alongside) using hand-written math. One common approach is to feed a learning program both the data and the physics rules as it trains. This talk tackles a different angle: when you're trying to simulate something that has parts at many different size scales—atoms bouncing, then molecules jiggling, then materials warping, then structures shaking—how do you connect these views? Machine learning can learn the equations that stitch these scales together when the equations are too hard for a person to write down by hand.
core_problem: Real-world systems happen at many size scales at once: electrons and atoms (quantum scale), groups of molecules (atomistic scale), bunches of molecules acting together (coarse-grained scale), bulk materials (continuum scale), and swirling flows at large scales (turbulence scale). To predict real properties—how strong a material is, how a fluid flows, how heat spreads—you need these scales to talk to each other in your simulation. The hard part is writing down the 'connectors' between scales: the equations that describe how the smaller-scale details add up to affect the larger scales. These connectors are often too tangled and complex to write by hand.
first_principles_model: Each scale has its own successful description. At the atomic scale, you use quantum rules. At the molecular scale, you track the jiggling of atoms. At the material scale, you write down how the material stretches and bends. The job is to move information between scales: smaller-scale details should tell you what effective rules apply at the next scale up. For instance, molecular jiggling should tell you what viscosity (how thick or goopy a fluid is) to use in a larger-scale fluid simulation. Machine learning lets you learn these connection equations—the potentials (energy descriptions), the rules for how a coarse material responds to forces, the reduced equations for large systems—when writing them by hand is too hard or too time-consuming.
key_claims: Real systems require connecting models across many size scales to build simulators that actually predict what happens.
The bottleneck is writing the equations that link scales; those equations are often too complicated to work out by hand.
Machine learning can learn flexible versions of these linking equations from data.
Concrete uses include atomic simulations, models where many atoms act as one blob, thick fluids that don't behave simply, and shrinking large systems into smaller equations.
The chain goes: quantum rules, density descriptions of electrons, atomic jiggling, clumps of atoms, bulk materials, swirling large flows.
The real goal is not to throw out physics, but to learn the specific pieces that connect one physical picture to the next.

important_terms.meaning: Building a simulation by connecting together separate descriptions that work well at different size scales—tiny (atoms) to large (structures)—so they can all predict what happens.

A replacement rule that says what the tiny-scale details add up to when you don't track each tiny detail separately in a larger-scale simulation (like saying 'friction here is this much' instead of computing every tiny collision).
A simulation that treats a bunch of atoms as single blobby units instead of tracking each atom separately, making the calculation much faster.
A liquid or gas whose thickness (how hard it is to pour or stir) changes depending on how hard you push on it, unlike water which stays the same thickness no matter how fast you stir it.
A simplified rule at one size scale that captures what all the messy physics at smaller scales actually adds up to, without having to compute each tiny piece.

stanford_connections: This talk connects to Kaushik Bhattacharya's work on teaching programs to become simulators (neural operators) that handle systems across multiple scales.
It ties directly to machine learning for materials, because learning energy descriptions (potentials) is a concrete way to jump from smaller-scale atoms to larger-scale material behavior.
It reinforces a repeating thread across these talks: machine learning works best when it fills in the gaps that physics-based simulations cannot fill on their own.
practical_caution: A rule learned from data can look perfect within the data it trained on, yet still break physical laws (like energy or momentum must be conserved), become unstable in new situations, or fail when moved to a different scenario. This happens if the learned rule is not grafted into the full simulation in a way that keeps the physics consistent across all scales.
selected_evidence: Multi-scale modeling... aims at unifying the different physical models at different scales.
Practical success on really challenging problems has been limited.
Limited ability to represent complex models and complex functions.
Machine learning has emerged as a promising tool for overcoming the difficulty.
A hierarchy of physical models... quantum mechanics... molecular dynamics... continuum mechanics.
takeaway: The core idea is that multiscale machine learning is about learning the glue that holds together descriptions at different physical scales. The real win comes when learned rules let you trust your full simulation to work at every scale.
worked_example: Illustrative: Multiscale molecular dynamics (MD) coupled to continuum PDE. MD region has 10³-10⁴ atoms; continuum domain is discretized on macroscopic grid. ML learns the closure: macroscopic strain/stress history → coarse-grained force field. Example: polymer chain under load learns effective potential from MD ensemble averaging.
deeper_mechanics: Heterogeneous multiscale method (HMM) solves macro-PDE, queries microscale model at sampling points. Neural network closure g_θ(history; μ) replaces expensive microscale solve: F_macro = g_θ(u_coarse, ∇u_coarse; μ). Loss: minimize ||F_fom - g_θ(·;μ)||² over trajectories. Coarse-grained time-stepping: u_{n+1} = u_n + Δt × (linear + g_θ(u_n)).
failure_boundary: Closure is parameter-μ dependent; transfer to new μ fails if training set doesn't span parameter range. Microscale stochasticity (thermal noise) requires ensemble averaging; small ensemble → biased closure. Causality violation if network output depends on future history.

title: Daniel Floryan: Charting Dynamics From Data
speaker: Daniel Floryan
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things move and change by learning from real data instead of hand-written math. This talk shows how to find the true number of dimensions (the simplest way to describe what's actually happening) by using overlapping local maps and learning the motion rules on each map separately.
core_problem: Many real systems are so complicated that writing down their motion rules from first principles is impossible or takes too long. But when you plot their behavior over time, the path the system traces often lives on a much simpler surface hidden inside the high-dimensional recorded data. The challenge is finding local coordinate systems that fit this hidden surface and the motion rules that work there, so you can build a simplified model that still captures how the system actually evolves.
first_principles_model: Imagine a crumpled or curved surface (like a sheet of paper folded in 3D space). You can describe any point on it using overlapping local coordinate systems, where each system covers just one flat patch. From time-series data, you group trajectories into overlapping neighborhoods, learn a local coordinate system on each neighborhood, figure out how things move within each local system, and then stitch all the pieces together into one continuous dynamical model. The result is a simplified description that uses only as many coordinates as the system truly needs, rather than as many as you happened to record.
key_claims: Learning models from data is most useful when the real motion rules are unknown or when there are so many rules written down that computing them is too slow.
Systems in nature typically move along lower-dimensional surfaces, even when you record hundreds or thousands of measurements.
Overlapping local coordinate systems can cover any curved surface, no matter how twisted.
Time-series data can be split into overlapping groups that each get their own local coordinate system.
Learning how the system moves within each local coordinate system creates simplified models that use only the number of dimensions you really need.
Local coordinate systems let you tell the difference between the true shape of the system and artifacts that come from your measurement choices, and both of these improve predictions.

important_terms.meaning: A space that may twist and curve when you look at it from far away, but in any small local region looks like ordinary flat space.
A collection of overlapping local coordinate systems that together cover an entire curved surface, the way pages of an atlas cover Earth.
One local coordinate system that describes one small flat patch of a curved surface.
The true minimum number of coordinates you need to keep track of to specify exactly where the system is, without any redundancy.
A record of measurements taken one after another over time that shows how a system's state changes moment by moment.

stanford_connections: This approach expands on earlier work discovering hidden structure in data by providing a concrete geometric method that uses local maps.
It shares the same goal as reduced-order models: finding small-dimensional descriptions of how systems evolve in time.
It ties together the study of curved surfaces, nonlinear motion, and building models that you can use to control what happens next.
practical_caution: The local coordinate systems only work well if your data samples the entire hidden surface and covers the transitions between neighborhoods. If the data leave gaps or skip over where one neighborhood transitions to the next, the learned coordinate systems can create artificial jumps and give wrong predictions for how the system evolves.
selected_evidence: Learn minimal dynamical models directly from time series data.
Natural systems tend to live on small or low dimensional manifolds.
A manifold is... an atlas of charts.
Time series data... lie on or near a manifold.
Cluster the data into overlapping patches.
takeaway: When you simplify a dynamical system by finding its true dimensions, you're not just squashing numbers — you have to make sure that the way things move still makes sense in the new simpler coordinates. Picking the right local coordinates is how you separate the real shape of the system from the clutter that came from how you happened to measure it.
worked_example: Circle example: 40 equally-spaced points, 2D ambient data reduced to 1D intrinsic manifold with 3 overlapping patches. Error nearly perfect after training. Torus periodic orbit: 3 patches, 1D reduction from 3D ambient space, high fidelity over 10 periods. Quasi-periodic torus (incommensurate): 6 patches from 3D to 2D representation with minor phase-speed offset but excellent reconstruction. Reaction-diffusion spiral wave: 20,000+ dimensional system reduced to 1D model with minimal reconstruction error between high-res and learned dynamics. Kuramoto-Sivashinsky system: periodic case maps to 1D model with high fidelity; disparate time scales (factor of 100) captured from single time unit of training data; intermittent dynamics with non-periodic bursts: 6-patch atlas yielding 3D dynamical model, qualitatively correct but quantitative quiescence duration off (attributed to logarithmic divergence inherent to saddle points).
deeper_mechanics: Atlas of overlapping patches (coordinate domains) with local coordinate maps (invertible neural networks / autoencoders) flattening curved manifolds to Euclidean spaces. K-means clustering with overlap procedure creates boundary/internal point distinction. Under-completed autoencoders encode/decode local dimensionality reduction (forward and inverse mappings). Neural networks approximate dynamics in reduced coordinates: either ODEs (dx/dt via neural net) or discrete time-delta flow maps. Strong Whitney embedding theorem (bound 2n for worst case) shows theoretical limit without charts. Dissipation mechanism drives trajectories to inertial manifolds. State space decomposition into regions of distinct behavior; local models compose via chart transitions.
failure_boundary: Manifold learning methods without charts fail to recover intrinsic dimension (non-injective mappings cause information loss). Cannot globally flatten topologically non-trivial manifolds (e.g., torus always collapses when flattened as single chart). Sample complexity depends on intrinsic (not ambient) dimension but unknown a priori—must empirically determine number of patches. Hyperparameter selection (patch count, local dimension per patch) requires trial/iteration. Noise robustness: transitions between patches amplify disagreement where manifold intersections occur under noisy data. Limited to systems with clear dissipative structure enabling inertial manifolds; chaotic systems with logarithmic divergence capture gross structure but fail on quantitative timescale details. Global methods (single autoencoder without patching) achieve only order-of-magnitude worse reconstruction even at 2n dimensions per Whitney bound.

title: Petros Koumoutsakos: Artificial Intelligence And Scientific Computing For Fluid Mechanics
speaker: Petros Koumoutsakos
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples. Fluids — air, water, wind — are especially hard because they change in countless connected ways at the same time. This talk is about why letting a learning program (a system that tunes itself by trial and error) predict fluid motion alone often fails, and shows how to build a hybrid: mix the trial-and-error learning with traditional step-by-step math solvers that engineers have used for decades, then pick the right balance between them.
core_problem: Fluid mechanics studies how water and air move and push on things around them. The challenge has many layers: motion is nonlinear (small changes can cause huge effects), chaos shows up at many size scales at once (tiny swirls mix with big currents), turbulence (chaotic, irregular motion) dominates, and objects in the fluid push back on it as it pushes on them. Over decades, engineers built slow, careful step-by-step math (numerical solvers — programs that predict what happens next by tiny increments) to handle this. Now people want learning programs (systems that tune themselves by trial and error on data) to do the same job, faster. The real problem is: how do you combine old math solvers, new learning programs, and human knowledge to predict and steer fluids in ways you can trust?
first_principles_model: Two tools exist. The old tool: step-by-step math solvers. They follow the rules of physics exactly (or nearly) and know how to avoid numerical crashes if you set them up right. The new tool: learning programs with millions of adjustable dials that learn patterns by trial and error on data. They are flexible and can spot trends humans miss, but they have no built-in physics knowledge. The smart move is to combine them: use the solver to generate data or to check that the learning program's answer makes physical sense; use the learning program to learn a smaller description of the full motion (so you only track what matters); and use reinforcement learning (learning by trial and reward signals from a simulated environment) to discover good ways to steer the fluid.
key_claims: AI has grown because of more powerful computers and more available data, but claims about AI for fluids need hard proof to separate fact from hope.
Complex flows and steering should combine learning programs with numerical solvers rather than trust learning alone.
One successful hybrid approach: use detailed or high-resolution simulations to teach a smaller model that still captures the important motion patterns.

The equation-free method (a technique developed years ago by Kevrekidis and others) showed how to learn smaller descriptions of complex systems; this is a direct ancestor of modern learned reduced models.
Multiple independent agents learning together (each adjusting actions based on rewards from a simulation) can solve fluid steering and interaction problems when mixed with scientific computing.
Both successes and failures matter because they show whether the underlying physics structure is truly necessary.

important_terms.meaning: A calculation system that weaves together step-by-step math solvers, learned models, trial-and-error tuning, and traditional physics knowledge into one integrated process.
A simplified description that captures how a complex system evolves at the particular scale or detail level you actually care about.
The coupled dance between a moving fluid and solid objects inside it that can shift position or bend in response to the fluid's push.
A method where several independent entities each learn by taking actions in an environment and receiving reward signals, often learning to work together or compete.
Using algorithms and computers to solve the step-by-step math rules that describe physical systems, turning abstract equations into numerical predictions.

stanford_connections: This lecture builds directly on earlier work by Kevrekidis about equation-free methods and effective dynamics, adapting those ideas specifically to fluid motion.
It connects to later talks about surrogate acceleration because the goal is not just speed but keeping predictions accurate and staying in control.
It also joins with talks on reinforcement learning in scientific control, where simulations become the training ground for learning strategies.
practical_caution: In fluids, disaster hides in the details. A learned model might predict one test case perfectly, then fail completely when conditions shift slightly. Predictions can drift over hours of simulated time because tiny mistakes compound. When you feed a learned prediction back into a real system — steering a plane wing, for example — small errors can grow fast. Any hybrid system must include checks: does the prediction violate conservation laws? Does it stay stable over long times? Does control actually work when tested?
selected_evidence: There is an ever-increasing amount of hype... regarding the capabilities of learning algorithms.
Forming alloys of AI and simulations for the prediction and control of complex flow systems.
Models and numerics and... machine learning tools... I call this computing alloys.
Learning the effective dynamics of complex systems.
Equation free framework... simulations in the microscales.
takeaway: The lesson is that AI for fluids must be built as a partnership between step-by-step math solvers and learning programs, with continuous checks that the answers make physical sense. The real question is not whether to use AI or solvers, but how to combine them so the result is stable, stays accurate, and can actually be controlled.
worked_example: Petaflops compressible-flow simulation on 13 trillion computational elements in 2013 (line 141-143), 30x improvement in time-to-solution via petsc/trilinos optimization reaching high % of peak performance. Blood-cell simulation at sub-micron resolution: 13 trillion dissipative-particle-dynamics particles (line 164), tens of millions of timesteps, 1.4 billion RBCs resolved in 0.3 mL of blood (line 166-168). Kuramoto-Sivashinsky prediction: LSTM trains on 20 SVD modes capturing sufficient energy, predicts 0.5-1.0 training periods before chaotic divergence (line 628-641). Cylinder flow (Reynolds 100): 100x speedup via latent-encoded dynamics (LED), errors in vorticity small, drag captured to 5% error (line 843-851) vs Reynolds 1000 showing 20% error, demonstrating Reynolds-number generalization limit (line 858-861).
deeper_mechanics:
Covariance-matrix adaptation evolution strategy (CMA-ES) learns probability distribution of optimal parameters. Start with Gaussian (mean, covariance); sample λ points, weight by fitness, recombine good points, update covariance via rank-one + full-matrix update (line 358-385).
