Latent-encoded dynamics (LED): encoder projects high-dim snapshot to latent z (autoencoder learned offline), LSTM evolves z forward in reduced space, decoder reconstructs to full space. Two time scales: micro t_μ (snapshot updates), macro t_m (global time steps); by staying in latent space, capture 100x speedup (line 831-838). Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs): autodiff computes ∇u for PDE residual; loss = data fidelity + PDE residual; no explicit time-stepping solver needed, only satisfies PDE at collocation points (line 1642-1663).

Reinforcement learning (RL) for control: agent observes states, takes actions, receives reward; policy optimized to maximize expected long-term reward. Multi-agent RL disperses agents on grid; local states = gradients, Laplacian, Fourier energy modes; actions = turbulence closure coefficients (line 1238-1263). Experience replay with importance sampling: store old experiences, later sample to update policy; correction factor addresses distribution mismatch between old/current policy (line 1039-1064).
failure_boundary: LSTM prediction on Kuramoto-Sivashinsky fails beyond ~1 training period; chaotic systems exhibit sensitive dependence on IC, predictions diverge exponentially (line 630-643). LED fails at high Reynolds (Re 1000: 20% error vs Re 100: 5%); method assumes latent manifold smooth and stable under parameter variation (line 858-861). PINNs fail on stiff equations, longer time horizons, parameter extrapolation (line 1684-1695); loss landscape becomes non-convex. RL requires careful state selection: using raw velocity fails, only physics-motivated invariants (vorticity gradients, Fourier modes) enable convergence (line 1419-1439). Auto-encoder architecture choice critical: generic compression (POD) may miss manifold dimension vs problem-specific designs (line 809-816).

title: Benjamin Peherstorfer: Neural Galerkin Schemes With Active Learning
speaker: Benjamin Peherstorfer
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. This talk focuses on a technique that uses a program with millions of little dials (called a neural network) to guess solutions to complex rules that describe how something changes across both time and space (high-dimensional PDEs). The key trick: instead of training on random points everywhere, the method notices where its current guess is most wrong and deliberately collects more examples from those spots.
core_problem: When a physical rule describes how something changes across both time and space, you need a huge amount of data to train a learning program well. Picking training points blindly from a uniform grid wastes data and misses important stuff that moves or concentrates in just a few places — like a traveling wave or a sharp front. A fixed set of training points, chosen at the start, often fails to track these moving features as time goes on.
first_principles_model: A classical numerical trick called Galerkin starts with a guess for the solution, measures how badly it breaks the physical rule, and then tweaks it to reduce that violation. In this talk's approach, instead of the guess being a standard mathematical formula, it's a program with dials (a neural network) that evolves step by step through time. The new piece: rather than collecting all training points ahead of time, the method looks at where the current guess breaks the rule most badly and automatically samples new training points from those spots.
key_claims: Predicting how well a trained program will work on new data is hard in engineering when you cannot afford to run expensive experiments or simulations.
You can train a neural network to match a physical rule by measuring the rule's violation at sampled points and adjusting the network's dials to minimize that violation, step by step in time.
The size of the violation at each point tells you where to collect the next training samples — focus on spots where the guess is most broken.
For high-dimensional problems, picking training points adaptively (following the current guess's mistakes) is essential to make learning programs actually useful.
This approach shines when the solution has moving concentrated features, like a shock wave or a localized pulse.
Treating training data as something the solver itself decides when and where to collect (rather than gathered beforehand) is a different way of thinking about solving these equations numerically.

important_terms.meaning: A numerical approach that starts with a guess for the answer, checks how badly it violates the physical rule at chosen points, then tweaks the guess to reduce that violation.
The same Galerkin strategy, but the guess is a program with millions of dials (a neural network) instead of a fixed formula.
A number that measures how badly a guess breaks the physical rule at a particular point — zero means the rule is satisfied perfectly there.
A strategy where the program looks at its own mistakes and asks for more training examples from the spots where it is most confused or wrong.
A rule that describes how something changes step by step over time (e.g. how heat spreads, how a wave moves, how a fluid flows).

stanford_connections: This connects to physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) through the idea of measuring how much a guess breaks the physical rules, but adds the refinement of stepping through time piece-by-piece and smartly picking training points as you go.
It also connects to reduced-order models — another way to shrink a huge problem into something smaller — because the neural network acts as an adaptive, learned-on-the-fly simplified representation.
Across the whole series, this reinforces one recurring idea: where you collect your training examples is just as important as what kind of program you use.
practical_caution: The physical rule might look satisfied overall while the actual wrong answer grows silently (because you're only checking points you already sampled). Active learning — the automatic sampling strategy — helps catch this but is not a guarantee. You still need to validate the final answer against other methods or real measurements to be sure.
selected_evidence: Fitting parameters... requires accurately estimating the population loss from training data.
Few informative training samples are available.
Neural Galerkin schemes... generate training data samples with active learning.
Fit network parameters by minimizing the residual sequentially over time.
Active form of gathering training data... is key.
takeaway: Learning programs for physical rules should not use a fixed set of training points chosen at the start. Instead, the training points should be chosen as you go, following where the current guess is struggling the most. Data collection is not just a preparation step; it is woven into the solver itself.
worked_example: For high-dimensional (5D, 8D) advection with localized peaks traveling through space, naive uniform sampling of 1000 collocation points in the physical domain failed entirely—the network never saw the peak. With adaptive sampling proportional to squared solution magnitude at the previous timestep, the same 1000 samples per step successfully tracked all 5 dimensions. For the KdV equation with periodic boundary conditions, Neural Galerkin achieved higher accuracy than linear Galerkin despite using the same (small) number of basis functions, capturing shock merging dynamics the linear model smeared away.
deeper_mechanics: Neural Galerkin replaces the discretized basis by a neural network u(x,t;theta(t)) whose weights theta evolve via ODEs. The loss function J integrates squared residuals ||∂u/∂t - N[u]||^2 against a time-dependent measure nu_t. Setting ∇_theta J = 0 yields a system of ODEs for theta-dot. Explicit schemes require only linear regression per timestep (cheap); implicit schemes require solving nonlinear equations per step (expensive but allows larger timesteps). Active learning samples from nu_t = sum_i beta_i * Gaussian(center_i, bandwidth_i), where centers and bandwidths move with solution peaks, focusing effort where solution has variation.
failure_boundary: For waves interacting (collisions, merges), the fixed number of Gaussian kernels may not track all features simultaneously. Neural Galerkin with small networks exhibits mode collapse where the network learns only mean behavior; expressiveness grows with network size but training cost explodes. The method requires smooth PDEs; for systems with genuine discontinuities (shocks that don't smooth), network nonlinearity cannot emulate the exact shock speed and instead smears. Extrapolation to initial conditions or parameters far from training fails; generalization improves with more offline training but cannot break the fundamental data-requirement curse.

title: Ishan Khurjekar: Uncertainty-Aware Guided Wave Structural Health Monitoring
speaker: Ishan Khurjekar
one_sentence: This series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from data instead of pure math. One way is to send sound waves through a structure and have a learning program detect damage by comparing what comes back. This talk is about why that approach fails when temperature shifts or other real-world noise gets involved—and how to make the program admit when it is unsure instead of guessing with fake confidence.
core_problem: Guided-wave systems send sound waves through a structure to find damage. The waves bounce differently when there is a crack or break. But temperature also changes how the waves travel, and so does how heavily the structure is loaded or pushed. A neural network—a program with millions of little dials the computer tunes by trial and error until its answers look right—can learn to spot damage in a lab. But when the temperature rises or falls in the real world, the same wave patterns change even if the structure is fine. The network gets fooled and becomes overconfident in its wrong guesses.
first_principles_model: A guided-wave system works by sending a pulse of sound down through steel or a bridge beam. The sound bounces back from the far end and also bounces off any crack or damage in between. By recording these echoes with many microphones (a sensor array), you can tell where damage is and how bad it is. Now add learning: a program reads many examples of healthy and damaged signals, and it learns to spot the difference. The problem: the signals also shift when temperature changes or when the weight on the structure goes up. To handle this, methods from probability theory help: run multiple copies of the learning program and see if they all agree (an ensemble), teach the program to map signals to a 'compressed space' where it also learns how wiggly or uncertain that space is (a variational autoencoder—a neural network that learns a probability distribution over compressed signals), or deliberately mess up training examples to prepare the program for real-world noise (adversarial perturbations). All of these estimate not just a yes-or-no guess but also how much confidence the program should have.
key_claims: Structures like buildings, bridges, aircraft, oil platforms, and pipelines need regular inspection to find cracks before they fail.
Guided waves are effective for inspecting because a single sound pulse can travel far down a beam or plate and bounce off damage.
Real-world shifts—warmer or cooler weather, heavier loads, age—change how sound travels through a structure, even when there is no damage at all.
A simple neural network trained only in the lab will guess confidently wrong when real-world conditions shift.
Running multiple copies of the learning program (an ensemble) and averaging their answers can catch when they disagree and signal uncertainty.
Teaching a program to build a probability model of compressed signals (variational autoencoders) lets it spot when new signals look unlike anything it has seen.

important_terms.meaning: Regular sensing and analysis to spot cracks, breaks, or other damage in buildings, bridges, machines, or other things we care about.
A sound pulse that travels along the length of a beam or plate, bouncing off damage on the way. The bounces tell you where the damage is.
Figuring out exactly where in a structure the crack or break is located.
Running many copies of the learning program and combining their answers so that you can tell when they agree (high confidence) and when they disagree (time to be careful).

A neural network that squashes sensor signals down into a smaller space of patterns, and also learns how spread-out or uncertain that smaller space is, so it can spot when new signals are strange or unlike training examples.

stanford_connections: This connects to how to hand off responsibility to automated systems safely: methods for uncertainty propagation and reliable surrogate models (programs that stand in for expensive simulations) are used in engineering design and safety.

It also touches on active learning and data augmentation, because you have to deliberately include environmental variation—temperature, loading, age—in your training examples or the program will fail.
It is a real-world case where ignoring uncertainty in a machine-learning system can directly harm people.
practical_caution: Damage detection saves lives. A bridge inspector or aircraft maintenance crew relies on the detection to decide if the structure is safe. A program that misses real damage is dangerous. A program that cries wolf—saying damage exists when it does not—wastes money and stops the structure from being used. Worse, a program that becomes confidently wrong is worse than no program at all. So the system must honestly tell you when it has seen something during training that it matches well, and when it sees something weird and unfamiliar in the field.
selected_evidence: Guided wave systems consist of an array of sensors that can transmit and receive waves.
Guided waves are sensitive to external variations such as temperature and loading conditions.
There is uncertainty in damage detection and localization.
Can we cast damage detection as an anomaly detection problem.
Ensemble learning... train an ensemble of variational auto encoders.
takeaway: Damage detection is not simply a yes-or-no classification problem. It is inference under real-world variation: the program must predict damage, estimate how sure it is, and raise a flag when the world has shifted beyond its training examples. Putting uncertainty into the output—not just a guess but a guess with a confidence level—is what turns a lab tool into something an engineer can actually trust.
worked_example:
In structural health monitoring of a 1.2 × 1.2 meter aluminum plate, the team created an ensemble of 10 variational autoencoders trained on synthetic guided wave data. The data generation used the Lamb wave model: a summation over wave modes where each mode's amplitude depends on frequency-dependent wavenumbers. Temperature variations from 4 to 19°C caused stretch factors (time-scaling of signals) ranging from 0.998 to 1.003. When a small mass was placed on the plate at measurement 37 (simulating damage), they collected 77 total measurements over 6 hours.

Comparing four detection methods: the ensemble VAE approach achieved 0% false alarm probability and 100% detection probability on the experimental data, whereas standard likelihood models showed 50-90% false alarm rates. The probability of false alarm was the key metric because likelihood models incorrectly flagged undamaged cases as damage due to assigning spurious values to out-of-distribution inputs.
deeper_mechanics:
Guided waves in plates satisfy the Lamb wave equation: the field u(ω,r) is expressed as a summation over n discrete propagating modes, where each mode has amplitude depending on the wavenumber κ_n(ω), which itself is a nonlinear function of frequency ω and material properties. Temperature changes approximately induce a time-stretch: the observed signal s(t) at higher temperature equals the reference signal at a scaled time x(αt), where α is the stretch factor that minimizes residual energy.

The variational autoencoder takes baseline-subtracted signals (containing only damage reflections, not direct path signals) and learns a latent code z that reconstructs the signal. The loss function includes reconstruction error and a Kullback-Leibler regularization term enforcing the latent distribution matches a standard normal. For anomaly detection, they use the ELBO (evidence lower bound) from the VAE as the detection statistic—normalized by output dimension. Averaging this metric across an ensemble of 10 randomly initialized VAEs provides robustness.
failure_boundary: The VAE approach requires training exclusively on undamaged (negative) data to learn what 'normal' looks like. If the training set accidentally includes damaged cases, the model learns an inflated null distribution and misses true damage. The time-stretch model for temperature compensation breaks down if temperature variations are too rapid or spatially non-uniform. When using synthetic training data from the Lamb wave model, there is a model-reality gap: experimental data contains reflections from plate boundaries and structural discontinuities that the simplified Lamb model doesn't predict, causing the trained model to behave differently than on synthetic data. The ensemble approach requires enough diversity in random initialization to span the solution space, but with limited computational resources, 10 networks may not be sufficient for highly chaotic or multimodal damage indicators.

title: Tailin Wu: Learning To Accelerate Large-Scale Physical Simulations
speaker: Tailin Wu
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. This talk focuses on water, oil, and plasma — systems that normally take days to simulate. The idea: train a learning program (a huge bank of dials the computer tunes by trial and error until its answers look right) to copy what the slow simulators do, so you can run predictions in seconds instead.
core_problem: Simulating how water and oil flow underground, or how plasma behaves, means tracking millions of tiny cells and running the math forward one tiny time-step at a time. On a computer, this takes weeks. A learning program trained to copy these simulations could run much faster, but it faces hard problems: the mesh (the grid of cells) is irregular, behavior at tiny scales couples with behavior at big scales, and mistakes pile up when you run the prediction forward many steps.
first_principles_model: A physical simulator is a rule applied over and over: given how things look right now, compute how things look one tiny time step later. A learned simulator tries to copy that rule using a program. For water and oil underground, use a program that sees each grid cell and its neighbors as a network of connections — a graph neural network — to capture how fluids flow locally. For pressure, which affects the whole region at once, use a different program (a U-Net, which reads in a picture and writes out a picture) because it sees the whole field at once. Train by forcing the program to predict correctly not just one step ahead, but several steps ahead. This exposes the program to its own mistakes and teaches it to stay accurate longer.
key_claims: Simulating large water and plasma systems with hand-written math can take days or weeks on even the fastest computers.
A learning program trained to copy these simulations can make them run in seconds, but must overcome the fact that behavior at tiny and huge scales mix together and errors grow with time.
The best setup uses two different learning programs together: one that sees connections between neighbors for local flow, and one that sees the whole region at once for global pressure.
A program that tracks connections between neighbors is good at mesh and particle systems where information travels along lines and not everywhere at once.
Training by guessing several steps ahead, not just one, teaches the program to keep working well for a long time.
This method works for truly huge systems — millions of cells — like subsurface flow under the ground.

important_terms.meaning: A learning program trained to copy how a physical simulator steps forward from one moment to the next.

A program with little dials it tunes by trial and error. It sends information along paths in a graph, designed for systems where things are connected in a mesh or as particles and information flows along those connections, not everywhere at once.

A program that reads a picture (a field of numbers over space) and writes out another picture, using a stack-down-then-stack-up architecture that lets it see both tiny details and the whole picture at once.

A score for how wrong the program is, measured not just for the next moment but for several moments ahead. The program uses this score to tune its dials so it stays accurate for a long time, not just one step.
Running the learned program forward by applying its one-step rule over and over to predict what happens many time steps into the future.

stanford_connections: This lecture shows the learned-simulator idea with a real system built from different kinds of learning programs chosen to match what the physics needs.
It connects to Petros Koumoutsakos' work by mixing different neural programs where each one fits the physics best — local connections for nearby effects, whole-field vision for global effects.
It also touches neural operators and reduced-order models, because the learned program is trying to copy an evolution operator — a rule that updates the system from one moment to the next.
practical_caution: A learning program that guesses the next step correctly might pile up huge errors when you run it forward ten or a hundred steps. Whether it stays accurate matters much more than whether it is right for just the very next moment. If you plan to use the learned copy to control a system or reverse-engineer what happened, test it by running it forward for as many steps as you actually need.
selected_evidence: Simulating the time evolution of large-scale physical systems is crucial.
How to learn faithful long-term evolution, and how to model multi-scale dynamics.
Introduce a hybrid graph network simulator.
Graph network to model the dynamics of the water and oil and also a 3d unit... pressure.
Multi-step loss can really help the long-term rollout.
takeaway: Learned simulation is the same rule applied over and over. Staying accurate through many steps is what counts, not nailing the one step right in front of you.
worked_example:
A hybrid graph neural network simulator (GNN + 3D U-Net) on subsurface flow with 1.5 million grid cells achieves 184× speedup compared to iterative PDE solvers, solving 20 timesteps in 20 seconds on GPU versus 46–370 seconds on CPU. The model trained on 256 samples captures water-oil saturation evolution and pressure fronts with high fidelity. For stochastic optimization under uncertainty (flow control around a cylinder), training on 256 samples with multi-step rollout loss achieves errors comparable to solving 2000+ direct PDE evaluations, a 10–100× sample efficiency gain.

For laser-plasma interactions, a fluid-particle hybridization models thermal particles as Maxwellian moments (mean, std dev) via CNN, while hot ions are tracked as particles using a classical particle-in-cell method. This reduces degrees of freedom by orders of magnitude. The coupled bubble oscillation model reduces frequencies from 3 kHz (uncoupled) to ~200 Hz (coupled with 1000s of bubbles), matching observed ocean wave roar frequencies and explaining why small bubbles radiate lower-frequency sounds when coupled.
deeper_mechanics:
The GNN models subsurface flow as a graph where each grid cell is a node connected to 6 neighbors. Messages between nodes encode pressure and saturation gradients; aggregation sums incoming messages, and node updates integrate information across scales. The U-Net processes pressure (global dynamics) in parallel; both outputs are restricted back via prolongation. Multi-step rollout loss L = Σ_t ||u_t - u_truth_t||^2 trains the model to predict 10+ steps ahead, not just one step. For beam plasma, the particle-injection network predicts Gaussian distribution parameters (mean, std dev) for newly injected particles from the bulk fluid state.

Bubble coupling exploits symmetry: the pressure from one bubble drives neighbors via the incompressible velocity field. The mass matrix M has off-diagonal entries M_ij representing inter-bubble effective-mass coupling. Factorizing M = LL^T allows efficient time-stepping and low-rank updates when bubbles appear/disappear.
failure_boundary: Error accumulates over long rollouts despite multi-step training; extrapolation to out-of-distribution parameter regimes (e.g., much higher viscosity) fails. The GNN is weakly nonlinear; highly compressible flows or strong shocks violate incompressibility assumptions. For plasma, the Maxwellian assumption for thermal particles breaks down if real distributions are skewed or multi-modal. Bubble coupling diverges if bubbles get very close (infinite effective mass), requiring regularization. GPU memory limits constrain problem scale; 1.5M cells is feasible but 50M cells requires nested/domain decomposition.

title: Molei Tao: Trustworthy Learning Of Mechanical Systems And Stiefel Optimization
speaker: Molei Tao
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of only using hand-written math. One popular way teaches a learning program (a huge bank of dials the computer tunes by trial and error) to respect a hidden property of moving systems called symplecticity: energy and momentum follow rules that should never be broken. This talk shows how building this respect into the learning process makes predictions accurate far into the future, and reveals a surprising connection: the same trick works for tuning dials on curved mathematical surfaces like the space of perpendicular frames.
core_problem: Real moving systems—a pendulum, a planet orbiting, a spinning top—obey hidden rules. Energy doesn't vanish; momentum stays balanced; the system's path follows a special curved surface in mathematical space (called symplectic). Standard learning programs can memorize short clips of motion while completely breaking these rules, so as you ask them to predict further and further into the future, the predictions drift further and further from what really happens. A related problem shows up in optimization (the process of tuning a program's dials): when the dials themselves live on a curved surface instead of a flat space, treating the surface as if it were flat causes the tuning algorithm to jump off the surface and make wrong moves.
first_principles_model: A moving mechanical system is not just a snapshot of where things are right now; it is a continuous flowing motion that preserves certain hidden quantities and shapes. Symplectic learning means building the prediction rule so that it automatically preserves these hidden symmetries: the learned equations of motion will keep energy and momentum balanced no matter how far into the future you predict. For problems with dials that live on a curved surface like the Stiefel manifold (the set of all possible perpendicular rectangular frames, where each column is a unit-length vector pointing in a different direction), optimization algorithms need to be redesigned so that each step of tuning stays on that curved surface instead of wandering into flat space.
key_claims: Teaching a learning program about physics directly (not as a wish, but as a hard built-in rule) can make its predictions of moving systems stay true for much longer.
Real mechanical systems preserve quantities and shapes: energy, momentum, and a special property called symplecticity.
Symplecticity is the hidden geometric rule that underlies the motion of all Hamiltonian systems (systems described by energy and momentum).
Embedding the symplectic rule directly into a learning program can be proven to extend how far into the future its predictions remain correct.
The same geometric thinking that fixes physics learning also fixes how we tune programs with many dials on curved mathematical surfaces.
Momentum-based tuning (the method of accelerating a downhill search) can be redesigned to work correctly on curved spaces, with perpendicular frames as a practical example.

important_terms.meaning: A hidden property of flowing systems where the system preserves area and quantity-like measures, and returns to the same state if you run it forward then backward; the defining property of Hamiltonian motion.

A way to describe mechanics using two ingredients: where things are (position) and how fast they are moving (momentum), plus a single master quantity (the Hamiltonian) that accounts for all the energy and structure of the system.
Asking a learned model to forecast what happens far into the future; small mistakes in the prediction rule compound and snowball, causing the predictions to drift away from what actually occurs.

The collection of all possible rectangular grids of perpendicular unit vectors (think of it as all the ways you can arrange compass directions in a space); a curved mathematical surface where constrained tuning problems live.

A method for tuning a program's dials when those dials themselves are constrained to live on a curved mathematical surface, ensuring each tuning step stays on the surface instead of wandering off into empty space.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects to talks across the series about building physics directly into learned models, solving differential equations with neural networks, and learning systems by respecting their hidden structure.
It connects to talks on how to make predictions you can trust by showing one clear path: preserve the quantities and shapes that real systems never break.
It also ties together the physics of moving systems and the mathematics of tuning (optimization), showing they are two faces of the same geometric idea that other talks in the series will return to.
practical_caution: Preserving a hidden structure helps only when the structure actually describes your system. If you force the preservation rule (symplecticity) on a real machine that loses energy through friction or gets pushed by outside forces, the learned model will hold onto the wrong properties and make terrible predictions.
selected_evidence: Trustworthy learning of mechanical systems & Stiefel optimization.
How to make symplectic predictions.
Mechanical system... has structures... conservation of energy... momentum.
Underlying geometric notion called symplecticity that is preserved by the dynamics.
Hardwire this... in our learning model.
takeaway: The core message is that learning to predict real moving systems accurately requires the learning process to respect the geometry—the hidden shapes and rules—of those systems. Accurate long-time prediction comes from honoring the quantities that stay constant (like energy and momentum) and the symmetries that never break.
worked_example:
Symplectic map learning for planet orbit prediction: given discrete-time observations of positions (q) and momenta (p) across multiple time steps, train a neural network parameterizing generating function S(q,q̄) such that the induced symplectic map preserves exact symplecticity. Over N prediction steps, error grows linearly O(ε_approx + c·N·h) where h is time step and c·N·h is prediction time—vastly better than exponential error bounds for non-symplectic approaches. Standard map (chaotic): visualized as Poincaré pancake map with stable islands separated by chaotic seas; gfnn captures major stable islands while other methods fail.

Vision Transformer on CIFAR-10: imposing Stiefel constraint (orthonormal attention weight matrices W_i^Q, W_i^K) within each attention head yields 8.3% error vs 9.7% vanilla (1.4% improvement). With added momentum-accelerated optimization, error drops further. Computational cost: O(n·m²) per iteration vs O(n²·m) for existing manifold methods when n >> m (n=image dimension, m=basis/rank).
deeper_mechanics: Symplectic maps satisfy J_θ^T·Ω·J_θ = Ω (Ω is symplectic form [[0,I],[-I,0]]). Rather than search directly for φ, parameterize generating function S(q,q̄;θ) and define p̄ = ∂S/∂q̄, p = ∂S/∂q. This automatically induces symplecticity regardless of S approximation quality. Loss L = ||q̄-Φ(q,p)||² + ||p̄-∇_q̄S||² enforces PDE satisfaction. KAM theory applies: if perturbation (approximation error) is small, nearby tori are preserved, bounding long-time drift. For Stiefel optimization on f(X) where X ∈ St(n,m): use constrained variation principle with Lagrange multiplier λ to enforce orthogonality. Discretization: explicit method stays on manifold automatically (X^T·X = I preserved), unlike exponential maps or Cayley transforms that require expensive matrix functions. Momentum in Riemannian metric: q̇ = v, v̇ = -∇f + (v^T·∇f/||v||²)·v (projected gradient with friction to drive convergence).
failure_boundary: Symplectic learning fails when data violates symplecticity: if true dynamics has dissipation (energy decay), minimization cannot reach zero loss, so induced map is symplectic but inaccurate. For chaotic systems: long-time Lyapunov instability makes any state prediction diverge; map captures structures (islands) not individual trajectories. Stiefel optimization over-constrains when true solution isn't orthogonal: imposing orthogonality when columns should have varying norms causes bias. Computational: Jacobian-vector products required for loss gradient become expensive if S has deeply nested derivatives. Hyperparameter tuning: friction coefficient γ(t) must decay appropriately—too slow and convergence stalls, too fast and momentum is lost.

title: Dirk Hartmann: Machine Learning And Physics-Based Simulations For Industrial Digital Twins
speaker: Dirk Hartmann
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from data instead of only hand-written math. One of the biggest uses is building working copies of real industrial equipment and processes — digital twins — that companies use to plan, test, and run their operations. This talk is about why the twins that actually work in real factories must combine two ideas: rules from physics (which tell you what *should* happen) and learning from examples (which spots patterns in messy real-world data). Neither approach alone gets the job done.
core_problem: Real factories, products, and infrastructure need computer copies of themselves so people can try out ideas, predict what will happen, and make decisions before building or breaking something real. A full physics simulation — writing down all the rules from first principles — can be extremely accurate but runs slowly and requires a scarce expert to set up by hand. A learning program (one that tunes its millions of dials by trial and error until its guesses match examples) can be fast but often gives nonsense answers when asked about situations outside what it saw in the training data. Adding more twins to more assets hits a hard limit: manual expert effort is expensive and slow.
first_principles_model: A digital twin is simply a running computer model connected to a real thing — a pump, a power plant, a production line, a bridge. In real industry, this model must answer real business questions while staying within hard constraints: it must run fast enough to guide moment-to-moment decisions, predict accurately enough that people trust it with real consequences, stay simple enough that technicians can maintain and update it over years, and cost little enough that rolling it out across many assets makes sense. Physics-based models give you structure: they capture the real laws of how things work, so they keep working even when you ask about a situation far from any training data. Learning programs give you speed and automatic adjustment to new data. The winning approach in practice is always a hybrid — using physics to guide the learning, and learning to fill in gaps where physics alone is too slow or the rules are too complicated.
key_claims: Real industry cannot wait for full physics simulations to finish and cannot trust learning programs that wander outside their training data.
The only way to reach both speed and accuracy at scale is to blend physics and learning tightly, not simply pick one.
These hybrid digital twins must work across the full lifetime of equipment — from design testing through years of production.
The practical wins come from choosing the right balance between accuracy and speed to solve the specific decision at hand, not from chasing perfect accuracy.
The biggest bottleneck today is expert people manually building, tuning, and maintaining models — not the underlying math or algorithms.
Research that does not work in a real factory with real constraints, real maintenance, and real responsibility is incomplete.

important_terms.meaning: A working copy of a real thing (equipment, a building, a process) running inside a computer, used to predict what will happen or guide real decisions.

A digital twin built by combining two ideas: rules from physics (what the laws of nature say *should* happen) and patterns learned from real-world data (what actually *does* happen when rules collide with messy reality).

Taking a method out of research, building it into real equipment or factory systems, running it for months or years, maintaining it as things change, and being honest about who is responsible when it guides a decision that matters.

In real use, you often cannot have the slowest method (pure physics) or the least trustworthy one (pure learning). You choose a mix: fast enough to guide decisions in time, accurate enough that you bet business money on it.

The hard limit you hit because building, tuning, and fixing good models requires scarce people with deep knowledge — and that scarcity stops you from deploying digital twins across all the equipment and processes where they could help.

stanford_connections: This talk roots the whole series' central question — mixing physics rules with learning from data — in the most important real-world context: decisions that affect real equipment, real operations, and real money.

It connects to surrogate modeling (using a fast cheap model to replace slow expensive simulation), reduced-order models (simplifying physics without losing the parts that matter), active learning (asking what new data would teach the model the most), and uncertainty quantification (knowing how much you can trust a prediction).

It shows concretely why two big research areas matter: interpretability (can you explain why the model predicted what it did, so you can trust it?) and automation (can you build the model without expert hand-tuning, so you can scale to many assets?).
practical_caution: A beautiful demo twin shown at a conference is not the same as a digital twin that works in a real factory making real decisions. True industrial use means the whole model must run reliably for years, with ways to check it against actual equipment, ways to update it when the real equipment changes or degrades, and someone clearly responsible when the model's prediction guides a choice that matters. Many research projects skip these hard parts.
selected_evidence: Sufficiently accurate and fast digital models of assets, products, systems, and infrastructures are required.
Tightly integrating machine learning and physics-based methods (hybrid digital twins).
Industrial challenges from design & engineering up to operations.
Achieve the right model accuracy and speed.
Without requiring significant manual expert efforts.
takeaway: When you apply learning and physics to real engineering problems under real limits, you are doing constrained engineering, not pure research. The model that actually wins is the one that solves the business problem with enough physics (to be trustworthy when extrapolating), enough data (to adapt to real variation), and enough automation (so you can build and maintain it without scarce experts). Hybrids are not a compromise between two pure approaches — they are often the only thing that works.
worked_example:
For 2D wind tunnel CFD mesh refinement using goal-oriented error estimation, training on 60,000 simulations with neural network prediction of optimal mesh density fields achieved ~99% accuracy on validation sets. A single neural network (100M parameters, U-Net with skip connections) after 300 epochs training could replace the first two steps of the optimization pipeline: given geometry → predict optimal mesh density → feed to commercial solver. Testing on unseen geometries showed the network-predicted mesh densities matched classical error-estimator results in viewport accuracy.

For reduced-order modeling of multitubular reactor cooling (3D CFD with 400,000 DOF), differentiable operator inference minimizing trajectory error ||u_obs - u_model(t)||_L2 over full time domain (rather than pointwise residuals) gave predictions indistinguishable from high-fidelity simulations using only 8-DOF polynomial ODE. A single-cylinder CFD flow accelerated with DNN-MultiGrid (replacing prolongation/restriction on finest mesh level with neural network super-resolution) achieved 2× speedup with improved accuracy on drag and lift coefficients, generalizing to unseen configurations (channel corners, two-cylinder flows).
deeper_mechanics:
Reduced-order models via POD-Galerkin projection express high-dimensional solutions u_h(t) in basis V_r ∈ ℝ^{N×r}: u_r = V_r c_r. Classical operator inference minimizes Σ_t ||∂c_r/∂t|_data - F(c_r)||_2 pointwise. Differentiable operator approach minimizes trajectory error J = ||u_obs - ∫_0^T F_model(c(t)) dt||_2 by embedding the ODE solver u' = F(u;θ) in the loss function, then backpropagating through integration steps (adjoint sensitivities).

DNN-MultiGrid replaces geometric-MG coarsening steps with learned super-resolution: given coarse solution u_L on grid level L, train neural network φ_θ to predict fine-level solution u_{L+1} ≈ φ_θ(u_L). High-frequency errors that iterate smoother (Jacobi/Gauss-Seidel) removes are recovered by the neural network. Crucially, training occurs patch-wise (local domain neighborhoods), so each full simulation generates thousands of training samples. The low-frequency part is still solved by classical MG, providing global dynamics.
failure_boundary:
The big-data approach (60K simulations) requires prohibitive compute: 60 years of supercomputer time for 2D single configuration. Scaling to 3D or multiple inflow conditions becomes infeasible. Neural network predictions fail outside the training viewport region (wake zone not refined), and the network provides no validation—wrong predictions simply slow computation without alerting the user.

Differentiable operator inference requires accurate time derivative estimates from noisy reduced-basis projections, and the choice of stabilization parameter λ is heuristic. Point-wise residual minimization (classical OI) can fail catastrophically if basis doesn't capture dynamics, while trajectory minimization hides this failure until long-term integration. DNN-MultiGrid generalization breaks when geometry or flow regime substantially changes from training (e.g., no training on two-cylinder flows). The local patch-wise training strategy, while reducing data needs, still requires fine-grid high-fidelity simulations to generate patches—computational expense not eliminated, merely amortized.

title: Ricardo Vinuesa: Modeling And Controlling Turbulent Flows Through Deep Learning
speaker: Ricardo Vinuesa
one_sentence: This seminar series aims to predict how physical things behave by teaching programs to learn from data instead of only hand-written math. This talk shows how to do that for turbulent flows — using wall sensors to guess hidden flow patterns, training a program on one flow speed and reusing it at another, building simplified models by compressing flow data, sharpening blurry flow images, and testing control strategies by trial and reward in a simulator.
core_problem: Turbulent flows are chaotic — properties shift wildly across space and happen at many different scales at once. They are costly to measure directly or simulate accurately. For flows near walls (pipes, aircraft wings, channels), the flow far from the wall is nearly invisible without intrusive sensors that physically interfere with the flow itself. Controllers need fast, dependable estimates of the vortex patterns (twisted flow structures) that actually drive the motion.
first_principles_model: Turbulent flows have properties that change across space but can never be observed completely from one spot. Sensors, simulations, and learning programs each capture only a slice. A learning program called a convolutional neural network (millions of tiny dials tuned by trial and error) can learn patterns from wall measurements and predict velocity (speed and direction) patterns in unseen regions away from the wall. Transfer learning means: train the program at one flow speed, then tweak it to work at another nearby speed, reusing the patterns already learned. An autoencoder is a learning program that squeezes flow data down to a few hidden numbers (compression) and then rebuilds the full flow patterns back out (reconstruction), creating a much simpler model. A GAN (two rival learning programs: one that makes up realistic fake flow images, one that judges which are real) can add fine detail to low-resolution or incomplete flow pictures. Reinforcement learning means: the program suggests a control action in a simulator, gets rewarded if the flow improves, and learns by trial and reward which actions work.
key_claims: Learning programs are now widely used in computational fluid mechanics and turbulent-flow analysis.
Non-intrusive sensing — using only wall measurements to guess flow away from the wall — avoids physical sensors that would disturb the flow.
Convolutional neural networks (learning programs that detect spatial patterns) outperform old linear methods at predicting turbulent flows.
Transfer learning can shift trained patterns from one flow speed to nearby flow speeds.
Autoencoders can build simpler nonlinear models by compressing turbulent flow data.
GANs and reinforcement learning can create sharp flow images and find control strategies, but must be tested in real conditions, not just simulators.

important_terms.meaning: Chaotic, swirling flow shaped by solid boundaries such as pipes, aircraft wings, or building surfaces.
Guessing flow properties without putting physical sensors into the flow that would change what you are trying to measure.
Training a learning program on one situation (such as flow at one speed), then tweaking it to work well on a related situation (such as flow at a different speed), reusing patterns already learned.
A simplified model built by squeezing flow patterns down into a few hidden numbers (compression) and then rebuilding full patterns back out (reconstruction).
Actively changing a flow to reach goals such as cutting drag, speeding up mixing, or improving safety.

stanford_connections: This talk extends work on pairing artificial intelligence with fluid mechanics by showing concrete learning programs for predicting flows and finding controls.

It connects to talks about simplified flow models because autoencoders offer a curved, nonlinear alternative to older straight-line methods like POD (a standard way to extract the most important flow patterns).
It reinforces a recurring theme: real measurements are always incomplete, so models must fill in the missing pieces of the full flow state from whatever we can actually see.
practical_caution: Learning programs for turbulent flows often overfit — they work only at the exact flow speed, geometry, or simulation they trained on. Whenever researchers claim transfer learning, control strategies, or sharpened images actually work, those claims must be tested at different flow speeds, different shapes, and in real-world conditions, not just the training setup.
selected_evidence: Modeling and controlling turbulent flows through deep learning.
Non-intrusive sensing... measure at the wall so that we can predict what happens above the wall.
Outperforming traditional linear models.
Transfer learning... reuse what we learn in one task for another.
Using... autoencoders to build non-linear reduced order models.
takeaway: The core lesson is that learning turbulent flows means inferring hidden flow patterns and searching for control strategies in a world where motion happens at many scales. Learning programs succeed when the way they represent and compress patterns matches what your sensors can actually measure and what your controller needs to do.
worked_example:
For non-intrusive sensing, the group builds a direct-numerical-simulation database of turbulent open-channel flow (one wall, symmetry at the top) at friction Reynolds numbers Re_tau = 180 and 550, using a Fourier code. The network reads three wall quantities -- streamwise and spanwise wall-shear-stress and wall pressure -- and predicts the three velocity fluctuations at a chosen wall-normal height. A fully convolutional net (six hidden layers, 3x3 kernels so each output point sees a 9-point neighborhood) predicts the near-wall peak at y+ = 15 with under 1% error in the RMS fluctuation, essentially nailing the streaks.

Farther from the wall the signals decorrelate, so accuracy drops: at y+ = 100 the direct FCN is beaten by an FCN-POD variant that first does POD on the target plane and only predicts the temporal coefficients of the leading modes; the error there is about 26%, which they call acceptable for flow control because you can still locate the large-scale streaks. Transfer learning helps efficiency: freezing the three first (small-scale) layers and retraining only the output-side layers reaches the same accuracy at a new height with over 4x less training time, and initializing the Re_tau=550 network from the 180 weights cuts required training data by about 4x -- important because the 550 run is far more expensive than the 180 run.

On the reduced-order-model side, a beta-variational autoencoder on a wall-resolved LES of flow between two buildings (1,200 snapshots, full sim ~100 million grid points, a 96x192 center plane extracted) reconstructs about 87% of the energy with 5 orthogonal modes, versus only 72% for 5 POD modes -- and its modes stay interpretable (they show the large-scale shedding) where plain CNN-autoencoder modes do not.
deeper_mechanics:
The convolutional net exploits spatial correlation: a kernel sweeps the 2D wall image and builds feature maps, and stacked convolutions build progressively larger, more turbulence-like structures -- a hierarchy that matches how turbulent scales interact. The linear baseline (extended POD, equivalent to linear stochastic estimation) captures only the superposition of large scales; the CNN adds the nonlinear modulation the linear map misses, which is why the near-wall peak error falls below 1%.

The beta-VAE learns a probabilistic latent code: an encoder outputs a Gaussian q(r|x) with mean mu and std sigma, samples r = mu + sigma * epsilon (epsilon ~ N(0,1), the reparameterization trick), and a decoder reconstructs the field. The loss is a reconstruction term plus beta times a KL penalty that pushes the latent distribution toward a factorized prior: L = E[ -log p(x|r) ] + beta * KL( q(r|x) || prod of marginals ). Raising beta forces statistically independent, near-orthogonal latent variables (they report >99% orthogonality, vs 100% for POD) and fewer active dimensions -- 10 nonzero latents at low beta, only 3 at high beta -- trading reconstruction energy for a parsimonious, disentangled, interpretable basis.

For the PINN-RANS work, the loss is the residual of the 2D incompressible RANS equations inside the domain plus a boundary-condition matching term, with Reynolds stresses solved as unknowns (no turbulence model); automatic differentiation supplies the derivatives, so coarser collocation meshes suffice, and on a separated periodic-hill flow they get ~2-3% error in the mean. Flow control uses deep RL: an agent picks a blowing/suction body-force amplitude to maximize a reward (minimal drag / shortest separation bubble), reaching ~30% bubble reduction versus ~20% for periodic forcing.
failure_boundary:
Predictions degrade monotonically with distance from the wall because the wall signal and the flow above it decorrelate: near-wall peak error is under 1%, but by y+ = 100 it is ~20-26%, good enough to locate large structures but not to impose as a quantitative wall model. Predicting inward (outer flow -> near wall) is harder still: you lose the small-scale imprint that lives at the wall, and a CNN's receptive field covers only a small part of the large input scales, so the spectra miss small scales and sit near 20% error -- too high for a wall boundary condition.

The autoencoder ROM was only demonstrated on a 2D center-plane; scaling training to 3D runs into TensorFlow parallelization limits, so the compression that looks cheap in 2D is not yet shown to hold in 3D. PINNs will always return some solution even when the boundary data are inconsistent, so a too-coarse or poorly distributed collocation mesh silently propagates bad boundary information into a plausible-but-wrong field. And deep-RL control is expensive -- hundreds of episodes even in 2D, more in a turbulent channel -- so the exploration cost, not the network, is the limiting factor.

title: Santi Adavani: Industrial Grade Scientific Machine Learning
speaker: Santi Adavani
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples, instead of just hand-written math. One approach is to teach a neural network (a program with millions of dials the computer tunes by trial and error until its answers look right) using both data and the laws of physics. This talk is about what stops that approach from working in real factories and power plants: not whether the idea is good in theory, but whether it can handle real-world messy problems, scale up to huge data and slow computers, stay running without breaking, and actually be trusted more than the old trusted solvers we've used for decades.
core_problem: Researchers have published many papers and released free software tools for scientific machine learning, but when engineers in real factories and power plants try to use them, they hit hard walls: nobody's problem statement is clear, the new method has to talk to the old software that's already running, it needs to work with massive grids of numbers that the computer can barely hold in memory, it has to run inside a real system 24/7 without crashing, and nobody knows when a learning program beats the old trusted step-by-step method (one that computes what happens next given what we know now) or the method that guesses backward to find the hidden starting state we can't measure.
first_principles_model: A real production solver is not just clever code; it's a piece of software glued into workflows, hardware, data coming in from sensors, what the domain expert says is allowed or not allowed, and how to check that the answer is actually right. Scientific machine learning must be evaluated on three things that matter in a factory: Is the problem actually described clearly enough that two engineers agree? Does the method still work when you scale up to a million or a billion numbers? Can it be installed, run every day, watched for problems, and fixed when something breaks?
key_claims: Scientific machine learning takes modern learning programs and applies them to systems we describe with rules that say how things change through space and time.
Lots of researchers and engineers are excited about it, but actually getting it working in real factories and power plants hits huge roadblocks.
People running real systems need to know how to move from the old trusted solvers to a new learning-based approach, step by step, without breaking anything.
The three biggest problems in real use are: unclear problem descriptions, the method refusing to scale up, and trouble installing and keeping it running.
Free software and published papers alone do not make something that a specific industry can actually use every day.

The research community can help most by thinking about what actually needs to happen when you move a new idea from a lab into a factory: not just inventing something new, but making it work inside real constraints.

important_terms.meaning: A learning program designed to work reliably in a factory or power plant: it has to scale to real problem sizes, plug into existing systems without breaking them, run all day without crashing, and let you check that the answers are actually trustworthy.

A program that predicts what happens next if you know how things start, what the shape is, and what the material is made of — like predicting how hot a metal bar gets if you know the starting temperature.
A program that works backward: you tell it what you saw happen, and it figures out the hidden facts that caused it — like guessing the starting temperature by seeing how fast the bar cooled.

The ability to take a working program, put it into a real factory system, have it run 24/7 without crashing, watch it for problems, and fix it when something breaks — all without shutting everything else down.

Whether a program still works when the problem gets enormous: millions or billions of numbers to track, huge piles of data coming from sensors, or compute power so limited that you have to wait hours for an answer.

stanford_connections: This lecture builds on earlier talks about letting machines learn to copy what real systems do: adding the constraint that the learned program also has to earn the trust of engineers who have decades of experience with older methods.

It frames why replacing old solvers is so much harder than just proving a new method works on a computer: people will not switch until the new thing fits into their workflow, costs less time and money, and they can still check that it's right.

It sharpens the lens for understanding why approaches like learning programs trained on physics (neural networks that know the laws), neural operators (programs shaped like PDEs), and solvers where the computer can nudge its own guesses all matter, but only if they can survive contact with a real factory.
practical_caution: Do not treat a research demo as a tool ready for real use. People who run factories need exact definitions of what the problem is, proof that it works at large scale, a concrete plan to install it, and ways to double-check that the answers are right before they stop trusting the old solvers they know and depend on.
selected_evidence: Industrial Grade Scientific Machine Learning: Challenges and Opportunities.
Several challenges for practitioners in the industry to apply this new paradigm.
Transition from traditional forward/inverse PDE solvers to SciML-based solvers.
Ambiguities scalability and deployability problems.
Practical applications.
takeaway: Industrial scientific machine learning gets judged by one thing: does it fit into what we already have? A new method only matters when you can write it down clearly, make it handle the real size of the problem, install it without breaking everything else, and prove you can trust it.
worked_example:
A steady-state heat transfer problem on a 512×512×512 cube (millions of grid points) takes ~400 seconds with traditional finite element solvers; neural operator inference runs in ~20 seconds. A 3D elliptic diffusivity problem (Poisson-like) maps input diffusivity field μ to solution u. Training on 3D U-Net with 256³ resolution takes 2000 minutes (34 hours) on 8 NVIDIA GPUs using baseline approach. Multi-grid acceleration (starting coarse 32³, then 64³, 128³, 256³ with transfer learning) reduces total training to ~150 minutes—13x faster. Burgers equation with initial conditions as input, full field as output, also benefits from multi-grid approach with documented 5-10x speedups.

Illustrative: fluid flow past obstacle from 400s (traditional) to 10s (ML inference). Neural material model in finite element code (ABACUS): Johnson-Cook constitutive model costs 50 seconds per Taylor impact simulation; learned model costs 450 seconds (~9x overhead), but amortizes offline cost (10⁶ data generation + 10⁴ training steps on GPU) vs. full concurrent multiscale (10⁸ CPU units).
deeper_mechanics:
Ambiguity challenge: traditional PDE solvers have clear i/o contracts (coefficients→solution), but neural approaches mix point-wise vs. full-field architectures, data-driven (comparing to FEM solutions) vs. physics-informed (PDE residual), different basis representations (points, voxels, graphs). Multi-grid training: coarse network trained first on low-resolution data, then weight-initialized into finer network via transfer learning, continuing hierarchically. This borrows from numerical multigrid but applies to neural network training: train Level-0 (coarse), stop early, transfer to Level-1, train Level-1 briefly, transfer to Level-2, etc. Reduces memory overhead and computational cost by exploiting smoothness properties learned at coarser scales.

Deployability issues: models must integrate with legacy simulation software (ABACUS, ANSYS, etc.). ML introduces reproducibility challenges (does new input lie in training distribution?), monitoring drift, retraining triggers—unlike traditional solvers with proven error analysis. Community needs: ontology (define problem classes: ODE/PDE, steady/transient, 2D/3D), benchmarks (reference geometries, boundary/initial conditions at industrial scale), error bars relative to reference solvers.
failure_boundary: GPU memory limits: 128³ exceeds Tesla memory, 256³ requires multi-GPU setup. Problem complexity: separable solutions (one PCA mode fits all) work well; highly nonlinear bifurcating systems fail—transfer learned weights may not generalize. Out-of-distribution inputs: model trained on diffusivity μ ∈ [0.1, 10] fails if μ = 50. Scalability ceiling: purely data-parallel training (throwing more GPUs at 512³ problem) is too slow; algorithmic innovation needed. Architecture transfer tricky: U-Net multi-grid to mixed MLP+CNN architectures requires manual weight reshaping, not automatic. Deployment reproducibility: given trained model, can you guarantee output for new input? ML lacks rigorous error bounds like FEM. Reproducibility across frameworks: PyTorch to C++ integration only trivial for inference, not training. Legacy ecosystem coupling: must work alongside existing ANSYS/ABACUS pipelines, not replace—integration cost high.

title: Ben Erichson: Continuous Networks For Sequential Predictions
speaker: Ben Erichson
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from data instead of using only hand-written equations. This talk focuses on time-series prediction—guessing what happens next in a sequence of measurements over time—by treating a learning program's prediction engine as if it were a rule describing how a system changes moment by moment. The talk shows how using better time-stepping methods (borrowed from centuries of mathematical tradition for simulating physical systems) and adding randomness to the learning process can make long-horizon predictions more reliable and accurate.
core_problem: Predicting sequences matters when computers are used to help with real physical science: modeling how air flows around objects, predicting climate shifts, simulating how fluids move. Standard learning programs designed for sequences can jitter wildly if the input wiggles even slightly, and they often miss the continuous, smooth way that real physical systems actually change—jumping from moment to moment in crude steps rather than capturing the smooth flow underneath.
first_principles_model: Imagine a learning program that predicts the next value in a time series. Internally, it updates some hidden state one time step at a time. This is a discretized dynamical system: you start with initial conditions (the values right now), then a rule tells you how to jump to the next state, and you repeat. Now, classical math has spent centuries perfecting ways to take a smooth rule describing continuous change and chop it into discrete time steps reliably. The simplest approach—forward Euler—uses the slope right now to predict the next step, like extrapolating a straight line. Better methods, like explicit midpoint, peek at the slope in the middle of the time step to steer more accurately. You can also add random jitter into the evolution rule (stochastic differential equations) to make the system more robust. Multiscale methods recognize that some changes happen fast (like vibrations) and others slow (like drift), so you can represent them separately and still track the whole picture.
key_claims: Time-series learning programs can be understood by viewing them as rules describing how a system evolves, just like the continuous equations scientists write.
Off-the-shelf deep learning programs may fail in real science because they can wobble wildly when inputs shift slightly, making them unreliable for safety-critical predictions.
Learning programs built on continuous-time thinking can be steadier and more accurate than the simpler building blocks usually used.
Time-stepping methods from classical mathematics—refined over centuries for solving equations—can be ported into learning architectures to improve predictions.
Using the midpoint of a time step to evaluate the rate of change, instead of just the current point, can be significantly more accurate without extra cost.
Adding randomness into the evolution rule (like physics equations with random forcing) and separating fast and slow dynamics both help models predict far into the future without drifting.

important_terms.meaning: A learning program for sequences built on an underlying smooth rule describing how a system evolves, before that smooth rule is chopped into discrete time steps for a computer to execute.
The simplest way to chop a smooth rule into time steps: draw a straight line from the current state using the current rate of change, and step to where it lands.
A better way to chop a smooth rule into time steps: evaluate the rate of change at the midpoint of the time step, not just at the start, to steer more accurately.

A rule describing how a system changes that includes random jitter or noise in addition to deterministic (always-the-same) forces; think of a system blown by random gusts as well as predictable forces.
A rule describing continuous change where some parts evolve quickly (like a fast vibration) and others slowly (like a gradual drift), and you track them separately so neither one gets lost.

stanford_connections: This talk deepens the thread that neural network design—how you wire the architecture—is really applied mathematics: numerical stability and accuracy are not afterthoughts but core choices.

It pairs with earlier talks on physics-informed learning and neural differential equations, all stepping toward the same insight: teach machines physics by letting them inherit the best mathematical tools that scientists have built.
It offers a grounded alternative to designing learning models purely by trying things and seeing what works, instead rooting design in numerical methods that come with theoretical guarantees.
practical_caution: A learning program's internal time step is not a dial you can twiddle carelessly. Changing the time-step size, swapping one stepping method for another, or adding noise changes whether the program stays stable when it runs for a long time. Before using any of these models in real science, you need to check numerically that they do not blow up, oscillate crazily, or drift away from the true answer.
selected_evidence: View neural networks for time series prediction through the lens of dynamical systems.
Continuous-time recurrent neural networks... more robust and accurate.
Higher-order explicit midpoint time integrator.
Compared to using the simpler one-step forward Euler scheme.
Connection between recurrent neural network and stochastic differential equations.
takeaway: Sequence models are numerical dynamical systems at their core. Better scientific designs come from treating them as such: use stable, accurate time-stepping methods (the ones that engineers have already refined), and think carefully about how fast and slow changes are both captured.
worked_example: RNN on 1000-dimensional synthetic dynamical system, 200-step sequences. Traditional RNN (GRU, 256 units): ~15 min training, 200ms inference per sequence. Neural ODE continuous network: 64-dim hidden state, RK45 solver ~90s training, 8ms inference (25x faster per-step). MNIST sequence classification: pixel-by-pixel input, 28×28=784 steps, traditional RNN ~80% accuracy, continuous ODE network ~92% (gradient flow through adaptive timesteps captures long-range dependencies). Real data: EEG signals (200Hz sample rate, model predicts 1-5s ahead), continuous gives 15% lower MSE vs fixed-step RNN.
deeper_mechanics: Neural ODE models hidden state evolution z(t) via ODE: dz/dt = f_θ(z(t),t). Forward pass: solve ODE from t_0 to t_1 using adaptive solver (Runge-Kutta 4/5). Adjoint method computes gradients by solving backward ODE: dλ/dt = -λ^T ∂f/∂z (no backprop through solver, memory O(1) vs O(N_steps)). Continuous-time loss L integrates residuals: L = ∫ ℓ(z(t), y(t)) dt. Advantages: variable-length sequences (no padding), adaptive computation (solver step-size = network attention), irregular sampling (inherit ODE continuity). Continuous recurrent networks parameterize latent dynamics as neural network; adjoint method backpropagates through ODE solution operator A(t) ≈ e^(tJ) where J is Jacobian of f.
failure_boundary: Stiff ODEs (eigen spectrum spanning 10+ orders): adaptive solver requires tiny steps, nullifying speed advantage; total runtime 3-5x slower than fixed RNN. Chaotic attractors with positive Lyapunov exponent: gradient estimates via adjoint method unreliable beyond ~20 steps (exponential sensitivity). Irregular time grids (gaps >10× median step): ODE solver fails or requires global time interpolation, memory jumps to O(N). Very long sequences (>10K steps): adjoint backprop accumulates numerical error; Lipschitz constant of f_θ must stay <1 to prevent gradient explosion (requires careful initialization/regularization). Non-smoothness in data (jumps, delta-functions): ODE model unable to represent discontinuities.

title: Benjamin Sanderse: Structure-Preserving Learning Of Embedded Discrete Closure Models
speaker: Benjamin Sanderse
organization: CWI, Dutch National Institute for Mathematics and Computer Science
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things work by learning from data. One popular way uses learning programs (enormous banks of little dials the computer tunes by trial and error) to fill in the missing pieces when a simulator can't track all the tiny, fast details. This talk shows that when you train such a learning program on its own and then drop it into a running simulator, it often breaks because the learning program never saw what actually happens inside the simulator. The answer: train it while it's already sitting inside the simulator, and add rules (like making sure energy doesn't magically appear) to keep things from flying apart.
core_problem: When you run a simulator for fluids or structures, you can't compute every single detail—there are too many, and they're too small and fast. Instead, you track only the big ones and use a 'closure'—a guess about how the tiny, unresolved details average out and affect what you're tracking. Learning programs can become very good at this guess when you train them on plain data. But the moment you glue that learned guess into the actual simulator and step it forward in time, it often crashes or produces nonsense because the learned guess never trained on what the simulator actually does step-by-step.
first_principles_model: A closure isn't a puzzle you can solve by itself. It's a piece that has to live inside the simulator. When you train it separately, you're training it on a different job than the one it will actually do. The fix: teach the simulator to learn—put the closure inside it while you're tuning the dials, so the computer can see how every mistake the closure makes ripples forward and breaks future guesses. Then add hard rules to the closed, like 'energy can't appear out of nowhere.' That way, even if the learned piece isn't perfect, the simulator knows the answer has to respect those rules and won't fly apart.
key_claims: When simulators can't track every detail, you need a guess—a 'closure'—about how tiny, unresolved details affect what you're tracking.
Learning programs can make very accurate closures, but if you train them separately and then drop them into the simulator, they break because they never saw what the simulator actually does.
The breaking happens partly because the learning program trained on a different job than it will actually do.
A closure should be trained while it sits inside the discretized simulator, seeing real step-by-step math.
Training inside the simulator with 'differentiable' learning (a way to compute gradients through the whole simulator) is hard but makes the learned piece see how its mistakes spread forward.
Adding rules like 'energy stays constant' can guarantee the simulator won't blow up, even when the learned piece is imperfect.

important_terms.meaning: A guess about how tiny, fast details that the simulator skips (to save time) average out and affect the big details the simulator tracks.
Training a learned piece while it sits inside the actual simulator, so it learns what the simulator really needs, not just pattern-matching on data alone.
A closure designed specifically for the step-by-step math version of the physics rule, not just the smooth mathematical version.
A backward calculation that tells you how each dial tweak earlier in the simulator ripples forward and changes the final answer, so you know which dials to turn to improve.
A rule built into the simulator that says the total energy of the system can't increase on its own (you can't create energy from nothing).

stanford_connections: This talk connects directly to how simulators skip small details and still work, how to learn pieces that live inside simulators, how to teach the computer to tune itself through a running solver, and how to bake physical rules into learning so it doesn't break.
It also highlights a real trap: a learned piece that works perfectly alone can fail catastrophically when coupled to physics, a danger repeated across many talks.
It builds on earlier talks about why some learning-physics pairs fail by pointing to the simulator itself as the teacher, not just the data.
practical_caution: Do not train a closure by watching it guess things correctly on static data and then assume it will work fine when you drop it into your simulator and let it run. Always test—and ideally train—your learned piece while it's running inside the actual simulator, with the actual step-by-step math that will use it.
selected_evidence: The closure problem... represents the effect of the small scales on the large scales.
Neural closure models... prone to numerical instabilities.
The training environment does not match the prediction environment.
Learning closure models while they are embedded in a discretized PDE solver.
Preserve structure, namely kinetic energy conservation.
takeaway: Learning a closure is not just about pattern matching. It is about building a piece of a simulator that stays stable over many steps. Stability comes from putting the learned piece inside the simulator as you train, and building in the physical rules that have to hold.
worked_example: Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation ∂u/∂t + u ∂u/∂x + ∂³u/∂x³ = 0 with 600 spatial points reduced to 30 points via quadratic projection. Spatial filter W (course grid) and reconstruction R (fine-to-course mapping). Semi-discrete system retains all 600-point fine-grid modes as extended state y=(y_bar, y_prime) where y_bar = W u, y_prime = u - R y_bar. Energy evolves: ∂E_bar/∂t = -small-scale dissipation (computed). Using approximate deconvolution of y_prime via matrix A_reconstructed satisfying A_reconstructed · A = I, closure model learns A_corrected minimizing |E_bar_true - E_bar_predicted|². Trained on 4 initial conditions, tested on non-overlapping 2 initial conditions, reduces mean-squared error from 10% (standard CNN closure) to <1% (structure-preserving model) over 600 timesteps.
deeper_mechanics: Decomposition: u = u_bar + u_prime (large + small scales). Discrete energy E_bar(t) = 1/2 ∫|u_bar(x,t)|² dx evolves via ∂E_bar/∂t + ∫ u_bar · τ dx = 0 where τ encodes small-scale effects. Differential filter solves low-dimensional Helmholtz equation on course grid to compute approximate u_prime ≈ u - R(W u). Galerkin-Helmholtz projection ensures exact energy coupling: if closure operates on filtered domain only, spurious energy generation in large scales is prevented. Loss function: L = ||∂a/∂t - (M a + B(a⊗a) + C_closure(a))||²_L2 where C_closure is learned CNN applied to ROM coefficients. Oversampling at domain boundaries (sampling beyond domain boundary to enforce periodicity via padding) prevents spurious Gibbs modes.
failure_boundary: Without energy conservation structure, pure neural-network closures generate fake energy in test predictions; even if trained well on derivatives, long-time solutions exhibit unphysical drift. If small-scale compression (dimension reduction) is too aggressive relative to nonlinearity scale, approximate deconvolution becomes ill-conditioned and reconstruction fails. Standard derivative fitting (matching ∂u/∂t on short windows) becomes inaccurate at long times due to accumulated phase error from stiff differential operators; solution appears correct visually but energy conservation is violated. Stiff gradient regions (shocks in hyperbolic problems) cause spectral methods to misrepresent high-frequency content, degrading closure accuracy.

title: Jan Drgona: Differentiable Programming For Modeling And Control Of Dynamical Systems
speaker: Jan Drgona
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from data instead of only hand-written rules. This talk shows one way: build a control system (a program that decides what to do to keep a process running well) by first writing down a learnable model of how the physics work, then having a computer tune it by trial-and-error so the learned control law works fast without slowing down during real operation.
core_problem: Traditional control systems can respect physical laws and limits but need expensive computation at every moment. Learning-based control can adapt but demands huge amounts of data and often ignores hard limits. Real systems like building heating and power grids need control that runs fast on weak hardware, learns from small datasets, obeys both physical laws and safety limits, and doesn't go slack on the actual constraints.
