first_principles_model: Differentiable predictive control works like this: write the control rule (what to do next) as a learnable calculation built from a model of the physics—one where tiny changes in inputs create tiny changes in outputs, so you can measure how tweaking any dial affects the final answer. Keep the classical idea of model predictive control: guess what the system will do over the next few seconds, pick actions that minimize waste or harm, enforce limits. The change is that you do all the trial-and-error tuning beforehand on a computer, so when the system runs in real time, it just executes the already-learned control rule instead of solving a new math problem every instant.
key_claims: Smoothly-differentiable programming gives a clear way to build control for systems that change over time.
Differentiable predictive control joins classical control tuning with scientific machine learning.
The method uses custom learnable physics models to train the control policy before it runs.
Hard limits on actions or states can be baked directly into the training process.
Real systems tested include building temperature control and electrical power grid scheduling.
The method can run fast and efficiently on weak hardware for deployed control systems.

important_terms.meaning: A way to train control policies where the controller learns using models where tiny input changes cause tiny output changes (so you can measure how each dial affects the answer) and where limits are written in the same learnable way.
A control strategy where the system repeatedly predicts what will happen over the next short window of time, picks the best actions under that prediction, and applies them.
Training a control strategy in advance using simulations or models, so it runs fast when deployed without needing to solve new math problems during real operation.
A hard limit or rule (like 'power output cannot exceed 5000 watts') written using curved or bent math, not straight lines.
Packaging a learned control algorithm so it can be reused across different systems or plugged into other applications.

stanford_connections: This lecture directly connects differentiable programming to the control problem, placing it within the DDPS seminar's focus on teaching how to learn physical behavior from data.
It bridges reinforcement learning and flow-control talks by showing how to combine learned models with classical mathematical optimization that guarantees safety.
It also touches digital twins because real control systems need fast, exact models tightly linked to the machines they operate.
practical_caution: Control policies learned offline only work if your physics model is accurate and your safety constraints are hard rules, not soft nudges. Real deployment means testing against surprises and keeping a backup safety shutdown when things go unexpected.
selected_evidence: Differentiable programming perspective on optimal control of dynamical systems.
Differentiable predictive control (DPC).
Integrates the principles of classical model predictive control (MPC) with scientific machine learning.
Offline policy optimization subject to nonlinear constraints.
Building control and dynamic economic dispatch problems.
takeaway: The core insight: making everything smoothly-differentiable (so tiny changes lead to tiny changes) turns control design into a learning problem. But the learned controller is only as good as the physics model underneath, how strictly you enforce the constraints, and how careful you are before letting it loose in the real world.
worked_example:
Double integrator stabilization: trains 100 epochs under 1 min. Nested MPC unroll with 16 collocation points (parametric scenarios) + time horizon 5s. Comparison: interior-point solver ~100ms online; differentiable programming <1ms (100x speedup) with suboptimal cost gap <5%. Multi-zone building 20-state HVAC control: 30 days data (10 train/10 val/10 test). Linear model diverges after ~7 days; neural model with domain priors (dissipative envelope, bounded heat rates) stays robust >25 days.

Power grid 9-bus economic dispatch: 7-8 orders of magnitude (10^7-10^8x) speedup for online control vs iterative solvers (minutes → microseconds). Solutions within 2-3% of interior-point optimality. Quadrotor ball tracking with Raspberry Pi microcontroller: memory <50MB vs 200MB+ for full MPC, trades learning offline (hours) for real-time deployment (<10ms per control update).
deeper_mechanics:
Parametric optimization via Lagrangian: min_θ E_ψ[L(u(θ, ψ), ψ)] s.t. inequality/equality constraints g(u, ψ), where u=network(θ), ψ=scenario samples. Penalties: L_total = L_obj + λ_g·max(0, g)^2 + λ_eq·|g_eq|^2 (augmented Lagrangian). Backprop through control policy network → optimizer gradients ∇_θ via chain rule through dynamics unroll and constraint satisfaction.

Inductive priors (spectral maps): parameterize weights as V_SV where V,S,U orthogonal (SVD factorization), clamp singular values σ ∈ [σ_min, σ_max] for stability (contraction). Lyapunov functions and control barrier functions learned as auxiliary networks to enforce convergence/safety.
failure_boundary: Suboptimality gap grows with problem complexity and high-dimensional parameter space; no hard optimality guarantees like convex solvers. Requires pre-computed offline solution map—cannot adapt online if dynamics change. Unstable learning landscapes with chaotic sensitivity to weight initialization; stability margins need separate verification. For stochastic systems, sampling density in parametric space crucial; sparse regions show poor generalization. Memory still prohibitive for very large systems (100M+ network parameters); transfer learning across similar problems unexplored.

title: Eric de Sturler: Cheap And Robust Adaptive Reduced Order Models For Nonlinear Inversion And Design
speaker: Eric de Sturler
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from data instead of only hand-written math. When we want to find unknown parameters in a physical system (like guessing what material an object is made of from how it moves), or to design something to work better, we run the same math over and over. Using simplified stand-in models can speed this up, but only if we check whether the stand-in is still giving correct answers. This talk shows how randomization (adding controlled dice-rolling to calculations) and models that get smarter as we go can keep things fast and trustworthy.
core_problem: Finding unknown quantities in a physical system or designing something to meet goals often means running expensive math many times. When we have a mathematical model of the physics (a rule that says how something changes from moment to moment or place to place), solving it once can take a long time. Doing it tens or hundreds of times exhausts computer time and money. One idea is to build a smaller stand-in model that mimics the full physics for different settings — but even building that stand-in and running it repeatedly can be slow. Worse, there is no quick way to ask: is my stand-in still trustworthy right now?
first_principles_model: A stand-in model only helps if the person using it knows when to trust it. We can use randomization (adding controlled chance to mathematics) to quickly build smaller models or to check how far off they are without doing a full expensive run. Adaptive models update themselves when checks show they are drifting away from correct answers. Once updated, we use a specific optimization method — one that takes steps only within a region where the stand-in model is believed to be accurate — to guide the next move safely.
key_claims: Finding unknown parameters or designing better systems requires running expensive physics math many times.

Methods like Newton's approach (a standard way to hunt for answers) also need a second kind of expensive solve — the backwards step through the math that tells you how sensitive your answer is to tweaks.
Building a smaller model that works across different parameter settings can cut the total computation dramatically.
Building that smaller model in real time (while the search is running) can still be expensive.
Smaller models built to work across parameters usually have no quick way to check if they are drifting toward wrong answers.
Randomization can help build smaller models quickly and check whether things are still on track — both things that trust-region methods need to take steps safely.

important_terms.meaning: Finding unknown quantities or properties from what you observe, when the connection between the unknowns and the observations is not a straight line (does not follow a simple rule).

Adjusting things to reach a goal, but the things you adjust must always follow a rule that says how something changes from moment to moment or place to place (what physicists and engineers call a differential equation).
A smaller stand-in model built to copy the behavior of a full expensive model across different settings or conditions, without having to run the full model each time.
Using controlled chance or random choices inside calculations to speed things up, to check whether answers are still correct, or to pick which directions or pieces of data matter most.

A way to search for the best answer by taking small steps only in directions and distances where a simpler stand-in model is believed to be reliable, then checking and updating that trusted area as you go.

stanford_connections: This lecture ties smaller models to the hard problems of finding unknowns and improving designs, not just to running simulations forward.
It also ties to the question of knowing whether a stand-in model is trustworthy, because using smaller models is only safe if you know when they are lying.
It speaks to industry and science by asking how to make smaller models cheap enough and honest enough to run through many design loops without wasting money or leading you in the wrong direction.
practical_caution: A smaller model can make the search faster but steer it in the wrong direction if its mistakes are not being watched. Checking if the stand-in is still good (using trust-region logic or randomized error tests) is not optional — it is baked into the algorithm itself, not something you add on later only if you feel like it.
selected_evidence: Nonlinear inverse problems and other PDE-constrained optimization problems... require the repeated solution of many discretized large linear systems.
For Newton-type methods we also need solutions for the adjoint problem.
Parametric model reduction or other surrogate models as well as by randomization.
Reduced order models do not come with (cheap) error bounds.
Monitor the difference between the reduced model and full model objective function improvement.
takeaway: Finding the right answer with repeated runs needs more than just a cheap model — it needs a model that is honest about its limits. Before each step in the search, the stand-in must signal whether it is ready to guide that step safely.
worked_example: Diffuse optical tomography inverts for absorption μ from 1000 frequency-domain measurements using parametric ROM. Full-order model requires 1000 solves × frequencies of a 400×400 mesh = 1.1M large linear systems per Newton step. With parametric ROM (360 basis vectors from 5 parameter samples × sources/detectors), reduces to 250×250 systems. Adding stochastic source subsampling cuts this further 3× (effective 12 random samples vs. full 360). Total 3D test: 23,000 solves (full) → 63 solves (adaptive ROM with updates) = 365× speedup while achieving <1 percent reconstruction error with stochastic accuracy checks updating ROM mid-optimization.
deeper_mechanics: Parametric ROM constructs basis V_R spanning range of interpolation systems [sI - A(p)]^{-1} B over sample points in frequency/parameter space. Interpolatory projection guarantees reduced model matches full model transfer function H(s, p) and its s and p derivatives at interpolation nodes. At node p*, reduced model gives exact same step as full model—critical for trust-region optimization. Stochastic Trace estimate via Hutchinson samples approximates misfit ||C^T(I - VW^T[sI - A_R(p)]^{-1}W^T)B||_F^2 with O(1) solves, enabling cheap residual-based error detection. When error exceeds threshold, efficient rank-1 update adds corrective basis vectors via SVD of residual projection.
failure_boundary: ROM breaks when parameter space has high intrinsic dimension—exponential sampling needed for dense coverage. Interpolatory methods assume smoothness in (s,p) plane; non-analytic behavior (critical points, phase transitions) requires denser sampling. For ill-posed inverse problems (high-dimensional tomography), even modest ROM dimension r still requires many basis solves if parameter space is large. Stochastic error estimates with few samples underestimate true error; concentration inequalities suggest O(10) samples needed for probabilistic guarantees but this contradicts efficiency gains. Updates fail if residual is dominated by unobserved model-data mismatch rather than ROM approximation error—practitioner cannot distinguish.

title: Zorin Mitran: Data-Driven Information Geometry For Stochastic Model Reduction
speaker: Zorin Mitran
organization: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
one_sentence: This whole series is about teaching computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples instead of hand-built math. But what if your system has randomness in it — heat jiggling in a bar, noise in a sensor, molecules bouncing unpredictably? Then we care about probability distributions, not single answers. This talk shows how to shrink down complex models with randomness by respecting the actual shape of those distributions, rather than treating them as if they lived in flat featureless space.
core_problem: Most reduction methods chop a large model down to a smaller one by putting data onto a flat straight space and measuring distance the ordinary way. But a stochastic system (one with randomness and jiggle) is not really a collection of individual states — it is a collection of probability distributions (the odds of finding the system in each state). Probability distributions have a natural curved shape; they do not live in flat space the way ordinary vectors do. And for systems far from equilibrium, you might not even have a clean formula for what distribution shape to use.
first_principles_model: Think of probability distributions as living on a curved surface (like how the globe is curved, not flat). Information geometry is the study of how these surfaces curve and where distributions sit on them. Instead of squashing your data onto a flat subspace (a straight line, a plane), you can move along curved paths on the surface where distributions naturally belong. When you do not have a named distribution family ready, you can build one by taking small neighborhoods around your data points, finding the bell-curve shape that fits each neighborhood using a standard matrix trick called SVD, and gluing these bell-curves together to make a personalized curved surface for your data.
key_claims: Standard reduction methods project data onto flat straight spaces and use ordinary distance.
Models with randomness are fundamentally about probability distributions, not single answer values.
Probability distributions have natural curved shapes; you can think of them as living on geometric surfaces.
For systems far from equilibrium, you may not have a standard named distribution family available.
You can build a personalized curved surface from your data by taking small neighborhoods, fitting bell-curves to each one using matrix decomposition, and connecting them.
Moving along curved paths (geodesics) on this surface gives you a reduced model that respects how distributions behave.

important_terms.meaning: The study of probability distributions as shapes on a curved surface; how to measure distance and direction between different distributions.
A curved surface (like a globe or a potato chip) where each point on the surface stands for one specific probability distribution.
The shortest or most natural path between two points on a curved surface, like a great circle on Earth; it is curved in ordinary flat space but straight on the surface itself.
A bell-curve (Gaussian) shape you fit to a small pocket of data points around one spot.
Shrinking a complex model down to a simpler one when the model includes randomness, jiggle, or uncertainty in its states or answers.

stanford_connections: This lecture extends the reduction-modeling theme from simple point-value systems to systems where what matters is the probability distribution, not a single answer.
It touches uncertainty quantification because instead of tracking one state value, you are tracking an entire probability distribution.
It also connects to learning the shape of data: the reduced space sits on a curve you learn from data, not on a pre-made flat space.
practical_caution: If you treat probability distributions as if they live in flat space and measure distance the ordinary way, you can lose or distort their true structure. For a model with randomness, how you measure distance and define your reduced space actually changes what the reduced model predicts, so the curved surface you build must match how your actual distributions sit and move in your data.
selected_evidence: Reduced-order models are often obtained by projection onto a subspace.
Extension... from flat spaces to curvilinear manifolds of probability distributions.
Information geometry is the study of statistical manifolds.
Envelope of local normal distributions obtained from the singular value decomposition of data.
Reduced-order models are obtained by geodesic transport.
takeaway: How you do stochastic reduction depends on geometry — the shape of the space you are working in. If you are modeling probability distributions, your reduced model should live on a surface that respects how those distributions actually behave, not on a flat artificial space.
worked_example: Stochastic PDE: ∂u/∂t + N[u] = σ ξ(x,t) (multiplicative noise). Data-driven ROM via snapshot POD on random realizations, then project to reduced space: u_rom(t; β) = Σᵢ βᵢ(t) ϕᵢ. Information geometry: measure manifold of distributions via Wasserstein or Fisher metric, adaptively refine basis when KL divergence between FOM and ROM exceeds threshold.
deeper_mechanics: Fisher information matrix F_ij = -E[∂²log p(u|θ)/∂θᵢ∂θⱼ] encodes local geometry of likelihood surface. Geodesic on manifold parameterized by (reduced state, noise intensity σ). Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence: D_KL(p_fom || p_rom) = E_fom[log(p_fom/p_rom)]. Greedy: find μ_new = argmax KL(p_fom(·,μ), p_rom(·,μ)) to extend ROM basis.
failure_boundary: Computing Fisher/Hessian requires densities p(u); Monte Carlo estimation needs many samples (~10³). Curse of dimensionality in parameter space: Fisher matrix is P×P. Method assumes Gaussian or mild non-Gaussianity; heavy-tailed noise breaks information-geometric assumptions.

title: Michael Brenner: Scientific Uses Of Automatic Differentiation
speaker: Michael Brenner
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. This talk focuses on something deeper: a tool called automatic differentiation — a way to compute gradients (the direction and slope to move toward a better solution) through any computer program — might be more useful to science than the learning programs themselves, because it turns scientific discovery into a general optimization problem.
core_problem: Many scientific problems hide inside optimization: solve a PDE (a rule that says how something changes from moment to moment or place to place, like how heat spreads or air pushes), design a material with specific properties, find an unstable water or gas flow state (one that doesn't stay put by itself), figure out the sequence of steps a molecule takes during assembly, understand how organisms grow, or design a way to drive a system far from equilibrium (away from balance) to achieve something specific. Traditionally, each problem needs hand-written math for gradients (the direction to change inputs for a better result), custom tricks for working backward through the math, or brute-force search trying every combination. This limits the size and flexibility of the problems scientists can tackle.
first_principles_model: Automatic differentiation means you can take any program — a simulator, a measurement of how far you are from a goal, a model of a physical process — and ask: if I change the inputs slightly, how does the output change? You get back gradients (which direction and by how much to adjust things). If you write a scientific problem this way, you can do large-scale optimization: state what you want to achieve, write the computation, compute the gradients automatically, and search for designs, hidden states, or governing structures.
key_claims: The tools running machine learning, especially automatic differentiation, can matter more to science than the learning programs themselves.
Automatic differentiation enables large-scale optimization for scientific discovery.
Automatic differentiation can support new algorithms for solving PDEs.
The same approach can design energy landscapes and the sequences molecules take during self-assembly.
Optimization can discover unstable solutions that organize fluid instabilities.
Automatic differentiation-based scientific computation can extend to organismal development, nonequilibrium statistical mechanics, fluid properties, and protein self-assembly.

important_terms.meaning: A computational method that exactly computes how outputs change when inputs change, by applying the chain rule (a calculus rule for how derivatives stack through composite operations) through every step of a computer program.
Solving problems with thousands or millions of choices to make, made practical by computing gradients (directions to move to improve the result) efficiently instead of guessing randomly.
A map showing the energy at every possible state a system could occupy, which determines which states are stable and how the system transitions between them.
The series of steps a system goes through as it evolves, such as the sequence of molecular clusters that form as a material assembles.
A mathematically valid state or trajectory that would fall apart if disturbed slightly, but which still organizes the behavior of nearby states.

stanford_connections: This lecture grounds differentiable programming, embedded closure learning, DPC, and inverse design talks by showing why differentiability matters.
It reframes machine learning infrastructure as scientific infrastructure: when scientific workflows become differentiable, they become optimizable.
It also connects to equation discovery and digital twins because differentiable programs can search over mechanisms, designs, and hidden dynamics.
practical_caution: Computing gradients through a program does not mean your goal makes sense scientifically or that the math stays numerically stable. Automatic differentiation gives you directions to move; scientists still need valid models, constraints that capture reality, and experiments to verify the answer works.
selected_evidence: A primary opportunity is not machine learning per se.
The tools underlying the ML revolution yield significant opportunities for scientific discovery.
Primary among these tools is automatic differentiation.
Automatic differentiation and large scale optimization to solve science problems.
Developing new algorithms for solving partial differential equations.
takeaway: Automatic differentiation changes what scientists can optimize over. When any scientific computation becomes differentiable, it becomes optimizable — turning scientific problems into a single general language: define your goal, encode the physics, compute gradients, and search for solutions.
worked_example: Smoke dynamics inverse problem (autograd example): optimize initial velocity field so smoke evolves into target image (peace sign). Full solution in ~15 lines of Python code via autograd. Burgers equation on 32x mesh spacing coarser than training resolution: learned scheme outperforms classical finite-volume, flux-limiter, and WENO schemes. Komogolev turbulence (2D, Reynolds 1000, 2048² training grid, 64² coarse test): learned interpolation-based scheme achieves 80x speedup vs DNS while maintaining accuracy to 3 Lyapunov times. Vorticity correlation: learned model performs between 512² and 1024² resolution (compared to raw 64² direct solve). Statistics (spectra) match higher-resolution schemes. ML inference cost: 12.5x more FLOPs than baseline CFD but only 12x slower wall-clock on TPU V4 (better utilization). Speedup calculation: 10³ mesh refinement × 10 time-stepping factor ÷ 12 ML overhead = ~833x net speedup. Higher Reynolds number generalization (1000→4000): scaling law (1/√Re in 2D) yields valid model after mesh rescaling; performance degrades slightly but enables substantial upscaling.
deeper_mechanics: Automatic differentiation: unroll computation graph, apply chain rule to obtain exact forward and backward derivatives without numerical approximation. Adjoint method for PDE-constrained optimization: solve forward problem (x_t), then backward adjoint problem (λ_t) for design derivatives independent of parameter count. Loss function minimization via gradient descent on learned neural network interpolation coefficients. Update rules with learnable stencil coefficients C_NMK (nonlinear functions of velocity field) replacing polynomial interpolation. Finite-volume time stepping with learned flux interpolation. Three architectural choices: (1) pure ML emulator (full neural network update rule); (2) learned interpolation (NN-based flux computation + physics update); (3) learned corrections (standard scheme + NN correction term). Chart-space vorticity projection; spectral analysis via Fourier coefficients.
failure_boundary: Coarse-grid interpolation without learning: classical finite-volume produces instabilities; flux limiters add excessive diffusion and smear shocks. Chaotic flow sensitivity: beyond ~3 Lyapunov times, correlation with DNS decays (fundamental prediction limit for chaotic systems, not method-specific). Pure ML emulators fail generalization: good on training forcing/Reynolds number but collapse on unseen forcing patterns, larger domains, or different Reynolds numbers. Learned interpolation generalizes better but requires fine-tuning per problem class. Memory overhead: storing full computation graph for autodiff requires more RAM than adjoint methods. Numerical solver (Jack CFD) currently limited to single GPU/TPU—higher Reynolds scaling requires distributed implementation. Runtime scaling n/k^{d+1} with ML overhead factor 12 (pre-factor C_ML/C_physics); even with 10x grid coarsening in 3D, speedup only ~1000x before hitting memory/compute wall mentioned for turbulence (~Re^{9/4} grid points needed). Model interpretability lost: learned stencils are black boxes (though Burgers experiment recovered WENO-like behavior post-hoc).

title: Andrea Manzoni: Deep Learning For Reduced Order Modeling
speaker: Andrea Manzoni
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. One way to speed this up is to work with a smaller, cheaper version of the problem — but when the physics is highly nonlinear, those small versions become expensive too. This talk shows how a program that learns by trial and error (what we call deep learning) can build small versions that stay both accurate and fast, even when the physics twists in complicated ways.
core_problem: When engineers solve real physics problems — how heat spreads through a metal, how a plane's wing flexes, how fluids swirl — they often need to solve the same problem many times with different starting conditions or boundaries. The math (a differential equation, which is a rule saying how something changes moment by moment) might take minutes or hours to solve even once. One trick is to make a smaller, simpler version that runs in seconds instead — we call this a reduced model. It works well for simple physics, but breaks down when the physics behaves in deeply nonlinear ways (when tiny changes at one place can cause huge effects somewhere else). The challenge is building these smaller versions without digging into the original solver's code, which in real industry is often locked down or proprietary.
first_principles_model: Start with a high-resolution solution — a detailed picture of what the physics does (temperature at every point, velocity at every point). We want to squash this into a few key numbers (like 10 instead of 1 million) that still capture the essential behavior. A classical approach: find the simplest fixed basis vectors that matter most, then project everything onto them. A program that learns by trial and error can improve this in several ways. First, it can learn a squashing rule (we call this an encoder) to compress the high-resolution picture into those few key numbers, and a reconstruction rule (a decoder) that expands them back. Second, it can learn the rules for how those key numbers evolve in time or across different conditions. Third, it can mix the best of both: use the classical fixed basis vectors but also teach the program nonlinear tweaks on top. The goal is fast predictions without needing to open up and modify the original solver.
key_claims: Reduced models — simplified versions of expensive physics solvers — are necessary for real-time prediction and repeated evaluations when uncertainty needs to be quantified, systems need to be controlled, or digital twins must run fast.
A program learning by trial and error can build reduced models by looking only at saved snapshots of the high-resolution physics, without modifying the original solver.
Learning programs are especially useful for the nonlinear maps that simple basis vectors struggle to represent.
Mixing classical basis vectors with neural learning can combine speed, accuracy, and interpretability.
A learned reduced model can compress not only the state variables but also the operators and intermediate terms that classical reduction struggles with.
The main payoff is speed: nonlinear physics that takes hours to solve can be approximated in milliseconds.

important_terms.meaning: A fast approximation made by squashing a huge, expensive physics problem into a smaller version with just the most important pieces, so predictions run in seconds instead of hours.
One saved example showing the full detailed state of the physics at one moment (temperature and pressure at every point, velocity at every location) — used as training data.
A reduced model built by a learning program: the computer finds the squashing rule and unfolding rule and the evolution rules by trial and error on examples.

A hybrid approach: start with classical fixed basis vectors (found by a statistical trick called POD, which identifies the most important patterns in the data), then layer on a learning program to handle the nonlinear parts that the fixed vectors miss.
A reduced model built by observing examples from the original solver without ever needing to look at or edit its code — the solver remains a sealed box.

stanford_connections: This talk builds on earlier discussions of reduced basis methods and POD, showing how to mix them with programs that learn from data.
It connects to real-world digital twins, where real-time simulation of many scenarios is the entire point — a reduced model is often the only way to run fast enough.
It relates to the broader search for cheap replacements to expensive physics solvers, including other learning-based surrogates and operators that act on data directly.
practical_caution: A program trained on snapshots (saved examples of the physics) only knows patterns from those specific examples. If you ask it to predict behavior for a new set of conditions it never saw during training — a different shape, a new temperature range, a sudden transient event — it may fail or drift away from the true answer. You must always test whether the model is still trustworthy before using it in real decisions.
selected_evidence: Reduced order modeling... efficient approximation of parametrized differential problems.
Real-time simulation... data assimilation... predictive digital twins.
Exploit deep neural networks... to build ROMs for parametrized PDEs in a fully non-intrusive way.
Deep learning-based ROMs (DL-ROMs).
POD-enhanced DL-ROMs.
takeaway: Deep learning helps here because it can learn the twisted, highly nonlinear rules that simple fixed basis vectors cannot capture well. When classical methods are cheap but not accurate enough, and the physics is too tangled for simple compression, teaching a program to learn the nonlinear map is what saves the day.
worked_example: Illustrative: deep neural network learns projection from parameter space μ to reduced coordinates z, then solves reduced problem with basis V: q_rom = V*z. Training on 100+ FEM simulations with varying parameters; each produces high-dimensional solution (e.g., 50k-200k DOFs). Network maps thermal field image (input parameter) to latent z; during inference, Galerkin projection minimizes ||V^T r(V z)||. Speedup 50-100x typical for elastoplastic problems. Compared to POD-only, deep network captures nonlinear parameter dependence.
deeper_mechanics:
Encoder: CNN or autoencoder compresses parameter space μ → latent z. Decoder: learned matrix V or neural network reconstructs displacement q = V z. Loss combines: (1) FEM residual ||r(V z)||₂ ensuring solution satisfies physics, (2) reconstruction error if regression on explicit snapshots used. For nonlinear systems, decoder learns how reduced basis V should depend on parameter: V(μ). Galerkin method projects Navier-Stokes or elasticity onto span(V): V^T [M q_rom + C(q_rom)q_rom + K(q_rom)q_rom] = 0, solving smaller (~10-100 DOF) problem.

Surrogate model chains: parameter → encoder → z → LSTM/RNN → predict z(t+1) → decoder → q(t+1). Training on snapshot pairs with supervised loss. Transfer learning: pre-train encoder on large dataset, fine-tune on specific problem.
failure_boundary: Encoder mislabels parameter space regions → wrong z → wrong reduced basis selection → large residual errors. When parameter space has abrupt transitions (e.g., bifurcations), piecewise-linear decoder insufficient. Overfitting: network fits training parameter samples but extrapolates poorly beyond training range. Hyper-reduction (energy sampling) per cluster adds memory; storage scales linearly with #clusters × basis size (from ROM-net analysis). Decoder produces non-physical solutions (negative pressures, unphysical strains) if training set incomplete.

title: Ralph Smith: Parameter Subset Selection And Active Subspaces
speaker: Ralph C. Smith
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of hand-built step-by-step math. In engineering and biology, when scientists build models, they have dozens or hundreds of tuning dials but measurements from the real world that don't reveal what each dial actually does. This talk is about finding which dials matter most, which dials work together, and then tuning only those dials to match real-world data without running millions of slow simulations.
core_problem: Scientists and engineers build complex models with dozens or hundreds of adjustable parameters — the tuning dials inside the program. But when they try to pin down what those dials actually are using real-world measurements, they run into a wall: the measurements just don't give enough information. You could try running the full model millions of times to explore what each dial does, but that takes weeks or months of computer time. The real question: Which of these dials (or which combinations of dials) actually change what you measure in the world?
first_principles_model: Imagine a model with 200 dials, but here's the main idea: most of the time, most of the action happens along just a few directions through the dial space. Parameter subset selection picks out the individual dials that matter most — the ones you can actually learn from data. Active subspaces go further: they find certain combinations or directions through the dial space where nearly all the output changes happen. Once you find these few important directions, you can build a quick approximation instead of running the slow full model, you can make Bayesian calibration (the trial-and-error method for matching model dials to real measurements) focus only on what the data can teach you, and you can trace how uncertainty ripples through the model in a much smaller space instead of all 200 dimensions.
key_claims: Most engineering and biology model dials cannot be pinned down to a single value from real-world measurements, because many different dial settings produce nearly the same result.
Running full-fidelity models many times is too expensive to do Bayesian calibration (fitting dials to data) or to trace how uncertainty flows through the model.
Sensitivity analysis can rank which inputs have the strongest effect, but this ranking has blind spots.
Parameter subset selection directly identifies which dials have the most noticeable effect on outputs.
Active subspace techniques find important directions in dial space (combinations and patterns), not just single dials.
Bayesian calibration done in the reduced active subspace can estimate both the values and the uncertainty ranges for physical dials.

important_terms.meaning: When real-world measurements cannot distinguish between different dial settings because they produce nearly identical results. The measurements are too weak or too few to nail down what each dial is.
A collection of methods that measure how uncertainties in the input dials get translated into uncertainties in what the model predicts.
Picking out the smaller group of dials that either can be learned reliably from data or have the largest effect on model outputs.
A low-dimensional space (often just 2, 3, or 5 dimensions instead of hundreds) made up of specific combinations of dials that accounts for most changes in model outputs.
The process of guessing what the dial values must be by combining initial beliefs, what the model predicts at different dial settings, and observed real-world measurements.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects three Stanford themes: measuring and managing uncertainties in models, solving inverse problems (figuring out dial values from real-world measurements), and building quick approximations by reducing the dial count.
It complements talks about faster models by shrinking the number of input dials instead of simplifying the equations themselves.
It opens a practical path for digital twins: discover which dials the real-world data can teach you about, then calibrate only those rather than chasing dials the measurements cannot reveal.
practical_caution: Ranking dials by how much each one alone changes the output can fool you if the dials interact (if turning one dial only matters when another is set a certain way) or if the thing you're measuring matters less in some situations than others. Active subspaces sound perfect but they need careful checking: you must verify them for the exact quantity you care about and the regime of data you're using, because they can shift if either one changes.
selected_evidence: Parameters which are nonidentifiable... not uniquely determined by measured responses.
Computational cost of high-fidelity simulation codes often precludes their direct use.
Isolate influential parameters for subsequent surrogate model construction.
Parameter subset selection and active subspace techniques.
Bayesian calibration on active subspaces.
takeaway: Not all tuning dials in a model matter equally. Smart calibration starts by finding which dials and which directions the data can actually reveal.
worked_example: For neutron transport with 7700 parameters (cross-section library), active subspace projection reduced the problem to 1D: gradient-based methods identified k_eff (multiplication factor) depends primarily on one linear combination of all 7700 parameters. For the Burgers equation with unknown viscosity, the posterior distribution from Bayesian inference concentrated sharply on the true value 0.01/pi after observing noisy solution snapshots; parameter subset selection revealed viscosity is identifiable but interactions with other parameters matter. For a minimal PBPK drug model, only 3 out of 36 parameters informed the posterior during inference; activity scores (squared singular vector components) correctly identified these before inference ran.
deeper_mechanics: Active subspaces use the gradient matrix G whose (i,j) entry is ∂f_i/∂θ_j. The outer product C = G^T G (scaled Fisher-information-like matrix) has eigendecomposition C = U Λ U^T. Parameters are rotated into W_active (directions of large eigenvalues) and W_inactive (small eigenvalues). Projecting onto W_active compresses thousands of parameters to tens or single digits. For Bayesian inverse problems, the marginal likelihood is approximated using only the active subspace, turning a high-dimensional sampling problem into low-dimensional Markov-chain Monte Carlo that mixes well.
failure_boundary: Active subspace identification requires accurate gradient computation; finite differences on noisy simulators introduces numerical error and false structure. Complex step derivative (perturbation size ≈10^-30) avoids cancellation but fails on codes with internal discretization or non-smooth operations. Highly nonlinear parameter-to-output maps have parameter-dependent active subspaces that change region-by-region, so a single global projection misleads. When the gradient matrix has slowly decaying singular values (no clear gap), the distinction between active and inactive becomes ambiguous and the reduced model loses predictive power. Local subspaces exist but require multiple training points and adaptive switching, complicating deployment.

title: Ajay Harish: Uncertainty Quantification And Deep Learning For Water-Hazard Prediction
speaker: Ajay Harish
one_sentence: This series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples. This talk focuses on one high-stakes prediction: when a hurricane or tsunami hits a coast, how much damage does it cause? We'll see why this is so hard—the water height isn't the only thing that matters—and how a learning program that also estimates its own uncertainty can help decision-makers prepare.
core_problem: Storm surges, tsunamis, and coastal floods push enormous forces on buildings, roads, and communities. How much damage occurs depends on far more than just the water level: it depends on uncertain starting conditions (how high is the ocean before the storm?), how waves bounce off structures, whether debris gets swept in, how sediment moves, what the building is made of, and how strong the structure actually is. To make real decisions about protection—where to build, what walls to reinforce, who evacuates—we need numbers for all these uncertainties and how they combine to produce damage.
first_principles_model: A hazard prediction model takes uncertain inputs (initial surge height, building strength, sediment thickness) and produces uncertain damage outputs. We can use three tools together: Bayesian calibration, which means adjusting the model's guesses about unknown numbers by comparing predictions to real measurements; neural networks, which are fast stand-ins for slow, detailed simulations (a program with millions of little knobs it tunes by trial and error until its predictions look right); and uncertainty tracking (following how uncertainty in the inputs spreads through the model to affect the final answer). Together, these produce not just one damage prediction but a full range of possible outcomes—a picture of how likely each damage level is.
key_claims: Storm surge is the rise of the ocean above its normal level, caused by wind and low air pressure from a storm.
When surge combines with normal waves and high tides, it can lift the average water level by several feet over a large region, flooding cities built near shore.
Predicting damage to buildings and infrastructure is harder than predicting water flow alone because buildings behave differently depending on materials, age, and how they were built.

Big sources of uncertainty include the initial water level before the storm, floating objects that get swept into buildings, how the seafloor shifts, and whether concrete or steel fails the way engineers expect.
A learning program trained on examples, plus methods for updating guesses with real data, can help us measure and predict extreme-event impacts with better precision.
To protect cities, you need damage estimates tied to specific buildings and roads, not just water-flow predictions for the whole region.

important_terms.meaning: The unusual rise in ocean level caused by storm winds pushing water toward shore and by low air pressure underneath the storm.
A damaging event driven by water—such as storm surge, tsunami, coastal flooding, or a large wave hitting a structure.
An estimate of how much physical harm or money loss a hazard event will cause to buildings, roads, or other assets.
A method of adjusting the numbers inside a model by comparing what it predicts to real measurements, so the model's guesses about unknown values improve.
The chance that buildings, roads, utilities, and other structures built near a coast will be harmed by a hazard event.

stanford_connections: This is an applied case study in uncertainty quantification that builds directly on earlier talks about how to track uncertainty as it flows through a system and how to monitor the health of structures.

It connects to digital twins—computer copies of real infrastructure—because good decisions about protecting cities require fast, calibrated models that run in real time to show different possible futures.
It also relies on surrogate modeling: simulating extreme events with many different conditions requires a fast replacement for slow, detailed simulations, and a learning program can provide that.
practical_caution: A single-value flood map tells you 'water rises to 10 feet here' but hides the fact that it might actually be 8 or 12 feet depending on winds, starting conditions, or how you measured the building. Real decisions need the full picture: this damage might be 2 million dollars, but it could realistically be 1 million or 4 million depending on factors we don't know yet. Ignoring that uncertainty leads to under-prepared cities.
selected_evidence: Storm surge... difference in the observed and regular sea level.
Storms coincide with the periodic high tides.
Modeling the impact of storm-surge events on urban infrastructure are extremely complicated.
Uncertainties in the flow... and in the structure.
Bayesian calibration, Neural networks... quantify the impact of such extreme events.
takeaway: Hazard prediction is really uncertainty tracking that flows into decisions. A learning program helps when it can measure and communicate risk faster and more precisely than older methods.
worked_example:
For tsunami propagation modeling, the team set up a hypothetical magnitude-7 earthquake on the Alaska fault and simulated wave propagation to Crescent City, California and Honolulu, Hawaii using shallow-water equations. The computational domain used adaptive mesh refinement from level 1 (deep ocean, ~110 km grid spacing) to level 6 (coastal zones, ~15 meter resolution). The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami reached 30 meters at some coastal locations after traveling thousands of kilometers. In their Crescent City simulation, the first wave reached 6 meters high, followed by smaller peaks of 2-3 meters over several hours.

For storm surge modeling, they observed 15-20 meter storm tides from low-pressure atmospheric systems. The computational speedup was dramatic: using graph neural networks trained on 100,000 CFD snapshots, they reduced inference time from 360 core-hours per simulation to a tenth of a second, while preserving correlation structure between coupled fields (density and magnetic field in MHD simulations).
deeper_mechanics:
Shallow-water equations reduce the full Navier-Stokes to depth-averaged form by integrating over the water column. The key equations are continuity (∂η/∂t + ∂(Uh)/∂x = 0, where η is free surface height, U is depth-averaged velocity, h is water depth) and momentum conservation with pressure gradient driving flow. The semi-implicit discretization requires a projection operator that partitions the domain into wet cells (nonzero water depth) and dry cells (land), which transitions during inundation.

For structure-water interaction, they coupled shallow-water solutions via boundary conditions into 3D CFD (OpenFOAM using finite volume method). The challenge is interpolating between the 2D depth-averaged velocity field from shallow-water solutions into full 3D velocity profiles for CFD initialization. Deep neural networks serving as surrogate models learn the nonlinear operator mapping initial conditions → forcing parameters → field solutions. Graph neural networks exploit mesh topology by computing edge features (forces between adjacent particles) and aggregating messages.
failure_boundary: Shallow-water equations break down in steep-sloped regions or near vertical cliffs where the depth-averaged approximation fails. The wet/dry cell treatment creates numerical discontinuities and requires careful handling to avoid spurious oscillations. When mesh resolution transitions abruptly (adaptive refinement interfaces), reflections and diffraction patterns sometimes appear that are purely numerical artifacts. Graph neural networks trained on one mesh topology may not generalize to different mesh structures or resolutions. Conservation laws (mass, momentum, energy) are not automatically satisfied by neural surrogate models—they may produce physically unrealistic predictions (e.g., water disappearing or appearing from nowhere). For extreme events (mega-tsunamis over 20 meters), the surrogate model often extrapolates poorly because training data rarely includes such rare scenarios.

title: Spencer Bryngelson: Competitive Physics-Informed Networks
speaker: Spencer Bryngelson
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of hand-written math. One popular way is to add physics rules directly into the trial-and-error tuning: a program (with millions of dials it adjusts to fit the data) is also told that its answer must respect those rules. This talk is about why that approach, called a PINN, often gets stuck and gives up improving when the physics rules are written one way, but a new method called Competitive PINNs gets much further by creating a second referee program that learns to spot exactly where the first program is wrong, and the two compete until the answer is almost perfect.
core_problem: Standard PINNs train by taking each physics rule, measuring how badly it is broken at different spots, squaring those measurements, and adding them all together to get a single score to improve. But this method hits a ceiling: on even simple physics problems, the answer stops getting better even though the program could do much better. One reason is a hidden danger in squaring: when you square those measurements, you also square a number that measures how sensitive the whole calculation is to tiny wobbles in the input—big numbers get much bigger when squared, which makes the trial-and-error tuning jerky and unstable, fighting against improvement.
first_principles_model: Competitive PINNs turn physics solving into a two-player game. The solution network—the program trying to learn the physics—wants to minimize how much the physics rules are broken at each spot. A second referee network (the discriminator) is rewarded whenever it finds a spot where the solution network is still doing badly. The best answer both networks can reach in this competition is the same as if a mathematician had solved the physics perfectly by hand. By switching to this competitive setup, the method changes which mistakes get penalized most, which avoids some of the numerical wobbling that comes from squaring measurements.
key_claims: Standard PINNs write their goal as the sum of squared measurements of how badly each physics rule is broken, but this causes the tuning to get stuck on most problems.
Competitive PINNs add a second program trained to find where the original PINN's answer is wrong.
The two programs form a competition where the best answer either can reach matches the exact solution to the physics rules.
This competitive approach avoids the numerical wobbling that comes from squaring those large sensitivity numbers in physics discretization.
On a simple standard test problem, Competitive PINNs made answers ten thousand times more accurate than strong comparison methods.
The method made answers so precise they matched what a computer can store exactly, with improvement continuing smoothly at each training step.

important_terms.meaning: A program with millions of dials that the computer tunes by trial and error until its predictions both match the data you show it and also obey the rules governing how a physical system changes in space and time.
Two programs in a competition: one learns to predict the physics while the other learns to spot its mistakes, and they keep pushing each other until the answers are nearly perfect.
A referee program trained to identify exactly where another program's answer is breaking the physics rules.
A competition where one player's gain is exactly the other player's loss, so they want opposite things and push each other to find the best strategy both can reach.
A number measuring how much a calculation gets jittery and unreliable when the inputs wobble slightly; large values mean tiny changes in input make huge wild swings in output.

stanford_connections: This talk directly builds on earlier lectures about why PINNs stop improving, and offers an adversarial solution.
It shows how sensitivity and numerical stability problems in optimization tie directly to why physics goals can plateau, putting the math of stability at the center of the story.
It sits alongside Neural Galerkin and structure-preserving closure talks as different ways to build neural physics solvers you can actually trust in real work.
practical_caution: Adversarial training (where two networks compete against each other) introduces its own tuning choices and stability issues. Before trusting Competitive PINNs, you should check whether the method works across different physics problems, not just on one carefully-chosen example where it shines.
selected_evidence: PINNs... currently cannot produce high-accuracy solutions.
Competitive PINNs (CPINNs).
Train a discriminator that is rewarded for predicting mistakes the PINN makes.
Discriminator and PINN participate in a zero-sum game.
Errors four orders of magnitude smaller than the best-performing PINN.
takeaway: The core lesson is that how you write the goal (the score to minimize) decides whether the trial-and-error tuning will work well. If squaring measurements of broken rules causes the tuning to get jerky, changing the game setup—having a referee spot mistakes instead—can make the method actually learn.
worked_example:
A competitive physics-informed neural network (CPINN) on a 2D Poisson problem reaches single-precision error (~10^-7 L2 relative error) within a few orders of magnitude fewer forward passes than standard PINN with Adam optimizer, which decreases by less than one order of magnitude over all iterations. For the steady Navier-Stokes lid-driven cavity flow, standard PINN barely decreases error (factor of 2 over all passes), whereas CPINN converges to reasonable accuracy; convergence is slower than for Poisson but demonstrates tractability.

The method replaces the standard squared-residual loss min_u ||PDE_residual||^2 with a min-max game where a discriminator (neural network D) penalizes large residuals, creating a saddle-point problem. An ablation study shows that among various optimizers (Adam, SGD, L-BFGS, several recent variants), competitive gradient descent (CGD) with the Nash equilibrium update consistently outperforms all alternatives.
deeper_mechanics:
Standard PINN solves min_π ||A^T A π - A^T b||^2, where A encodes PDE derivatives and π are network parameters. This squares the condition number κ(A), making convergence poor. CPINN reformulates as min_π max_D ⟨D, F(π)⟩ where F(π) is the PDE residual and D is a discriminator. The linearized local approximation yields two update equations for π and D that include cross-derivative terms (Hessian off-diagonals). The Nash equilibrium is found via a truncated LU decomposition raised to an infinite power, yielding an update that incorporates what each player would do knowing the other's strategy.

The loss now has the form L = ||D · F||_2^2 instead of ||F||_2^2, which avoids squaring the condition number of the differential operator.
failure_boundary: CPINN is slower per iteration than standard PINN because it requires computing Hessian-vector products for the cross terms; speedup is measured in forward passes, not wall-clock time. Navier-Stokes results show convergence is noisy and significantly slower than Poisson; the method remains sensitive to initialization. Highly heterogeneous coefficients (conductivity jumping 1000×) or singular perturbation problems (steep boundary layers) are not addressed. The approach assumes the problem is well-formulated; if boundary conditions are not properly imposed or the PDE residual is numerically unstable, the discriminator cannot fix it.

title: Soledad Villar: The Passive Symmetries Of Machine Learning
speaker: Soledad Villar
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples. One big obstacle: when we write down data, we make arbitrary choices—which directions to call x and y, which units to measure in, how to number things. This talk is about why learning programs that ignore these choices and give the same answer no matter how we write things down end up predicting better on new situations they've never seen.
core_problem: Whenever we measure and record data, we make choices that have nothing to do with reality: we pick a coordinate system (which way is x? which is y?), we pick units (meters or feet?), we label nodes in a diagram with numbers or names. The learning program doesn't know these choices are meaningless. If it shifts its answers when we rotate the coordinate system or switch units, it's learning noise from how we happened to write things down, not the actual structure of what's happening in the world.
first_principles_model: A passive symmetry is what stays the same about reality when we change how we write it down. If you rotate your coordinate axes, swap units from meters to feet, relabel nodes in a graph, or pick a different measurement direction, the real thing doesn't change—only its description does. A smart learning program should treat these as the same input and give the same output for them. One way to build this into the program: set it up so that when you transform the input in a predictable way, the output transforms in a matching way (this is called group equivariance—a matching pair of transformations, one on the way in and one on the way out, that fit together like gears).
key_claims: The same real situation can be written down many different ways, and each way creates an exact symmetry—the model should recognize all versions as identical.

Passive symmetries come from coordinate rotations, unit conversions, relabeling (like numbering nodes differently in a graph), and gauge choices (alternative mathematical conventions that describe the same physics).
These are not hidden features of nature—they are explicit consequences of our choices in writing things down. Yet they control whether a learning program generalizes well.
You can build these symmetries directly into the structure of a neural network (the program with millions of adjustable dials) using group equivariance.
Models that respect these symmetries predict better on situations they have never seen before.
This work bridges machine learning practice to deep ideas from physics and causality.

important_terms.meaning: A sameness that appears when you change how you describe something but the thing itself stays the same—like describing the same chair with different coordinate systems.
The fact that you can describe any object using infinitely many different coordinate systems (different choices of which direction is x, y, z) without changing what the object actually is.
Different mathematical write-ups that represent one and the same physical state, like different choices for the zero-point of voltage in an electrical circuit.
When you switch measurement units (say from inches to centimeters), all quantities scale together in a consistent, predictable way—the real relationships don't change.
A property where the model transforms its output in a matching way when its input is transformed—for example, if you rotate the input image, the output also rotates by the same amount.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects to equivariant neural networks and graph models that learn while respecting symmetries throughout this seminar series.

It explains why symmetries matter in actual practice: learning programs need to ignore arbitrary notation choices so they zero in on the real world, not artifacts of how we happened to write things down.
It directly improves generalization (predicting well on new data): models that dismiss meaningless notation choices learn structure that transfers to situations they have never encountered.
practical_caution: Not every sameness should be forced into a model. A model should ignore arbitrary choices like coordinate systems or measurement units, but it must recognize real differences when they exist. For example: water really does flow downhill, and a model that treats 'uphill' the same as 'downhill' would be fatally wrong.
selected_evidence: Any representation of data involves arbitrary investigator choices.
Each choice leads to an exact symmetry.
Passive symmetries... include coordinate freedom, gauge symmetry and units' covariance.
Implemented as group equivariances.
Valuable when the goal... is to generalize out of sample.
takeaway: If a learning program gives the same answer regardless of arbitrary choices in notation and measurement, it's focusing on the real structure instead of accidents of how we wrote things down. That's what makes it work better on new situations.
worked_example:
Double pendulum with springs under gravity: O(3) equivariance (rotations in XY plane) plus Hamiltonian energy conservation. Learned as equivariant neural ODE dx/dt = F_θ(|pairwise inner products|), where scalar invariant functions (sums of relative distances) parameterize position updates. Adding rotation symmetry: error → 8.2%. Adding Hamiltonian constraint (learn H, integrate with canonical equations): error → 6.5%. Adding time translation (energy conservation via Hamiltonian integrator): error → 4.1%. Vanilla unconstrained network: error → 15%. On point cloud with n particles in R^d, invariant energy learned as E(x) = ∑_i<j f(||x_i - x_j||²) (rotation-invariant by construction); equivalent force = ∑_j≠i g_ij(distances) · (x_i - x_j) where g_ij are learned coefficient functions.

Graph neural network task (node classification on 100-node graph): message passing ensures permutation equivariance by definition (aggregates from neighbors only, independent of adjacency matrix ordering). Classical network fitted ~85% accuracy; permutation-invariant GNN fitted ~91% on same graph size.
deeper_mechanics: Active symmetries (conservation laws via Noether): energy conservation ↔ time translation; momentum conservation ↔ spatial translation; angular momentum ↔ rotation. Passive symmetries (representation choices): change of coordinates (rotation matrix R), change of units (scaling factors). First fundamental theorem of invariant theory: rotation-invariant function of point cloud {x_i} can be written as f(pairwise inner products {x_i·x_j}). Equivariant function (output transforms with input): ∀g∈G, ∀θ: F(g·x;θ) = g·F(x;θ). Implement via irreducible representations (group representation theory decomposes tensor products into irreducible blocks; equivalent maps preserve block structure) or invariant theory (multiply scalar invariants by input vectors). Hamiltonian neural network: parameterize H(q,p), compute ∂H/∂p → q̇, -∂H/∂q → ṗ automatically preserves Poisson bracket {·,·} structure.
failure_boundary: Over-specification: imposing all known symmetries when some are violated weakly (e.g., slight dissipation) introduces bias. Graph isomorphism barrier: message passing networks cannot distinguish non-isomorphic graphs if they're locally identical; need higher-order invariants or subgraph kernels. Sparse data: enforcing strong symmetry constraints shrinks hypothesis class; if true solution is barely equivariant or uninvariant, generalization error increases despite smaller model class. Dimensional analysis failure: Buckingham π theorem requires all relevant physical variables to be present; missing variables break dimensional consistency. Stiffness: symplectic/Hamiltonian integrators require smaller time steps than explicit methods, increasing computational cost despite theoretical advantages.

title: Victor Zavala: Bayesian Optimization With ML Models, Physics, And High-Throughput Experiments
speaker: Victor M. Zavala
organization: University of Wisconsin-Madison / Argonne National Laboratory
one_sentence: This series chases one goal: getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from data instead of only using hand-written math. When you can run experiments but they cost time or money, one approach is to use a smart search method called Bayesian optimization. This talk shows how to combine three things: a starting physics model that captures basic behavior, a learned model that fixes what the physics model gets wrong, and the ability to run many experiments at once.
core_problem: Bayesian optimization is a way to search smartly when each experiment or simulation takes effort or money. You start with a fast substitute model (called a surrogate: a quick guess-maker trained on past experiments) and you track how sure you are about its guesses. Standard versions struggle when your model is huge, when you have physics knowledge sitting around unused, or when you have the ability to run many experiments in parallel at the same time. The real puzzle is how to use physics and parallelism together while still having your search guided by your uncertainty—how confident your surrogate is in each prediction.
first_principles_model: Bayesian optimization picks the next experiment by scoring all possible choices with a formula called an acquisition function. This formula uses a surrogate (fast substitute model) and uncertainty estimates to score what you'll learn. If you have a physics model (a rough first guess built from known scientific laws), you can split what happens into two parts: what the physics model predicts plus the gap left over (called the residual—the leftover bits the physics model misses). Train a Gaussian process (a statistical tool that assigns likelihoods to different possible models, so you get both a guess and a confidence level) on just the residual part. This focuses your limited experiments on catching exactly what physics gets wrong. The physics model also lets you carve up the design space so parallel experiments don't repeat effort, and it helps build acquisition formulas that work on large models.
key_claims: Bayesian optimization can combine large-scale learned models, physics knowledge, and batches of experiments all at once.
You can split what happens into two pieces: a physics-based starting model plus a learned model that captures what's missing.
Training a statistical model on just the missing parts speeds up your search.
A physics-based starting model can divide the design space so parallel experiments don't duplicate effort.
Running many experiments at once requires Bayesian optimization methods that score groups of choices, not one at a time.
Acquisition formulas can extend Bayesian optimization to large models by using simple counts of uncertainty instead of exact calculations.

important_terms.meaning: A search method that builds a statistical model of past results to make quick guesses about which experiments will teach you the most, then runs those experiments rather than trying everything.
A starting model, often built from physics or known science, that captures the overall pattern of how outcomes change as you vary inputs.
A learned model that captures the errors or corrections the reference model misses—the leftover gap between what physics predicts and what really happens.
A statistical tool that builds a model by assigning probabilities to different possible patterns, letting you estimate what will happen and how confident you should be in that estimate.
A scoring formula that decides which experiment or simulation to run next by balancing what looks like it will work well against how much you still need to learn about that region.

stanford_connections: This talk connects to active learning and experimental design across the playlist, and to how you build and tune digital copies of real systems.
It extends hybrid physics-plus-learning modeling by treating physics as a strong starting point rather than the complete answer.
It shows the optimization side of building substitute models while carefully managing confidence in predictions.
practical_caution: A weak or wrong physics model can steer your search down the wrong path. When using Bayesian optimization with physics built in, pay close attention to how well-behaved the residual is and how honest your confidence estimates are, rather than trusting the physics model everywhere.
selected_evidence: Bayesian Optimization... exploiting machine learning models, physics and high throughput experiments.
Decomposes the performance function into a reference model... and a residual model.
Learning the residual from data using a Gaussian Process.
Partition the design space and enable parallel search.
Acquisition function.
takeaway: The core idea is that Bayesian optimization is smart experimentation when you have uncertainty. Physics works best when it points your search in the right direction while still letting you learn where it falls short.
worked_example:
For HVAC plant controller tuning, model predictive control depends on horizon parameter and constraint tuning. A single 1-year simulation runs 3 hours, making brute-force search infeasible. Using Bayesian optimization with low-fidelity reference model (simplified physics), the algorithm identified optimal control parameters within the flat region of cost landscape (millions of dollars/year range) in ~20 experiments, versus 60+ required by standard BO without reference model.

For microbial community optimization, recurrent neural networks trained on limited high-throughput experiments achieve only neighborhood-level accuracy (not globally accurate), yet enable parametric BO to find improved bacterial species compositions. Even with inaccurate predictions, the closed-loop framework converges to better concentrations and community configurations that standard random experimental design cannot achieve.
deeper_mechanics:
Bayesian optimization decomposes performance f(x) = g(x; reference physics) + r(x; residual learned from data). The Fisher Information Matrix H = Σ J_i^T J_i (where J_i = ∂f/∂θ|_{θ_opt}) captures parameter sensitivity; acquisition function maximizes μ(x) + λσ(x) to balance exploitation (expected performance) vs. exploration (uncertainty reduction). Parametric models use Laplace approximation: σ^2(x) = (J^T H^{-1} J) ∝ posterior variance at x. Non-parametric Gaussian Process models with kernel k(x,x') and hyperparameter Θ: mean prediction m(x), variance v(x) from covariance structure.

High-throughput partitioning via level sets: decompose design space into regions where reference model predicts high/low performance. Run parallel BO agents in each partition with shared central model for global optimization. Recurrent neural nets for dynamics: y_t = RNN(x_t, h_{t-1}; W,b) where hidden state h_t encodes system memory; loss minimizes ||y_pred - y_data||_2 over trajectories, not pointwise errors.
failure_boundary:
Gaussian Process models scale poorly with number of observations (O(N^3) complexity for covariance matrix inversion). Fisher Information approach requires computing second derivatives and inverting large Hessians—prohibitive for deep neural networks. Non-parametric BO is inherently sequential (one experiment per cycle), making high-throughput parallelization difficult; standard acquisition functions cannot easily propose multiple candidate experiments simultaneously.

Parametric BO with neural networks is sensitive to model architecture and training; inaccurate models can drive search into wrong regions if acquisition function doesn't adequately explore. Neighborhood-level accuracy suffices locally but fails globally—recurrent neural nets trained on microbial communities exhibit poor long-term trajectory prediction, so the method only works in closed-loop iterative cycles. Reference models with incorrect physics can mislead partitioning, causing BO to ignore promising regions. Noise in input data (not output) is difficult to handle; no straightforward way to incorporate input uncertainty into gaussian process framework.

title: Hassan Babaee: CUR Matrix Decomposition For Scalable Reduced-Order Modeling
speaker: Hassan Babaee
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things change (air over a wing, heat through metal, water sloshing) by learning from examples instead of hand-written formulas. One way to predict faster is to use a shrunk model that only tracks the most important patterns. This talk shows how to use a selection method called CUR—pick the most informative rows and columns from a matrix—to make these shrunk models work for complicated PDEs (rules that say how something changes place-by-place and moment-by-moment) where change isn't just proportional, and to make the code easier to build.
core_problem: A shrunk model with bases (sets of directions) that change as time goes forward can solve big PDEs by tracking only a few evolving patterns instead of tracking everything. But when the PDE has complications (change that isn't proportional) and those complications aren't simple polynomials (terms like x², x³), the cost of computing the shrunk equations becomes as expensive as solving the whole original problem. On top of that, writing the code to do this is tedious and error-prone.
first_principles_model: Start with a PDE solution that is huge and complicated. Instead of tracking every detail, represent it as a few time-changing patterns—vectors and numbers that evolve. To find which patterns matter most, compute them by minimizing how wrong the model's guess is compared to the real answer. For complicated terms (the non-proportional parts), CUR does this: it picks the rows and columns of a matrix that carry the most information, then approximates the whole matrix using just those rows, columns, and a small computed piece where they overlap. This way, the time-changing patterns stay shrunk because you only compute the complicated terms at the informative spots you picked.
key_claims: Time-changing patterns pull out the real correlations hiding in big PDE solutions.
These patterns are built by minimizing error as you go, not by analyzing data that was computed beforehand.
Shrunk models stay cheap for simple PDEs (where change is proportional) and for polynomials (sums of powers like x + x²), but non-polynomial complications force you back to full cost.
Non-proportional terms that aren't polynomials are especially hard to handle in shrunk models.
Picking which rows and columns to use (CUR selection) makes shrunk models for complicated PDEs actually stay cheap.
This method cuts down the amount of code you have to rewrite when applying shrunk models to new PDEs.

important_terms.meaning: Pick a few columns and a few rows from a huge table of numbers; compute a small connecting piece where they cross; use those to approximate the whole table.
Represent a complicated, evolving system by keeping only a few time-changing directions—compressing the information needed to describe what happens.
A small set of directions that evolves during the simulation—it doesn't stay frozen, it updates moment-by-moment to stay closest to the real answer.
Compute complicated nonlinear terms at only a few carefully chosen spots (not everywhere), and use those spots to approximate the terms wherever you need them.
A non-proportional term you can't write as a simple sum of powers (like x + 3x² + x⁵); computing a shrunk version of it is much harder than for simpler terms.

stanford_connections: This talk continues the line of work on shrunk models: instead of just finding patterns in data, this method picks which parts of the calculation matter most and only computes those.
It connects to other paths for making shrunk models practical, like learning from data and adapting the shrunk model as time goes forward.
It also links to smarter ways of picking which data points or rows/columns to actually compute, based on which ones carry the most signal.
practical_caution: Picking which rows and columns to keep must be done carefully: the error from the shrunk representation has to stay small. If you miss rows or columns where the non-proportional behavior is happening, the shrunk model will run fast but give answers that are wrong.
selected_evidence: CUR Matrix Decomposition for Scalable Reduced-Order Modeling.
Dynamical low-rank approximation... high-dimensional partial differential equations.
Time-dependent bases.
Residual minimization.
Adaptive sparse interpolation algorithm based on CUR matrix decomposition.
takeaway: Making shrunk models that run fast needs two things working together: a shrunk structure (low-rank) and a way to compute complicated terms cheaply. CUR gives you the selection method that picks which pieces matter, so shrunk models for complicated PDEs can actually stay shrunk.
worked_example:
A reacting-flow example has 23 chemical species, so the full PDE system is 23 coupled equations; realistic mechanisms reach ~1000 species, which is out of the question to store on a DNS grid. The time-dependent-basis ROM writes the state as a matrix (species/samples x grid) and evolves a rank-r SVD-like factorization on the fly, with no offline data generation -- only the initial and boundary conditions.
