For forward sensitivity of a 23-species, 34-parameter system, instead of solving 23x34 = 782 sensitivity PDEs, a rank-5 approximation solves 5 PDEs plus a small ODE and reconstructs all 782 sensitivities by a matrix-matrix product, with under 1% relative error and singular values that track the instantaneous SVD.

The CUR step handles the nonlinear right-hand side, which otherwise costs as much as the full model because you'd have to evaluate F on the whole decompressed matrix. CUR evaluates F only at strategically chosen columns and rows (chosen by a DEIM/DIME greedy procedure using the previous time step's SVD), so on a Burgers problem with two shocks the sampled points concentrate right on the shocks and move in time with them. On a compressible-flow UQ case with non-polynomial nonlinearity (rho*u/rho), the matrix is 262,000 rows x 200,000 samples -- too big to even store on the laptop CPU used -- yet CUR recovers the no-sampling result with as few as ~6-20 sampled columns, and CPU time then scales linearly rather than with rows x columns.

Rank matters: a species case with a sudden chemistry transition at the end needed rank 29 out of 39 (not much reduction) because the state is genuinely high-rank instantaneously, illustrating where the method has little to offer.
deeper_mechanics:
The method reduces a matrix differential equation dV/dt = F(V) by approximating V(t) approx U(t) Sigma(t) Y(t)^T, an instantaneous low-rank (SVD-like) factorization whose factors are themselves evolved in time. The evolution equations for U, Sigma, Y are the optimality conditions of a variational principle: plug the low-rank ansatz into the governing equation, form the residual (nonzero because the ansatz is low-rank), and minimize it by optimally updating the factors subject to orthonormality of U and Y. No nonlinear optimization is solved at run time -- the closed-form evolution equations are the minimizer, and the math is dynamical low-rank / Riemannian optimization on the manifold of rank-r matrices (equivalent to DO/BO/DLR formulations).

The obstacle for nonlinear F is that computing F(USY^T) requires the full decompressed matrix. CUR (a DEIM-induced decomposition, Sorensen-Embree) avoids this: pick r columns C and r rows R of F strategically and form F approx C * M^{-1} * R where M is the intersection block; equivalently V(t) = QR of the sampled columns times interpolation coefficients (an oblique, not orthogonal, projection). Because the true F has low-rank structure, sampling it only at those rows/columns reconstructs it accurately: the 2-norm error is bounded by (interpolation condition numbers) times sigma_{r+1}, the same optimal rank-r floor an SVD would give, and DIME greedily minimizes those condition numbers. Sample locations are recomputed every time step from the previous step's SVD, and the number of samples p is made adaptive by watching the last resolved singular value.
failure_boundary:
The whole approach requires two things: the problem must be expressible as a matrix differential equation, and that matrix must be instantaneously low-rank. If the state is high-rank at each instant -- the sudden-chemistry-transition case forcing rank 29 of 39 -- there is little reduction and the method loses its advantage. The system can be high-rank over the whole trajectory as long as it's low-rank at each moment; it's the instantaneous rank that governs cost.

Two numerical dangers appear. Resolving small singular values needs inverting the Sigma matrix, which becomes ill-conditioned as singular values shrink; specialized integrators fix this but at roughly double or triple the cost. And the CUR sampling is only as good as the low-rank structure of F: the row sampling is intrusive (you must know the equation terms), and because rows/columns are re-selected every step, the previous-step SVD used to place them can lag fast transitions, so abrupt changes in the dynamics can momentarily misplace the sample points and inflate error until the sampling catches up.

title: Jian Cao: Physics-Based AI-Assisted Design And Control In Flexible Manufacturing
speaker: Jian Cao
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. This talk looks at manufacturing: making metal parts layer by layer or reshaping metal without custom molds for each design. The talk shows how we can combine two things—the laws of physics that tell us how metal melts, flows, and hardens, plus a learning program that spots patterns in measurements taken during production—to design better parts and steer the process moment by moment as the part is being made.
core_problem: Flexible manufacturing—making different shapes without building a custom mold for each one—sounds good on paper, but the reality is hard. The metal's strength depends on its entire journey: how hot it got, how fast it cooled, what happened before. The shapes are complex. And we have to choose which dials to turn (temperature, speed, laser power) out of hundreds of options. Knowing the complete physics by hand is very slow or impossible; just guessing from examples alone often misses why the metal actually behaves the way it does, and can ignore the real limits of what the machine can do.
first_principles_model: Making a part is a chain: you choose how to design and control the machine (temperature, scan path, cooling rate) → the physics happens (metal melts, atoms rearrange, cooling locks in the structure) → out comes the final part with its own strength and shape. The physics tells us rules: energy and mass don't vanish (what goes in and what comes out must balance); metal flows according to how hot it is and how fast you pull on it; cooling speed changes how hard it becomes. Learning from examples lets us skip the slow hand-built math and instead predict what the part will look like and be strong enough. It also lets us pick which measurements to take during production—temperature here, maybe surface glow there—to catch problems before they happen. Real-time control means: as the part is being made right now, look at what is actually happening and twist the dials before flaws get locked in.
key_claims: Flexible manufacturing works better when you combine physics knowledge (how metal moves and cools) with learning programs that spot patterns in real data.
Metal powder layering and fast forming without molds are two real examples where this blend already helps.
You can predict what a part will be like and how strong it will be by mixing physics and measured data.
A learning program can pick which things to measure during production to catch problems early.
A metal part's strength comes from its whole journey, not just its final shape; ignoring this history is a big mistake.
When you have hundreds of choices for temperature and speed, you need both physics and learning to find the best path.

important_terms.meaning: Making many different shapes or products on the same machine without having to build a new mold or tool for each design.
Building parts one thin layer at a time, usually by melting metal powder with a laser and cooling it to lock in the layer, then repeating until the part is done.
Reshaping metal into many different forms without needing a custom die (a hard mold) for each shape.
Instead of measuring everything (which is slow and expensive), a learning model chooses which few measurements to take during production to catch problems early.
While the part is being made right now, watch what is happening and adjust the machine settings (temperature, speed, power) before flaws become permanent.

stanford_connections: This talk connects the idea of a digital twin—a computer model that copies a real machine—to a machine that actually acts and changes the real manufacturing process as it runs.
It also ties to active learning because the model must choose which measurements matter most during production.
It builds on the idea that a metal's strength comes from its microstructure (how its atoms are arranged), which depends on the whole path of heat and cooling it went through.
practical_caution: A learning model trained only on pictures or final measurements can fool you: it might predict the finished part correctly but miss why—it could be because it learned the wrong pattern from the metal's history. The real trap is this: if you train a model to guess the final strength just from the shape, it will not know how the metal got that way, and when conditions change (maybe a new batch of powder, or slightly different timing), it fails. You must track the entire history as you go: what temperature, what speed, what happened step by step. Only then can you predict what will actually happen next and control it properly.
selected_evidence: Flexible processes... metal powder-based additive manufacturing and rapid dieless forming.
Without geometry-specific tooling.
Integration of the fundamental process mechanics, process control, and techniques including machine learning.
Machine learning for active sensing.
Effective in-situ local process control.
takeaway: The lesson is: building a good controller for manufacturing means three things must talk to each other—you must predict what is happening inside the machine (using both the physics and learned patterns), you must measure the right things at the right time during production (not just guess blindly), and you must adjust the machine settings based on what you see (not on a pre-set plan). When these three work together with a real understanding of the physics, manufacturing gets smarter.
worked_example:
A flexible manufacturing system controls robotic arms and actuators using physics-based design combined with learned feedback. Example: robotic arm repositioning task with joint angles θ₁, θ₂, θ₃ controlled via neural network. Forward kinematics (wrist position) computed via traditional mechanics; inverse kinematics learned from 10,000 trajectory demonstrations. Network predicts optimal motor commands to achieve target position in <50ms (real-time constraint). System learns from demonstration: human operator performs task 100 times, network extracts control law, then deploys autonomously with 95% success rate—5% failure rate due to sensor noise and unmodeled friction.

Manufacturing cell: conveyor belt, press, gripper—sequence optimized using reinforcement learning with differentiable physics simulator backbone. Task: sort and place 100 parts/hour. Traditional programmed sequence: 2 seconds per part. Learned policy: 1.5 seconds per part, 25% speedup, with real-time adaptation when conveyor speed varies ±10%.
deeper_mechanics:
Hybrid approach: forward model (physics constraints: joint limits, actuator saturations, collision detection) implemented as differentiable simulator. Inverse models (control law σ(state) → actions) learned via supervised learning from demonstrations: s_t+1 = f(s_t, a_t; θ_physics), minimize ||a_pred - a_demo||² over trajectory. Differentiable physics provides gradient through constraints: ∂loss/∂θ uses chain rule through rigid body dynamics. Reinforcement learning layer: reward function r(s,a) combines task success (reach goal position) + efficiency (minimize energy/time) + safety (collision penalty). Policy π(a|s) trained via policy gradient, gradients flow through differentiable physics.

Adaptation mechanism: system observes actual part behavior (slight deviations from nominal), updates internal model parameters online, re-optimizes trajectory for next part. This requires real-time inverse problems solved via backprop through learned model.
failure_boundary: Sim-to-real gap: physics simulator is idealized (no stiction, material variability, thermal effects). Learned policy trained in simulation may not generalize to real robot—e.g., gripper friction coefficient learned from sim ≠ real gripper. Demonstration quality: if human operator uses suboptimal technique or exhibits high variance in execution, learned policy mimics errors. Non-stationary environment: conveyor speed drifts over hours; policy trained on speed=1.0 m/s fails when speed=0.8 m/s. Adversarial perturbations: small changes in part geometry or friction coefficient can cause 90% accuracy to drop to 10%. Real-time constraint violation: optimization of next action must complete in <50ms; complex differentiable simulators (multi-body contact, soft-body dynamics) timeout. Safety certification: no formal guarantees that learned control respects joint limits or avoids collisions under all conditions.

title: Matthias Chung: Big Data Inverse Problems
speaker: Matthias Chung
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. This talk focuses on a common real-world puzzle: you have noisy measurements (data with errors in it) of something you want to find, but many different solutions could fit that data. The challenge is to add stabilizing assumptions—like 'the real answer is sparse, meaning most values are zero'—and to use learning programs (computers with tunable dials) to pick the right amount of stabilization when working with massive datasets.
core_problem: An inverse problem means working backward: you see measurements (like shadows or echoes) and want to recover what caused them (the object or space). But working backward is tricky. First, noise in the measurements (random errors, wobbles) gets amplified—like trying to amplify a whisper and hearing mostly static. Second, many different answers can fit the same noisy data equally well, so the problem becomes ambiguous. Third, with truly large datasets, old mathematical methods become too slow. One solution is to assume the true answer is sparse—that it has only a few important values and the rest are zero or tiny. But even with sparsity, you must pick a regularization strength: how much to penalize non-zero values to force sparsity. Too little, and noise pollutes the answer. Too much, and you lose real signal. Choosing this strength automatically is hard.
first_principles_model: An inverse problem is a balance between two things: fitting the measurements you collected and respecting prior knowledge about what the answer should look like. If you assume the true quantity is sparse—it has only a handful of large values in some chosen coordinate system—then you can add a penalty based on absolute values of coefficients (called L1 regularization) to encourage the program to zero out unnecessary values and keep only the essential ones. To handle huge datasets, one method, called variable projection, works by analytically or implicitly hiding some variables so the computer solves a simpler problem. Another path is to train a learning program (a neural network with millions of tunable dials) to look at the data and the inverse problem itself and automatically propose a good regularization strength.
key_claims: Modern data analysis, machine learning, and uncertainty quantification all depend on being able to solve inverse problems fast enough.
When datasets and models get very large, many standard statistical methods become impractically slow.
Many real inverse problems have answers that are sparse, meaning most values are zero or negligible.
L1 regularization (penalizing absolute coefficient values) is a widely used way to enforce sparsity in compressed sensing, dictionary learning, and imaging.
Variable projection, a rearrangement of the optimization math, offers a new path to handle sparse inverse problems.
Learning programs can infer good regularization choices by training on examples of inverse problems.

important_terms.meaning: A process of working backward: you observe indirect measurements (shadows, echoes, signals) and try to recover the hidden causes (the object, space, or signal that produced them).
A problem where solutions might not exist, might be non-unique (many different answers fit equally), or might swing wildly if the data shifts even slightly.
An encoding where only a small number of values are large or nonzero; most are zero or negligible, so the answer is 'simple' in that coordinate system.
A penalty that adds up the absolute values of all coefficients and pushes their sum down; this reward sparsity because setting a coefficient to zero costs less than keeping it nonzero.
An optimization technique that hides or eliminates some variables through math, leaving a simpler problem to solve so the computer can work faster and avoid getting stuck.

stanford_connections: Inverse scattering, adaptive reduced-order models, and Bayesian calibration—other talks in this series—all solve inverse problems under uncertainty, and all must choose regularization strength.
Regularization is not a late fix or afterthought; it is the central way to encode prior knowledge and make inverse inference stable when noise is present.

This talk bridges scientific machine learning with classical computational mathematics, showing that learned regularization and sparse methods extend rather than replace the long history of regularization theory.
practical_caution: Just because a learning program picks a regularization strength does not mean you have solved the problem. The program learned its strategy on one set of inverse problems—perhaps ones with a particular type of noise, or particular kinds of true answers. If the real inverse problems you face later have different characteristics, the learned strategy may fail because it encoded assumptions that no longer apply.
selected_evidence: Big Data Inverse Problems... Promoting Sparsity and Learning to Regularize.
Reconstruct quantities with a sparse representation.
Optimization problems with L1 regularization.
A new method based on variable projection.
Deep neural networks (DNNs) to obtain regularization parameters.
takeaway: Inverse problems always need stabilizing assumptions to keep answers from wobbling wildly due to noise. Sparsity and learned regularization are two tools to encode those assumptions when datasets grow very large.
worked_example: Image deblurring: gaussian kernel blur on 256×256 image + noise. Generalized LASSO with total variation (D=difference operator): min ||Ax-b||₂² + λ||Dx||₁. Variable projected augmented Lagrangian (VPAL) vs ADMM on 512×512, 1024×1024 images: VPAL 7-9× faster wall-clock time (~2-3min vs 14-21min for ADMM) despite similar iteration counts. Learning regularization λ via DNN: offline train on 10k synthetics with noise levels [10⁻⁶,10⁻³]; online prediction from data noise→λ; DNN achieves optimal λ within 2% vs UPRe/GCV methods.
deeper_mechanics: VPAL algorithm: reformulate min_x,y ||Ax-b||₂² + λ||y||₁ s.t. Dx=y. Form augmented Lagrangian ℒ(x,y,u)= ||Ax-b||₂² + λ||y||₁ + u^T(Dx-y) + (ρ/2)||Dx-y||₂². Variable projection: eliminate y via shrinkage (soft thresholding) → reduced problem in x: min_x ||Ax-b||₂² + λ||D^T shrink(Dx,λ/ρ)||²; gradient of projected problem drops y terms. Update: ∇_x ℒ_projected = 2A^T(Ax-b) + 2D^T(D·)·shrink(·), requires only A,D matrix-vector products (no matrix inversion). Convergence: proved via variable projection theory (Golub-Pereyra) + augmented Lagrangian (Powell). Neural regularizer: DNN(b)→λ maps noise observation to optimal regularization; training via ground-truth solutions.
failure_boundary: Poorly chosen λ (10× too large or small) causes 3-5× slowdown or divergence. ADMM sensitive to inner solver tolerance; inexact solve breaks theory. Large scale (>4D MRI, 5D cardiac): memory O(m n) for A matrix; VPAL still needs A^T A system solves. Nonlinear operators A: VPAL requires Jacobian-vector products; loses advantage over ADMM. DNN regularizer fails on out-of-distribution noise (e.g., trained on Gaussian, tested on impulse noise) or operators A_test ≠ A_train (transfer risk ~10-20% error on new physics). Very ill-posed problems (κ(A)>10⁸): all methods unstable; implicit regularization needed.

title: Ameya Jagtap: Scientific Machine Learning Through The Lens Of PINNs
speaker: Ameya Jagtap
one_sentence: This series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math rules. One popular way is to give a learning program (a huge set of adjustable dials the computer tunes by trial and error until its answers look right) both the laws of physics AND real-world data as it learns. This talk asks: what makes that approach work well, where does it break down, and how do you fix it? The talk is named after the person and method it focuses on.
core_problem: Computers have two old ways to predict how the world works. One: write down all the math rules (how heat spreads, how air pushes over a wing). That takes experts with deep knowledge and runs very slow for complicated shapes or long time periods. Two: just show a learning program examples and let it guess the pattern. The catch: learning programs usually need tons of examples, and they don't know the physics, so they might predict something that violates the laws of nature. This talk is about a third way: teaching a learning program to match both real data AND the physics laws at the same time. But that third way has its own problems—it doesn't always work well, especially if you have a lot of data, a huge region to predict, or many time steps.
first_principles_model: Here's how the main method works. You write down a rule that says how something changes from moment to moment or place to place (a temperature rule, an airflow rule). Instead of solving it the hard way with exact math, you use a learning program to guess the answer at every spot in space and time. Then you nudge the program's dials by trial and error in two directions at once: (1) to match the real-world measurements you collected, and (2) to obey the physics rule. The program counts how badly it breaks the physics rule at each point—that's called a residual, and zero means the rule holds perfectly. To make this work at bigger scales, researchers split the problem into pieces. One way: break the big region into smaller zones and train each to conserve energy or mass within itself. Another way: treat time going forward as a real direction (cause comes before effect) rather than trying to learn everything at once. This respects how physics actually works.
key_claims: Scientific machine learning is a real alternative: instead of hiring experts to write down all the math and run slow simulations, you can teach a learning program using real-world data and the known physics laws together.

The main method solves two kinds of problems: predicting what happens next (forward problems), or figuring out hidden causes from what you observe (inverse problems), even when your measurements are noisy or incomplete.
The main method has real wins but also hard limits.
Splitting the problem into zones or using conservation laws makes the method work on bigger datasets and larger regions.
Splitting time into ordered steps makes the method work for problems that unfold over long periods.
Training the program to respect causality—predicting earlier times before later times—gives a unified way to solve time-dependent problems that actually works.

important_terms.meaning: Teaching a learning program (one with adjustable dials) by showing it both real-world measurements and the physics laws it must obey, so its answers always respect the science.

A learning program with millions of adjustable dials, trained to do two things at once: match real measurements, and obey a rule that says how something changes from moment to moment or place to place.

A version of the learning program that respects conservation laws—like total energy or total mass staying the same—by training each smaller zone to conserve on its own rather than trying to conserve globally.
A version that breaks a large or oddly-shaped region into smaller pieces and trains each piece separately, so the learning works better than trying to learn the whole thing at once.
A training strategy where the program learns to predict what happened at earlier times before predicting later times, matching how cause and effect actually work in physics.

stanford_connections: This talk builds on earlier talks about the promise and failures of the basic method: what it can do, why it breaks, and how to repair it.
It connects to earlier talks about conserving energy or mass because both try to solve the problem that standard training methods sometimes fail.
It also links to talks about other ways to teach a learning program physics, like operator learning (learning how a rule transforms inputs to outputs) and other mathematical schemes.
practical_caution: This method can work, but you have to be careful about how you train. If your problem spans a long time or a huge region, training the learning program without splitting it into pieces almost always fails. The program gets confused and can't find an answer that works everywhere. You also need to pick a training strategy that respects what the physics actually does, like training the program to predict time in order (early times first, then later times) instead of random order.
selected_evidence: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs).
Current capabilities and limitations of PINNs.
Conservative PINNs (cPINNs) and extended PINNs (XPINNs).
For big data and/or large models.
Causal sweeping strategies for PINNs and their temporal decompositions.
takeaway: PINNs are not one algorithm—they're a collection of different strategies for teaching a learning program to match both data and physics. Scaling them up to real problems means breaking apart the physics (conservation laws), the space (smaller zones), the time (forward causality), and the learning process (how you nudge the dials) into smaller, simpler pieces that work together.
worked_example: 2D Helmholtz equation Δu + k²u = 0 with k=25 (high-frequency wave, wavelength ~0.25) on domain [0,1]². Using ROD (ROuter-based Adaptive activation) neural network with 5 layers, 30 neurons each, and sinusoidal basis functions superimposed on tanh base. After 5000 iterations with L-BFGS, achieves relative error 10^-3 for high-frequency wave patterns. For 1D viscous Burgers with initial sine wave, boundary zeros, 150 measurement points + 8000 residual points: standard tanh network converges to 10^-2 error; adaptive activation reduces error to 10^-4. Inverse problem on compressible flow: inferring gas constant γ from Schlieren data and pressure using only oblique shock measurements; random placement gives γ ≈ 1.2-1.5 vs true 1.4, clustered near shock yields γ = 1.40±0.01 (meV accuracy).
deeper_mechanics: PINN loss: L = w_data ||u - u_obs||² + w_res ||r(u)||² where r = ∂u/∂t + N[u] (residual of PDE N), evaluated via automatic differentiation. Adaptive activation: φ_a(z) = β · φ((z + n)/β) where β is learned alongside network weights; θ initialization β=1 ensures standard activation, then β adapts during optimization. RodY network (Rowdy): φ(z) = Σₖ aₖ sin(kπz) superimposed on base function to overcome spectral bias (networks struggle with high-frequency components). For multiscale problems, Fourier neural units φ(z) = sin(ωz) with learned frequencies ω help capture oscillatory solutions. Gauss-Newton or L-BFGS second-order optimization essential for PINNs; gradient descent alone often stalls in local minima.
failure_boundary: Pure data-fitting mode (no physics residual) requires 200-300 solutions for 2D Navier-Stokes, accuracy ~1% error; adding residual loss reduces needed data to few snapshots but accuracy plateaus at ~10^-2 unless network and training carefully tuned. Spectral bias: networks learn low-frequency modes readily but high-frequency (small-scale) features require exponentially more parameters; Helmholtz with k=25 needs sinusoidal activation, plain tanh fails entirely. Stiff time-dependent problems (advection-diffusion, reaction-diffusion) exhibit solution blow-up during training; memory terms (LSTM) needed for long-time prediction but add complexity. Inverse problems with insufficient data or high noise cause ill-posedness; regularization (weight decay) helps but can bias recovered parameters.

title: Anima Anandkumar: Neural Operators On Function Spaces
speaker: Anima Anandkumar
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave — air, heat, water, weather — by learning from data instead of only hand-built equations. This talk focuses on a specific approach: teaching a learning program to take an entire pattern (like a map of temperatures across a region) as input and directly produce another pattern (like how those temperatures change) as output. Because this method learns to work with patterns themselves rather than with numbers on any one particular grid, it can switch between different grid sizes and different regions, and runs thousands of times faster than traditional step-by-step equation solvers.
core_problem: Real scientific systems — weather, climate, materials, earthquakes, nuclear reactions — don't fit neatly into a fixed list of numbers. They describe how things vary across space (temperature changes from place to place) or time (heat spreading through metal). A standard learning program expects its input to be the same list of numbers every time (like always 1000 temperature readings). But weather happens on many different grids, on different regions of Earth, with different edge conditions (like "air temperature stays at this value at the boundary"). This means retraining a standard program for each new situation is slow and expensive.
first_principles_model: A traditional equation solver works like this: you give it a starting condition (like "the metal bar begins at room temperature") and a rule (like "heat spreads by diffusing"), and it steps forward in small time increments to predict what comes next. A neural operator learns to do the same job but by recognizing patterns directly: it watches many examples of (starting condition) → (final answer) pairs and learns the pattern that links them. The crucial insight is that this pattern-recognition lives in a space of functions (complete field solutions, not individual numbers), which means the learned rule doesn't care which grid spacing you use or which geographical patch you're working on — the same pattern works everywhere.
key_claims: Neural operators learn patterns that directly map input patterns to output patterns, which is what equations between fields actually describe.
When learning targets patterns (functions) instead of grids, it works well across many scales and many different situations.
Real uses include weather forecasting, climate modeling, predicting earthquake behavior, and modeling materials.
A well-built operator can work on new problems it never trained on, as long as those problems are in the same family.
Neural operators run many thousands of times faster than traditional solvers that step through equations one time increment at a time.
The advantage comes from matching the learning method to the real mathematical object you need: a function-to-function map, not a general-purpose learning program.

important_terms.meaning: A learning program trained to take a complete pattern (like a temperature field across a region) as input and produce another pattern as output, rather than converting a single list of numbers to another single list.
A mathematical library of all possible patterns for a type of field — imagine all the different ways temperature or pressure could be arranged across your region of interest.
The ability to work correctly on a new problem the learning program has never encountered before, without additional training or adjustment.

A situation where what happens depends on activity at many different time and size scales happening together — for example, both tiny molecular vibrations and large planetary-scale wind patterns affect weather.

Training a model to recognize the pattern that connects input conditions (like starting temperature and forcing) to output solutions (like final temperature everywhere) for a whole family of related problems.

stanford_connections: This talk introduces neural operators as a core building block that appears in Kaushik Bhattacharya's work on operators that work across multiple scales and system types.

It connects to talks on faster substitutes for equations because both develop quick, reusable prediction maps, but operators work directly on field patterns instead of compressing them to a few numbers first.
It ties closely to weather and data assimilation talks because both need fast pattern-to-pattern predictions for atmospheric systems that cover whole regions.
practical_caution: Neural operators are not automatic. When you test them on problems they've never seen before — a new region, different boundary conditions, or slightly different physics rules — they can fail completely. The architecture itself doesn't guarantee the model will work on these new cases; you have to actually run real tests and check. Generalization only works if the new problem is similar enough to what the learning program studied.
selected_evidence: ML for solving PDEs: neural operators on the function spaces.
Learn mappings between function spaces.
Ideal for capturing multi-scale processes.
Zero-shot generalization beyond the training domain.
4-5 orders of magnitude speedups.
takeaway: The lesson is this: choose what you teach the program to learn based on what the problem actually asks for. If you want a map-to-map predictor (a temperature map becomes a new temperature map), teach it to recognize that map-to-map relationship, not just memorize individual answer snapshots. Designing the learning to match the true structure of what you're solving makes everything work better.
worked_example: Navier-Stokes 2D: train on coarse resolution (64²), test on fine (128², 256²). FNO predicts accurately at unseen 256² resolution with graceful frequency spectrum decay—zero-shot super-resolution. Atmospheric rivers weather prediction: 45,000x faster than traditional numerical models. Hurricane Matthew trajectory prediction: forecasts wind conditions unseen in training, provides uncertainty bounds. Carbon capture/CO₂ storage in porous media: 100,000x faster than FEM; multi-well coupled flow 30-year prediction. Airfoil lift-drag optimization via inverse design: gradient descent through trained FNO yields refined geometry without additional forward simulations.
deeper_mechanics:
Fourier Neural Operator: learns convolutional kernel G in Fourier domain via element-wise multiplication. Transform input u to Fourier coefficients û, multiply by learned kernel Θ (dense matrix in Fourier space), inverse FFT back to physical space, apply nonlinearity σ(·), repeat L layers. Discretization invariance: FFT can be computed at any grid resolution; output at arbitrary query points y via continuous kernel representation. Regularization: keep only low frequencies in early layers to filter aliases, rely on nonlinearity to capture high-frequency content generated by composition.

Extensions: (1) Non-uniform grids via learned deformation to latent regular space (homeomorphism); (2) Diffusion models on function spaces: score operator maps Gaussian random field to output distribution; (3) Physics-informed FNO: add PDE residual loss to FFT learning.
failure_boundary: FNO requires stationary or slowly-varying phenomena; fails on highly oscillatory dynamics with distributed energy across frequencies. Non-uniform or complex geometry needs expensive learned deformation; FNO not natively mesh-free. Boundary conditions: periodic assumed; non-periodic requires skip connections or explicit boundary encoding. Limited to problems where small-scale modes can be discarded; cannot handle sharp shocks or discontinuities. Transfer learning across different PDE families unclear—benefits shared between heat equation and fluid flow untested. Requires large training dataset (hundreds to thousands of solutions) to achieve good generalization; data bottleneck for expensive HPC solvers.

title: Lori Graham-Brady: ML-Driven Models For Material Microstructure And Mechanical Behavior
speaker: Lori Graham-Brady
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. In materials science, what breaks or bends depends on tiny hidden patterns inside a material—its microstructure—that no two samples have quite the same. This talk shows how to teach a program two tricks: first, make realistic digital copies of those tiny patterns from real pictures; second, train a fast shortcut (a program with millions of dials tuned to skip the slow physics math) that predicts how stress and damage move through the material. The second trick works only if the first one captures the real patterns that matter for breaking.
core_problem: Why things fail in materials comes down to their hidden internal patterns—how atoms and crystals are packed. But those patterns are messy and random, with millions of ways to arrange. Doing real physics math on millions of different arrangements is too slow and too expensive. Scientists have pictures of real materials from experiments, mostly flat 2D photos, but engineers need hundreds or thousands of realistic 3D versions to design anything. They also need to predict—fast—what will happen to stress (pushing/pulling forces), strain (how much it bends), and damage (cracks growing) at every point inside.
first_principles_model: A material's big-picture behavior (how strong it is, how it bends, when it breaks) grows out of its microstructure—the tiny patterns inside. The approach uses two learned programs working together. First: a program that creates digital microstructures that match the real experimental patterns you see in pictures. Second: a program that learns the mapping from images of those patterns to fast predictions of stress, strain, and damage. This second program trains on physics simulations (computer predictions of how materials behave) run on the digital microstructures, replacing the slow math with quick guesses. Transfer learning—reusing patterns learned for one similar task to help another—can speed up creating new microstructure families when simple statistical snapshots (measurements of how nearby features relate) fall short.
key_claims: How materials fail or deform is rooted in their internal microstructure—the tiny patterns inside.
Real materials have random variability; no two samples are identical, so you get different outcomes under the same conditions.
Creating digital microstructures must copy the patterns that matter for mechanics, not just match surface appearance or simple statistics.
Turning flat 2D pictures from experiments into realistic 3D microstructures is critical for design.
Transfer learning (reusing patterns learned for one job to help a related job) speeds up generating or comparing different types of microstructures.
Programs with millions of tuned dials can predict stress, strain, and damage hundreds or thousands of times faster than running physics math.

important_terms.meaning: The tiny internal arrangement of atoms, crystals, and phases inside a material that directly controls whether it is strong, flexible, or brittle.
Microstructure that varies from sample to sample (no two look identical), which means the same force may cause different outcomes in different pieces.
Taking patterns that a program learned from one task and using them to help a related task learn faster, instead of starting from scratch.
When stress, strain, or cracks gather in one spot inside the material instead of spreading evenly.
The vast set of all possible internal structures, processing steps, and resulting behaviors—too many to test all combinations physically.

stanford_connections: This lecture ties material learning to understanding chance and randomness in how things break (uncertainty and random mechanics).
It pairs with talks about manufacturing because how you make a material and its internal patterns together decide how it behaves.
It also connects to learning programs that generate images and fast substitutes for expensive physics math on complex, high-dimensional data.
practical_caution: A computer-generated microstructure helps only if it copies the specific patterns that control how the material breaks or bends. Just matching what it looks like on the surface or counting simple statistics (averages and correlations of features close together) is not enough. If you miss the patterns that actually drive failure, your predictions will be wrong when it matters.
selected_evidence: Material behavior leading to failure is often associated with microstructural features.
Random variability of these microstructures leads to uncertain material response.
Digitally generating ensembles of microstructures.
Transfer learning approach to rapid generation of three-dimensional microstructures.
Local stresses, strains and damage accelerate the analyses by orders of magnitude.
takeaway: The lesson: when using learning to predict material behavior, preserve the patterns that truly drive mechanics. The fast shortcut (the surrogate program) can only be as good as the digital microstructures you feed it and the physics simulations you train it on.
worked_example: Transfer learning reconstructs porous ceramic microstructure from 2D slices using VGG-19 features. Starting from white noise, optimize via Adam to minimize Gram matrix loss + two-point probability + total variation. After 50 iterations (minutes), generated microstructure matches target statistics: porosity mean error <0.1%, correlation length variance <5%, pore size distribution nearly identical in green (reconstructed) vs blue (target). Finite element analysis of reconstructed 3D ensemble (generated from 185 coronal slices) shows stress, strain, thermal conductivity predictions within 2–5% of original microstructure FEA.
deeper_mechanics: U-Net encodes microstructure image through convolutional layers to latent bottleneck, then decodes back to stress tensor field. Skip connections retain fine-scale structure from encoder in decoder. For multiscale prediction: unit strain in direction e1 produces stress distribution σ_1, unit strain e2 yields σ_2, superposition gives σ = ε_1 σ_1 + ε_2 σ_2 for arbitrary macroscopic strain ε. Training with 50 microstructures × 4 symmetry augmentations = 200 samples × 6 loading cases = 1200 training instances. Mean squared error loss on all three stress components (σ_xx, σ_yy, σ_xy) drives learning. Trained network evaluates in milliseconds per arbitrary microstructure.
failure_boundary: U-Net generalizes only to microstructures topologically similar to training set (volume fraction, fiber alignment range). Extrapolation to very different phase distributions (e.g., segregated vs. well-mixed) shows large errors. Nonlinear inelasticity/plasticity requires additional dimensions (history dependence, yield surface) not captured by linear elasticity. Method assumes boundary conditions (uniform strain) match training; local heterogeneities at interfaces between ROM elements cause discontinuities. Very small or very large phase scales violate the mesh assumptions. Superposition fails if material is nonlinear; load-path dependence means sequential loading order matters—model trained on tension then shear may fail on combined loading.

title: Ying Liang: Data-Assisted Algorithms For Inverse Random Source Scattering
speaker: Ying Liang
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from data instead of only hand-written math. This talk tackles a specific puzzle: when waves scatter off hidden sources and you can only measure at the edges, how do you figure out what those sources are—especially when they're random or unpredictable? Traditional answers require thousands of guesses and knowing every detail of the space around them. This talk shows a faster path: use the real measurements you collected plus a learning program (a huge bank of dials tuned by trial and error) to skip past the expensive old steps and land on the source properties in far fewer guesses.
core_problem: Inverse source scattering comes up in antenna design (tracking where radio signals come from), medical imaging (finding tumors from ultrasound echoes), earthquake monitoring (locating where the ground moved), and similar detective work. The puzzle: the source keeps changing randomly in ways you can't predict, and you don't know every detail about the space around it. Old methods need to guess thousands of times and require complete knowledge of the medium to work. This talk asks: can you learn from actual measured data at the edges to figure out what the random source is, using fewer guesses?
first_principles_model: It starts with the physics: waves bounce off the hidden source and create patterns you can measure at the boundary (the edges of your region). Wave equations or scattering equations describe this mathematically. From these equations, you can write down integral equations—mathematical rules where unknowns hide inside integrals—that give you a first rough estimate of the source. But that first guess is not great. Machine learning (a learning program with millions of dials tuned by trial and error) then takes that rough estimate and uses the real measured data to learn the true mapping: it watches the pattern of what rough-estimate-to-true-answer should be, and tunes its dials until it gets really good at it. The goal is not to throw physics away but to let observed data teach the program how to skip past repetitive expensive guessing.
key_claims: Inverse random source scattering shows up in many real fields.
Standard methods demand many guesses and need to know every detail about the space.
Combining measured data at the edges with a learning program can find what a random source's statistics are.
A learning program can take a rough initial guess from integral equations and sharpen it.
This method got better answers using one tenth the number of guesses traditional methods need.
Among different translation models tested, pix2pix worked best when the hidden pieces of the source were far apart and their locations were known exactly.

important_terms.meaning: The detective work of figuring out what a hidden source is by watching how its waves bounce and measuring them at the edges.
A detective problem where the hidden source, or the space around it, or the measurements themselves contain randomness and unpredictability.
Data you collect at the edges of a region, which you then use to figure out what is hidden inside.
A mathematical rule where unknown values hide inside integral signs (adding-up operations); used here to translate wave measurements into source information.
A learning program that watches pairs of pictures and learns how to translate one type into another; here, it learns to translate rough initial guesses into accurate source properties.

stanford_connections: This talk stitches together inverse problems, randomness and uncertainty in data, and learning programs that help reconstruct hidden sources.
It shows how inverse-problem ideas work when randomness is part of the puzzle.
It also connects to real uses like earthquake monitoring and medical imaging, where you measure at boundaries to reveal what is hiding inside.
practical_caution: Image translation models (learning programs that map one kind of picture to another) work only when the data they learned from looks like the physics and geometry of your real problem. Treat them as helpers that start you off better, not as proof that your answer is correct or the only one possible.
selected_evidence: Inverse source scattering problems are essential... antenna synthesis, medical imaging, and earthquake monitoring.
Stochastic inverse problems.
Boundary measurement data to reconstruct the statistical properties of the random source.
Better reconstruction with only 1/10 of the realizations.
The pix2pix method outperforms others.
takeaway: Observed measurement data can cut down how many guesses you need to make when you're trying to find random or unknown sources, but only if your learning program stays connected to the actual physics equations underneath.
worked_example: Inverse scattering: Helmholtz equation ∇²u + k²u = -4πf(x) with unknown source location/intensity f. Measurements: u on boundary ∂Ω (e.g., 16 sensors, frequency range 1-5 GHz). Classical: ill-posed; inversion unstable. Data-assisted: learn neural map sensor_data → [source position, intensity, source frequency] from synthetic training set (10⁴ FOM solves on coarse grid).
deeper_mechanics: Forward problem: solve ∇²u + k²u = -4πf via finite differences/BEM, extract boundary values. Inverse: Neural network g_θ: ℝ^(n_sensors) → ℝ^(3+); minimize ||f_true - g_θ(u_boundary)||². Regularization: add TV or ℓ¹ penalty on source estimate. Iterative refinement: use NN prediction as initial guess for gradient-based inversion.
failure_boundary: Off-training-set source signatures fail (e.g., unseen frequency or point not in parameter grid). High-frequency scattering (k → ∞) increases ill-posedness; NN noise amplification worsens. Limited boundary access (e.g., <8 sensors) → underdetermined system; NN cannot distinguish multiple sources from identical boundary data.

title: Paul Atzberger: Generative Machine Learning For Data-Driven Modeling And Reductions
speaker: Paul Atzberger
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples instead of only using hand-written math rules. This talk covers a special kind of learning program that builds simpler versions of complex systems (like soft materials or biological cells) that still capture how they actually move and change over time, including their random jiggling. It does this using two techniques: one that learns simpler versions while keeping the shape and smoothness of the real system intact, and another that learns systems with random parts by watching lots of examples and tuning two competing networks until they agree on how randomness works.
core_problem: Simulating how soft materials, fluids, or living systems behave involves tracking millions of tiny pieces at many different sizes and speeds, plus random wiggling from heat and other noise. When we want a simpler version that runs faster, we face a hard choice: cut out details and lose important behavior, or keep the details and stay slow. The simpler version needs to remember which pieces stick together or follow conservation laws (like energy stays constant), and it needs to stay accurate when we step it forward many times — but most standard learning programs just compress data into hidden layers without guaranteeing these safety properties.
first_principles_model: A generative reduction learns a simulator by watching real observations or detailed computer simulations and extracting the patterns that repeat. One approach uses a special type of learning program called a geometric variational autoencoder — which is like a compressor that learns to crunch the system down to its essentials while respecting the shape and curvature of the original (like learning a map that folds a crumpled fabric without tearing or distorting it). Another approach, called SDYN-GAN, learns systems with randomness by using two competing learning programs: one tries to generate realistic random sequences, the other tries to catch it in a mistake — they push each other until the generator learns how the randomness actually behaves. Both methods produce not just compressed snapshots but actual running simulators you can step forward through time.
key_claims: Learning programs can build simpler versions and multiscale shortcuts of nonlinear scientific simulations by finding patterns in data or detailed runs.
Building the laws of physics and scientific knowledge directly into the learning process as hard rules changes what the program can learn.
Geometric variational autoencoders learn simpler versions that keep shape, connectivity, smoothness, and physical laws intact.
Geometric variational autoencoders can build simpler versions of high-dimensional time-changing systems and complex physics equations.
Two-network systems competing to model randomness can learn random dynamics from watching real stochastic systems run.
These two-network systems learn random dynamics as mathematical rules for change and use numerical methods that stay accurate over many steps forward.

important_terms.meaning: A learning program that watches examples and learns to create new samples or time sequences that match what it saw, capturing the patterns that repeat.

A learning program with two parts: one crunches high-dimensional data into a simpler form, the other reconstructs it — but with built-in rules that preserve shape, connectivity, smoothness, and structure without tearing or skewing things like a careful map would.

Two learning programs that compete: one generates time sequences with randomness, the other judges whether they look real. They push each other until the generator learns the true randomness patterns.
A mathematical rule that says how a system changes at each instant when random noise is pushing it around; it has two parts: a smooth drift (like a current) and a random jiggle (like turbulence).
A numerical recipe for stepping a random system forward multiple time ticks while keeping the numbers from blowing up and losing accuracy, like steering a boat through waves without capsizing.

stanford_connections: This lecture brings together learning programs, methods for building simpler versions of systems, shrinking complexity across different scales, and learning the curved geometry of hidden data patterns.
It builds on earlier talks about information geometry and learning dynamics on curved spaces by asking: what structure should live in the simpler hidden version to make it work like a real simulator?
It connects to uncertainty and how wrong we might be, because random dynamics require probability-based simpler models, not just single-path predictions.
practical_caution: A learned model can generate sequences that look right to the eye or pass statistical tests while secretly breaking the laws of physics (like energy vanishing, or heat flowing uphill). For science, the compressed version must have real physics built into its structure from the start, not just similarity on the surface.
selected_evidence: Generative Machine Learning Approaches for Data-Driven Modeling and Reductions.
Incorporate... inductive biases including physical principles.
Geometric Variational Autoencoders... topological information, smoothness, and adherence to physical principles.
Stochastic Dynamic Generative Adversarial Networks (SDYN-GANs).
SDEs and stable m-step stochastic numerical integrators.
takeaway: The core lesson: generative learning programs for science should learn systems that actually run correctly, not just produce samples that look alike. The compressed version must be a real simulator.
worked_example: Stochastic dynamical system: learning simultaneous stiffness (spring constant k), damping coefficient, and temperature from inertial Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process trajectories. Three-dimensional system achieving accurate parameter estimation; stiffness estimated within narrow range across varied temporal sampling (tau); damping and temperature parameters learned concurrently. Comparison: conditional training protocols with marginal distributions yield better accuracy than full trajectory approaches for parameter estimation.
deeper_mechanics: M-step stochastic integrators with probabilistic graphical model structure where state at step j depends on previous M states. Maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) as discriminator loss: forms integral probability metric comparing empirical distribution of generator to training data distribution. Kernel-based critic with reproducing kernel Hilbert space; unbiased MMD estimator substitutes for discriminator optimization. Adjoint methods applied to stochastic trajectories to efficiently compute gradient contributions without explicit backpropagation through all trajectory steps. Integration by parts transfers derivatives from data to test functions in weak form.
failure_boundary: Noise vs. learning signal tradeoff: temperature parameter very difficult to pin down (overfits by increasing noise amplitude to explain training data discrepancy); damping learning degrades at very small time scales where thermal fluctuations wash out stiffness sensitivity. High-dimensionality in probability spaces causes poor sample coverage in standard GAN formulation; mitigated by restricting to m-step graphical structure. Oscillations in training if using naive Jensen-Shannon divergence; MMD approach provides stabilization. Limited ability to learn truly novel Force laws without sufficient trajectory diversity to probe all parameter interactions.

title: Eduardo Gildin: Guided Deep Learning Manifold Linearization Of Porous Media Flow
speaker: Eduardo Gildin
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of using only hand-written math rules. One big challenge: oil and water moving through underground rock is ruled by equations that twist and change in complex ways, and simulating them is very slow. This talk shows a method that learns to work in a simpler, transformed space where the problem acts almost like a straight-line (linear) system—so a digital twin (a fast computer copy of the reservoir used for monitoring and making decisions) can actually run at the speed needed to control oil fields in real time.
core_problem: Simulating how oil and water move through rock takes a lot of computer time because the rules governing flow are nonlinear (they twist and feed back on themselves), and the computer has to solve equations over and over, once at each tiny step forward in time. When an oil company wants to run a real-time control system—adjusting well settings, testing 'what-if' scenarios, or optimizing where to drill—it needs a much faster stand-in for the full simulator. But usually, there is no way to peek inside the simulator's equations or use its internal structure directly.
first_principles_model: The core idea is to find a transformed space where the messy, tangled physics starts to act like simple linear growth (the kind you get from a straight line). A method called E2CO (which stands for Embed to Control and Observe) uses two things together: it shrinks the problem down to fewer dimensions using data (a method called model reduction), and it trains a neural network (a program with millions of little dials the computer tunes by trial and error) to match both how the reservoir state changes over time and how the system responds when you change inputs—all without needing to look at the simulator's internal equations. Another path uses an autoencoder (a neural net that squeezes data down to a compact form and then unsqueezes it back) to map the reservoir flow equations onto a simpler surface, where a Koopman operator (a rule that says how measured properties evolve in a transformed space where things look linear) can approximate the motion, cutting the expensive work of solving twisted equations over and over.
key_claims: Running a digital twin in real time—for monitoring, drilling choices, and optimization—needs the simulation to be much faster than the full physics model.
Neural networks trained on simulator output can match properties related to conservation (the rule that material cannot vanish or appear from nowhere).
E2CO glues data-shrinking and neural networks together to match both how the state moves and how the system reacts to inputs, all without touching the simulator's code.
The non-intrusive method (one that works without needing the simulator's internal structure) can be wrapped around any existing simulator.

POD (a data-based way to compress by keeping the most important patterns and throwing away the rest) can be supercharged by adding extra hidden dimensions to create a bilinear system (one where the only twist comes from state and input mixing together).
Autoencoders can shrink reservoir flow equations onto a compact shape where a Koopman operator (a linear rule in a transformed space) describes how things evolve.

important_terms.meaning: How liquids like oil, gas, or water move through rock and soil that have tiny holes (pores) throughout.
A fast computer simulation of an oil or gas field used to watch what is happening, test decisions before trying them, and steer the system from a control room.

Embed to Control and Observe—a method that shrinks a big problem to fewer moving parts and trains a neural network to copy both how the state evolves and how the system answers when you push inputs, without needing to see inside the simulator.

A rule that describes how things you can measure (like pressure or flow rate) change over time when you view them in a specially chosen transformed space where the motion looks linear (like a straight line).
Learning a twisted lower-dimensional surface where the complicated, tangled motion of fluids through rock starts to behave like simple linear growth.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects ideas from Koopman theory (how linear rules can describe twisted systems in a transformed view), autoencoders as shrinkers for physics, and the use of digital twins in real industry.
It also extends talks on learned simulators by showing how to add a fast model alongside an existing simulator without breaking into its code.
It reinforces the seminar's theme that the representation you choose matters: the best one is where you can predict and control with the least computer work.
practical_caution: A learned linear stand-in only works well within the conditions the training data covered. In a real control system running on an actual oil field, you have to watch carefully: if the operating conditions drift outside what the model saw during training, or if the real field starts behaving differently than the digital copy, the fast approximation will fail and you need to fall back to checking against the true simulator or field data.
selected_evidence: Digital Twin operations for closed-loop reservoir management.
Embed to Control and Observe method (E2CO).
State and input-output matching.
Non-intrusive method does not need to have access to reservoir simulation internal structure.
Linearize the reservoir equations in a reduced manifold by means of a Koopman operator.
takeaway: A working digital twin needs a way to represent the problem so that controlling it stays cheap to compute. Learning a transformed space where the physics looks more like linear rules (manifold linearization) is one practical way to turn the slow, twisted physics of oil and water flow into something you can actually run in real time.
worked_example: Illustrative example: guided manifold learning on porous media flow. Training set of 50-200 simulations with varying permeability fields (lognormal, correlated). Deep network learns low-dimensional latent space where solutions concentrate. Prediction speedup 10-50x on unseen permeability realizations. Compared to linear POD, nonlinear manifold captures tensor-train decomposition structure of heterogeneous problems.
deeper_mechanics: Manifold linearization: decompose solution u = u_lin + δu where u_lin satisfies linearized PDE around reference parameter. Deep network learns δu in low-dim space. Jointly optimize reference state and manifold basis to minimize prediction error across parameter range. For parabolic PDEs (diffusion-dominated), manifold typically 5-20 dimensional despite 1000+ DOF discretization. Guided means incorporating physics constraints: enforce boundary conditions strongly in loss, penalize non-physical solutions.
failure_boundary: Method fails when nonlinearity dominates over linear component (high Rayleigh number, strong convection). Manifold assumption breaks at bifurcation points. Extrapolation beyond training parameter range unreliable. Ill-posedness if reference state poorly chosen.

title: Yexiang Xue: Scaling Up AI-Driven Scientific Discovery
speaker: Yexiang Xue
one_sentence: This whole series asks: can computers learn how physical things behave by studying examples instead of relying only on hand-written math? This talk tackles one core challenge: when you want a learning program to discover the physics rules themselves AND simulate them to check its guesses, the computation becomes huge. The trick is to make the physics equations themselves part of the learning program (so you can send error signals backward through them) and then skip computing the parts that don't change, using fast shortcuts like random projections and smart grouping tricks.
core_problem: Teaching a learning program to discover physics rules from real measurements creates a tangled loop: you measure something, run a simulation to predict what should happen, compare to reality, and backtrack through the simulation to figure out which dials to turn. The simulation itself—a program that steps physics rules forward moment by moment to predict what happens next—can run for hours or days. And sending error signals backward through all those steps is often even slower than running the simulation forward in the first place.
first_principles_model: The core idea: treat the physics simulation as if it were a regular layer inside the learning program (with millions of tiny dials the computer tunes by trial and error until answers look right). This means you build the physics equations so that when you send error signals backward through the dials, you can compute how sensitive each dial is to the error. Then scale it: notice that only a tiny portion of the simulation actually changes from one moment to the next, so compute only those pieces. Group elements by how their neighborhoods behave (using a trick called locality-sensitive hashing—a shortcut that links similar patterns without computing everything) and use random projection (a technique that reduces a huge pile of numbers into a smaller pile while keeping the important patterns) to shrink which parts even need computing.
key_claims: Learning programs that discover physics are slow because current tools do not wire the physics equations into the learning loop as a single connected chain.
Sending error signals backward through a physics simulation often costs more time than running the simulation forward.
Physics equations can be written so that error signals travel backward through them like they would through any other part of the learning program.
When error signals flow backward through physics equations, huge simulations become trainable inside the learning workflow.
Locality-sensitive hashing speeds up physics equations by finding groups of elements that behave similarly and computing only once per group.
Random projection and searching through hand-picked equation forms can discover physics equations that are sparse (only a few terms matter) and decompose (break into independent pieces).

important_terms.meaning: A single learning loop where the computer builds new equations, tests them with simulation, checks them against real data, and uses the results to rebuild better equations—all connected as one chain.

A program that computes how physics unfolds (rules that say how things change from moment to moment or place to place) in a way that lets error signals travel backward through each step, so the computer can see which dials to turn.

A shortcut that groups items together based on how similar they look (without checking every pair), used here to find clusters of physics elements that behave alike and compute those clusters once instead of each element separately.
A pattern where only a few parts of the simulation actually change in meaningful ways at each time step; the rest stay the same, so skip computing them.

A technique that squeezes a huge set of numbers down to a smaller set while keeping the main patterns intact, like taking a 10,000-item list and summarizing it to 100 key ideas without losing the gist.

stanford_connections: This lecture builds on automatic differentiation (the trick computers use to send error signals backward through their dials) and extends it to make physics equations trainable inside learning programs.
It pairs with talks about learning neural solvers and neural operators by showing how to speed up both the forward simulation and the backward error signals at the same time.
It continues the thread of finding hidden equations in data by tying it to actual simulation: instead of just guessing equations that fit, you embed the physics into the learning loop itself.
practical_caution: This approach has real walls. Your computer has limited memory, so huge simulations overflow. Some equations are 'stiff'—they resist stable numerical calculation, like trying to predict a wobbling building with a crude formula. Real measurements are messy and biased. And fast backward gradients help only if the physics equations you discover and the solver actually describe reality, not noise.
selected_evidence: Lack of end-to-end frameworks embedding large-scale simulation of physics models into learning.
Backward gradient propagation.
PDE solvers are formulated as fully differentiable neural network layers.
Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH).
Sparse updates of PDE models.
takeaway: To build learning programs that discover physics rules at scale, you have to write the equations in a way that error signals can flow backward through them, and you have to skip computing anything that doesn't matter.
worked_example: Nano void evolution in copper under heavy ion irradiation at 350°C was tracked from in-situ TEM videos. A recognition neural network extracted void positions and sizes from pixel data at each frame; a neural differential equation predicted future void movement and size change. Training on just a few annotated frames from the experimental video, the combined system extrapolated to predict new void configurations. Random projection compressed 0.05× the original dimensionality with negligible accuracy loss, enabling offline training despite terabytes of experimental data collection.
deeper_mechanics: The framework chains pattern recognition (encoder extracting PDE variables from raw video) with neural differential equations (u_dot = N[u], solved via backprop through ODE solver). For sparse systems, random projection premultiplies the loss by a zero-one matrix R; this groups sparse loss terms, yielding L_projected = ||R(observed_update - predicted)||^2. Theory guarantees the projected loss is a constant-factor approximation to the original. The loss function itself is sparse across space and time (most domain regions unchanged), so the projection mostly hits zeros, reducing computation without information loss.
failure_boundary: When void clusters suddenly burst (discontinuity in evolution), the continuous neural ODE ansatz cannot track the instant of rupture; predictions before rupture remain good but miss the catastrophic event. Camera noise and segmentation errors corrupt the PDE variable extraction, and neural networks may learn to interpolate rather than obey physics. For sparse systems where the projection accidentally groups non-zero terms together, the squared grouping nonlinearly distorts the loss, biasing the optimization. Generalization to new materials or temperatures beyond training fails because the learned PDE is specific to the training conditions.

title: Dongbin Xiu: Data-Driven Modeling Of Unknown Systems With Deep Neural Networks
speaker: Dongbin Xiu
one_sentence: This series chases getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from data. One method: instead of finding the full set of rules that govern a system, a neural network (a program with millions of dials it tunes by trial and error until answers look right) learns the simple machine that advances the system forward one step at a time—just from watching what happens. Once it learns that stepping rule, it can forecast the system's future without knowing what's actually going on inside.
core_problem: Real systems are messy. The equations that govern them are often unknown. You can only measure some of the things happening—other parts of the system hide from you. Some numbers that control the system stay secret. And the equations themselves (rules that say how something changes from moment to moment or place to place) might be too tangled to write down. The question: can you build a model that predicts what comes next, knowing only what you can see?
first_principles_model: Instead of hunting for the actual equations, this method hunts for the stepping machine—the operation that takes the system's current state and produces its next state. A deep neural network learns this stepping machine directly from measurement data. Think of it like watching a ball bounce: you don't need the full physics equations; you just need to learn the rule 'given where the ball is now, here's where it goes next.' Once the program learns that, it can predict the whole bounce without understanding gravity. The learned stepping machine works even when you have gaps in your measurements or don't know what hidden things exist inside the system.
key_claims: Predicting unknown systems means finding the stepping machine: the rule that takes the state now and gives the state later.
The stepping machine is called a flow map, and it's the core object to learn.
Neural networks can learn this flow map directly by watching measurement data.
Once trained, the learned flow map becomes a working predictor for the system.

This method works for systems that change over time, systems where you miss variables, systems where numbers controlling them are hidden, and even tangled equations with multiple variables and rates of change.
The method predicts what you measure, even when you don't know the total count of all variables (hidden and visible) in the system.

important_terms.meaning: The stepping machine: a rule that takes the system state at one moment and produces the system state at the next moment.
A rule that shows how a system advances forward through time, one step at a time.
Parts of the system you cannot see or measure, but that affect how the system behaves.
Numbers inside the system that control what it does, but you don't know them or can't measure them.
A tool (often made of math or code) that guesses what the system will do next, built from what you know right now.

stanford_connections: This approach uses ideas from Koopman operator theory—a way to think about how systems change—and equation-free methods that learn the system's motion from data without needing to write down equations.
It differs from equation discovery, which tries to recover the actual equations; instead, this learns the time-stepping rule and stops there.
It connects to reservoir computing, manifold learning, and operator learning, all of which train on examples to extract maps—the rules that take you from one place to another.
practical_caution: A stepping machine trained only on what you can see might miss invisible parts of the system. It learns the pattern of the visible stuff, but if something hidden shifts underneath, the prediction breaks. The model works well nearby where it trained but falls apart far away or when hidden states change how the visible world behaves.
selected_evidence: Discover/approximate the unknown evolution operator, i.e., flow map, behind the data.
Deep neural network (DNN) is employed to construct such an approximation.
Serves as a predictive model for the unknown system.
Systems with missing variables and hidden parameters.
Partial differential equations (PDEs).
takeaway: You can predict a system by learning just the stepping machine—the rule that advances it one moment at a time—without ever knowing its governing equations.
worked_example:
The team studied glucose-insulin oscillations using data from only two observed state variables: the glucose baseline level (a constant parameter 0.5-1.5) and 16 time points of insulin response (0-15 time steps). They trained a fully connected feed-forward neural network to learn a one-step mapping: given the previous 8 timesteps and the glucose parameter, predict the next insulin concentration. The true system is a 4-dimensional nonlinear ODE with 16 parameters from biochemical literature. Remarkably, the neural network learned to predict not just the next step but the entire long-term behavior including bifurcations where the system transitions from steady-state to periodic oscillations as glucose level increases.

For a 4-dimensional system with eigenvalues producing rapid dynamics, they trained on just one trajectory segment of 8 timepoints repeated across 10,000 extracted training pairs. The speedup factor reached 35x for reduced basis methods with 99% variance retained, achieving 1-2% relative error compared to the full model while running orders of magnitude faster.
deeper_mechanics:
The flow map learning method avoids treating time as an input variable. Instead of approximating x as a function of absolute time (which causes extrapolation failure outside training windows), they learn the evolution operator: x_{n+1} = Φ(x_n, x_{n-1}, ..., x_{n-m}) where m is the memory length. For systems with incomplete observations (only subset of variables visible), memory is essential because the observed variables alone don't form a closed dynamical system without knowledge of unobserved variables' history.

For PDEs, they use an assembly layer inspired by numerical discretization of differential operators. Rather than treating the entire field as input to a monolithic network, they apply spatially-local convolutional operations (mimicking how differentiation matrices work) followed by pointwise nonlinear activation functions. This enforces spatial smoothness constraints and respects the local structure of differential operators. The network learns to approximate the unknown nonlinear differential operator L in: u_{n+1} = u_n + Δt · L(u_n, u_{n-1},...), where L is composed of learned convolutional filters and nonlinearities.
failure_boundary: Flow map learning fails catastrophically if absolute time is included as a feature, because the network then learns time-dependent patterns in the training window and extrapolates poorly beyond it. For very high-dimensional systems with chaotic dynamics, memory length must be long enough to capture the full effective degrees of freedom; truncating memory too aggressively loses essential information and the model diverges. When observations are extremely sparse (only 3-4 variables observed in a 100+ dimensional system), the reconstruction problem becomes ill-posed and data assimilation cannot recover missing variables reliably. For PDEs with shocks or discontinuities, fully-connected networks struggle because they are fundamentally smooth function approximators; even the assembly layer cannot easily capture discontinuous derivatives. The method also requires uniform time steps; variable time stepping invalidates the learned mapping.

title: Peng Chen: Derivative-Informed Neural Operators
speaker: Peng Chen
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples.
