This talk focuses on teaching a learning program (a neural network) to do two things at once: predict what happens when rules for how things change in space and time are given some starting values, AND tell you how sensitive that prediction is—if you nudge an input a little, how much does the prediction shift? This matters when you're doing detective work to find hidden values from messy data, choosing where to measure next to learn the most, or finding the best decision when some values are uncertain.
core_problem: Many real problems involve a rule that says how something changes in space and time (like heat spreading or air flowing), combined with random or uncertain starting values. To solve these problems—say, to figure out an unknown number from data, or pick the best action when inputs are uncertain—you need to run the rule forward many, many times. Each run is slow and expensive. And you don't just need the answer; you need to know how it shifts when you nudge an input, so your method can find the best answer.
first_principles_model: A neural network can learn to mimic a rule for how things change, without running the slow rule forward each time. But for finding the best answer, you need more than just a good prediction—you need accurate sensitivity: if I shift an input by a tiny amount, how much does the prediction shift? The approach here trains a neural network in a reduced (squeezed-down) space that learns both the prediction and the sensitivity at the same time, using fewer slow rule-runs than before.
key_claims: Many problems involve a rule for how things change in space and time, combined with finding unknown values from data, choosing measurements wisely, or making good decisions when values are uncertain.
Traditional methods are too expensive because they require running the rule forward many times.
A neural network can learn to approximate both the prediction and how the prediction responds to small changes in inputs.
Using a squeezed-down space inside the neural network makes it practical for problems with many uncertain variables.
Training with a limited amount of slow rule-runs can give high accuracy for both the prediction and the final answer.
Sensitivity information makes learned models useful for finding the best answer, not just for guessing what happens next.

important_terms.meaning: A learning program trained to predict what happens when a rule for change is run forward, plus how that prediction shifts if you nudge an input by a tiny amount.
Detective work: using messy data to figure out hidden values, treating each unknown as something that could be different with different odds.
Picking where and how to measure so you learn the most about the system with the fewest measurements.
Finding the best choice when some values are uncertain or random instead of fixed.
A way to build a neural network that squeezes outputs into fewer dimensions, making training faster and predictions more accurate.

stanford_connections: This work extends learned models into inverse problems (finding unknowns from data) and design, where how-much-does-the-output-shift matters.

It connects to finding the few most important input directions, adjusting unknown numbers to match data, and automatic sensitivity calculation, because all three need to know how outputs respond to input changes.
It builds on earlier talks about compressed-space models by putting those compressed spaces inside neural networks.
practical_caution: A neural network that predicts what happens accurately might still get sensitivities wrong. If you use those wrong sensitivities to guide decisions (like choosing a better design), you will make poor choices. Test the sensitivities before you trust them to guide important decisions.
selected_evidence: Derivative-informed neural operators.
Approximate not only the mapping... to the PDE state, but also its derivative.
Reduced basis architecture.
Limited number of training data.
Bayesian inverse problems... optimal experimental design... stochastic optimization.
takeaway: Finding the best answer under uncertainty needs more than fast predictions. It needs trustworthy sensitivities—accurate answers to 'if I nudge this input a tiny bit, how much does the output shift?'—from a learned model.
worked_example:
Derivative-informed neural operators (DerivINOs) for a log-normal diffusion inverse problem reduce map-point error by one order of magnitude (~1% L2 error) when Jacobian training is included versus ~10% without. For a 64×64 mesh, this translates to finding maximum-a-posteriori estimates that are 10× more accurate. For stochastic optimization in flow control (2D Navier-Stokes), 256 training samples with Jacobian loss achieve results comparable to solving 2000+ direct PDE evaluations, a 10-100× sample efficiency gain. A 3D Navier-Stokes problem solved in under one minute using the trained surrogate (instead of hours per single evaluation) enables rapid design iteration.

For sensor placement optimization (A-optimality: minimizing trace of posterior covariance), the reduced-Jacobian projection method correlates 99% with ground truth Hessian estimates despite 150× reduction in effective dimensionality.
deeper_mechanics:
A neural operator maps parameters θ to observables f(θ). The projected architecture uses active-subspace input reduction (SVD of ∇_θ f) and POD output reduction. Crucially, the training loss includes L_Jac = ||J_pred - J_truth||^2 where J is the parameter-to-output Jacobian. This is the key to Bayesian inference and optimization: J is needed to solve for the map point via Newton methods or to compute the Hessian of the posterior.

For optimal experimental design, the posterior covariance is approximated via Gauss-Newton: H ≈ J^T Σ^{-1} J + Γ^{-1}, where Σ is the measurement noise and Γ is the prior. Rather than compute the full Jacobian (millions of derivatives), the method projects: first onto the active subspace, then vectorizes and applies a second SVD to the Jacobian matrix, yielding a low-dimensional surrogate.
failure_boundary: Jacobian learning is harder than function learning; errors in ∂f/∂θ amplify in downstream optimization. Active-subspace projection assumes sufficient spectral decay of the Hessian ∇²_θ f; if eigenvalues are flat, compression fails. Dimension reduction is problem-specific: the active subspace for map-point reconstruction differs from the subspace for Jacobian approximation, requiring separate projections and added complexity. Out-of-distribution parameters can produce untrustworthy Jacobians. For time-dependent PDEs, the method is not yet developed; extension to full fields (not just discrete observables) is an open challenge.

title: Alvaro Coutinho: Enhancing Data-Driven Workflows For Complex Simulations
speaker: Alvaro Coutinho
organization: Federal University of Rio de Janeiro
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. This talk tackles a hidden enemy: when simulations run on huge computers and produce enormous amounts of data, the bottleneck isn't usually the calculation itself—it's moving data from fast computer memory to slow disk storage. Researchers are learning to analyze and compress data while the simulation runs, not after, so the real-world I/O speed doesn't cripple the science.
core_problem: When you set up a simulation (a program stepping a physical situation forward in tiny increments to predict what happens next) for something complex—like fluid flowing, structures bending, or temperature spreading—the math produces high-dimensional state vectors: thousands or millions of numbers describing every little piece of the problem. Modern computers can do the math incredibly fast. But writing all those numbers to disk is slow. The disk can't keep up with how fast the calculation produces data. If the workflow waits until the simulation finishes to save and analyze everything, the slow speed of moving information between memory and disk becomes the bottleneck that slows down the whole science.
first_principles_model: A data-driven simulation workflow is really a two-part machine: calculation and data movement working together. Methods that learn from the data—discovering hidden patterns, building simpler stand-in models that capture the essential behavior, creating ML models trained to follow physics equations, and steering the simulation in real time—all need snapshots from the running simulation. Large simulations can't always save every snapshot. The answer is to rethink when things happen: analyze data while the simulation runs instead of after; compress or summarize data before writing it to disk; update the learning models during runtime as new snapshots arrive; steer simulations based on intermediate results; and merge simulation code directly with machine-learning code so they share memory instead of passing files back and forth.
key_claims: Learning methods are now standard in engineering and scientific simulations.
Large, changing, nonlinear PDE simulations (rules describing how things change from moment to moment or place to place) produce data with so many numbers that disk systems struggle to keep up.
The gap between how fast the calculation runs and how fast data can be written to disk makes it nearly impossible to save everything for later analysis.
Data must be analyzed while the simulation runs or compressed before being saved to disk.
Algorithms can update learning models during simulation as new snapshots arrive, without waiting for the simulation to end.
Special tools can merge simulation code and machine-learning code so they work together without moving data back and forth through files.

important_terms.meaning: Analyzing data while the simulation is running, instead of waiting until it ends and reading everything from disk.
A slowdown caused by the speed at which data can be read from and written to disk, which is much slower than how fast the calculation produces data.
An algorithm (a step-by-step recipe the computer follows) that updates during simulation as new data arrives, without waiting for the simulation to finish.
Compressing or summarizing simulation data by keeping only the most important numbers, so storage takes less space and analysis is faster.
Changing how the simulation runs or what gets analyzed next, in real time, based on results from the data being produced right now.

stanford_connections: This talk adds to other talks about large-scale simulation and learning by solving a practical problem many researchers miss: moving data fast through the workflow, not just building better models.
It builds on simpler stand-in models (reduced-order models) because compression during simulation can avoid saving full state vectors in the first place.
It also teaches a real-world lesson about machine-learning in practice: methods only work if you can actually deliver the data they need.
practical_caution: If your system can't move data fast enough, no cleverer math will fix the bottleneck. Data-driven simulations are also systems engineering problems. The learning algorithm can only work with data the workflow can afford to move from memory to disk. If you ignore compute speed, storage space, and I/O speed from the start, the model will fail no matter how good it is.
selected_evidence: One must be cautious regarding I/O operations.
Disparity between computing and I/O speed.
Large simulations to output to disk a large amount of data.
Data should be analyzed while the simulation is running.
Merge... simulation workflow and the Machine learning workflow.
takeaway: Data-driven simulation is systems engineering as much as mathematics. The model can only learn from data the workflow can actually deliver.
worked_example: Hydrodynamic simulation at Re=10^6 (1000 snapshots) compressed with ZFP lossless algorithm: PSNR (peak signal-to-noise ratio) remains above threshold with 60% storage reduction. DMD (Dynamic Mode Decomposition) extracts 100-200 dominant modes from full ~50M cell dataset, reducing online cost to O(n^{4/3}) from O(n^3) for full solver. Computational time breakdown: 80% on physics solver execution, 20% on data I/O and ROM projection. For CFD with temporal sampling: collecting 1000 snapshots at Δt = 0.01 covers ~10 time constants. Post-processing overhead (file I/O, compression, mode extraction) scales as O(n log n) with smart selection of critical timesteps; total workflow time reduced from days (full simulation) to hours (surrogate + validation).
deeper_mechanics: DMD constructs Krylov subspace: given snapshot matrix X = [x_1, ..., x_n] and X' = [x_2, ..., x_{n+1}], find A ≈ X'·X^† (pseudo-inverse). Eigendecomposition A = U·Λ·V^H yields DMD modes (columns of U) and exponential growth rates (diagonal Λ). Loss function: ||X' - A·X||_F². ZFP compression: lossy integer representation with exponent range and mantissa precision; user specifies tolerance ε, solver automatically allocates bits per field. Adaptive magic points: rather than all n spatial points, select m << n collocation points where residual evaluation is most sensitive (QR-pivoting on Jacobian matrix). Workflow orchestration: data staging (filesystem → fast memory), mode caching, checkpointing to prevent redundant computation.
failure_boundary: Spectral bias: DMD captures exponentially decaying modes well but misses sharp transients or shocks; frequency content beyond Nyquist (2Δt)^{-1} aliases into low-frequency modes. Adaptive sampling fails when criticality changes: magic points selected during training phase may be uninformative during deployment if physical regime shifts. Compression artifacts: ZFP lossy reconstruction differs from exact values; error propagates through multi-step ROM updates, causing divergence after ~50-100 steps. Scaling breakdown: for extreme Reynolds numbers or multi-scale phenomena, DMD modes no longer separate cleanly; need hybrid ROM (combine global DMD with local basis refinement). Curse of dimensionality: storing 200 modes × 50M spatial points = 10B numbers; I/O bottleneck dominates if not carefully managed.

title: Thomas Beckers: Physics-Enhanced Gaussian Processes For Electromechanical Systems
speaker: Thomas Beckers
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. Machines like motors and generators are tricky to predict from data alone — you need enough examples, and the predictions can break the laws of physics. This talk shows how to combine two ideas: a statistical method (called a Gaussian process) that doesn't just guess what happens next but also estimates how uncertain that guess is, and a way to write the rules for motion (called Port-Hamiltonian systems) that automatically preserves energy. Put them together, and you get a model that learns from data, stays physically correct, and tells you how sure it is — all without adding penalty tricks during training.
core_problem: When you try to predict how motors or generators behave using only data and machine learning, two problems show up. First, you need a lot of examples to get good predictions. Second, the model will happily make predictions that violate physics — say, claiming energy appears from nowhere. You can add penalties during training to discourage bad behavior, but the model still often breaks physics or demands very careful tuning to work well.
first_principles_model: A Gaussian process is a statistical method that describes a cloud of possible functions instead of picking just one. For any prediction, it gives you both a best guess and a range showing how confident it is. Port-Hamiltonian systems are a way to write down the rules for how things change over time such that energy is never created or destroyed — it only flows, gets lost to friction, or stored. When you combine these two ideas, you build a cloud of possible motion-rules that all obey Port-Hamiltonian structure, rather than having the computer learn a single hidden behavior. Even fancier versions use Gaussian processes with a special structure (Green's functions, which show how simple linear systems respond to a quick push) baked into the hidden layer, so the hidden behavior itself respects what physics should look like.
key_claims: Data-driven models of motors and generators should encode the laws of physics to learn from fewer examples and avoid predictions that break physics.
Gaussian processes let you learn models that don't assume a fixed number of dials to tune, and they track uncertainty in every prediction.
You can enforce physical correctness by building it into the model itself, rather than punishing the computer during training when it breaks physics.
A Gaussian process model of a Port-Hamiltonian system uses data to form a cloud of possible motion-rules, each one conserving energy.
Adding Gaussian processes with a special prior structure (Green's functions) to the hidden layer makes that hidden behavior physically plausible too.
Green's functions, which describe how a simple linear system responds to a sudden push, let you encode physical knowledge into the similarity measures that Gaussian processes use.

important_terms.meaning: A statistical method that treats functions as random clouds, giving you both a best guess for what happens next and a range showing how sure you are.
A way to write the rules for how things change over time such that energy is conserved: it tracks energy storage, energy lost to friction, and how different parts push on each other.
A model where the laws of physics are wired directly into how it's built, rather than added as a penalty the computer must follow during training.
A mathematical tool showing how a simple linear system responds when you give it a single quick input; used to teach the Gaussian process what physics-respecting behavior should look like.
The motion rules that happen inside a learned hidden layer or compressed space, such as the squeezed code in a machine that learns to compress and uncompress data.

stanford_connections: This lecture combines uncertainty-aware learning with motion rules that preserve energy and physical structure.
It builds on earlier talks about symplectic and Hamiltonian systems by adding uncertainty estimates so you know how much to trust the prediction.
It also connects to talks about physics-informed similarity measures and Green's functions elsewhere in this seminar series.
practical_caution: A physics-based structure only works if the real system actually follows that structure. If your physics assumptions don't match the true system, the model can be very confident and systematic in predictions that are wrong in the same way every time.
selected_evidence: Physics-enhanced Gaussian processes.
Gaussian Process Port-Hamiltonian systems (GP-PHS).
Physically correct by design.
Distribution over all possible Port-Hamiltonian systems.
Green's function... included in the kernel function.
takeaway: You can bake both uncertainty estimates and physical structure directly into how the model is built, instead of bolting physics on as a penalty after the computer has already learned.
worked_example:
For an electromagnetic coil attracting an iron ball (a toy electromechanical system), physics-enhanced Gaussian processes trained on roughly 20-30 sparse data points. Using a port-Hamiltonian prior structure, the method recovered energy conservation accurately even in regions without training data: total energy stayed constant when the coil was on and decreased when the coil switched off, across all posterior samples. A vanilla GP with no physics structure produced predictions that diverged wildly outside the training region.

For a pendulum swinging in water (nonlinear friction), about 30-40 data points sampled in phase space (angle vs. angular velocity) were enough. The Hamiltonian (energy) always decreased due to water friction, a property preserved by structure-aware sampling. A physics-enhanced variational autoencoder learned latent dynamics from around 50 video sequences, respecting the known spring-mass equation while inferring the unknown external excitation.
deeper_mechanics:
Port-Hamiltonian systems are written ẋ = (J - R)·∇H(x) + G·u, where H is total energy, J is skew-symmetric (J^T = -J, routes energy without loss), R is symmetric positive-semidefinite (dissipation), and G maps inputs. The skew-symmetry of J guarantees energy conservation and passivity by construction. A GP prior is placed on the Hamiltonian H via a structured kernel K_ph(x1,x2) built by applying the linear operators (J, R, and derivatives) to a base RBF kernel.

Each sample drawn from this GP yields a deterministic port-Hamiltonian system ẋ = (J - R)·∇H_sample(x) + G·u that preserves energy conservation exactly—so uncertainty is expressed as a spread over physically valid dynamics, not arbitrary functions. For nonlinear friction, the dissipation matrix R is itself modeled by a GP, which loses the closed-form posterior and requires variational inference. The physics-informed VAE encodes video into a latent (x, ẋ) pair and models the latent dynamics as a linear ODE ẋ = A·x + B·u using a Green's-function kernel.
failure_boundary:
Gaussian processes scale as O(N^3), limiting exact inference to roughly 1000 samples; beyond that requires inducing points or variational approximations (as used for the nonlinear-friction case), which reduce analytical tractability. Modeling nonlinear friction by placing a GP on the matrices J and R loses the closed-form solution, and the variational approximation weakens uncertainty guarantees.

The port-Hamiltonian structure is restrictive: the choice of Hilbert space for H is difficult to generalize beyond electromechanical systems with a clear energy definition. Posterior variance from sample spread can be loose and does not directly quantify prediction error. The sparse-data advantage diminishes as state dimensionality grows; high-dimensional systems (beyond ~10-12 states) are rarely reported because both data needs and covariance-inversion cost climb sharply.

title: H. S. Udaykumar: Data-Driven Multi-Scale Simulations For Energetic Materials
speaker: H. S. Udaykumar
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. When you design an explosive or rocket fuel, the material's behavior depends on tiny details at many different scales — from atoms up to the size of the whole chunk. This talk is about how to stitch predictions from the smallest scales all the way up to the biggest ones using a computer program that learns which effects at each scale matter most for the final result.
core_problem: Explosives and rocket fuels are sensitive: whether they burn safely or badly depends on what's happening at atoms, at grains you can almost see, at clumps of grains, and at the whole piece. Running full atomistic simulations (computing forces between all atoms) for something the size of an actual device is impossible — it would take centuries of computer time. So you need predictions that cross scales: simulations at one scale must inform simulations at the next bigger scale. Each jump from a smaller scale to a larger scale loses detail: how do you capture what matters from the details you're throwing away?
first_principles_model: To design these materials, you need to know: what structure (atoms arranged how?) makes what properties (hardness, how fast it burns, how sensitive to shock), and what properties lead to what final performance (safe ignition, full energy release). Multiscale simulation climbs upward: simulations at the atom level tell you what happens in messy grain boundaries, those predictions feed into medium-scale simulations that show how a bunch of grains behave together, and those feed into full-device simulations. The hard part is that each jump up requires a summary: a formula or a learned model that captures the small-scale effects your bigger model can't resolve. Machine learning trains on data from smaller-scale simulations to learn these summaries automatically, then uses them to quickly predict how different material designs will perform.
key_claims: Sensitivity in explosives and rocket fuels arises from physics happening at atoms, at grain boundaries, at grain clumps, and at the whole piece — and these scales are linked.
You cannot run atom-by-atom simulations for real-sized objects, so smaller-scale simulations must train models that predict the effects larger scales care about.
Computer programs that learn from examples can create these connecting models (summaries of unresolved small-scale effects) instead of hand-writing them.
The chain from material structure to material properties to final performance is the map you need for design.
Building a library of medium-scale simulations and fitting learned models to them is one way to create these structure-to-performance maps.
Deep learning, reusing knowledge across similar materials, and mixing cheap and expensive simulations can speed up learning across different energetic materials.

important_terms.meaning: A solid or liquid that stores energy in its chemical bonds and releases it rapidly when disturbed or ignited — examples: explosives, rocket propellants, pyrotechnic powders.
Passing what you learned from simulations at one size scale (say, atom-scale) into simulations at a bigger size scale (say, grain-scale), so smaller-scale details can shape larger-scale predictions.
A formula or learned model (trained by a computer program on data) that summarizes small-scale effects that a bigger-scale simulation cannot see but needs to account for.

The chain of cause and effect: the way atoms are arranged determines material properties (like hardness or burn rate), and those properties determine how the material actually behaves in use (whether it ignites safely or too slowly).

Using a mix of simulations that differ in accuracy and speed: expensive atom-scale simulations that are very accurate, cheaper medium-scale simulations that are faster, and faster formulas that are rough but quick — and teaching a learning program to combine them well.

stanford_connections: This work connects learning applied to material structure with learning how to bridge scales correctly, the key theme of the series.
It pairs with talks on building digital twins and optimizing manufacturing by showing how to create design loops that predict material performance from first principles.
It reinforces the series' core problem: bridging scales and learning unresolved effects accurately is what separates predictions that work from ones that fail.
practical_caution: When you learn these summaries from one energetic material, you might hope to reuse them for a similar one. But similar materials can fail differently under shock — the small-scale details that break one may not break the other. Reusing a learned summary from one material to predict another sounds like a shortcut, but you must check whether the underlying physics at all scales is really the same.
selected_evidence: Telescoping physics from the nano- and micro- and meso-scales.
Meso-scale models must provide closure to macro-scale simulations.
Data-driven closures which upscale key (localization) physics.
Structure-property-performance (S-P-P) relationships.
Transfer learning and multi-fidelity modeling strategies.
takeaway: Designing materials is really a multiscale closure problem: at each step from atoms up to the device, you must represent the effects you cannot see accurately. Machine learning shines when it learns the right small-scale effects and carries them faithfully up the chain.
worked_example:
The target is the sensitivity (James) curve of pressed HMX: shock pressure on the x-axis, pulse width on the y-axis, with a critical envelope separating detonation from no-detonation. Two microstructures are studied -- class 5 with about 14% porosity and R10 with about 7% porosity, void sizes centered near 0.5 micron -- and predictions are checked against Eglin AFB experiments. The MESO-scale route (MESSAGE) runs hundreds of single-pore reactive collapse simulations in a couple of days, sweeping shock pressure and void diameter, and fits a hypersurface (dynamic kriging, a Gaussian-process surrogate with active learning that adds simulations where RMSE is high) for the ignition and growth rates of hot spots from one pore.

From each single-pore collapse they read the reacted-mass-fraction curve and take its slopes: F_dot_ignition (initial rate as the pore collapses and ignites surrounding material) and F_dot_growth (steady growth rate once a critical hot spot survives). To close the macro model they multiply by porosity: Lambda_dot = porosity x F_dot, feeding exactly the ignition-and-growth form used in Tarver-style reactive burn. Propagating a 1D shock through the homogenized material and interrogating the hypersurface cell-by-cell reproduces the class-5 James curve in good agreement with experiment, and the recovered critical energy matches the measured value.

The deep-learning route (PARC) learns from about 35 DNS pore-collapse simulations and predicts hot-spot temperature and area evolution in seconds where a DNS takes days on HPC; a saliency analysis (dT/d(microstructure)) reveals only a small subset of voids go critical, and those critical voids are on average smaller and oriented more transverse to the shock than the non-critical ones. The two routes straddle the experimental curve -- MESSAGE and PARC agree well at high pressure and diverge in the hard low-pressure region below ~5 GPa.
deeper_mechanics:
The physics chain is molecular -> meso -> macro. At the mesoscale, a shock (6-10+ GPa) collapses pores nearly hydrodynamically, jetting produces a hot spot, the hot spot ignites reaction, and if reaction couples to the shock you get shock-to-detonation transition. The closure fed to the macro hydrocode is the ignition-and-growth reaction-rate model: a pressure-dependent ignition term plus a pressure-dependent growth term for the reacted fraction lambda, classically fit to experiments but here fit to simulations instead -- 'data-driven burn model.'

MESSAGE is a Gaussian-process surrogate: it builds F_dot_ignition and F_dot_growth as functions of (shock pressure, void diameter/shape) over a sampled design space, with dynamic kriging and an active-learning acquisition that places new single-pore runs where predictive variance is largest until RMSE converges. Void-void interaction, absent from single-pore data, is added as a separate surrogate. PARC ('physics-aware recurrent convolution') instead treats hot-spot evolution as a dynamical system for a state X = (temperature field, pressure field, microstructure field) and learns its time evolution with paired differentiator and integrator networks inside a recurrent net -- it approximates dX/dt from DNS and integrates forward, so void-void interaction is captured intrinsically because it trains on full DNS. Both extract the same Lambda_dot ignition/growth to plug into the macro solver (Scimitar3D, a Cartesian level-set sharp-interface compressible multi-material code). Microstructures are generated/edited by a GAN over latent variables, letting them dial void size and orientation.

The temperature field is sharp and well predicted; the pressure field has smaller gradients and is predicted less accurately.
failure_boundary:
The method is trustworthy in the high-pressure, hydrodynamic-collapse regime and degrades below about 5 GPa. There the collapse is no longer purely hydrodynamic jetting -- it shifts to a sideways-pinching closure mode where shear bands and material strength matter, physics the current strength model handles poorly. So the low-pressure branch of the James curve is exactly where MESSAGE and PARC disagree and both straddle the data, and the speaker attributes the discrepancy more to missing physics (strength, shear-band collapse) than to the data-driven layer itself.

That regime is also the most sensitive to reaction chemistry: because void-collapse temperatures near threshold are borderline, the predicted criticality curve can slide all the way across the plane depending on which global kinetics model is used, and an inverse fit picks a specific one-equation model as best. Trust is further limited by data scarcity (only two well-characterized microstructures, ~35 DNS for PARC) and by void size -- void-void interactions are weak near ~1 micron voids but strong for larger voids, so a surrogate calibrated at one void scale should not be extrapolated to another. Extrapolation to genuinely out-of-distribution microstructures (very different porosity, a third PBX class) is flagged as untested and in progress.

title: Amir Arzani: A Flexible And Generalizable XAI Framework For Scientific Deep Learning
speaker: Amir Arzani
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples instead of only hand-written rules. One challenge: when you train a learning program (a huge bank of dials the computer tunes by trial and error until its answers look right) to predict something physical, it often refuses to explain why it made those choices, and it fails when given inputs unlike anything it saw during training. This talk shows a method to solve both problems: take a trained network and fit a much simpler set of mathematical rules (integral equations — formulas that sum effects together) to what it learned, then test those rules against real physics to make sure they actually work.
core_problem: Learning programs trained to predict physical behavior often suffer from two linked failures: first, they give no explanation for their choices, so you can't tell if they're actually capturing real physics or just getting lucky; second, they tend to fail badly when you ask them to predict something at a temperature, size, or condition they never saw during training. The root cause: real experiments and measurements rarely cover every possible condition a model might meet, so the learning program never learns what to do in those gaps.
first_principles_model: The method starts by taking a trained learning program and asking it: what patterns did you pick up on? It pokes the network with inputs across the range it learned from, then takes all those outputs and fits a much simpler, readable model (built from integral equations — formulas where one quantity is defined as a sum of effects calculated across space or time using a kernel weight and other rules). The goal is to find the sparsest set (fewest terms, most important ones only) that still captures what the network learned. This simpler model acts like a translator: it can explain what the network discovered and also predict outside the training range, much like how operator learning (a method where you teach the computer one general rule that works across a whole family of problems) tries to capture general patterns rather than specific cases.
key_claims: Making models readable and making them work on new inputs are deeply connected: both depend on the network truly learning real physics, not just memorizing training data.
When physics-based learning tasks cannot create exhaustive data covering all conditions, models trained on limited data will predict poorly on new conditions.
The proposed method works both during design (to guide which physical rules matter) and after training (to explain a finished model).
You can extract understanding from a trained network by testing it carefully across the input space it learned on.
A small set of carefully chosen mathematical rules can often replace a huge network while staying readable.
This approach trades some raw prediction speed for the ability to read the rules and trust them against real physics.

important_terms.meaning: Methods that let humans understand why a model made a particular prediction by showing the reasoning in a way humans can read and judge.
Using a model to predict when the input falls outside the range of examples it trained on — the situation where most models guess badly.
An explanation of what a model learned applied after the model has already been built and trained, rather than built into the training itself.
A collection of different mathematical rules (each one sums effects across space or time using a kernel function and other operations) that can be mixed and matched to build a readable model.
A method that picks out only the most essential terms from a long list of candidates, throwing away the rest so the final model stays simple and readable.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects interpretability with operator learning (a method that teaches a single rule across a whole family of similar problems), Green's functions (mathematical solutions that show how effects spread and accumulate), and sparse regression techniques (picking the most important terms from many candidates).
It builds on Miles Cranmer's scientific-debt talk by offering a concrete path to write down equations that capture what a network actually learned.

It also addresses out-of-distribution reliability — why models trained on limited data fail on new conditions — a problem that repeats across surrogate models and digital twins (virtual copies of real systems used to test ideas safely).
practical_caution: The simpler model you extract only captures what the original network learned — it does not automatically describe the true physics. Before you trust this extracted model, you must check it against real measurements and compare it to known physics rules that must always hold true, so you catch cases where the network merely got lucky on its training data.
selected_evidence: Lack of interpretability and generalization are key challenges.
Out-of-distribution (OOD) inference.
Applied in either by-design or post-hoc fashions.
Library of integral equations.
Sparse regression similar to SINDy.
takeaway: Prediction of physical systems can be made readable by converting what a trained network learned into a sparse set of mathematical rules you can actually write down and understand. But that extracted model is only the network's guess — you must always verify it against real physics to confirm it is not just pattern-matching noise.
worked_example:
Illustrative: Neural network trained to predict fluid velocity from pressure field (surrogate for Navier-Stokes). Input: 256×256 pressure map; output: 256×256 velocity magnitude map. Network achieves 5% RMSE on test data. XAI analysis reveals: attention weights concentrate on 8 spatial patches (high-gradient regions near flow recirculation zones). Saliency map shows input gradients cluster at vortex cores. Integrated gradients attribute 72% of prediction error to pressure near boundaries (boundary conditions dominate prediction), 20% to interior pressure, 8% to spurious noise. This insight leads to redesigning loss function: give 3x weight to boundary residuals, reducing test error to 2% with same network architecture.

Scientific discovery: PDE coefficient learning. Network maps observational data → unknown PDE parameter λ (diffusivity). Feature importance analysis reveals that measurements far from boundary carry zero information for learning λ (interior is nearly smooth), forcing redesign of sensor placement.
deeper_mechanics: XAI taxonomy: (1) Attribution methods (gradients, saliency, integrated gradients, DeepLIFT): measure ∂output/∂input or cumulative effect. (2) Attention/occlusion: mask input regions, measure performance drop. (3) Feature importance: train surrogate interpretable model (decision tree, linear regression) on network outputs. (4) Uncertainty quantification: Bayesian neural networks provide prediction intervals showing where model is confident. For PDEs: use PDE residual as signal—high residual at some points signals model struggles there. Physics-informed explanations: if network predicts shock location, ask: does it align with predicted gradients of solution? Rationality checks: verify that learned operator respects physical symmetries (rotation, translation, scaling).
failure_boundary: Post-hoc explanations can mislead: saliency map says boundary matters most, but this doesn't mean the network learned correct boundary physics—may have simply memorized boundary values. Attribution methods are fragile: perturbing model slightly changes attributions significantly (adversarial attack on explanations). Attention weights are not causality: high attention on a region doesn't mean causally important—the network may be using it as a distractor (adversarial pattern). Out-of-distribution robustness unknown: XAI reveals behavior on training data distribution; no guarantee how model will explain predictions on OOD inputs. Computational cost: computing attributions (gradients×input + N forward passes for occlusion + expensive Bayesian sampling) can exceed training cost. Interpretation gap: even with XAI, determining why a feature matters physically requires domain expertise—automated interpretation without human-in-the-loop is unreliable.

title: Khalid Jawed: Reduced Order Modeling And Inverse Design Of Flexible Structures
speaker: Khalid Jawed
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. This talk focuses on bendy structures like cables and springs that twist and stretch a lot. Instead of tracking every tiny part of the structure (which takes forever), a learning program can learn a shortcut using far fewer variables—then use that shortcut to design what shape the structure should be or how to actuate it to hit a target configuration.
core_problem: When a structure bends and deforms a lot, the math gets complicated because the geometry itself changes, and the material behavior (how it resists bending) changes too. Simulating the full structure precisely, tracking every piece, costs a lot of computing time. And when you want to invent a new shape—deciding what design choices or what forces to apply—you have to try many possibilities. Each try needs a full simulation, and there are too many combinations to test by hand.
first_principles_model: A structure like a slinky has a shortcut: instead of tracking the whole twisting helix at every point, you can just track the position and twist of the helix's center line. A learning program trained on real simulations (precise 3D simulations of how a chain of rigid segments bends and stretches) can learn what forces show up at each segment in this reduced coordinate system. Then that learned force law lets you simulate the slinky's motion much faster. For a morphing structure (like a flat sheet that needs to fold into a 3D shape), a learning program learns to map a design choice—the pattern cut into the flat sheet—directly to what 3D shape it makes.
key_claims: Structures that bend and stretch a lot need simulators that handle the changing geometry and changing material resistance.
Learning programs can cut down the number of variables and make simulation vastly faster.
A slinky's deformation often comes down to tracking just its center helix axis, not every piece of the metal.
Learning programs can store the effective forces in the reduced coordinate system.
Precise simulations of chains of rigid segments (called Discrete Elastic Rods) provide the training data.
Designing morphing structures—going from a flat pattern to a target 3D shape—becomes much faster when a learning program learns that mapping directly.

important_terms.meaning: A structure that bends and stretches so much that the shape changes dramatically, and the forces resisting that motion change as the shape changes.
A compact description using far fewer numbers than tracking every piece; for a slinky, it might be just the center line instead of the full helix.
A learning program that copies how something changes continuously over time; instead of breaking time into steps, it learns a smooth rule for how things flow.
A precise method that simulates thin elastic structures (cables, springs, rope, or helices) by treating them as chains of stiff segments connected by joints that resist bending.
Working backward from a desired outcome to find what design choices or forces make it happen; instead of 'what shape does this design make,' it asks 'what design makes this shape.'

stanford_connections: This talk brings together reduced models (shortcuts for complex systems), learning programs that mimic differential equations (continuous-time rules), and inverse design (working backward from a goal) all in the real-world setting of bending and flexing structures.
It builds on manufacturing and materials research because how you cut and build a structure, what material you pick, and how it actually bends are all tangled together.
The best shortcuts come from understanding the physics first, not just trying to compress data—so good judgment about what matters saves a lot of work.
practical_caution: A shortcut coordinate only works when the structure moves the way it did during training. If the structure bends, twists, folds, or collapses in a new way not seen in training, the learned force law will give wrong answers. You need to check that your training covered all the deformations that will actually happen.
selected_evidence: Highly deformable structures... nonlinear geometry and nonlinear material.
Reduce the number of variables and speed up the simulation by orders of magnitude.
The axis of the helix is a reduced-order representation.
Neural ordinary differential equations.
Discrete Elastic Rods (DER).
takeaway: Getting inverse design right for bendy structures depends on picking the right reduced coordinates—ones that capture how the structure actually deforms. Once you have the right coordinates, learning programs can speed up the simulation by thousands of times and search through designs quickly.
worked_example:
Take a Slinky-like helical rod. The precise way to simulate it is Discrete Elastic Rods (DER): chop the rod into a chain of short cylinders connected at nodes, and track the position of every node plus the twist of every segment. For a long helix that is a lot of degrees of freedom, and every timestep you must recompute the bending, stretching, and twisting forces on all of them.

Jawed's shortcut collapses the 3D rod onto its center line: instead of the full helix, you track only the center line as a 2D beam, described by a small set of constitutive parameters he calls theta (bending stiffness, twisting stiffness, damping, and so on). A neural network is trained on precise 3D DER runs to predict the reduced forces in these coordinates. He reports the reduced beam model runs roughly 50 to 60 times faster than the full 3D discrete elastic rod simulation.

Inverse design then becomes tractable: for a target shape (say a soft robot or a bacteria-inspired flagellum that must coil a certain way), you search over theta or over the actuation, running the fast reduced model thousands of times instead of the 3D model. Because each forward evaluation is ~50-60x cheaper, a design sweep that would take hours of full DER finishes in minutes.
deeper_mechanics:
The precise model is Discrete Elastic Rods: the rod energy is the sum of stretching, bending, and twisting terms, E = E_stretch + E_bend + E_twist, and forces are f = -∂E/∂x on each node x plus a twist degree of freedom per segment. Jawed reduces a 3D rod to a 2D beam center line, so the state shrinks from (node positions + per-segment twist for the whole helix) to a beam described by constitutive parameters theta.

The learned piece is a force law: a neural network maps the reduced beam configuration to the effective forces that would have appeared in the full 3D DER, so the reduced simulation reproduces the 3D motion without resolving the helix. To use precise time integration he splits the second-order equation of motion into two first-order equations (position rate and velocity rate), then steps them forward. The theta parameters are not always known for a real object, so he back-calculates them: run the fast model, compare to observed shape, and adjust theta to fit — an inverse fit that closes the loop before design search begins.

Inverse design minimizes a mismatch J(theta or actuation) = ||shape_reduced - shape_target||^2 over the design variables, using the cheap reduced model for each trial shape. Because the reduced forces are differentiable, gradients dJ/d(design) can be taken through the model to steer the search rather than sampling blindly.
failure_boundary:
The shortcut assumes the rod's behavior is well described by its center line and a fixed set of theta parameters. That breaks when the real deformation is not center-line-dominated — sharp local kinks, contact and self-collision between coils, or buckling where the helix snaps into a new shape. The reduced beam has no coordinate for those events, so it will predict a smooth shape while the true rod jumps, and the design search will converge to a target the physical structure never reaches.

The learned force law is also only trained over the range of 3D DER runs it saw. Push the design outside that range — much larger curvature, a different aspect ratio than the beam assumption (length no longer much greater than width), or strong material nonlinearity — and the network extrapolates. The practitioner sees the reduced model and a fresh full 3D DER check disagree, and the back-fit theta stops being stable across shapes, which is the signal that the center-line reduction no longer holds.

title: Eleni Chatzi: Twinning And Model Discovery For Engineered Systems
speaker: Eleni Chatzi
one_sentence: This whole series is about teaching computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from data instead of only hand-written math. Here's one powerful way: build a living computer copy of a real structure (a bridge, a building, a plane wing), feed it measurements from sensors scattered around the real thing, and use that copy to spot damage, measure how bad it is, guess how long it will last, and decide what to fix. This talk is about why that works—and what you have to do to make it work right.
core_problem: Real structures—buildings, bridges, aircraft—are complicated, exposed to weather and heavy use, and change over time as materials wear. We have sensors that pick up vibrations and movements. These sensors can tell you 'something is wrong here', but they don't automatically tell you how bad the damage is, when the structure will fail, or what to fix. The sensors see only a few spots. The structure is everywhere. To make smart decisions about repairs, you need to connect what the sensors see to the whole structure, account for the fact that you don't know everything (the sensors have noise, materials vary), and imagine what happens under future stress.
first_principles_model: A digital twin is a computer copy of your real structure that stays up to date. Sensors feed real measurements into this copy. Physics equations (the rules describing how structures bend, how forces spread, how materials degrade) let the computer spread those few sensor measurements to places you can't measure and into the future. Model discovery means tuning that computer copy until it matches what the real structure does—by learning what damage it has, what the materials are actually like, or what its current state is. When the twin is built right, it tells you: is damage there? where exactly? how much? what will happen next? should we fix it now?
key_claims: Detecting damage is easiest; then you must locate it, measure how big it is, and finally predict when it will fail—each step is harder than the last.
Just fitting numbers to sensor data is not enough for the harder jobs, like measuring damage or predicting how long the structure lasts.
A real digital twin of a monitored structure must be built from physics equations, not just recorded data.
A good twin represents the structure as it actually is right now, including damage and wear—not just as the engineers designed it.
A twin can imagine how the structure will hold up under future loads and stresses if you give it the right information.
A useful twin should tell you what to do (fix it, inspect it, leave it alone), not just show you numbers.

important_terms.meaning: The job of placing sensors on a structure, reading their signals, and deciding whether there is damage, where it is, how bad it is, and when things might break.
A computer copy of a real structure that is constantly updated with fresh sensor readings and uses physics equations to understand the whole structure, not just the spots where sensors sit.
How much longer a structure or part can keep working safely before it wears out, breaks, or gets so weak that it has to be replaced.
Taking the few measurements you have from sensors and using math and physics to figure out what is happening everywhere in the structure—even the spots with no sensor.

Using the real measurements from sensors to tune a computer model, adjusting numbers for damage, material properties, or the structure's actual state until the model matches what the real thing is actually doing.

stanford_connections: This lecture brings together digital twins, damage detection, uncertainty accounting, and the job of learning what a structure's properties actually are—all aimed at making decisions about real structures in the field.
It moves forward from earlier talks about spot damage detection to the larger question: how do we predict what happens next and decide what to do about it?
It shares thinking with reduced-order models and fast surrogate models because twins need to run fast enough to be useful, while still respecting the physics of how structures actually work.
practical_caution: A screen showing sensor numbers is not a digital twin. To actually use a twin for repair decisions, you need the physics equations, you need to track your uncertainty (sensors wiggle, math isn't perfect), and you need to think about what could stress the structure in the future. Skip any of those, and your twin will steer you wrong.
selected_evidence: SHM comprises a hierarchy... detect, localize and quantify damage.
Offer a prognosis over the system's residual life.
Purely data-driven methods are found to be lacking.
Furnishing a digital twin of a monitored structure.
Augmented twin representations... anticipating performance under future stressors.
takeaway: A useful digital twin does three separate jobs. First, it figures out what the structure looks like right now (state estimation). Second, it uses physics to guess how it will behave (mechanics). Third, it tells a human what action to take—fix it now? check it later? (decision support). Sensors alone, without the other two jobs, don't give you a real twin.
worked_example: Digital twin of a damped pendulum: physical system generates position measurements y_obs(t), model is ∂²θ/∂t² + c·∂θ/∂t + sin(θ) = 0. PINN simultaneously learns the true state trajectory u(t) and parameter c. Training on 50 time measurements over [0, 10s], PINN recovers c ≈ 0.25±0.01 (true value 0.25) and predicts θ(t) beyond training window with <2% error. For engineered system (e.g., structural vibration sensor network with 100 nodes), sparse measurements at 10 sensor locations constrain model; PINN infers missing DOFs and locates damage (stiffness reduction) to within 5% of true location.
deeper_mechanics: Physics-informed discovery combines constraint enforcement with supervised learning: L_total = λ_data L_data + λ_physics L_physics where L_data = ||u_pred(t_i) - y_obs(t_i)||² measures fit to observations, L_physics = ||∂u/∂t - f(u,μ)||² enforces dynamics (μ are unknown parameters or system matrices). Automatic differentiation computes ∂u/∂t, ∂²u/∂t² via chain rule through neural network. Parameter discovery: if μ appears in loss via residual, gradient descent updates both network weights θ_net and parameters θ_μ simultaneously: ∂L/∂μ_j = ∫ (∂r/∂μ_j) · r dt. This couples model error with parameter error, allowing joint identification.
failure_boundary: If model structure is wrong (e.g., assuming linear damping c·ż when system is nonlinear frequency-dependent), parameter identification fails catastrophically; discovered c varies with amplitude and time. Sparse measurements (few sensors) combined with complex dynamics (high-dimensional state) leads to unobservable modes; PINN latent representation can fit noise while predictions outside sensor region are phantom. Long-term prediction (beyond training window) accumulates phase error; solutions that match training data closely can diverge exponentially if true system is chaotic or stiff. If measurement noise is high (>5% of signal), parameter uncertainty propagates and identified parameters become meaningless.

title: Lu Lu: Deep Neural Operators With Reliable Extrapolation
speaker: Lu Lu
one_sentence: This series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. One way to do that is to teach a neural network (a program with millions of little dials the computer tunes by trial and error until answers look right) to learn how to transform one kind of information into another—not just guess a number, but learn a whole process. This talk covers how to build these neural operators so they work well beyond the examples they learned from, especially when facing new physical conditions, different scales, or situations where multiple physical systems interact.
core_problem: Neural operators—programs that learn transformations between entire functions, not just single numbers—can master complex systems. But the trial-and-error learning process usually works best when the computer is guessing about data similar to what it saw during training. Real science has a different demand: predict what happens in completely new regimes—different physical conditions, different precision needs, new types of inputs, problems where multiple physical forces interfere—where a neural operator trained only on old examples might give terrible, confident-sounding wrong answers.
first_principles_model: DeepONet works by splitting the job into two parts: one program reads in the input signal and captures its essence; another program evaluates the answer at specific points; then you combine them. Related ideas build from there: some handle problems where multiple physical systems push on each other; some use proper orthogonal decomposition (a technique that keeps only the most important patterns and throws away noise), which compresses the data before learning; some take multiple inputs at once instead of one; some use patterns from Fourier analysis (breaking signals into repeating waves); some combine measurements that cost different amounts to get. To make predictions trustworthy outside the training range, you need to measure how hard that leap is and create checks that warn when the model might be failing or fix the prediction.
key_claims: Neural networks can learn transformations between entire functions—not just mappings from one number to another number.
DeepONet can learn transformations that represent both deterministic equations (rules with no randomness) and stochastic equations (rules with randomness built in).
DeepM&Mnet extends operator learning to problems where different physical systems interact and push on each other.
POD-DeepONet combines proper orthogonal decomposition (a method to find and keep only the most important patterns while discarding noise) with operator learning.
MIONet handles transformations with multiple inputs, while multifidelity DeepONet mixes data from sources that cost different amounts to collect and have different accuracies.
For science to trust these models, you need to measure how hard extrapolation is and design workflows that spot problems or improve predictions when the model ventures outside its training range.

important_terms.meaning: A neural network (a program with millions of dials tuned by trial and error) designed to learn transformations from one function to another, using one program that reads and understands the input and another program that produces the output at specific points.

A version of DeepONet that first uses proper orthogonal decomposition (a technique for keeping only the most important patterns in data and throwing away noise and clutter) before applying the operator network.
A neural operator network (a program that learns transformations between functions) built to handle transformations with multiple inputs instead of just one.
Training a model using data from different sources where some are cheap and approximate and others are expensive and accurate—mixing them together to train faster.
A way to measure or describe how hard it is for a model to make correct predictions when it runs into data or situations completely different from what it learned on.

stanford_connections: This talk adds to neural-operator discussions beyond Fourier neural operators, specifically diving into the DeepONet family of approaches.
It connects to Anima Anandkumar's operator talk through learning in function spaces, but focuses on the hard question: do predictions stay right when the model meets brand-new data?
It also ties to other talks in the series on mixing data at different price-points and precision-levels, multiscale problems, and situations where multiple physical systems interact.
practical_caution: Learning operators does not automatically solve the problem of extrapolation—predicting in new territory. A model can work perfectly on the exact functions it learned from but collapse when it meets new physics, new scales, or interactions it never saw during training.
selected_evidence: Deep operator network (DeepONet).
DeepM&Mnet for multiphysics problems.
POD-DeepONet.
Multifidelity DeepONet.
Quantify the extrapolation complexity.
takeaway: The real lesson is that neural operators should be tested not just on how well they remember known data, but on whether they get the right answer for entirely new types of problems.
worked_example:
Structural mechanics: cantilever plate with notch under traction. DeepONet trained on boundary conditions, predicts displacement field L² error ~2%. Advection-diffusion PDE with multiple inputs (boundary, diffusion coefficient, source): maps 3-input functions to solution, handles parametric variations.

Geologic carbon storage (multiphysics 3D): 24 snapshots over 30 years, coarse-fine spatial coupling (100m wells, million-meter far field). Multi-fidelity hybrid: pod-DeepONet reduces parameters 33M → 3M, GPU memory 16GB → 6GB, training 42h → 12h while maintaining accuracy R²=0.99. Predicts unseen time snapshots t=2,4,6 (trained only on t=1,3,5,7) by conditioning on temporal coordinate.

Waveform inversion seismic: 2D acoustic domain, 5 source locations, various frequencies. Predicts subsurface velocity from noisy pressure records. Tests: Gaussian noise +50%, missing traces 50% dropped, source noise in wavelet—DeepONet robust across all; baseline networks fail at noise levels >20%.
deeper_mechanics:
Multiple-input DeepONet (μ-net): m branch networks {φ_i} each processes one input function v_i, concatenate outputs, trunk network ψ(y) encodes query location y. Merge: G(y)=Σ_k[⊙_{i=1}^m φ_i(v_i)]·ψ_k(y) (element-wise product then sum reduces tensor explosion). Fourier-μ-net: replace element-wise merge with Fourier transform layer + 2D/3D UNet to preserve spatial structure while reducing parameters. Temporal extension: add time t as additional trunk input, condition solution continuity over time.

Multi-fidelity: cascade two DeepOnets: low-fidelity G_lo trains on 10k samples, high-fidelity G_hi learns correction Δ = G_hi - G_lo using few high-quality samples (<5k) and penalizes correlation mismatch.
failure_boundary: Extrapolation minus (smoother training distribution, rougher test) succeeds; extrapolation plus (complex training, smooth test) fails catastrophically due to spectral bias. Wasserstein-2 distance between training and test function spaces predicts error magnitude in log-log scaling—requires pre-computed reference for new problem class. Cannot handle phase transitions or regime switches (e.g., laminar-turbulent, nucleation) without separate operator per regime. Stochastic noise in source signal amplifies through wave propagation—architecture sensitive to input noise distribution. Memory scaling: m-input problems still require m branch forward passes; not amortized if m >> 1.

title: Krishna Garikipati: Fokker-Planck Inverse Reinforcement Learning
speaker: Krishna Garikipati
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. In biology and physics, we often see an agent or system move through a sequence of states—a cancer cell growing, an animal foraging—and want to figure out what it 'wants' (its goal, or reward) and what rules it obeys. This talk tackles the harder problem: when neither the goal nor the rules are known, can we infer both at once from watching the system move, using the math of random motion and probability spread?
core_problem: Most methods that try to infer why an agent behaves a certain way (what goal it is trying to reach) assume someone already told them the rules—how states change, how actions lead to new states. But in real science and biology, those rules are often hidden. Cancer cells, bacteria, animals: we see what they do but not the instruction manual. This talk asks: what if we have to figure out both the hidden goal and the hidden rules at the same time from just watching?
first_principles_model: Think of a system as a jar of colored sand grains. Each grain is in some state (position, age, whatever matters). At each step, each grain can take an action or get pushed by randomness, and most grains spread out into new states. We can track the odds: what fraction of grains are in each state at each time? A Fokker-Planck equation (a rule that says how the spreading happens moment by moment) describes those odds. The lecture shows that this spreading math and the decision-making model (called an MDP: a way to describe choices with states, actions, odds of where you land, and what reward you get) can be made mathematically the same. That match is the key: it lets us run a fitting procedure (adjust the invisible goal and invisible rules over and over until they predict the observed trajectories well) that finds both the goal and the rules at once.
key_claims: You can work backward from observed motion to find the goal (reward) an agent is trying to reach.
Most existing methods assume the transition rules are already known or given.
When both the goal and the rules are unknown, the problem gets much harder.
Random motion in a system (like probability spreading) can be described by the Fokker-Planck equation.
This equation and decision-making models (MDPs) have the same mathematical structure underneath.
Using that match, you can infer both the transition rules and the reward from just watching what happens.

important_terms.meaning: Looking at what an agent actually does and asking: what goal or reward is it trying to reach? Then guessing the goal from the actions.

A model that describes choice-making: a system has states (situations), actions (choices), odds of moving to the next state, rewards for being in states or taking actions, and decision rules for picking actions.
A rule that says how the spread of likely locations (the probability of being in each state) changes moment by moment in a system with random motion.
The rule that says: if you are in this state and take this action, what are the odds of ending up in each possible next state?
Finding the hidden rules of a system by adjusting guesses repeatedly to minimize how wrong they are, using calculus-based weak forms of the equations.

stanford_connections: This lecture brings together stochastic dynamics (random systems that change over time), inverse problems (working backward from what you observe to find hidden causes), and reinforcement learning (learning to choose actions) in a setting driven by real physics and biology.
It connects with other talks in this series on Fokker-Planck equations, SDEs (rules with randomness), and stochastic model reduction.
It shows a recurring theme: when a problem seems impossible because too many answers fit the data, adding physics structure can cut down the ambiguity and make learning work.
practical_caution: Here is the trap: many different goals and many different rule-sets can all lead to the same behavior. A person might share because they like others or because they fear punishment—same action, different motives. When the lab adds physics rules that narrow down which answers make sense, that helps. But we still have to check: does the inferred goal match what we know about the real system from other experiments? Do not assume the math gave us the true answer just because it fits the trajectories.
selected_evidence: Inverse Reinforcement Learning... revealing the rationale underlying the behavior of autonomous agents.
Estimate the unknown reward function... from observed agent trajectories.
IRL needs a transition function.
Fokker-Planck (FP) equation.
Simultaneously infer the transition and reward functions using only observed trajectories.
takeaway: To understand why something moves the way it does, you need two things: the goal (what reward it gets) and the rules (how states change). The Fokker-Planck equation is the math for how random motion spreads. By connecting that spreading math to decision-making, the method lets us infer the hidden goal and hidden rules together from watching alone.
worked_example: Breast cancer cells in scratch assay show heterogeneous chemotaxis: K-means clustering reveals 3 populations from ~300 cells each. Cluster 0 moves leftward (toward chemoattractant), Cluster 1 moves rightward (against gradient), Cluster 2 ambivalent. Fokker-Planck inference over velocity states yields potential functions ψ_i and diffusivities D_i for each group. Using inverse Bellman equation, reward structure is recovered: leftward+upward yields high reward (low AKT, high ERK). Biologist validation: chemical knockdown of ERK reduces velocity 50%, knockdown of AKT increases velocity 10%—exactly matching IRL prediction.
deeper_mechanics: Fokker-Planck equation ∂ρ/∂t = -∇·(ρ∇ψ) + D∇²ρ governs probability density evolution. Potential ψ encodes drift; diffusivity D represents noise. Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) theory: steady state ρ* ∝ exp(-ψ/D) minimizes free energy F = ∫ρψ + D∫ρ log ρ. In Markov decision process, state-action value Q(s,a) satisfies Bellman optimality; conjecture identifies Q ↔ ψ structurally. Policy π(a|s) ∝ exp(Q(s,a)/D) matches Boltzmann distribution. Weak-form system identification fits ψ as polynomial in state/action coordinates; transition probabilities follow from FP solution; inverse Bellman recovers reward R = ∇·(∇ψ) ∘ (dynamics) avoiding backpropagation.
failure_boundary: Fokker-Planck assumes continuous, quasi-stationary states; discrete populations (cell clusters) become sparse and mean-field breaks. Inferring ψ from <300 cells per group on 20×20 grid (400 states) requires strong regularization; noisy/missing data amplifies aliasing. Moving to 4D state-action space explodes grid size; 20^4 = 160K nodes with inverse RL becomes 4–24 CPU-hours even with GPU acceleration. Assumption of Gaussian diffusivity D (isotropic) fails if cells exhibit directional persistence or velocity-dependent drag. Polynomial basis for ψ captures only smooth potentials; sharp energy barriers or multi-modal distributions aren't represented. Cell division/death (reaction terms) treated as unobserved changes in population size—not modeled.

title: Alice Cicirello: Integrating Physics Knowledge In Machine Learning Strategies
speaker: Alice Cicirello
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. One popular approach is to feed physics knowledge into that learning at four different points: the data you collect, the shape of the learning program itself, how you train it, and a separate model that catches where your physics rules fall short. This talk uses friction-force identification to show how all four work together.
core_problem: Learning programs trained only on data often fail when faced with new situations, make predictions that break physics (like a ball falling upward), and struggle when you have few measurements or little data. Real engineering problems give you some physics knowledge—some equations you know, some you don't—along with measurements that are noisy and scarce. The question is: where and how should you inject physics knowledge into your learning process?
first_principles_model: Physics knowledge can enter learning at four places. Observational bias shapes the data by choosing what to measure or creating artificial measurements that physics tells you matter. Inductive bias builds physics rules, symmetries, or conservation laws directly into how the learning program is structured. Learning bias changes the training process itself—what cost the program tries to minimize, rules it absolutely cannot break, or how it searches for the best answer. Discrepancy bias adds a separate program that catches the gap between your partial physics equations and what you actually see. Friction identification shows how finding which forces matter most and using a method that represents uncertainty in predictions can use all four types together.
key_claims: Physics knowledge improves prediction on new situations when you have small to medium amounts of training data, and can enforce that predictions respect physics even with lots of data.
Training only on data without physics can hide biases in your data and produce impossible predictions.
You can control data bias by collecting measurements through physics-guided choices or creating new artificial examples that physics tells you should exist.

You can embed prior knowledge such as boundaries, conservation laws (energy or momentum never disappears), and symmetries (unchanged behavior under transformations) directly into the program's structure.
You can change the training process: the cost you minimize, hard rules the program must follow, or the algorithm you use to find the best answer.
You can use partial physics knowledge or fix known gaps between simplified equations and real data, as shown through friction-force identification.

important_terms.meaning: Physics-informed choices about which data to measure, which to create artificially, or which to emphasize when training a learning program.
A built-in assumption or constraint that the learning program carries from the start, woven into its structure or how it represents information.
Physics information introduced through the cost function (what you minimize), hard rules the program must satisfy, or the search method itself.
A separate program trained to catch the gap between an imperfect physics model and real observations.
Finding friction forces or friction rules in a moving system from data and physics constraints, when friction is the main unknown quantity.

stanford_connections: This lecture gives a clear taxonomy that unifies earlier talks on physics-informed learning, physics-guided learning, and physics-enhanced learning.

It connects to physics-informed neural networks (learning programs that include physics rules), finding the few most important forces in a system, learning methods with physics starting-points, and models that catch gaps between simplified physics and real data.
It gives precise language for deciding where physics should enter a program, moving past loose advice to simply add physics.
practical_caution: Adding physics knowledge carelessly can fail or give wrong answers. For example, adding a soft penalty (a gentle nudge in the cost function) may not work when a physical law must never be broken—you need a hard constraint built into the structure itself.
selected_evidence: Four different biases... observational, inductive, learning, and discrepancy.
Poor generalization performance and extrapolation.
Physically inconsistent or impossible prediction.
Friction forces in a dynamical system.
Sparse system identification... Gaussian Processes.
takeaway: Physics can enter learning at four points: the data, the program's structure, how you train it, and the discrepancy model. Good physics-informed learning chooses where to insert physics deliberately rather than piling it in everywhere.
worked_example: Learning fluid dynamics closure: ∂u/∂t + u·∇u + ∇p = ν∇²u + g_θ(u,x,t), where g_θ is a neural network learning unresolved stress. Train on LES data (coarse grid 32³, true solution from 512³ DNS at high cost). Loss: ||∂u_coarse/∂t + u_coarse·∇u_coarse + ∇p_coarse - ν∇²u_coarse - g_θ||^2. Regularization: add physics constraints (e.g., energy conservation, positivity of eigenvalues).
deeper_mechanics: Physics-informed regularization penalizes violations: L_total = L_data + λ₁ L_conservation + λ₂ L_positivity. Conservation loss: integral of energy dissipation must match ∫(g_θ · u) dV. Positivity: eigenvalues of stress tensor must lie in physical cone. Symbolic regression or graph neural networks learn sparse combinations of invariants (||∇u||, tr(∇u⊗∇u), etc.).
failure_boundary: Regularization weights (λ₁, λ₂) are problem-dependent tuning parameters; wrong choice prioritizes one constraint over accuracy. Graph/symbolic methods scale poorly in high-dimensional parameter spaces (>20 degrees of freedom). Extrapolation beyond training Reynolds number or geometry fails; NN lacks generalization.

title: Jinlong Wu: Data-Driven Closure Modeling Using Derivative-Free Kalman Methods
speaker: Jinlong Wu
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of hand-written math. When you can't track every tiny detail—like every swirl in turbulent air or every water droplet in a cloud—you need a stand-in that says what those small, invisible details do to the big patterns you can see. This talk shows one way to learn that stand-in from real measurements: a method that updates guesses by running many parallel copies of your system and comparing them to what actually happened, without needing to compute how sensitive your answer is to each dial you turn.
core_problem: Real systems like turbulent flows and clouds have far too many tiny parts to track at once. Engineers handle this by writing a stand-in—a description that says what all those untracked small parts do to the big-scale flow you can see. Making a good stand-in is hard: the traditional hand-built ones miss real physics, need to be tuned differently for each case, and learning from data gets even harder when your measurements are indirect, scattered, or noisy.
first_principles_model: A stand-in takes what you can observe directly—the large-scale variables—and predicts what the unobserved small-scale motion does to them. One approach treats the unknown parts of the stand-in as hidden pieces and updates them by using many parallel copies of your system (ensemble-based assimilation, meaning you blend many estimates together to gradually match the real data). This works without ever computing how sensitive the answer is to each input, so you can learn stand-ins from measurements that don't directly show what you want to learn.
