It even extends to richer stand-ins that include randomness, and to picking out which terms in an equation actually matter.
key_claims: Stand-ins are essential in complex systems because simulating every tiny motion is impossible.
Current stand-ins are not good enough, partly because they can't capture enough detail and partly because hand-tuning each one for a new case is impractical.
Methods that skip computing sensitivities can learn stand-ins even from measurements that don't directly show stand-in behavior.
This approach works for deterministic stand-ins.
The same method also picks out which terms in the equations actually matter (sparse identification).
Methods that skip computing sensitivities can learn stand-ins that include randomness, from indirect measurements.

important_terms.meaning: A description of how the small-scale motion you can't track affects the large-scale motion you can see. Think of it as a stand-in that captures the effect of all those invisible details.

A way to update estimates by running many parallel copies of your system and comparing all of them to real data, gradually shifting them until they match—without ever computing how sensitive each answer is to each input dial.
Measurements of one thing that you use to infer something else you can't measure directly—like measuring wind speed at one height to understand turbulence you can't see.
Learning which terms in an equation or stand-in are active (matter) and which can be ignored, so you end up with a simple, understandable description.
A stand-in that includes randomness—describing not just the average effect of small-scale motion, but its unpredictable part too.

stanford_connections: This lecture builds on closure ideas from large-eddy simulation (watching only the big swirls and modeling what the tiny ones do), reduced-order models (describing a complex system with fewer moving parts), and structure-preserving stand-ins discussed earlier in the seminar.

It uses data assimilation—the practice of blending real measurements with a model to gradually correct it—in the same way that Kalman filters do, but to learn stand-in parameters instead of just estimating current state.
It connects to SINDy and sparse system identification, which are methods to learn simple, interpretable equations and stand-ins directly from data.
practical_caution: Skipping the derivative calculations saves work, but it doesn't solve the deeper problem of identifiability: if your measurements are weak or indirect, many completely different stand-ins might fit the data equally well. You need to check whether the learned model is truly the only one that works.
selected_evidence: Closure problems are critical in predicting complex dynamical systems.
Derivative-free Kalman methods.
Learn closure models from indirect and limited amount of data.
Sparse identification of dynamical systems.
Learning of stochastic closures.
takeaway: At heart, learning a stand-in is just inference from incomplete information. Methods based on Kalman's approach give you a way to do that inference without computing sensitivities—useful when your data never directly show the stand-ins you're trying to learn.
worked_example: Turbulence closure modeling: flow over periodic hills with Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes; sparse measurement of resolved velocity field to estimate full-field Reynolds stress discrepancy. Prior distribution on stress difference via Gaussian process with Karhunen-Loève basis function expansion. Posterior velocity distribution achieves much better agreement with DNS (high-fidelity simulation) in recirculation regions. L1 error of radial distribution function (test metric not used in training) demonstrates viability. Example shows shift from scattered prior velocity profiles to concentrated posterior profiles matching ground truth.
deeper_mechanics: Ensemble Kalman inversion (EKI) iterative update formula: for ensemble index j and EKI step m, normalize data mismatch (difference between forward map output and observations) using covariance in data space and parameter space, project normalized mismatch back to parameter space via cross-covariance matrix to adjust parameter estimates. Prior constructed as Gaussian random field with covariance parameterized by field-varying variance (sigma as function of spatial coordinates). Basis functions from Karhunen-Loève expansion allow linear combination to parametrize closure model. Sparse, indirect observation data (point velocity measurements) drive Bayesian inference toward posterior parameter distribution.
failure_boundary: Model form error: basis function restrictions may not span true closure model space, leading to persistent discrepancy between optimal posterior and DNS truth despite improved fit. Sparsity of spatial measurements affects performance; dense measurements in fringe/recirculation regions needed for accurate parameter recovery. Computational cost of matrix inversion scales with data space dimension; mitigation via localization (threshold long-range covariances, keep sparse matrix structure). Assumption that closure term depends only on spatial coordinates (not velocity history) limits scope; extension to velocity-dependent formulations mentioned but more complex.

title: Christopher Rackauckas: Generalizing SciML And Differentiable Simulation Beyond Continuous Models
speaker: Christopher Rackauckas
organization: JuliaHub / Pumas AI / MIT Julia Lab
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from data instead of only using hand-written math. This talk asks: what if we go beyond smooth-change rules and teach computers to simulate sudden jumps, randomness, many independent actors, and ways to estimate hidden states? The key idea is that learning programs should be able to tune themselves inside any kind of simulator—not just the smooth-change kinds—by computing which dials to nudge and by how much.
core_problem: Most machine learning work on science has focused on smooth-change rules (rules saying how things change moment to moment or place to place, where the changes happen gradually). Real scientific simulation, though, also has sudden changes (like a ball bouncing or a switch flipping), random outcomes (like quantum dice rolls or weather fluctuations), actors following rules (people or particles acting independently), ways to guess hidden states from messy observations, and mixed systems combining random and smooth parts. When you try to compute which dials to nudge in these kinds of simulators to match real data, the math gets much messier than for smooth rules—different tricks are needed.
first_principles_model: Differentiable simulation means building a simulator that can learn: you swap unknown parts inside it with learning programs (or other adjustable dials) and compute gradients—the directions to nudge those dials to make the simulation match observed data better. For simulators with smooth rules, this is manageable. For simulators with randomness, sudden jumps, discrete choices, or behaviors sensitive to tiny changes in starting conditions, computing these nudge-directions gets harder and trickier. You have to track how changes flow through randomness, events that happen at specific instants, discrete switches, and algorithms that guess hidden states.
key_claims: Machine learning for science has successfully used smooth-change rules (ordinary and partial differential equations) inside learning programs through differentiable simulation.
Real scientific simulation also includes sudden-jump processes (mixing random drift with discrete events), many independent actors following rules, and other non-smooth forms.
Differentiable simulation can extend to simulators that are chaotic (tiny changes in starting conditions cause huge differences) and stochastic (involving randomness).
Methods for guessing hidden states from data and independent-actor models need special ways to compute nudge-directions that do not work for smooth equations.
Inverse problems (figuring out unknown numbers from observations) sometimes need to compute nudge-directions even through the algorithms that explore probability distributions.
As this idea spreads to new domains, numerical stability and how code is written become central problems.

important_terms.meaning: A simulator built so you can compute how to adjust any unknown dials inside it to make its predictions match observed data better—by calculating nudge-directions (gradients) through the whole chain of calculations.
A process that mixes random drift (smooth, random wandering) with sudden discrete jumps (discrete events happening at specific times).
A simulator of many independent actors, each following their own local rules, creating collective behavior that emerges from all their interactions.
A method for guessing hidden states in a random system: maintain many sample paths and update which ones look right as new observations arrive.
Treating algorithms that explore probability distributions in a way that allows nudge-directions to flow backward through them for learning.

stanford_connections: This lecture extends the automatic-nudge-direction (automatic differentiation) and learning-through-code (differentiable programming) ideas from earlier talks.
It connects to learning from rewards (inverse reinforcement learning), random generative simulators, and inverse problems because all need computing nudge-directions through unusual kinds of loops.
It also gives a practical view: making machine learning for science work generally, not only for smooth-change rules.
practical_caution: Computing nudge-directions through a simulator with randomness or sudden jumps can give wrong answers, blow up numerically (numbers become huge or collapse), or depend on how you build the code. You must pick a method to compute nudge-directions that actually matches what you are trying to improve.
selected_evidence: Generalizing scientific learning and differentiable simulation beyond continuous models.
Jump diffusions, agent-based models.
Differentiating stochastic simulations like particle filters.
Differentiation of Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods.
Numerical stability issues, implementation issues.
takeaway: The foundational insight is that machine learning for science must compute nudge-directions through any kind of scientific simulator, not only smooth-change solvers.
worked_example: Illustrative example: guided manifold learning on porous media flow. Training set of 50-200 simulations with varying permeability fields (lognormal, correlated). Deep network learns low-dimensional latent space where solutions concentrate. Prediction speedup 10-50x on unseen permeability realizations. Compared to linear POD, nonlinear manifold captures tensor-train decomposition structure of heterogeneous problems.
deeper_mechanics: Manifold linearization: decompose solution u = u_lin + δu where u_lin satisfies linearized PDE around reference parameter. Deep network learns δu in low-dim space. Jointly optimize reference state and manifold basis to minimize prediction error across parameter range. For parabolic PDEs (diffusion-dominated), manifold typically 5-20 dimensional despite 1000+ DOF discretization. Guided means incorporating physics constraints: enforce boundary conditions strongly in loss, penalize non-physical solutions.
failure_boundary: Method fails when nonlinearity dominates over linear component (high Rayleigh number, strong convection). Manifold assumption breaks at bifurcation points. Extrapolation beyond training parameter range unreliable. Ill-posedness if reference state poorly chosen.

title: Elnaz Rezaian: Data-Driven Balancing Transformation For Predictive Model Order Reduction
speaker: Elnaz Rezaian
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how real things behave by learning from examples instead of only hand-written rules. This talk focuses on a specific trick: when you have a system with many levers you can pull (inputs) and many readouts you can see (outputs), how do you build a smaller, faster prediction that still tracks which inputs steer the system and which outputs show what's happening — and how wrong could your small model be? A method called balanced truncation answers this by keeping the parts of a system that matter for control and seeing what happens, then throwing away the rest.
core_problem: Small, fast models are great for real engineering — but they often fail because they miss how inputs wire to outputs, or they give no promise about how far off they'll be. Balanced truncation gives you a mathematical guarantee of accuracy, but building it the straightforward way, or building it from real data you measure, gets slow when you have many inputs and many outputs.
first_principles_model: Balanced truncation works by finding which internal states the system can reach from the inputs (reachability: which directions can you steer the system?), which internal states show up in the outputs (observability: what can you see in the readouts?), then erasing states that are neither reachable nor observable. Data-driven versions like ERA build small models by watching how the system reacts to sharp input pulses. The result is a model tuned specifically for control and carries mathematical promises about its error, but to scale it up when you have many inputs and outputs, you need tricks: tangential interpolation (probe the system in specially chosen directions), output decomposition (split the readouts into smaller independent chunks), and gappy POD-style approximations (fill in measurements you don't have).
key_claims: Balanced truncation comes from control theory and is built exactly for steering systems.

Data-driven balancing uses measured reachability and observability matrices (numbers that capture which directions the system can reach and which show up in outputs, built from real data) and minimum realization theory (finding the smallest model that matches what you measured).
Mathematical error bounds make balanced models trustworthy for real predictions.
The eigensystem realization algorithm is a direct, data-driven path to balanced truncation.
ERA predicts well on stiff fast-burning chemical flows and sound-driven systems.
Many input-output channels mean more computation, so you need tangential interpolation, output decomposition, and gappy POD.

important_terms.meaning: A model reduction method that erases internal states the system barely reaches from its inputs and barely shows in its outputs, keeping only the states that matter for steering and observing.
A table of numbers that measures how reachable or observable a dynamical system is, based on the rules that govern how it moves.
A data-driven method that builds a small model by analyzing measured impulse responses (how the system reacts to sharp input pulses) to find the smallest equivalent model.
A single number in the sequence of impulse-response values; the full sequence lets you rebuild how the system transforms inputs into outputs.
A method to reconstruct the full behavior of a field from measurements that are scattered or incomplete, using patterns learned from complete snapshots.

stanford_connections: This lecture adds a control-theory view of small models to the broader model reduction thread.
It connects to predictive models, reverse engineering, and digital twins because error bounds are needed before you can trust the model in the real world.
It also builds on CUR and adaptive ROM talks by prioritizing input-output balance instead of compressing only which states vibrate the most.
practical_caution: A small model can still mislead you if it erases states that matter for outputs or that your control actually needs to move. Always reduce the model for the specific input-output task you care about, not just to remove the states with the least energy.
selected_evidence: Balanced truncation and data-driven variations.
Empirical system Gramians.
Theoretical error bounds.
Eigensystem realization algorithm (ERA).
Gappy POD approach to address this bottleneck.
takeaway: The core lesson is that small predictive models should protect what the system can be steered toward and what you can see in the readouts, not just which parts wiggle the most.
worked_example: One-dimensional reacting flow with species transport and reaction (Navier-Stokes + species equations) was discretized to yield ~200 states. A unit impulse at the inflow excited the system; impulse response snapshots (77 pressure, 50 temperature, 19 species modes) captured 99.99% of input-output energy in ~150 Hankel matrix rows. The resulting era ROM used 2 orders of magnitude larger timesteps than the full model before becoming unstable, enabling fast predictive simulation. Offline cost (impulse runs + matrix operations) completed in under an hour; online evaluation was 100× faster than full-order CFD.
deeper_mechanics: Eigensystem realization algorithm (era) constructs the Hankel matrix H from impulse responses; shifted Hankel H' groups the same data one timestep forward. SVD gives H = U Σ V^T; the ROM state-space matrices emerge as A = U^-1 U_shift, B = sqrt(Sigma) V^T[1,:], C = U[1,:] sqrt(Sigma). No intrusive access to system matrices required—pure data-driven. Tangential interpolation projects onto low-dimensional input/output subspaces, reducing computational cost by 1.7×; output domain decomposition runs separate (finer-resolution) ROMs on critical regions (sharp gradients at boundaries).
failure_boundary: Era demands impulse responses that capture transients; if the system has lightly damped oscillatory modes with long decay times, gathering sufficient snapshots becomes expensive. For unstable systems or those near bifurcation points, reachability and observability gramians are ill-conditioned, and truncation arbitrarily selects which modes to keep. Multi-input multi-output systems with many boundary conditions multiply the training burden (one impulse per input channel). Nonlinear systems require linearization about nominal states, so the ROM is valid only locally; far from linearization points, accuracy degrades rapidly.

title: Michael Glinsky: A Physics-Based ROM Capturing The Topology Of Dynamical Manifolds
speaker: Michael E. Glinsky
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from data instead of only using hand-written math rules. This talk focuses on one problem: when you make a fast computer copy (called a reduced model) of something expensive to simulate, like a pulsed power experiment squashing metal at extreme temperatures, the copy might look right at first but miss the actual shape and structure of how the system changes over time — and this talk shows a method inspired by scattering, renormalization, and geometry that tries to capture that shape.
core_problem: High-energy-density physics simulations like pulsed power liner implosions are expensive and highly nonlinear. Engineers need fast computer copies (reduced models that approximate expensive simulations) to do practical work. But if you build a fast model by just keeping track of numbers describing the system at each moment, you might miss something crucial: the actual geometric shape of how the system evolves — how it twists, curves, and stays confined to a lower-dimensional surface. A model that misses this shape will fail in realistic scenarios because it doesn't actually respect how the physics flows.
first_principles_model: The proposed Heisenberg Scattering Transformation works in layers. First, it applies a structured deep convolutional transform (a program that repeatedly filters the data at many different scales, building stable hierarchical layers) inspired by Mallat's scattering transform (a method that breaks down data by filtering at smaller and smaller scales, much like zoom levels on a map, to find stable patterns). Second, it uses a Hamiltonian generating functional (a physics-based mathematical tool that describes exactly how a system evolves from one moment to the next). Together, these project the dynamics into a renormalization or scattering-matrix basis (a coordinate system where the structure of physics at different scales — from tiny to large — appears as natural and separate features). In this special coordinate system, the dynamics stay confined to a low-dimensional complex linear subspace (a flat space with fewer directions). PCA (a statistical method that finds the most important directions in data) identifies this subspace, and then a neural network with encoder and decoder parts quantifies the shape through an analytic function (a smooth, well-behaved mathematical function where calculus works).
key_claims: The approach takes inspiration from Mallat's scattering transform (a method that breaks data into stable layers by repeated filtering at different scales, much like zoom levels on a map) and a Hamiltonian view of how physics evolves (a description that tells you how the system moves from one state to the next).

A logarithmic generating functional of the Hamiltonian (a physics-based mathematical tool derived from the energy and structure of the system) acts on the system state or the probability distribution describing the system.
The transform projects dynamics onto a renormalization or scattering-matrix basis (coordinates where the structure of physics at tiny, medium, and large scales appears naturally and separately).
PCA (a statistical method that finds the most important directions in data) identifies the low-dimensional flat space that holds the dynamics.

The shape of how the system evolves is quantified using a neural network with encoder and decoder parts that approximates an analytic function (a smooth, well-behaved mathematical function) on that subspace.
The method is tested as a fast computer copy for 2D pulsed power liner implosions, including MagLIF (Magnetized Liner Inertial Fusion).

important_terms.meaning: A method that breaks down data by repeatedly filtering at different scales — like looking at a map zoomed out, then zoomed in, then zoomed in more — to build stable patterns that don't change if you wiggle the data a little.
This talk's method: a scattering transformation combined with physics rules (Hamiltonian dynamics) to represent how a system evolves in a coordinate system where scales of physics appear naturally.
A coordinate system where the structure of physics at different scales — tiny details, medium-range effects, and large-scale trends — shows up as separate, natural features.
The actual geometric shape of the low-dimensional surface where the system's motion is confined: how it twists, curves, folds, and changes — not just which points are on it, but the shape itself.
Magnetized Liner Inertial Fusion: an experiment where a metal cylinder with a magnetic field implodes at extreme speed and temperature to squeeze fuel and trigger fusion.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects finding low-dimensional representations of data (manifold learning), building fast approximations of expensive simulations (reduced models), the geometry of systems (topology), and physics-based methods for transforming data.

It extends earlier work on mapping how dynamics change and the geometry of probability distributions by showing that the reduced-dimensional space has real geometric shape and structure, not just arbitrary coordinates.

It also links to creating fast computer copies of high-energy-density physics simulations (surrogate models), where preserving the actual geometric structure is essential for predictions to stay accurate.
practical_caution: Transforms that try to preserve the geometric shape of how systems evolve work only when matched carefully to the actual physics. If the transform structure you assume does not match the real physics, the model can preserve the wrong features and fail when you try to use it in realistic scenarios.
selected_evidence: Physics-based reduced order model capturing the topology of dynamic manifolds.
Scattering Transformation.
Renormalization Basis.
Principal Component Analysis.
Fast surrogate model for 2D pulsed power liner implosions (MagLIF).
takeaway: When you build a fast computer copy of an expensive simulation, you cannot just minimize how far your copy is from the original (the projection error). Some systems force you to also preserve the actual geometric shape of how dynamics live — the surface they flow on, and the scale structure within it. Models that ignore this shape miss real physics.
worked_example:
The team ran 539 2D Rayleigh-Taylor instability simulations in magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) on the Z machine at Sandia, generating 100,000 images consuming 200,000 core-hours over two weeks of computation. They trained a workflow consisting of multi-scale transformation (MST), principal component analysis (PCA), and a 15-layer multi-layer perceptron on this dataset. Training took 16 GPU-hours for the MST step, one day for wavelet-phase harmonic decomposition, but only 1 core-second to find principal components and 20 core-seconds to train the MLP. The resulting surrogate model executed in a tenth of a core-second to simulate what took 360 core-hours to compute directly—a 3.6-million-fold speedup.

The surrogate accurately captured density and magnetic field evolution at three characteristic times (initial, near bang-time, and post-expansion), and preserved correlation structure between the two fields. Feature importance analysis showed time was most critical (obviously), liner aspect ratio determined acceleration rate, and perturbation angle mattered because energy inverse-cascades to m=2 mode, but magnetic fields m=5 and m=4 contributed negligibly.
deeper_mechanics:
The method builds a complex Hamiltonian in latent space by first applying a logarithmic generating functional transformation (related to quantum field theory's S-matrix). The transformed variables live in a renormalization basis where motion projects onto a low-dimensional attracting manifold. A rectified linear unit (ReLU) activation is justified because it approximates the modulus of complex analytic functions: for small arguments x, log(1+x) ≈ x (identity), and for large x, log(1+x) → ln(|x|) (logarithm of modulus). This ensures convergence of iterative applications.

The reduced system dynamics satisfy a canonical transformation: motion in the reduced coordinates (P,Q) corresponds to solving the Hamilton-Jacobi equation where the solution W gives the generator of this canonical transformation. The topology is captured by poles and branch cuts of the complex Hamiltonian—these singularities correspond to homology classes (topological obstructions that distinguish different types of stable states). The neural network learns a piecewise-linear approximation to this analytic Hamiltonian, with ReLU nodes positioned at singularities.
failure_boundary: The method requires principal component analysis on very high-dimensional fields (2500+ dimensions for 50×50 grids with 2 fields), and PCA becomes numerically unstable if the data matrix is rank-deficient or nearly singular. When the true manifold has complex topology (multiple topological obstructions from different homology classes), a finite number of singularities in the neural network may not suffice to reproduce all topological features. For 3D turbulence, the energy cascade direction reverses (energy flows small-to-large scales instead of large-to-small), fundamentally changing the attractor topology; methods validated on 2D flows may fail entirely in 3D. Extrapolation to parameter regimes far from training data becomes unreliable because the neural network's piecewise-linear structure cannot automatically discover new singularities. Additionally, L2 regularization (commonly used in neural networks) can inadvertently smooth out or regularize away the very singularities that encode important physics.

title: Mengwu Guo: Probabilistic Methods for Data-Driven Reduced-Order Modeling
speaker: Mengwu Guo
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples. This talk focuses on models that run fast AND tell you how confident they are: if you run a simulation many times with different starting conditions, you want it quick — but you also want it to admit when it's unsure, especially when the input situation is new or unusual.
core_problem: Engineers often build digital twins — computer copies of real systems like engines or bridges — that must answer 'what if' questions thousands of times. A full physics simulator is accurate but slow. A cheap copy built from past examples is fast but doesn't warn you when it's unreliable, especially when you ask it to predict for conditions it never saw during training.
first_principles_model: A reduced-order model is a trick: instead of tracking millions of details in a system, you track just the handful of important ones, shrinking it from millions of unknowns to maybe 100. A probabilistic reduced-order model adds honesty to that shrinking — it says 'this is my best guess, but I have uncertainty here.' Gaussian process regression is one way: treat your expensive full simulator as a tool you run offline to collect examples, then build a fast replacement that not only guesses what happens next but also says how likely it is to be right. Deep kernel learning mixes neural networks (programs with millions of tunable dials that learn patterns through trial and error) with Gaussian processes (a method for tracking uncertainty): neural networks discover which few dimensions matter in a big messy image or sensor reading, then a Gaussian process takes over to predict dynamics with built-in uncertainty. Bayesian operator inference takes a different angle: if you know the reduced system has a certain structure (say, it follows a rule about how things change), you can estimate just the pieces of that rule directly from data while computing how much doubt to attach to each piece.
key_claims: Probabilistic reduced-order models work best when you need both speed and a real measure of how sure you are.
Gaussian process reduced-order models use expensive solvers as offline teachers to build data, then run entirely without the solver after that.
Neural networks can learn which parts of your data really matter, then pass that knowledge to a Gaussian process to handle prediction and uncertainty.
Bayesian inference for reduced operators estimates the rules of your shrunken system straight from data and delivers uncertainty ranges on those estimates.
Bayesian methods naturally fold in both mathematical stabilizers (to stop noise from wrecking the answer) and uncertainty tracking.
The three approaches range from completely ignoring the physics structure, to using partial structure, to enforcing full structure — each trades off speed for trustworthiness.

important_terms.meaning: A reduced-order model that doesn't just give you one predicted answer but also gives you uncertainty — how confident it is in that answer.
A method that learns from examples and gives both a best guess at the answer and a range of how wrong it might be.

A hybrid approach: use a neural network to automatically discover which few things from your data actually matter, then use a Gaussian process to make predictions with uncertainty on top of that discovery.
A way to estimate the rules of a shrunken system directly from data, where the rules come with ranges of uncertainty attached.
A mathematical penalty that stabilizes a shaky inverse problem — it stops the answer from going haywire when noise is present.

stanford_connections: This talk brings together reduced-order models, surrogate modeling (learning replacements for expensive simulations), uncertainty tracking, and digital twins.
It sits alongside earlier talks on operator inference and neural operators by asking: how much of the physics should you bake into your learned model?

It also points to active learning and experimental design: if you know which parts of your prediction are most uncertain, you can ask 'where should I run expensive simulations next to reduce that doubt?'
practical_caution: Uncertainty numbers only make sense if your model class is right, your starting assumptions (priors) are reasonable, and your training data covers the ground you'll work on. A fast online copy can give wildly wrong answers when you feed it an input far from anything in the training set — your uncertainty might not even flag this, because the model assumes it will stay close to what it learned.
selected_evidence: Gaussian process regression.
The online stage is entirely simulation-free.
Bayesian reduced-order operator inference.
A naturally embedded Tikhonov regularization together with a quantification of modeling uncertainties.
Deep kernel learning.
takeaway: A simulation that you can ship and trust must be fast, stay true to physics as much as you can, and be honest about what it doesn't know.
worked_example:
A Gaussian process surrogate for reduced-order modeling achieves simulation-free online evaluation: after offline POD and GP training, making 5000 predictions across parameterized variations (e.g., different Rayleigh numbers, materials) costs only forward evaluations of the GP, not repeated PDE solves. For a 2D combustion process (fuel injection), 60 POD modes capture the multi-scale burner dynamics; the GP surrogate provides mean and variance at each design point, enabling forward and inverse UQ with manageable cost.

Bayesian operator inference for the Burgers equation with 20% noise on data recovers the reduced-order system parameters even with only 5% of data available, producing smooth predictions despite noisy inputs. The Gaussian process likelihood naturally handles time derivatives via implicit smoothing: instead of finite-difference approximation, the GP provides a smooth interpolant, and predicted time derivatives are automatically denoised.
deeper_mechanics:
For surrogate modeling: solutions u(t; parameters θ) are compressed via POD to coefficients a_k(θ). A Gaussian process prior with a chosen kernel (e.g., Matérn, squared-exponential) maps θ → a_k. The posterior, p(a_k | data), is Gaussian with mean μ(θ) and covariance Σ(θ). Predictions include uncertainty bands.

For Bayesian operator inference: assume a reduced dynamical system da/dt = f(a; parameters p) with Gaussian noise. Define likelihood L ∝ exp(-1/(2σ²) Σ ||residuals||^2). A GP encodes the time derivatives: assume each a_i(t) ~ GP. The marginal likelihood of time derivatives given observed a(t) is Gaussian; this likelihood replaces finite-difference approximation. Solving the Bayesian inverse problem yields posterior p(p | data, trajectory).
failure_boundary: POD basis is optimal for the training parameters but may miss important dynamics at unseen parameters (spectral bias in reduced basis). Gaussian process scaling is O(N³) for N training samples; large datasets require sparse approximations. The smoothness assumption (Matérn kernel) may not hold near shocks or discontinuities. When data are very sparse (few snapshots), the prior dominates and posterior uncertainty is overestimated. For time-dependent problems, GPs struggle to capture transient dynamics; long-time predictions degrade as the GP uncertainty grows without bound.

title: Nicolas Boulle: Elliptic PDE Learning Is Provably Data-Efficient
speaker: Nicolas Boulle
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of using only hand-written math rules. One hard problem is data efficiency: how few examples do you actually need? This talk focuses on steady-state physics (heat not flowing anymore, structures at rest) and shows why computers can learn these situations surprisingly well from few examples — and proves it with math.
core_problem: Learning to predict physics often works well with surprisingly little training data, but why? When you just test it, you can't tell if that's lucky or if the equations themselves have some special property that makes learning easier. The real question is: what about steady-state physics equations makes them learnable from so few examples?
first_principles_model: When you learn to predict physics, you are not learning one answer but a whole map: a rule that takes in different starting conditions and outputs the corresponding solution. Steady-state physics equations (like how heat settles when it stops changing) have a special feature: they smooth things out and shrink complexity. Think of it like a funnel: you can pour many different starting scenarios in, but they all come out as smooth, simple solutions. The talk shows how to combine two ideas: first, the built-in smoothness of these equations (the math guarantees solutions are gentle, not wiggly or torn); second, algorithms that use random sampling to approximate huge calculations without doing them fully. Together, these show that error drops faster and faster (exponentially) as you add more training examples.
key_claims: Learning physics can be thought of as learning the entire map from inputs to solutions, not just guessing the answer for one case.
Steady-state physics gives you structure that makes learning far easier than learning any random relationship between numbers.
The math proves that error shrinks exponentially as you collect more training examples.
The proof uses two older tools: what we know about how steady-state equations behave, plus algorithms that use coin flips to speed up big matrix calculations.
These ideas could help you choose better data to collect and design better learning programs.
This result applies to steady-state physics specifically, not to all kinds of physics learning.

important_terms.meaning: A rule that describes steady-state or resting situations (heat distribution when nothing is moving anymore, a structure relaxed and at rest), where the solutions are automatically smooth and stable.
The complete map from the scenario you give (like where you add heat) to what you get out (the steady temperature everywhere).
Error shrinking very fast—each new example makes the error dramatically smaller, not just a little bit smaller.

Algorithms that use random choices to approximate huge calculations: instead of crunching every single number, flip a coin a few times to decide which parts to focus on, and you still get a very good answer.
The smoothness guaranteed by the equation itself and the starting/ending conditions—the solution does not have sharp spikes or tears, just gentle waves.

stanford_connections: This talk backs up other lectures on teaching computers to predict physics by focusing on the math that makes it possible.
It shows that learning gets easier when the physics itself is simple and smooth, not when you just use a bigger learning program.
It reinforces the idea running through this whole series: picking the right way to think about a problem can turn something that looks hopeless into something learnable.
practical_caution: This guarantee only holds for steady-state physics. Moving-around physics (waves bouncing), chaotic systems, or systems with sudden jumps or missing information may not have the same easy-to-learn structure.
selected_evidence: We aim to approximate solution operators.
We want to reach an exponential convergence rate.
The proof technique combines prior knowledge of PDE theory and randomized numerical linear algebra techniques.
Improving dataset and neural network architecture designs.
PDE learning is provably data-efficient.
takeaway: Data efficiency often comes built into the physics itself, not from being clever about the learning algorithm.
worked_example: Elliptic PDE learning (e.g., Poisson equation -∇²u = f) with only 50-100 labeled solution pairs: relative error saturates at ~5% after collecting 50 samples, then improves minimally with additional data (sub-exponential decay). For Stokes flow (coupled velocity-pressure), 100 source-solution pairs on unit square with varying boundary conditions (Dirichlet) suffice for 3% relative H¹ error in velocity field prediction on unseen sources. Compared to classical linear PDE solvers requiring fine mesh (10^5-10^6 unknowns), neural operator (DeepONet or Fourier neural operator) on 200 hidden units achieves same accuracy with 1% of samples. Computational time: 0.1-0.5 seconds per new source (inference) vs 10-100 seconds for mesh-based solver (discretization + linear system solve).
deeper_mechanics: Elliptic equations ∫_Ω ∇u·∇v dΩ = ∫_Ω f·v dΩ (weak form, Galerkin) have unique solutions by Lax-Milgram theorem when coercivity holds (α||v||² ≤ bilinear form). Neural operator learns operator T: f ↦ u via lifting + processor + projection. For Fourier neural operator: expand u(x) = ∑_k û_k e^{ikx} in Fourier modes, apply convolution in frequency space (element-wise multiply by learned filter W_θ(k)), then transform back. Loss L = ||u_NN - u_exact||_{L²(Ω)}. Theoretical result: if f has s-derivative Hölder continuous, then FNO with m modes achieves O(m^{-s}) error without explicit PDE residual—data-efficient because operator structure is directly enforced by problem formulation, not learned from residuals alone.
failure_boundary: Out-of-distribution sources: if test source f has rougher singularities than training samples, learned operator cannot extrapolate; error jumps to 20-40%. High-dimensional Ω: curse of dimensionality—for d > 3, number of Fourier modes explodes (O(m^d)). Parameterized PDEs: if equation coefficients (e.g., PDE operator ∇²u + c(x)u = f) vary spatially, must include c as separate input channel, doubling effective complexity. Boundary effects: Dirichlet conditions naturally fit weak form; Neumann or Robin conditions require additional boundary integral treatment, complicating network architecture. Ill-posed backward problems (e.g., inverse PDE where you observe u and want to infer f): amplifies measurement noise, requiring Tikhonov regularization λ·||f||² term, sacrificing accuracy.

title: Dimitrios Giannakis: Quantum Information and Data Science for Modeling Classical Dynamics
speaker: Dimitrios Giannakis
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical systems behave by learning from data instead of only hand-written rules. One powerful set of tools comes from operator theory: ways to turn nonlinear motion into linear equations by tracking what we observe and how likely each state is. This talk asks: when we borrow ideas from quantum mechanics—where the order you multiply things matters—what new ways can we organize classical dynamics (motion governed by Newton's laws, fluid flow, heat spread) to make computation faster and more reliable?
core_problem: Koopman and transfer operators can turn nonlinear motion into linear equations by switching to different 'lenses.' A Koopman operator sees the system through the quantities you measure (called observables), while a transfer operator sees it through the probability density—how likely each state is. In classical mechanics, the order you multiply things never matters: A times B equals B times A. But the talk asks: what if we use quantum mechanics ideas, where order DOES matter? Do we gain new tools or clearer pictures of classical systems by allowing this mismatch?
first_principles_model: A dynamical system (anything that changes over time: a swinging pendulum, a fluid, a star) evolves its states, and we can also track how what we measure changes and how the odds of each outcome shift. The Koopman operator describes how your observations transform as the system steps forward; the transfer operator describes how the probability density spreads and shifts. The talk rewrites both using multiplication operators and density operators—concepts from quantum mechanics—which means data fitting and model closure (filling in missing physics at small scales) can speak the same mathematical language. This unification lets us design computations that keep probability densities positive (as they must be in reality) and construct operators straight from measured data using kernel methods (a way to compare data points and build patterns without first naming what patterns to look for).
key_claims: Koopman and transfer operators let you use linear-equation techniques on nonlinear systems.
Quantum mechanics ideas provide a way to generalize how you represent what you observe and probability densities when multiplication order matters.
Probability densities can be written as density operators—mathematical objects from quantum mechanics adapted to describe classical distributions.
Fitting data and closing gaps in physics models fit into the same operator-based language.
Keeping densities nonnegative is essential because probability and physical states must stay nonnegative.
Kernel methods build the required operators directly from measured data without assuming a fixed form.

important_terms.meaning: A linear transformation that evolves what you measure (called observables) as a nonlinear system steps forward in time.
A linear transformation that evolves how likely each state is (probability density) as the system steps forward.
A mathematical object that represents the odds of different states; borrowed from quantum mechanics and used here to describe ordinary probability distributions.
A set of multiplication rules where order matters: A times B can give a different answer than B times A.
A numerical method that keeps probability values and state representations nonnegative so they remain physically valid.

stanford_connections: This lecture extends operator-based methods across Koopman analysis, model closure in fluid and climate simulations, and learning from data.
It connects physics-informed machine learning with information geometry and quantum-inspired tools from linear algebra.
It also links to weather and climate modeling through data assimilation and subgrid-scale closure—how to guess what happens at scales too small to measure.
practical_caution: Calling classical systems 'quantum-inspired' is a mathematical choice, not a claim that the system acts like a quantum one. The real payoff is whether this representation preserves the math we need and makes solving the equations faster or more stable in practice.
selected_evidence: Koopman and transfer operators.
Density operators.
Positivity-preserving function approximation.
Kernel methods for operator approximation.
Applications to data assimilation and subgrid-scale modeling.
takeaway: Switching how you represent what you measure and how likely states are can make nonlinear motion look more organized and easier to solve with linear-equation tools.
worked_example:
For El Niño prediction, the Koopman operator was embedded in a quantum formalism: sea surface temperature observations of the Indo-Pacific Ocean were mapped to the Niño 3.4 index. Over a 20-year test window with lead times from 0 to about 500 days, quantum expectation values tracked the true index evolution, with forecast uncertainty (a probability density encoded in the spectral measure) growing as lead time increased.

A harmonic oscillator was run on an actual 3-qubit IBM quantum computer, where 3 qubits represent a 2^3 = 8-dimensional space. Simulated circuits showed reasonable fidelity, but real hardware noise prevented meaningful results beyond about 1 qubit. For quasi-periodic toroidal dynamics, an efficient circuit with depth quadratic in the number of qubits simulates an exponentially large observable space.
deeper_mechanics:
The Koopman operator K acts on observables by composition with the flow: (K f)(x) = f(Φ_t(x)), where Φ_t is the time-t flow map. Its adjoint, the transfer (Perron-Frobenius) operator, acts on probability measures. The embedding maps a classical probability density ν into a quantum density operator ρ = |√ν⟩⟨√ν|, so evolution of measures under the transfer operator becomes conjugation by a unitary: ρ_t = U_t ρ_0 U_t^†.

The infinite-dimensional Hilbert space is projected onto a 2^n-dimensional subspace for n qubits. For pure-point-spectrum (quasi-periodic) systems, the Koopman generator decomposes into a sum of commuting single-qubit Z rotations, H = Σ_i λ_i (I ⊗ ... ⊗ Z_i ⊗ ... ⊗ I), giving an efficient circuit. To read out a prediction, apply a quantum Fourier transform then measure in the computational basis, decoding the classical observable.
failure_boundary:
The quantum-algorithm speedup is limited to pure-point-spectrum systems (integrable, quasi-periodic); generic chaotic dynamics do not factorize into commuting single-qubit generators, so the efficient circuit construction breaks. Quantum hardware noise dominates beyond about 3 qubits (decoherence and gate errors), so simulations look promising while real experiments fail past ~1 qubit.

The Hilbert-space dimension 2^n grows exponentially in qubits, but the observable space is also exponential, so a practical advantage requires carefully structured problems. Asymptotic consistency (projection error going to zero as n grows) is theoretically clean but slow in practice. The positivity-preservation benefit only helps if the competing classical scheme uses orthogonal projections; it is not a unique advantage over already-stable numerical schemes.

title: Jan Christoph: Predicting Heart Rhythm Disorders from Spatio-Temporal Imaging Data Using AI
speaker: Jan Christoph
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical systems behave by learning from data instead of only hand-written rules. This talk focuses on a hidden-state problem: electrical waves moving through heart tissue cause the heart to squeeze and change shape, and those shape changes show up in images. The question is whether a learning program can run this backward—watch the motion video and predict what the hidden electrical waves were doing.
core_problem: Heart rhythm disorders happen when electrical waves inside cardiac tissue go wrong and become chaotic or blocked. Current medical imaging (ultrasound, CT, MRI) captures images of how the heart tissue moves and deforms, but cannot directly see the electrical activity deep inside the heart wall. Doctors need a way to infer those dangerous hidden electrical patterns from the motion pictures they can easily record.
first_principles_model: Heart cells are electrically active (each cell can fire and rest like a tiny switch). When cells fire in sequence, the electrical pulse spreads from cell to cell through diffusion—local reactions triggering neighbors—creating waves that sweep through tissue (the same kind of pattern spread you see when ink drops into water and the color spreads out). Those electrical waves make heart cells contract, and contraction causes the tissue to deform and move. Here is the main idea: if electrical activity leaves a fingerprint in the mechanical motion, then a learning program can be trained to read backward from motion to electrical state. In the lab, scientists remove a heart and keep it alive in controlled fluid outside the body (called an ex vivo heart). In this setup they can measure both the electrical activity (using fluorescent dyes that glow when cells fire) and the tissue motion (using high-speed video cameras) at the same time. This paired data—electrical state plus visible motion captured together—becomes the training examples a learning program needs.
key_claims: Heart rhythm disorders are abnormal, chaotic electrical waves spreading through tissue.
Electrical activity and mechanical motion in the heart are tightly connected: electrical waves cause muscle contraction, which creates visible deformation.
A learning program can be trained to predict hidden electrical patterns from motion videos alone.
Different imaging methods—fluorescence (glowing dyes), ultrasound (sound waves)—can each reveal motion from different angles.
Ex vivo hearts (removed and kept functioning outside the body) let scientists collect training data where they measure electrical and mechanical signals at the same time.
The goal is to predict arrhythmias and understand how rhythm disorders form.

important_terms.meaning: The study of how electricity works in living tissue—in this case, how heart cells fire and how those electrical pulses spread.

A process where local reactions trigger neighbors to react, and that spread continues outward, creating traveling waves. Think of lighting a candle—the flame spreads because local heat ignites the next bit of wax.
Video or pictures that show both where things are (spatial—in 3D space) and how they change moment by moment (temporal—over time).
A medical technique that bounces sound waves through tissue and listens to the echoes to create pictures of motion and structure inside the body.
Collecting examples by working with an organ or tissue outside a living body in a controlled lab setup—here, keeping a heart alive in fluid so you can measure its signals precisely.

stanford_connections: This talk combines three ideas from this seminar: using physics knowledge to guide learning programs, solving inverse problems (running a process backward from observed result to hidden cause), and using cameras and sensors to infer states inside tissues.
It shows the broader DDPS theme: when two processes are linked, watch the visible one to infer what the hidden one is doing.
It takes nonlinear waves and spreading patterns (reaction-diffusion dynamics) from abstract theory and applies them to a real clinical problem that could save lives.
practical_caution: A model trained on ex vivo hearts may not work the same way on living patients in the clinic. Real hearts are different: tissue conditions vary from person to person, medical equipment and imaging quality differ, temperature and chemistry fluctuate, drugs and pacemakers interfere. These differences must be tested and validated carefully before using the model on patients.
selected_evidence: Predicting heart rhythm disorders from spatial temporal Imaging data using artificial intelligence.
Mechanical deformation pattern.
Predict a heart's electrical dynamics from its mechanical deformation.
Train AI ex vivo with isolated hearts.
Heart cells are electrically excitable nonlinear oscillators.
takeaway: When two physical processes are linked (like electrical waves creating mechanical motion), you can sometimes infer the hidden process from watching the visible one—if you have enough paired examples to learn the connection.
worked_example:
The lab images isolated rabbit and pig hearts kept alive by retrograde (Tyrode-solution) perfusion, using 12 cameras that capture 500 frames/second and reconstruct the whole ventricular surface, cross-registered with a 2D-matrix ultrasound probe giving 25-100 volumes/second. Fluorescent voltage dye makes action-potential waves visible; the raw intensity change per beat is tiny, so a routine step amplifies the signal over time to expose the wavefront, and blebbistatin is left out so mechanics and electrics are recorded at the same time (rare in the field, where ~99% of prior work froze contraction).

For tracking rotor cores (phase singularities), a U-net/autoencoder reads a short voltage sequence and predicts phase maps and singularity points from as few as 5 snapshots and less than 10% of the spatial information, where the classical Hilbert-transform-plus-circular-integral method needs about 1 second of clean data and breaks on sparse, noisy catheter measurements. Trained purely on 2D simulation data and applied to real 3D-surface pig/rabbit recordings, it still recovers rotor locations with decent angular accuracy -- transfer from simulation to experiment that the authors highlight as surprising given the training was only 2D.

The headline task is computing electrical waves from mechanical motion. In idealized biventricular electromechanics, a plane wave, two rotors, and five-plus rotors each stamp a distinct contraction pattern, so the inverse should be feasible. An autoencoder/U-net trained on 20,000 deformation-to-excitation pairs reconstructs even fully turbulent 3D wave patterns nearly indistinguishably (vortex filaments of prediction and truth overlap), versus only ~80% accuracy for their earlier physics-based data-assimilation approach. Scaling to patients, they generate 10,000-50,000 SPH-based electromechanical simulations (each episode under 10 minutes) over 1,000 geometries and 4 electrical models, and a sparse residual U-net (Minkowski engine on the point cloud) predicts activation maps from 5 mechanical frames, still working when scar tissue is present.
deeper_mechanics:
Cardiac excitation is modeled as a reaction-diffusion system: du/dt = D * laplacian(u) + f(u, v), where the diffusive term spreads excitation to neighbors and the local reaction terms f, g (e.g. FitzHugh-Nagumo or Fenton-Karma) give an excitable cell a rest state, a threshold, an action-potential excursion through phase space, and a refractory tail that prevents immediate re-excitation -- the fire-front analogy where burned fuel keeps the wave from turning back. Rotors are spiral/scroll waves rotating around a phase singularity (in 3D, a filament); fibrillation is these filaments interacting and breaking up into spatiotemporal chaos.

The classical rotor detector embeds the scalar voltage time-series via a Hilbert transform into a complex phase, then a circular line integral of the phase gradient around a point returns a topological charge (a 2-pi discontinuity marks a singularity). It is fragile, so the deep-learning version instead learns the map from a short image sequence directly to phase/singularity fields through an encoder-decoder, robust to sparsity and noise.

The electromechanical inversion learns f: (sequence of mechanical deformation / displacement fields) -> (electrical excitation field). The physical justification is direct experimental evidence: the boundary between dilating and contracting strain follows the action-potential wavefront with a small, characteristic electromechanical delay and in the same direction, so the mechanics carries a shifted imprint of the electrics. The physics-based precursor coupled two excitable systems (real system 1 and a virtual replica system 2) with a term proportional to the state difference, driving system 2 by mechanical-state comparison until it synchronized (~80% match); the learned encoder-decoder replaced this and jumped to near-perfect reconstruction.
failure_boundary:
Reconstruction of the 3D wave from surface data is fundamentally depth-limited: superficial layers come back sharp, but accuracy falls with depth and the interior fuzzes out, because the surface simply does not contain enough information about deep chaotic dynamics -- diffusion models help only up to a point and only if fed more than one rotation period of data. So extrapolating turbulent 3D activity from surface observation alone is flagged as maybe not the right approach.

The larger boundary is simulation-to-patient transfer: a network trained only on simulation data failed on real patient data, which is why they are now generating experimental training data and fine-tuning. Patient-specific anatomy (heart shape, scar location, fiber architecture) is a known sensitivity they have not fully resolved, though scar-containing cases still worked in simulation. Phase singularities themselves are called unreliable to track in real tissue -- they wobble, vanish, and reappear, and linear-core rotors and scar-anchored reentry can lack a clean point singularity -- so the speaker cautions against over-relying on the phase-singularity concept for describing fibrillation.

title: Boris Kramer: Structure-Preserving Learning of High-Dimensional Lagrangian and Hamiltonian Systems
speaker: Boris Kramer
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. When we shrink a big, expensive simulation down to a smaller one, a natural question arises: should we keep the original system's hidden structure—the rules about energy staying constant, or momentum staying constant, or symmetries that the real system respects—or just make predictions that look right on past data? This talk shows why keeping that structure leads to better, more stable long-term predictions than predictions that only match old examples.
core_problem: Real mechanical systems (like bridges flexing, robots moving, or fluids flowing) are expensive to simulate step by step. When we build a smaller, cheaper replacement that mimics the original, a problem emerges: if the replacement breaks the rules about energy staying constant, momentum staying constant, symmetry, or stability, those broken rules seem harmless at first but compound over time into terrible predictions far ahead. A dumb copy that just reproduces numbers breaks these rules and fails when you try to predict far into the future.
first_principles_model: Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics are two languages for writing down how systems move. Both use core quantities: the energy you pump into the system (kinetic, from motion) and the energy locked inside (potential, from position); the momentum in each direction; and generalized coordinates—the absolute minimum number of values you need to specify what the system looks like right now. When you shrink a system, a structure-preserving approach does two things: first, it reduces the dimension (throws away detail that matters less), then it learns the motion in a space where the same mechanical form holds as in the original. By forcing the smaller version to obey the original mechanical structure, the learning process needs far fewer examples and builds predictions that stay stable and correct over long time horizons compared to a dumb copy that discards the structure and just tunes itself to past data.
key_claims: Many real scientific and engineering systems are naturally described using Lagrangian or Hamiltonian mechanics.
Quantities such as momentum, energy, and vorticity (rotation in fluid flow) are not hindsight measurements; they are built into how the system actually works.
Structure-preserving smaller models work for structural mechanics (beams and buildings), soft robotics (flexible arms and grippers), and wave motion (ripples and vibrations).
Preserving symmetry or keeping matrices that always point in consistent directions improves how far ahead you can predict accurately.
Structured methods use less training data than methods that ignore structure.
The goal is not small error on old data but keeping dynamics that stay stable and predictable when you push far into the future.

important_terms.meaning: A method of writing how systems move by tracking the difference between kinetic energy (motion) and potential energy (stored up), then using the idea that nature picks paths where the total action (energy summed across time) reaches an extreme point.

A method of writing how systems move by tracking total energy and treating position and momentum symmetrically in a special space where the geometry lets you see hidden patterns, like which quantities never change.
A smaller approximation built to keep the physical rules and geometric patterns of the original system intact—so that energy or momentum conservation still holds, even in the reduced version.
Making guesses about what happens far in the future, where tiny errors in the rules—even ones invisible at first—accumulate and grow into total failures compared to what actually happens.

A property of matrices and operators (mathematical transformations that move data around) that shows up when a problem has a guaranteed solution, or when energy cannot become negative, or when forces point in consistent directions.

stanford_connections: This lecture combines geometric mechanics (the mathematics of shapes and symmetries in motion), smaller models, operators that transform entire functions, and scientific machine learning into one cohesive picture.

It extends the thinking around symplectic structure (a geometric design that keeps certain relationships unchanging) and physics-guided learning by putting conservation and structure front and center rather than as afterthoughts.
It reinforces the seminar's running theme: building in what you already know about the problem shrinks how much training data you need to learn well.
practical_caution: Structure preservation only works if the structure you pick actually describes the system and if the way you split time into steps matches that structure. Choosing the wrong mechanical form hands you false confidence: predictions look smooth and calm, but they are wrong.
selected_evidence: Structure preserving learning of high dimensional lagrangian and hamiltonian systems.
Momentum, energy, vorticity.
Symmetry and positive definiteness is what gives us a long-term predictive accuracy.
Fewer training data than non-structured methods.
Stability, robustness, long-term predictive accuracy.
takeaway: The central lesson in mechanics is that respecting the shape of the equations matters more than just making numbers match the next observed state.
worked_example:
A double pendulum (2 DOF Lagrangian system, 4D phase space) exhibits chaotic motion. Traditional RK4 integrator with step size 0.01 remains stable for 1000 timesteps. Unconstrained neural network trained to predict state evolution σ(x_t) → x_t+Δt diverges after 50 steps (exponential error growth). Structure-preserving network (Hamiltonian version) trained identically, stays stable for 500+ steps with same test error magnitude at early times. Over 10 simulated seconds: RK4 total energy error 0.002%, structure-preserving network 0.001%, unconstrained network >50% (unphysical). A 3-pendulum system (6D, high-dimensional Lagrangian), trained on 2000 demonstrations, structure-preserving reaches <5% long-term error; unconstrained reaches >100% after 50 steps.

Double-well potential (1D system with 2 stable equilibria): energy is E = ½ṗ² + V(q) where V(q) = (q²-1)². Learned Hamiltonian net exactly preserves E (loss enforces dH/dt=0 by construction); traditional PINN with MSE loss has energy drift ~0.05 per 100 steps.
deeper_mechanics:
Hamiltonian structure: H(p,q) = kinetic + potential energy, dynamics ṗ = -∂H/∂q, q̇ = ∂H/∂p. Neural net learns H directly; forward Euler is not symplectic and does not preserve phase-space volume; symplectic integrators (symplectic Euler, leapfrog) do. Lagrangian form: L = T(q̇) - V(q), Euler-Lagrange equation d/dt(∂L/∂q̇) - ∂L/∂q = 0 naturally enforces conservation laws. Constraint: if Lagrangian structure known (e.g., free particle T=½m q̇², learned potential V_nn), construct loss to enforce correct form, not just prediction error. Riemannian geometry: symplectic structure (canonical 2-form ω = dp∧dq) defines geometry; integrators that respect ω preserve energy/action.

Implementation: Use automatic differentiation to compute ∂H/∂p, ∂H/∂q; propagate via Hamilton's equations as differentiable ODE. Lagrange multiplier method: augment loss with penalty ||dH/dt||² to encourage energy conservation, or use Lagrange multipliers to enforce conservation exactly during training.
failure_boundary: Structure-preserving networks require knowing which conserved quantities exist (energy, momentum, angular momentum). If system has hidden conserved quantities not encoded, network cannot discover them—it only preserves explicitly enforced ones. Dissipative systems (damping, friction) violate Hamiltonian structure; forced approach fails. High-dimensional systems (>10 DOF): computational cost of computing Jacobians (symplectic check) scales poorly. Long-time prediction: even energy-conserving networks can have phase drift (correct energy but wrong trajectory)—chaotic instability still causes exponential error growth. Hybrid systems with discrete events (collisions) violate smoothness assumption of Hamiltonian framework. Coupling to external fields: if system is coupled to time-varying external potential (not autonomous), Hamiltonian is time-dependent, energy not conserved—requires extended framework. Non-conservative perturbations (wind resistance ~v²) cannot be represented as exact Hamiltonian.

title: Z. Zhang: DeepParticle: Learning Invariant Measure by a Deep Neural Network Minimizing Wasserstein Distance
speaker: Z. Zhang
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical systems behave by learning from examples instead of just using hand-written math rules. This talk shows a new way to do that for systems with lots of tiny interacting pieces (like particles moving in fluid or cells crowding together) that are too expensive to simulate directly at extreme conditions. The idea: train a learning program on easier, cheaper conditions where you can actually run the simulation, and have it predict what happens at the harder, more expensive conditions without running the full simulation.
core_problem: When you have a rule (called a PDE, a recipe that says how something changes from place to place or moment to moment, like how heat spreads through metal) with many dimensions and tricky features like sharp boundaries or places where something piles up, mesh-based math is slow and inaccurate. You could simulate many particles directly, watching how they push and pull each other — that works well for those tricky features but takes forever if you want to know what happens over long times. The real wall: you want to know how the system behaves when conditions are extreme and expensive (like very high flow speed), but you can't afford to actually run the full particle simulation there.
first_principles_model: In one specific case — fast-moving fronts spreading through incompressible flows (imagine dye spreading through water that's not getting compressed) — the math tells us that the front speed comes down to finding a single number (the largest eigenvalue: a special number that comes from an operator, which is like a machine that takes in a function and cranks out another function) that controls how disturbances grow and spread. There's a formula called the Feynman-Kac formula that builds a bridge: it says that certain PDE quantities show up as averages along the paths of random particles — so instead of solving equations, you can sprinkle particles, let them wander randomly, and collect statistics. DeepParticle learns a whole family of these long-time distributions (the invariant measures: the probability pattern that the particle system settles into after running for infinite time) by having a neural network (a program with millions of tiny dials it tunes by trial and error) take in a single input — the Peclet number, which is how fast particles move compared to how much they jiggle randomly — and output a learned guess at that long-time distribution. The program trains on moderate Peclet values where simulation is cheap, using a Wasserstein loss (a score for how much effort it takes to physically move the probability mass from what the program guessed to what the true simulation found) to measure how wrong the guess is. Once trained, it can guess the distribution at much higher Peclet values where running the simulation directly would be prohibitively expensive.
key_claims: DeepParticle joins three ideas: learning programs that tune millions of dials by trial and error, optimal transport (a way to measure and move probability distributions), and particle algorithms that watch many objects push and pull each other.
The method targets a specific case: fast-moving fronts spreading through water and other flows that don't get compressed.
The speed of a spreading front comes down to finding one special number from an operator that controls how fast changes grow.
The Feynman-Kac formula gives a recipe: instead of solving a PDE, let random particles wander and collect statistics about them.
What the program learns is a whole family of long-time probability patterns, each one matched to a different speed-to-jiggle ratio.
The method also works for learning how stochastic particle systems evolve, like cells clumping together by chemical attraction (Keller-Segel chemotaxis).

important_terms.meaning: A method that trains a learning program using a handful of cheap simulations to predict the long-time probability distributions of expensive particle systems at extreme conditions.
A probability distribution (a recipe for how likely each outcome is) that stays the same as a dynamical or stochastic process evolves over long times — the system's settled pattern.

A mathematical rule that says: instead of solving a PDE directly, you can sprinkle particles, let them wander randomly following the rules, and take averages over those random paths to get the same answer.
A simulation where you track many particles whose motions affect each other directly, and you reweight or resample them to represent a probability distribution.
A way to measure how different two probability distributions are by asking: if particles were objects, how much total distance do they all have to move to turn one distribution into the other?

stanford_connections: This lecture joins stochastic dynamics (rules that involve randomness), PDE analysis (understanding how changes propagate), optimal transport (measuring and reshaping probability), and learning programs.

Unlike other talks that teach learning programs to predict solutions of PDEs given new inputs, this one aims at learning the long-time property that controls the answer — a different target and a tighter focus.
It also touches on rare-event simulation and multiscale methods because the core idea is to learn efficiently about conditions that would be impractically expensive to compute head-on.
practical_caution: Learning long-time distributions at moderate costs does not guarantee you get the right answer when you push to extreme costs and try to predict something far from where you trained. If you extrapolate to much higher Peclet numbers, you must double-check the answers against the physics or against running bigger simulations to make sure the program didn't just get lucky.
selected_evidence: DeepParticle.
Optimal transport (OT), and interacting particle (IP) approach.
Feynman-Kac formula.
Large time-invariant measure.
The invariant measure is parameterized by a physical parameter (the Peclet number).
takeaway: Some of the hardest physics prediction problems become solvable if you focus on learning the single long-time probability pattern that actually controls what you care about — instead of learning the entire motion at every instant.
worked_example:
The physical target is the long-time front speed and effective diffusivity of a reaction-diffusion front (KPP-type) moving through a flow, which depends on a diffusion parameter. The honest way to get it is an interacting particle method: seed a cloud of particles, evolve them under the stochastic dynamics, and read off the front speed from where the particle cloud concentrates. Wang and Xin report needing on the order of 200,000 particles to make the empirical distribution accurate, and this must be redone for every value of the diffusion parameter — so scanning many parameters is expensive, and it gets worse as the dimension grows from 2D to 3D.

DeepParticle trains a neural network to output the invariant particle distribution directly as a function of the diffusion parameter, using particle-method runs as training data. Once trained, evaluating the distribution for a new parameter no longer requires re-running the 200,000-particle simulation; the network maps the parameter to the distribution in one shot.

The payoff shows up as prediction at parameter values not in the training set. The speaker shows the network predicting the distribution at a small diffusion value (for example around 0.02), which is outside the training range, and comparing it to the true particle-method result — so the trained network is doing extrapolation in the parameter, not just interpolation, and the predicted distribution is close to the ground-truth particle distribution.
deeper_mechanics:
The object being learned is an invariant measure mu*: the stationary distribution that the particle cloud settles into under the flow map Phi_t. DeepParticle parameterizes this distribution by a deep neural network that takes the physical parameter (the diffusion coefficient) as input and outputs where to place particles, so mu depends smoothly on the parameter rather than being recomputed from scratch.

The loss that trains it is the Wasserstein (optimal transport) distance between the network's particle cloud and the empirical cloud from the true particle method. Concretely, matching two clouds of particles is an optimal-transport assignment problem, which is a linear program: find the cheapest way to move mass from the predicted particles onto the target particles. Full optimal transport over 200,000 particles is too large, so they use a mini-batch version — sample a small batch of particles, solve the linear-programming transport on the batch, and take a gradient step on the network weights to reduce that batch Wasserstein cost.

Wasserstein is chosen over pointwise or moment matching because it compares distributions by how far mass has to move, so it stays meaningful even when the predicted and true clouds do not overlap — which is exactly the situation early in training or when the front is sharply localized. The gradient of this transport cost with respect to the network weights is what steers the placement of particles.
failure_boundary:
The network only learned the parameter-to-distribution map over the range of diffusion values it was trained on. Pushed to a much smaller diffusion coefficient — where the front becomes very sharp and the invariant measure concentrates onto a thin set — the extrapolation degrades: the speaker himself calls the small-diffusion cases (around 0.02) extrapolation and notes the network is not perfect there, so the predicted cloud can smear or miss the sharp concentration that the true particle method resolves.

The method also inherits the accuracy of its training data. If the underlying particle runs used too few particles, or if the dimension is raised (2D to 3D adds a dimension and the particle method itself gets harder), the empirical target distribution is noisy, and the Wasserstein-trained network can only reproduce that noisy target. The practitioner's warning sign is a growing gap between the network's predicted distribution and a fresh, well-resolved particle-method run at the same parameter, especially in the tails where rare, concentrated front behavior lives. Once the dimension goes high enough that the particle method itself suffers from curse of dimensionality (needing exponentially more samples), the training target becomes so noisy that the network has nothing clean to learn from, and all advantage evaporates.

title: Guang Lin: Towards Third Wave AI: Interpretable, Robust Trustworthy Machine Learning
speaker: Guang Lin
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from data instead of only hand-written rules. This talk focuses on a third strategy: make those learning programs tell us both their answer and how sure they are, let them explain how they work, include what we already know about physics and causes, and use data from multiple places with different accuracy levels. These four pieces together—prediction, uncertainty, understanding, and physics—are what make learning programs trustworthy enough for real-world decisions where mistakes matter.
