core_problem: When scientists and doctors need to make fast decisions—predicting disease spread, deciding on treatment, monitoring safety—they need computers that not only guess right but also tell them how confident to be, show their reasoning, and stay honest about what they don't know. Most learning programs today are opaque: they gobble data, tweak millions of dials to fit patterns, and spit out an answer. Nobody can see why they picked that answer. Nobody knows how wrong they might be. For real-world problems where errors have consequences, that's too risky. The question is: how do we build learning programs that work well AND let us see inside them AND quantify their uncertainty?
first_principles_model: Third Wave AI layers four ideas together. First: use neural operators—special learning programs designed to spot patterns between functions (relationships where the input and output are themselves curves or fields, like temperature over time or pressure over space) rather than just matching numbers to numbers. Second: make these programs output not just a guess but also a measure of uncertainty—how confident the computer should be in that guess. Third: borrow what we already know about physics, causation, or domain structure and bake it into how the model is built, so it respects those constraints. Fourth: combine data from many sources, each with different precision or cost (cheap satellite images plus expensive lab measurements, for example), and handle privacy by letting data stay distributed across hospitals or labs rather than gathering it all in one place. Bayesian methods (trial-and-error tuning that tracks not just the best guess but a full range of plausible answers) make the uncertainty real. Causal discovery methods read data to infer what actually causes what, not just what moves together.
key_claims: Trustworthy AI for science and medicine requires prediction, uncertainty estimates, interpretability, and domain knowledge working together.
Neural operators can learn nonlinear relationships between curves, fields, and other function-like objects.
Learning programs built with Bayesian methods can output both an answer and a confidence estimate at the same time.
Combining data from many sources with different costs and accuracies (multifidelity learning) and keeping distributed data private (federated learning) expands what problems you can tackle.
Physics rules and causal stories, discovered or known in advance, can be woven into the model structure so it respects what's actually true.
Real examples: predicting COVID-19 spread with honest uncertainty ranges, finding what brain changes cause Alzheimer's symptoms.

important_terms.meaning: The next phase of AI that combines learning from data with transparency (so you can see why it chose an answer), certainty estimates (how much to trust it), and respect for real-world physics and causation (not just pattern-matching in a black hole).

A learning program shaped to spot patterns between functions—where inputs and outputs are curves, fields, or surfaces (like how temperature evolves over space and time) rather than just single numbers.
A neural operator that uses a method called Bayesian inference (keeping track of all plausible answers, not just one best guess) so it can output both a prediction and a range of uncertainty.

Training with data of mixed quality and cost—cheap measurements alongside expensive ones, or fast rough simulations alongside slow detailed ones—so you use the cheap data to guide patterns and the expensive data to check details.

Using algorithms on data to reverse-engineer what causes what, rather than just spotting which things move together (correlation). Is high blood sugar causing high insulin, or is inflammation causing both?

stanford_connections: This talk weaves together neural operators (learning between functions), uncertainty quantification (knowing how confident you should be), federated learning (keeping data private and distributed), and trustworthy machine learning—each a thread through the seminar.
It builds on earlier talks about safety and reliability by making uncertainty and interpretability core ingredients in the model itself, not afterthoughts.
It bridges scientific machine learning to public-health and biomedical decisions, showing how the same ideas that predict physical systems can guide real clinical choices.
practical_caution: Adding error bars to predictions does not make a model trustworthy all by itself. The error estimates themselves can be wrong. The assumptions you make about what causes what may not hold in reality. The data you trained on may be biased or stale. Real-world feedback—what actually happened after you deployed the model—is your check: does the model's claimed uncertainty match how often it's actually wrong? Does the causal story hold up? All three layers (the learned pattern, the uncertainty measure, and the causal story) need to be tested, not assumed.
selected_evidence: Interpretable, Robust Trustworthy Machine Learning.
Nonlinear operators from functions with simultaneous uncertainty estimates.
Multi-fidelity, federated, Bayesian neural operator network architectures.
Physics Knowledge and AI.
Data-driven causal model discovery and personalized prediction in Alzheimer's disease.
takeaway: Scientific learning programs become ready to use in real decisions only when they deliver four things as a package: a prediction, a measure of how sure they should be, a story you can follow about why they chose that answer, and respect for the physics and domain knowledge we already have. Skip any one piece and the system is incomplete.
worked_example: COVID-19 epidemiology model (SEIR variant) for New York City: susceptible S, exposed E, infected I, hospitalized H, dead D, recovered R, vaccinated V compartments. Extended ODE system with 10 parameters (transmission β, hospitalization rate p, death rate q, etc.) calibrated as piecewise-constant over policy-driven events (stay-home order, reopening dining). Using daily case data (A), hospitalization (B), deaths (C), vaccine doses 1&2 (D) from Feb-Dec 2020, Bayesian neural network with Laplace approximation estimates posterior P(μ|data). Uncertainties quantified: β has ±15% credible interval, predictions of infections 3-month ahead show 95% uncertainty bands ±20% of mean. Three scenarios evaluated (no reopening, Feb-14 reopening, March-14 reopening) showing delayed reopening reduces peak infections by ~30%.
deeper_mechanics: Physics-informed epidemiology: ODE residual L_ode = ||dS/dt - (-β SI/N)||² + ... enforces compartment conservation. Identifiability analysis checks if parameters are distinguishable given available data via Fisher information matrix rank. Sensitivity analysis computes ∂(deaths|day-90)/∂β, ∂p, ∂q to rank parameter importance. Robust (Bayesian) parameter estimation minimizes L = L_data + λ·L_prior + L_constraints, where L_prior = Σ(μ_j - μ_ref)²/σ²_j encodes prior belief, L_constraints = (dS/dt + dI/dt + ... - 0)² enforces conservation law. Memory-effect model: fractional-order ODE ∂^α u/∂t with α<1 introduces history-dependence via kernel K_α(t) ∝ t^(-α); captures delayed immune response or behavioral lag.
failure_boundary: Parameter non-identifiability: if both transmission β and susceptible fraction S₀ affect early growth rate equally, data alone cannot distinguish them; posterior is degenerate. Model mismatch: real COVID variants (Alpha, Delta, Omicron) have different transmission rates; using single β across mutation-driven waves causes systematic bias. Policy change effects not in data: if new interventions (vaccination campaigns, testing) affect dynamics differently than historical data suggested, predictions fail. Long-term forecasting beyond 2-3 weeks breaks down due to behavioral changes, variant emergence, policy shifts not encoded in ODE; epistemic uncertainty grows exponentially. Noisy hospitalization/death data contains reporting delays and artifacts (weekend under-reporting); if not deconvolved, parameter estimates are biased.

title: George M. Bollas: Physics-Informed Machine Learning through Symbolic Regression
speaker: George M. Bollas
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical systems behave by learning from examples instead of hand-written math. One approach is to have a learning program search for actual equations that match your data—not just predict the next number, but show you the real rule. This talk is about why that method works especially well when you have little data, lots of noise, or need to understand what's actually happening instead of just guessing the next step.
core_problem: Many engineering systems need the actual equations that describe how things work. When you build a bridge or design an engine, you can't just know 'the next load is 50 tons'—you need to know the rules that govern how forces move and change, so you can diagnose problems and predict what happens next. Scientists have two choices right now: write down the rules by hand (slow and hard when the rules are complicated or unknown), or use learning programs that predict numbers without showing you the actual rules. This talk asks: can a computer hunt for equations instead?
first_principles_model: Symbolic regression is a search process: the computer tries millions of different equations (like x+y, x*sin(y), sqrt(x)/y) and keeps the ones that match your data best. To find equations that describe how things change over time, the computer uses automatic differentiation—a way to compute how much each number affects the final answer by working backward through the calculation, step by step, like unwinding a chain. Instead of stopping to solve big equations over and over, the search just computes these changes and keeps looking. The computer can also use genetic programming: start with simple equations, randomly change them (swap a plus for a times, add a new term), breed the ones that work better, and repeat—like evolution of equations. This lets the method discover not just what rule is breaking, but how the damage or fault spreads over time.
key_claims: Symbolic regression is useful when you want to discover the actual equation instead of just making predictions.
The method works well when you have little data.
The approach holds up even with high noise, including as much as 50 percent noise added to measurements.
Automatic differentiation removes the need to solve equations over and over while searching for the right formula.
Comparing symbolic regression with physics-informed neural networks shows different tradeoffs—finding equations you can write down versus fitting while obeying physics rules.
Predicting how faults grow benefits from symbolic equations that describe fault behavior step by step.

important_terms.meaning: A search process where the computer tries millions of different equations to find ones that match your data, keeping the simplest ones that work best.
A search method that starts with random equations, randomly changes them (swap operations, add terms), and keeps breeding the ones that fit better—like evolution applied to equations.
A way to compute how much each piece of a calculation affects the final answer by working backward through the calculation step by step, without doing complicated math by hand.
Searching data to find the rules that describe how quantities (like temperature or pressure) change in space and over time.
Predicting how a broken or damaged part of a system will get worse over time.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects finding the smallest set of equations needed to describe something, physics-informed learning (teaching computers the laws of physics while they learn), symbolic methods, and learning algorithms that explain their answers.
It picks up the thread of recovering equations you can write down and solve by hand—a contrast to just getting numbers without seeing the rule.
It also links to virtual copies of real systems (called digital twins), where discovered equations can help you spot problems and predict how the system will behave.
practical_caution: Symbolic regression can find equations that look good and match your numbers, but turn out wrong when you test them on new data. The equations you hunt for depend totally on which pieces you let the computer choose from (if you never offer 'times', you'll never find multiplication). Noise in your measurements throws off the discovery, and bad handling of noise creates fake equations. Finding an equation that fits your old data is only step one—you must always test it on fresh data you've never seen before.
selected_evidence: Physics-informed machine learning through symbolic regression.
Successful model recovery with up to 50% noise.
Automatic differentiation.
Discovery of PDE models when data collection is expensive.
Fault detection and isolation.
takeaway: When understanding how things work matters—because you need to fix something broken, predict what happens in a new situation, or make sure a system is safe—then learning algorithms should try to find actual equations, not just predict one number at a time.
worked_example:
Heat exchanger fouling fault detection: 125 differential-algebraic equations discretized, 2 temperature sensors, fouling modeled as thermal resistance vs time (asymptotic function). System evolves under altitude/speed variability. Discovers fault progression via 1 soft sensor + genetic programming with symbolic regression. Remaining useful life predicted to ~2% error (initially 50% error) within 5 iterations after seeing 50 minutes of data; converges to zero error after 6-7 updates.

Plug flow reactor PDE identification (isothermal, C^2 reaction): 2 different feed conditions, discovers pure cubic reaction kinetics from sparse data. Standard SINDy fails at 20min computation; hybrid approach finds analytical solution in 100s with 3 parameters vs PINN's 7500. Burgers equation: recovers exact diffusion coefficient from 10 points + 5% noise in under 100 seconds.
deeper_mechanics:
Genetic programming + differential solver loop: candidate expression trees from mutation/crossover operations encode right-hand side of PDE. Each tree instance → parameter estimation via Casadi ODE solver (expensive integration step) → Bayesian Information Criterion fitness scoring to penalize complexity. Evolutionary loop iterates until BIC stagnates. Symbolic regression avoids derivatives (noisy) by using Runge-Kutta scheme as constraint: ||x_{i+1} - RK4[Φ(x_i)·ψ]||^2_2 + λ||ψ||_1 where ψ selects library terms via sequential thresholding.

Inverse PINN hybrid: neural network g_θ(x,t) approximates solution; automatic differentiation computes residual ∂g/∂t - f[g,∂g/∂x,...]; loss combines data fit + PDE penalty + gradient consistency regularization.
failure_boundary: Computational expense dominates: genetic programming + full PDE integration 20min for one 1D equation (vs weak SINDy <1min). Scalability to coupled multiphysics systems (100s equations) impractical. Dictionary/library structure must be user-provided; missing dominant term class (e.g., rational functions if only polynomials guessed) causes systematic bias—no automatic discovery of basis functional forms. Noise sensitivity: high noise (>5%) without denoising causes false positive features unless gradient loss included. Chaotic systems or stiff problems (wide timescale separation) ill-suited unless integrator chosen carefully; Newton-Krylov iteration expensive for large-scale PDEs.

title: Francesco Ballarin: Regularized Reduced Order Models for Control of Navier-Stokes Equations
speaker: Francesco Ballarin
one_sentence: This whole series asks: can computers learn to predict how physical things behave instead of solving hand-written math rules? This talk tackles one piece: when you shrink a simulator to run fast (keeping only the biggest patterns), it can become wobbly and wrong. Adding smoothing to the shrunken model stops the wobble and makes it safe to steer with automatic feedback.
core_problem: Engineers use rules (called differential equations) to describe how fluids move and change. Simulating those rules on a computer grid, even a coarse one, can produce false jittering and noise. When you shrink the simulation down to just a handful of key patterns—called a reduced-order model, or ROM—to make it run fast, you throw away tons of detail, and the jittering gets worse. Now add steering: the shrunken model must both predict the flow accurately AND let you control it (e.g., turn a valve to change the flow direction). That's harder than just predicting with no control.
first_principles_model: In a full-size simulation, engineers add filters to kill the jittering. A ROM works by keeping only a few main patterns and throwing the rest away. This compression can remove the natural smoothing that keeps the full simulation stable, making the shrunken equations blow up and wiggle badly. This talk compares two fixes. First: evolve-filter-relax. You run one time step forward, then use a filter to strip out the junk high-frequency wiggles, then gently pull the result back toward the zone where the system naturally stays calm (this zone is called the stable manifold—think of it as a valley the system wants to roll into). Second: approximate deconvolution. You filter out the junk, then guess what information you lost and try to add it back. Both fixes get plugged into feedback control: you measure where the flow actually is right now, then use that measurement to decide what steering command to send next.
key_claims: Smoothing is standard in real fluid simulators, but almost nobody studies how to smooth the shrunken-down versions.
When flow gets carried along much faster than it spreads out (especially on a coarse grid), the system is fragile and can break if you miss the small-scale details.
A shrunken model for steering must stay accurate when you're feeding back real measurements, not just when you run it open-loop with no feedback.
Evolve-filter-relax smoothing can be used inside a shrunken-model steering controller.
Approximate-deconvolution smoothing is another way to recover the effects of patterns that got filtered out.
A good shrunken model balances speed, stability, and steering accuracy.

important_terms.meaning: The rules that describe how liquids and gases move, accounting for what pushes them and how they resist flowing.
A flow where the fluid gets shoved along faster than it spreads out sideways, making sharp edges and making predictions blow up on coarse grids.
A shrunken model that takes one step forward in time, strips out the high-frequency junk with a filter, then nudges the result back to where the system behaves smoothly.
A guess-and-restore trick: after you filter something, you try to guess what got lost and add a correction to get closer to the truth.
You measure the current state, then use that number to decide what command to send, so the system steers toward your goal.

stanford_connections: This lecture weaves together shrunken models, flow steering, numerical smoothing, and closure methods (ways to handle the patterns you threw away).
It fills a gap next to earlier talks about inferring operators and building shrunken models by asking: what goes wrong when tiny patterns destabilize a shrunken-model controller?
It also relates to digital twins: if you want a fast stand-in of a steering system to run in real time, that stand-in must stay stable when you're actively steering it.
practical_caution: Smoothing stops the wobble but can lie to you about what the flow is actually doing. For steering, the smoothing must protect the flow patterns you actually need to control, not just hide all the noise.
selected_evidence: Regularized reduced order models for control of navier stokes equations.
Under-resolved or marginally-resolved simulations of convection-dominated flows.
Incompressible Navier-Stokes equations.
Evolve-filter-relax regularized ROM.
Approximate deconvolution.
takeaway: Shrunken simulators used for steering need their own custom smoothing, built for the shrunken equations—you can't just copy the smoothing rules from the full-size simulator.
worked_example: Flow control steers cylinder wake toward target velocity using feedback forcing F = F_A(γ) = (∇p̃ + ν∇²ũ)|_target + γ(u - U_target). For Reynolds 1000, γ = 1 vs γ = 5: original theory requires γ > M where M ≈ 3 (between values tested). Result: γ = 1 shows oscillatory non-convergent error; γ = 5 converges monotonically to near-zero. New formulation F_B(γ) = F_A + correction term guarantees convergence for any γ ≥ 0, even at Re=1000 (ν small). Adaptive regularization via evolved filter-relax: full FE model with filter radius δ²~h, relaxation parameter χ~Δt reduces effective error plateau 10×, enabling efficient POD ROM with r=20 to match higher-dimensional solutions.
deeper_mechanics: Feedback control law u_t + (u·∇)u + ∇p = F_B(γ) where F_B depends linearly on error e = u - U_target. Linearization around target shows error evolution e_t ≈ -γe - (correction), proving exponential decay rate γ + c₀ν. Evolved filter-relax has three stages: (1) solve feedback system; (2) solve Δu_bar = u with filtering radius δ; (3) u_new = χu + (1-χ)ū. Analysis shows ||e_n|| ≤ ρ^n ||e_0|| + plateau, where ρ = exp(-(γ + c₀ν)) and plateau ~ χ. Adaptive switching: while first term dominates (χ enabled), use regularization; when first term < threshold, disable (χ=0) to eliminate plateau.
failure_boundary: Convergence proof assumes smooth target velocity and compatible boundary conditions; mismatch or discontinuities cause feedback instability. Theory holds only for sufficiently small ν and smooth domains; complex geometries with thin boundary layers violate assumptions. Feedback gain γ + c₀ν can become very small if ν → 0 and γ is chosen conservatively, slowing convergence catastrophically. Nonlinear solver for full system at each step may not converge if error is initially large or system is highly nonlinear (inertial-dominated). Evolved regularization introduces additional error that may not decay with mesh/time refinement if filter parameter δ is not tuned correctly. ROM basis (POD from uncontrolled flow) may not span controlled dynamics well—basis update required for very different target velocities or high Reynolds numbers outside training regime.

title: Yanlai Chen: GPT-PINN and TGPT-PINN
speaker: Yanlai Chen
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. One popular way is to let a learning program (a huge bank of dials the computer tunes by trial and error until its answers look right) also be told the laws of physics as it learns. But when you want to solve physics equations that change as one value—like thickness or temperature—shifts, training the whole learning program over and over is too slow. This talk shows how to reuse a trained learning program from one value and bolt it together with other versions at different values, feeding the result into a tiny network that learns how the answer shifts as the value changes—giving you accurate answers fast.
core_problem: Physics equations that change as parameters shift (like thickness, angle, or pressure) are everywhere in engineering. Right now, the slow way is to train a learning program from scratch each time the parameter changes. We waste time and also waste computing power because the same size network might be overkill for one setting and too small for another. We need a way to train once and reuse that work for many different parameter values.
first_principles_model: Start with a learning program trained on one physics equation at one parameter value—it has millions of dials tuned to make its predictions match the physics. The new idea: take these trained programs from selected parameter values and treat each one as a single unit (the way a simple rule or a sensor is a unit). Stack them together and feed the results into a second, much tinier learning program. This tiny program only needs to learn how the answer shifts as the parameter changes, not rediscover the physics from scratch. That's the first version. The second version adds a mixing layer before each trained unit, allowing the tiny program to stretch or squeeze the trained outputs into new patterns—like translating between different languages—so it can reuse them even more flexibly.
key_claims: Training a learning program for each new parameter value is too slow when you have many values to solve.
You can treat already-trained learning programs as building blocks inside a much smaller network.
The outer network can be shrunk to just one hidden layer with far fewer dials than the original.
You can add exactly as many dials as you need by building the layer one dial at a time.
This approach gives accurate answers across all parameter values with far less computation.
Adding a mixing layer before the trained blocks lets the outer network reuse them in even more flexible ways.

important_terms.meaning: A learning program trained to predict physics by having two goals: match real observations and also obey the physics equation (the penalty for breaking the equation is added to the training score).
A method that takes already-trained learning programs from a few parameter values and feeds their outputs into a smaller learning program that learns how the answer shifts across all parameters.
The version with a mixing layer added—the smaller program can stretch and squeeze the trained outputs before using them, letting it adapt them to new situations.
A physics equation whose answer changes as you change one or more values (like how the temperature pattern in a heated rod changes as the rod gets thicker or the heat input rises).
A learning program that sits on top of other learning programs and learns how to combine or switch between them, treating them as tools rather than training from scratch.

stanford_connections: This work sits at the crossroads of three ideas: training learning programs to respect physics rules, compressing big learning programs into smaller ones that still work, and learning how to reuse trained programs across many situations.

Earlier talks showed neural operators—ways to train one learning program that works for all parameter values at once. This talk does something related but different: it stacks pre-trained programs together instead.
The repeated pattern in this whole seminar is: how do we avoid re-training and re-computing the same physics over and over? This talk answers it by showing how trained work can become reusable parts.
practical_caution: The trained programs you reuse are only useful if you picked parameter values that actually cover the kinds of answers that appear. Pick wrong values, and the tiny program might confidently give answers that are completely off. It's like training someone to recognize animals by only showing them cats and dogs, then asking them about a llama.
selected_evidence: Generative Pre-Trained PINN (GPT-PINN).
A brand-new meta-learning paradigm for parametric systems.
Its outer-/meta-network is hyper-reduced.
Grows this hidden layer one neuron at a time.
Transformed GPT-PINN, TGPT-PINN.
takeaway: Physics equations with changing parameters get faster and cheaper to solve when you reuse trained learning programs (like building blocks) in a smaller network rather than training from zero each time.
worked_example: PDE: ∂u/∂t + u∂u/∂x = ν∂²u/∂x² (Burgers' equation, parameter ν). Baseline PINN: minimize ||∂u_net/∂t + u_net∂u_net/∂x - ν∂²u_net/∂x²||² over collocation points + BC loss. GPT-PINN transfers: pre-train on ν ∈ [0.01, 1], then fine-tune on ν=0.005 with <10 gradient steps. TGPT-PINN: time-stepping version, solve in windows (t ∈ [0,Δt], then roll forward), stabilizes long-term integration.
deeper_mechanics: PINN loss: L = α L_r + β L_ic + γ L_bc where L_r = ||r(x_c,t_c)||² (residual), L_ic, L_bc are boundary/IC losses. Auto-differentiation computes ∂u/∂t, ∂²u/∂x². Transfer learning via meta-learning: compute gradient on ν₁ data, transfer to ν₂. Time-stepping PINN applies PINN on short windows u(t+Δt) = integrator(u(t)), reduces total loss depth.
failure_boundary: Gradient-based methods struggle with shock formation (Burgers' ν → 0). Meta-learning requires sufficiently similar source/target PDEs; transfer across equations fails. Spatial high-frequency modes ill-resolved by standard neural networks (spectral bias).

title: Burcu Beykal: A DDPS Engineering Approach for Supply Chain Management and Enterprise-Wide Optimization
speaker: Burcu Beykal
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical systems behave by learning from data. This talk shifts focus: instead of predicting motion or heat flow, it asks how to help a company make good decisions across interconnected layers — planning what to make, scheduling when to make it, managing supplies — where each layer's choices affect what other layers can actually do.
core_problem: Real factories and supply chains don't operate in isolation. A decision made by the planning team (make 500 units next month) only works if the scheduling team (who decides the day-to-day timetable) can actually fit it in, and if supplies are available when needed. If you optimize each layer separately, you often get a plan that looks good on paper but is impossible to execute because the layers conflict with each other. The problem: many interconnected decisions depend on each other, and finding a solution that works at every level is hard.
first_principles_model: Think of supply-chain decisions as a chain of bosses making decisions. A top manager (the leader) chooses a high-level plan: how much to make, which customers to serve. Then the operating teams (the followers) look at that plan and decide the detailed schedule: which equipment runs when, which workers shift when. But often the followers discover the leader's plan is impossible—there isn't enough time or equipment. In math, this two-level game is called bi-level programming: the leader picks first, then the followers react, and the leader has to pick something the followers can actually execute. The real difficulty is that at the operating level, decisions come in two flavors: continuous (a machine can run for any amount of time) and discrete (a shipment either goes out or doesn't). Mixing these two types of decisions creates enormous math problems that regular solvers struggle with. A data-driven process systems approach uses three tools together: learning patterns from historical data about what the factory can do, thinking of the factory as a network of connected parts that constrain each other, and using smart algorithms to find a plan that works at all levels.
key_claims: Real factories serve many products at once and must handle many different kinds of decisions, making them inherently complicated.
To keep a factory running well and making profit, different teams (planning, scheduling, supply) must coordinate and not work against each other.
The two-level leader-follower structure captures this: the planner must choose something the operator can execute.
The operating layer has many yes-or-no decisions (which pieces get made, which routes get shipped) mixed with smooth decisions (how long things run), and that mix makes the math very hard to solve.
Thinking of supply chains through the lens of process systems (how materials flow through interconnected stages) gives structure to otherwise overwhelming optimization problems.
Using data to learn realistic models of what plants can do, combined with smart optimization, makes enterprise decisions more reliable and practical.

important_terms.meaning: Making the best decisions across all the layers of a company — planning what to make, scheduling when and how, managing supplies — at once, rather than having each team decide alone.

Keeping track of and coordinating everything required to get materials and finished products where they need to be: buying supplies, shipping, storing, moving through the factory, and getting to customers.

A math structure where one decision-maker (the leader) chooses a plan first, then another (the follower) has to execute it and can only do certain things; the leader has to pick something the follower can actually carry out.

A math problem involving two types of decisions mixed together: smooth choices (like how much of something to make, which can be any decimal number) and yes-or-no choices (like whether to run a machine, which must be 0 or 1).

The field that studies how materials, energy, and information flow through interconnected industrial processes, combining math models, optimization, and decision-making to run factories and chemical plants well.

stanford_connections: This talk takes the data-driven approach the series started with and moves it from predicting physics (heat, flow) to solving practical business decisions.
It connects machine-learned models with constrained optimization: using what data teaches us about realistic operations as part of deciding what to do.
It also mirrors a big problem in planning systems: local choices (what my team should do) must align with global goals (what the whole company needs).
practical_caution: A smart computer program that recommends decisions can steer you wrong if the model of "what's actually possible" oversimplifies the real operating layer. If the detailed constraints are left out or weakened too much, the planner might recommend something that scheduling or operations cannot execute. Before acting on any recommendation, the operations team must verify it actually works in practice.
selected_evidence: Supply Chain management and Enterprise wide optimization.
Multi-dimensional, multi-purpose, and multi-product systems.
Optimal coordination of each element and their robust response to changing market conditions.
Bi-level programming is well-suited.
High numbers of integer variables are present in the scheduling problems.
takeaway: Supply-chain and factory decisions form a nested stack: every choice only succeeds if it remains doable at the detailed operating level. Decisions are only truly good when they survive the whole chain from planning all the way down to execution.
worked_example: Bilevel planning/scheduling integration: 7-day production planning with 2 products and dynamic demand profile (low, peak midweek, decline). State-task network with 3 feeds, 4 units, 8 tasks producing 2 products. Upper level: minimize inventory + production cost; lower level: minimize production cost subject to continuous-time schedule constraints. Demand peak at midday 3 results in production targets; scheduling must verify realization. Cost difference between Nomad (sample-based) and Argonaut (model-based) reflects ~5-30 unit material discrepancy depending on parametrization; both achieve feasible, optimal schedules. Extension to quadratic variable costs and cubic inventory costs (NLP-MIQP) shows cost Amplification at small carryover differences.
deeper_mechanics: Bilevel program (upper minimizes over x, lower solves MINLP yielding y*(x)): upper objective subject to constraint 'y* is globally optimal for lower level given x'. Complementary slackness from KKT conditions introduces nonlinearity even in LP-LP case. Domino framework: design-of-experiments on upper-level variables, deterministic solution of lower level to global optimality (via CPLEX, BARON, Antigone), derivative-free optimization (Nomad via compass moves, Argonaut via Kriging surrogate + bound tightening) on upper level. Quadratic programming problem with L1 regularization (sparsity constraint) formulated via auxiliary variables (+, -) for absolute value decomposition. Inventory balance equations: ending_inventory = production + prior_day_inventory - demand.
failure_boundary: Feasibility not guaranteed without global optimality of lower level (feasible solution must have lower level globally optimal). Branch-and-bound suffers with variable count; genetic algorithms lack constraint handling robustness. Mixed-integer formulations prevent KKT-based reduction to single level. Sample-based optimizers very sensitive to starting point for highly nonlinear lower-level problems; 121 seconds per sample for complex 3-charging-tank scheduling makes Nomad exhaustive. One infeasible run observed in 3-tank multi-product case; Argonaut unable to find solution within 24 hours. Stochastic demand adds dimension: must solve scheduling for each scenario branch, increasing computational burden; no guarantee worst-case solution generalizes to all scenarios.

title: Yexiang Xue: Vertical Reasoning Enhanced Learning, Generation and Scientific Discovery
speaker: Yexiang Xue
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of only using hand-written rules. One approach is to combine two different kinds of computer thinking: learning (a program tuning millions of dials by trial and error until its answers match reality) and reasoning (a program that checks if answers obey explicit rules). This talk shows why mixing them together—not one after the other, but tangled inside each other—works better: reasoning can shrink the space of wrong answers a learning program needs to search, so it finds solutions faster, and checks them against the rules as it goes.
core_problem: Learning programs are good at spotting patterns hidden in data. Reasoning programs are good at enforcing rules that must always be true. Self-directed scientific agents need both, but nobody has figured out a clean way to weave them together so they help each other instead of getting in the way.
first_principles_model: Vertical reasoning means building a structured reasoning step inside or alongside a learning program, not just using it after the program finishes. In image generation, a system called SPRING weaves spatial reasoning directly into the generator: as it builds an image, it checks that new parts obey the constraints, so the output respects the rules on data it has never seen before. In finding mathematical equations from data, reasoning cuts down which equations are even worth trying—it skips equation forms that contradict the data structure. In discovering physical equations, the same idea applies: reasoning removes impossible forms first, leaving fewer candidates for trial and error. In a logic-and-counting problem (combining yes-or-no rules with counting tasks), reasoning over parity constraints (odd-even checks that simplify the search) helps the solver give stronger guarantees about what it found.
key_claims: Automated reasoning and learning are two different kinds of thinking that work well together in AI.
Spatial reasoning can be woven directly into a program that generates images.
Checking rules as you go improves the final answer and makes it easier to explain why.
Reasoning steps make it faster to find mathematical equations from data and discover physical equations.
Organizing logic constraints (especially odd-even rules) helps solvers work through counting problems.
The big goal is self-directed agents that mix learning and reasoning together, not pick just one.

important_terms.meaning: A layer of rule-checking built inside or woven into a learning program, so it enforces rules while learning, not after.
A program that generates images and has a spatial reasoning module built inside it—so as it builds the image, it checks that each part follows the constraints.
Searching over possible mathematical equations to find one that matches the data you collected.
A problem type that mixes yes-or-no logical rules with counting or probability questions—asking: which combinations of answers satisfy both the rules and the counting goals?
Odd-even parity rules (one thing is on, the other is off, but not both and not neither) that can be organized to speed up a solver's search.

stanford_connections: This talk anchors to the series goal: computers learning to predict physical behavior. It shows why mixing reasoning directly into learning helps solve harder discovery problems.
It connects to other talks in the series that find equations from data and discover physical laws, and to talks on generating images that obey constraints.
It also connects to the broader theme: as we build agents that need to solve real problems, learned models alone often fail—they need reasoning steps and verification built in when rules matter.
practical_caution: Building reasoning into learning can make the system more reliable, but only if the rules themselves are correct. If you state a constraint wrong, or leave out an important rule, the system can confidently solve the wrong problem instead.
selected_evidence: Vertical reasoning enhanced learning generation and scientific discovery.
Spatial Reasoning INtegrated Generator (SPRING).
Embeds a spatial reasoning module inside a deep generative network.
Expedite symbolic regression, and to learn Partial Differential Equations.
XOR constraints enables solvers with constant approximation guarantees.
takeaway: Reasoning acts as a built-in support structure for learning and generation: it guides the program toward correct answers, cuts down the space of possibilities, and checks progress along the way—especially when the task has explicit rules to use.
worked_example: Illustrative example: guided manifold learning on porous media flow. Training set of 50-200 simulations with varying permeability fields (lognormal, correlated). Deep network learns low-dimensional latent space where solutions concentrate. Prediction speedup 10-50x on unseen permeability realizations. Compared to linear POD, nonlinear manifold captures tensor-train decomposition structure of heterogeneous problems.
deeper_mechanics: Manifold linearization: decompose solution u = u_lin + δu where u_lin satisfies linearized PDE around reference parameter. Deep network learns δu in low-dim space. Jointly optimize reference state and manifold basis to minimize prediction error across parameter range. For parabolic PDEs (diffusion-dominated), manifold typically 5-20 dimensional despite 1000+ DOF discretization. Guided means incorporating physics constraints: enforce boundary conditions strongly in loss, penalize non-physical solutions.
failure_boundary: Method fails when nonlinearity dominates over linear component (high Rayleigh number, strong convection). Manifold assumption breaks at bifurcation points. Extrapolation beyond training parameter range unreliable. Ill-posedness if reference state poorly chosen.

title: Gianluca Iaccarino: AutoEncoders for Aerodynamic Predictions
speaker: Gianluca Iaccarino
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from data instead of only hand-written math. This talk focuses on a specific tool: autoencoders, which are programs that squeeze aerodynamic flow data down to a handful of numbers and then rebuild it, so computers can quickly predict what flow looks like over many different wing shapes.
core_problem: Predicting aerodynamic flow over many wing shapes requires generating new flow cases fast. The problem: flow fields have many dimensions (many numbers needed to describe them), and they twist around in nonlinear ways (the math doesn't follow straight-line rules). Squeezing the data using only straight-line math can miss important structures, especially when flow peels away from the wing surface. Using curved-line squeezing raises a harder question: can you trust the predictions, and can you measure how uncertain they are?
first_principles_model: An autoencoder takes a high-dimensional flow field (many numbers describing the air motion) and compresses it into a handful of numbers—a compact summary called a latent code. Then it rebuilds a flow field from that summary. the main idea is that with a well-built dataset, those handful of numbers can line up with things engineers care about: wing geometry and performance measures. The lecture compares curved-line compression (autoencoders) against a statistical method (Gaussian process regression) and straight-line compression, while tracking uncertainty from three sources: how you build the network, the tuning choices you make, and how much training data you have.
key_claims: Autoencoders can squeeze aerodynamic flow data nonlinearly into a handful of numbers.
Those numbers can support prediction for new wing geometries the network has never seen.
A well-built training dataset can make those numbers line up with aerodynamic performance in ways you can understand.
The method works for both attached flow and separated flow regimes.
Uncertainty comes from three places: how you build the network, the tuning choices you make, and how much training data you use.
Comparing curved-line compression, statistical methods, and straight-line compression shows when curved-line actually helps.

important_terms.meaning: A program with millions of dials that learns two things together: first, how to crunch many numbers into a small handful (the encoder), and second, how to rebuild many numbers from that handful (the decoder). It tuned by trial and error on examples until the rebuilt version looks like the original.
A handful of learned numbers that capture the most important ways the original data changes. Think of it as a fingerprint—different fingerprints describe different flows.
A flight regime where the air sticks poorly to the wing and peels away, creating swirling wake behavior downstream—more complex than when air hugs the surface smoothly.
Uncertainty caused by decisions you make in building the network or assumptions you embed—separate from noise in the raw data, and often hard to spot.
Squeezing many numbers into a handful using curved surfaces and bent rules, instead of only straight-line formulas.

stanford_connections: This talk ties together autoencoders, simplified models that run fast, compact summaries of data, and aerodynamic prediction while tracking uncertainty.
It builds on earlier talks about simplified nonlinear models by asking a harder question: do those learned numbers actually correspond to things engineers care about?
It also applies directly to design: when you have thousands of possible wing shapes to evaluate, this method can rank them without running slow step-by-step physics simulations each time.
practical_caution: A smooth, simple-looking summary can appear to make sense while hiding danger when you predict in new regions the network has never seen during training. To trust the results, check three things: does slightly changing how you build the network wreck the results, does your training data cover the wing shapes and flight conditions you actually care about, and how well does the network predict flow it has never encountered?
selected_evidence: Auto encoders for aerodynamic predictions.
Non-linear compression to construct a low-dimensional latent representation.
Generate new (unseen) cases.
Latent variables that can be interpreted in terms of aerodynamic performance.
Uncertainties due to the autoencoder architecture, the hyperparameters and the amount of the training data.
takeaway: Useful aerodynamic prediction compresses flow into a handful of numbers that predict accurately, explain what is happening, and track uncertainty so you know when to doubt the answer.
worked_example: A database of 30 airfoil geometries (different thickness and angle of attack) was simulated at full CFD fidelity. A shallow autoencoder with latent dimension 2-3 trained on concatenated (geometry+flow solution) tensors learned to compress 40,000 CFD outputs to 2 latent numbers. At latent size 1, the model correctly captured the linear regime (low angle-of-attack) but failed when stall occurred, showing clean interpretability: multiple latent-1 values map to the same angle for pre-stall, but they split when stall physics emerges. Reconstruction time: 0.1 seconds per case on single GPU vs. hours for full CFD.
deeper_mechanics: Deterministic (not variational) autoencoder with convolutional+fully-connected layers bottlenecks to latent vector z. Sequential training starts at P=1, then P=2, P=3, conditioning each higher layer on lower-layer latent codes to preserve interpretability across dimensions. Latent space conditioning builds a mapping from input (thickness, angle-of-attack) to latent variables via polynomial regression. Decoder reconstructs flow field; loss = ||data - decoder(z)||^2. Ensemble of 100 autoencoders with architectural variations (layer counts, activation functions) captures model uncertainty; quantile bands show where data is scarce.
failure_boundary: Limited training data (30 cases) means extrapolation beyond the database (new airfoil families, operating regimes) produces hallucinated fields that violate physics. When training data has a gap (e.g., angle range 5-25° excluded), the latent space becomes non-smooth and interpolation in the gap yields non-physical solutions. Noise in input CFD data corrupts latent representations; high-resolution features (boundary-layer separation details) compress poorly to 2-3 numbers, so reconstructions blur sharp gradients. Multi-fidelity (viscous vs. inviscid) datasets mixed without explicit metadata cause latent codes to entangle different physics, degrading generalization.

title: Fabio Giampaolo: Learning Paradigms for Neural Networks: The Locally Backpropagated Forward-Forward Algorithm
speaker: Fabio Giampaolo
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. One method teaches neural networks using small steps within each layer instead of one big step from the output all the way back to the input. This talk shows how that method, called locally backpropagated forward-forward, works: each layer gets its own score for how good its answer is, instead of waiting for error signals to bounce backward from the end.
core_problem: Backpropagation—the standard way to train neural networks by sending error signals backward through all layers—runs into trouble when models have pieces that don't change smoothly (so you can't compute how to fix them), when computers doing the learning are scattered across different machines, or when they include physics simulators that can't be fed into a single chain of calculations.
first_principles_model: Backpropagation squeezes a single error signal backward through the whole network to nudge every dial in the right direction. The forward-forward algorithm instead gives each layer its own job: look at correct answers versus wrong answers and learn which one looks right. The locally backpropagated forward-forward strategy combines these ideas—it uses calculus-based direction-finding inside each layer (like backpropagation) but lets each layer work more on its own, without needing one giant error signal flowing all the way through.
key_claims: Backpropagation is still the most common way to train neural networks.
Real-world and physics-based settings show where backpropagation sending signals backward through the whole network hits a wall.
Pieces that don't change smoothly can block error signals from flowing backward.
When training is split across different types of computers, it pushes us toward methods where each part works more on its own, without needing one central signal.
The locally backpropagated forward-forward algorithm merges backpropagation's calculus-based tuning with forward-forward's layer-by-layer learning goals.
The aim is to make deep-learning methods work in more places and situations.

important_terms.meaning: The standard method for training neural networks: use calculus to figure out how much to nudge each dial, by sending error signals backward through all layers step by step.
A training method created by Geoffrey Hinton that scores each layer by looking at correct answers and wrong answers separately, without computing backward error signals.
Training where each layer or section of the network uses its own score or goal, instead of having one error signal from the final output control everything.
A piece of the model where small changes to input don't cause smooth, predictable changes to output—this breaks the calculus chain that backpropagation needs.
A collection of different computers or processors—perhaps fast ones and slow ones, with different memory or designs—all working together on one job.

stanford_connections: This talk connects to how we design rules that make neural networks learn, how to spread that learning across many computers, and how to build learning systems for science and physics.
It builds on earlier talks where smooth calculus doesn't hold—showing what to do when models break those normal assumptions.
It also fits into broader conversations about what makes learning succeed beyond just the network design itself—the actual training rules are what drive progress forward.
practical_caution: When testing new training methods, look at whether they stay steady while learning, whether they scale up to bigger networks, and whether they actually get right answers on real jobs—not whether they sound like how brains work or fit nicely on scattered computers.
selected_evidence: Backpropagation is the most widely used method for training Neural Networks.
Non-differentiable components within neural architectures.
Distributed learning on heterogeneous devices.
Locally Backpropagated Forward Forward training strategy.
Merges the effectiveness of backpropagation with the appealing attributes of the Forward-Forward algorithm.
takeaway: Training that happens layer-by-layer, with each layer working toward its own goal, can make learning more separated and modular. But it still has to solve the credit-assignment problem: each part of the network has to figure out which of its own changes help or hurt the final answer, and it needs to do that well enough to keep up with backpropagation.
worked_example:
The team trained deep neural networks on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST datasets using the forward-forward algorithm as an alternative to backpropagation. With the pure forward-forward approach, layers accumulated errors that didn't propagate backward, so deeper layers (3, 4, 5) performed worse than early layers (1, 2). They then introduced a locally backpropagated forward-forward (LBFF) hybrid: splitting the network into blocks, applying backpropagation within each block while training blocks according to forward-forward principles across blocks. With 10 blocks (approximately 2 layers per block), the convergence pattern smoothed dramatically—the three training curves (stacks of 1-3, 1-10, and 1-15 layers) that previously separated at epoch 50 remained coherent through training, with overall accuracy improvement of approximately 5-10% depending on configuration.

For random partitioning with 5-epoch intervals, computational cost per epoch dropped to nearly that of the pure forward-forward algorithm while maintaining accuracy comparable to standard backpropagation. The overall wall-clock time for training was faster than backpropagation-only approaches on the same hardware.
deeper_mechanics:
The forward-forward algorithm replaces the forward-backward pass of backpropagation with two forward passes. Each layer has its own local loss function based on a goodness metric: neurons compute activation magnitudes and compare them to a threshold θ. For positive data (real samples), the loss encourages high goodness above threshold; for negative data (corrupted samples), it encourages low goodness below threshold. Mathematically: L = (||h||^2 - θ)^2 for positive data and (θ - ||h||^2)^2 for negative data, where h is the hidden activation vector.

The weight update rule becomes: ∂w ∝ (goodness - θ) · h · input, which is purely local—each layer only needs information from its immediate inputs and outputs. The locally backpropagated variant partitions the network into K blocks, applying backpropagation's chain rule within each block while enforcing the forward-forward objective between blocks. This creates a hybrid: information flows both ways within blocks (full gradient propagation) but only forward between blocks (local learning rules). A randomized partitioning strategy—varying block boundaries at fixed intervals during training—ensures all layers experience both local and global optimization pressure.
failure_boundary: Pure forward-forward networks struggle to learn hierarchical representations because deeper layers receive no gradient signal from the output loss. On MNIST, accuracy plateaus around 95-97%, worse than standard neural networks. Adding convolutional architectures makes the approach even harder because convolutions have spatial structure that doesn't decompose naturally into independent layer-wise goodness measures. The method requires generating negative data (corrupted versions of real samples), and the quality of this negative set dramatically affects learning; choosing a poor corruption strategy causes the network to learn trivial patterns. Goodness is a global property (norm of activations) so it cannot distinguish between different modes of failure. The hyperparameter θ (goodness threshold) must be tuned per layer, and there's no principled way to set it—practitioners must search empirically. On high-dimensional tasks (ImageNet scale), the method's advantage over backpropagation diminishes because communication of layer information through sparse negative samples becomes bottlenecked.

title: Doug James: Recent Progress in Reduced-Order Modeling for Computer Graphics and Sound
speaker: Doug James
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples. This talk covers a trick for making those predictions faster: instead of computing what happens to every tiny piece of a cloth or water surface, you compute what happens to just a few key pieces, then guess the rest. The talk shows how this trick works for making movies (cloth folding the right way) and sound (splashes that sound real).
core_problem: When you want to make a movie or video game where cloth drapes naturally or water splashes sound real, you need a program that simulates what happens. But simulating every tiny piece—every thread in the cloth, every water ripple—takes forever and costs a fortune. If you skip to a coarser version to save time, the cloth might fold differently and the sound might be wrong. So artists and programmers are stuck: they want cheap and fast, but also correct.
first_principles_model: Here's the trick: instead of tracking everything, track only the most important wiggles—the big folds, the main vibrations. A program can learn which few pieces of cloth or water matter most, simulate just those, then figure out where the rest goes. For cloth and thin shells (things that bend and fold), you start with a coarse guess, then gradually add finer detail without breaking what was already right. For water sound, you model a few coupled bubbles (imagine bubbles inside the water pushing and pulling each other)—when bubbles oscillate (expand and shrink), they create vibrations in the water, which your ear hears as sound.
key_claims: You can start simulating cloth and thin shells at coarse resolution, then add finer detail in a way that keeps the original coarse behavior correct.
By tracking only a few key vibration modes of cloth or water, you can make simulation cheap while keeping it plausible.
Progressive simulation—starting coarse and gradually refining—lets artists control and direct the physics interactively.
When you change simulation resolution (go from coarse to fine), the appearance should stay consistent; the cloth should fold the same way, just with more wrinkles.
Coupled bubble oscillators (vibrating bubbles that push and pull on each other) can synthesize water sounds that sound physically grounded.
Physics simulation in graphics and sound must satisfy two masters: it must be numerically close to reality and also remain steerable and reliable for artists.

important_terms.meaning: A workflow where you start simulating something at rough resolution, then gradually add finer and finer detail without changing how the coarse version looked.
Choosing how fine or coarse to make your simulation depending on what you need—coarse when you want speed, finer when you need to see tiny wrinkles.
A method for making sure that when cloth or deformable objects touch each other or an obstacle, the collision is handled smoothly and realistically without tears or wild jumps.
A model where small bubbles in water oscillate (expand and shrink) and influence each other's vibrations; these vibrations travel through water and become the sound you hear.

Physics simulation that stays plausible and true to the laws of nature, but also responds to what an artist wants—cloth can be tugged where needed, or vibrations can be tweaked to match a sound design.

stanford_connections: This talk shows one way to use reduced-order models—not only in engineering and prediction, but in art and interactive media where speed and control are as important as accuracy.
It bridges the gap between mathematical techniques learned in other talks and the real world of film, games, and interactive design where you need to run physics in real time.
It also reveals that multiscale modeling (looking at systems at many different size scales at once) solves practical problems in creativity and perception, not just in academic prediction.
practical_caution: These reduced models are judged by two things: do they look and sound plausible to a human eye and ear? Do they stay physically close to the full detailed version? A model can be mathematically correct but fail because an artist cannot steer it (cloth won't drape the way the director wanted), or because tiny artifacts appear on screen that break the illusion.
selected_evidence: Recent progress in reduced-order modeling for computer graphics and sound.
Progressive simulation for art-directable physics.
Coarse-to-fine, level-of-detail simulation methods.
Up-res and still get consistent, higher-fidelity results.
Reduced-order vibration models for synthesizing water sound using coupled acoustic bubbles.
takeaway: Reduced-order models are not only a tool for engineers to predict physical behavior faster in lab settings. They are also a way to make physical simulation usable in real creative work—movies, games, interactive design—where speed, control, and plausibility all matter at once.
worked_example:
Progressive cloth quasi-statics: a coarse mesh (1500 triangles) solves instantly; when refined to high resolution, the solution is consistent with the coarse result (same rough crease pattern, no mesh-lock artifacts). Compared to direct fine-scale simulation (prohibitively slow) or cascadic approaches (which bake in coarse artifacts), this achieves interactive design plus high-quality offline refinement.

For water-bubble sounds: coupling 10,000+ small bubbles reduces frequency from 3 kHz (uncoupled) to ~200 Hz (coupled). GPU wave-equation solver on time-frozen geometry evaluates sound radiance 1000× faster than CPU approaches. Spectrogram analysis shows the lower-frequency lobe appears only when coupling is included, matching recordings of ocean wave crashes.
deeper_mechanics:
Progressive simulation minimizes E(x) = E_membrane + E_bending + E_contact where contact is barrier method (repulsive potential). When prolongating (mesh refinement), the coarse model uses fine-scale elastic energies restricted to coarse degrees of freedom. Newton's method solves: ∇E = 0, using the Hessian H = ∇²E in the Newton step. The Hessian includes both contact (at current mesh level) and elastic (from fine scale). Inexact Newton accepts coarse Hessian, avoiding full fine-scale cost.

For bubbles: the mass matrix has diagonal stiffness K (gas pressure, surface tension) and dense mass M (inter-bubble coupling via incompressible flow). Time-stepping via M dv/dt = -K u uses Cholesky factorization of M; regularity ensures positive-definiteness. Sound radiation solves the time-domain wave equation ∂²p/∂t² = c² ∇²p with bubble surfaces as Dirichlet boundary data. A frozen-geometry approximation evaluates this independently for each time frame, then sums contributions.
failure_boundary: Progressive mesh refinement can lose contact constraints if new mesh nodes penetrate obstacles; continuous collision detection and edge-based inflation fix this at cost. Strain limiting (preventing excessive stretching) adds energy; poorly tuned limits create artifacts. For bubbles, the Maxwellian injection assumption breaks down if actual particle distributions are non-Gaussian. Near contact, the barrier potential becomes numerically stiff, requiring tiny timesteps. Wave equation is only valid in linear regime; large-amplitude pressure fluctuations (supersonic flow) violate assumptions. Coupling mass matrix can lose positive-definiteness if bubbles coalesce; regularization is heuristic.

title: Francesco Romor: Intrusive Model Order Reduction Using Neural Network Approximants
speaker: Francesco Romor
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. One popular shortcut is to throw away unnecessary details and keep only the most important numbers—a process called model reduction. This talk shows one way to do that: use a learning program (a system with millions of little dials tuned by trial and error) to spot the smooth curved surface where all the solutions live, then run the actual physics equations on that compressed shape during prediction, so you get the speed of learning plus the trust of keeping the real physics visible.
core_problem: When you want to predict how something physical behaves—say, how heat spreads through a complex metal part—you can either write down all the rules (a rule that says how something changes from moment to moment or place to place) or let a computer learn from examples. A fast way to do both is to compress the problem: find a much smaller set of numbers that hold the key information. The old standard way does this with flat mathematical sheets (picking just a few main directions where solutions move), but this fails when the actual solutions wiggle around in a curved shape that flat sheets can't capture well. Learning programs are good at spotting curved shapes, but most of them forget the physics rules entirely once they've learned, turning into pure guesses with no connection to the real equations.
first_principles_model: This method keeps the actual physics equations running during prediction instead of abandoning them. It uses a learning program—specifically one that compresses data by squeezing it through a narrow middle layer, then rebuilds it on the other side—to find the curved surface where answers actually live. This squeezed shape has far fewer numbers than the original problem, so the physics equations run much faster on it. Then techniques that avoid computing expensive parts (only checking whether the physics rules hold at a few key spots rather than everywhere) make the cost even lower. The payoff is that you get both the speed of a compressed model and the visibility and trustworthiness of keeping the real equations in the loop.
key_claims: When solutions form a curved shape that doesn't lie flat, traditional compression methods (keeping only main directions) can't capture it well without keeping too many numbers.
Learning programs can spot curved surfaces accurately in data.
Most current learning-based reduced models toss away the equations after training and become pure guesses.
A model that stays intrusive—keeps the equations running during prediction—gives you both speed and visible physics.
A learning program that compresses by squeezing through a narrow middle layer can reduce the number of important numbers while keeping curved surfaces.
Techniques that evaluate physics rules at only a few key spots (instead of everywhere) make the compressed model fast enough to use.

important_terms.meaning: Compressing a physical problem while keeping the actual governing equations running during prediction, so you stay connected to the real rules.

A number that measures how many main directions (like finding just the 3 most important compass directions out of infinite directions) you need to capture a curved surface well; if it decays slowly, you need many directions.
The smooth curved surface or shape traced out by all the different answers as you change the input numbers or physical parameters.
A learning program that compresses data by squeezing it through a narrow middle layer with fewer numbers, then rebuilds it back to full size; the narrow middle layer captures the essential patterns.
Techniques that speed up an equation solver by checking whether the physics rules hold true at only a few selected spots instead of everywhere, cutting computation time dramatically.

stanford_connections: This talk brings together three big ideas from the seminar: how to compress high-dimensional problems, how learning programs can spot curved shapes in data, and how to keep equations visible while adding learning.
It contrasts with talks about pure data-driven learning by explaining why keeping the original physics equations matters for trust and speed.
It also relates to talks about finding the main directions in data by showing that curved surfaces—not just flat sheets—can hold the key to fast, accurate predictions.
practical_caution: This approach requires that you have access to the actual governing equations and the numerical program that solves them, not just examples of past predictions. That's a strength—you can see and verify the physics—but a weakness when you only have a simulator that spits out answers without letting you look inside. It's harder to set up than methods that just learn from data alone, and when you move it to a new computer or new problem, it requires careful handling of the equations themselves.
selected_evidence: Intrusive model order reduction of parametric PDEs using neural networks.
Slowly decaying Kolmogorov n-width.
Neural networks as solution manifold approximants.
Retaining the underlying physical and numerical models during the predictive/online stage.
Autoencoders to further compress the dimensionality.
takeaway: Using a learning program to spot curved shapes works best when you treat it as a helper alongside the physics, not as a replacement for it. The equations stay, the learning program just compresses the search space.
worked_example: Heat transfer on unstructured mesh (32,000-200,000 cells): ROM with 300 modes computed via randomized SVD (RSVD) in <5 seconds. Latency: 74 ms per inference vs 10-100 seconds for full CFD solve. Speedup: 135-1350x depending on problem complexity. Adaptive magic points: instead of projecting residual onto all basis vectors (cost O(n_dof·n_modes²)), select 150-200 critical sample points where residual varies most (QR-pivoting on Jacobian at these points). This reduces projection cost from O(n) to O(m) where m = magic point count << n. Tested on Burgers equation (2D domain, 1000 snapshots): ROM error stays <1% for 50 timesteps forward prediction, then grows linearly (~0.1% per additional step). For 500-step prediction, error reaches ~5%.
deeper_mechanics: Intrusive ROM: given full discretization du/dt = F(u), project to reduced basis V ∈ R^{n×k}: d(V^T u)/dt = V^T F(V·(V^T u)). Cost: evaluating F still requires n FOM operations, but ROM state (V^T u) is only k-dimensional. Magic points reduce this: select m collocation points where F evaluated, approximate full projection by interpolating (Empirical Interpolation Method, EIM). Loss: ||V^T F - W·diag(f_m)||_F where W ∈ R^{k×m} weights the interpolated values and f_m are FOM evaluations at magic points only. Basis update via POD: SVD(snapshots matrix X) = U·Σ·V^T, keep top k singular vectors as V. RSVD uses randomized projections to compute this in O(n·k·log n) time.
failure_boundary: Basis decay: POD spectrum (singular values Σ) saturates for chaotic flows; many modes contribute equally, defeating compression. Magic point placement is fixed during training; if dynamics shift into unexplored regions, interpolation error explodes. Long-time integration: nonlinear ROMs drift away from attractor; residual grows quadratically in prediction time T. Parameter dependence: single ROM trained on one set of boundary conditions/Reynolds number fails on new parameters; must recompute basis for each case. Stiffness in ROM: temporal dynamics in reduced space can become more stiff than full model, requiring tiny timesteps despite dimensional reduction.

title: Alberto Padovan: Model Reduction via Optimization of Projection Operators and Reduced-Order Dynamics
speaker: Alberto Padovan
one_sentence: This whole seminar series chases one goal: getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of hand-written math. This talk takes on a specific puzzle: when you have data measurements from a system but can't see the equations running underneath, how do you build a fast, smaller version of the system that still predicts well? The answer is to let the computer learn not just which directions to pay attention to, but also how to project the data onto those directions—without needing the original equations.
core_problem: When engineers want to speed up predictions for a complicated system, they often start with a method called POD: a program that looks at measurement data and finds the strongest repeating patterns by looking for the directions where the data bounces around the most. But POD assumes you project by dropping perpendicular (like a shadow straight down). When a real system has huge sudden swings during its transient behavior (the wild motions before it settles down), perpendicular projection can twist and ruin those transient dynamics even though POD spotted the right lower-dimensional directions to work in. Many systems also hide their equations behind opaque solvers—software you can't see inside—so learning a better way to reduce them from measurement data alone would be useful, but the standard POD method doesn't provide it.
first_principles_model: A reduced model of a system needs two pieces: first, a low-dimensional subspace—a direction or plane in the data to project onto; second, a direction to do the projecting—which decides how the full high-dimensional state maps down to the low-dimensional space. Perpendicular projection is simple and common (it points straight in), but it can miss transient behavior you care about. Tilted projection (directions that don't point straight in) can protect input-output relationships or the system's wild early motions, but usually you need the governing equations to compute it. This method solves that by learning both the tilted projection directions and simplified polynomial equations directly from measurement sequences. It does this by solving an optimization problem—a search over special curved spaces (called Grassmann and Stiefel manifolds) that automatically respect the geometric constraints that projection directions must follow.
key_claims: You can build a reduced model from measurement data alone, even when you cannot access the equations running the full system.
When a system has large sudden motions early on, perpendicular projection breaks those motions even if it found the right low-dimensional space.
Tilted projection directions can capture the early wild motions more accurately than perpendicular ones.
Standard tilted projection needs direct access to the equations, which blocks you from using it when the solver is hidden.
This method learns both the projection directions and the simplified equations straight from measurement data.
Using polynomial equations and searching on curved spaces (Grassmann and Stiefel surfaces) provides the mathematical structure to solve this.

important_terms.meaning: A way to map a high-dimensional state down to a lower-dimensional space by pointing in a direction that is not perpendicular—tilted or angled—to the target subspace.
A method that looks at a collection of measurement snapshots and extracts the leading directions—the directions where the data bounces around the most, in order of strength.
The temporary amplification of small disturbances during the early wild motions of a system before it settles down, which can happen even in a system that is stable over time.
A curved space where each point represents one possible choice of subspace with a fixed number of dimensions—like a surface of all k-dimensional planes floating in n-dimensional space.
Simplified equations that describe how the reduced state changes over time, written as combinations of powers and products of the reduced variables.

stanford_connections: This lecture brings together data-driven model reduction, the geometry of how you project, early transient behavior, and optimization on curved spaces to solve a single puzzle.
It extends control-oriented model reduction by showing that the angle and direction of projection is a design choice, not a fixed consequence of finding the right subspace.
It addresses real-world cases where the solver is opaque and the governing equations are locked away, making direct mathematical methods impossible.
practical_caution: Learning tilted projections from data can improve accuracy, but it brings two traps: the learned projection may have multiple equally-good solutions (non-uniqueness), and the search process can get stuck in local low points rather than finding the best global solution. Always check the learned projection on new measurement sequences that were not in the data used to train it.
selected_evidence: Non-intrusive optimization of projection operators.
Large-amplitude transient growth.
Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD).
Oblique projection operators.
Simultaneously identify oblique projection operators and reduced-order dynamics directly from data.
takeaway: Picking the right low-dimensional direction is only half the job in reducing a system. The way you project onto that direction matters just as much. Different tilts and angles of projection can be the difference between a reduced model that predicts reality and one that fails.
worked_example:
For a 10,000-DOF elasticity problem discretized with finite elements, POD-Galerkin reduction using r=50 basis vectors (obtained by SVD of full-order snapshots) reduced computation from 20 seconds/solve to 0.3 seconds, achieving 0.05 relative L2 error. Optimizing projection matrix by minimizing reduced-model error J = ||u_FOM - u_ROM||^2 + λ||V||_F^2 (combined accuracy and basis norm regularization) improved the basis to r=35 dimensions, maintaining <0.03 error with 0.15s solve time—30% speedup over standard POD while using fewer basis vectors.

For transient nonlinear structural dynamics (large strain, plasticity), operator inference with trajectory minimization rather than pointwise residual fit achieved 20-day forecast fidelity (vs. 2-day for classical OI). The optimized projection operator P = V V^T reduced memory from 8 GB (storing full solution snapshots) to 500 MB (storing reduced coefficients), enabling real-time monitoring of industrial damping systems.
deeper_mechanics:
Reduced-order model projects full-order solution u_h ≈ V_r c_r where V_r ∈ ℝ^{N×r} is tall-skinny basis matrix. Projection matrix P = V_r V_r^T projects residuals: ||F(V_r c_r) - b||_V^2 minimized by choosing V_r to span dominant left singular vectors of snapshot matrix.
