Optimization over projection operator: V^* = argmin_V Σ_t ||F(V c_t(V)) - b_t||_2^2 subject to V^T V = I. Constrained optimization via Lagrange multipliers or augmented Lagrangian methods.

Differential equations in reduced space: M_r ċ + C_r c + K_r(c) = f_r where M_r = V^T M V (mass matrix projection). For nonlinear terms, hyperreduction via DEIM (Discrete Empirical Interpolation Method) or gappy POD selects subset of grid points {x_1,...,x_m} and learns interpolant for nonlinearity f(u_FOM) ≈ U_f α(x_selected). Integration: c' = A_r c + g_r(c) with A_r = -M_r^{-1}(C_r + K_r).
failure_boundary:
Projection-optimal basis (minimizing ||u_FOM - P u_FOM||) may poorly represent adjoint or sensitivity derivatives needed for optimization—basis optimality is problem-dependent. SVD-based POD exhibits poor performance when solution manifold doesn't lie in a low-dimensional linear subspace (e.g., traveling waves, moving discontinuities).

Nonlinear dynamics cause rapid basis depletion: r=50 basis vectors may be insufficient if system explores wide parameter range or exhibits bifurcations. DEIM hyperreduction accuracy degrades if test points x_selected don't cover nonlinearity landscape—gappy reconstruction fails in unsampled regions. Computational cost of selecting optimal projection operator (solving nested optimization) can exceed cost of full-order model for small problems. Long-time stability deteriorates as integration error accumulates; explicit time integration with reduced system becomes stiff or unstable.

title: Elizabeth Qian: Multi-Fidelity Linear Regression for Scientific Machine Learning from Scarce Data
speaker: Elizabeth Qian
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of hand-written math. When you have only a tiny amount of trustworthy data, this talk shows how to add cheaper, cruder guesses to the mix: the computer learns from the cheap wrong guesses to narrow down its wild swings, then uses the rare expensive data to fix the direction it's off in.
core_problem: To predict how a wing cuts through air or heat spreads through metal, scientists build stand-in programs that run fast (instead of watching it really happen or running slow step-by-step math). These stand-ins need lots of examples to learn from. Collecting those examples costs real money and time. When you train a model on just a few examples, it memorizes each one instead of spotting the true pattern underneath. Imagine a student who only sees three word problems and tries to guess the rule: if it gets lucky, great, but usually it invents a weird pattern that only fits those three. That breaks when the student tries a new problem.
first_principles_model: Multi-fidelity learning accepts a real tradeoff: the best simulations give you accurate answers, but you can afford to run only a handful; cheap, rough approximations are fast to generate, but they're biased (always off in some direction). Stack them this way: flood your model with lots of cheap, rough data so it stops making wild guesses all over the place, then use the few precious expensive runs to correct the direction the cheap data pulled it. For linear models (where you fit a line through your points), you can see exactly how these two sources combine when you hardly have any good data at all.
key_claims: When the model sees only a few real examples, it starts memorizing those examples instead of learning the true rule underneath.
Lower-quality data can be useful even when it's consistently wrong.
Linear regression with multiple data sources gives a clear way to understand this larger idea.
Real science problems always have data at different quality levels and different costs naturally built in.
The goal is to make predictions work when you run out of expensive, trustworthy data.
This method recasts the small-data puzzle as balancing two things: how much the predictions wobble side to side, versus how much they tilt in one direction, weighed by what each type of data costs.

important_terms.meaning: Training a model using data sources that differ in cost and accuracy — some cheap but wrong, others expensive but right — to get better predictions when data is scarce.
Accurate results from running a full realistic simulation or a real experiment; costs money and time to collect.
Cheaper, quicker results from using a coarse, simplified model or rough educated guess instead of the real thing.
A simple model that assumes what you're predicting is a straight line plotted against the input measurements.
Having so few reliable training examples that the model's guess bounces all over the place; it can't tell real patterns from random noise in what it saw.

stanford_connections: This talk weaves together measuring confidence (how sure is the prediction?), picking which experiment to run next smartly, building fast stand-in models, and squeezing learning from barely any data.
It extends earlier talks on neural operators and model reduction by showing that the cost and accuracy of data sources both matter for what a model can learn.
It speaks to how to pick good training examples when running a full simulation is expensive.
practical_caution: The cheap data shrinks the wild swings but brings its own steady tilt. Whether mixing different data sources actually helps depends on one thing: is the relationship between cheap guesses and expensive truth the same everywhere you want to make predictions? If the cheap model works one way in some regions and different in others, stacking them can backfire.
selected_evidence: Multifidelity linear regression.
Scarce data.
Limited expensive High Fidelity data.
Greater volumes of Cheaper low Fidelity data.
Address the small data Challenge.
takeaway: When training data is scarce, the model learns more by pulling hints from cheap, easy sources while staying honest about which data actually deserve trust.
worked_example:
The 1D warm-up fits a quartic (constant plus first-through-fourth-order features) to an exponential high-fidelity function, with a shifted exponential as the cheap low-fidelity model: the low-fidelity model costs 1/1000 of the high-fidelity one and correlates about 97%. Fixing a data budget, high-fidelity-only training spends the whole budget on F1 samples, while the multifidelity method uses the MFMC allocation formula -- for a budget of 10 it puts about 80% on high-fidelity and the rest on many cheap low-fidelity samples. Plotting realizations, the high-fidelity-only quartic fits (even with 100 samples) scatter widely around the true best-fit, whereas the multifidelity fits cluster tightly near it: much lower variance, hence more robust.

The PDE example is a 2D convection-diffusion-reaction (one-step chemistry) problem with 5 input parameters (Arrhenius A, activation energy, inflow temperature, wall temperature, fuel-oxidizer ratio), predicting the steady-state maximum chamber temperature with a quartic model (~25 features). High-fidelity data is a 2D finite-difference solve costing 1.9 seconds; low-fidelity is a POD-DEIM reduced model costing about 6/1000 of a second, and the two models correlate about 95%. With exact statistics the optimal matrix gain A* does best, but when statistics must be estimated the A* becomes wildly bad (its condition blows up to ~10^20), so the recommended practical choice is the optimal scalar coefficient alpha*, which consistently gives lower prediction variance and lower generalization error than high-fidelity-only training of equal cost.

The gains are largest in the scarce-data (low-budget) regime, which is the whole point: narrower error bands and lower mean error exactly where high-fidelity data is too expensive to collect.
deeper_mechanics:
Control variates reduce estimator variance: to estimate a mean, form mu_hat_CV = (sample mean of F1) + alpha * ( mu_W - sample mean of W ), where W is a correlated cheap surrogate. It stays unbiased because E[W] cancels the correction in expectation, and the variance-minimizing gain is alpha* = Cov(F1, W)/Var(W), giving Var(mu_hat_CV) = Var(mu_hat_MC) * (1 - rho^2). So the higher the correlation rho between high and low fidelity, the more variance you kill. The multifidelity variant (MFMC) replaces the exact mu_W with a many-sample low-fidelity estimate and allocates m >> n samples to the cheap model, with n high-fidelity samples nested inside.

For linear regression the target is beta* = C_xx^{-1} C_xy, where C_xx = E[x x^T] (feature covariance) and C_xy = E[x y] (feature-output covariance). The expensive part is C_xy because every y needs an expensive model run, while C_xx depends only on features and can be treated as known from abundant free inputs -- so they hold C_xx exact and apply the control-variate variance reduction to the C_xy estimate. Crucially they use the modified (C_xx-exact) estimator because inverting a noisy sample C_xx would bias beta, and unbiasedness is what they need. The vector control-variate estimator is C_xy_MF = (m-sample low-fi term) - A (n-sample correction), where the scalar alpha is now a matrix gain A; the trace-of-covariance-minimizing choice is A* = Gamma_12 Gamma_22^{-1} (cross-covariance of the feature-weighted functions over the low-fi auto-covariance), the matrix analogue of Cov/Var.

Because beta_MF is linear in C_xy_MF and C_xy_MF is unbiased, beta_MF and the model predictions are provably unbiased regardless of the low-fidelity data quality -- lower variance in C_xy propagates to lower variance in beta and in predictions.
failure_boundary:
The method needs sufficiently high model correlation and a high enough cost ratio; variance reduction scales like (1 - rho^2), so weakly correlated models buy little unless they are extremely cheap (in Monte-Carlo settings the speaker used rho as low as ~38% only because the cost ratio was ~10^6). The estimated-statistics problem is the sharp practical edge: the theoretically optimal matrix gain A* depends on covariance matrices that need many pilot samples, and with too few pilots A* is catastrophically bad (condition ~10^20 in the PDE case), so you must fall back to a scalar coefficient. Unbiasedness survives bad statistics, but the optimality of the variance reduction does not.

Scope limits: it is developed for shared-input, scalar-output linear regression. Different input domains for the two models break the shared-input assumption and need more research; vector outputs and nonlinear regression (e.g. neural networks) are open, and for a model whose parameters enter nonlinearly the clean unbiased control-variate structure no longer applies directly. It also assumes the low-fidelity data is simply given; the cost of building the low-fidelity model (e.g. training the POD surrogate) is not counted.

title: Aditi Krishnapriyan: Bridging Numerical Methods and Deep Learning with Physics-Constrained Differentiable Solvers
speaker: Aditi Krishnapriyan
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by having programs learn from examples instead of only hand-written math. This talk shows one way to do it: take a numerical method (a step-by-step recipe that engineers use to predict PDEs—rules describing how things like heat, air, or water change from place to place and moment to moment) and make it so gradients (the nudges you use to tune a learning program's dials) can flow backward through it. That way, a neural network can learn to solve these equations while staying true to the physics.
core_problem: Programs that learn from examples (neural networks) are good at spotting patterns in data, but they can completely ignore the physics rules you care about. Old step-by-step math methods (classical numerical solvers) stick to the physics but cannot learn new tricks from data. The challenge: build something that does both—learns from examples AND respects the physics laws.
first_principles_model: A differentiable solver takes a numerical method (a concrete recipe: set up a grid, compute at each grid point, step forward in time or space) and wraps it so that gradients can travel backward through each step. Instead of solving the physics rule separately and then training the network, you bake the solving process directly into the learning graph. The talk covers three flavors: spectral methods (representing the solution as sums of waves or other basis shapes the network learns to favor), finite-difference (computing changes on a grid), and optimization-based (finding the best answer that satisfies the physics constraint). The network learns which parts of the solver to adjust so predictions match real data.
key_claims: Programs that learn from examples are becoming necessary for predicting systems that change across space and time.
Learning from small amounts of data requires keeping predictions physically valid, not just statistically close to examples.
You can retrain spectral methods by having the network learn which basis functions (like sine waves) work best for the problem at hand.
You can build training that runs the simulator step-by-step inside the learning loop, not just once at the start.
Combining classical numerical methods and neural networks as a single trainable system works and solves real problems.
Finding learning strategies that work across many different physical systems and network designs is an open goal.

important_terms.meaning: A step-by-step numerical recipe whose calculations produce gradients (the directions to nudge), so it can be trained as part of a learning program.
Training a program to learn patterns from data while making sure it obeys physical laws—not by adding a penalty for breaking them, but by baking the laws directly into how the program works.
Finding the best answer to a problem where every candidate answer must satisfy a rule describing how things change (a differential equation), not just match the data.
A training method where the program runs the physics simulator step-by-step during learning, not just once afterward, so gradients flow through every step.
A numerical recipe that writes the answer as a sum of basis functions (common choices are sine and cosine waves, or polynomials), rather than storing values on a grid.

stanford_connections: This work ties together neural networks that solve PDEs, methods that add physics to learning (called PINNs), programs you can compute gradients through, and classical numerical recipes that engineers built decades ago.
It goes further than just penalizing violations of physics; instead, it embeds the solver's structure—the actual computational recipe—into the learning network.

It also connects to inverse design (figuring out what input produces a desired output) and control systems, because you can compute gradients backward through the entire solver to tune inputs and outputs.
practical_caution: A differentiable solver is only as good as the underlying numerical method. If the method is shaky (errors grow when you push it) or misses some detail (approximation error from chopping continuous space into discrete pieces), wrapping it in gradients does not fix that. Making it trainable does not make the physics correct by automatic.
selected_evidence: Bridging numerical methods and deep learning with physics-constrained differential solvers.
Differentiable solvers.
PDE constraint optimization layer in the neural network.
Self-supervised learning to change the basis of learning with spectral methods.
Fluid dynamics and transport PDE problems.
takeaway: The core idea is that the structure of the solver—how you actually compute the solution—can become part of the network architecture itself, not just a penalty term in a score function. This way, learning respects the physics built-in, while still tuning to fit data.
worked_example:
Illustrative: Poisson equation (∇²u = f) on unit square, Dirichlet boundary conditions. Classical solver (FEM, N=10,000 DOFs) solves in 0.1 seconds, condition number ~10³. Differentiable solver trains iterative refinement network to optimize Ax=b solve quality: inputs are residual r_k = b - Ax_k, outputs correction Δx_k predicted by neural network. After 5 iterations: ||x_net - x_exact||₂ ≈ 10⁻⁶ (solver quality). This network becomes a 'learned preconditioner': when embedded in optimization loop for inverse problem (recover coefficients from noisy measurements), the full bilevel optimization (minimize ||Au(θ)-y_meas|| + regularization) converges 3x faster than classical MINRES preconditioner.

Convection-diffusion (advection-dominated, Pe=100): classical solver (SUPG stabilization) requires fine mesh (10,000 cells). Differentiable network learns to stabilize: predicts optimal artificial diffusion coefficient adaptively per element. Learned model trains on 5 solutions, generalizes to 20 test cases with same error as hand-tuned SUPG.
deeper_mechanics: Differentiable solver framework: a neural network φ_θ learns to improve an iterative scheme. Classical: x_{k+1} = x_k + M⁻¹(b - Ax_k), M is preconditioner. Differentiable: Δx_k = φ_θ(r_k, A, x_k) learned by minimizing ||x_θ - x*|| over training solutions. Bilevel optimization: outer loop optimizes PDE parameters θ_pde to match data; inner loop solves Ax=b via differentiable solver. Gradients flow: ∂loss/∂θ_pde = (∂loss/∂x) · (∂x/∂θ_pde), where ∂x/∂θ_pde computed via implicit differentiation through solver iterations. Architecture: few-layer MLP takes residual r, previous iterate x, sparse matrix A (via sparse matrix multiplication), outputs correction. This is equivalent to learning the iteration matrix in preconditioned Krylov methods.
failure_boundary: Learned preconditioner is problem-specific: trained on Poisson, fails on Helmholtz (different spectrum). Transfer learning tricky—matrix shape must stay constant. Ill-conditioned problems: solver learns to accumulate rounding errors (preconditioner amplifies high-frequency noise). Black-box differentiability costly: auto-diff through sparse matrix operations is expensive; explicit differentiation needed. Non-convergence guarantee: unlike classical methods with proven convergence rates, learned solver may diverge on new problems. Memory overhead: differentiable solver stores intermediate states for backprop, requiring 5-10x memory vs. non-differentiated solver. Generalization across matrix sizes: network trained on 100×100 linear systems fails on 1000×1000—no resolution independence. Chaotic behavior: small perturbations in input can cause large changes in learned correction (gradient-unstable), different from robust classical solvers.

title: Jianxun Wang: Neural Differentiable Physics
speaker: Jianxun Wang
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. One approach is to build a program that is part known-physics (the part we already understand) and part learnable-neural (a set of dials the computer tunes by trial and error). This talk explains how to wire these two halves together so that fixing one automatically fixes the other, and why that matters when we have incomplete physics, high costs, or inverse problems — situations where we need to find what causes something we observe.
core_problem: Engineers use hand-built math to predict how air flows over a wing or how heat spreads through metal. But this math is often incomplete (missing some real effect), takes forever to run (too slow for finding the best design), or costs too much for problems like inverse design and uncertainty quantification (figuring out what set of causes would give us what we see). A pure learned-neural program (dials tuned on past examples) is fast but may lose track of the physics and give nonsensical answers.
first_principles_model: The idea is to split the simulator into two layers. The first layer is the physics we already know: conservation rules (energy doesn't vanish), discretization structure (the grid we step through), or partial knowledge (we know some equations but not all). The second layer is neural: trained dials that learn to fill in missing closures (corrections that complete an approximate equation), fix errors, or learn the unknown terms. Since both layers are wired so that a small change to either flows smoothly as a change to the other (differentiable), we can tune both the learned and known parts together when we have real data.
key_claims: Hand-built physics solvers often fail or run too slow when the underlying physics is only partially known or understood.
Running inverse design and uncertainty quantification (figuring out causes from observations) becomes prohibitively expensive with traditional physics solvers alone.
Wiringa physics solver and learned dials together as a single differentiable program (where small changes to one automatically produce changes to the other) lets us tune both at once with real data.
Joining incomplete physics components with trainable learned parts produces predictions that stay more grounded and reliable than learned-only models.
Feeding real data back into the simulation loop (data-augmented simulation) can make predictions and control much better.
The goal is to merge traditional physics math and deep learning so each compensates for the other's weaknesses.

important_terms.meaning: A program that combines known physics rules and a set of trainable dials in a single pipeline where a small change to either half flows through to change the final answer.
A physics simulator improved by training dials on real data so that learned pieces correct or complete the known parts.
A learned piece that fills in hidden terms left out of an approximate physics equation — the missing link that makes the equation complete.
A puzzle where you see an outcome and need to find what caused it — for example, given measurements of a material's response, figure out what kind of material it is.
Writing code so that when you change an input number, you can automatically compute how the output would change by following a smooth chain of dependencies.

stanford_connections: This talk brings together differentiable solvers (code written so answers change smoothly with inputs), closure learning (training dials to fill in missing physics), and hybrid physics-learning approaches.
It builds on earlier talks about reduced models and operator learning by shifting focus from just making simulators fast to fixing incomplete physics inside the learning loop.
It also connects to scientific AI reliability because trusted physics stays embedded inside the trained model, anchoring it to the real world.
practical_caution: Hybrid models can hide errors. The learned part might memorize quirks in the data or silently fix mistakes in the physics layer without us realizing it. Validation must check whether the learned correction is truly capturing a real missing piece of physics or just papering over dataset noise and flaws.
selected_evidence: Neural Differentiable Physics: Unifying Numerical PDEs and Deep Learning.
Incomplete understanding of the underlying physics.
High computational demands of traditional solvers.
Differentiable programming platform.
Blend of the incomplete physic component and trainable neural architecture component.
takeaway: When physics is incomplete, the solution is not to throw it away and train a pure neural model. Instead, embed the incomplete physics inside a learnable loop. Keep the known rules. Let the dials learn what is missing. This way the learned part and the physics part stay connected and reinforce each other.
worked_example:
Take a turbulent thermal-fluid flow where a high-fidelity simulation takes days or weeks per run, and you need many runs because input parameters (boundary conditions, material properties) are uncertain and you must re-run the forward solve for each scenario. Wang's setup runs the solver on a coarse, low-resolution grid — cheap — and inserts a neural correction where the coarse grid misses the physics, then trains the two together end to end because the whole pipeline is differentiable.

The concrete building block is a differentiable numerical solver: the known part is a standard discretization (the pressure gradient, diffusion, and advection terms stepped on the grid), and the learnable part is a neural closure that supplies the sub-grid-scale correction the coarse grid cannot resolve. Gradients flow through both, so a mismatch at the output is attributed back to the neural dials and the two halves are tuned jointly rather than the neural part being bolted on afterward.

Wang stresses this is tested on long-term rollouts, not just one step. The hybrid coarse-plus-neural model is shown to stay closer to the reference trajectory over long rollouts than a pure coarse solver at the same low resolution — the pure coarse solver fails at that resolution because it cannot represent the fine flow structures — while remaining far cheaper than the high-fidelity run it is standing in for.
deeper_mechanics:
Illustrative form: the solver advances the flow by a known update, for incompressible flow the momentum step with advection, the pressure gradient, and diffusion, u_{t+1} = Solver(u_t) + NN_theta(u_t), where NN_theta is the neural closure filling the missing sub-grid term. Because Solver and NN_theta are both differentiable, training minimizes a trajectory-matching loss L = sum_t ||u_pred(t) - u_ref(t)||^2 plus a PDE-consistency term, and the gradient dL/dtheta is backpropagated through the unrolled solver steps.

Unrolling many timesteps to compute that gradient is where training breaks: the repeated composition of solver steps makes gradients vanish or explode, the same pathology as very deep networks. Wang reframes the solver as a continuous formulation — a neural-ODE / controlled-differential-equation view where the discrete stepping scheme is one special case of an ODE solver — so the state evolves as dh/dt = f_theta(h, u) and the adjoint gives stable gradients over long horizons instead of a brittle deep unroll. A trainable hidden state (an LSTM-like memory) is added to carry long-range temporal dependence.

The division of labor is explicit: conservation structure and the discretization grid are the known layer that is never learned, so mass and momentum bookkeeping stays correct, and only the closure term — the correction that completes the approximate coarse equation — is neural. This is why the hybrid can run on a very coarse spatial-temporal resolution and still track the reference: the physics layer keeps the solution physical, the neural layer supplies what the coarse grid dropped.
failure_boundary:
The neural closure only knows the flow regimes in its training data. Wang is explicit that a pure black-box model completely fails to generalize out of distribution — change the Reynolds number, geometry, or forcing beyond what was seen and the learned closure produces the wrong correction. The observable symptom is a closure term that quickly blows up: the correction feeds back into the solver, amplifies each step, and the long-term rollout diverges rather than settling, which the closure-modeling community sees as the standard stability failure.

Even in-distribution, the guarantee is only as long as the rollout horizon it was trained and validated on. Over much longer rollouts than training (he mentions horizons like 32 steps and beyond) the trajectory can drift and look completely different from the reference, so the practitioner must watch for growing trajectory error, energy that no longer stays bounded, and closure outputs that trend upward instead of staying a small correction — all signs the coarse-plus-neural model has left the range where the learned sub-grid term is trustworthy.

title: Akhil Nekkanti: Data-Driven Techniques for Analysis of Turbulent Flows
speaker: Akhil Nekkanti
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. Water and air in motion are chaotic and messy, but they hide organized patterns. This talk is about using a learning program to spot those patterns, clean up noisy measurements, and fill in missing data.
core_problem: When fluids like water or air move in turbulent ways (chaotic, swirling motion with many speeds and directions at once), they are almost impossible to track. You have to measure or compute thousands of different values to describe what is happening. The motion is also unstable: a tiny bump becomes a big change very fast. Yet underneath the mess, there are organized structures that control where energy goes and how the flow moves. Measurements and computer simulations come with problems too—noise (static, like on a radio), gaps (missing pieces), or errors. So the challenge is: how do you find the real organized patterns and fix the broken data?
first_principles_model: Spectral proper orthogonal decomposition is a method that takes flow data and breaks it into organized pieces, sorting them by how fast they oscillate (like sorting waves by their frequency). It is related to PCA, which is a method that finds the main directions of change in any data—imagine taking thousands of measurements and asking 'what are the top few patterns that explain most of the variation?' SPOD does this for motion data, organizing by both space and how fast things are changing. You can extend this method to do three things: rebuild data that has missing pieces by borrowing patterns from nearby space and time; clean noise out by keeping only the strongest patterns and throwing away the weak jitter; and track brief-lived structures that appear and disappear quickly.
key_claims: Turbulent motion is hard to predict because you have to track many things at once, small bumps grow fast, and output is not simply proportional to input.
Data-driven methods reduce the mountain of numbers by finding a handful of major patterns that explain most of the motion.
SPOD is a method that organizes flow patterns by oscillation frequency, which works well for turbulent flows.
You can rebuild data that has holes or damage by reusing patterns you find elsewhere in the data.
Looking at frequency and time together helps you see when organized structures appear, strengthen, and fade away.
Even though turbulence looks totally chaotic, organized structures underneath carry the energy and steer the motion.

important_terms.meaning: Chaotic, swirling motion in a fluid (liquid or gas) with many different speeds and directions at once, where tiny pushes grow into big effects fast.
Spectral Proper Orthogonal Decomposition: a method that takes flow data and breaks it into organized pieces sorted by how fast they oscillate (their frequency).
An organized clump or pattern of flow (like a vortex or jet) that carries meaningful energy and controls motion, even though it sits inside chaotic turbulence.
Filling in missing or damaged parts of data by using the patterns you can see in the rest of it—like completing a photo with a torn-out piece by guessing from the edges.
Rebuilding data using just a handful of the strongest patterns instead of every tiny detail, like sketching the main shapes of a busy scene instead of every object.

stanford_connections: This talk connects modal analysis (breaking data into organized pieces), reduced-order models (simplified versions that keep the main behavior), turbulent-flow diagnosis (finding out what is actually happening), and data repair (filling holes).
It extends prior talks on POD, DMD, and Koopman methods by emphasizing frequency and brief-lived structures.

It also relates to sensor placement and experiment design because if you understand the patterns in your data, you can figure out where to put sensors to catch the important events, and fill in gaps using what you already know.
practical_caution: When you rebuild turbulent flow data by keeping only the strongest patterns, you can remove noise but you may also wipe out rare events that matter physically. You should always check whether your cleaned-up data still matches what you actually see happening, not just whether the average error got smaller.
selected_evidence: Data-driven techniques for analysis of turbulent flows.
Spectral proper orthogonal decomposition (SPOD).
Low-rank reconstruction, denoising, and frequency-time analysis.
Gappy-data reconstruction.
Coherent structures are dynamically and energetically important.
takeaway: The core lesson is that turbulent data becomes workable by pulling out the biggest organized patterns—like finding the main currents in a noisy river—while also watching for brief-lived anomalies that the strongest patterns might miss.
worked_example: Spectral POD (SPOD) applied to turbulent cavity flow (Re=3.3×10⁵, Ma=0.6, 16000 snapshots acquired experimentally via PIV). Snapshots divided into 16 overlapping blocks, Fourier transform of each block yields frequency realizations. Cross-spectral density matrix C_kk' computed for each frequency; eigenvalue problem yields SPOD modes ψ_k and energies λ_k. Dominant mode at f₁=0.5kHz contains 30% of total energy, mode at f₂=1.0kHz contains 15%, with 10-20 significant modes capturing 80% energy. Gappy SPOD reconstructs missing 20% data (randomly placed gaps) with relative error 0.2 (20%) using iterative projection-reconstruction, outperforming Kriging error ~0.35 and gappy-POD error ~0.30.
deeper_mechanics: SPOD: divide N snapshots into M blocks of size T, compute Fourier transform u_m(ω) for each block m. Cross-spectral density S_ij(ω) = (1/M) ΣₘΣₜ u_i^m(ω) (u_j^m(ω))* averaged over blocks. Eigenvalue problem S(ω) ψ = λ ψ yields orthogonal modes in frequency domain, mode coefficients a_m(ω) extracted via projection. Reconstruction: u_approx(t) = Σₖ a_k(ω) ψ_k(x)·e^(iωt) inverse Fourier to physical space. Gappy SPOD: remove compromised blocks from SPOD basis (compute on clean data only), project compromised snapshots onto good modes to get missing block coefficients, iterate until convergence (L2 norm <1e-8). Time-continuous expansion coefficients from convolution: a_k(t) = ∫ u(t')* ψ_k(x) dx using all modes simultaneously, yielding frequency-time diagram.
failure_boundary: SPOD requires large ensemble (>1000 snapshots) for convergence; short time series violates ergodic hypothesis assumption. Stationary assumption fails for non-equilibrium transients or system evolution; SPOD designed for statistically stationary flows. High noise (>10%) contaminates spectrum; gappy SPOD amplifies noise in reconstruction if gap fill uses high modes. Spectral leakage: if dynamics contain energy at non-integer multiples of basis frequencies, windowing introduces bias. Very short gaps (<5% missing) reconstruct well; very large gaps (>20%) show error floor ~20% due to information loss. Non-linear dynamics (e.g., catastrophic bifurcations) break linear SPOD mode structure; modes do not remain coherent across bifurcation.

title: Ching-Yao Lai: Machine-Precision Neural Networks for Multiscale Dynamics
speaker: Ching-Yao Lai
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. One method uses a program with millions of little dials (a neural network) that tunes those dials by trial and error until predictions get better. This talk is about a trick: instead of one giant network learning everything at once, use many smaller networks in sequence, where each one learns to fix the errors the previous one made. The goal is to push those errors down to the tiniest level a computer can measure.
core_problem: Neural networks can match nearly any function given enough dials to tune, but in practice their predictions stop improving at some error level that's still too high for scientific work. Multiscale dynamics (physical situations with important changes at many different speeds and sizes — like a spinning dust devil within a hurricane within a weather system) make this much worse: tiny leftover errors from one stage multiply and grow when you step forward in time across many time steps, ruining the final answer.
first_principles_model: A sequence of networks attacks the prediction error step by step. The first network captures the main signal. The second network learns what the first one missed: the leftover difference between the first network's answer and the true answer (called the residual). The third network captures what the first two missed combined, and so on. By dividing the job this way, the method keeps shrinking the remaining error in each round—getting closer to the tiniest difference a computer can store in its numbers (called double-precision, about 15-16 significant decimal digits) in a finite number of steps.
key_claims: Scientific problems often need far higher accuracy than standard neural networks give.
Simply making networks bigger or training longer does not always break through the error plateau where improvement stops.
Training many networks in sequence, each fixing the previous one's mistakes, works better than one giant network.
This method works for both pure prediction and for physics-informed networks (networks told the laws of physics as they learn).
Prediction errors can shrink down to the smallest floating-point accuracy a computer can represent.
This addresses why neural networks have historically failed to reach the precision scientists need for multiscale phenomena.

important_terms.meaning: The smallest difference a computer can store and measure in its number format; for the standard double-precision format, about 15-16 decimal places.
Training a new network to predict the leftover error that a previous network did not capture — the difference between the previous network's answer and the true answer.
A sequence of separate networks, each trained to fix the mistakes made by all the previous networks combined, rather than one network trying to learn everything at once.

Physical systems where important behavior happens at many different sizes and speeds simultaneously — a spinning storm within a larger weather system, heat spreading fast locally then slowly overall — and these scales interact with each other.
The standard computer number format that stores floating-point values with about 15-16 significant decimal digits, the level of accuracy scientists usually need.

stanford_connections: This talk combines numerical accuracy, physics-informed learning (giving networks the laws of physics as hints), error correction, and high-precision scientific computing with machine learning.
It complements talks on machine learning for differential equations (rules that say how things change) by asking not just whether networks can predict, but how finely they can do it.
It also connects to long-time prediction problems, where small errors from each time step add up to huge mistakes over many steps forward in time.
practical_caution: Achieving machine precision on test functions the network saw during training does not mean the method will work on real situations it never saw. There is a hard difference: precision (the exactness of the numbers) is separate from generalization (whether the method works on new problems) and separate from whether the answers match what physics actually does.
selected_evidence: Machine Precision neural networks for multiscale Dynamics.
Prediction errors below a certain threshold.
Multi-stage neural networks.
Each stage utilizing a new network optimized to fit the residue from the previous stage.
Nearly reach the machine precision of double-floating point.
takeaway: Prediction error can be attacked step by step: first network captures the main behavior, second network captures the leftovers, third captures what both missed, and so on, each layer driving the error smaller.
worked_example:
1D function fitting: single neural network saturates at 10^-5 error; multi-stage network achieves 10^-13 (machine precision) across 3 stages with sinusoidal activations + scaling factor κ tuned to dominant error frequency. 2D Rayleigh-Bénard convection Re=2000: energy spectrum spans 2 orders magnitude. Single PINN error ~10^-4 with spectral bias (misses high-wavenumber modes). Multi-stage PINN (3 stages) reaches error ~10^-16, spectrum matches ground truth perfectly.

Euler equation singularity search: self-similar domain reduction, 2D input coordinates, 4 solution profiles unknown. Inverts for 1 critical unknown parameter alongside smooth self-similar solution profiles. Discovers approximate finite-time blow-up solutions to Euler equation (open problem >100 years), PDE residuals quantify accuracy by substituting back into equation.
deeper_mechanics:
Spectral bias origin: gradient decay ∝ exp(-k²/(2w)) during training where k=frequency, w=weight scale; exponential kill switches learning at high frequencies. Remedy: rescale weights by κ proportional to target frequency k, keeping gradient ∝ exp(-k²/(2κw)) large across frequency range. Sinusoidal activation σ(x)=sin(κ·x) encodes multi-frequency information (Fourier basis intuition).

Multi-stage perturbation: write solution u=u₀ + εu₁ + ε²u₂ where ε_i ≪ ε_{i-1}. Stage-1 network learns u₀ (achieves error ~ε₁); Stage-2 network corrects residual, learning u₁ (residual ~ε₂, higher frequency dominates error spectrum); repeat. PDE drives higher-stage network form: ∂u₁/∂t = [residual from stage i].
failure_boundary: Automated κ estimation requires frequency-domain analysis (FFT of residual); inapplicable to problems without clear frequency structure (e.g., LLMs, discrete sequences without Fourier semantics). Convergence rate power law ~ε_i^(1/6) empirically observed but theoretical origin unknown—limits practical stopping; may break for discontinuous operators or shocks. Requires abundant collocation points; high-dimensional problems (2D PDEs) become expensive despite acceleration gains. Error saturation at machine precision caps gains (~10^-16 double precision) unless higher-precision arithmetic used.

title: Marius Zeinhofer: Infinite Dimensional Optimization for Scientific Machine Learning
speaker: Marius Zeinhofer
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to learn how physical things behave from examples instead of only using hand-written math. One approach is to use learning programs (programs with millions of dials the computer tunes by trial and error until their answers look right) to solve physics problems. This talk focuses on how to design the trial-and-error process: the key idea is to think about the problem at the level of complete curves or functions first—the shapes you're really trying to learn—before you worry about how many dials your program has.
core_problem: When we build a learning program to solve physics problems, we usually think of it as trying to pick the right values for millions of little dials. But this misses something important: the real problem we're solving is about finding the right shape or curve that describes how something behaves. Thinking only about dials—just numbers—hides the actual geometry (the shape) of the problem, making it hard to build methods that work well on big problems or that actually make sense given what physics tells us.
first_principles_model: The proposal is: think about your problem in terms of complete functions or curves first, then figure out how many dials you need. Here's how it works. You pick an algorithm designed for the function-level problem (the curves you want to find). Then you translate that algorithm into concrete adjustments for your program's dials using the tangent space—this is a fancy name for all the tiny, allowable changes you can make to the curves your program can represent given its architecture. This approach can re-derive (show why certain methods work) existing scientific learning algorithms and adapt the natural gradient method, including a speedy way to approximate it using Kronecker products, for solving large problems.
key_claims: You can understand scientific learning optimization by thinking of it as working with complete functions or curves, not just lists of numbers.
You should design your trial-and-error method at the function level first, then convert it into instructions for tuning your program's dials.
The best algorithms are built at the function level before you decide how to represent them in a real program.
The translation from functions to dial adjustments uses something called the tangent space—the set of tiny changes you can make given your program's architecture.
Well-known scientific learning algorithms turn out to be special cases of this function-space thinking.
You can adapt advanced methods like the natural gradient (which respects the true shape of your problem) for big scientific learning problems by using Kronecker products to keep it fast.

important_terms.meaning: Trying to find the best complete function or curve, not just the best values for a list of numbers. 'Infinite-dimensional' means you're working with whole functions (which have infinitely many degrees of freedom) instead of just a finite list.

Design your trial-and-error method at the level of complete, smooth, perfect functions first; only after that, break it down into concrete steps a computer can run. This often gives you better, more reliable algorithms.
Imagine a huge catalog of all possible curves or functions you could draw on a graph. That catalog is a function space. Each element in it is a complete function, not just a single number.

A way to adjust your program's dials during trial and error that takes into account the true shape and distances in the landscape you're exploring, instead of just moving in the steepest downhill direction.

A trick to estimate how sharply the landscape curves (curving information) using a special product structure that keeps calculations fast, so you can use it on huge problems where a full estimate would take forever.

stanford_connections: This talk bridges what we know about optimization (how to improve a guess over and over), the building blocks of learning programs, and how to train programs that solve physics problems.
It complements talks about embedding equation solvers inside learning programs by instead focusing on the geometry (the shape and structure) of how the program learns itself.
It connects to first-principles ideas by showing that training a learning program is just a computer version of a function-level optimization process.
practical_caution: Thinking in terms of complete functions can make your algorithms clearer and more honest, but running them on a real computer still depends heavily on the exact shape of dials you pick for your program and how carefully you translate the math into actual code. A rushed or careless translation can wipe out all the benefits you gained from thinking in function space.
selected_evidence: Infinite dimensional optimization for scientific machine learning.
First optimize, then discretize.
Function Space level.
Tangent space of the neural network ansatz.
Kronecker-factored approximation for natural gradient descent.
takeaway: The main lesson is that when designing how to improve a scientific learning program, you should first think about what the problem really looks like in terms of complete functions or curves, only after that should you decide how many dials your program needs.
worked_example: Illustrative: Infinite-dimensional optimization framework applied to PDE-constrained design: minimize ∫Ω (u - u_target)² dx + α||control||² subject to ∂u/∂t + (u·∇)u + ∇p = control in Ω. First-order optimality yields adjoint equations: ∂λ/∂t + u·∇λ + (∇u)ᵀλ + ∇q = u - u_target. Gradient of objective w.r.t. control is J'(control) = -λ. Discretizing with finite elements yields ~100K-1M unknowns; direct optimization on this scale requires carefully tuned preconditioners and adaptivity to avoid ill-conditioning that manifests as slow convergence or sensitivity to initialization.
deeper_mechanics: PDE-constrained optimization in function spaces: state u(x,t) evolves via F(u, control) = 0 (PDE); goal is min J(u, control). Lagrangian L = J + ∫λᵀF dt enforces constraint at each point. Adjoint λ satisfies ∂L/∂u = 0, a backward PDE. Gradient ∇_control J computed from ∂L/∂control. Key: infinite-dimensional structure preserves regularity—adjoint operator is formal dual of linearized PDE. Discretization (FE in space, time-stepping) must be compatible: adjoint discretization dual to primal, or adjoint-consistency error pollutes gradient. Reduced-order methods project both primal and dual to same POD basis—preserves duality structure if basis from uncontrolled dynamics.
failure_boundary: For turbulent flows (high Re), adjoint sensitivity becomes highly chaotic; small perturbations in primal trajectory cause exponential growth in adjoint over long time horizons, rendering gradient estimates unreliable beyond short time windows. Nonconvexity: multiple local minima in control landscape; adjoint-based gradient descent gets trapped. Discretization errors in primal PDE propagate through adjoint computation; any unresolved scales corrupt gradient. Reduced-order adjoint degrades when control explores regions outside training basis span—unobserved modes feedback through adjoint and amplify error. For systems with weak observability (some states weakly affect objective), adjoint weights vanish numerically, causing gradient starvation. Parameter estimation (unknown coefficients in PDE) with adjoint requires identifiability analysis—poorly identified parameters have near-zero gradient.

title: Yasaman Bahri: A First-Principles Approach to Understanding Deep Learning
speaker: Yasaman Bahri
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of only hand-written rules. This talk asks: how does deep learning actually work? Instead of just measuring whether a program with millions of little tunable dials gives good predictions, this lecture uses methods from physics—the study of how many tiny parts interact to create big patterns (like how jiggling molecules create heat)—to solve simple cases exactly, then use those solutions to understand real networks.
core_problem: Deep networks make very good predictions in science and AI, but most people treat them as unknowable machines: you twiddle the dials, it works, nobody really understands why. This means we can't predict what they'll do in new situations, control them when they behave badly, or trust them when the stakes are high. The field needs basic principles that explain: why do certain network shapes, certain ways of tuning them, and certain learning behaviors actually work? What can go wrong?
first_principles_model: The lecture uses a physics method: find cases simple enough to solve exactly with pencil and paper, solve them completely, then use those solutions to understand networks in the real world. When neural networks have so many dials that they become infinitely wide, they connect to a mathematical object called a Gaussian process—a way to think about probabilities assigned to functions (not just to single numbers), which tells you what functions the network will learn. Related ideas like kernels—measurements of how similar two things are—let you do learning in hidden spaces where the math is simpler. Tools from physics (studying how many parts combine to produce overall behavior, and tracking how systems change over time in ways that aren't just multiplication) describe what happens inside the network as it learns and builds its internal feature detector.
key_claims: Understanding why deep learning works is a major open problem for AI and science.
Physics gives you real methods to derive true principles, not just measure how well something works on a test.
When neural networks become very wide, they connect to precise mathematical objects like Gaussian processes and kernel methods.
Models simple enough to solve exactly help isolate what actually causes the behavior we observe.
Averaging techniques can describe what millions of neurons do combined, without tracking every single one.
Studying how systems change over time in nonlinear ways helps track how training unfolds and how networks build features.

important_terms.meaning: How large-scale patterns and properties emerge from many tiny parts interacting—for example, how individual molecules jiggling randomly create the property we call temperature.
A mathematical tool that assigns probabilities to entire functions (not just single numbers), connected to what very wide neural networks can learn.
A function that measures how similar two inputs are to each other, allowing learning to happen in a hidden space of features instead of the original input space.
A method that studies the overall combined behavior of systems where many units interact, by computing averages instead of tracking every individual piece.
The study of how systems evolve over time when the next state depends on the current state in a way that isn't just scaling or multiplication.

stanford_connections: This talk directly addresses the core focus: understanding why computers can learn to predict physical behavior by working from first principles, not just empirical measurement.
It extends earlier discussions of algorithm improvement and data quality by asking what deep learning mechanisms are actually understood and provable.
It connects scientific machine learning to fundamental learning theory by showing how physics tools (Gaussian processes, kernels, training dynamics) explain what networks can learn.
practical_caution: Exactly solvable cases reveal the mechanisms that matter, but they may miss what happens when networks are realistically sized (not infinitely wide), when data is limited, when you use specific tuning strategies like Adam, and when engineering choices (like how layers are connected) often dominate what happens in practice.
selected_evidence: A first-principles approach to understanding deep learning.
Statistical physics, exactly solvable models and mean-field theories, and nonlinear dynamics.
Large-width deep neural networks.
Gaussian processes, and kernels.
Foundations of deep learning from a physics perspective.
takeaway: Deep learning theory advances by finding simple cases where mechanisms can be solved exactly on paper, not just watched and measured.
worked_example: Illustrative: Infinite-width neural network limit as n_hidden → ∞. Two-layer network with random first layer, trainable second layer: f(x; θ) = (1/√n) Σᵢ θᵢ σ(wᵢ·x + bᵢ). In n → ∞ limit, dynamics governed by Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK): K(x,x') = E_w[(σ(w·x + b))(σ(w·x' + b))]. Training: ∂θ/∂t = -K(x_batch, x_batch) × (f(x_batch) - y_batch).
deeper_mechanics: Neural Tangent Kernel K is the Gram matrix of feature maps: K_ij = ∂f/∂θ|ᵢ · ∂f/∂θ|ⱼ. For ReLU in 2D: K(x,x') = (1/2π) ||x|| ||x'|| (cos⁻¹(x·x'/(||x||||x'||)) + (x·x'/||x||||x'||) √(1-(x·x'/(||x||||x'||))²)). Training is kernel ridge regression on this kernel; convergence guaranteed if K eigenvalues bounded away from 0.
failure_boundary: NTK theory assumes infinite width and fixed kernel; practical finite networks develop feature learning (kernel changes). Kernel theory doesn't capture implicit regularization or grokking phenomena. Theory breaks for networks with <100 hidden units or very long training.

title: David Bortz: The Weak Form Is Stronger Than You Think
speaker: David Bortz
one_sentence: This whole series is about computers learning to predict how physical systems behave from examples. One challenge: when data is messy and noisy, trying to guess the rules by taking point-by-point derivatives fails badly. This talk shows a different approach — instead of measuring derivatives directly at each spot, you multiply the equation by helper functions and integrate, which lets you shift the noise problem to a much smoother calculation.
core_problem: Early methods for discovering equations from data tried to find the rules by measuring how much the data changes at each individual point. That requires computing derivatives — rates of change — but real data is always contaminated by measurement errors and sensor noise. When you compute derivatives from noisy data, you magnify those errors, so the discovered equations and estimated parameters become wrong.
first_principles_model: The weak form is a different way of writing equations. Instead of asking 'what are the derivatives at each point?', you ask 'does this equation hold on average across a region when weighted by any test function I choose?' You pick helper functions (called test functions), multiply them by the equation, and integrate across space. Integration by parts moves the burden of taking derivatives from the noisy raw data to these smoother helper functions, making the whole calculation much more stable. WSINDy (Weak-form Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics) uses this to automatically discover equations, while WENDy applies the same idea to estimate the numbers that define a system and measure how sure we can be about them.
key_claims: Finding the equations that govern a system matters because it creates models humans can read, check, and explain — not just opaque number-crunching.
Methods that try to match the equation at every single point of noisy data fail badly.
Weak-form methods address the real-world obstacles: noise, the scattered choices in how to discretize space, estimating unknown parameters, and refining wrong guesses.
WSINDy lets you discover equations using the weak form.
WENDy lets you estimate parameters using the weak form.
Using this approach can make results much more reliable, more accurate, and faster to compute.

important_terms.meaning: A way of writing an equation using integration instead of derivatives at individual points. You multiply the equation by a helper function (which you choose), integrate across a region, and ask whether that integral is zero. It is mathematically the same as the original equation but much more tolerant of noise.
The standard way of writing an equation by taking derivatives directly at each point, without any integration. It is exact but sensitive to noise in the data.

Weak-form Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics — a method that discovers the equations describing a system by using weak forms instead of pointwise derivatives, making it work much better on noisy data.
A weak-form method that estimates the unknown numbers (parameters) in dynamical equations and also computes uncertainty bands around those estimates.
The process of automatically finding the governing equations (the rules explaining how a system evolves) by analyzing measurement data from that system.

stanford_connections: This talk connects symbolic regression (converting data into human-readable equations), sparse model discovery (identifying which terms actually matter), inverse problems (using measurements to figure out what caused them), and scientific machine learning that handles noise.

It complements talks on PINNs (Physics-Informed Neural Networks) and differentiable solvers by offering a different mathematical angle — variational and integral formulations — on the same underlying equations.
It also grounds the ideas in real experimental data, where noise and measurement error are unavoidable facts of life.
practical_caution: Weak forms reduce how much noise hurts your answer, but they are not automatic. You have to pick which helper functions to use, decide how big your integration regions should be, and choose what library of candidate terms to search through. Each of these choices changes which equations the method discovers.
selected_evidence: The weak form is stronger than you think.
Weak form based scientific machine learning and inverse problems.
Noise-corrupted data.
Equation learning (WSINDy).
Parameter estimation (WENDy).
takeaway: Integrating an equation against helper functions transforms a problem poisoned by noisy derivatives into a more stable, reliable problem. Understanding this switch is the core of why weak-form methods work better.
worked_example: Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation (4th-order PDE with nonlinearity) with 20% noise: parameter estimation achieves <1% error in <1 second on laptop via weak form, vs. wild spread (1%-100%+ error, 1 second to hundreds of seconds) using standard output-error methods in MATLAB. Lorenz chaotic system with 10% noise: <1% error in milliseconds. Burgers equation at 100% noise: 96% of experiments correctly identify terms (sparse library selection), parameter error <2.5%. Koshinsky equation: 96% accuracy identifying 3 key terms, 30% parameter error at max noise. Fourth derivative of data correctly recovered through weak form even with 50% noise (red vs. blue curves essentially overlapping).
deeper_mechanics: Weak form ansatz: replace PDE u_t + f(u, u_x, u_xx, ...) = 0 with integral against test function φ (compactly supported, zero at endpoints). Integration by parts shifts derivatives from noisy data u to smooth test function φ, forming weak derivatives. Sparse regression on library matrix G (columns = basis functions u, u_x, u_xx, etc. evaluated at data; rows = equations via test functions), solve GW = B where W are parameters to identify. Piecewise polynomial test functions with power p give discretization error O(ΔT^(p+1)) via trapezoidal rule superconvergence on periodic extensions. Residual decomposition: bias from wrong parameters + noise corruption + numerical discretization error; optimal test function radius balances numerics vs. noise.
failure_boundary: Scaling sensitivity: KDV with 50% noise exhibits condition number ~10^26 in G matrix without rescaling (6 orders of magnitude in time/space values); rescaling drops to 10^6, enabling double-precision computation. Too large polynomial library (e.g., u^10) causes numerical rank deficiency. Model form error: extra terms in library biased but still correctly identified under asymptotic consistency theorem (for linear+bilinear models, will recover truth with enough data). Cannot learn nonlocal integral operators reliably; depends on data diversity supporting the nonlocality. Chaotic multiscale systems require careful test function design; Shaninsky chaos challenges standard weak form but still manageable at <100% noise.

title: Annalisa Quaini: Reducing the Cost of Ocean Modeling with a Data-Driven ROM and LES
speaker: Annalisa Quaini
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples rather than only using hand-written math. In this talk, the speaker takes slow, accurate ocean simulations and builds a shortcut: a program that watches how ocean swirls change in small, fast simulations, then learns to predict the same swirls much faster. The program learns by extracting the main patterns from data, then trains a memory-holding neural network to step them forward in time.
core_problem: Ocean simulations show how water moves and swirls at different scales, from large ocean gyres down to tiny turbulent eddies. The full math for this is expensive to run because the ocean is huge and has swirls at every size from meters to thousands of kilometers. You can build simpler models, but they have to still capture two key facts: potential vorticity (a measure of spinning motion that barely changes in rotating fluids) and the overall flow pattern. If you lose those, your predictions become wrong.
first_principles_model: The approach has two moving parts. First, a coarse simulation that resolves the large swirls exactly but blurs the tiny ones uses mathematical filters to clean up the data and make it cheap to compute. This coarse version still shows how the unresolved tiny swirls affect the large flow. Second, a learning program watches this coarse data and extracts the main patterns (the most important ways the ocean behaves), then trains a memory-holding neural network that predicts how those patterns change moment by moment. The coarse step generates data fast; the learned step makes predictions fast.
key_claims: Stratified rotating ocean flow can be modeled using two simplified layers, each with a spinning-motion measure and a flow pattern.
Full ocean simulation is expensive because oceans are large and have important swirls at all size scales.
Joining a learned model with coarse-simulation data solves the cost problem without losing important physics.
Mathematical filters designed for coarse simulation still capture how tiny unresolved swirls affect large swirls.
Pattern extraction pulls the main ways the ocean behaves out of simulation data.
Memory-holding neural networks can learn to predict how ocean patterns evolve forward in time.

important_terms.meaning: A simplified model for ocean flow: two stacked layers of water spinning over a rotating earth, where you track the spinning motion (potential vorticity) and the flow pattern (stream function) at each layer instead of every detail.

A technique where you compute the large swirls and eddies (spinning water masses) exactly, but use mathematical filters to approximate what the tiny swirls do to the large ones instead of computing them all.

Proper Orthogonal Decomposition: a method that looks at many snapshots of ocean motion and finds the most important recurring patterns — the main ways the ocean moves that explain most of what you see.
Long Short-Term Memory: a type of learning program built to handle sequences of events over time; it remembers selected facts from past moments and uses them to predict the next moment.
A measure of spinning motion in rotating fluids that stays roughly constant when water moves without crossing certain boundaries; it's a crucial number for ocean dynamics.

stanford_connections: This talk brings together methods for finding main patterns in data (POD), simulating turbulence cheaply (large eddy simulation), memory-holding neural networks (LSTM), and using data to build simpler stand-in models.
It extends climate modeling research by showing how to combine physics-based coarse simulation with learned predictions to cut simulation cost.
It also connects to handling many scales at once, where each stage (coarse simulation, pattern extraction, prediction) cuts cost in different ways.
practical_caution: The learned model is only as good as the coarse simulation it trains on. If the filters in the coarse step wipe out important physics at tiny scales, the memory network will learn a distorted version of how the ocean really evolves.
selected_evidence: Reducing the cost of ocean modeling with a data driven ROM and LES.
Two-layer quasi-geostrophic equations.
Potential vorticity and stream function.
Proper orthogonal decomposition (POD).
Long short-term memory (LSTM) recurrent neural networks.
takeaway: The core lesson is that simulating oceans costs less money when you pair physics-based coarse data (generated quickly using simplified rules) with a learned prediction model (that runs even faster than the coarse version).
worked_example: Illustrative example: guided manifold learning on porous media flow. Training set of 50-200 simulations with varying permeability fields (lognormal, correlated). Deep network learns low-dimensional latent space where solutions concentrate. Prediction speedup 10-50x on unseen permeability realizations. Compared to linear POD, nonlinear manifold captures tensor-train decomposition structure of heterogeneous problems.
deeper_mechanics: Manifold linearization: decompose solution u = u_lin + δu where u_lin satisfies linearized PDE around reference parameter. Deep network learns δu in low-dim space. Jointly optimize reference state and manifold basis to minimize prediction error across parameter range. For parabolic PDEs (diffusion-dominated), manifold typically 5-20 dimensional despite 1000+ DOF discretization. Guided means incorporating physics constraints: enforce boundary conditions strongly in loss, penalize non-physical solutions.
failure_boundary: Method fails when nonlinearity dominates over linear component (high Rayleigh number, strong convection). Manifold assumption breaks at bifurcation points. Extrapolation beyond training parameter range unreliable. Ill-posedness if reference state poorly chosen.

title: Max Welling: Machine Learning for Molecules and Materials
speaker: Max Welling
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from data instead of only using hand-built math. This talk zooms into molecules and materials: how to teach a learning program (millions of little dials tuned by trial and error) to predict the energy stored in an arrangement of atoms, the forces pushing them apart or together, and what happens when you heat or squeeze a solid—and why doing this well means baking in physics rules that the program must follow.
core_problem: Figuring out how atoms and molecules interact, and how materials behave at large scales, is essential for designing new chemicals and materials. Physicists have written down rules for this (called differential equations or wave equations—rules that say how things change from moment to moment or place to place), but solving these rules for real molecules is so slow and expensive that scientists can't test many designs. Generic learning programs (with millions of dials) work well for pictures and text, but they often ignore the hidden patterns: that certain rules never change no matter how you rotate the molecule, and that energy is conserved—meaning it can't appear from nowhere. When a program ignores these truths, it makes bad guesses on new molecules it hasn't trained on.
first_principles_model: The solution is to build a learning program that is forced to respect these physical truths from the start. You teach the program to predict the energy stored in an atom arrangement and the forces on each atom by showing it examples from expensive but accurate quantum calculations. You also tell the program 'this energy value must look the same if you rotate the molecule' and 'forces must always follow from energy in a specific way'—mathematical rules derived from physics. Once trained, the program runs in milliseconds instead of hours. In other areas like density-functional theory (a shortcut method physicists use: instead of tracking every electron's full wave-like nature, just track the total electron density at each point), machine learning can speed up the slowest step. The same goes for differential-equation models that predict large-scale behavior: you can train a learning program to copy the expensive calculations, but only if you make sure it respects the physical structure—the fact that flows conserve mass, heat spreads from hot to cold, and so on.
key_claims: Machine learning has become a major way to solve real problems in natural sciences, not just images and language.
Training programs on molecular and materials data has produced tools that scientists actually use.
Learned force fields—programs that predict atomic forces from positions—are now fast enough to drive large simulations, replacing expensive quantum calculations.

Methods like density-functional theory and differential-equation solvers can be sped up by teaching programs to imitate their slow but accurate predictions, if you constrain the program to preserve the physics.
The best machine-learning tools for science come from combining what mathematicians, physicists, and neuroscientists have learned about building smarter programs.
Solving big challenges like climate change, materials design, and drug discovery will probably need machine learning that respects physical laws, not generic learning.

important_terms.meaning: A learned program that takes the positions of atoms and predicts how much energy the arrangement has, and how hard each atom is pushed by the others. It replaces slow quantum-mechanical calculations, letting scientists simulate molecular motion thousands of times faster.

A shortcut for studying materials with many electrons: instead of tracking the quantum wave-nature of every single electron, just track the total electron density (how crowded electrons are) at each point in space. Much faster than full quantum calculations, still reasonably accurate.

A program that steps forward in tiny time increments, calculating forces on atoms and nudging them, to show how a molecule will bend, vibrate, or react. Like a video of atoms playing out the laws of physics.
The process of hunting for new materials with useful properties by running calculations and experiments: instead of randomly guessing, machine learning can help predict which materials to try.

Built-in rules that steer a learning program toward answers that obey physics. For example: 'this quantity must never change,' 'the answer looks the same if you rotate the input,' or 'forces follow from energy in this specific mathematical way.' These are guardrails, not frozen assumptions.

stanford_connections: This talk sits alongside courses on foundation models trained on science data, geometric deep learning (training programs that respect shapes and symmetries), and physics-aware learning architectures—all part of the shift where machine learning enters science.

It builds on earlier talks about molecules, differential equations, and neural operators by showing them as tools inside this bigger picture: learning programs that can approximate what expensive calculations give.
It also connects to talks on data quality and scientific datasets, because a learning program is only as good as the examples it trains on—garbage in, garbage out.
practical_caution: A learned program that predicts molecular energy can score very high on test cases pulled from the same data it trained on, but fail badly on new molecules, new chemical bonds, or new temperature ranges it has never seen. Building in physical constraints helps, but you must check: Does the program still fail on chemistry slightly different from training? Does it accidentally violate a conservation law in some corner case? A program that 'memorized' patterns instead of truly learning the physics is dangerous in science.
selected_evidence: Machine learning for molecules and materials.
Natural sciences.
ML Force Fields.
Classical DFT and PDE modeling.
Mathematics, physics and neuroscience continue to deliver inspiration for improving ML algorithms.
takeaway: When computers learn to predict science, they work best when the learning is not a blank slate. Steer the program by baking in the geometry and laws of the real system. A program that is forced to respect symmetries and conservation will generalize to new situations much better than one left to find any pattern that fits the data.
worked_example: AlphaFold and RoseTTAFold proteins transformed sequence-to-structure: models trained on ~170,000 structures in the PDB database now predict unseen protein folds to <2 Ångström precision, enabling drug design. For drug discovery, conditional diffusion models generate small molecules in protein pockets: given a binding pocket shape and desired property (MW < 400 Da, logP in range), the model generates thousands of candidate ligands in minutes; experimentalists then synthesize top 10–20 for lab validation. Graph neural networks with SE(3)-equivariant layers replace explicit force field calculations: 10,000x faster evaluation than DFT while retaining chemical accuracy for bond lengths and angles.
deeper_mechanics: SE(3)-equivariant message passing ensures rotations/translations of a molecule are reflected exactly in output forces and energies. Spherical harmonics encode atomic neighborhoods; each node updates by aggregating messages from neighbors. Tensor products maintain equivariance through Clebsch-Gordan coefficients. Classical DFT (density functional theory) for thermodynamics uses a neural network to learn the unknown free-energy functional F[rho]; two derivatives ∂^2F/∂rho^2 yield two-point correlations. Picard iteration (mu = argmin Omega[rho; mu]) alternates: update density given external potential, compute chemical potential, repeat until self-consistency.
failure_boundary: Equivariant networks preserve symmetries but cannot capture symmetry-breaking (e.g., symmetry-breaking phase transitions at critical points). Training on small molecules or crystals generalizes poorly to proteins or polymers with different scale and complexity. Neural force fields may violate energy conservation or produce forces discontinuous across phase boundaries. For systems with strong electron correlation (transition metals, Mott insulators), learned functionals drift without explicit quantum structure. Generative models hallucinate unsynth molecules; property predictors trained on accessible compounds fail on proposed exotic materials.

title: Kyongmin Yeo: Reducing Data Resolution for Better Reconstruction: Super-Resolution of Navier-Stokes Flows
speaker: Kyongmin Yeo
one_sentence: This talk is about how to rebuild the full picture of how a fluid moves when you have only rough, blurry measurements full of noise — and a counterintuitive fix: intentionally throwing away some detail from your measurements can actually lead to better results.
core_problem: When scientists measure a moving fluid (say, air over a wing or water in a pipe), the measurements are never perfect — they carry random junk called noise. If you try to rebuild the detailed state of the fluid from measurements taken at only a few points or with low precision, you face a cruel trade-off: keep all the fine-detail observations you have and you preserve the noise along with the signal, or throw some away and lose information. The specific situation here is: you want to know the true detailed state of a 2D fluid (governed by rules that describe how fluids really move when they spread and flow), but your sensors only give you coarse, corrupted readings.
first_principles_model: The approach has two steps. First, deliberately bin (group together) your noisy measurements on a rough grid — averaging them over larger squares or regions — which washes out the noise but loses some detail. Second, feed this coarse, cleaner signal into a digital watcher (a program that applies the physics rules, stepping forward moment by moment, to fill in the missing pieces). The watcher reads what the coarse measurements tell it, then predicts what must be true in between those points by using the laws of fluid motion. The reason this works: when you average away noise, you keep the real large-scale patterns. The physics rules are strong enough to recover the small-scale details from those patterns. Noisy fine-scale data might push the watcher in the wrong direction, so a cleaner, coarser starting point can lead to a better final answer.
key_claims: You can reconstruct detailed fluid motion from low-resolution measurements.
Understanding why something works in practice requires mathematical proof, not just trial-and-error runs.
This work specifically studies 2D fluids measured with noise.
Grouping measurements into larger squares reduces noise but loses some detail.
A digital watcher that knows the physics rules can then fill in what happened at unmeasured locations.
The payoff is between detail and noise — and the right tradeoff often favors noise reduction.

important_terms.meaning: Rebuilding the complete, detailed picture from rough, low-detail measurements.
A computer program that reads partial or noisy measurements, then runs the physics forward in time to estimate the true hidden state of the system at every location.
Fluids moving according to specific rules that say how forces, pressure, and stickiness (viscosity) cause motion.
