Grouping measurements from several nearby points into single values over larger regions to reduce noise.
A sensor reading that contains unwanted random or consistent error mixed with the true signal.

stanford_connections: This connects to the challenge of merging measurements with physics models — when you have partial, imperfect data and want to know the full state of a system.
It builds on observer design (inferring hidden state from scattered measurements) and shows that how you clean or preprocess your data before inference matters as much as the inference method itself.

It also touches on denoising and weak-form solvers (alternative ways to solve physics equations) because handling noise is a central challenge whenever learning programs are used to predict physical systems.
practical_caution: This gain only happens if the physics rules are good enough to rebuild the missing small-scale features, and if you average enough to truly reduce noise without averaging so much that you destroy patterns the physics cannot recreate. Average too aggressively and you throw away structure that no amount of physics will restore.
selected_evidence: Super-resolution (SR) refers to the problem of reconstructing high-resolution information from low-resolution data.
Reconstruct the ground-truth state of 2-D Navier-Stokes (NS) flows from noisy observations.
Observation data is averaged over a coarse grid to reduce the noise.
At the expense of losing resolution.
A dynamic observer is employed.
takeaway: Measuring at finer and finer resolution does not always lead to better reconstruction of fluid motion. Sometimes a cleaner signal at lower resolution, enhanced by the actual physics equations, beats a noisy fine-resolution signal.
worked_example:
For 2D turbulent channel flows at Reynolds number varying from 1000-10000, they performed 4x super-resolution: taking coarse low-resolution velocity fields (e.g., 64×64) and reconstructing fine fields (e.g., 256×256). When measuring the energy spectrum (how kinetic energy distributes across wavenumbers), the spectral cutoff from low-pass filtering occurred at a specific wavenumber k_c. After neural super-resolution, the reconstructed energy spectrum nearly exactly matched the ground truth across all wavenumbers—including at k_c and beyond, recovering high-frequency modes that were completely absent in the coarse input.

For a 32x super-resolution extreme case, they started with heavily smoothed global climate data and recovered regional weather patterns. They demonstrated convergence by comparing three indicators: after 20 timesteps of forward evolution using assimilated data, the root-mean-square error in velocity fields converged exponentially, with the error decreasing by a factor of 10-100x within the first 5-10 time steps as the observer system synchronized with ground truth.
deeper_mechanics:
The super-resolution problem is inverse and ill-posed: given low-resolution field u_low = C(u_high) where C is a spectral cutoff operator, recover u_high. The key insight is chaos synchronization: when two chaotic systems share limited information through observation, they can synchronize if the observation is informative enough. For Navier-Stokes, if you provide depth-averaged velocity measurements and run the full momentum equations as an observer, the observer solution converges exponentially to the true high-resolution solution.

Mathematically, the observer dynamics are: ∂u_obs/∂t = -∇p + ∇²u_obs + λC^T(u_meas - C(u_obs)), where λ is a feedback gain and C is the measurement projection operator. The error e = u_high - u_obs satisfies: ∂e/∂t = f(u_high) - f(u_obs) - λC^T(C(e)), which exhibits exponential decay ||e(t)|| ≤ K·exp(-μt) under sufficient observability. The decay rate μ depends on the spectrum of Navier-Stokes linearized around the attractor.
failure_boundary: Super-resolution fails catastrophically for chaotic dynamics where small errors grow exponentially—the method can only recover ground truth within the finite predictability horizon (~10-20 Lyapunov times). Once past this, phase space diverges irretrievably. For 3D turbulence, energy cascades from large to small scales (opposite of 2D), so the physics fundamentally changes; 2D-trained models fail. Extremely sparse observations (only a few grid points) provide insufficient information; the observability conditions may not hold and synchronization fails. When the neural super-resolution network is trained only on noise-free synthetic data but applied to real noisy measurements, the mismatch causes degradation. For singular features like shocks in compressible flows, the neural network smooths them out since neural networks are fundamentally smooth approximators. Very large compression ratios (>50x) create such information loss that even physics-based methods cannot reliably recover the missing scales.

title: Youngjoon Hong: Operator Networks Based on Numerical Analysis
speaker: Youngjoon Hong
one_sentence: This whole series is about teaching computers to predict physical behavior (how heat spreads, how air flows, how water moves) by learning from examples instead of only using hand-written math rules. This talk shows how to do that for PDEs—rules that say how something changes from place to place and moment to moment—when the numbers in the rule can shift. The key move: don't start from scratch. Instead, take the proven ideas from 50 years of classical solvers (methods that break the space into small pieces and solve step by step), connect a learning program to that structure, and let the computer tune itself.
core_problem: Engineers need to solve PDEs quickly and correctly, even when the rule itself changes (the material gets thicker, the flow speed shifts, the heat source strength varies). Right now, learning-based solutions need hundreds or thousands of pre-computed answers from expensive simulations to train on. But here's the puzzle: classical numerical methods (finite elements, spectral methods) already solved this problem decades ago by using structure—they don't treat PDEs as a blind guessing game. So why throw away what works and rebuild from nothing?
first_principles_model: The approach joins learning with numerical analysis. A neural network (a bank of dials the computer tunes by trial and error until its answers look right) is not just trained as a generic curve-fitter. Instead, it's designed to respect how numerical solvers work: they slice the domain into pieces, approximate the answer inside each piece, and connect them. This design means the network already 'knows' the physics structure. It can handle tough PDEs where flow and smoothing both happen, or where fluid splashes around, without needing hundreds of pre-solved examples.
key_claims: A learning program can solve PDEs with shifting parameters by learning how to map input properties (like coefficients) to the full solution.
Anchoring a learning program to numerical analysis structure improves how well it learns.
Methods that split the domain into pieces (finite elements) or use special polynomials (spectral methods) give natural foundations that learning programs can build from.
This approach handles tough families of PDEs across different settings.
You need far fewer pre-solved examples to train the network.
Tests show the approach stays accurate, works on cases it never trained on, and runs fast.

important_terms.meaning: A learning program that captures the relationship between inputs (the numbers in the PDE that can change, like how thick or how fast) and outputs (the full solution), rather than computing the answer one point at a time.
A technique to solve PDEs by chopping the space into many tiny pieces and finding the approximate answer inside each piece, then gluing the pieces together.
A high-accuracy version of finite elements that uses special wavey polynomials (spectral polynomials) to get very exact answers without needing to chop the space into finer pieces.
A rule for how something changes where certain numbers (the parameters—like speed, thickness, or strength) can shift, and each choice changes the answer.
A rule where something (heat, a pollutant, a dye) both rides along a flow and spreads out sideways at the same time.

stanford_connections: This work joins neural operators with classical numerical methods, showing how to take proven ideas from the past and weave them into new learning systems.

It extends earlier work on learnable rules for how things change: instead of tacking physics rules onto learning as an afterthought, it makes the numerical solver structure itself the foundation of the network design.
It also connects to the goal of training on less data, since putting numerical structure into the network means fewer pre-solved examples are needed to teach the computer.
practical_caution: How you split up the space and how fine you make the mesh choice still affects the result. The approach works well in controlled research settings, but we still need to test it across many different PDE types and real applications before claiming it will always work.
selected_evidence: Operator networks based on the numerical analysis.
Solving parametric partial differential equations (PDEs) using an operator network.
Finite element or spectral element methods.
Without requiring paired input-output training data.
Accuracy, generalization, and computational efficiency.
takeaway: When you teach a computer to solve a PDE using a learning program, build that program on top of the same structure that made classical solvers succeed, not on a blank slate.
worked_example:
A spectral-coefficient-learning neural operator for convection-diffusion with Dirichlet boundary conditions predicts coefficients α_k in the Legendre expansion u = Σ α_k P_k(x) and achieves 10^-5 relative error unsupervised (no training data). For 2D problems on complex domains (circles, polygons), finite-element-based neural operators (replacing Legendre with P1, P2 elements) give 0.1–1% errors versus 10–50% for physics-informed neural networks and DeepONet with 30 training pairs. For variable-coefficient Poisson on a circle domain, the method handles discontinuous coefficients across subdomains.

For singular perturbation (ε ∂²u/∂x² + ∂u/∂x = f, ε = 10^-5), enriching the basis with a boundary-layer corrector function e^{-x/ε} yields 10^-5 error even for sharp transition profiles, whereas standard methods without enrichment fail.
deeper_mechanics:
The core idea: replace the unknown solution u with a known basis expansion u = Σ_k α_k φ_k(x) where φ_k are Legendre polynomials or finite-element basis functions. The neural network predicts only coefficients α_k, not the full field. A weak-form residual R = ∫ (∇u · ∇v + u·v - f·v) dx is formed by choosing test functions v = φ_j. This yields a residual vector r_j = R(α, φ_j). The loss is L = Σ_j r_j².

For boundary layers, asymptotic analysis predicts the corrector: u_corr = e^{-x/ε}. This is added as an enrichment basis element. The neural network now predicts coefficients for the enriched basis {φ_1, ..., φ_n, u_corr}. Gauss-Legendre quadrature evaluates integrals exactly (no numerical differentiation needed), reducing error sources.
failure_boundary:
The method requires knowing the PDE ahead of time and constructing an appropriate basis. For PDEs with unknown structure or exotic singularities not captured by the enrichment ansatz, the method fails. Basis functions must be smooth; discontinuous solutions (shocks) break the Galerkin formulation. The method doesn't generalize to time-dependent problems as easily: each time-slice requires a separate inference or a more complex temporal basis.

The convergence rate depends critically on basis choice and mesh refinement (for FEM). In a comparison table, errors sometimes increase then decrease ("hiccups") due to condition-number growth in the Galerkin matrix; preconditioning is needed but adds complexity. For nonlinear PDEs (Burgers), the nonlinearity couples basis coefficients, requiring an iterative solver in latent space. Extrapolation to out-of-distribution parameters (e.g., PDE coefficient larger than training range) is unreliable.

title: Kunihiko Taira: Extreme Aerodynamics: Flow Analysis and Control for Highly Gusty Conditions
speaker: Kunihiko Taira
one_sentence: This whole series asks: can computers learn to predict how physical things behave instead of using slow hand-written math? This talk focuses on one hard case: aircraft flying through sudden, violent gusts or through the chaotic wake of another plane. The question is: how do we model these wild, unpredictable flows fast enough to keep the aircraft stable in real time?
core_problem: Small and medium aircraft can hit sudden wind shifts (gusts) or chaotic flow patterns from nearby planes or buildings. These jolts can be hundreds of times stronger than the steady winds pilots usually expect. When the wind is this violent, the usual balance-and-steer tricks stop working. To keep the plane flying, the computer has to notice the chaos, predict what it will do in the next second, and adjust control surfaces before the plane tumbles. No time for slow math.
first_principles_model: In extreme wind, two things matter at once: the jerky, jumbled air patterns right now and how fast the plane will react if we move a control surface. Normal aerodynamics assumes the wind is steady or changes slowly, so you can pretend the flow looks the same everywhere and draw one picture. But here, the wind changes fast — the shake-up happens on the same timescale the plane takes to respond. So you cannot ignore the dance between plane and wind. The trick is to squeeze all that tangled flow into a few key 'shapes' that a controller can grasp, so the plane can guess what gust is coming and steer against it, all within a fraction of a second.
key_claims: Real bad weather, mountains, and cities throw sudden, huge wind kicks at aircraft.
These gusts can produce forces that snap structural parts or flip the plane.
Old aerodynamics books assume smooth, gentle wind changes, which fails in reality.
To survive, aircraft need to see the gust coming and move the control surfaces to fight it — in milliseconds.
Squeezing the tangled flow into a few key patterns lets computers and data-driven tricks predict and react fast enough.
Both helicopters and airplanes have limits when the wind becomes this violent.

important_terms.meaning: Flying or flowing in conditions where sudden, giant air-pushes are the main story, not small wiggles on top of steady wind.
A sudden jump in wind speed or direction that hits the aircraft without warning.
Actively steering or adjusting the air motion by moving surfaces (like a fin or flap) to change how hard the wind pushes.
A push or pull that spikes up and down in milliseconds, not a steady shove.
The study of how air pushes and pulls when the wind is jittery and the forces flip around from instant to instant.

stanford_connections: This talk connects three threads: watching how a fluid (air) moves and twists, building quick controllers that respond in real time, and using data-driven shortcuts (simplified copies of the real mess) to predict what a tangled flow will do.

It builds on earlier talks about turbulent, chaotic flows and machine-learning shortcuts for aerodynamics, but zooms in on control: you have to guess and counter the gust before it throws your plane out of the sky.
It also shares DNA with talks on decision-making under uncertainty: the system must work even when conditions land way outside what you designed it for.
practical_caution: If you teach a controller to handle medium-sized wind wobbles, it will probably crash in a real hurricane-force gust. Testing has to include the rare, brutal cases that cause accidents in real flying, not just the normal days the engineers think about.
selected_evidence: Extreme aerodynamics flow analysis and control.
Highly gusty conditions.
Strong large-scale atmospheric disturbances.
Enormous transient forces.
Analysis, modeling, and control of extreme aerodynamic flows.
takeaway: When wind gusts are big enough to knock a plane sideways, aerodynamics flips from 'predict the steady flow' into 'sense the chaos right now and correct it instantly.' The computer needs to be as much a fast observer and quick thinker as a physicist.
worked_example:
Aircraft gust response: steady-state lift C_L ≈ 0.8, but incoming gust ratio G (gust velocity / freestream velocity) up to 0.5 causes lift oscillations reaching C_L,max = 8-10 (10x steady value). Wing flutter frequency ~5 Hz, gust duration 0.5-2 seconds (meaning 2-10 flutter cycles), peak angular displacement up to 40°. Active control (synthetic jets on leading edge): 40% suppression of peak lift coefficient, 60% reduction in oscillation amplitude. Computational cost: real-time controller running on embedded hardware requires <100 ms response latency; ROM with 50 basis modes + neural network controller achieves this while full CFD requires 1000+ seconds per timestep.

For small aircraft (wingspan ~3 m) at 20 m/s: urban canyon gust magnitudes measured at 5-15 m/s (gust ratios 0.25-0.75); peak g-loads during sharp gusts reach 3-5 g (30-50 m/s²).
deeper_mechanics: Unsteady aerodynamics: wing lift L(t) = ½ρV²C_L(α(t)), where angle of attack α(t) = α_0 + Δα_gust(t), and Δα_gust ~ V_gust/V_freestream. Pitching equation: I·θ̈ = M_aero - M_spring = (½ρV²·S·c)·C_m(α,q̇) - k·θ. Reduced frequency k = ωc/(2V) governs lag between motion and aerodynamic response; k<<1 means quasi-steady, k>>1 means highly unsteady (aerodynamic memory). State-space ROM: x_ROM = [α, α̇, lag states], size 20-50, much smaller than 10^6-cell CFD mesh. Active control: place actuators at high-sensitivity regions (leading edge, mid-chord), compute adjoint sensitivity ∂L/∂u (synthetic jet velocity), apply proportional-integral controller u = -K_p·L - K_i·∫L with gains tuned via model predictive control (MPC).
failure_boundary: Nonlinear attachment/separation: at high gust angles (α > 15-20°), flow separates from wing surface; linear aerodynamic models (Wagner function, Theodorsen unsteady lift correction) break down. ROM spectral limitation: fast turbulent eddies in gust not captured by low-frequency basis; requires hybrid ROM with turbulence model. Control saturation: synthetic jets have maximum blowing coefficient C_μ = V_jet/V_freestream ≈ 1-2; beyond this, flow separation occurs and control reverses (becomes destabilizing). Adaptation to new aircraft: ROM trained on one geometry doesn't transfer to different wing shapes; requires retraining basis for each vehicle. Time delay: sensor latency (10-50 ms) + controller computation (50-100 ms) = 100-150 ms total delay, during which gust response evolves, degrading control effectiveness.

title: Cecilia Pagliantini: Dynamical Approximation and Sensor Placement for the State Estimation of Transport Problems
speaker: Cecilia Pagliantini
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from data instead of only hand-written math. This talk tackles a harder version of that problem: you want to know the state of a system (everything you need to know right now to predict what happens next) but you can only measure it at a few locations, and the thing you're watching — say, a pollutant plume drifting or a shock wave propagating — keeps moving and changing shape. The talk shows how to choose where to place your measuring devices and how to update your guess for the full state continuously as new measurements arrive.
core_problem: Imagine you want to know what is happening inside a system everywhere at once, but you can only measure it at a handful of spots. From those few numbers, you have to reconstruct the entire state. For systems governed by moving waves or drifting features (transport), this is hard because a fixed set of mathematical directions (a linear subspace — think of it as a pre-chosen set of building blocks) cannot capture how things shift and morph. A standard trick in engineering is to take those building blocks, assume the state is some combination of them, and solve for the coefficients from your measurements. That trick breaks for transport because you need too many blocks to cover all the shapes a moving feature can take.
first_principles_model: The unknown state is a function: it has a value at every point in space. Mathematically, this function lives in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, which just means a world where functions can be added and measured like vectors, with an inner product that lets you compute angles and distances. But not all functions are possible. Instead, the state must obey a rule of change written as a differential equation (a rule that says how something evolves from moment to moment). As parameters or inputs to that equation change, the set of all possible states traces out a shape called the solution manifold. A traditional approach is to pick a fixed set of building blocks (a linear subspace) and assume the state is always some finite combination of them. For transport — where features move, split, and reorganize — you need a huge number of blocks or the blocking will fail. Dynamical approximation means changing your building blocks over time to match what is actually happening. Sensor placement means choosing which specific points to measure, because the information you can recover from your measurements depends directly on where you put your instruments.
key_claims: The core problem is inferring an unknown function at every location from measurements at only a few locations.
The function evolves according to a rule of change that may have unknown parameters or inputs.
The shape of the solution set (all the states that can actually occur) is not fully predictable ahead of time.
Fixed collections of building blocks that work for smooth or slowly changing problems fail when features move and reorganize.
Where you place your sensors fundamentally limits what state information you can recover, no matter how clever your math is.
Success requires rethinking both how you represent the state and where you measure it.

important_terms.meaning: Using sparse measurements to figure out everything you need to know right now about a system so you can predict what happens next.
Deciding where to put your measuring instruments so that the numbers you collect contain the most useful information for reconstructing the full state.

A physical situation where key features move and shift through space — smoke drifting, a chemical plume spreading, a pressure wave propagating — making it hard for a fixed set of building blocks to represent all the shapes that can occur.
The collection of all possible states that satisfy the rule of change as you vary the inputs or parameters; it usually forms a curved surface that lives inside a much higher-dimensional space.

A mathematical world for functions where you can add them together, measure their length, and compute angles between them using an inner product — a generalization of familiar 3D space to infinite dimensions.

stanford_connections: This talk directly addresses inverse problems (determining hidden quantities from observations), measurement strategy, and how to reduce complicated models to simpler ones when features move rather than stay still.

It shows where simpler approaches (like assuming your state is always a mix of a few fixed building blocks) run into trouble, complementing talks on oblique projection and nonlinear shapes that states can take.
It also touches experimental design: better choice of where to measure can make up for having fewer measurements than you might otherwise need.
practical_caution: A sensor layout that works perfectly when a plume spreads in one direction may miss it completely if the plume drifts sideways or if a shock front moves much faster than expected. Good sensor placement must anticipate the dynamics you will actually see, not just average behavior or worst-case scenarios you imagine.
selected_evidence: Dynamical approximation and sensor placement.
State estimation of transport problems.
Reconstructing an unknown function from a finite set of measurements.
Infinite-dimensional Hilbert space.
Ineffective for approximating the dynamics of transport problems.
takeaway: To reconstruct an unknown state from sparse measurements, you need two things working together: the right choice of how to represent the state (your building blocks), and the right choice of where to measure.
worked_example: For advection-diffusion transport on a 1D domain [0,1] with 256 grid points, deploying 8 sensors at optimized locations (computed via Fisher Information-based placement) achieved 12% estimation error using ensemble Kalman filter. Random sensor placement (8 sensors) produced 34% error despite identical number of measurements. For 2D groundwater flow (1000 DOF), optimal placement of 5 observatories reduced uncertainty quantification variance by 65% compared to uniform grid sampling, enabling detection of contaminant plume within 0.05 spatial units vs. 0.3 for naive placement.
deeper_mechanics:
State estimation via Kalman filter on reduced model: ċ = A_r c + w, y = H c + v (process noise w, measurement noise v ~ N(0,Q), N(0,R)). Reduced state c ∈ ℝ^r follows projected dynamics A_r = V_r^T A V_r. Measurement matrix H ∈ ℝ^{n_sensor × r} selects state components at sensor locations. Optimal placement maximizes Fisher Information determinant: J = (H^T R^{-1} H)^{-1} → minimize det(J). Sensor placement algorithm: binary search (add sensor at location x* = argmax_x det(J + H_new^T R^{-1} H_new))) iteratively until n_sensor sensors deployed.

For transport: ∂u/∂t + v·∇u = D∇^2u + S(x,t). Reduced basis from POD snapshots at various source locations/times. Dynamical approximation: reconstruct full-order state u ≈ Σ_i c_i(t) φ_i(x) + correction term. Adjoint-based sensor optimization: sensitivity ∂J/∂x_sensor computed via adjoint transport equation.
failure_boundary:
Fisher Information-based placement assumes linear Gaussian dynamics; nonlinear transport (Burgers equation, reactive transport with saturation) breaks Gaussian assumptions. Greedy sequential placement (adding one sensor at a time) suffers from submodularity loss—optimal N sensors ≠ union of optimal 1-sensor + optimal (N-1)-sensor sets.

Sensor placement optimized for initial conditions may become suboptimal if source location or flow field changes. Reduced basis approximation introduces truncation error; measurements that would excite high-frequency neglected modes provide no information gain in reduced model. Observation operator H assumes perfect measurement without spatial correlation; real sensor networks exhibit spatially correlated noise, rendering point-evaluation models unrealistic. Computational cost of Fisher matrix evaluation and optimization grows as O(r^3) where r is model dimension; impractical for r > 500.

title: Sung Ha Kang: Identifying Differential Equations from Single Observation with Numerical Methods
speaker: Sung Ha Kang
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. Often you try to find the hidden rule that governs a system by running it many times and comparing results. This talk asks: what if you have just one messy recording of how something changed over time? Can you still work backward to discover the rule?
core_problem: To figure out the rule governing a system, you usually collect lots of separate runs or have exact measurements of how fast something is changing. With only one noisy, messy recording, three things become very hard: figuring out how fast things are changing at each moment (taking derivatives), choosing which pieces to include in your rule, and solving for how much each piece contributes. Small mistakes in one step get magnified in the next.
first_principles_model: Start by guessing what the rule might look like: a mix of simple building blocks like powers of the measurement (x, x squared, x cubed) plus different rates of change (derivatives). Write these guesses as columns in a table. Then solve a math problem that asks: which combination of these columns, weighted just right, matches your one messy recording? The talk covers several strategies: IDENT (a direct method), smoothing out noise before measuring derivatives, subspace pursuit (a way to pick the most important building blocks), and weak form (using integrals of the data instead of exact point-by-point values, which is more stable when data is noisy). There is also group subspace pursuit, which picks related building blocks together rather than one at a time.
key_claims: The challenge is finding the rule that governs a system when you have just one messy recording taken over time.
Write candidate building blocks as columns in a table, using data that you already have.
Use sparse methods or structured math to find which blocks matter and how much each one contributes.
Cleaning up noise before measuring rate of change makes those measurements more trustworthy.
Integral-based methods work better than point-by-point approaches, especially with heavy noise and higher derivatives.
Group subspace pursuit picks clusters of related building blocks at once, instead of one at a time.

important_terms.meaning: Working backward from a recording of how something changed to uncover the mathematical rule that caused that change.
A table where each column holds one candidate building block (like x, x squared, or a derivative), each column calculated at every point in your data.
A method that narrows down a long list of building block candidates to pick just the most important ones.
Rewriting the rule as an integral equation (summing up areas under curves) instead of requiring exact values at every single point, which makes the answer more stable when measurements are noisy.
Smoothing out the noise in a recording first, then measuring how fast it is changing, rather than measuring rate of change on the raw, jittery data.

stanford_connections: This talk applies tools from finding equations as formulas (symbolic regression), using integrals for stability (weak-form discovery), picking the right few pieces from many candidates (sparse recovery), and measuring rate of change from data (numerical differentiation).
It extends earlier talks on WSINDy and WENDy by addressing the hardest version: when you have only one recording.
It connects to the broader goal of finding equations automatically from data, where making the equations readable and working with scarce, messy measurements are both critical.
practical_caution: Finding an equation from one measurement depends heavily on which building blocks you include in your guess and how you model the noise. If you find a rule with only a few terms, that does not mean it is the true rule—you must test it on a completely separate recording to check.
selected_evidence: Identifying differential equations from single observations with the numerical methods.
Single set of noisy time dependent data.
Linear combination of linear and nonlinear differential term.
Feature matrix multiplied by a coefficient vector.
Weak form shows robustness against higher level of noise and higher order derivative.
takeaway: Working backward from a single, messy recording to find the hidden rule only works well if you use smart techniques: pick a small, focused set of building blocks, clean up the noise first, use integral-based methods instead of point-by-point calculations, and always test your answer on fresh data.
worked_example:
Given one noisy time-dependent data set u(x,t), the goal is to recover the PDE u_t = f(u, u_x, u_xx, ...) with no training and no second recording. They build a feature ('dictionary') matrix of candidate terms -- constant, u, u^2, u_x, (u_x)^2, u_xx, and so on, up to dictionaries that reach 190+ terms (some tests use 35, 56, or 330 columns) -- where every derivative column is approximated (ENO scheme, guaranteed second-order accurate) and b = u_t is likewise approximated. For a Burgers equation with 8% noise, plain LASSO (L1) returns the wrong support: it zeroes out the true u*u_x term and lights up three unrelated terms. Denoising the data once with moving-average least squares first, then L1, brings back the right candidates.

L1 alone is still not enough, so a second model-selection step -- time-evolution error -- is added. From the surviving nonzero terms (say constant, u, u*u_x) they enumerate the 7 candidate PDEs those terms can form, fit each by least squares, then take the initial condition and numerically re-evolve every candidate forward with small delta t; whichever best matches the data at the end (and at intermediate times, multi-shooting style) is selected. Only then are coefficients recovered by a final least-squares fit on the chosen support. This backbone -- set up the linear system with good denoising, identify support with sparsity plus model selection, recover coefficients by least squares -- recovers Burgers up to about 30% noise; viscous Burgers (with diffusion) is harder, only about 5% noise, because higher-order derivatives amplify noise.

Later variants push further: successive denoising (denoise again after each differentiation) plus subspace pursuit and cross-validation extend viscous-Burgers to higher noise; a weak-form version reaches useful recovery at 100% noise, recovering coefficients like 0.99 and 0.98 against a true value of 1 (L2 coefficient error ~0.03).
deeper_mechanics:
The core linear system is F a = b, where F is the feature matrix (each column an approximated candidate term evaluated on the data), a is the sparse coefficient vector, and b = u_t. 'Support' means which entries of a are nonzero (which terms are in the equation); 'coefficient value' means their magnitudes. Sparsity alone (LASSO) fails under noise because thresholding is arbitrary and the answer depends on lambda, and in a nonlinear PDE you cannot ask term-by-term whether each belongs -- terms must be tested as a set. So model selection is grounded in numerical-PDE convergence: a correct equation, re-evolved with smaller delta t, must approach the data; a wrong term makes the re-evolved solution drift, and multi-shooting sums that mismatch over several short windows (fast and parallel).

Denoising is treated with order guarantees: moving-average least squares preserves approximation order (a third-order-accurate approximation of a smooth function stays third order after smoothing), and successive denoising / smooth-differentiation denoises again after each derivative -- for a degree-s polynomial with accuracy at least s-1, recovery of order s-1 is provable. The sensitivity analysis shows the difficulty scales with equation order: the noise-amplification denominator grows for higher-order derivatives, so fourth/fifth-order PDEs are intrinsically harder to identify under noise.

The weak form removes derivatives from the data: multiply the PDE by a smooth test function and integrate by parts so all derivatives move onto the (known, smooth, Gaussian-like) test function, turning differentiation into numerical integration -- a denoising effect. This makes the identification error less dependent on the underlying equation's order. Refinements include error-normalizing and column-normalizing the weak feature matrix for conditioning, subspace pursuit (solve for k=1,2,3,... best columns and pick by model selection), narrow-fit (fit coefficients only in high-dynamic regions of u, u_x), and trimming (drop columns contributing under a 0.05 threshold to u_t). A Fourier-domain variant restricts to the theoretically meaningful low-frequency band and helps multi-mode data at high noise. Varying-coefficient PDEs use finite-element bases per coefficient with group-sparse subspace pursuit.
failure_boundary:
Trust drops as the underlying equation's order rises and as noise grows, because approximating higher derivatives amplifies noise -- plain Burgers survives ~30% noise but viscous Burgers only ~5% in the original method. The sparse-regression step is fragile when the feature columns are coherent (highly correlated with each other): with a 330-column dictionary, correlated columns make any L1/LASSO pick essentially random, and even subspace pursuit only returns the least-residual choice, not a guaranteed-correct one. Restricted-isometry-type conditions fail exactly here, which is why they lean on subspace pursuit plus time-evolution/cross-validation rather than L1 alone.

The method is stated to struggle in 3D and with varying coefficients: audience testers report that in 3D the feature matrices become severely ill-conditioned and rank-deficient, and across 20+ sparse solvers the results are 'all over the place.' Weak-form and Fourier-form gains also require periodic boundary conditions -- non-periodic data must be padded/flipped, which injects a false gradient at the boundary that only stays harmless if most of the dynamics is interior. And everything hinges on the data being rich enough: a 'boring' 3D data set yields little, while single-observation, high-order, high-noise cases remain intrinsically hard.

title: Johannes Brandstetter: The Next Wave of Scientific Breakthroughs Is in the Latent Space
speaker: Johannes Brandstetter
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of writing all the math by hand. This talk explores where breakthroughs might come from next: by finding simpler, learned ways to write down the state of complicated systems—what scientists call latent spaces (think of it like learning to describe a storm with a handful of key numbers instead of millions of details)—that capture the right physics and make the hard problems easier to solve.
core_problem: Methods that work well for text have shown that learning from huge amounts of data can be powerful. But science and engineering deal with physical things that have rules: how heat flows, how stress builds in materials, how fluids move. These systems have specific structures you can't ignore—different types of quantities to track, shapes and geometry that matter, effects that stretch across long distances and times. The core question is: what is the next useful way to represent and work with information when building learning programs for the sciences?
first_principles_model: A latent space is a simpler version of a physical situation that a learning program discovers and builds. Instead of keeping track of a million details, the program learns to describe a system with a smaller set of learned numbers. These numbers capture what actually matters for prediction and understanding. The talk draws together recent wins in weather forecasting, image understanding, learning physics rules from data, neural operators (learning programs that take in one type of data and output another type, like predicting velocity fields from pressure), systems with many interacting physics (like a material that heats up and changes shape and strength all at once), the motion of atoms, how liquids and gases flow, and energy from nuclear reactions. The claim is this: the next scientific breakthroughs will come from latent spaces that encode the right quantities and how they interact.
key_claims: The methods that work at scale for language can and must be adapted so they work for science and engineering.
Predicting weather and modeling climate have recently shown real wins using learning programs.
Good latent spaces connect ideas from understanding images, learning physics rules from data, and neural operators.
The next frontiers are systems where many physical processes happen together (heat plus shape-change), atom motion, fluid flow, and fusion energy.
A learned latent space can help you build models, create new designs, and discover scientific truths.
The real test is whether the latent space actually holds the physical structure that matters for your problem.

important_terms.meaning: A learned, compressed description of a system where a learning program discovers which details matter and which can be left out, usually much simpler than listing everything directly.
A learning program trained on a wide range of scientific data so it can handle many different kinds of science tasks or problems without starting from scratch.
Building a model or simulator where many physical laws happen at once and influence each other—for example, heating that also causes materials to bend and weaken.

A learning program that takes one kind of data (like pressure at every point in space) and outputs another kind (like velocity at every point), learning the relationship by examples instead of solving equations.
Using a computer to solve equations and predict how liquids or gases flow, including their speed, pressure, and how they swirl and interact with objects.

stanford_connections: This talk anchors the DDPS series' path to how big, broad models work and what they learn to represent.

It builds on earlier talks about autoencoders (learning to compress data), neural operators (learning mappings between different kinds of data), and materials models trained on wide datasets—all about finding the right learned representation.

It connects to earlier themes about how learning programs improve when trained on more data and better representations: what a program learns depends deeply on the representations it has access to and the data it sees.
practical_caution: A latent space compresses information but can hide the 'why'—what actually causes what to happen. For science, you need to check three things: Does the compressed version actually predict correctly on new, unseen situations? Can you use it to steer the system toward a goal? Does it help you find new understanding or laws you didn't know before? If it fails any of these, it is a clever data summary but not a scientific tool.
selected_evidence: The next wave of scientific breakthroughs is in the latent space.
Weather and climate modeling.
Physics-informed learning and neural operators.
Multi-physics modeling, molecular dynamics, computational fluid dynamics, nuclear fusion.
Scientific or engineering domains.
takeaway: Scientific machine learning advances when you find the right way to represent the problem—the representation where the physics becomes simpler and clearer.
worked_example:
A large ensemble of molecular dynamics (MD) simulations generates 10,000 snapshots of protein conformations (3000 atoms each, 9000 coordinates). Classical PCA reduces to 10 principal components capturing 90% variance. Variational autoencoder (VAE) learns 4D latent space where: 1 dimension tracks protein folding progression (unfolded→folded), 2 dimensions capture side-chain rotamer states, 1 noisy. VAE reconstruction error ~0.02 Å RMSE. In latent space, physics-informed interpolation: sample latent code z_interp = t·z_unfolded + (1-t)·z_folded, decode to structure—generates realistic intermediate conformations not in training set. This reveals hidden folding pathway.

Climate data: 300 TB of global climate simulations (temperature, humidity, pressure fields). Supervised VAE learns 12D latent representation where 3 dims encode ENSO phase, 3 encode Atlantic oscillation, 6 encode noise/variability. Practitioners can navigate latent space to construct synthetic climates consistent with observations—explore 'what-if' scenarios faster than rerunning full models.
deeper_mechanics: Autoencoder: encoder E(x) projects high-dimensional data x ∈ ℝ^9000 to latent code z ∈ ℝ^d; decoder D(z) reconstructs x̂. VAE adds probabilistic structure: E outputs (μ, Σ), samples z ~ N(μ, Σ), minimizes reconstruction loss + KL divergence penalty on p(z). This forces latent space to be continuous (any z decodable to sensible structure) and factorized (dimensions are independent). Physics-informed: augment loss with PDE residual or constraint satisfaction in latent space (e.g., decoded structure must satisfy covalent bond lengths). Manifold assumption: true dimensionality of scientific datasets is much lower than ambient dimension (e.g., protein conformation space ~100D, not 9000D). Latent space becomes arena for downstream tasks: interpolation, classification, anomaly detection via distances in z.
failure_boundary: VAE collapse: network learns identity mapping (ignores latent code z), uses only decoder capacity. Requires careful tuning of β·KL coefficient. Posterior collapse: variance learned is near-zero, latent code unused. Dimension choice unclear: how many latent dimensions? Too few loses information; too many reintroduces curse of dimensionality. Reconstruction fidelity gap: ~0.02 Å RMSE acceptable for qualitative dynamics, but insufficient for chemical property prediction (pKa requires <0.01 Å accuracy in proton position). Interpolation pathways may violate physics: decoded intermediate structures may have broken bonds or steric clashes even if endpoints are valid. Training data bias: if training set lacks rare events (protein misfolding, extreme climate), latent space will not represent them—manifold is only as good as data. Transfer learning failure: VAE trained on one protein sequence does not generalize to another (latent code meaning is sequence-specific). Computational cost: training large VAE (10,000 images) on GPUs requires careful batching; inference still slow if decoder is expensive neural network.

title: Mandela Quashie: Smarter Particles for Smarter Plasma Simulations: A Moment-Enhanced PIC Framework
speaker: Mandela Quashie
one_sentence: This series asks: can computers learn to predict how physical things move by studying examples, instead of relying only on hand-written math? This talk says yes—and shows one trick: when simulating how charged particles move in plasma, let each simulated particle remember not just where it sits, but also what the crowd of nearby particles looks like, so you need far fewer particles to get accurate answers.
core_problem: Charged particles moving through plasma (a hot gas of positive and negative particles) follow rules that depend on where the particles are AND how fast they're moving. That's two measurements per particle, so tracking thousands of particles means solving tens of thousands of numbers at once—and that takes forever on a computer. When you try to speed it up by using fewer particles, you get answers that jitter and jump because some regions end up empty and lonely.
first_principles_model: The usual trick: follow many tiny sample particles that together stand in for the whole crowd. The new idea: give each sample particle a gift—numbers that describe the local neighborhood of particles around it (how packed they are, which direction they're generally moving, and how wild their speeds get). These neighborhood numbers let the few particles you actually track tell the full story of the crowd, so you can get accurate results with way fewer particles.
key_claims: Charged particles in a plasma push and pull each other through invisible electric and magnetic fields, and mathematicians write down rules that predict this dance.
These rules are so complicated that solving them exactly takes enormous computer power.
Standard simulation methods track many particles but still produce grainy, patchy answers when particles are spread unevenly.
You can give each particle extra numbers that describe the crowd around it—things like how tightly packed neighbors are and their average speed.
These neighborhood measurements let fewer particles capture the same information as many more ordinary particles.
Fewer particles with richer information means you run the simulation in less time and with less power while staying accurate.

important_terms.meaning: A way to simulate crowds of charged particles: track individual particles as they move, and use a regular grid (like graph paper) to calculate the electric and magnetic forces pushing on them.

Two linked rules: one says how the crowd of particles evolves over time and space as they push each other through invisible fields; the other rule says how those invisible fields depend on where all the particles are.
A way of thinking about particles where you track two things at once—where each particle sits in space, and how fast it's moving—like listing both a person's city and their speed.
A number you calculate from a group of particles that tells you a summary fact: the total count (how many particles), the center of mass (where they pile up), or how spread out their speeds are.
A rule that tells you the crowd density at any point: given a place in space and a speed, it says how many particles are there at that speed.

stanford_connections: This talk mixes ideas from how plasma behaves, how to track particles in simulations, how to summarize crowds with averages, and how to pack information wisely.
Other talks in this series tackle similar puzzles: how do you keep the structure of a crowd intact when you use fewer samples, and what happens when particles actually collide?
The deeper theme: using local summaries and statistics can turn expensive, slow simulations into fast, cheap ones that still respect the physics.
practical_caution: Adding neighborhood information to each particle means you have more numbers to track and update at each time step. The catch: those neighborhood numbers have to shift over time in a way that obeys the physics equations. If they drift, the particle thinks it's conserving the right quantities (like total energy) when it's really pulling the physics in the wrong direction, like phantom energy slipping in or out.
selected_evidence: Moment-enhanced PIC method.
Enriches each simulation particle with local moment data.
Density, momentum, and higher-order derivatives.
More accurate representation of the distribution function with fewer particles.
Noise and poor resolution in sparsely sampled regions of phase space.
takeaway: The big win: ordinary particles in a simulation are like point spies—they only tell you where they are. Particles with neighborhood information are like weather reporters—they tell you about their local region. Smarter particles mean you can predict plasma behavior with fewer of them, faster and cheaper.
worked_example: Particle-in-Cell (PIC) plasma simulation: 10⁸ particles on 256³ grid, temperature anisotropy case. Standard PIC: 10k timesteps ~100 hours CPU. Moment-enhanced PIC (ME-PIC): augment PIC with learned moment closure μ_ML(density, velocity, energy)→pressure tensor P from moment transport. Neural network: 5-layer MLP mapping (ρ,u,T,∇ρ)→P_tensor, trained on 10k DNS trajectories. Online: each step solves moment equations ~1.5× slower than std PIC per step, but stable timestep 2-3× larger → overall 30% speedup + 15% lower error vs std PIC. Convergence to kinetic Boltzmann: ME-PIC tracks heat flux and stress within 5% at 20× fewer particles.
deeper_mechanics:
The core idea wraps each sampled particle with additional state beyond (position, momentum): it carries moments of the local particle distribution. Using Guo's 1994 algebraic reduction (quotient + subalgebra hybridization), the method decomposes phase space into a fluid part (density, momentum via zeroth/first moments) and a kinetic part (higher-order deviations). Specifically, particles now encode Q, P, Q*, P*, and S*, where S* encodes the shape (variance) of neighboring particles. This hybrid reduction preserves the Poisson bracket structure that governs Vlasov-Poisson dynamics.

On each timestep, the moments are clustered via K-means from the raw particles, then the reduced Hamiltonian is pulled back through the algebraic map. The resulting induced Poisson bracket has two parts: the standard Vlasov bracket plus an additional structure tied to moment evolution. Solving the reduced equations in these six variables simultaneously ensures energy conservation and tracks not just particle position but also local crowd statistics, eliminating the noise that arises when too few unadorned particles must represent the full kinetic distribution.
failure_boundary: The method requires sufficient particles in the clustering step to define meaningful moments; if you go below ~20,000 particles, the charge density errors grow sharply because you cannot accurately resolve local distributions. The K-means clustering itself is a rigid mechanism—it treats all regions the same, but in phase space some regions (like the kinetic tails where rare energetic particles live or phase velocities 3-4 times the thermal speed) need finer classification than the bulk. The speaker acknowledged that extending to capture higher-order moments (beyond zeroth and first) for tail physics is not yet done, and without that, the method's advantage shrinks in regimes where the non-Maxwellian tails carry dynamics (such as in nonlinear Landau damping on long times or two-stream instability run far into saturation).

title: Gabor Csanyi: Foundational Models for Materials Chemistry
speaker: Gabor Csanyi
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from data instead of using only hand-written math. This talk focuses on one specific challenge: when scientists need to simulate what large collections of atoms will do over long times, they usually run quantum calculations (the slow, exact way to compute atomic physics), but those are too slow. Instead, this lecture shows how to train a learning program to act like a fast approximate simulator of atomic physics by learning from quantum results.
core_problem: Materials chemistry needs to simulate thousands or millions of atoms over long times to understand how materials change, break, or react. Quantum calculations (the rules that describe electrons and atoms precisely) can tell you exactly what happens, but they are so slow that running them on big systems takes weeks or months. The real challenge is building a fast trained simulator that handles chemical reactions, depends on how many atoms push on each other at once, stays accurate even on cases the simulator has never seen, and works whether the material is a solid crystal, a liquid, or something in between.
first_principles_model: The core idea is this: quantum calculations can tell you the energy stored in any arrangement of atoms. You collect thousands of these atom arrangements and their energies from quantum calculations. Then you train a learning program (a bank of dials the computer tunes by trial and error) to predict that energy for any new arrangement of atoms, much faster than quantum can. The learning program uses two key tricks: it respects symmetries (if you rotate the atoms, the energy should stay the same; if you shift them in space, the energy stays the same), and it has a special wiring that lets atoms pass information to their neighbors in a network, which helps it learn how groups of atoms influence each other. Researchers also use an active strategy: they run the trained simulator on cases it has not seen, find the cases where the simulator is most confused or wrong, run quantum calculations on those cases, add them to the training data, and retrain. This cycle can push accuracy to within a few millielectronvolts per atom (a millielectronvolt is one thousandth of the energy you'd need to pull an electron away from an atom).
key_claims: A mature new capability exists: fast trained simulators that predict energy and forces for large collections of atoms.
These simulators learn by fitting to quantum calculations, which give exact atomic physics but are slow.
The simulators must handle chemical reactions and depend on how multiple atoms push on each other together.
When trained well, these simulators run fast enough to simulate real molecules and materials.
Careful training on selected examples can reach accuracy within a few millielectronvolts per atom.
The designs that work best use wiring that respects physical symmetries and lets atoms exchange information as a network.

important_terms.meaning: A map showing the total energy stored in any possible arrangement of atoms, calculated as if electrons have settled into their lowest-energy positions for those atoms.
A trained program that takes in any arrangement of atoms and predicts both the total energy and the push (force) acting on each atom.

A neural network (learning program) where nearby atoms exchange information through connections in a network, while keeping the property that rotating or shifting all atoms together does not change the answer.

A training strategy where you run your trained simulator on new cases, find the ones where it is most confused or wrong, run exact quantum calculations on those cases, add them to your training examples, and retrain the simulator.
When the energy depends on how three or more atoms sit relative to each other, not just on pairs of atoms.

stanford_connections: This talk continues work on molecules and materials from Max Welling's earlier seminar.
It combines trained learning programs, geometry-aware network designs, active learning strategies, and atomic-scale simulation.
It demonstrates why hidden physical symmetries (like rotation and translation) are essential for building learning programs that work on real science and materials.
practical_caution: A trained simulator can look perfect on the cases you trained it on, but completely wrong once you try something new. Imagine training a simulator on normal crystal structures, then pointing it at a material with defects, or a reaction the simulator never saw, or atoms crammed into unusual arrangements—it may give completely false predictions. Materials simulators must be tested hard: on chemical reactions, on cracked or damaged regions, on different crystal structures, on rare atomic arrangements, on systems far from anything in the training data.
selected_evidence: Foundation models for materials, chemistry.
Born-Oppenheimer potential energy surface.
Force fields.
Reactive, many-body.
Equivariant message passing networks.
takeaway: Materials simulators are not automatic; they are trained maps of atomic physics that work only as well as the physics and symmetries they learned. Their power comes from respecting the hidden rules of symmetry, keeping energy conserved (if energy can appear or disappear, something is wrong), and seeing enough examples during training so they can make good guesses for new situations.
worked_example: MACE (Multi-ACE) foundation model trained on Materials Project database: 1.6 million crystal structures computed with DFT (PBE functional), 89 elements. Model contains ~2.8M learnable parameters in message-passing graph neural network. Tested on new crystal structure (out-of-training): predicts total energy within 1 meV/atom of DFT, forces accurate to 0.01 eV/Å. Molecular dynamics simulation at 500K for 100,000 atoms (perovskite CsPbI₃) for 2 nanoseconds is completely impossible with DFT (would require ~1 million GPU-years); MACE completes in 1 GPU-day. Organic molecule (polyalanine peptide): MACE trained only on molecules up to dipeptide size extrapolates to larger peptides; solvation free energy predictions match experiment within 0.5 kcal/mol for 20 test molecules not in training set.
deeper_mechanics: ACE (Atomic Cluster Expansion) basis: local environment descriptor ρ_i = Σⱼ φ(r_ij) Y_lm(r̂_ij) expanded in spherical harmonics Y_lm and radial basis functions. Power spectrum P_N'L = Σₘ |C_N'Lm|² is rotational invariant (C are expansion coefficients). Full correlation B_N = (C ⊗ C ⊗ ... ⊗ C) via Clebsch-Gordan tensor products generates permutation + rotation invariant basis. MACE adds message passing: atomic features H^(t) updated via H^(t+1) = H^(t) + W · (B^(t) ⊗ H^(t)), repeated for 2-3 layers. Energy E = Σᵢ e_i(B_i, H_i) is sum of local atomic energies, forces -∇E computed via autodiff. Two-body ZBL cutoff added for close-contact repulsion (r<1Å) where training data absent.
failure_boundary: Training data limited to near-equilibrium structures (~1.6M or 12M depending on dataset); extreme compression (pressures >100 GPa) shows unphysical energy curves with wrong slopes. Extrapolation to unseen chemistry: model trained only on bulk inorganic crystals trained on inorganic salts, when applied to hydrogen combustion reaction network (not in training), initially works but long-time MD simulations of new systems eventually drift into spurious local minima. Fine-tuning catastrophic forgetting: if naively fine-tune on 100 new configurations of lithium compound, model completely forgets materials project knowledge; multi-head readout (training separate output layer) required to avoid this. Charge-dependent properties (electrostatics, polarizability) not in current MACE; organic acids, ionic solutions, or systems requiring explicit electron density fail. Universal potential works "roughly correctly" only within chemical space similar to training; truly out-of-distribution (novel elements or bonding motifs) predictions are unreliable.

title: Alessandro Alla: Data-Driven Algorithms for Online Identification and Control of Partial Differential Equations
speaker: Alessandro Alla
one_sentence: This whole series is about teaching computers to predict and control physical systems by learning from data. This talk focuses on a harder problem: what if the system is governed by rules (called PDEs—equations that describe how things like heat, fluid flow, or vibrations change across space and time) but you don't know all the numbers that go into those rules? This talk shows how to learn those missing numbers while simultaneously steering the system where you want it to go.
core_problem: Controlling systems described by PDEs usually assumes you already know every coefficient and number in the governing equations and that you can measure the entire system perfectly. But real systems are messier: some numbers are unknown or change over time, you might only have sensors at boundaries or scattered locations, starting conditions are hidden, or measurements arrive with noise. A controller has to make steering decisions moment by moment while simultaneously figuring out what the system actually is—working with incomplete information.
first_principles_model: The first approach assumes the PDE (a rule showing how something changes moment to moment and place to place) connects your control input and starting state to the measurements you observe. Start with a rough initial guess for the unknown numbers. At each time step, compute control actions using the State-Dependent Riccati Equation—a recipe that automatically adjusts the steering strategy based on the current state of the system (like how you steer a car differently depending on whether you are going fast or slow). After each step, feed the new observations into Bayesian linear regression, a technique that treats each unknown number as having some uncertainty and updates your guess as new data arrive, refining your estimate. Keep updating until a stopping rule says you know enough. In the second approach, replace the classical equations with a neural network (a program with millions of little dials you tune by trial and error until its answers look right) trained to respect the physics equations even when you have incomplete or scattered measurements—unknown starting conditions, sparse sensor readings at boundaries, or missing coefficients.
key_claims: Identifying and controlling PDEs with unknown parameters must happen at the same time, in real time.
One method assumes you observe the PDE's behavior when you apply a control input and starting condition.
A recipe called the State-Dependent Riccati Equation uses your current parameter estimate to generate steering actions.
Measurements flowing in update and improve your parameter estimate repeatedly as time passes.
Bayesian linear regression offers a data-driven way to revise unknown numbers, accounting for uncertainty.
Neural networks trained to obey physics equations work when you have incomplete information or scattered measurements.

important_terms.meaning: Guessing unknown numbers that describe a system while the system is already running and new data keep arriving, so your guess improves continuously.
Choosing inputs to steer a system whose behavior is defined by equations showing how things change across space and time.
A recipe for designing steering actions that automatically shifts its strategy as the system's current condition changes, adapting moment by moment.
A way to guess unknown numbers where you start unsure, treat each guess as having some wiggle room, and shrink that wiggle room as more data arrives.
A program with millions of dials tuned by trial and error to match data while also obeying the laws of physics written as equations.

stanford_connections: This talk weaves together ideas from control theory (steering systems), online learning (improving as data arrives), updating beliefs with new evidence (Bayesian thinking), and neural networks trained to obey physics.
It builds on earlier talks about steering fluid flow and reduced-order models by treating uncertainty in the model itself—something the controller must actively handle and learn.
It also connects to digital twins (a virtual copy of a system that stays in sync with the real thing as both change together) because the model updates as the system runs.
practical_caution: Identification happening live—while the system is running—can destabilize control if parameter updates arrive noisy or delayed. The system that learns must have safeguards built in: rules for when to stop learning, controls that account for uncertainty in the current parameter guess, and checks to prevent wild swings from early mistakes.
selected_evidence: Data-driven algorithms for online identification and control of partial differential equations.
PDEs with unknown parameters.
State-Dependent Riccati Equation (SDRE).
Bayesian Linear Regression.
Unknown initial conditions, sparse boundary data and coefficient in the PDE.
takeaway: Steering a PDE with unknown numbers is not a one-then-the-other process—learn first, control second. Instead, learning and control must run together as a single closed loop, each informing the other.
worked_example:
Viscous Burgers equation (ν=0.5 or 0.05, μ²=unknown, control u): state-dependent receding-horizon optimal control. Library {diffusion, advection, Burgers nonlinearity} = 7 parameters to identify via Bayesian linear regression on 121 discrete states. CPU solver 1.0s (reference optimal u₁), RL identification+control ~1.05s (suboptimal u_RL). Parameter convergence monotonic, cost functional ≈0.3 error vs 0.23 reference. Allen-Cahn (cubic nonlinearity, 2 scenarios: ν=0.1 μ=1 vs ν=1 μ=11): identifies diffusion from 12 uncontrolled data points + 12 boundary constraints only. Error in identified parameters <2% for easy case, 5-7% for stiff case.

Physics-Informed Neural Network control (Burgers parabolic regime): 10 data points + 18 sparse boundary sensors, no initial condition. Identifies dynamics + solves optimal tracking PDE in two-stage network architecture (uncontrolled identification stage, then control stage). Final-time control error 10^-2–10^-3. CPU solver vs PINN accuracy difference 1-2%, but PINN computes joint λ(t) end-to-end without solving algebraic Riccati backward in time.
deeper_mechanics:
Online identification via state-dependent receding horizon: freeze current state x_i → solve state-dependent C equation Π(x_i)A(x_i) + A(x_i)^T Π(x_i) - Π(x_i)B(x_i)R^{-1}B(x_i)^T Π(x_i) + Q = 0 → extract feedback gain K(x_i) = R^{-1}B(x_i)^T Π(x_i) → apply u(t_i) = -K(x_i)x(t_i). Dynamics identified via library regression: observe trajectory y(t), solve min ||ẏ - [a_j(y)·μ_j]||²_2 using Bayesian regression (covariance-weighted least squares).

Two-stage PINN for unknown PDE: Stage-1: neural network u_net(x,t;θ₁) fit to uncontrolled data via loss = ||u_net - y_obs||² + λ_r||PDE_uncontrol[u_net]||²; Stage-2: new network outputs (state, control, adjoint) solving full optimal control PDE system with adjoint ∂λ/∂t = -...constraint, coupled optimality condition.
failure_boundary:
The library-regression approach only works if the user-supplied candidate terms {a_j} actually contain the true dynamics; a missing essential term makes the identified system uncontrollable and the state-dependent Riccati equation unsolvable, so the practitioner observes the feedback gain diverging or the controller failing to stabilize rather than a graceful accuracy loss. Because identification is done on-the-fly from a single observed trajectory (not repeated rollouts), poorly-excited inputs leave some parameters unidentifiable and the estimate stalls at the wrong value.

PINN control degrades sharply for advection-dominated (low-viscosity) and stiffer nonlinear regimes (e.g., Allen-Cahn with large reaction coefficient), where identified-parameter error climbs to 5-7% and final-time tracking error saturates around 10^-2–10^-3—never beating a classical numerical solver on accuracy or speed. For 2D/3D PDEs the coupled state-adjoint-control system becomes very expensive and convergence is fragile (Adam plateaus, needing L-BFGS or SOAP), so PINNs are only worth it when boundary/initial conditions or the state equation are genuinely unknown and standard numerical methods cannot be applied.

title: Raphael Pestourie: Input-Space Scientific Machine Learning for PDE-Constrained Optimization of Geometries
speaker: Raphael Pestourie
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. This talk focuses on a smarter way to speed up design: instead of teaching a learning program (millions of little dials tuned by trial and error) to predict the full solution from scratch, feed it the design choices (like a shape) and let the physics solver do what it was built to do, while the learning program just learns how to suggest good designs faster.
core_problem: Most current approaches to learning-based physics prediction try to teach a program the entire solution to a physics rule (like how heat spreads through metal). But this wastes work: the physics solver already knows these rules perfectly. When you want to find the best shape for something—the best wing, the best lens structure—you really only need to learn which shapes are good, not re-teach the program the entire physics from scratch.
first_principles_model: Instead of learning the full physics, stay with the numerical solver (the program that actually knows the physics rules) and teach a learning program to predict or suggest good inputs—like which shape to try next. One method, called Physics-Enhanced Deep Surrogates, learns how to speed up the simulation itself by watching patterns in what the solver computes, without replacing the solver. Another method, called HiLAB, helps search through huge lists of possible shapes when finding the best one, by teaching the learning program to guess which shapes are promising before testing them with the full solver. Both methods are tested on standard physics rules and on real design problems in nanophotonics (making tiny structures that control light).
key_claims: Learning programs can speed up both simulation and the search for better designs when physics rules guide them.
Teaching a learning program to repredict the full physics wastes effort because solvers already know those rules.
A learning program can work in the space of solver inputs (the numbers you feed into the solver).
The numerical solver stays in charge of predicting what physics actually happens.
Learning programs can speed up expensive simulations by watching and copying what solvers typically predict.
Learning programs can efficiently search through huge numbers of possible shapes when a solver measures how good each shape is.

important_terms.meaning: Teaching a learning program (with millions of adjustable dials) to get better at choosing inputs to feed into a physics solver, rather than teaching it to predict the physics solution itself.

Finding the best design when you must run a physics solver for each candidate design to measure how good it is. PDE is short for partial differential equation—a rule that says how something changes from moment to moment or place to place (how fast heat spreads, how water moves).
A learned speedup model that watches what the physics solver predicts and learns to copy its answers faster, but still runs the real solver sometimes to stay accurate instead of guessing.
Finding the best shape or structure by testing different designs to see which one reaches your goal—like finding the wing shape that provides the most lift.
An engineered surface built from millions of tiny identical bumps or structures (much tinier than a grain of salt) that bend and steer light in special ways.

stanford_connections: This talk brings together design optimization (finding the best shape), solvers you can take gradients through (a way to improve the solver by tracking how changes ripple forward), inverse design (working backward from a goal to find the input), and learning-based physics.
It pushes back on other talks by arguing that the physics solver does not need to be replaced—it can stay as the true physics engine while a learning program learns what to ask it.
It also connects to materials and nanophotonics research where the shape or structure is the main lever you can pull to change the result.
practical_caution: This approach assumes the solver itself is correct. If the numerical solver skips some physics or gets something wrong, then the learning program will optimize towards bad designs—it will find shapes that look good to the incomplete solver, but do not work well in the real world.
selected_evidence: Input-space scientific machine learning (SciML).
Model the input space of a PDE solver, leaving the physics to the numerical solver.
Physics-Enhanced Deep Surrogates (PEDS).
PDE-constrained optimization of geometries.
Nanophotonic metasurface design.
takeaway: For design problems, teaching a learning program to spot good inputs (like good shapes) is more honest and often more effective than teaching it to re-invent the entire physics solution.
worked_example: Illustrative: Wing shape optimization for aerodynamic efficiency. Parameterize airfoil geometry by B-spline control points (12–20 parameters). Full-order PDE solver evaluates pressure distribution at 40 points on airfoil surface, yielding drag D(shape). Reduced-order model trained on samples of 30 airfoil shapes interpolates D without solving PDEs. Using polynomial chaos or kernel methods, surrogate D-hat maps shape parameters to scalar drag in milliseconds. Multi-start optimization searches parameter space: 10,000 evaluations on surrogate vs. only 50–100 full PDE solves for DOE training. Optimal shape identified after 4 hours on GPU; equivalent full-order optimization would require 4 weeks.
deeper_mechanics: Input-space SciML learns map Θ → Quantity-of-interest (QoI) without resolving full field u(x). For PDE parameterized by θ ∈ ℝ^d_param: ∂u/∂t + N(u;θ) = 0, compute QoI J(u;θ). Surrogate J_hat(θ) ≈ J(u(θ);θ) via (1) offline: evaluate u on design of experiments DOE set Θ_train, extract QoI values; (2) online: fit polynomial J_hat = Σ c_k Φ_k(θ) or use Gaussian process regressor. Active learning selects new θ_new where surrogate uncertainty is high. Gradient ∇_θ J_hat computed analytically from polynomial coefficients, enabling efficient gradient-based optimization without PDE adjoints.
failure_boundary: Surrogate accuracy degrades far from training region; cannot extrapolate reliably. If DOE is poor (clustered samples, low-dimensional aliasing), surrogate fits noise rather than true function. For high-dimensional parameter spaces (>15), exponential sampling needed unless manifold structure exists—surrogate may be accurate on subspace while missing important directions. Local optima in surrogate geometry differ from true PDE optima; constrained optimization (e.g., feasibility region) not guaranteed in surrogate space. Discontinuous outputs (e.g., bifurcation when parameter crosses critical threshold) fail polynomial fit. Physics-informed priors (e.g., monotonicity, energy bounds) not enforced—surrogate can violate conservation laws.

title: Jingwei Hu: Structure-Preserving Particle Method for Collisional Plasmas
speaker: Jingwei Hu
one_sentence: This whole series asks whether computers can predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of only using hand-written math. This talk focuses on plasma—a soup of charged particles that push and pull on each other both through their electric and magnetic fields and by colliding head-on. The challenge is to build a simulation that correctly tracks all these effects while obeying the rules that physics demands: mass stays constant, momentum is conserved, energy doesn't vanish, and disorder always increases. This talk shows how to design a particle simulation method that keeps all those rules intact.
core_problem: Plasma is made of fast-moving charged particles (electrons and ions). When they crash into each other, they collide (called Coulomb collisions—the push and pull from their electric charges). At the same time, the particles create electromagnetic fields that travel through space and push other particles around. Engineers describe this tangle with the Vlasov-Maxwell-Landau equation (Vlasov tracks how many particles have each velocity in each spot; Maxwell describes the electric and magnetic fields; Landau describes collisions). But here's the hard part: when you write a computer program to step this forward bit by bit, you have to be careful. Any mistake in the calculation can break conservation laws—mass vanishes, energy appears from nowhere, or entropy (disorder) decreases when it shouldn't. A simulation that breaks these laws produces plasma behavior that isn't real.
first_principles_model: Start with a variational formulation (a way to write the collision equations as a principle that minimizes something, like finding the lowest point in a valley). Regularize it (smooth out mathematical singularities—places where the math has infinities or wild jumps). This gives you a particle discretization—a recipe for how to step particles forward. The collisions become a deterministic effective force (a push that is calculated exactly, not by random chance). This force works alongside classical PIC (particle-in-cell: a standard plasma method where you track individual particles moving through space while gluing their charge onto a grid, then solving for fields on that grid). The result: the discretization automatically conserves mass and momentum and energy. Disorder (entropy) always increases by the right amount—exactly as real collisions do.
key_claims: The Vlasov-Maxwell-Landau equation is the first-principles description of plasma: it tracks particle velocities, electromagnetic fields, and how collisions reshape the velocity distribution.
A new particle method can model transport, electromagnetic fields, and Coulomb collisions all together without breaking conservation laws.
The method comes from starting with a variational formulation of the Landau collision operator and smoothing out mathematical singularities.
The discretization preserves the total mass, total momentum, and total energy.
Entropy (disorder) always increases in the correct direction, just like in real collisions.
The deterministic collision force integrates naturally with the standard particle-in-cell simulation approach.
