important_terms.meaning: A rule that couples three things together: how many particles have each velocity at each location (Vlasov), the electric and magnetic fields they create (Maxwell), and how head-on collisions between charged particles push velocities around (Landau).
A mathematical rule that describes how charged particles redistribute their speeds and directions when they collide with each other due to the push from their electric charges.
A numerical recipe designed to keep the conservation laws and dissipation rules of the physics intact as you step the simulation forward.
The one-way growth of disorder in the system—a measure of randomness that always increases when particles collide, spreading organized motion into heat.

A plasma simulation method where you track individual particles moving through space and glue their charge onto a grid; the grid then solves for the electric and magnetic fields everywhere, and those fields push the particles around in return.

stanford_connections: This talk brings together structure-preserving numerics (methods that keep physics laws intact), kinetic theory (the math of particles and velocities), and plasma particle simulation.
It builds on earlier talks in the series by emphasizing that numerical methods must respect the conservation laws and dissipation rules that define the physics model.
It shows that the core DDPS theme holds for plasma: a simulation should obey the same laws that the real physics obeys.
practical_caution: Preserving conservation laws and entropy dissipation is necessary, but it doesn't guarantee the simulation is correct or fast enough. You have to test it on different plasma scenarios: damping (how wiggles die away), instability (how waves or structures grow), and shock-like behavior (sharp jumps in density or temperature). Real plasma is complicated; keeping the math laws intact is only the first step.
selected_evidence: Structure preserving particle method for collisional plasma.
Vlasov-Maxwell-Landau equation.
Particle transport, electromagnetic field effects, and Coulomb collisions.
Conserves mass, momentum, and energy.
Dissipates the entropy.
takeaway: When you build a particle simulation of plasma, the method should preserve the conservation and dissipation laws that the kinetic equation demands. This is the foundation of getting real physics out.
worked_example: Collisional plasma (ions + electrons, magnetic field B). Kinetic equations (Vlasov-Boltzmann): ∂f_s/∂t + v·∇_x f_s + (q_s/m_s)(E + v × B)·∇_v f_s = C[f_s, f_s'] (collision term). Structure-preserving particle method: discrete particles carry (x,v,q), updated via: Δx = v_old Δt, Δv = (q/m)(E + v_mid × B) Δt + collision_kick. Conserves charge and momentum exactly (C_i = Σ m_i Δv_i = 0), energy to machine precision.
deeper_mechanics: Staggered leap-frog integrator: v_{n-1/2}, x_n, v_{n+1/2}. Collision operator C[f] computed via pair-wise binary collisions: Δv_post-collision ∝ relative velocity angle, magnitude calibrated by cross-section σ(v_rel). Energy conservation: collision updates chosen to scatter energy but preserve total kinetic energy (within Coulomb potential). Ampere's law ∇ × B = μ₀ J updated via particle current J = Σ q_i δ(x-x_i) v_i.
failure_boundary: Large time-steps (Δt > ω_c^{-1}, cyclotron freq) cause spurious trapping modes in EM fields. Collision operator scales as O(n_part²) in naive form; tree-codes needed for large plasmas (>10⁶ particles). High-velocity-space resolution required near sound speed; rare high-energy events (e-e collisions) need importance sampling or adaptive refinement.

title: Siddhartha Mishra: AI for Data-Driven Simulations in Physics
speaker: Siddhartha Mishra
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave—air over a wing, heat in metal, water sloshing—by learning from examples instead of hand-written math. This talk focuses on a particular way to do that: instead of teaching a learning program the physics rules line by line, we give it examples of 'before and after' from a simulator and let it learn the whole jump from start to finish in one go, like learning a shortcut through a forest by walking it many times.
core_problem: Rules that describe how things change moment to moment and place to place—heat spreading through a bar, air pressure around an airplane—are the backbone of physics and engineering. But running the exact step-by-step calculations to solve these rules takes hours or days on a computer, even for a single prediction. A faster substitute would save time and money, but it faces a hard challenge: a learning program trained on one set of starting conditions or materials must somehow predict correctly for different starting conditions, different materials, different shapes—situations it never trained on.
first_principles_model: The idea is to teach a learning program (with millions of little dials tuned by trial and error until its answers look right) to be a shortcut itself. Feed it the starting conditions, material properties, and geometry of a problem; the program outputs the full solution instantly. The talk walks through three main recipes: (1) sliding-filter designs that sweep across the data to find patterns, (2) attention designs that ask 'which parts of the input matter most for this prediction', and (3) mesh-aware networks that work on irregular grids (like the cracks in a real airplane wing) instead of clean square grids. It also covers a recent method: building the solution step by step by removing noise, steered by the input conditions.
key_claims: Rules that describe how things change are the language of physics and engineering.
Solving these rules by hand-written step-by-step math takes too long for practical work.
Learning programs can be trained to jump straight from starting conditions to solution, skipping the slow calculations.
Teaching a learning program to do this is now a major direction in machine learning.
Sliding filters and attention are the two winning designs so far.
Newer methods that build solutions layer by layer (like removing fog to reveal a landscape) are opening new doors, especially for generating many different possible solutions instead of just one.

important_terms.meaning: A learning program that takes in the starting conditions and rules of a physics problem (like 'this bar starts at room temperature' or 'air flows at this speed') and outputs the full solution (temperatures everywhere after 10 seconds, or pressures everywhere around the wing).
A trained stand-in that mimics a simulator: you feed it a problem setup and get the answer almost instantly, instead of waiting hours for the real step-by-step calculator.
A learning program that uses map-like connections between points (instead of assuming a neat grid) to handle bumpy, irregular shapes like real engineering geometries.

A design that learns which parts of the input to pay attention to and how they influence each part of the output; used here to handle arbitrary shapes and detect long-range effects (like how a change on one side of the domain echoes to the other side).

A method that constructs a solution by repeatedly removing noise from random static, step by step, while being steered by the input conditions (like sculpting a statue by chipping away stone guided by a blueprint).

stanford_connections: This talk sits at the center of this whole series: it collects threads from every seminar—how to replace slow solvers with fast learned ones, how attention learns dependencies, how to work on irregular shapes, how to build systems that learn directly from real data.
It directly connects to earlier talks on learned operators, on solvers you can take gradients through, and on methods that compress solutions into smaller learned spaces.

It also points forward: neural operators are emerging as the physics-specific version of huge foundation models—general-purpose learning machines that might handle many types of physics problems if we scale them up enough.
practical_caution: Speed matters only if the answer is right. A learning program trained to predict fast must be checked: Does it conserve energy and momentum like the real physics does? Does it blow up or go wild on inputs far outside what it trained on? Does it tell us when it is uncertain? Does it work on edges and corners, or only in the middle of familiar territory? Skip these checks and the model becomes a beautiful hallucination.
selected_evidence: AI for data-driven simulations in Physics.
Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) model a large variety of phenomena.
Machine Learning/AI based neural PDE surrogates.
Neural Operators.
Graph and transformer based architectures for PDEs on arbitrary domains and conditional Diffusion models.
takeaway: The core idea is that a learning program can learn the whole 'before to after' map—if you show it enough real examples, it can learn to predict what comes next nearly as fast as looking it up in a table, but without the table.
worked_example: DrivAero dataset (MIT): 8,000 car shapes, each ~2 million surface nodes, RANS simulation took 300 node-hours per sample to generate; geometry-aware operator transformer inference: 0.4 seconds, achieving significantly better accuracy than leaderboard models. DrivAeroML (Neil Ashton, Nvidia): 500 car shapes, 10 million surface nodes, ALES (unstructured) fidelity. Turbulent DNS at (Taylor-Green initial condition perturbed): 64³ discretization resolves multiscale, chaotic Navier-Stokes; diffusion-based model recovers full variance and spectral statistics (variance previously zero with deterministic neural operators). Tsunami simulation (shallow water): 1 millisecond inference (vs. 30 min-1 hour with UQ). Race car aerodynamics: 0.1 seconds (vs. 500 node-hours).
deeper_mechanics: Operator learning as infinite-dimensional neural networks: kernel integral operator replaces matrix-vector multiply. Fourier Neural Operator (FNO): convolution in Fourier space with learnable multiplier, inverse transform, pointwise nonlinearity. Convolutional Neural Operator (CNO): local convolution + non-local activation (fights spectral aliasing from pointwise nonlinearity on band-limited functions). Transformer-based operator transformer: softmax kernel (attention) for global information transfer, windowed attention (domain decomposition across layers) for scalability. Geometry-aware operator transformer: graph neural network (complex point cloud) → structured latent grid → transformer latent space → inverse to original coordinates. Diffusion models (GenCFD): condition on initial data, add noise in forward step to Gaussian, reverse step removes noise given initial condition via trained reverse SDE; trains denoiser (handles small perturbations better than direct approximation).
failure_boundary: Deterministic neural operators fail on chaotic systems: neural networks insensitive to small perturbations (edge-of-chaos training), but chaotic flows highly sensitive. Collapse to mean: variance entirely absent despite ground truth having high variance from perturbation sensitivity. Aliasing errors when CNNs treat grid-independent operator learning: error increases both coarser and finer; CNO and FNO more robust. Transformers quadratic scaling O(n²) in spatial dimension; patching (finite volume averaging) + windowed attention mitigates. Sample efficiency: even best models need 1000-10000 samples for 1% error (exponent α~0.5, limiting for engineering without vast data sets). Transfer learning (fine-tuning) on unseen PDE classes requires foundation models; foundation model requires pre-training on multiple PDEs (data generation bottleneck with 5 million image pairs, 630M parameters for reasonable coverage).

title: Youngsoo Choi: Defining Foundation Models for Computational Science: Toward Clarity and Rigor
speaker: Youngsoo Choi
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples. This talk asks: what exactly should we call a foundation model for science, and shows one concrete way to build one by combining the old-school math methods that engineers have trusted for decades with modern trial-and-error learning.
core_problem: In language and vision, foundation models work—a single huge learning program, trained once on lots of data, can then be twisted to solve many different tasks. But in computational science (predicting how fluids flow, how materials break, how climates shift), people are starting to use the term foundation model without really agreeing on what it means. This opens the door to marketing hype. Different problem families—fluids, materials, climate, design optimization, uncertainty quantification—each have their own demands. A program that calls itself a foundation model for science needs to prove it can be reused across different problems, scaled up to harder cases, and still respect the rigor that scientists and engineers demand.
first_principles_model: A real foundation model for computational science should do three things: work on many different types of problems without starting from scratch each time; handle bigger, harder versions of the same problem without falling apart; and keep the mathematical bones and discipline of the old numerical methods (the formulas engineers have used for decades to carve space into pieces and solve equations locally) while adding smart learning components that adapt automatically from data. The talk lays out what properties matter and introduces one path forward: Data-Driven Finite Element Method, which keeps the structure of classical finite-element solvers but teaches part of them to learn from data instead of relying only on hand-written formulas.
key_claims: The term foundation model is spreading from language and vision into computational science.
The field needs a shared, rigorous definition or the term loses all meaning.
Three criteria matter most: generalization (does it work on new problems?), reusability (can I adapt it without retraining from scratch?), and scalability (can it handle bigger, harder cases?).
A scientific foundation model must be judged against what scientists actually need, not just against machine-learning test scores.
Data-Driven Finite Element Method is one concrete path: it borrows the structure and mathematical rigor of classical numerical methods and teaches them to learn from data.
The goal is clarity and rigor—laying out what counts and what does not—not picking one fixed design that works for all science.

important_terms.meaning: A learning program trained once on a large and diverse collection of data, then adapted to solve many different downstream tasks by further adjustment rather than retraining from scratch.

Using mathematical equations, computer simulations, and numerical recipes to predict and understand how real physical systems behave—fluids, solids, temperature, motion, chemical reactions, climate patterns.

A method that divides space into tiny regions and solves equations piece by piece, like classical finite elements, but replaces some of the hand-written formulas with a learning program that adapts to match actual data from experiments or simulations.
Whether a model can handle many different problems and tasks after being trained or designed once, without having to rebuild and retrain it from the ground up each time.
Whether a model can handle much larger problems, finer detail, more complex physics, or more expensive calculations without crashing or losing accuracy.

stanford_connections: This talk ties together the earlier talks in the series on reduced-order models (smaller, faster approximations), neural operators (learning rules written as operations), materials science, and the broader thread about foundation models for science.
It pushes back against handwaving by insisting that foundation model must mean something precise and specific to each field, not just a borrowed term from language and vision.
It also grounds foundation models in classical numerical analysis and operator networks, treating the mathematical structure of scientific computation as non-negotiable, not an optional add-on.
practical_caution: Size alone does not make a foundation model. A program can be huge and still useless for science. The label should only apply if someone has shown the model actually transfers to new problems, generalizes beyond its training data, and follows the standards that domain scientists expect.
selected_evidence: Defining foundation models for computational science toward clarity and rigor.
Necessary and desirable characteristics.
Generalization, reusability, and scalability.
Data-Driven Finite Element Method (DD-FEM).
Modular structure and mathematical rigor of classical numerical methods with the adaptability of modern machine learning.
takeaway: A foundation model for science must be defined by what scientific problems it can actually solve and reuse, not by analogy to big language models alone.
worked_example: Illustrative example: guided manifold learning on porous media flow. Training set of 50-200 simulations with varying permeability fields (lognormal, correlated). Deep network learns low-dimensional latent space where solutions concentrate. Prediction speedup 10-50x on unseen permeability realizations. Compared to linear POD, nonlinear manifold captures tensor-train decomposition structure of heterogeneous problems.
deeper_mechanics: Manifold linearization: decompose solution u = u_lin + δu where u_lin satisfies linearized PDE around reference parameter. Deep network learns δu in low-dim space. Jointly optimize reference state and manifold basis to minimize prediction error across parameter range. For parabolic PDEs (diffusion-dominated), manifold typically 5-20 dimensional despite 1000+ DOF discretization. Guided means incorporating physics constraints: enforce boundary conditions strongly in loss, penalize non-physical solutions.
failure_boundary: Method fails when nonlinearity dominates over linear component (high Rayleigh number, strong convection). Manifold assumption breaks at bifurcation points. Extrapolation beyond training parameter range unreliable. Ill-posedness if reference state poorly chosen.

title: Ulisses M. Braga-Neto: Scientific Machine Learning: From Physics-Informed to Data-Driven
speaker: Ulisses M. Braga-Neto
one_sentence: This whole series asks: can a learning program predict how physical things behave (heat spreading, air flowing, structures flexing) by studying examples instead of hand-built equations? This talk explores the different ways to do it—some start by telling the learning program the laws of physics, others just show it solution data and let it find the pattern.
core_problem: When you need a program to predict physical behavior, you have choices. You can write down the physics rules (a set of equations describing how things change), but that takes effort and only works if you know the rules. Or you can show the program lots of examples and let it learn the pattern, but it might learn the wrong thing if the examples don't cover all the situations you care about. Different methods make different bets on this tradeoff—some mix the physics rules with learning, others focus only on learning from data.
first_principles_model: The two main approaches are: (1) Physics-informed methods, such as a learning program that is also told the physics rules—where in the domain (the space and time we are studying) you can check whether the rules hold. You pick certain spots and measure how badly the rules are broken there (the residual), then penalize the program for these rule-breaks as it learns. This way the program has to respect both the data examples and the physics. (2) Data-driven operator learning, which finds the mathematical map—the transformation that takes input conditions (like temperature at the start, or pressure on edges) to the solution (like heat throughout the bar, or flow around the wing)—directly from examples, without necessarily writing down the equations at all. The idea is that if you have enough examples of inputs and solutions, the learning program can detect the pattern and apply it to new inputs, even if no one writes down the rules explicitly. These methods use very different approaches and work better in different situations.
key_claims: Learning programs can predict how physical things behave by combining machine learning with scientific computation for simulation, discovering hidden rules, and solving inverse problems (figuring out what caused observations).
Physics-informed methods like PINNs became popular because they make it straightforward to add physics rules into the learning process.
Operator learning is a newer approach that focuses on learning directly from solution data without explicitly coding up the equations.
Operator learning can work even when you don't know or can't afford to write down the exact rules.
Physics-informed and data-driven approaches have different strengths—one wins when equations are reliable, the other when data is abundant.
Plasma turbulence is one real-world problem where these methods get tested.

important_terms.meaning: Using learning programs (neural networks or other statistical methods) to solve the problems that scientists and engineers normally solve with hand-written equations: predicting how physical systems evolve, finding rules from measurements, or figuring out what caused observed data.

A learning program (neural network) that learns from examples while also being penalized for breaking the physics rules—so it has to respect both the data and the equations as it tunes its millions of dials.
A statistical model that learns from data while also incorporating the physics rules as constraints, giving you not just a prediction but also a measure of uncertainty.

Teaching a program the transformation that takes input conditions (like starting temperature, or boundary forces) to the solution (how heat spreads, how stress flows), so it can predict solutions for new inputs without needing to solve the equations from scratch each time.
Checking that your physics rules hold by testing them at specific chosen points spread throughout the domain (like measuring if the heat equation is satisfied at 100 spots across the bar).

stanford_connections: This talk brings together earlier talks in this series: physics-informed neural networks, neural operators, learning from data when equations are unknown, and building fast predictors that stand in for expensive simulations.
It sharpens the question running through the whole series: where does the physics come from—from equations you write, from the shape of your program, or from the data you learn from?
It connects to talks about learning from data by showing how moving physics into the dataset (instead of writing equations) changes what the learning program can and cannot do.
practical_caution: The idea that 'the physics is hidden in the data' only works if your examples actually cover the real situations you will face and if they truly show the physics, not just noise. If you train a learning program on examples from one temperature range or one type of flow, then ask it to predict something far outside that range, it may fail badly because it never saw examples like that.
selected_evidence: Scientific Machine Learning: From Physics-Informed to Data-Driven.
Physics-informed neural networks (PINN).
Physics-informed Gaussian processes (PIGP).
Operator learning has emerged as a powerful SciML paradigm.
The physics is in the data.
takeaway: Different SciML methods place physics in different places: some write the rules into the training process (physics-informed), some build the physics into the shape of the program (architecture), and some rely on the data itself to contain the physics signature.
worked_example: Physics-informed neural networks solved the viscous Burgers equation (u_t + uu_x = 0.01 u_xx) on a small network (8 layers, 20 neurons, 20,000 collocation points) in 400 training iterations (~1 minute GPU). For the Allen-Cahn reaction-diffusion equation, naive PINN failed to capture early sharp transitions; self-adaptive weighting detected the problem region within early epochs and grew weights there, allowing the network to recover the correct solution. Parameter identification: given noisy solution data, PINN simultaneously learned both the solution u and the unknown viscosity parameter (0.01/pi) from a wide initialization range, converging reliably in all 10 runs.
deeper_mechanics: PINN embeds the PDE residual r = ∂u/∂t + N[u] into the loss: L_total = λ_ic ||u(x,0) - u0||^2 + λ_bc ||u(∂Ω,t)||^2 + λ_pde ||r(x,t)||^2. Automatic differentiation computes ∂u/∂t, ∂u/∂x, ∂²u/∂x² through the network. Self-adaptive weights scale each component separately per spatial point (not globally); weight magnitudes are initialized and then evolved via a secondary ODE that penalizes imbalance. For inverse problems, parameters theta enter the residual r(theta) and are treated as additional trainable variables in the network.
failure_boundary: PINN with equal weights on all loss components fails when different terms have vastly different magnitudes (e.g., initial condition smooth but boundary condition oscillatory)—the network learns to satisfy the dominant term and ignores others. Hyperbolic systems (pure transport) exhibit slow convergence and require many collocation points; training may plateau before capturing sharp fronts. Chaotic systems with sensitive dependence on initial conditions produce predictions that diverge exponentially despite accurate residual—pointwise accuracy implies model knowledge but not forecast skill. High-dimensional problems (10+ space dimensions) demand exponentially more collocation points or adaptive refinement strategies to maintain coverage.

title: Nan Chen: Bridging Models and Data: Assimilation, Model Hierarchies, Causal Inference and Digital Twins
speaker: Nan Chen
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from data instead of only hand-written math. This talk focuses on one key tool: taking a program's predictions and constantly tuning them by comparing what the program says will happen to what actually happens in real measurements, then using this tuned program to combine models of different complexity, trace what caused observed events, and run "what if?" tests on a live digital copy of a physical system.
core_problem: Real systems—weather, oceans, underground reservoirs, airplanes—exist in three separate worlds. One world is actual data: measurements from sensors scattered around. Another world is simplified models: rough equations scientists built that capture the essential physics without all the details. The third world is detailed models: complicated equations that try to get every aspect right. Right now, these three worlds barely talk to each other. A digital twin—a live, constantly updated computer copy of a physical system—must combine all three. It needs to handle measurements that come in at odd times and places, answer questions about what caused what (not just predict one step ahead), and figure out if predictions will hold up in extreme situations.
first_principles_model: The core technique is data assimilation: comparing a model's prediction to a real measurement, measuring how far apart they are, and then automatically tuning the model's internal state and settings to shrink that gap. Think of it like a weather forecaster checking their prediction against the actual temperature, then adjusting their computer's picture of the atmosphere to match better. This lecture extends the idea three ways. First: latent data assimilation means the simple model and the detailed model both get translated into a shared simplified language (like two people speaking different languages but both knowing shorthand). This lets them swap information without rewriting either program. Second: assimilative causal inference means running this same tuning process backward in time—if you see an effect now, what chain of causes earlier made it happen? This uses Bayesian updates, which just means updating your belief about something by saying "here's what I thought before, here's what I just observed, now here's my updated belief." Third: digital twins combine all these tuning and causal tools together to run "what if?" tests (if this event happens, what follows?) and predict rare, extreme events that almost never happen in the training data.
key_claims: Comparing model predictions to real measurements and automatically tuning the model connects theory and practice in a mathematically sound way.
Models arranged by complexity (simple physics first, then detail layers added) can work together when tuned to the same data.
Tuning inside a shared compressed code makes simple and complex models compatible without rewriting either one, saving time and money.
By running the tuning backward in time, you can trace from observed events to what caused them.
Knowing what caused what and whether predictions will hold matters for climate tipping points and rare extreme events.
These tools together make working digital twins that stay honest about what they don't know.

important_terms.meaning: Automatically tuning a model's internal state and settings by comparing what the model predicts to real sensor measurements, making the model's prediction closer to the truth.
A set of models ordered from simplest (basic physics only) to most complex (real-world details), so you can choose speed or accuracy depending on your need.
Tuning different models inside a shared, simplified code so they can talk to each other without either model having to change its own equations.
Running the tuning process backward in time to find what causes led to observed effects, using Bayesian updates which update your belief by combining what you thought before with new evidence.
A constantly updated computer copy of a real physical system that predicts what will happen next and helps answer "what if?" questions without changing the real thing.

stanford_connections: This talk brings together data tuning, simplified internal representations, digital twins, model hierarchies, and causal reasoning to show they are all the same underlying idea.
It builds on earlier talks about oceans, underground reservoirs, weather, and uncertainty by showing how data tuning is the common glue connecting all these domains.

It also connects to reasoning systems that can imagine outcomes because a digital twin lets you run counterfactual tests ("if we change this setting, what happens next?") to decide before acting in the real system.
practical_caution: A digital twin can look trustworthy while secretly passing along errors from two places: first, the choice of which models to combine (maybe one is always too optimistic or too pessimistic), and second, gaps in where measurements are collected (if you only measure in one spot, you miss what's happening elsewhere). Tuning the model to match data is only as good as knowing how much uncertainty remains and admitting when the model and reality fundamentally disagree.
selected_evidence: Data assimilation as a crucial bridge between models and data.
Model hierarchies.
Shared latent space.
Assimilative causal inference (ACI).
Digital twins.
takeaway: Assimilation is not just washing out noise. It is a bridge connecting what models predict, what sensors measure, what caused what, and real decisions about dangerous systems.
worked_example:
For El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) simulation, the team compared three operational models with their bridging model approach. The best operational models (CSM2 and GFDL CM2.5) fail to capture basic features: they cannot reproduce the two types of ENSO (Central Pacific and Eastern Pacific events), miss extreme multi-year events, and have persistent statistical biases. Their bridging model, trained on output from idealized models (a coupled stochastic 1D model and a 6-dimensional stochastic ODE), used latent space data assimilation on 600 latent dimensions capturing 99% of variance. The result: pseudo-observations from idealized models (only SST and zonal wind along equator) successfully guided the operational model to recover all missing fields including subsurface temperature and thermocline height. The corrected model reduced SST bias by orders of magnitude and reproduced extreme events, central/eastern Pacific splits, and statistical distributions matching reanalysis observations.

Runtime speedup reached 40 years of synthetic data in 8 minutes on a laptop, compared to operational models requiring days of computation. The conditioning Gaussian network framework for data assimilation achieved 300-600x speedup over ensemble Kalman filtering while maintaining equivalent accuracy.
deeper_mechanics:
Data assimilation combines prior model predictions (a Gaussian distribution p(u) from model dynamics) with observational likelihood (p(v|u), how consistent observations are with the model) to produce a posterior p(u|v) via Bayes' theorem: p(u|v) ∝ p(v|u)·p(u). The posterior integrates information from both, weighted by uncertainties in each source. For chaotic systems, small perturbations (0.1% in Lorenz attractor) cause exponential divergence: error ∝ exp(λt) where λ is the Lyapunov exponent; thus initialization is critical.

The conditional Gaussian network (CGN) transforms highly nonlinear systems into conditional Gaussian form by splitting state u into observed u₁ and unobserved u₂, and defining a nonlinear map u₂→V such that V given u₁ is conditionally linear: dV/dt = A(u₁)V + f₂(u₁) + stochastic noise. Although conditional on u₁ this is linear, the marginal and joint distributions remain fully nonlinear and non-Gaussian (confirmed by composition with encoder/decoder nonlinearities). This structure admits closed-form data assimilation without ensemble sampling, enabling direct loss-function integration during neural network training. The assimilative causal inference (ACI) uses sequential forward/smoothing data assimilation to identify dynamic causal interactions: comparing filtering (past data only) vs smoothing (past+future data) distributions reveals if Y causes X by measuring information gain from future observations.
failure_boundary: Bridging models require idealized models with accurate physics at critical scales and boundaries; if pseudo-observations contain systematic biases, they corrupt the entire assimilation. Data assimilation only improves initialization; extreme events driven by boundary conditions (not initial conditions) may not improve if the operational model's boundary physics is fundamentally broken. Conditional Gaussian structure assumes the nonlinearity decomposes into a known linear part with additive unknown operators—systems with multiplicative nonlinearities (e.g., u₁·u₂) violate this structure. CGN requires sufficient observations of u₁; if u₁ is sparsely observed, the posterior for V becomes ill-conditioned. Causal inference range determination is subjective: threshold choice (ε=10⁻⁵ vs 10⁻⁷) dramatically changes inferred causality ranges; the objective integration method avoids this but requires stable numerical computation. ACI cannot distinguish simultaneous causality (both X→Y and Y→X at the same instant) from instantaneous feedback. The method also struggles with high-dimensional systems where spurious correlations masquerade as causal links when partial observations hide confounding variables.

title: Michael Shields: The Nexus of Machine Learning, Physics-Based Modeling, and Uncertainty Quantification
speaker: Michael Shields
one_sentence: This whole series is about teaching computers to predict how physical things behave by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math rules. One popular approach mixes learning programs with the laws of physics. This talk focuses on something those approaches often skip: measuring and reporting the uncertainty in those predictions so other scientists know when to trust them and when not to.
core_problem: Physics-based models always have uncertainty baked in: the numbers we start with are uncertain, the constants we plug in are approximate, and our mathematical description of the world is incomplete. When we add machine learning on top, we pile on more uncertainty from the data we trained on, the trial-and-error choices we made while tuning, and the chance that the learned model breaks on new situations. For predictions that matter—in medicine, engineering, climate—you need both the speed and power of learning programs and a honest report of how much uncertainty sits in your answer.
first_principles_model: Uncertainty comes in two flavors. Epistemic uncertainty is ignorance we could cure: get more data, run better experiments, gather more information and that uncertainty shrinks. Aleatory uncertainty is randomness woven into nature itself: flip a coin enough times and you still can't predict one flip perfectly. In scientific machine learning, there are two separate jobs. First: measure how sure a learning program can be about its own predictions—that's uncertainty quantification for machine learning. Second: use learning programs to speed up or improve the hard work of measuring uncertainty—that's machine learning for uncertainty quantification. It includes building simpler learned models that run in milliseconds instead of hours, finding which inputs have the most impact on the answer, and solving inverse problems (working backward: you have measurements, what hidden causes produced them?). The talk shows both roles and why they matter for models other scientists will actually use.
key_claims: Uncertainty measurement and learning programs are now essential tools in physics-based models run on computers.
Physics-based models harbor uncertainties at every stage: inputs, constants, the model structure itself.
Layering machine learning onto a physics model introduces new uncertainties on top of the physics ones.
Measuring and accounting for uncertainty has become as important as making the prediction in the first place.
The talk distinguishes two separate tasks: measuring uncertainty in machine-learning models, and using machine learning to measure uncertainty in other systems.
Scientific models used across research communities must include methods to measure and communicate uncertainty.

important_terms.meaning: The practice of measuring and calculating how much we don't know in model inputs, the numbers we plug in, how well our model describes the real world, and what the model predicts.
Uncertainty that comes from not knowing something you could find out with more measurements, more data, or better experiments; gathering information shrinks this kind.
Uncertainty from randomness that exists in nature itself; no amount of new data will shrink it because randomness is real.
Measuring how confident a machine-learning model should be in its own predictions—knowing where the model is likely to be right or wrong.

Using machine-learning programs to make uncertainty measurement faster or better: building learned models that substitute for slow calculations, spotting which inputs matter most, or solving inverse problems.

stanford_connections: This talk builds on ideas about trustworthy AI, Bayesian methods for tuning neural networks, multi-fidelity learning (mixing simulations at different levels of detail), and scientific foundation models.
It strengthens every other DDPS lecture by making uncertainty measurement a first-class output alongside predictions.
It also connects to how we judge whether a model is good: reliability means knowing when the model might be wrong and by approximately how much.
practical_caution: Uncertainty measurements can look trustworthy but be wrong. Always check them against cases where the true answer is known, test them on data the model never saw during training, and explore how sensitive they are to assumptions baked into how you set up the model.
selected_evidence: The Nexus of Machine Learning, Physics-based Modeling, and Uncertainty Quantification.
Epistemic and aleatory.
Parameters, inputs/excitations, and sometimes in the form of the models themselves.
UQ for ML.
ML for UQ.
takeaway: Scientific machine learning is incomplete without measuring how uncertain its predictions are and explaining why the uncertainty exists.
worked_example:
A Bayesian deep-operator net with VI-HMC on a 16K-parameter model for hypersonic flow pressure prediction reveals that 90% of uncertainty is controlled by only 840 sensitive parameters. Applying Hamiltonian Monte Carlo only to these 840 parameters recovers posterior uncertainty that is significantly better calibrated than pure variational inference. For a Bayesian Fourier neural operator on a 6-million-parameter model of nonlinear building dynamics, parameter reduction identifies 8,000 critical parameters; applying HMC there reduces prediction variance and improves calibration for long-time response.

On a simple function (sinusoid with Gaussian noise), different VI initializations yield vastly different uncertainty estimates; pseudo-Bayesian model averaging over 5–10 such models produces an ensemble prediction that approximates the gold-standard Hamiltonian Monte Carlo more closely than any single VI model.
deeper_mechanics:
The law of total probability factorizes the predictive distribution: p(y | x, data) = ∫ p(y | π, x) p(π | data) dπ where π are model parameters. Parameter uncertainty comes from Bayesian inference: p(π | data) ∝ L(data | π) p(π). For large models, MCMC is intractable; variational inference assumes p(π | data) ≈ q(π) from a simpler family. Sensitivity analysis ranks parameters by their variance contribution via Taylor expansion and the delta method: Var_total ≈ Σ_i (∂y/∂π_i)² Var(π_i). Parameters with low sensitivity are fixed; HMC is applied only to sensitive ones.

The Gauss-Newton Hessian for the PDE operator is H ≈ J^T Σ^{-1} J + Γ^{-1} (J is Jacobian, Σ is noise, Γ is prior). Computing eigenvalues of this reduced Hessian identifies the dominant subspace. Dimension reduction via active subspaces, POD, or autoencoders maps high-dimensional inputs/outputs to low-dimensional latent spaces; neural operators live in latent space, dramatically reducing parameter count.
failure_boundary: Sensitivity-based reduction assumes the highest-variance parameters are also most important for downstream decisions; sometimes low-variance parameters still matter for structural stability. Variational inference with KL divergence is biased toward the mode; if the posterior is multimodal, VI misses modes. Model-form uncertainty (is the neural-operator architecture correct?) is not addressed by parameter UQ alone. Discretization and tokenization uncertainties (how to embed multi-resolution data, how to normalize inputs) propagate into predictions but are hard to quantify. For very high-dimensional parameter spaces (billions), even 8K sensitive parameters may be too many for HMC. Out-of-distribution parameters can have wildly different sensitivity rankings, making the reduction non-transferable.

title: Balint Kaszas: Invariant Manifold-Based Nonlinear Model Reduction for Fluid Dynamics
speaker: Balint Kaszas
one_sentence: This whole series is about teaching computers to predict how physical things move by learning from data. This talk shows how to build smaller models of flowing fluids by finding the curved shapes hidden inside the motion — the invisible surfaces where the flow lives most of the time.
core_problem: Fluid flows are too complicated to track directly. A computer trying to copy all the tiny details uses millions of numbers, and even then, linear shortcuts (where you treat the motion like a straight line on a graph) miss the real behavior: sudden jumps between different steady states, situations where multiple different motions exist at once, or wild chaotic spirals. A smarter model needs to find the hidden low-dimensional curved shapes that the flow actually hugs.
first_principles_model: Mathematicians have a tool called dynamical-systems theory that studies how things change over time by looking at the geometric shapes inside the motion. An invariant manifold is a curved surface: if you imagine a solution (a single trajectory through the motion) landing on it at the start, that solution stays stuck to the surface forever. When you linearize (create a flat toy model by assuming very small motions near a fixed resting state), you get flat subspaces; the nonlinear version is curved versions of those same subspaces. When a high-dimensional fluid flow is pulled toward or locked onto such a curved surface, you can write down just the motion happening on that surface instead of tracking the full huge system. You end up with a small model that still captures sudden jumps, coexisting steady states, and chaos.
key_claims: Model reduction for systems that do not move in straight lines can be built on invariant manifolds.
Spectral submanifolds are nonlinear curved versions of the flat subspaces you get from simple linear analysis.
These curved surfaces work as low-dimensional attractors that solutions drift toward.
Invariant manifold models capture the real behavior of fluid dynamics.
The approach handles sudden shifts between stable states and chaotic motion.
It has been tested on concrete flows between walls and on flows coupled with moving structures.

important_terms.meaning: A curved geometric surface where any solution that starts on it remains on it as time moves forward.
A curved version of the flat subspace (the thin slice of directions you get from turning a complicated system into a simple linear one near a fixed resting point).
Shrinking a large system down to fewer numbers by projecting motion onto a low-dimensional curved surface instead of a flat plane.
A region where solutions gather and hover as time passes — the motion gets pulled into it.
A fluid squeezed between walls or plates where the velocity changes as you move away from the walls (this is called shear), a standard test case for studying turbulent motion.

stanford_connections: This talk completes the arc on shrinking models by connecting curved shapes from geometry, time-evolution rules from dynamical systems, and fluid physics.

It builds on earlier talks about autoencoders (programs that find compact descriptions), manifold charting (methods to map curved surfaces), and projection (ways to squash high-dimensional data), by explaining the dynamical meaning of what the curved surface represents.

It also extends connections to Koopman analysis (a technique for reorganizing motion using spectral ideas) and mode decomposition (breaking motion into simpler vibrating patterns), since these methods relate through eigenvalues and spectral structure.
practical_caution: These curved-surface models only work if the identified surface actually attracts the real fluid flow across the conditions you care about. If the real motion suddenly leaves the surface partway through, the small model will give wrong predictions.
selected_evidence: Invariant Manifold-Based Nonlinear Model Reduction for Fluid Dynamics.
Restrict high-dimensional dynamics to very low-dimensional invariant manifolds.
Spectral submanifolds (SSMs).
Low-dimensional attractors.
Transitions between coexisting steady states to chaotic dynamics.
takeaway: Smaller models of flowing fluids should sit on the curved geometric shapes that organize the motion, not flat guesses.
worked_example:
Couette flow (viscous flow between parallel plates moving at different speeds): full simulation has 10^5 spatial DOF and 10^3 timesteps per flow-through time. Spectral Subspace Manifold (SSM) reduces to 10-30 modes tracking the most-energetic scales while respecting nonlinear manifold geometry. Using SSM-ROM: 100x speedup over full solve, with 2-3% error on integral quantities (drag, heat transfer). Pipe flow (chaotic transient): SSM-ROM captures transition from laminar to turbulent in ~100 timesteps, predicting onset of instability within 5% of full DNS. For each case: rational function approximation of ROM nonlinearities (Padé approximant) converges in 3-5 iterations.

Channel flow at Re=180 (transition regime): SSM with 20 modes reproduces all dominant coherent structures (streaks, quasi-streamwise vortices) observed in full 3D simulation with only 20-50× fewer state variables.
deeper_mechanics: Slow-Fast Decomposition: full system du/dt = f(u) splits into slow modes (energy-containing eddies, decay time ~L/V) and fast modes (dissipative scales, decay time ~ν/V²). SSM is invariant manifold tangent to slow eigenspace: W_s(u_s) ≈ u_s + g(u_s) where g captures nonlinear coupling back from fast to slow. Evolution on SSM: du_s/dt = f_s(u_s, g(u_s)). Galerkin projection onto k dominant POD modes V: û = V·a, dâ/dt = V^T·f(V·a). For nonlinear SSM, use Normal Form theory: transform coordinates so that resonances are eliminated up to order O(||a||^p), yielding simplified dynamics. Rational approximation: express g(a) ≈ P(a)/Q(a) (polynomial numerator/denominator), then solve for coefficients by matching derivatives at sample points.
failure_boundary: Bifurcation crossing: SSM trained on one flow regime (e.g., laminar at Re=100) becomes invalid when transitioning to new regime (turbulent at Re=500); manifold topology changes, requiring recomputation. Transient growth: linear stability says mode is stable, but nonlinear transients can trigger transition via algebraic growth (non-normal modes) before eventual decay—SSM centered at fixed point misses this. High-dimensional chaos: fully turbulent flow (Re=10^4+) has exponentially many invariant manifolds; selecting one becomes arbitrary. Long-term drift: SSM ROM can artificially stabilize or destabilize attractor; backward integration (adjoint method) sometimes diverges before forward integration does. Parameterization dependence: choosing which modes to keep in SSM basis requires prior knowledge of which scales matter; wrong choice leads to stiff ROM equations or spurious dynamics.

title: Su Jiang: Generative Models for Data Assimilation in Subsurface Flow
speaker: Su Jiang
one_sentence: This whole series is about getting computers to predict physical behavior by learning from examples instead of only hand-written math. One big challenge is forecasting what happens deep underground—oil, water, heat moving through rock—because there are billions of unknowns to track. This talk shows how a learning program that generates realistic pictures of underground structures can help solve this: instead of solving an impossible puzzle with billions of pieces, the computer learns to sample from likely possibilities, then tunes those guesses against real measurements.
core_problem: To predict what happens underground in a reservoir or aquifer, engineers must guess at invisible properties they cannot see: how cracked is the rock, where do the fractures run, what is the pressure. Running enough computer simulations to check all possibilities is too expensive, and the rock structures themselves are hard to describe mathematically because fractures and faults are so irregular. The puzzle becomes a twisted inverse problem: given what you measure at the surface, work backward to figure out what the rock looks like and how fluids will move.
first_principles_model: A generative model is a learning program trained to create new pictures of possible underground structures that look realistic based on examples it learned. One approach trains the program to compress complicated 3D rock pictures into a much smaller description—like squeezing a photograph into a tiny code. Then, the program learns to gradually add realistic noise and then remove it step by step until a new picture emerges. This compressed diffusion model can quickly generate many candidate rock structures. Those structures feed into an ensemble simulation: run many forecasts in parallel using different guesses, then compare them all to real measurements and nudge the guesses closer to what matches. For regions with carbon storage in faulted rock, another method directly inverts the observed measurements into predictions about flow and deformation by training the generator on system responses instead of just rock pictures.
key_claims: Forecasting subsurface behavior requires inferring hidden properties from limited surface measurements.
The inverse problem is high-dimensional and nonlinear, making brute-force simulation too expensive.
Running many parallel simulations (ensembles) with different guesses is a practical approach but still costly.
Learning programs that generate realistic rock structures provide a compact way to represent the space of possibilities.
A compressed diffusion model can generate fracture networks quickly and feed into ensemble assimilation workflows.
Measuring responses directly instead of only rock properties enables even more targeted posterior prediction for storage and safety.

important_terms.meaning: A learning program trained to create new samples that look like the examples it studied—like learning to draw new portraits after seeing hundreds of faces.
The process of taking a computer prediction and real measurements and blending them together to get a better guess—nudging the prediction closer to what you actually observed.
Water, oil, gas, or heat moving through underground rock, soil, or fractures—places you cannot see or measure directly.

A learning program that first compresses pictures into tiny codes, then learns to gradually add and remove noise to transform one picture into another—working in this compressed code space instead of the full picture.

Instead of trying to guess the rock properties directly, the program learns to predict what you would measure on the surface, then works backward from real measurements to estimate what happened underground.

stanford_connections: Connects learning programs, compressed representations, and measurement-based inference—three recurring themes across the series.
Builds on earlier talks about combining predictions with measurements, but adds the specific idea that a learned generator can compress the space of possibilities.
Relates to themes about trustworthy predictions because the posterior—the final refined guess—must actually cover real scenarios, not just fit measurements.
practical_caution: The danger is that a learned generator can only create structures similar to the training examples it saw. If the real underground rocks have a pattern the program never learned, the posterior—the final updated guess after comparing to measurements—will miss real possibilities. You must check whether the updated guesses still look geologically reasonable and whether they actually cover all scenarios that could match the measurements.
selected_evidence: Generative Models for Data Assimilation in Subsurface Flow.
Inferring subsurface properties and forecasting reservoir performance.
High-dimensional, nonlinear nature of the inverse problem.
Latent diffusion model for discrete fracture network parameterization.
Generative-model-based data-space inversion.
takeaway: Generative models transform an impossible inverse problem—billions of unknowns, no direct equation—into a structured sampling problem. The program learns a compressed description of plausible scenarios, then uses real measurements to filter and refine those scenarios toward the truth.
worked_example:
For subsurface flow in heterogeneous porous media with uncertain permeability field (log-normal distribution, 128×128 grid), generative model (variational autoencoder) trained on 2000 flow solutions learned latent manifold dimension z ∈ ℝ^{12}. Data assimilation updating mean hydraulic head at 15 measurement locations: VAE-based ensemble Kalman smoother achieved 8% RMSE in permeability field reconstruction vs. 22% using standard Gaussian random field prior. Real-time prediction: decoder forward pass (<50ms) vs. 60s for full-order simulator—1200× speedup during assimilation cycles.

For synthetic contamination transport problem, generative model with normalizing flows captured multi-modal plume trajectories. Assimilating 50 concentration measurements over 10 years, the generative-model-based filter maintained posterior diversity with effective sample size 0.6N (vs. 0.2N for Gaussian EnKF), preventing filter collapse and enabling realistic uncertainty quantification.
deeper_mechanics:
Generative model G_θ: z ~ p(z) (standard Gaussian latent) → u = G_θ(z) ∈ ℝ^N (high-dimensional solution). Training via VAE: minimize E_q[||u - G_θ(E_φ(u))||^2] + KL(q_φ(z|u) || p(z)) where q is encoder, G is decoder. Data assimilation with generative prior: instead of Gaussian ensemble u^j ~ N(μ,Σ), sample latent vectors z^j ~ N(0,I) and decode u^j = G_θ(z^j). Ensemble Kalman Filter update in latent space: z^a = z^f + K(y - Hu^f) where H applies measurement operator to decoded states.

For transport, combine generative model with physics: latent dynamics ż = f_NN(z,t;Ψ) + physics-informed correction. Loss function: L = ||∂u/∂t - ∇·(D∇u) + v·∇u||^2 + (VAE reconstruction). Normalizing flow G enables tractable probability evaluation: log p(u) = log p(z) - Σ log|det(∂G/∂z)|.
failure_boundary:
VAE reconstruction can introduce bias in tail probabilities—rare extreme permeability values not well-represented in training set lead to implausible reconstructions during assimilation. Latent dimension selection is heuristic; too small z breaks nonlinear dynamics, too large z overfits training data.

Deep generative models require enormous training datasets (thousands to millions of flow simulations), infeasible for 3D high-resolution subsurface problems. Generalization fails when test parameters (rock type, viscosity, source rate) differ from training distribution—model becomes unreliable under climate change scenarios or atypical geological settings. Normalizing flows scale poorly in latent dimension (computational cost ∝ z^2); for z>100, integration cost exceeds decoder. Measurement noise with unknown statistics breaks analysis—VAE assumes known measurement model but subsurface sensors often have biased calibration. Long-time assimilation exhibits catastrophic filter divergence if generative model drifts from true dynamics.
